Śrī.
The *Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*, composed by the venerable *Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra*.
(The second part: the Section on Mantras.)
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
I bow to the god with the face of an elephant, who is praised by Indra and the other gods, and whose beautiful, reddish luster is lovely like a mass of vermilion. 15.1

This world, known by the name of the "Ganas," is the manifestation of the power arising from the qualities of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, Ākāśa, Vāyu, Agni, and Kṣiti; its Lord is Gaṇapati, who is Śiva himself. (15.2)

This Puruṣa, Śiva, indeed performs everything by his power through his desire to act; and by his will, he expands that protection as well as its withdrawal, distinguished by various forms of embodiment. (15.3)
Even the gods, headed by Hari, Viriñca, and Maheśa, are struck down in this world by hosts of obstacles;
therefore, they indeed perform the worship of Gaṇapati, for he is the all-pervading Vināyaka. 15-4.
Indeed, that All-pervading Lord cast off all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) in order to protect the world;
then, for the welfare of the worlds, he assumed a form and became the elephant-faced one (Gajamukhī).
[She is] the one in whom the entire multitude of paths has fully converged, who is endowed with the sixfold [mantras] consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*), elements (*dhātu*), and seeds (*bīja*),
whose ritual procedure for the limbs is established by the six supreme limbs, and who consists of the six pairs joined with the excellent forms.

She who generates the sole prosperity of the world, who is ageless, and who is surrounded by Kamalā, Ambujākṣī, Girijā, Giriśa, Rati, Manmatha, Avana, Varāha, and the four-faced Brahmā with his speech.
Or he who remembers this very Gaṇanāyaka daily along with his mantra and ritual procedure, and recites it after performing worship—he indeed becomes a vessel for all desired objects. (15.8)
(2) Following the *praṇava* and the *vāgbhava*, there is the other [seed-syllable] joined with the *māyā*, *girijā*, and *smara* seeds;
it resides in the *avanībīja*, has its arms in the middle, and possesses the left eye enriched by the digit of the moon. (15.9)
Following that, the middle arm of Gaṇapati joined with the staff (daṇḍa) is indeed this excellent seed-syllable;
one should extract these six excellent seed-syllables in their proper order, which bring about all accomplishments.

Then, one should extract the first four syllables as follows: "udakamakṣi" (water-eye), followed by "yutam" (joined), then "kathitam" (declared), then "tataḥ" (then), "pavanasārathi" (wind-charioteer), "rūḍha" (mounted), and "vilocanam" (eye);
then "sanayanau" (with eyes), "atha" (now), and "khaḍgibhujaṅgau" (sword-bearer and serpent). Thus one should extract the four syllables at the beginning.
Hīṇāśa ca haṣa haṣa ḍaṭ! Bring the hearts of all the worlds under my control! Ṭhaṭ!

Furthermore, by means of the collections of one's own syllables, calculated according to the qualities of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, together with the separately stated seed-syllables (bīja), and joined with the classes beginning with "all-knowing" (sarvavit), [the mantra is formed]. || 15.12 ||

To the omniscient, eternally satisfied, beginningless awakening, independent, whose power is undiminished, and whose power is infinite—having thus joined [the syllables] with their own vowels in this sequence, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) come to be. Then, let him perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramanu*), and place the limb-mantras (*aṅgamanu*) upon the fingers.

Thereafter, he should place the weapon-mantra in the center of the palms; and likewise, upon the body, [he should place them] according to the letters of the alphabet, the seed-syllables (*lipivarṇa*), and the root-words (*mūlapada*).

Therein, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the ancillary mantras (*anaṅgamantra*) starting from the heart and ending with the eyes, from the thumb to the little finger; and having placed the weapon mantra (*astramantra*) on the palms of the hands; and thereafter, having thrice placed the six seed-syllables beginning with the letters of the *lipi* (alphabet) in the mouth; and having placed the six groups of consonants—*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*—along with the six words of the root mantra beginning with its modifications, upon the two arms, the two feet, the two sides, the back, the navel, and the heart; one should then meditate upon oneself as Gaṇapati, together with his Śakti, seated within the lotus of the Mātṛkās. This is the meaning.
Then, one should perform the assignment of the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to the heart and other parts, as well as the assignment of the directions from one's own weapon-mantra;
furthermore, one should fashion a blazing rampart all around with the weapon-mantra using the index finger.
Furthermore, some declare that the sage Vāmadeva was his [son], as well as Gaṇaka;
and after him, Nivṛt is said to have been the Lord, the sovereign of the host of the Prapañca.

Having received the mantra from the mouth of the Guru and with his permission, one should then construct a new monastery somewhere on the bank of a mountain river, in a temple, or another such location, possessing all the desired and charming characteristics. || 15-16 ||

Having gathered the materials for worship as prescribed, performing the daily obligatory rites without omission, and restricting his food according to the rules declared by those who observe vows, let him— possessing an unwearied mind— recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Thus, when the preliminary practice has been performed according to the prescribed rule, this mantra bestows supreme accomplishment.
For those who worship it daily with sacrifices, fire-offerings, and recitations, their desired goals are attained without delay. (15–18)
Now, its excellent procedure is being written down; by the mere recollection of which the mantra is perfected.
Having painted a most wonderful picture-scroll (*citrapaṭa*), one should worship it with material wealth if available, or otherwise with the mind alone. (15–19)
Then one should contemplate the ocean as being filled with sugarcane juice, most beautiful with hundreds of waves and ripples,
and shimmering with its waters teeming with schools of whales, crocodiles, conchs, fish, and the great timiṅgila fish.

And in its center was a great sandy bank and a massive mountain of jewels, its peaks densely covered; it was surrounded on all sides by hundreds of tamāla and tāla groves, and by *sarala*, *sāla*, and *ghanasāra* trees.

Its delightful banks are graced by clusters of *sakada*, *nimba*, and *nikurumba* trees, as well as hundreds of coconut palms used for play, and by groves of excellent *kuṇḍa*, *hāli*, and *nicula* trees, along with forests of mangoes and plantain groves.
It was made sweet by the mingling sounds of flocks of intoxicated, restless bees, and by the fragrance of fresh betel-nut trees,
nāga-vines, sallakī, lavalī, and black pepper, along with cloves, bilva, and bakula flowers.
It was graced by the songs of cuckoos intoxicated by tasting the flavor of mango buds;
it was frequented even by the *cāmara* yakṣas and inhabited by the foremost among gods, *kinnaras*, and *asuras*.
This place is exquisitely adorned by creeping vines that bear a profusion of blossoms— buds opening, clusters forming, and thick with fresh shoots— and it is filled with flocks of birds.
It was adorned with blue water-lilies and lotuses, and possessed the same essence as the lakes through their cranes;
in some places it was graced by white lilies and blooming blue lotuses, as well as by *kuravaka* flowers and flocks of swans.

It was also served by breezes laden with the weight of spray from waterfalls cascading down the slopes, enchanting like the ichor of elephants, and carrying the fragrances of swaying sandalwood, campaka, and ketakī flowers.
On one side, the sky was brightened by the rising moonlight of the full moon and a cluster of stars;
elsewhere, it shone with the rays of the emerging sun and was also graced by clouds.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, when the sky was filled with the months of Bhādrapada, Āśvina, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and Māgha,
the ascetic attained a wealth of flowers through his penance, which was equal to the month of Tapas and associated with the month of Sahas.

One should contemplate a golden and beautiful bank, its forest exquisitely adorned by a multitude of seasons that produce identical qualities, and where the abundance of flowers is perpetually gathered. (15.30)
In the center of that [palace], upon a golden peak with a ground of jewels and gold, there are seven ramparts with walls radiant with gold.
Therein, one should meditate on seven courtyards strewn with hundreds of celestial palaces (vimānas), each distinguished by high, towering gate-towers (gopura). (15.31)

Situated in their midst, one should meditate upon a divine golden pavilion with high peaks, covered by the luster of infinite jewels; its floor is adorned with moonstones, and it is vast, square, and exceedingly beautiful. (15.32)
Its center was graced by a canopy adorned with strings of pearls; it shone with golden jars variegated with the finest jewels and diamonds;
and its doors on all four sides were provided with arches fashioned in the shape of wonderful sea-monsters.

The interior of the pavilion was adorned with various kinds of hanging sweet fruits, ripe fruits, excellent garlands of flowers, the finest grains of rice, golden sprouts, and sweetmeats suspended from above.

On all sides, it was adorned with rows of sprouts, with jewel-lamps and gold lamps, with vessels containing incense, flowers, unbroken grains, and perfumes, and with fly-whisks, svastikas, conchs, and lotuses. || 15.35 ||
It was resplendent here and there with mirrors, full water-jars, and jars filled with parched grain;
it was adorned on all sides by groups of attendants, including dwarfs, hunchbacks, and others, who stood composed in their places.
Then, having sprinkled the fragrance, flowers, one's own self, the water for the *arghya*, and the sacrificial pavilion with that water,
one should first worship the *Ādhāraśakti* even beneath the surface of the earth.
Then, having worshipped that infinite upholder of the earth and the earth itself as the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha),
one should duly sacrifice to its feet, which consist of Ananta and have Dharma and the other [virtues] as their stated bodies.

Having meditated upon the stalk and the lotus as consisting of rajas, tamas, and sattva respectively, one should conceive of the sun, fire, and moon as being, in order, its petals, its filaments, and its pericarp. (15.39)

Having meditated upon that lotus of the Mātṛkās, adorned with the letters of the alphabet according to the method previously described, one should worship within it the eight Mothers and Rudras together with their pedestals, following the sequence of the petals, corners, and coverings of the directions. (15–40)
In the east is Śrī Kāmarūpa, and likewise in the southern direction is the mountain Kollagiri;
in the west is the seat (pīṭha) named Sopāra, and in the northern direction is Oḍḍiyāṇa.
Likewise, in the southeast is the Malaya mountain, and in the southwest is the venerable Kulānta.
Jālandhra is in the portion of Vāyu, and likewise Devikoṭṭa is in the green direction of the Three-eyed One (the North).

The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Caṇḍikā, are described here individually. Among them, the former are joined with the long vowels; they are joined with the crescents of the moon (the short vowels) and the short bindu-vowels.
Furthermore, Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍaka, and the one named Krodhana are mentioned.
Then another, intoxicated with pride, was called Kapālī; thereafter, Bhīṣaṇa and Saṃhṛti were named. || 15-42 ||

The word *pīṭha* (seat), joined with the name of the seat and preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), shall have a long vowel; then, accompanied by the respective names of the Mothers in the dative case, it is the heart-mantra (*hṛd*).
The short vowels, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*), are said to be the names beginning with *sitāṅga*.
And likewise to the eight Śaktis, and salutations to Bhairava and to his sandals as well.

The goddesses, beginning with Brahmāṇī, carry weapons resembling those of their respective fathers; they are black, red, transparent white, yellow, like the dawn, like a parrot, and possessing the luster of gold and copper.
The Bhairavas are richly adorned, their lotus-faces smiling, and they hold rosaries and skull-cups in their hands.
They should be meditated upon as having the moon as their crest-jewel, three eyes, wearing saffron-colored garments, and adorned with ointments and garlands. || 15.44 ||

Āmoda, Pramoda, and after them Sumukha and Durmukha; likewise the other known as Vighna and the one named Vaināyaka—these six elephant-faced ones are richly adorned with divine ornaments and garments.
Siddhi, Kānti, Samṛddhi, then Madanavatī, Klinnā, and Kledanī—
With those Śaktis resting upon your left lap, you should be worshipped, charming with the sentiment of love (smararasa). || 15-45 ||
On the right and left sides [of the central deity] are the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, their bodies embraced by the powers Vasumatī and Vasudharā; they are well-worshipped as they shower wealth.
These six Gaṇeśas are to be embraced by their beloveds and are to be worshipped on the petals of the lords of the gods, water, fire, Īśa (the northeast), the Rakṣas (the southwest), and the wind.
The two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, showering riches, are to be worshipped on the southern and northern petals.
The limb-mantras (aṅga-mantras) situated within that [central area] are the elephant-faced ones; however, the heart and other [limbs] are to be worshipped on the coverings of the corners.
Having worshipped their faces in the cardinal directions with the Eye-mantra, one should worship them by their own names ending in "namaḥ" with the five services (pañcopacāra).

Then, having visualized the orb of the moon situated in the midst of a white lotus in the sky, which showers down a rain of droplets consisting of white nectar flowing from a thousand rays of the moon’s digits; 15.48.

And one should contemplate within its center a subtle form, consisting of Śiva, radiant with light resembling the flickering flame of a lamp, beautiful, and the rising sun of the supreme point (bindu) shining forth intensely.
Having brought [the mantra-body] from this [place], cool as a spray of lunar nectar, subtle, and via the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the head, one should place it upon the lotus;
there, one should contemplate Gaṇeśa, whose body is the mantra, a mass of radiance shining like molten gold. (15.50)

Having joined his own hands in the añjali gesture filled with flowers and having placed divine light within the center of that lotus, he should meditate upon the God of beautiful form, resembling gold and other precious substances, whose radiance is equal to the rising of a thousand suns. (15.51)
May he protect us— he who has twelve arms, whose crest is the moon, who possesses three eyes, and whose beautiful body shines like the face of the Lord of Beings;
who holds in his hands that dispel fear a conch, a discus, a goad, a noose, the bow of the Mind-born, arrows tipped with lotuses, a wish-fulfilling tree, a golden pitcher, a mace, and a trident.
Seated upon a lotus, accompanied by Śakti, may Gaṇapati—who holds a jeweled goblet on the head of an elephant—be with you. || 15.52 ||

He whose lotus-feet are forgiveness, whose body is space, whose belly is the [taste] element, who has the sun, moon, fire, and the three eyes, whose sound is the wind, whose movements are the primary matter, intellect, and the senses, and whose universal form is the abode of all worlds. (15.53)
His garment was like saffron-colored silk; the entire world rested upon his long-hanging belly;
his broad chest shone with various necklaces; and he wore the lord of serpents as his sacred thread.
To the Lord, whose golden crown is fixed upon a mass of beautiful matted locks; who has the crescent moon of knowledge as his crest-ornament;
whose lovely form consists of the sciences of the phenomenal world; and who is the sole abode of all beauty and excellence. (15.55)

Adorned with golden neck-chains, armlets, and neck-ornaments, with various wonderful bracelets and finger-rings; beautified by gems set within dark-blue jewels, and with golden anklets radiant with tawny-colored gems.

One should meditate upon his right lotus-foot, which bestows all desired objects, as it rests gracefully before a golden jar that has the face of a lotus, while he himself sits comfortably within the heart of a lotus.
I bow to the Sovereign of all, who rests upon my left lap; she whose nature consists of the three qualities, the imperishable, the inexhaustible Mother of the worlds;
she who is enchanting with her auspicious form and who leans against a great coral tree.
One should contemplate her as being like a divine creeper of garments that grants all desires. || 15-58 ||
With pollen possessing the luster of bandhujīva petals, reddened by the glow of her own limbs,
she whose radiance was white as the moonlight of a smile as tender as a kunda bud,
and who was darkened by the mass of her flowing, wavy, and shimmering black tresses—
The wise call her the first of the Maṅgas, the Unborn, and indeed the Primordial Nature (prakṛti). || 15-59 ||
Her pair of lotus-feet has outshone the terrestrial lotuses with its radiance;
her pair of shanks has surpassed the auspiciousness of a peacock’s throat with their splendor;
and her pair of thighs possesses the beauty of a plantain trunk, as lovely as her own body.
And with his beautiful girdle, he [embraced] the lovely woman of slender waist.
Bearing upon her slender waist a most delicate line of hair as dark as collyrium, and likewise possessing three charming folds;
with breasts like a pair of golden jars and arms like fresh pārijāta creepers—
And she was exceedingly auspicious with a neck adorned with lofty jewels. || 15-61 ||
Her face is like the autumn moon; her eyes are like fresh blue lotuses trembling on the waves;
she wears jeweled earrings whose radiance sways upon her beautiful pair of ears;
and with her lovely nose, she possesses a charming pair of cheeks and a radiant forehead.
Her eyebrows were curved like the bow of Māra, and her locks were as beautiful as a swarm of bees.
She is the abode of the excellence of the flowing essence of all beauty,
like the autumnal moonlight of stainless radiance that never fades;
she is worshipped even by the lords of sages, the best of gods, and those with faces like Indra and the moon.
[She] whose body consists of the earth, speech, and the wives of the gods, [and who is] the pleasure-ground for the daughter of the mountain king.
Embracing him with her right arm, she touches his chest with her hand out of love;
and the God, embracing her with his left arm marked by the flower-bow, touches her at the knot of her lower garment.
Having meditated properly upon such a primordial power (mūlaśakti) and likewise upon the deity of the aforementioned form and attire,
one should worship them with ritual offerings after performing purification according to the sequence to be described.
Having first washed the arghya vessel with a mantra and filled it with water, unbroken rice, fragrance, and flowers,
one should place therein the root mantra together with its limbs, along with white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, fruits, milk, and a bundle of kūrca grass.
Having visualized that [liṅga] as filled with the flood of nectar from the dvādaśānta and endowed with consciousness by means of the *haṃsa*,
one should then display the *dhenu-mudrā* and worship it with incense, flowers, and the water of the *arghya* using the *kūrca*.

Having sprinkled water upon one's own head, as well as the support and the materials such as water and flowers, one should purify them by means of contact with drops of that water and by gazing; this applies also to the water for the feet and the water for welcoming.

Wearing a crest of excellent flowers and dūrvā sprouts, and having applied a tilaka on his forehead with fragrant paste, he, bowing with devotion, should worship the gurus in the north-eastern direction with the five-fold offerings. (15.69)

Oṃ, homage to the gurus! Oṃ, homage to the supreme gurus! Oṃ, homage to the gurus who are the preceptors of the highest state! Oṃ, homage to the gurus who are the ancient teachers! Oṃ, homage to the great venerable ones, the ancient perfected ones (pūrvasiddhas)!
They are adorned with red garlands, garments, perfumes, and ornaments; they are well-adorned and seated upon lotus thrones.
All of them are established in yoga with a support (sālambana-yoga) and have attained the goal of all the eight qualities of sovereignty. || 15-70 ||

Then, one should perform, in due order, the rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*sthāpana*), and presence (*sannidhāna*) according to the path taught in the chapter on ritual service (*upacaryāpaṭala*), as well as the rites ending with confinement (*nirodhana*) and veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), by means of the six ancillary limbs (*tadaṅga*).

The *arghya*, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*) should be offered to him with the *hṛdaya* mantra; likewise, perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, and incense should be given.
His bath should be performed with the six ancillary mantras joined with the root mantra, as well as with Vedic hymns (*sūtra*). || 15.72 ||

One should offer garments, garlands, ornaments and the like, as well as perfumes, unbroken rice grains, incense, and lamps with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; the mirror with the *netra-mantra*, and the food offering (*naivedya*) also with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). (15.73)

And that [offering], superior even to the most excellent previous path, is joined with four kinds of clarified butter, fruits, and condiments; together with curd, honey, sugar-candy, and clarified butter, as well as *laḍḍukas*, *modakas*, *maṇḍakas*, and so forth.

Having offered cool water, coconut water, parched grain flour, and sweet parched rice soaked in molasses, and having given water for the hands and water for sipping (ācamana), he should present betel leaf endowed with its eight ingredients.
"Phaṭ oḍaṣāṃ vidmahe, vakratuṇḍāya dhīmahi, tanno gaṇapatiḥ pracodayāt.
This is the Gāyatrī of Vighnarāja; it should be employed at the beginning of the food offering (naivedya), as well as in recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa).
Having praised him with hymns and having prostrated like a staff, the assemblies seated in the enclosures should also be worshipped here. || 15-76 ||
Padma and Mahāpadma-nidhi are at the eastern gate; then at the southern [gate] are Makara and Kūrma;
at the west are Mukunda and Ananta-nidhi; thereafter, Nīla-nidhi and Śaṅkha are to be worshipped.

Within the inner enclosure, outside the pavilion, in the east, south, west, and north, four wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) of golden form should be worshipped; they are joined with jeweled reliquaries (ratnacaitya).
And those [trees] are shaped like the *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *udumbara*—that is to say, they are *kalpavṛkṣas*.
(p. 9) Beneath the *bilva* are Śrī and Kamalākṣa seated upon a lotus; Gaurī is on the right at the root of the *pippala*;
beneath the *nyagrodha* are Kāma and Rati; to the west of that [tree] are Kroḍa and Bhū, and likewise beneath the root of the *udumbara*. (15.79)

These [deities] should be meditated upon as holding, in sequence, a lotus, a conch, a discus, a battle-axe, and a boar’s tusk; likewise a noose, a goad, a flower-arrow, and a bow; and finally, they bear an utpala lily, a cluster of fruits, a mace, and an enemy-slaying sword, like a wish-fulfilling creeper with rows of ears of rice.

The eight [deities] beginning with Śrīmukunda should be meditated upon as standing in pairs upon lotuses facing Gaṇeśa; they hold their weapons, such as the lotus and others, with their upper hands, while their lower hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture. Adorned with graceful attire, ornaments, and the like, they eternally pray for uninterrupted conjugal bliss with one another. Furthermore, in the intermediate directions between these couples, there are Apsarases, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas.
Performing instrumental music, song, and dance beginning with the fire-quarter (south-east), they should indeed be meditated upon for the attainment of their desired fruits. (15.81)

Outside of them, situated at the four gate-towers of the Vedas, one should visualize the Lotus-born Brahmā, accompanied by Sarasvatī; he holds a water-pot and a rosary in his hands, sits upon a lotus, and bears a book and a jar, adorned with white ornaments. 15.82.

There, in the middle of the gate-towers, in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, Sanaka and the others, Dakṣa and the others, the Bālakhilyas, and the Seven Sages should be remembered as seated comfortably, meditating according to their respective offices.
Then, at the third gate, one should worship the World-Guardians (lokapālas) stationed in their own directions, together with their attendants and their sacrificial offerings (svāhā):
the ancestors (pitṛs) in the south, the serpents (nāgas) under the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) in the north along with the hosts of Yakṣas.
One should worship those Daityas and Dānavas, together with their sons and wives, who reside in the fourth enclosure;
then one should worship the sages, and in the fifth enclosure, all the Maruts.

In the sixth enclosure, having worshipped the Guru and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) to the north, one should worship the Sun in the center, the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter in the cardinal directions, Venus in the southeast, and Mars and the others in the [remaining] directions starting from the southeast. (15.85)
In that [mandala], one should duly worship the planets, Skanda and his attendants, the spirits, and the Mothers;
those who dwell in heaven, the atmosphere, the earth, and the oceans, together with the Kinnaras, are to be contemplated during the final enclosure.

Thus, outside, those who dwell in the seven enclosures as previously described—the couples, the wish-fulfilling trees, the gods and other beings belonging to the aforementioned groups—should be worshipped duly by those intent on the worship of Gaṇeśa. || 15.87 ||

(10) Worship with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) by their respective names according to what is available has been described for these [deities]. Likewise, one should satisfy Gaṇeśa together with his retinue in the fire with the remains of the oblation of clarified butter (ājya). || 15.88 ||

The mudrās, beginning with the Śaṅkhāri-mukha, should be displayed: having placed the arm at the mouth like an elephant’s trunk, with the tips of the middle fingers bent and joined with the thumbs—this is the Gaṇarāja-mudrā. (15.89)

Then, one should daily perform recitation according to one's ability; and having offered the recitation and the worship with water from the hollowed palms, one should present them at his lotus-feet in sequence with the mantras that will be stated here.
Oṃ!
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us, so that through your grace, success may abide in me and in you. (15.91)
O Lord! Whatever good or evil deed we ever perform, O Śaṅkara, consume and destroy that for me as I abide in the state of Śiva. || 15-92 ||
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire universe;
Śiva is victorious everywhere, and he who is Śiva is indeed myself. (15.93)
O Lord! This worship, accompanied by recitation and burnt offerings, which has been performed by me—be gracious, accept it, and grant me my desired success. (15.94)
Then, having composed himself and having consecrated the fire with the specific rites as prescribed,
the twice-born man, having offered oblations into the mouth of the fire, should invoke Gaṇeśa into that mouth and offer oblations for the sake of success.
Having offered white flowers and incense on the full moon and other auspicious days, one who offers ten thousand white lotuses mixed with ghee,
jaggery, and honey— or half a hundred thousand bilva fruits with ghee, honey, and milk— attains inexhaustible prosperity like the Lord of Wealth himself.

Having fasted for three nights beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, and having offered ten thousand or even more than a hundred thousand oblations into the fire with lotuses and the "three sweets" on the fourth day, one truly beholds Lakṣmī or even a treasure. (15.97)

Or, on the day of the lunar mansion Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), with thousands of *nandyāvarta* flowers; or on the fifth day (*pañcamī*) with *puṇḍarīkākṣa* flowers; or on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), or likewise on a bright festival day (*śuklaparvan*), having thus offered oblations with white lotuses, one shall become a lord of wealth (*dhaneśa*).
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times daily in the forenoon with arms raised and eyes fixed on the sun, one will become wealthy.
Furthermore, having uprooted an udumbara tree and offered it entirely as an oblation within a mandala, one attains prosperity.
Having prepared a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) cooked with the shadow of a single tree, the offspring of a cow, and cow’s milk, one should either touch it or consume it after repeated practice.
Or, while gazing at the sun in the waters of a river that flows both ways to the ocean, one who recites [the mantra] shall become a lord of wealth (*dhaneśa*). (15.100)

With *nālikera*, *apanasa*, sugarcane, *rambhā*, sesame flour, parched rice, and flattened rice—all mixed with sweet substances—and combined with *modakas* in equal proportions, this indeed is the sacrificial oblation that is like a wish-fulfilling tree. (15.101)

Having offered oblations for the sake of cloth, one obtains threads from a spider; by means of white, red, and other flowers, one attains garments of those respective colors, or beautiful clothes through beautiful white water-lilies or lotuses.
By offering a thousand oblations of dūrvā grass sprinkled with milk and clarified butter daily, one shall be free from disease and long-lived;
through flowers, nourishment shall be attained; and by drinking water in which sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter have been steeped, one shall destroy diseases. (15.103)

Fuel-sticks of the *amṛtalatā* plant, measuring four finger-breadths in length, when well-offered and bathed in clarified butter mixed with curds and honey, destroy the fear of untimely death as well as the afflictions caused by the planets. (15.104)
By offering sacrificial oblations of fine rice (*paramānna*) with ghee and sugar, or milk with ghee and black sesame seeds on a new-moon day,
and by reciting the mantra over the root of the *pippala* tree while touching [the person], one may remove the fear of untimely death.
Having recited [the mantra] over a water-pot placed upon a lotus at sunrise, and by keeping vigil day and night,
one who consecrates [another] at the rising of the sun shall conquer misfortunes and even remove the diseases caused by malevolent magic.

Having thus filled the jar at sunrise with the remainder of the tenth part of the ghee-oblations, one who is consecrated by this bath when the sun has reached the meridian becomes fortunate and obtains prosperity and sons. (15.107)

Having consecrated water, food, fruit, and so forth with this mantra—which removes disease—one should partake of them; furthermore, when given, this "Priya-kūrca" bestows prosperity and delights the people. (15.108)

At the auspicious hour of Brahmā, on a festival day when the moon has waned, having obtained cow-dung from a Kapila cow on a lotus leaf in the sky, one should practice its recitation ten thousand times; buried at the doorway, it shall protect [the house] from disease, thieves, fire, and serpents.

Similarly, ashes produced from cow dung in fire, when empowered by that mantra, destroy epilepsy, minor spirits, planetary influences, and the like; they provide protection, bring prosperity, and, when applied with sandalwood and other substances, bring about subjugation. (15.110)

Having fasted for three nights prior to an eclipse, one who consumes a mixture of *vacā* powder and clarified butter in a copper vessel—consecrated with the mantra of Haṃsavāgīśvarī—attains the play of eloquence. (15.111)
Desirable rain occurs with fuel-sticks made from *vetasa* reeds, and sons are obtained with those made from the three-leaved tree (*tripatra*).
By offering oblations of grain-particles (*kaṇa*), one wards off rain in this world; likewise, with sweet arka flowers, one gains victory. (15.112)

By means of food and sweet substances, one should obtain [results]; through oblations with fuel-sticks produced from the *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *bodhi*, and *plakṣa* trees, one may, in due order, bring the castes beginning with the twice-born under one's control. (15.113)
By offerings of wood-apple fruits and lotuses, kings shall be brought under control; by white water-lilies, salt, ghee, and parched grain, the people of the countryside;
by honey with salt, maidens; by other oblations, women; and by night-blooming lilies, sesame seeds, rice, and sugar, entire villages. (15.114)

For the victory of kings over their enemies, one should construct an excellent pavilion—a square hall—in a distinguished location; it should be provided with gates and arches in the cardinal directions, well-adorned, and covered with fine cloths, fruits, flowers, and garlands. (15.115)
Having worshipped Gaṇanātha seated upon a lotus marked with a svastika, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations into the fire-pit using the three sweets;
and a tenth part of that number—three thousand—with edible offerings, sweetmeats, fruits, milk-rice, sugarcane products, and clarified butter.

Having bestowed choice food, gold, and garments upon those in the first stage of life, and likewise having given cows, horses, and gold to the officiating priest; and having gratified the best of the twice-born and performed sacrifices even for the gods—he who departs [from this world] shall indeed be a victorious lord of men.
By practicing with these, one may ward off predatory thieves, tigers and the like, or even elephants.
One may hold fire in one's hand and destroy jambhaka-demons, yakṣas, and classes of bhūtas. (15.118)
Having drawn forth a woman, one perfected in mantra may cause her to dance or agitate the entire world.
The collyrium or sandalwood paste practiced by him brings delightful affection to the eyes of women. (15.119)
If one first consecrates mustard seeds with mantras and places a thousand of them inside an *aśvattha* tree for seven nights,
then by repeatedly reciting those mantras over them once they have been empowered, one may drive away enemies and serpents by digging them into the ground at that location.
One should cause enmity by means of *kali* fuel-sticks, or else with neem leaves interspersed with husks;
one should instantly kill [an enemy] with the fuel-sticks of a funeral pyre and the *vibhītaka* tree, using blood and poison.

Having meditated upon the All-pervading Lord as intensely red and black, one should consecrate a bundle of forest darbha grass of equal measure to the height of a man; then, by scattering it along the path of the enemy, the foes shall be overtaken by disease.
One should meditate upon Gaṇapati, who resembles a blazing fire reaching the tongue;
by reciting the mantra and cutting him with that sharp goad, one conquers the opponent whose mouth is obstructed. (15.123)
Having fasted on the third day, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī), having offered oblations into the fire with fruits and other items according to his capacity on the fourth day,
and having devotedly presented milk-rice enriched with ghee to Him and likewise honored the best of the twice-born, shall obtain his desired goal.
Whether subsisting on milk or vegetables, he who recites the mantra one hundred thousand times shall attain complete perfection;
furthermore, by constantly honoring the foremost of the twice-born with desired gifts and the young students with offerings according to his ability, he shall also obtain [his goals]. (15.125)

To this it is replied: having worshipped Gaṇanātha according to the previously described form of Kuṇḍavara, and having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with milk and ghee, or even with flowers of the Arka plant and sand; || 15-126 ||

Having offered a hundred thousand oblations separately and in sequence with honey and food into the center of the sacrificial pit, one obtains a pill known as *vetāla*; by wearing it, one becomes perfected in the powers such as *aṇimā*.
In this way, the mantra-practitioner obtains whatever he desires, such as a sword, collyrium, sandals, and so forth.
What is there that cannot be obtained in these three worlds? Is there nothing for him? What is the use of saying more? (15.128)
With rice flour, plantain fruit, bean powder, sugar, and dehusked mung beans;
with coconut, honey, cumin, and salt; combined with the powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and cooked in ghee. || 15.129 ||

With *modaka* sweets, which are fragrant and delicious like the joy of the heart, this daily fire-offering (*homa*) performed according to one's own capacity is indeed a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) that grants the fruits of all desired objects to men. (15.130)

The milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with husked śāli rice, mung beans, sugar, and ghee, and offered as an oblation using coconut and the milk of a tawny cow, is said to grant all desired objects. (15.131)

An oblation of plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, cow’s udder-shaped sweets, jujubes, and other delicacies such as *laḍḍukas* and *maṇḍakas*, sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*), as well as an offering of black sesame seeds, shall grant all desires. (15.132)

The worship and oblation performed on the fourth lunar day, as well as the daily worship according to one’s means, and the satiation with water consisting of the nectar from the sky-lotus—these accomplish all desired objects and every single wish of men. (15.133)

Meditated upon as this deity, whose luster is white as the moon, he instantly destroys all poisons by sprinkling them with showers of nectar from the cups of his own hands; having recited [the mantra], he is the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) whose body consists of the manifest universe. 15.134

In the lotus of the heart, one whose body is as pure and beautiful as a fresh white lotus, possessing the splendor of a thousand moons, with a form the size of a thumb and sprinkled with the nectar of the upper waters—when meditated upon, he destroys even death and becomes the bestower of liberation. (15.135)
Thus, indeed, this Manu has been proclaimed here in the *Prapañca* [Tantra],
and likewise in the *Lalitāgama* and the *Makuṭa-vātula*; however, the Lord of the *Prapañca*, along with his ritual procedures, mantras, and rites—
It bestows success even in the Kali age upon those who seek the prosperity of the three goals of life.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Paṭala on Prapañcagaṇapati, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.

The syllables *tāra* (om), *śrī* (śrīṃ), *śakti* (hrīṃ), *kāma* (klīṃ), *kṣiti* (laṃ), and *gaṇapati* (gaṃ) are the six seed-syllables at the beginning; then follows the one ending in *caṇḍa* (phaṭ), the one ending in *na* (na), and the two ending in *ḍa* (ḍa); then *aṣaḍiḥ* (huṃ), followed by *marut* (ya), *yonigo* (ra), and *ambhaḥ* (va), which is red.
Water, fire, then three [times] that; thereafter, the word "sarva" is said; "janam me," this Vaināyaka mantra, ending with "vaśam ānaya agnipriyā" (bring under control, O Beloved of Fire). || 16-1 ||

As before, with the six seed-syllables beginning with *tāraka* (om), that Vighna-seed-syllable (*gaṃ*) is enriched with the long vowels; joined with its Lord and the [six] classes, those six limbs should be formed according to rule, ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). 16–2.
The sage is thus stated; the calculator (gaṇaka) is Kakubh; some say the meter here is Gāyatra;
its deity is Mahāgaṇeśa; and the accomplishment (siddhi) culminates in the fruit of the four aims of life. 16-3.
If one is not capable of that, one should recite the mantra a number of times equal to the count of existence, non-existence, and existence;
and having offered clarified butter ten times the number of the eight types of food, one becomes a perfected master of the mantra, possessing the power of Gaṇeśa.

One should meditate on a golden mountain, delightful with groves of various trees, situated in the midst of an ocean of jewels; on that mountain, one should visualize a divine garden enclosed by golden ramparts, its grounds composed of moonstone.
Then, in the middle of this hexagonal pedestal on dry land, one should visualize Gaṇeśa seated upon the previously mentioned lotus;
he is the size of a man, has a protruding belly, the luster of a hibiscus flower, and is adorned with various necklaces set with jewels. || 16-6 ||

May He who possesses ten arms—bearing the citron, mace, and the weapon of Smara; the goad, the enemy of the lotus (the discus), and the noose; as well as the blue lotus, the cluster of kalama rice, and His tusk—protect you. (16.7)
She was embraced by him, who had placed his arm upon her left shoulder; she held a white lotus in her hand, and her body was fully adorned with ornaments variegated with white pearls, gems, and gold.
Adorned with red perfumes, flowers, garments, and garlands, together with her, he is the Lord of the Gaṇas;
holding a lotus and a water-pot, he showers a rain of wealth upon the practitioner.
Then Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and likewise Durmukha;
Vighna and Vighnakartṛ, and then the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
Śakra, Agni, Īśāna, Varuṇa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu—these six are the lords of the quarters (Aśragās).
Gaṇeśa and the two treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma are situated in the south and north. (16.11)
The white, the red, and the black Vighnas, preceded by Āmoda, are to be known in sequence;
they have two upper hands holding an axe and a rosary, while their lower hands hold a tusk and food. (16–12)

The two treasures known as Śaṅkha and Abja, white and red in color, should be meditated upon with their two hands marked by those [symbols], facing one another in the guise of yakṣas, and vomiting forth a vast flood of wealth. (16.13)
Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Mohinī, Sogadā,
and Kāminī— these six most radiant powers are Āmodā and the others.

The five enclosures are to be worshipped in their proper sequence: first the limbs, then the obstacles together with the pair of treasures, then the *lakṣya* and so forth, then the Mothers, and finally Indra and the other deities.
Padmā and Ambujākṣa are in front at Bilva; on the south, beneath a banyan tree, are Girijā and Vṛṣāṅka;
behind at Bodhi are Rati and Puṣpabāṇa; and on the north, at Priyaṅgu, are Mahī and Varāha.
The two in front, Umā and Īśa, hold in their hands a pair of lotuses, a white conch, a noose, a goad, and a trident;
the other two hold a pair of blue lotuses, the bow of Smara, and flower-arrows, while they also bear a rice-stalk, a peacock feather, a discus, and a mace.
Desiring long-lasting happiness for their married life, they worship the Lord of Obstacles with palms joined in reverence;
externally, all these [deities] should be meditated upon as having green complexions, bearing weapons and vehicles, and adorned with divine ornaments, garments, and perfumes. (16–18)

Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the lotus (Sarojha), each by their own names as before, the Lord together with his five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa) should be worshipped duly with the primary offerings (upacāras) consisting of the root-mantras of the limbs (aṅga).

Having properly installed the Great Gaṇeśa on a wall, a cloth, or an image made of gold and other materials, one who has received mantra-initiation—or who was previously consecrated with the jars of Gaṇeśa—should worship him. (16–20)

One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and then perform oblations with eight types of edible foods ten times that amount—or according to one’s own capacity—while remembering Gaṇeśa even mentally; having thus sacrificed, the mantra will be perfected and his desired goal attained.
To the east, near Īśa, there shall be the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), Gaṇacaṇḍa, resembling a golden mouse and like a mountain peak;
he is to be worshipped as before with offerings of food and oblations. For one who is devoted at the lotus-feet of the Teacher, all goals are accomplished. (16–22)

One who desires spiritual perfection should constantly recite the mantra according to one's ability, satisfy [the deity] with water from the sky, the moon, and [ordinary] water, and give desired food and other offerings to the twice-born belonging to the first stage of life. || 16-23 ||
One should also place jars at the tips of the petals in the four directions, and the principal jar in the center of the lotus;
one should smear them with the waters of the four previously mentioned milky trees and likewise with medicinal herbs.

Having placed those jars, well-filled with gems, perfumes, fine flowers, and gold, and wrapped in cloths in front [of the altar], one should then install the god Gaṇeśa in the center; likewise, having worshipped the pairs [of deities] in the jars starting from the east (Indra’s direction).
Then, having adorned [the image] with garments and perfumes, and having worshipped it with its root-mantra and its constituent parts, one should make them "living" (sajīva).

Having recited the mantra according to one's ability and performed the fire-oblation, one should perform the consecration; for thus the mantra will succeed, and one shall obtain one's own desired goal. || 16-26 ||

One should offer oblations with cooked rice for the abundance of food, with honey for the attainment of gold, with cow's milk for the success of cattle, or with sesame and rice for the sake of Lakṣmī; one may also offer with clarified butter,
or with curd and sugar for the sake of fame, or with *aśvārī* and safflower.
One should worship the king with lotuses for the sake of clothing, the queen with night-lotuses, and his minister likewise. || 16-27 ||

One should bring the social classes (varṇas) under control with fuel-sticks of *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *plakṣa*; young women with sweetmeats or flour-cakes; and whatever is desired with the eight substances (*dravyāṣṭaka*).
Success is achieved with salts, and rain shall fall through the libation (*tarpaṇa*) of reeds (*vetasa*).
Then, by means of the mantra multiplied fourfold, all desires are attained through recitations or burnt offerings. || 16-28 ||
If one should desire [to perform this rite] in an elephant forest near a body of water, having first constructed a square sacrificial hall there,
one should worship the elephant-faced deity upon the central altar and offer oblations in an auspicious fire-pit in the northeastern direction.
Having invoked Mahāgaṇeśa into that fire, let him offer oblations by means of the path of prosperity;
then, having offered with the seed-syllables as well as the limb-mantras, he should likewise offer here first with the root-mantra.
Having divided the mantra into nine parts according to the three groups (varga), one should offer oblations with clarified butter;
then, having offered oblations with the entire mantra as many times as there are syllables, one should offer the eight kinds of edible foods smeared with the three sweets.

This [merit] is equal to the contemplation on the arising from existence multiplied by a hundred; furthermore, by feeding Brahmins according to one's ability and honoring them with garments, gold, and cows, those who fall within the banyan tree become elephants.
A sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) equal to one-tenth of the elephants obtained should be given to this best of mantra-knowers.
Then, having offered the oblation (*bali*) along with the ancillaries to the attendants, [he should worship] the fire together with Sahadeva.
One should join [the mantra] in one's own heart-lotus or in the lotus of the sky; thus there is the "seizing of the elephant.
This is the procedure for Mahāgaṇapati.
Others, however, declare that the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa is the "end of the five" (paṃ) joined with the nasal drop (bindu), which is the manifest seed. (16–34)

They pronounce [the mantra] ending with the vowel *au* and the bindu; the same procedure should be sought for these two. To Gaṇarāja, *ṭhaṭha*. To Ekadaṃṣṭra, *huṃ phaṭ*. Salutations, salutations to Acalakarṇin. Salutations, salutations to Gajavaktra. To Mahodara, who holds a staff in his hand, *huṃ phaṭ*. To Vināyaka, *vauṣaṭ*.
These six limbs, possessing their own respective seed-syllables, are declared in sequence up to the eyes. (16–35)
To Gaṇeśvara, ṭhaṭha! To Dhūmramukha, ṭhaṭha! To Dhūrjaṭi, ṭhaṭha! To Vighnarūpa, ṭhaṭha! Thus is the procedure for the binding of the eight directions taught.
To Vighnahantṛ, ṭhaṭha! To Lambodara, ṭhaṭha!
One should perform the calculation of the upper and lower directions.
The seer is Virāṭ by name, the metre is Gaṇaka, and its presiding deity is the one called Vināyaka. (16-36)

One who eats according to the vow should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times for the sake of preliminary purification, followed by a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth that number.
[The deity is] four-armed, with a dwarfed body, an elephantine face, a protruding belly, and a serpent serving as his sacred thread. (16.37)
Holding a bowl with a noose, goad, tusk, and food, his hand resting upon its lotus-shaped tip;
adorned with red garments, ointments, garlands, and jewels, he possesses a complexion tawny like saffron. (16.38)
Indeed, one should meditate [on the deity] beneath the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), seated upon a golden lotus throne and surrounded by those seeking its fruits;
having first worshipped the Guru and the Lord of the Field (kṣetrapati) in the northeast, as well as the Śakti consisting of the foundational support (ādhāra).
And the remainder is the earth, which is its infinite pedestal; it is adorned with the lotus-forms whose qualities have been described, beginning with Dharma.

Having brought that [consciousness] into the moon situated within the point (tāra) in the center of the moon, by means of a stream of nectar from the sky-lotus, [one should contemplate it] in the moon.

One should worship Vināyaka with his own [mantras], the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), and the elephant-faced mantras located on the petals of the directions; with the heart-mantra and others in the corners, the weapon-mantra in front of him, the eye-mantra, and the six lords of the Gaṇas who obstruct the binding of the directions.
One should likewise worship in due order the two treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma located in the cardinal directions and the corners;
then, having worshipped Indra and the other guardians of the worlds along with their mounts in their respective quarters, one should worship their weapons.
Then, in the fourth enclosure, one should worship one's own gurus in the northeast, as well as Gaṇacaṇḍa;
having worshipped them with offerings beginning with invocation according to the prescribed rites, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity.
Having given food and other such things to those in the first stage of life (brahmacārins), one obtains whatever wealth one desires.

By offering honey and meat to the king, sesame seeds to the ministers, white flowers to the best of Brahmins, molasses to the Vaiśyas, and salted rice to the Śūdras and others, and by sacrificing *mātuluṅga* flowers, one brings a maiden under one's control. (16.44)
Or, having offered balls of flour mixed with the eight substances, one shall quickly obtain all desired human goals.
With lotuses one gains wealth; with neem leaves, the act of inciting hatred; and with that same [offering], unguents, perfumes, and so forth become subject to one's control.
Having meditated on the person to be accomplished with his body bent down by one’s own goad, and having stepped upon him, that person comes under control for one who recites the mantra.
Likewise, a woman whose limbs are overwhelmed shall come under control; and by meditating on oneself as being identical [with the deity], one shall be victorious in combat or in debate. (16.46)

If one plants a row of *rājī* seeds within an *aśvattha* tree for seven days and buries them in the house of someone when the moon is full, there shall be the eradication of enemies, poisons, snakes, and the like; furthermore, by performing the recitation (*jāpa*) while unified with that [mantra], one destroys malevolent spirits and minor obstacles. (16.47)
Having established the fire with its ritual procedures within a mandala beneath a nyagrodha tree, and having invoked the Yakṣī to the south of the fire,
one should worship her with the root mantra and the limb mantras ending in "namaḥ," and also form the mudrā resembling an elephant's trunk.
First, having practiced for a thousand fires and then offered oblations of *aṅkola* oil, he indeed beholds a *yakṣī* within a month.
Whatever is desired is obtained, or he enjoys her; provided he bathes three times a day, he shall never be touched by weapons.
The ritual procedure for the single-syllable mantra of Vināyaka:
the water-pot (kumbha) joined with fire (agni), followed by the arms and so forth, then "ṛṣaḍī," "karṇānvitāṇḍāya," and "huṃ"—
these syllables are declared as the six-syllabled mantra of Vināyaka.
The seer is Śukra, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its presiding deity is the god Siddhavināyaka; the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgas) should be performed with long-voweled syllables. || 16-50 ||
Its seed-syllable is the sixth letter, and its power consists of the *nāda*.
One should place these syllables on the fingers beginning with the thumb of both hands, and the final one on the palms.
For the limbs, the placement is taught to begin with the little finger, and the weapon-mantra (*astra*) is placed on the palms.
One should place the syllables on the head, eyes, ears, mouth, heart, and feet, as well as the limbs, according to their respective locations.

May the blessed Gaṇeśa be for your prosperity—he who holds a noose and a goad in his two hands, who bestows boons, whose belly is pendulous, who has the face of an elephant, who is adorned with red garlands and perfumes, and who wears red garments, armlets, a crown, and variegated necklaces. 16-52.

At dawn, for the sake of attaining one’s desired success, one should gratify this Lord of the Siddhas, who is seated comfortably upon a white lotus on a jeweled throne within a golden pavilion radiant with gems, situated in a new lotus pond on the peak of the mountain where the sun rises. (16.53)

Then, having approached from the sky-lotus to the center of the lotus of qualities at the seat of the faces of Śakti and the other [deities], one should worship according to the ritual procedure; beyond the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti), the circle is joined by the eight Gaṇeśas and the enclosure of the world-protectors (lokeśa) and their pairs of directional elephants.
The obstacles (vighnas) are these eight: the one named Vināyaka in the east, Vīra, Śūra, another called Varada, Kṣipraprasāda, the one known as Gajavaktra, and Mahāgaṇeśa. || 16-55 ||
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Kumuda, Añjana, Vāmana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka—these are the elephants of the quarters situated in the directions beginning with the east. (16.56)

Those elephants, with four tusks like the tusks of the lord of elephants, though shedding the water of rut, were scattering abundant wealth of jewels; their lotus-like faces were illuminated by their own trunks. || 16.57 ||

Having thus worshipped Gaṇeśa together with his attendants either in an image such as one painted on cloth or within the lotus of the heart, one who observes the vow of fasting should mutter the mantra sixty thousand times; then, one should offer oblations of clarified butter in a number equal to one-tenth of that recitation.
Then this supreme mantra shall be constantly perfected; through recitation and other rites, one obtains all desired objects.
By offering food with ghee as an oblation, one gains food; and by an oblation of honey and parched grain, one finds a maiden.
By offering cakes or fruits made of eight substances and sprinkled with sweet liquids, one shall obtain all desires;
by offering dūrvā grass sprinkled with milk and clarified butter, one obtains long life; and by offering parched grain or vetasa shoots, one obtains a daughter or desired rain.
Through oblations of *apāmārga* and *brahmavṛkṣa*, victory shall be attained; with grains, one gains grain; and with blue lotuses (*utpala*) and the like, clothing.
One obtains a field by offering husks smeared with molasses, and everything is brought under control by offering pieces of *chinnā*.
Having drawn the body of another upon a cemetery ground, one should transfer the vital breaths into that form under that person's name;
by offering oblations of *vibhītaka* fruits wrapped in red thread with *sarājita* oil, one shall cause death.
The dark Lord of the Gaṇas, remembered as one with his own self, possesses a roar like that of a terrifying, dark cloud;
having weighed the enemy upon his own trunk, he shall cast him into the submarine fire, blowing him away.
Standing in that water, one who has been consecrated with handfuls of water from the ocean and the Indus shall remove the afflictions caused by the planets;
a woman desiring a son should drink vacā root mixed with milk, honey, ghee, and rock salt while reciting the mantra.

Those who meditate upon Gaṇeśa, the size of a thumb, within the lotus of the heart— surrounded by his powers (śaktis) in the maṇḍala of the eight-petaled city-staff form— they cross the ocean of saṃsāra without effort.

Having worshipped a jar, a small cup, parched grain, and a lamp filled with clarified butter, one should perform recitation at night; having consecrated a young girl there, she indeed speaks a continuous stream of meanings pertaining to the three times upon being gazed upon. (16.66)
Thus was this mantra of Viṣṇu, which fulfills the desires of sages, formerly uttered by Bhārgava.
For that lord of practitioners who would properly accomplish it, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that remains unattainable. (16.67)
The Ritual Procedure for Siddhavināyaka:
Having extracted [the portions] from the lap of Jhaṇṭī, one should then say the word "to Danta"; [the portions] from the bladder, the tail, and the anus are for Ucchiṣṭamātman. (16.68)
The spear is adorned with the *tārā* (the letter *a*) and the *aṅkuśa* (the letter *u*), along with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
The syllable *hrūṃ* is the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astra*), and the supreme Śiva is joined with the lips (*o*). (16.69)
This mantra, consisting of twenty-eight syllables and repeated twice, is known as Ucchiṣṭa-Vighnarāja; it bestows all perfections through recitation and other such practices. (16.70)

"Ṭhaṭha to Ucchiṣṭa! Having thus performed the sixfold assignment of the limbs, beginning with the heart, together with their seed-syllables in due order according to their respective locations, the practitioner Ucchiṣṭa shall accomplish this.
The seer is named Ucchiṣṭayāja; the meter is indeed Nicṛt.
With the word "ucchiṣṭa" preceding it, its deity is remembered as Gaṇapati. (16.72)

The elephant-faced Vighna is pot-bellied, white in color, holding a noose, naked, and carrying a goad; he is the size of a thumb, adorned with various jewels, possesses three eyes, and is to be worshipped as he dances, bestowing fearlessness and desired boons. (16.73)
Starting daily from the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
one who has consumed the remains [of the offering] should recite the mantra eight hundred times and perform oblations with fresh, sweet-smelling tooth-sticks;
by this, the mantra is mastered, and thereafter the mantra together with the name of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) [is effective].
Having drawn [the image] here and placed that Gaṇapati within it, one should summon him through the recitation of mantras.

Having cast this [mantra] into one's armpit, one shall obtain the desired object; having worshipped him with hundreds of oblations of gold-intoxicated [substances], and having placed her footprints in the dust, if one recites it at night, the desired woman will quickly come. (16.75)
If one desires mutual affection for a couple, one should recite the mantra while looking at their hands;
or, having consecrated it with recitation, one should offer perfume and so forth, as well as ghee, sandalwood, and sacrificial ashes, which bring them under control. (16.76)
Then, offering fuel-sticks the size of a thumb into a golden fire, one gains mastery over kings;
with flowers, one gains mastery over the twice-born; with fruits, over merchants; with leaves, over Śūdras; and with all these together, one gains mastery over everyone.

Having uttered "hastī," one should recite the mantra for the witnesses (*sākṣin*) by their side: *vānto* (vam), *dīrghaḥ* (dīrgha), *kūrcaḥ* (huṃ), and *māyayā* (hrīṃ), followed by the *sākṣimāṃsa* (the flesh of the witnesses).
Then *soṣṭhaḥ* (svā) and *caṇḍau* (caṇḍau), joined with *vahnijāyā* (svāhā); this is the *aucchiṣṭa* mantra for Vighna, as before. (16–78)

"Hastihṛdayāya namaḥ! Piśācaśirase svāhā! Likhē śikhāyai vaṣaṭ! Svāhā kavacāya huṃ! Saṅgha astrāya phaṭ! These are the limbs [of the mantra]. Kiṣkindha is the sage; its metre is indeed Virāṭ. As before, the deity is the same; it shall be perfected on the eighth lunar day through ten thousand recitations of the sun-mantra (the Gāyatrī).
He who, though impure from eating remnants, should mutter a hundred thousand of his own seed-syllable, for him there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished.
Whatever ritual act pertaining to the seed-syllable of Vighna has been prescribed, he shall obtain it by performing it while in this state of impurity.
The king of practitioners shall obtain through this that ritual action of the mantra beginning with the letter *e* which has been proclaimed. || 16.81 ||
One should bury an image made of beeswax, bearing a leaf inscribed with the name of the person to be accomplished along with the mantra;
then, by offering oblations into a fire of khadira wood placed upon it, one shall bring the entire object of the rite under control.

Furthermore, through the recitation of the mantra interspersed with the name [of the person], that person becomes submissive; likewise, if the name is written on birch bark and interspersed [with the mantra], it should be worn. Alternatively, for the sake of subjugation, one should perform oblations with clarified butter for seven nights.
The recitation of its mantra, the application of oil and collyrium, sandalwood paste, and so forth, as well as oblations made with golden flowers, bring about subjugation (*vaśya*).
Furthermore, Gaṇeśa should be meditated upon as being exceedingly crimson, naked, adorned with a noose and a goad, and accompanied by his own limbs. (16.84)
The Section on Ucchiṣṭa-Vighneśa:

Now, the mantra of Vighnapati beginning with the seed-syllable and ending with the heart-mantra (namas), containing the word "kṣipram" for swift accomplishment and consisting of ten syllables, shall indeed fulfill all desired objects; it is truly a wish-fulfilling tree. (16.85)
The ṛṣi, the meter, and all other ancillary elements shall be according to the procedure prescribed for the single-syllable mantra.
Through initiation, one hundred thousand recitations, and ten percent of those as oblations of sweet sesame seeds, success is attained. (16.86)

May the moon-crested Lord, who has the face of an elephant, who holds a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, a tusk, and a citron in his hands, and who is beautifully adorned, grant you swift grace. (16.87)

The one to be meditated upon is ruddy-hued, holding the three worlds in his mouth, adorned with white garments, seated upon a lotus throne, and showering wealth from the wish-fulfilling creeper held in his hand upon the head of the foremost practitioner. (16.88)
One should worship the one named Siddha with his four enclosures either within one's own form or in the heart-lotus;
having offered oblations with the previously mentioned substances such as ghee and milk-rice, as well as with lotuses, one shall obtain prosperity.
By constantly performing oblations of ghee and cooked food according to one's ability, the sustenance of the householders' families shall be ensured;
and if he gratifies them with floods of nectar-like water, he shall obtain whatever else is desired. (16.90)
Having offered oblations at night with portions of cold salted food sprinkled with curd and clarified butter, his desired goal will surely be accomplished.
Or, if he desires a reconciliation among enemies, by offering coconuts on the fourth lunar day, he attains that very result.

The five endings (the five *anta* letters) together with fire (*ra*), along with the left eye (*i*) and the staff-bearer (*ma*), [followed by] the spear (*śa*) enclosed between two *anusvāras*—this three-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu is thus declared.
Its limbs (*aṅgas*), joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), should be formed according to the vowels.

The meter is Virāj, the sage is Bhārgava, and its presiding deity is Gaṇapati; having practiced one hundred thousand syllables of this mantra, and having offered oblations according to the prescribed portions while feeding maidens and young brahmins with the five types of sacrificial foods (pañcabhakṣya), one indeed attains success. (16.93)
Having been initiated by the mouth of the Guru and having obtained the mantra, one should perform the worship according to the daily rites beginning with the ritual bath;
having meditated upon the golden lion-throne within a pavilion of jewels and gold, situated amidst the forest of the Kalpa tree on the surface of the earth consisting of the oceans of wine.

One should worship the heart-mantra and the others on the petals at the corners with the lotus-forms of the qualities such as power (*śakti*), and the eye-mantra in front and the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions; one should then worship the powers:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Śauṇḍī, Anantā, and Sumaṅgalā.
These, however, are situated respectively at the tips of the petals and in the center. || 16-95 ||

One should worship these obstacles— Gaṇa, Gaṇanātha, Vighneśa, Vināyaka, Bhakṣyapriya, Pañcakara, Lambahasta, and Mahodara— who have elephant faces, are reddish in color, and hold a noose, a goad, and a lotus, outside the lotus in the eight directions respectively, using their own names. Outside of that, one should also worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in the ten directions, who wear red garlands and scents and hold a noose and a goad.

Then one should meditate upon Gaṇapati, who is of the nature of the sky, moist with the nectar of the lotuses in the celestial lake, with the color of molten gold, wearing yellow garments, adorned with reddish ornaments, garlands, and perfumes, pot-bellied, three-eyed, and crowned with the crescent moon. (16.97)

Having visualized him with five hands holding a noose, a goad, a mango fruit, an elephant tusk, and a sweetmeat (*modaka*), short in stature, and his limbs variegated with various ornaments—one should, together with the root-mantra and the limbs, invoke him into the previously described pericarp of the lotus. (16.98)
Having worshipped with the root mantra together with its ancillaries (aṅga) and the primary offerings, one should present milk-rice, jaggery, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge,
cakes, fresh roots, fruits, sugarcane, parched grain, honey, and sweets such as *laḍḍuka*.
One should constantly recite the thousand-fold hymn at the three junctions of the day, meditate upon Gaṇeśa, and worship him according to one's means;
he bestows upon such a person wealth, excellent enjoyments, long life, freedom from disease, and all desired objects. (16.100)
Now the ritual applications (viniyoga) are described:

Having established the fire according to rule in a pit in the northeast corner of the altar, and having invoked the deity therein according to the prescribed rite, one should offer oblations of rice cooked in cow's milk or clarified butter, or milk-rice; within two months, one shall obtain one’s desired object and prosperity.
By offering clarified butter with cakes mixed with jaggery, or with the eight substances, one shall obtain desired wealth;
by offering parched grain mixed with sesame and sugar-candy, one shall bring a brahmin under control, and by offering honey, one shall subjugate a king.

If one performs oblations with jasmine flowers, one brings ministers under control; with honey, rice, and sugarcane, women; with meat mixed with honey, all Śūdras; and with fruits, sesame seeds with sugar, and parched grain, one shall bring everyone under one's sway.
By reciting the *saṃpuṭa* mantra while addressing her as "Kanyā," one should obtain that [image] made of flour and smeared with molasses;
having taken it, one should consume the remainder of that food and perform worship everywhere according to one's capacity. (16.104)
Having first offered to him the seed that is to be consumed by those [beings], one should sow ten thousand seeds in the fields after having performed the recitation;
by that means, there will be an abundant harvest of grain.
When the crop has ripened, one should set aside the first portion and perform a great worship of the Deity.

Furthermore, if one desires another field that is currently a subject of dispute, one should take earth from its center; by reciting [the mantra] on eight Saturdays while possessing the form of Gaṇeśa as one's own, one shall obtain it. (16.106)

During a solar eclipse, however, one who observes a fast should drink one *pala* of tawny clarified butter mixed with a powder of *vacā* in a one-fourth portion, having recited the mantra over it according to the rules;
as long as that ghee remains undigested, he shall become a retainer of what he has heard and an eloquent speaker. (16.107)

Having touched a gold coin (*niṣka*), or half of it, or even a quarter, along with turmeric, rock salt, white *vacā*, and *paśumūtra* (animal urine) ground together, a woman in her courses should drink it while reciting the mantra. Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa according to her ability, she shall obtain a son who is like Gaṇeśa himself. (16.108)

On a Tuesday, having worshipped Gaṇanātha with all his splendor, having offered and sacrificed edible foods, clarified butter, milk-rice, and sacrificial porridge, and having fed maidens, Vaṭu boys, and the best of the twice-born, one liberates all those who have fallen into bondage through the power of recitation. (16.109)
Having obtained a stone that has emerged from water, shaped like a bud and resembling a goad, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
then, by placing it upon the hand of a prisoner on a Saturday, he shall be released from his shackles—provided the stone was produced from white Sindhuvara flowers.
Having passed the night with the young brahmin boy, the two of them— having been bathed and adorned—
performed in the morning a great worship of the obstacle-remover (Vighna) with offerings of supreme rice-porridge, clarified butter, sweetmeats, and other delicacies.
Having placed the *kalaśa* upon the grain-altar and having worshipped it with water, scents, unbroken rice, flowers, and powders,
one should place upon it a new shallow dish filled with ghee, together with the honored lamp and the Lord of Obstacles (*Vighnarāja*).
That boy and the young girl shall indeed see here the lost wealth bound for the three times;
he himself should mutter [the mantra] while touching the two youths, and this same procedure is to be performed even with a mirror. (16.113)

If rain is desired here, one should perform a sacrifice to the Lord of Obstacles with devotion according to one's ability, using ghee, milk-rice, sweetmeats, fruits and the like, as well as excellent perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps. || 16.114 ||

Having invoked the Lord into the mouth of the fire in the sacrificial pit— which is beautifully adorned with banners, arches, auspicious sprouts, water-pots, fruits, canopies, and other ornaments— he should perform oblations for seven nights.

One should constantly perform three hundred separate oblations with flour-cakes made from plantain fruit, sugar, and other ingredients, cooked in ghee; likewise with boiled rice, cakes, fruits, milk-rice (pāyasa), sugar, clarified butter, and milk. || 16-116 ||
There will be a great rain. On a Tuesday— the day of Mars— during the asterisms of Arī, Naidhana, or Bhadra, by offering a thousand pieces of wood smeared with poison,
or likewise with nimba wood offered in the afternoon, enemies indeed meet their death within a fortnight.
Having written the name of the enemy along with his physical form on a funeral ground at midday on a Saturday,
and having worshipped the fire with fuel in the victim's belly, the enemy enters the world of death for the one who recites the mantra.
By offering ten thousand fruits of the poison-tree (viṣavṛkṣa) into a funeral pyre while reciting the name of the [target] written [on the oblation], he goes to his death.
By piercing the house of an enemy with a stake of neem wood during the afternoon of Mars, expulsion is clearly accomplished.
Enmity [is brought about] by its leaves. (p.

25) On a Tuesday coinciding with the Gaṇeśvara lunar day, having worshipped Gaṇanātha while well-seated upon a tiger skin, and having filled a water-pot there, one should mutter [the mantra] and perform oblations; then, having consecrated [the practitioner] with that [water], one shall pacify spells and diseases. || 16.120 ||

One should pacify the affliction of fever by offering oblations of milk, sugarcane juice, and clarified butter; for the pacification of elephants and horses, an offering of cakes and milk is prescribed.
By sprinkling them with that water and performing a ritual consecration (prokṣaṇa), there shall be both peace and prosperity in this world.
Thus the sage Bhārgava, for the welfare of the worlds, proclaimed this ritual procedure for the king of the Trivarṇaka community;
and the minister, having fed the maidens and the boys with sweet foods, obtained the desired fruit in every respect.
Having meditated upon the maiden Durgā and having meditated upon the youth Gaṇapati, one should feed them.

With their own names, one should separately satisfy the eight principal Gaṇeśas and the others mentioned, such as Vighna and Vināyaka, with the thought "I satisfy you" using the nectar-like waters of the moon; by so satisfying them daily, one obtains whatever is desired. (16.123)

At the beginning of the day, having meditated upon the lords of obstacles as they are described— quenching their thirst with the nectar-water flowing from the moon within the lotus of the sky— one should accomplish the entire range of desired objects by means of their respective mantras.

Having remembered the Lord of Elephants at dawn, having descended from the peak of the mountain of sunrise into the midst of the herds of female elephants via that path of golden stairs, and having offered libations, one shall obtain all desires. (16.125)

The offering of food and other items to Gaṇapati, the fire-oblation (homa), recitation (japa), libation (tarpaṇa), praise with hymns, and salutation should be performed daily according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, there is the worship of the fourfold [deities] every four days, consisting of forty-four [offerings].
That sacrifice is praised for one who may become beloved by the Sovereign Lord of Obstacles.
Thus, the mantras of Gaṇapati, which are seen in various Tantric divisions and described here individually in their many distinct forms,
as well as the entire web of ritual actions such as recitation (japa) and so forth that have been taught—
Manu is also the Lord of the Gaṇas; each preceding one is more venerable than the next.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on Gaṇapati with ten arms and other forms, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
First is the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], followed by the seed-syllable of Manmatha, then the letter Bha with the vowel *u* (Bhūḥ) and the letter Ra joined with grace (Raḥ).
This mantra of the three cities (Tripura), indeed like a young calf, is said to be a wish-fulfilling cow that grants all desires. (17.1)
Indeed, this Vāgīśvarī is joined with the Vidyā, the Vāgbhava, and the Kāmarāja [bījas];

she is manifested through the three fires, the three worlds, the three forms, the three libations, the Vedas, the qualities, and the causes— or whatever else may be threefold, it is revealed by Tripurā through her three syllables.
That object of knowledge, whose sphere is the name "Tripura," is called the supreme power (parā śakti). || 17-2 ||
Śrī is its seer (ṛṣi), Brahmā is its sage, and the Uṣṇih is said to be its meter; some say its deity is Vāgīśī, others declare it to be Śiva, and likewise others Bhairava.
The first [syllable] is called Vāgbhava, possessing the luster of the full moon, while the other is as red as the Bandhujīva flower.
They know the third seed-syllable to be as beautiful as a fully blossomed, red Karṇikāra flower. || 17-3 ||
*Tāra* (Om), *vyoma* (Hrīm), and likewise *bhṛgu* (Sakala)— this three-syllabled mantra is indeed called Śeṣa; one should fashion the limbs (*aṅgas*) of the Tripurā-mantra with this in due order,
endowed with their respective seed-syllables (*jātis*), and then again assign them to the two hands and the body.
Having performed the purification of the hands with water for the weapons, one should place the letters of those [mantras] upon the fingers and the limbs.

Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the little finger (kaniṣṭhāṅguli). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the ring finger (anāmikā). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the middle finger (madhyamā). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the forefinger (tarjanī). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the thumb (jyeṣṭhāṅguli).
Having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa) on the fingers of both hands in sequence according to the order of the three joints, [one should place]:

Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the upward face (ūrdhvavaktra). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the eastern face (pūrvavaktra). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the southern face (dakṣiṇavaktra). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the northern face (uttaravaktra). Oṃ hasauṃ, salutation to the western face (paścimavaktra).
In this manner, one should place [the letters] with the fingers directed toward the faces, beginning with the eldest (the thumb);
