then, accompanied by the remaining root-syllables, one should likewise place them separately on the two feet, the two knees, the generative organ, the navel, the heart, the throat, the palate, the bindu, and finally on the head. (5)
And in reverse order:
Kāmarūpa, Kollagiri, Sopāra, Oḍyāṇaka, Malayādri, Kulānta, Jālandhra, and Devikoṭṭaka. (17.6)

Thus are the eight seats of yoga (yogapīṭhas). Here, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Caṇḍikā are described individually; they are first joined there with the long vowels, then with the crescents of the moon (the short vowels), and then with the short bindu-vowels.
They should be joined with Asitāṅga, Ruru, and then Caṇḍaka; Krodhana by name, Unmatta, Kapālī, and thereafter Bhīṣaṇa and Saṃhṛti are declared. (17.7)
Then follows the name of the seat (pīṭha) joined with the word "Śeṣaśrī," and thereafter the word "pīṭha" with a long vowel.
Then, accompanied by the names of the Mothers, each [name] is in the dative case;
the short vowels are joined with the bindu, while the others are dark-colored (unaspirated), beginning with their respective initial letters.
Then, with those ending in *rbindva*, there should be "Obeisance to the one called Bhairava," and then "Obeisance to the sandals. || 17-8 ||
One should thus place [the mantras] separately in the navel, heart, throat, and mouth, then in the nose,
on the forehead, on the head, and likewise at the dvādaśānta, in due order.
The placement of the *pīṭha* and the sandals (*pādukā*):

In the secret place, the heart, and likewise on the forehead known as the *bindu*, one should separately place the remaining [syllables] beginning with *śeṣa* and the root-syllables in these three locations. (17–10)
The placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantranyāsa*).
The placement is first on the two hands, then on the faces, and then on the pedestal and the sandals;
it should proceed from the feet up to the head in reverse order, using both the root mantra and the limb-mantras (*aṅga*). Thus, there are six modes. (17–11)

Having entered the initiation and been consecrated by the Guru, performing his desired rites and specially instructed by him, he performed his daily obligations with the Guru’s permission; having purified himself and bound his body with mantras, he remained composed.
Adorned with white garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments, having worshipped Gaṇeśa and his preceptor with devotion,
he sat down appropriately on an auspicious seat, having gathered all the requisites for the ritual of worship.

Within the ocean of the jeweled palace in the interior of the cosmic egg, there is a garden brilliant with *kadamba* trees and a pavilion of gems, glowing with the crimson luster of shimmering rubies;
it is divine, with four gates guarded by as many reddish-brown *vaṭukas*.
One should meditate upon Him as being joined by the omniscient ones, who are resplendent in their attire of saffron robes and the like. || 17-14 ||
The first is the Kulavaṭuka, and likewise the second is the Akulavaṭuka; the third should be known as the Samayin, and the fourth is called the Sādhaka. (17.15)
At the four gates, these [deities] are to be worshipped; likewise are the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) and Gaṇeśvara.
These two, always well-adorned, are situated to the north and south.
In the center of that, upon a golden lion-throne, one should meditate on Śakti, red as the sprouts of coral;
and Ananta, encircling her eightfold with his coils, as well as a white lotus—thus [is she to be visualized].
His four feet are Dharma and the others; his lion-like faces are the qualities of Sattva, Tamas, and Rajas.
The bulbous root, the stalk, and the lotus are to be meditated upon in sequence as the three principles (Tattvas), the three worlds, and the three forms (Trimurti). (17–18)
The lotus has its upper covering as the *puryaṣṭaka*, and its four petals have the form of the lower covering;
it is strewn with a mass of shimmering filaments, and in its pericarp is the Root Power (*mūlaśakti*) above.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the Vāgbhava seed-syllable alone, which is bandhūka-red, beautiful, and triangular;
and upon Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, Rudra, as well as Īśvara and Sadāśiva.

Then [he beheld] the Goddess seated comfortably in their midst, her beauty reddened by the *japā* flower and *alaktaka* lac; her form serene with her legs bound in the *padmāsana*, her lotus-face adorned with three eyes. (17–21)
She wears matted locks and a crown upon which the cool-rayed moon is set; her ornaments, garments, and garlands are tawny-red;
she holds a rosary in her right hand and grants boons, while in her left hand she holds a book and displays the gesture of fearlessness. || 17-22 ||
Her face was like a mandala presided over by the full moon; she wore earrings of refined Jāmbūnada gold and jewels;
her neck was adorned with a niṣka ornament made radiant by its luster; and her well-formed, rounded, and elevated breasts were full. || 17-23 ||

Her breast-cloth was shimmering with a variegated pearl necklace, and she was adorned with rings and bracelets; possessing a lovely radiance reddened by the luster of saffron silk, she wore a golden girdle upon her hips.

She possessed a pair of shanks that were beautiful with their appropriately formed specific features, as charming as her thighs, tapering gradually toward the lotus-feet, which were adorned with anklets shimmering with various jewels. (17–25)

Having meditated upon the auspicious deity of the Tripuṭa, who is the singular beauty of the totality of all splendor, whose essence is the nectar of the beauty of fire, and who is one with oneself, one should worship her by means of practices infused with contemplative feeling.

Then, within the orb of the sky-lotus and moon, one should contemplate the consciousness that is of the nature of Śiva— partless, subtle, and exceedingly minute, possessing the brilliance of a star’s transition and the luster of a flash of lightning.
Then, having taken up [the breath] through the Suṣumṇā with one's own identity-deity (nijaikyadevī), one should lead it to the lotus of the heart.
Having contemplated her as endowed with consciousness for a moment, one should make the mind steady and inclined toward her. (17–18)

Having consecrated the Goddess of his own unity with the stream of nectar flowing from the moon of his own lotus— possessing the luster of white milk— and with the waters of nectar from the path of Brahman via the *suṣumṇā* channel, he should cause her to rejoice.
Having worshipped that [deity] mentally according to the ritual procedures and having flooded it with nectar,
one should then contemplate [the body] by means of the six internal substratum-mandalas and lotuses, through the *suṣumnā* which ascends from the body.

In the *mūlādhāra*, the anus, the generative organ, the navel, the heart, the root of the palate, and the head—these lotuses have four, six, ten, twelve, sixteen, two, and eight petals respectively, situated within the *brahmanāḍī*. (17.31)
Then, at its base, one should visualize the lunar mandala, nine koṭis of yojanas in extent;
having slightly contracted and fixed [the breath] there, one should contemplate the white lotus arising from it, with petals consisting of the kalās.
On the curved body, that lotus should be downward-facing; on the straight [body], it should be upward-facing with a long, smiling [petal].
Having visualized within its center the temple of Kāma—a liṅga with the form of a *kadamba* bud, radiant as the moon—[one should worship it]. (17.33)

Then Kuṇḍalinī, white as the fiber of a lotus sprout, having coiled herself three times around that [liṅga] while asleep, attains awakening through the agitation of the awakened abode of Madana; that first [liṅga] is said to consist of Vāgbhava. (17.34)

One should meditate here upon the fiery orb, red in color, as a ten-petaled lotus with the luster of the bandhūka flower; and in its center, one should contemplate that liṅga of the seed-syllable of Love (Mānmatha), possessing the brilliance of a ruby, which enchants and fascinates all people. (17.35)
The station of the Bindu is on the forehead, a yellow-colored mandala consisting of the sun;
there is a twelve-spoked lotus, brilliant as the sun, and the Linga is indeed yellow.
That seed-syllable of Sarasvatī arises as the supreme embodiment of speech, by whose power—
That which was proclaimed as the three Purāṇas seen here is indeed the Vidyā known as Traipurā.

Starting from this liṅga called Bāṇa by way of the Suṣumnā path, the subtle radiance with the luster of lightning—having passed through the second and third liṅgas via their centers as the Power (Śakti)—ascends to the city at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta). (17.37)

I, having become the individual soul (jīvabhūta), have here gradually united with my own lotus, which has arisen through the power awakened by the three signs; it possesses a thousand petals, its filaments are situated within the digits (kalā), and its center is a hollow aperture dripping with the essence of nectar.
Again, that very same power, having turned back from him with a stream of nectar, enters the aperture of Brahmā through the path of Suṣumnā as before;
flooding the three signs within in succession, it reaches the root-lotus here.
Having thus visualized the upward and downward movement [of breath], one's body is then filled with [light] as white as a conch shell, a kunda flower, the moon, or cow’s milk;
and being bathed by the flowing nectar-water dripping from the pores of the skin.

One should meditate on the deities stationed in the eight seats in sequence, as well as the limbs, the accomplishments (*siddhis*), and those abiding in the enclosure; then one should contemplate the Guru, the gatekeepers, the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), the pavilion, and the ocean. (17–41)
By constantly meditating on this mantra through the practice of repeated application, one shall obtain the objects desired by the mind within the three worlds;
having conquered death in this world, one shall attain mastery over qualities and speech, as well as liberation that is otherwise unattainable.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess through the realization of one's own identity with her and having worshipped her with mental offerings according to the rule,
one should properly draw the diagram of the Goddess on the outside for the sake of external sacrifice, exactly as before and according to the prescribed rite.

One should draw a wheel on a very beautiful surface measuring one cubit (*aratni*), using gold, silver, or copper, with water mixed with saffron from Kashmir, yellow orpiment, sandalwood, camphor, *kuṣṭha*, *rukmapatraka*, and cow dung.
In the center is a lotus with a pericarp and eight petals; outside that, twelve petals;
beyond that, a sixteen-petaled lotus; and likewise, on the outermost layer, there should be petals of passion (rāga). || 17-45 ||

The outer perimeter of that [mandala] is square; in this [square], the corners on the sides should be drawn resembling vases, endowed with the respective symbols of the noose, goad, conch, and lotus, in their proper order.
In the center, there should be the Vāgbhava syllable in the form of a triangle; within that, the two seed-syllables of Smara and Śakti should be written.
The vowels should be placed upon the petals located in the eight directions, and the Kāma syllable on the twelve outer petals.

Then, the mantra-practitioner should write the sixteen Śaktis upon the sixteen petals, and then the twelve Kāmas upon the twelve petals; furthermore, he should write the thirty-two letters beginning with *sa* and ending with *na*, accompanied by the *haṃsa* and the *bindu*, upon the petals of the thirty-two-petalled lotus.

p. 31) Then, on the outside, like a garland, one should draw the remaining mantra; outside the circle, there is a square within it. Likewise, one should duly draw the noose and the goad situated at the four corners in a most beautiful manner. (17–49)
Having drawn this wheel, which is designated as Tripura, one should perform the sacrifice within it;
then, having placed it upon a pedestal, the practitioner of mantra should worship it with those prescribed offerings. (17.50)
Worship of the Goddess in a painted mandala is likewise praised as being equal to that performed with one's own body; it is not to be done upon the bare ground.
If, out of delusion, he should worship her on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), he would fall away from the three aims of life as well as from the attainment of mantra-siddhi.

Having first meditated upon her as being united with the nectar-power (amṛtaśakti) at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta) through the application of the seed-syllables consisting of the three genders, one should worship her—who is of one body with oneself—upon one's own head with perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and water. (17.52)
Having invoked that speech, consisting of light, consciousness, and bliss, from the sky-moon-lotus as if it were before one,
one should sprinkle it with the nectars produced from the moon in the sky, within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Having worshipped in sequence with the mantras of the remaining limbs and roots as before, using great offerings (mahopacāra),
and having performed the immersion with drops of water filling the sky as previously described, one should worship the aforementioned enclosures (āvaraṇas).
One should worship the enclosure with the limbs (aṅgas) first, in due order, in the middle of the petals;
then, in the second [circle], one should worship those Śaktis situated at the tips of the petals, holding a pen and a book in their two hands.

Yogā, Satyā, Vimalā, Medhā, Śraddhā, Buddhi, and likewise Samṛddhi, and Jñānā—these [deities] in the east and other directions are red in color, their limbs adorned with divine garments and other ornaments. (17.56)

Then, in the third enclosure, one should worship the Mothers and the Bhairava-pādukās in sequence upon the eight seats; in the northeast, one should worship the five Gurus; and in the fourth [enclosure], one should worship the Kṣetrapāla along with the Vighnas and the Vaṭukas in the cardinal directions.

Having duly worshipped those lords of the world, together with their weapons, vehicles, and so forth, in the fifth enclosure with various types of ritual offerings, and having again honored the Goddess with flowers; || 17-58 ||
"Salutation to the Goddess, sovereign of the *ātmatattva*; salutation to the Goddess, sovereign of the *vidyātattva*; salutation to the Goddess, sovereign of the *śivatattva*.

Having offered three handfuls of flowers with these mantras separately in sequence, one should worship her also with the eight flowers of disposition (*bhāva*) by means of the practices of disposition (*bhāvasādhana*). (59)
Non-violence is the first flower; then comes restraint of the senses, forgiveness, devotion, compassion, meditation, non-greed, and knowledge as the eighth. (17.60)

With the principles (tattvas) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, separately as before, ending with *namaḥ*, one should perform the recitation at the beginning and end of the recitation; this is the procedure that effects the protection of the recitation. (17.61)
A rosary of crystal beads is indeed recommended for the recitation of mantras dedicated to Tripura;
one should also mentally offer the recitation to her with water consecrated by the nectar-mantra.
Then one should recite this hymn, which is the essence of the mantra to be meditated upon:
[I bow to her] who possesses the splendor of a flash of lightning and a cluster of *kadamba* blossoms, who is most slender,
as delicate as a lotus fiber, and who has emerged from the form of the three *liṅgas*.
We bow to that most partless Speech which, having transcended *saṃsarga*, *bindu*, and *nāda* in succession from that state, is drenched by the flowing essence of nectar.
In an ocean of nectar, upon a white ground, within a pavilion of moonstones, amidst a lotus that is the orb of the moon,
[he beheld] a fair-complexioned girl holding a book marked with the seal of awakening, along with a water-pot and a rosary for recitation.
We pay homage to the Speech, adorned with white garments and other ornaments, and enveloped in white radiance.

In the Himālaya hermitage, she is worshipped by the eight Mothers; she is seated upon a lotus-throne, possesses the luster of the moon, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness while holding a lotus and a book;
she is accompanied by Gaṇeśa and Ṣaṇmukha, as well as Dakṣiṇāmūrti and the Preceptor (Śiva).
We praise the goddess who is accompanied by Bhairava, who has three eyes, and whose hair is tied in a topknot. || 17-65 ||
By virtue of her own unity with [the Sun], she possesses a ruddy luster; wearing earrings of refined gold,
adorned with various ornaments and garments, she stands upon a lotus that fulfills all desires,
holding a noose and a goad in her hands, as well as the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
We bow to the speech that brings about prosperity, together with the treasures of the conch and the lotus.
One should visualize the Vāgbhava syllable on the lotus of the forehead with the brilliance of Indra’s bow;
then, upon the lunar orb at the head, the white-lighted [Māyā] together with Manmatha;
and in the heart-lotus, the solar disc situated within the orb of the sun.
We offer praise to the speech that distinguishes between the two for the sake of enjoyment and liberation.
The two worlds, heaven and earth, were reddened by the liquid lac of her own radiance;
she was adorned with flowers, arrows, and a bow, holding a goad and a noose,
clad in crimson garments and other finery, appearing as if she were one with herself.
We bow to the Speech that is remembered as the enchantress of the world and the attractor [of all beings]. || 17-68 ||
Because it is the birthplace of the power of speech for all the Vedas and Shastras, it is indeed the source of the play of refined language (Sanskrit) and other tongues;
and when remembered, it shines with the brilliance of a star within the temple of the god of love.
We praise that Speech, whose very nature it is to set words in motion.
Since the manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution of phenomenal existence proceed through the differentiation of the three forms, the Trimūrti is thus conceived;
it is preceded by the three qualities (*guṇa*), the three worlds (*jagat*), the three principles (*tattva*), and time.
Therefore, O Mother, we bow to that speech of yours which was preceded by the syllable *tri* in the past.
Or perhaps, being ignorant of the procedure for limb-worship, I worshipped you while lacking the mantras for the limbs, the ritual means, and so forth;
yet that was done by me, impelled by devotion toward your pair of lotus-feet.
O Mother! You have been distressed by me now; forgive my misconduct.
O Goddess! By your grace, may that worship of mine—devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of faith—become complete. (17.72)
Thus, from the Self (Ātman) up to the end of the three principles (Tattvas), ending with "namas," one should offer the fruit of worship and recitation to the Goddess with water from a handful.
Having bound the two ring fingers together with the two index fingers of the hands, [one should place] the middle fingers and the little fingers together on the palms which are turned upward. (17.74)
Having brought the two sides together at the tips so that they are straight and extended,
one should touch the roots of the two little fingers with the tips of the two thumbs.
This mudrā is known as Yoni; it belongs to Śakti and bestows the accomplishment of mantra.
Having bound it, one should show it to the Goddess; it will instantly produce delight. (17.76)

Then, having offered the *arghya* with the heart-mantra, and having paid homage and propitiated [the deity], one should [dismiss her] with this handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) for the Goddess together with her retinue: "O Stainless One! Go to dissolution! *ṭhaṭha*. (17.77)
Having taken [the substance] with the outpourings of nectar, one should place it in the center of the lotus of the mouth;
then, having offered the *arghya* with the heart-mantra, one should feed the young maidens.
One should also offer to the young students milk-rice, clarified butter, and honey according to one's ability;
however, during periods of birth-impurity and the like, one should not perform external worship or recitation of mantras.
One should perform the rites of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) and others according to the prescribed rules;
specifically, one should prepare the sacred threads here using silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*).
One may also perform the descent of the Gaṅgā and the rite of the bracelet;
however, fierce worship is not recommended here, and the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) is now being described.
An oblation of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sugar shall grant all-enchanting power;
likewise, one may offer bilva leaves, white fruits, or flowers for the sake of prosperity.
One offers oblations with black mustard and salt along with honey for supreme satisfaction;
by offering white flowers, one obtains knowledge.
In rites for subjugation and attraction, one should perform the practice with red materials;
by means of tips of *dūrvā* grass, one obtains a maiden, and with food mixed with clarified butter, one obtains excellent food. (17.84)
One may bring a courtesan under one's control by offering *śirīṣa* flowers mixed with honey.
By performing a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with white and other such flowers, one gains the arrival of women dressed in white and other garments. (17.85)
With apāmārga, aśvattha, nyagrodha, and udumbara [leaves], one may subjugate the four castes, beginning with the brahmins, by means of sweet [substances] in their respective order.
By performing oblations with *dhurdhūra* wood, enemies shall become insane;
by using neem and cotton, one effects enmity; and with poisonous poisons, one may cause death.
By performing oblations with the leaves of the *kākāri* and *pattrā*, one may cause others to be driven away (*uccāṭayet*).
In rites against base beings, one should meditate on her as black, along with her black retinues.
Through the homa offering of honey, clarified butter, and milk, prosperity shall become attainable.
Having smeared the area beneath a banyan tree with cow dung, the practitioner should spread darbha grass there. (17.89)
One should worship the Brahmayakṣiṇī with white flowers, parched grain, and unbroken rice;
having recited her mantra eight thousand times every night with a focused mind. (17.90)
Within a month, one shall behold the yakṣiṇī and also obtain one's desired objects;
moreover, water consecrated with that mantra, when drunk daily, is traditionally known to produce intelligence.
Having drunk water one hundred and eight times while touching it day and night,
and having gazed [at the object] with the mudrā bound, he shall paralyze their speech.
One should retain even unheard scriptures by mere sight;
what is the use of much prattle? [The Lord] bestows the power of eloquence through the play of speech. (17.93)
There is no mantra other than that of the Tripurā which bestows such glory, especially when it is devoid of all other mantras—that mantra which was declared first. (17.94)
The mantra designated as "Bāla" is to be recited by children alone and not by others;
it consists of all these remaining root-syllables, distributed according to their respective divisions.
The mantra of the three cities is indeed immovable and bestows all accomplishments;
it consists of the vowels and so forth in sequence, followed by the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* in two successive orders.
Indeed, those very mantras of Tripura arise in sequence from those internal vowels, together with the consonants [ending] in the sprouts of the left eye (the letter *i*). 17-97.
This triple city, consisting of Samyag, Itthā, and Muditā, is a cow of plenty that grants all desires; it is the very embodiment of knowledge.
By worshipping it, the gods, Guhyakas, and Siddhas attained their desired perfections and supernatural powers. (17.98)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Tripurā," in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter. Now, according to the specific instruction that has been declared, [the mantra consists of] Tripura, Haṃsa, Vāgīśvarī,
the Sky with the Bindu (M), Bhṛgu (S), and separately the vowels beginning with the letter 'Bā' (Ā).
This [syllable] is the enchantress of the world; it exists for the prosperity of all speech.
Then follows the sage seated upon the lotus, and thereafter the *uṣṇih* meter and Speech itself. 18-1.
One should sequentially place the vowels ending in the bindu (a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ) upon the mouth, the eyes, the nose, the lower lip, the face-circle, the two ears, the other mouth, the heart, the navel,
and the head throughout the entire body.

Oṃ haṃ saḥ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ, homage to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ). Oṃ haṃ saḥ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ña, svāhā to the head (śirase ṭhaṭha). Oṃ haṃ saḥ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhāyai vaṣaṭ). Oṃ haṃ saḥ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ, huṃ to the armor (kavacāya huṃ). Oṃ haṃ saḥ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ, phaṭ to the weapon (astrāya phaṭ). Thus, the arrangement of the limbs is declared here, by which the directions are bound and so forth. (18–2)
Having bathed your own body from head to foot and having occupied your desired seat,
remember the divine hermitage of the Siddhas on the shore of the ocean—
the palace of moonstones with its silver star-studded throne.
It has a great lotus as its base, with Mount Meru as the excellent pericarp, and the three qualities (guṇas) as its unfolding petals.
Salutation to the pericarp in the form of Meru.

Then, ending with "namas," one should worship the filaments according to the principles of the lords of the principal mountain ranges; salutations again and again to the filaments whose nature is that of the great boundary mountains.
In the same manner, one should worship the world-enclosing mountains, which consist of the renowned mountain ranges of the various regions (*varṣa*),
as being composed of petals;
and outside [that], one should worship the circle of the earth and the seven oceans.
In that same manner, one should worship Caṇḍikā, Gaṇapati, the Guru, and Kṣetrapa in the [respective] directions.
First, the sustenance of one's own limbs [is performed]; then, Rudra is in front upon a lotus, and likewise the four-faced Brahmā above him seated on a lotus; below is Vāsuki.
Above, the sun and moon serve as lamps in front.
The two excellent treasures named Saroja and Jalaja are bestowers of wealth. || 18-5 ||
White as a moonstone, with her right hands granting boons and holding a rosary, and her left hands holding a lute and a book, she has three eyes;
she wears a crown of matted hair adorned with the moon, and is graced with stainless necklaces, garlands, and other ornaments.
Bow down to Haṃsavāgīśvarī, whose form is the supreme nectar.

Having meditated upon his own divine form seated comfortably upon the pericarp of that lotus, he then sprinkled that one of stainless luster with the nectar of the clear lotus and moon on his head, and with the waters of the *arghya* offering.
And let him worship with fragrant flowers and other such offerings through his intellect.
Homage to Airāvata; homage to Puṇḍarīka; homage to Kumuda; homage to Añjana; homage to Vāmana; homage to Puṣpadanta; homage to Sārvabhauma; homage to Supratīka.
Thus one should worship the elephants of the directions situated in the quarters beginning with the East.
Homage to Dharā; homage to Dhruva; homage to Soma; homage to Āpa; homage to Anila; homage to Anala; homage to Pratyūṣa; homage to Prabhāsa. Thus [one worships] the eight Vasus.

Salutation to Ajaikapād; salutation to Ahirbudhnya; salutation to Virūpākṣa; salutation to Raivata; salutation to Tryambaka; salutation to Pinākin; salutation to Bhava; salutation to Īśvara; salutation to Kapālin; salutation to Sthāṇu; salutation to Bhava—thus [are] the eleven Rudras.

Salutation to Dhātṛ; salutation to Aryaman; salutation to Mitra; salutation to Varuṇa; salutation to Aṃśa; salutation to Bhaga; salutation to Indra; salutation to Vivasvat; salutation to Pūṣan; salutation to Parjanya; salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ; salutation to Viṣṇu—thus to the twelve Ādityas. Salutation to Kratu; salutation to Dakṣa; salutation to Sudhā; salutation to Stavya; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kāma; salutation to Dhuni; salutation to Kurumat; salutation to Madhumat; salutation to Rocanāman—thus to the ten Viśvedevas.

One should worship the Vasus in the east, the Three-eyed ones (Śivas) with the Lord of the Gods (Indra), the Bhāskaras (Suns) in the south with Yama, the Viśvakas in the west with the Moon, and then the Lords of the Worlds;
furthermore, one should worship the deities consisting of their weapons, preceded by the Praṇava, their names, and the heart-mantra. (18.8)

One should worship with perfumes and other offerings; eating moderately as is appropriate for a vow, wearing white perfumes, garlands, and garments, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) by reciting [the mantra] one million times with a rosary.
One should offer oblations separately one hundred thousand times each with white palāśa flowers, lotuses, jasmine, blue water-lilies, and fragrant fresh clarified butter.

Then that excellent practitioner clearly becomes a master of speech among the perfected ones (siddha-vāgīśvara) and a partaker of all accomplishments, attaining the state of the sole sovereign wealth of the three worlds;
likewise, he should recite [the mantra] every day and offer oblations of ghee and milk according to his capacity.
Having contemplated that identity with one's own self, one indeed conquers others in debate.

For the attainment of royal fortune, one should meditate upon Śivā, who possesses the luster of molten gold, has three eyes, and holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a sword, a thunderbolt, a lotus, and an excellent trident, while bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
One should remember the Goddess who enchants the world, who is as pale-red as the Japā flower.

I meditate upon Gira, who possesses a singular oneness with her consort, whose radiance is ruddy, who holds in her hands a lute resonating at the fingertips, a noose, a goad, a water-pot, and a rosary of beads, and who is adorned with ornaments of variegated jewels.
In recitations and other rites, this [mantra] is desired for subjugation; one should likewise attract [the object]. || 18-12 ||
One may subjugate Fortune (Śrī) with lotuses and bilva fruits, as well as a king and the common people with offerings of sweet milk and lotuses and bandhujīva flowers;
one may subjugate women with salt and rice, and the best of the twice-born with kunda and utpala flowers.
The Vaiśyas [should offer] with sesame seeds possessing their specific qualities, while the Śūdras and others [should offer] with honeyed sesame seeds.

By offering oblations of *viṣavibhītaka* seeds, there is the destruction and inciting of enmity against enemies; furthermore, by using its fuel-sticks or leaves, there is the paralyzing of the enemy's body.
By offering oblations of *viṣarājika* seeds with *viṣa* fuel-sticks, death shall occur.
Let him scatter [the dust] from his feet, mixed with rājikā seeds, upon his enemies. || 18.14 ||
By offering oblations of equal pieces of *galūci* wood, along with fragrant milk and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, one conquers all diseases; by offering sesame seeds, one overcomes death.
Whatever is desired here in the mind, all that is attained through recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*).
Through the realization of one's own identity, let him worship Haṃsavāgīśvarī.
What is the use of much description here? Whatever is accomplished by Tripurā, and whatever is desired by her, all that is fully attained through this Vidyā.
Therefore, indeed, through its application, the fruit is truly equal.
Surely, within the belly of the three worlds, there is nothing here that cannot be accomplished by these two.
The ritual procedure for Haṃsavāgīśvarī:
Having first uttered "Jalātri salilātri" and then "Vāgvādinī," this ten-syllable mantra, accompanied by the pair of *ṭha* syllables (*ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*), is the speech of the Goddess.
The seer was Dhiṣaṇa; others, however, know him as Kaṇva.
They also know Virāj as his deity, and Vāgīśvarī as his consort.

Oṃ hāṃ, speak! To the Heart of the Ṛgveda, namaḥ. Oṃ hīṃ, speak! To the Head of the Yajurveda, svāhā. Oṃ hūṃ, O Speech! To the Tuft of the Sāmaveda, vaṣaṭ. Oṃ haiṃ, O Speaker! To the Armor of the Atharvaveda, huṃ. Oṃ hauṃ, to the Three Eyes of the Six Limbs, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ haḥ, to the Weapon of the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Śāstras, svāhā phaṭ.
These are the mantras of the six limbs; initiated by an excellent guru, one who is intent on performing his own duties, wearing white perfumes, garlands, and garments—

Eating measured food appropriate for his vow and occupying a seat in a place declared as auspicious, let him recite the mantra one million times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should place the first syllable of "Manu" (Ma), together with the *tāra* (Oṃ) seated in the heart,
upon the nose, face, eyes, throat, breasts, thighs, knees, feet,
and likewise the belly; the remaining syllable is said to be for these [locations].
One should place [the mantra] in the lotus of the heart, and then one should place the Tāraka once again.
One should place the ten syllables in sequence upon the head, the pair of eyes and ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the heart, and the two feet.
This is another method; it is beautiful, being a single path for both.
Having performed the binding of the directions with the prescribed weapons, one should assign the limbs according to their respective measures.
Oṃ! Protect me, O Dakṣiṇāmūrti! O Vīrabhadra, homage be to you!
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, may you always protect us in our service at your feet. || 18–21 ||

With this [mantra], the practitioner should recite it first when going to his bed or seat, as well as when walking and when attending to the necessities of nature, for the sake of protecting his own body with mantras; furthermore,
by performing libations in the water at midday and at dawn, he shall destroy wandering [in saṃsāra].
If that practitioner here is pure and performs the recitation of the mantra, he shall be successful. || 18-22 ||

Then, during the rite of worship, facing the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the North), one should visualize a pavilion made of crystal situated in the midst of an ocean of milk, containing a cluster of lotuses;
it rests upon a golden lion-throne, is fully blossomed, white, and composed of the Mātṛkās.
A lotus with its pericarp and beautiful, scattered filaments in full bloom.

Then, having looked at and sprinkled with water one's own head, the place of refuge, and the entire collection of sacrificial materials, in sequence, by means of the nectar from the moon in the sky-lotus [arising] from the *arghya* offered upon one's own limbs,
[one should offer it] to Yama, Varuṇa, Arthanātha, and Indra.
One should worship [the deities] seated upon lotuses atop cushions made from the skin of the lion, the enemy of the deer.
In due order, one should visualize these four: first the Guru, who is Śiva accompanied by his consort and possessing the form to be described; then Gaṇeśa, clad in an elephant hide;
and finally [Śiva] himself, possessing the luster of the autumnal moon, three-eyed, and crowned with matted locks.
He who has the moon as his crest-ornament and who is seated upon a yogic posture with a cloth-band bound around him.
Bow down to Dakṣiṇāmūrti beneath the banyan tree, surrounded by a multitude of sages, holding a chisel, and wearing a rosary for the recitation of wisdom;
bow to the Guru, the supreme Guru, and the Guru known as Parameṣṭhi.
From the mantra of his own venerable guru, [he obtained] the mantra of the guru named Anantapūjya.
Bow down to these [deities] who delight in meditative absorption, who are clad in white perfumes and garments,
who are manifested from the eight groups [of deities], and who have reached the further shore of all that is to be known;
they hold in their hands a skull-cup, a trident, and the desired mudrā.
He has three eyes, is adorned with serpents, and wears the skins of an elephant and a hyena as his garments.
Bow for the sake of prosperity to the all-pervading Bhairava, who has a corpse as his lotus-seat, who wears a garland of the heads of brave warriors, and who is praised by gods and demons;
bow to the all-pervading one who has the splendor of a hibiscus flower, who has an elephant’s face, and a protruding belly.
Holding a noose and a goad, he bears his own tusk as his fruit.
I bow to the Lord of the Gaṇas, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, three eyes, and shimmering ornaments; who is the embodiment of the sky and the bestower of desired boons—
one who, when meditated upon with a concentrated mind, removes sins, suffering, and obstacles.
Having prostrated before the Goddess within the interior of the lotus, one should perform the invocation.
She possesses the luster of moonstones, moonlight, clusters of night-lotuses, and jasmine;

her matted locks shine with a crescent moon upon her head; she has three eyes; and she is clad in white garments and unguents, adorned with necklaces and garlands that captivate with their stainless purity.
[He beholds] Bhāratī, who holds the pen that grants fearlessness and the boon-granting book.
Likewise, let him worship her with the limbs and secondary limbs in sequence, and with ritual offerings;
let there be an oblation of pure rice-porridge with milk and ghee.
Then, having depicted her on a cloth or a wooden board in a painting for the sake of victory—
If not, one should worship [it] in a beautiful book written upon lotuses. || 18-31 ||
Or else, one should worship [the deity] residing in a sky-lotus, or within the orb of the sun, or even in water, according to one's own desire, with the equality of the essence of one's own power.
First, there is the sustenance of one's own limbs, and thereafter, by means of the Śaktis and the Mothers—
Let him perform the sacrifice ending with the invocation of the city (stadāhvayana) according to the sequence to be described. || 18-32 ||
Oṃ, homage to Yogā. Oṃ, homage to Satyā. Oṃ, homage to Vimalā. Oṃ, homage to Buddhi. Oṃ, homage to Smṛti. Oṃ, homage to Medhā. Oṃ, homage to Śraddhā.
These Śaktis, holding books and rosaries, resplendent with spotless necklaces and garlands, possessing the beautiful luster of the moon, reside at the tips of each petal.

With both hands joined in *añjali*, their matted locks crowned by the moon, possessing the forms previously described and bearing the characteristics of their respective deities, they are the Mothers. (18.33)
One should worship those situated in the third enclosure, beginning with Dakṣiṇeśa and Īśāna as previously described;
those situated in the fourth enclosure outside are the world-protectors (Lokapālas) headed by Indra (Śatamakha);
and then, one should duly worship the deities consisting of their weapons in the final enclosure.
Having worshipped thoroughly with fragrant flowers and other offerings, one should recite the mantra. || 18-34 ||
With water in his cupped palms, he should offer his recitation (*japa*), sacrifices, and other rites, saying:

"O Supreme Goddess, you whose form is the self, protected by that which is more secret than the secret! Accept this worship performed by me, along with the recitation and other acts, for the attainment of their fruit. (18-35)

With this [mantra], having performed the worship of all the powers and mantras at the two lotus-feet, one should ask for forgiveness from the deities through the sacrificial image; then, [one says]: "O Stainless One in the sky-lotus, go to dissolution! *Ṭhaṭha*!"
Or rather, let him unite her with that funeral pyre within the calyx of the heart-lotus.

Touching his face daily with his own hand, he should meditate upon her while reciting that mantra at the three junctions of the day; thus, by holding the support of a clenched fist with his left hand, he becomes a composer of prose, verse, and other literary forms.
Casting [the mantra] into the mouth of another, one should instantly paralyze their speech. || 18-37 ||

In an instant, one becomes a possessor of the power of retention (śrutadhara); [one should visualize the goddess] who has the luster of the moon, six arms, and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a rosary, a lotus, a water-pot, and a book;
she is white, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with white garments, garlands, ornaments, and the like.
Remembering her, whose high breasts were adorned with all manner of charming ornaments, he became [filled with longing]. || 18-38 ||
Then, meditating upon the previously described goddess who has eight beautiful arms, who is the sovereign of speech (Vāgīśvarī) identical with himself, and who possesses four lotus-like faces—
visualizing her within his own mouth and consecrating his own face— he indeed triumphs in debate over others.
As it has been said: "Even one who has not studied may speak the Vedas and the Śāstras. (18.39)
By offering white lotus flowers sprinkled with sweet milk into the fire,
one shall obtain poetic skill as well as prosperity here within six months;
he who, honored as the very embodiment of the mantra, recites it a thousand times at the break of day.
Indeed, within a year, he shall become one who has reached the further shore of all the sciences.
Having consecrated one hundred and ten measures of water with mantras, one should drink it at dawn;
or one should recite the mantra three thousand times while standing in water up to the heart;
or else, being armored by the mantra, one should recite it one thousand times at daybreak.
Moreover, by offering *bilva* fruits for a year, one becomes a composer of poetry. (18.41)
By offering oblations of fresh *palāśa* flowers or fuel-sticks,
one may obtain poetic skill as well as prosperity in this world;
or one may drink ghee called "born from a lotus" consecrated with this mantra.
One should immediately retain in memory whatever has been heard at home while accompanied by white vacā.
What is the use of much speaking here? Whatever is desired by this mind is not difficult to obtain within the three worlds through this knowledge,
for it effects the removal of the world’s calamities and fulfills the longing for established prosperity.
How can she be described, whom even the Lotus-born Brahmā himself adores?

For the sake of spiritual accomplishment, one should not eat onions, garlic, water from winnowing-grounds, leeks, *kalañja*, large *ālupa* tubers, *pajjapahaṇi*, nor *amlātaka* fruit at night, and likewise avoid betel leaf.
Let him not consort with women by day; if he does consort with them, let him consort with Vāgīśvarī.
The ritual procedure for Vāgīśvarī of ten syllables:
preceded by the Praṇava and joined with Śakti, she herself consists of ten syllables;
she who is renowned as the Siddha-Vāgīśvarī brings the world under her control here.
One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* recitation one million times, and furthermore,
offer oblations numbering one hundred and twenty-five thousand (*sapāda-lakṣa*) using guggulu resin, milk, and lotuses.
The six limbs are to be assigned individually with one's own pairs of syllables in their proper order; here too, the application according to the ritual rule is the same as previously stated.
Then, [one recites] "namo bhagavati," followed by the pair of words "vāgdevi" and "ṭha."
This Manu is considered to have accomplished his purpose before [the others] by means of the two [methods]. || 18-46 ||
Others say "wisdom, intelligence, learning, power, memory, the mistress of speech, and thought," while others say "well-being"; these are the powers of the mantras Vāgīśvarī and Manu.
For the sake of liberation, one should meditate upon Sarasvatī within the heart-lotus, having the form of a kadamba bud, possessing the luster of the sun’s orb,
situated in the center of a lotus and a bindu, and radiant with the light of the autumnal moon.
One should meditate upon her as being immersed in a flood of flowing nectar, the destroyer of worldly existence.
At dawn, recollecting the full moon in the sky-lotus from which streams of nectar flow,
and thereby satisfying his speech, he attains greatness and becomes a master of eloquence.
Thus has been declared the general purpose of mantra, worship, and so forth, arising from mastery over speech;
having understood this desired mastery over speech, one shall attain it for common purposes in the world. (18.50)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the Vāgīśvarī-paṭala, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 18.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Herein are written verses that serve as examples for the definitions and illustrations of *gaṇavṛtta*, *mātrāvṛtta*, and *chandovṛtta* meters.
Victorious is that Mother Lakṣmī of the world, through the falling of her compassionate glances.
The Noble One protects people with their desired prosperities, as if they were her own children to be nourished. (19.1) The Noble One:
Recollection of her lotus-feet nourishes grains, cattle, gold, fields, kingdoms, horses, elephants, and even the jewels of women in this world. (19.2) As before.

The letter *va* (vānta), mounted on fire (*vahni*), joined with the left eye (*vāmākṣi*), and enriched by the *bindu* and *nāda*, is indeed declared as the mantra for Lakṣmī; it leads to swift accomplishment through recitation as its proper regimen. [19.3] This king of mantras, known as the Heart of Śrī, is enclosed between the beginning and end of the *śakti*.
Through meditation, that which is received from the mouth of the Guru yields fruit; otherwise, it is equal to a mere verse (gāthā). [This is] the Pathyā-gāthā. (p.
45) There shall be a sage named Viṣṇu, and its meter shall likewise be Jāgata; its deity is Lakṣmī, who is indeed praised by the worlds. I shall now describe its constituent parts (aṅgas). As before.

Oṃ lakṣmyai hṛdayāya namaḥ | Oṃ śriyai śirase ṭhaṭha | Oṃ devajuṣṭāyai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ | Oṃ māyāyai kavacāya hum | Oṃ śrīṃ huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ | Oṃ haṃ saḥ | With this, there is the binding of the ten directions (*daśadigbandha*). Having received initiation, one should take up the *vidyā* during the month of Phālguna on the day of the *phālgunī* constellation; or even on a desired lunar day and auspicious hour, on a day favorable to one’s own birth star (*janmarkṣa*) and so forth. (19–6) [This is] the "Mukhapathyā" [verse].

When the sun is situated in Uttaraphalgunī, one who has bathed and is adorned with white perfumes, garlands, and new garments should worship both Āryā and Gajavadana (Gaṇeśa) through the preceptor and then mutter the mantra. This too is an Āryā verse.
First, let him mutter it on a riverbank, by a Bilva tree, on a mountain, or at the temples of Mukunda and Śiva.
Then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times separately according to the rules for meditation, he should worship her. || 19-8 ||
Meru, situated in the center of the earth-lotus, becomes its broad pericarp;
one should likewise visualize the golden peaks on its perimeter as its clusters of filaments.
But having entered the exceedingly beautiful center of that lotus, he himself becomes motionless, with a body straight and extended, and with his mind fully restrained. (19.10)

One should meditate upon a thousand-petaled lotus extending from the navel downward, as radiant as a hundred suns; its pericarp is the star, and here one should contemplate that reddish syllable of Power (Śakti).
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable *mā*, resembling moist gold, within the heart-lotus endowed with eight petals;
and likewise, the seed-syllable of Śakti within the thousand-petaled lotus between the eyebrows.
One should remember the extremely white letter *ṭa* with a bindu upon a hundred-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, together with a water-pot;
and one should also remember that lotus-face which rains down a flood of nectar.

In the first lotus, one should mentally recite the Śakti-mantra, which possesses a sweet sound like the resonance of a bell and is of incomparable brilliance, extending to the end of the Suṣumṇā path within the lotus of the heart. These are specific types of Āryā verses.
Within the heart-lotus is the Śrī-bīja, resembling a lamp-flame, permeated by the sound of Śakti.
Then, having reached the *pathyā* even higher than that, one should go to the *suṣumnā* at the *bindu*. This too is the *pathyā*. (p.

46) From the center of the eyebrows to the lotus of the head, along the path of Brahman (*brahmapatha*), one should lead the consciousness—the Goddess Lakṣmī—through the piercing of the *śakti* and *nāda* to the sky-lotus of the moon.

One should meditate in the heart upon her whose nature is consciousness and bliss, who has been brought down from the path of Brahman into the lotus of the heart, and whose form is flooded by streams of the supreme nectar of immortality.

Having repeatedly led this root power to the path of the moon (sudhāpatha), one should then lead it—which has reached the heart, ascended upward, and is eternally situated within the heart—to the heart once more. (19.18)
If the mind remains steady when this yoga known as *niṣkala* has been thus described, and if one recites [the mantra] with that mind, he perceives everything; he is omniscient.
Through such practice of the Śrī-hṛdaya, the scriptures shine for him, and there shall be abundance of grain, wealth, and power; he brings the entire world under his control. (19–20)

In this [chapter], I shall explain the complete meditation, joined with both external and internal worship, by means of external riches such as perfumes and so forth, and also by those [riches] perfected through the mind. This is an Āryā verse.
[The mandala is] a pavilion situated in the midst of the ocean of milk, surrounded by a forest of lotuses.

One should meditate on the Hiraṇya [Nidhi], which has vast openings at its mouth through which wealth flows out like treasures. (19–22) The Mukhavipulā [Nidhi] has a surface strewn with lapis lazuli and is endowed with beautiful fourfold gates and archways;
it is further adorned by female messengers with lovely faces and broad hips. (19–23) The Jaghanavipulā [Nidhi].
The pillars were variegated with pearls, emeralds, and gems, as were the canopies;
its four corners were made of crystal, and its walls were surrounded by jewels. Another [hall] was broad at the hips;
it carried the fragrance of the Saugandhika forest and the pollen of flowers such as the Pārijāta.

The gentle breezes from the Malaya mountains blew forth, vast and exceedingly pleasant. (19.25) [Mahāvipulā meter] In this place, the quarters of the sky, with their edges perfumed by pastes of camphor, black aloe, saffron, and sandalwood mixed with cool water, as well as by incenses, became as fickle as faces. (19.26) [Mukhacapalā meter]
Then, in the center of the pavilion, one should visualize the divine Maheśvara-maṇḍala;
in its center is the lotus-throne, which, with its own splendors, is exceedingly radiant. In this place, the sweet resonance of the lute and the sounds of the *sāna* and *paṇava* drums resound.
The *pathyā-gīti* is that which is continuous, with equal tempo and measured syllables, and likewise accompanied by the *mṛdaṅga* drum. (19.28) This is the *pathyā-gīti*. (p.

47) The *vipulā-gīti* is that where the song is heard to be sweet to the ear and expansive, like the songs of *kinnaras*, as well as of bees, and is perceived as being joined with the warbling of sweet-voiced cuckoos. (19.29) This is the *vipulā-gīti*.
One should then meditate upon the Śakti, Śeṣa, and the lotus upon the surface of the earth;
these are praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as being presided over by Fire, the Sun, and the Moon respectively.
(Upagīti) One should [meditate upon] the eight petals of the lotus and the Śaktis: Kānti, Puṣṭi, Dyuti, Dhṛti, and Kīrtimatī.
Contentment (Tuṣṭi) and Peace (Śānti) are the deities of these [petals], sung by their own names from the heart. This is the Āryāgīti meter.
Vāsudeva is in the eastern petal, and then Saṅkarṣaṇa is in the southern one;
Pradyumna is in the western direction, and the one named Aniruddha is declared to be in the direction of the Lord of Wealth (Vittanātha).

Holding conchs and discs in their hands, clad in yellow garments and adorned with divine garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, they are blue, white, crimson, and tawny in hue; by their radiance, they bear the Śrīvatsa mark upon their chests and possess the Kaustubha gem.
Then Airāvata, Kumuda, the one named Vāmana, and the elephant Sārvabhauma—these white-bodied ones, possessing four tusks, stand upon the corner petals together with jars of nectar. (19-34)

Ṛddhi, Sarasvatī, Svasti, Prīti, Kṣamā, Rati, Siddhi, and Ruci are said to be the female messengers in the eight directions; they hold garlands, garments, perfumes, ornaments, and fans in their hands. (19.35)

Then, on the fifth [day], one should worship the lords of the worlds, headed by Śakra, along with their weapons, retinues, and vehicles, in the enclosure; one should first worship the limbs at the tips of the filaments.
At the eastern gate, one should worship the messenger named Valākinī; at the southern gate, the one called Vanamālikā;
at the western gate, the one named Bibhīṣikā; and likewise at the northern gate, one should worship Śāṅkarī. (19.37)
And there let those beautiful, short-statured women carry swords and cane staves;
adorned with their own ornaments, they possess complexions that are dark, white, deep red, and honey-yellow.

Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, adorned with divine garlands and ornaments, should be meditated upon in the four corners; all of them are male in form, each possessing qualities and attire suited to their respective purposes. (19.39)
Then one should invoke her— the splendor of the moon-like lotus of the heart, consisting of a mass of radiance— either into the heart or upon the external lotus:
"Oṃ, come, come, O Goddess Kamalā, Mother of the World, [consort] of the Lord of the World!"
"Right here, on this very chest, you [should remain] for the prosperity of me, your devotee. (19.40)
(48) Accept this performed worship, offered according to one's means, with this mantra as an encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) according to the ritual rule. (19–41)
By means of that *arghya* which fulfills both the root and the ancillary mantras, one should purify oneself, the place, and the ritual implements through sprinkling;
if it concerns the image, it should be purified with the *pluta* mantras by adorning it with flowers and bathing it. (19.42)
One should offer the *arghya* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the *pādya* and *ācamana* with the *astra-mantra*, and the *aṅga-mantras* and the root-mantra (*mūla*) for the recitation;
likewise, the bath, garments, ornaments, and the five beginning with fragrance should be offered with the *hṛdaya* and the root-mantra.

The food offering (naivedya) should consist of ghee and milk-rice with sugar, pure boiled rice mixed with ghee, along with sweet fruits, side-dishes prepared with ghee, and likewise sweet-flavored modakas. || 19-44 ||
Having offered fragrant, cool water for the rinsing of the hands and mouth-scented substances,

one should perform the fire-oblation according to the rules, having first offered the "mouth of the fire" (the introductory oblations) and likewise the root-mantras of the limbs with offerings of clarified butter.
Jātyutpala, tulasī, vāsantī, mallikā, and the plant known as kubjaka-sahā; nandyāvartaka, damanaka, maruvaka, mālūra, nāga, punnāga, and śīphā. (19–46)
Or else, by skillfully arranging wild flowers or those that are white and fragrant, one may abandon the *droṇa* for the sake of pleasing Lakṣmī; thus proceeds this noble song (*āryāgīti*). (19.47)
[These are the Āryā-gītis.

Having bowed with devotion to Viṣṇu—the unborn, undecaying, immortal, and unique—within the realm of Śrī, one should compose these Āryā-gītis as a wholesome form of worship for the attainment of the four aims of life. (19-48)
[The Pathyā Āryā Gīti: If this practitioner desires to attain prosperity in this world, let him constantly recite the mantra within his mind;
abandoning extensive attachment to sense objects through his intellect, he becomes a vessel for Kamalā. (19.49)

[The Vast Noble Song: One who wears white garments, uses flowers and incense, performs daily fire-offerings, and is devoted to mantra-recitation and sacrifice; who possesses wealth through righteous means and has a mind fixed on truth—such a person shall attain the state that brings about the attainment of all prosperity. (19.50)
[The Āryāgīti in the Vipulā and Acapalā meters]
Thus ends the section on *gaṇa*-metres.
(p. 49) This [method] also succeeds quickly for women through the practice of exceptional devotion.
It bestows victory upon kings; one should please the families of the *vaitālīya* [verse] by means of the destruction of enemies. (19.51) [This is] the *vaitālīya*.
Adorned with white garments, perfumes, and ornaments, and having performed the specific auspicious *puṇyāha* rite, he should,
after providing a meal for the Brahmins in his residence, draw a white lotus together with its pedestal.
Having placed the fire upon a lotus, or else in a square fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa),
and having invoked Śrī into her heart within the mouth of the primary fire, one should offer oblations with the ritual implements as before.
There, the distinguished twice-born ones should perform the recitation of the Śrīsūkta according to the *aupacchandasika* meter.
All of them, holding water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*), should likewise recite the four Vedas here. (19.54) [In the *aupacchandasika* meter:

Having worshipped the Fire-god and Lakṣmī with bilva fruits, lotuses, white flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, perfumes, incense, and lamps, one shall obtain everything in the *aupacchandasika* meter. (19.55) As before.
One who desires wealth should offer oblations of *bilva* fruits or white lotuses mixed with clarified butter;
this establishes even fleeting fortune within one's own family for a very long time. (19.56) [Regarding "āpātalikā":
An oblation made with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and *kubjaka* flowers brings about the abundant acquisition of garments.
Through oblations of excellent rice and clarified butter, the Goddesses of Fortune approach him; this is the eastern practice (*prācyavṛtti*).

From the offering of *palāśa* fuel-sticks, there arises extraordinary intelligence; from flowers produced from those same trees, and from an oblation of *dūrvā* grass with clarified butter, there comes long life; this is the northern practice (*udīcyavṛtti*).

Eating only sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for half a year while worshipping Śrī and reciting [the mantra] every day, he shall attain the status of a king; or, if not Śrī, he shall attain a woman of lovely smiles (*cāruhāsinī*). With white rice mixed with milk and drenched in ghee and honey, one shall likewise become possessed of food.

By offering oblations of *sarala* wood on the day of Bhaga, one attains in this world a fortune that has no rival. (19.60) [Aparāntikā] If one recites [the mantra] while meditating on one's own identity before an angry person, that person becomes peaceful here in this world.
Furthermore, by reciting the *mātrāsamaka* mantra before a king, one shall make him a friend. (19.61) [Mātrāsamaka]
Upon seeing [a person], one should mutter [the mantra]; indeed, it brings under control even that forest-dwelling herd of deer.

If one performs bathing, recitation, and so forth at dawn, and practices with the *bilva* fruit, it removes bad dreams. (19–62) It removes misfortune (*dausthya*), as well as ill-repute (*viśloka*) and the faults caused by misconduct and quarrels. (p. 50) *Vānavāsika*.

Even great suffering arising from enemies [is overcome] by a fire-oblation (homa) combined with white lotuses and clarified butter. (19.63) If one desires sovereignty equal to that of a king, or wishes to personally protect a kingdom here, then through ten hundred days of recitation and oblation, one obtains a kingdom and even manifold prosperity. (19.64) [This is] the Citrā [chapter].
One should offer as oblations thirty-six hundred *bilva* logs, fruits, and leaves;
or, with abundant resources, one may perform the *upacitrā* sacrifice and attain great, immeasurable prosperity at the three times of day (*traiṣavaṇa*).
Regarding the *upacitrā*: at those specific times, there should be an offering of ghee and rice accompanied by milk, together with a meal for the twice-born (*dvija*).

If one desires to attain the status of a king, one should perform the *upacitra* and *apacitra* rites at night. As before, having touched a jar filled according to the ritual rules, he should mutter the mantra and contemplate the Fortune (*lakṣmī*) residing within it. Having worshipped and been consecrated as a lord of the earth, he shall proceed to the ground in the *pādākulaka* meter. (The *pādākulaka* follows).

Having given wealth and cattle to the *hotṛ* priest, as well as ornaments, garments, vehicles, grain, and even desired gifts to the Brahmins, one who has performed those sacrifices achieves his desire before long—just as before.
O Daughter of the Ocean of Milk! Be gracious toward the king’s mother’s longing.
Consecrated by Śrīkumbha, may this illustrious one live for a hundred years.
Thus one should address the Goddess.

Now, when the sun has risen, having offered oblations to men and the ancestors, [the practitioner]—whose nine jewels are weighed by the water from the nine jars placed upon the lotuses drawn in the auspicious ninth house, and who is adorned with garments, perfumes, flowers, and ornaments—should proceed. (19-70) [This is in the Gītyāryā meter.]

If one performs this supreme ritual bathing even for a most excellent king or for an ordinary man who delights in the praise of the preceptor of the best of gods and is devoted to virtues, then indeed it brings victory upon that person, even if their resolve is wavering, in this world. (19.71)
[Some say it is *caladhṛti*.

Having cast into [the vessel] rice, *dūrvā* grass, *bilva*, lotus, water-lily, the "ten flowers," sesame, black gram, *kuśa* grass, the four milks, tree-bark, and unbroken grains; having adorned the *brahmakūrca* with nets of pearls and himself with white garments and the like; having invoked the Goddess Śrī into the jar; and having recited the root mantra ten thousand times or one thousand and eight times; and having performed a great worship of Viṣṇu, he praises the God and Goddess together: "Victory, victory to you, O you who have crushed the sons of Diti with your claws and beak! Victory, victory to you, O you who were born from the excellent churning of the ocean!"
Victory, victory to you who hold the chariot of the ocean-born [Agni]! Victory, victory to you who have made your abode in the lotus-eyed one! (19.72) [Chūlikā, p.
51] Bow here to the slayer of Madhu, the refuge of the helpless, the incomparable one of immeasurable qualities and countless virtues;
the virtuous perceive him within as the Self of the universe, the Controller, the True One, the light of their own soul. (19.73) [Saumyā]

I pay homage to the goddess Lakṣmī, whose abode is the lotus and who was born from the ocean of milk; O Blessed One, may your pair of feet, possessing the luster of the petals of a fresh lotus, abide here within my heart. (19.74) [As before. Having thus concluded the hymn of praise, one should give wealth to the preceptor according to one's means.
One's own desired sovereignty and so forth arises before long in incalculable measure.
Now, in a square house provided with beautiful fourfold gates and archways,
the ritual of oblation performed here, adorned with fruits, flowers, and other offerings, brings about all-encompassing peace.
One should recite the Svasti-sūkta and Śrī-sūkta while facing the four directions with [offerings] resembling white lotuses;
one should also offer oblations of bilva fruits mixed with ghee at midday and at midnight.
Having offered even a tenth part of that ghee to Hari, one should feed the Brahmins;
one should also perform the water libation every day for the duration of a month.
He becomes fortunate and glorious, having pacified all worldly calamities and afflictions;
by offering this flower or its fragrance, one shall bring [the recipient] under one's control. (19.79)
Then, when the wind has entered the *amṛta* [channel], one should drink the breath of the sleeping person while performing recitation (*japa*).

Furthermore, by fixing the seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*), which is reddish in hue, upon one's own forehead within the city of fire (*dahanapura*), one brings [the person] under control. (19.80)

Having collected Sahadevī from a pure region and having consecrated it many times with mantras, one should apply it to the head or the arm; thus one shall attain victory in battles, disputes, and forests. (19.81)
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, as well as on the eleventh of the dark fortnight, one who approaches a woman with recitation shall bring her under control;
likewise, one may subjugate even a king, a man, or any other person.
One should draw a lotus with Śākta perfumes, having eight petals first and sixteen petals in sequence;
outside of this is a petal of passion (rāga), and further outside than that is one with twenty-four petals.
[The Noble Distinctions: The Section on Gaṇa, Chandas, Mātrā, Chandas, and Vṛtta. Now, concerning the Anuṣṭubh.]

One should write [the name of] the one to be protected located in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and on its eight petals, the *sādhivahninetradaṇḍa* mantra, which is exactly the same as the last [mantra]. [The word] *samānī* [is used].
Then, one should write the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) upon its sixteen petals.

On the petals numbered according to passion (rāga), one should draw the noose and the goad in sequence as before. Then, one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā, along with the eight syllables of Kāma and Śakti, and the Māyā, Japa, Arṇa, Tāra, and Kā letters, outside of that in their proper order.
That [liṅga], encircled by a stalk of gold and copper,
should be made into a pill and wrapped with a lotus-fiber thread and gold, as before. Then,
having meditated upon her as being worshipped within a circle of lotuses, one should worship her with the intellect.

One who possesses authoritative understanding should carry this *jaya-cakra* together with Viṣṇu and Śrī; it bestows authority, fortune, and long life. Indeed, in this world, it is truly a canopy that provides protection, wealth, prosperity, land, sons, and so forth. (19.88–89) [This is] the *vitāna*.

For the sake of victory over all enemies, having invoked the goddess Śrī Kṛṣṇā into a fire-pit shaped like a bow, adorned with jewels, provided with a canopy, and situated in the corner of the [sacrificial] qualities (guṇakoṇa),
one should spread out outside the fire various weapons such as arrows and swords.

One should offer oblations with *akṣa* fuel-sticks sprinkled with ghee and *navarājī*, as before. Being enraged and standing facing the enemy, one should recite the mantra situated within the vessel marked with the name of the foe,
using the *hana* and *abhi* [syllables], along with the armor (*kavaca*), the weapon (*astra*), and the fire-maiden (*agniyuvati*), as before.
Having offered oblations of ground weapons and cooked *paramānna* rice, one shall conquer enemies like Indra, even within a month—how much more so within a year. As before.
Thus has been described this wish-fulfilling tree known as the *Śrīhṛdaya*.
He is the jewel that is the essence of the three worlds, granting the fulfillment of the desires of those who worship him.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled the Śrīhṛdaya, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 19.

Now begins the twentieth chapter. I shall first describe the *vitāna* [canopy], which is the means for attaining the perfection of the Śrī-bīja; it bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and releases one from the expanse of sins. The *vitāna*.
Standing in water, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times using a rosary of lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*).
Likewise, one who is consecrated with water will become wealthy within three months. As before:
he who, having worshipped Śrī, should recite three million times at the beginning of the day.
And even in the *bilva* tree, which is the abode of Viṣṇu, one finds the fortune of variegated patterns (20.3). Regarding *citrapadā*:
"Even for those who worship it without prior ritual preparation (*puraścaryā*), this [tree] constantly brings forth wealth, grain, and other such things;
therefore, it is called the 'mouth' (*vaktra*) of the mantra that is the seed of Fortune (20.4). Regarding *vaktra*.
Its meter is Śrī, and the sage is Maṅkaṇa by name;

its deity is Lakṣmī, and it is perfected through recitation, meditation, and worship. This too is a [six-syllable] face, and its five limbs at the end are joined with their own respective seed-syllables.
O Mahāśrī, O Mahāvidyutprabhā! Ṭhaṭha! O Goddess Śrī, I sacrifice to you, svāhā! O Gaurī, O Mahābalā, bind! bind! Ṭhaṭha! Dhṛti, svāhā! Huṃ, O Mahākāya, O Padmahasta, huṃ phaṭ!
Others here say otherwise: "Śriye ṭhaṭha! Śrīṃ phaṭ! Śrīṃ namaḥ! Be gracious to Śrī, namaḥ! Śrīḥ phaṭ!"
One should resort to one of these two paths. This too is a *vaktra*.

Having received initiation from a guru and obtained the mantra, for the sake of the glorious practice (*sādhana*), one who has performed the daily rites and is restrained in his own path, beginning with the *pathyāvaktra*—this is the *pathyāvaktra*.

Wearing white garlands, garments, and so forth, dwelling in a beautiful and auspicious place, one should face either the east or the north; however, that which is the opposite should be avoided. [This refers to] facing away from the path or the mouth. One should meditate upon a fresh pavilion made of gold or sapphire situated within the heart.

The golden rampart, however, is adorned on all sides with the beauty of the faces of the *capalā* goddesses. (20.9) Regarding the *capalāvaktra*: the female messengers (*dūtī*) previously mentioned—those with lotus-like eyes and broad faces—and those with the faces of cranes (*valākinī*) at the gates, one should worship them in due order. (20.10) This refers to the *vipulāvaktra*.

(54) With rows of lamps, water-pots, and likewise the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala), that mandala was adorned with vast splendor from garlands and wreaths, and was exceedingly beautiful. (20-11) [This verse is in the Bhakāravipulā meter.
In its center was a lion-throne, radiant with gold and jewels.
A white lotus, rich with filaments and possessing a vast pericarp; [this is] the *ravipulā*.

One should worship Vāsudeva and the others situated upon the petals of that lotus in the cardinal directions, bearing their prescribed colors and weapons, with eyes as broad as lotuses; [this is] the *navipulā*.
Then, one should worship white elephants with large bodies and endowed with four tusks, stationed at the corners of the covering as before, beginning with guggulu incense. (20.14)
Those Guggulu, Guṇaṇḍa, Damaka, and Śalaya,
with golden palace-domes raised like lotuses upon their heads,
sprinkle me— who am filled with vast bliss— with waters of nectar. (20.15) [The meter is Vipulā.]
Then, as before, one should meditate with the mind upon this Śrī, the mother of the worlds, possessing the fullness of form and splendor, located within the pericarp; as previously described,
she holds two white lotuses aloft with her four arms.
Rich in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with her left [hands] and others expanded, she is equal in splendor [to the previous]. (20.17) This one also is Vipulā.
She has the luster of the interior of a fresh lotus, a face resembling a golden lotus, white perfumes and garments, is adorned with garlands, and possesses vast splendor. (20.18) [She is] Vipulā.
She is golden-hued, possessing a pair of lofty, beautiful, and excellent breasts,
with a face as tender as the full orb of the autumnal moon and a lotus.
Her lotus feet are worshipped by the people of all the worlds; she possesses a waist as slender as a *kara* (hand) and eyes like blooming blue and white lotuses. This is the *padacaturūrdhvā* meter.
If one remembers her, whose mass of hair is beautifully bound with a cluster of bees, within one's own heart, one becomes free from all suffering. (20-20) This is the *āpīḍa* [garland].
Now, the pair of treasures of Lakṣmī. (p. 55)

May he fully contemplate his own body as being filled with an abundance of great wealth— the lotus-feet known as Anujalabhava, which incessantly shower down rain from clouds that are light with pride. (20-21) As before.
If one meditates even once,
whatever wealth is obtainable here will come to pass;
and such a person constantly performs sacrifice, remaining devoted to the rites of recitation and oblation.
It seems to reject the Lord of Wealth himself while causing him to acquire riches. [This is] the *pratyāpīḍa* ornament.
For one who is naked indeed attains prosperity; let him not even enter the water for sleep.

Then, with his body moistened by oil and his frame covered in filth, he does not move at all, sleeping upon the ground which is impure and strewn with excrement; this is indeed the *pratyāpīḍa* posture.
[He performs] the direct consumption of sesame oil, salt, and [other substances].

One should also avoid Vaikuṇṭha. One should not touch with the head or the foot even a lotus, a bilva fruit, or the seed of the lotus-born [Brahmā]. One should not eat the flower-stalk nor break a cluster of blossoms.
[* Mañjarī:
One should not cut even a blade of grass, nor should one vainly scratch the earth,
nor should one apply ointment to the face at night.]
On the fifth, the seventh, and on the day of the Lord (the eleventh), one should avoid salt, *āmalaka*, sour things, and *lavalī*. [Regarding] *lavalī*:
having bathed, wearing unsoiled, pure, white garments, flowers, and perfumes, he should remain.
In the morning, his head crowned with *lakṣmī* flowers,
he should be a consumer [of food] while favoring all people with heart-touching words, as if with streams of nectar out of affection. (20.26) — *Amṛtadhārā*.

On the day of the Lord (Sunday), during the lunar mansion of the Serpent (Āśleṣā) and on Fridays, one should partake of sweet food; furthermore, one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) together with *bilva* fruits.
On the new-moon day, one obtains prosperity born of a noble lineage.
With rice-porridge mixed with ghee, with ghee, with white lotuses, and with milk-rice, [one attains this].
By offering oblations of *bailva* leaves and fruits perfumed with incense, he shall soon attain prosperity. [Regarding] *saurabhaka*:
he should then perform ablutions and recite mantras.
May he worship Śrī with hymns, and may he perform the ritual of oblation word by word; he shall soon attain the beautiful and resplendent prosperity of Lalitā. (20.29) —Lalitā.
He who daily offers oblations at sunrise with *nandyāvartaka*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *kubjaka* flowers,
and recites [the mantra] one thousand times;
He shall be happy with abundant wealth and cattle. (20–30) This is the *upasthitapracupita* meter;
it has four *hasta* units.
For the battle-cry: *namo pha vā śrīśe namaḥ*.
The rites beginning with the *ṛṣis* mentioned previously should be performed here in the same manner;
moreover, one should increase the offerings day by day.
He who here recites [the mantra] three million times while his throat is moistened with water—
He obtains abundant wealth here from Prajāpati. [This is] the *Vardhamāna* [diagram].
The rule for the lines of *Śrī*:
the heart (*hr*), Brahmā (*br*), then poison (*vi*), earth (*ma*), and water (*la*), each with a long vowel.

The ten-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā*, which begins with the letter *bhṛgu* (3) followed by *naya* (1), and concludes with other [letters], generates prosperity in this world for one who recites it with purity; it is the *śuddhavirāṭ*. (20.32) *Śuddhavirāṭ*.
The seer of this [hymn] is said to be Dakṣa, and she is called Virāj, indeed Upacitrā;
she is Kamalā, who dwells within the heart of the lotus.
Having worshipped the deity consisting of one hundred thousand syllables (Akṣaralakṣa), [one performs] the Upacitraka rite.
Homage to the Goddess; homage to Padminī; homage to the Consort of Viṣṇu; homage to the Bestower of Boons; homage to her whose form is the lotus.
The fivefold mantra-syllables of the limbs are to be recited in their proper order according to the procedure as previously prescribed.
The man who constantly worships this [goddess] Śrī will quickly obtain prosperity that is neither slow nor moderate. (20.34) [Regarding] *drutamadhyā*:
He shall become most wealthy in this world by offering *bilva* fruits or even lotuses by the tens of thousands.
Then, for sixty days, or twice that number, he should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire and perform recitation (*japa*) as before. (20.35) [As before.]

He who daily worships Kamalā, intent on meditation through sacrifice and burnt offerings, and who is constant in maintaining his risen vows, abandons the suffering of poverty along with Vegavatī. (20.36) [With] Vegavatī.
With white flowers as they are obtained—such as nandyāvarta, white water-lilies, lotuses, and so forth—
If one should offer oblations daily, numbering a thousand times, he shall become like Bhadravirāṭ, a lord of wealth. (20.37) Bhadravirāṭ:

One should offer oblations for three months with *gulā*, cow’s milk, white lotuses, and bilva fruits mixed with milk-rice and ghee; thus one shall conquer even an army with banners and likewise the earth. (20.38) Ketumatī.
The Chapter on Kamalāvāsinī. Herein, indeed, are proclaimed the mantras of Śrī as set forth in various tantras;
for those who worship her, they surely bring about the arising of fruits equal to their actions, just like the leap of a deer. (20-39) [The meter is] Hariṇapluta.

Whoever accomplishes even one of these [practices] taught by the goddesses dwelling in the lotus, Lakṣmī causes his lineage to flourish, like a flowering *kalpalatā* that has entered his home. (20-40) [The meter is] Puṣpitāgrā.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, concerning the Four Elephants and other [rites], in the *Tantrasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. (20)
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Victorious is the Sovereign Power of Śiva, the Mother of all speech and of all worlds;
for even by words born from the *aparavaktra* meter, that supreme state which is beyond cannot be praised. (21.1) [The meter] *aparavaktra*.
In the very first chapter, the primordial seed-syllable of Śakti was declared here as the universal form;
like a flowering creeper of the celestial tree, its expansion indeed bears fruit in the form of all desires. (21.2)
They say that even the Seer (Ṛṣi) is the Lord, and there may also be the metre known as Gāyatrī;
for Śakti herself is indeed the deity, and her seed-syllable (bīja) should be joined with the Bindu and Nāda. (21.3)
