The sky here is joined with the long vowels, and the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) should be joined with the six notes (ṣaḍja etc.).
The eye-mantra should likewise be placed before the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), which is "phaṭ"; one should perform the binding in the directions with this.
For she is the sovereign of the world, whose limits are submerged; she is this power that deludes the three worlds.
Even when residing in the heart-lotus, she is devoid of sound (nāda), yet possesses the luster of a ruddy sun and is endowed with a line (lekhā) within the heart.
Thus, the seed-mantra of Śakti is said to be threefold: in certain forms of worship it is joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*;
in the rules for fire-offerings (*havana*) it ends with *analapriyā* (svāhā); and in the matter of recitation (*japa*), indeed, it is the seed-mantra alone.
Having long served the supreme teacher and performed what was pleasing to him, he was initiated;
then, on a day chosen by himself during the bright fortnight, in a temple of Śiva containing a single, most beautiful liṅga.
Having worshipped his own chosen preceptor, who has the face of an elephant, he should wear white ashes as a covering and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
observing the vow with restricted food, remaining silent, dressed in pure garments, and facing the auspicious south, he should remain pure.

Having duly worshipped Śiva along with Śivā and their retinue with great offerings, and having also presented the sacrificial oblation (caru) prepared with milk and mixed with ghee and jaggery, he offered it as a libation into the fire for Agni. || 21.9 ||
One should recite one hundred thousand [mantras] of the Sun during the period beginning from the eighth day of the waxing moon and ending on the fourteenth day of the following month;
this is recommended as being neither too fast nor too slow. By means of those days of reality, the mantra becomes perfected.
The Section on Puraścaraṇa:

Now I shall clearly explain the worship of Śakti for the sake of attaining success through various specific rites; having bathed one's body with the limbs and root mantras, and having completed the procedure for one’s own intended goal, one should remain silent. (21.11)

Having entered the sacrificial hall with washed feet, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and with a sacred blade of grass (pavitra) in his hand, he should worship the Goddess before him with flowers, water for honor (arghya), and water from a vessel held in his hand. || 21.12 ||

At the right and left doors stand Jayā and Vijayā, with complexions like red and yellow; as follows: they hold canes in their hands, are adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments, and are endowed with beautiful forms. (21.13)
Similarly, above are the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, white and dark, bearing lotuses;
and in the middle is the splendor of the gateway, golden-hued, with a lotus pond and a pair of elephants.
Having first worshipped these [deities] and consecrated iron arrows (*nārāca*) with mantras,
he should expel the hosts of obstacles, enter within, and worship the Lord of the Site (*vāstvīśa*).

Having worshipped his own seat and immediately sat down, with his self purified by the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), he should then purify the pair of hands. From the *astra-mantra*, he should utter the *aṅga-mantras* upon the fingers of both hands.
He should then place that *astra-mantra*, joined with the *praṇava*, sequentially upon the two palms, ending at the little fingers.

One should place the root mantra upon the head, the two eyes, the mouth, the pair of ears, the heart, the navel and the waist, the genitals, the thighs and the shanks, and also upon the pair of feet. (21.17)
One should install [the mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*: for Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, Karālikā, and Mahocchuṣmā.
These five forms are indeed to be placed on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the feet. || 21-18 ||
One should assign Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra to the throat,
the two breasts, the two shoulders, and the heart;
then these six forms (mūrtis) are assigned again as previously stated to the left and right limbs.

One should assign the Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, to these locations by their respective names: the left shoulder, the left side, the abdomen, the right side, the shoulder, the back, and the heart. (21.20)
Thereafter, having placed the six limbs, beginning with the heart, separately upon the body in their respective locations,
one should then project outside the armor of weapons, resembling blazing fire, from the tips of the threatening fingers.
Up to this point, in this chapter, there are verses in the *puṣpitāgrā* meter and occasionally in the *āryā* meter. (p.
60) [The substances are] perfumes, flowers, and mustard seeds with the tips of *kuśa* grass.

Likewise, one should fill [the vessel] with unbroken grains, *dūrvā* grass, and fragrant water; one should respectfully offer the *arghya* for the Śakti, provided with barley, and worship her by name. As it is said: "It contains barley. (21–22) *Yavamatī*.
One should sprinkle the entire head [of the image] with the *kūrcaka* brush, as well as the materials upon which it rests, such as sandalwood and other substances.
One should then visualize that very place as a jewel-pavilion at the corners of the Vedas, and therein, a jeweled lion-throne.
One should likewise worship its Śakti below as Aruṇā; and similarly, the legs of the pedestal, preceded by Dharma.
In the center of that [pedestal], there is a red lotus with four petals at its base and eight petals [in total].
Its sixteen vowels shall be the filaments; together with the three circles, there shall be a broad pericarp (*karṇikā*).
There are eight powers (*śakti*) upon the filaments, beginning with Jayā, while Sumaṅgalā resides in the pericarp.

To Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, Vilāsinī, Śauṇḍī, Aghorā, and Sumaṅgalā. In all worship, it is the same to begin with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and end with *namaḥ*. One should worship those located on the corners and petals with the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra) and others; the *netra* (eye-mantra) is in front, and the *astra* (weapon-mantra) is on the cardinal petals.
One should worship outside, in order, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, the well-attired female messengers beginning with Anaṅgarūpikā.

One should worship [the goddesses] beginning with Praṇava and ending with Namaḥ upon the pedestal outside the lotus: Anaṅgarūpā, Anaṅgamadanā, Madanāturā, Pavanavegā, Bhuvanapālā, Sarvaśiśirā, Anaṅgadamanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā.
They bear a golden pitcher, a mirror, betel, an umbrella, a fan, and a parrot;
they hold chowries and flower-caskets, possessing beautiful forms and reddish limbs. (21–27)
Then, having meditated upon the Blessed Śakti, whose form and other attributes are to be described hereafter, one should invoke and worship her:
"O Goddess, whose pair of feet—with the jewels of their toenails—conquers the moon with the luster of the petals of a young, reddish lotus;
whose pair of feet rests above [all things], and whose form is truly incomparable throughout the entire universe—it is indeed impossible to describe. (21–28)
Her hips are worthy of praise, as is her slender waist, and likewise her pair of jar-like breasts and her two arms;
so too her neck, her lotus-face, her pair of eyes that have conquered the blue water-lily, and the crest of her broad tresses. (21.29)
The *śikhā* is the crest-lock.
[It is] the young women of the gods, demons, humans, and the best of serpents, whose dwellings and abodes are in all the worlds;
young women whose faces, eyes, and feet are like lotuses and who shine with the brilliance of the entire pure moon. (21–30)

She who creates [the world] as the sky, wind, fire, water, earth, the sun, moon, and stars—truly, even the Creator is not at all capable of enumerating the multitude of virtues in her exceedingly beautiful form. (21-31)
[Ṣaḍja | Chapter on Meters with Uneven Matras | Now, among the meters, regarding that which has been stated— ]
*Hrīgīryā* is *Śrī*. (21.32) The meter named *Śrī*.
Now, regarding *Atyuktā*: "I bow to the goddess Gaurī, the Śakti. (21.33) The meter named *Devī*.
In the middle [channel]:
"That which is subtle, consciousness, eternal, and to be meditated upon—that is Nārī. (21.34) "Nārī" is the name of the meter.
In the *Pratiṣṭhā* [chapter], it is said:
"She became a maiden (*kanyā*) in order to create and protect the entire world that was to be favored. *Kanyā* is the name of a meter.
In the state of *supratiṣṭhā*,

one should meditate upon her who, as the Sovereign of the Universe (*viśveśī*), assumes whatever form she desires— she who transcends all form yet is richly endowed with form. (21–36) This is the meter named *rūpāḍhyā*.
Now, regarding the Gāyatrī:

[one should meditate upon] the Goddess, whose form consists of splendor, whose limbs resemble the Bandhūka flower, who possesses a divine appearance and attire, and who has a slender waist. (21.37) She has a slender waist.
Clad in red garments and red perfumes, her crown radiant with jewels, she possesses a digit of the crescent moon and is enriched with divine ornaments.
Holding a noose and a goad in her hands, she is enriched with the gestures of protection and boon;
sixteen years of age, she is an ocean of the essence of beauty.
One should meditate upon Śakti as the sole mother of the universe, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, whose essence is the seed-syllable (bīja), as previously described. (21.40) [p.
62] In the Uṣṇih meter—

Having visualized that blessed Citi, whose limbs are as graceful as a youth's, within the moon of the sky-lotus, moist with the supreme nectar; [and] having visualized her while a profusion of flowers rests in one's own hand—this is the Kumāralalitā. (21.41) Kumāralalitā.
Having joined [the breath] from the sky-lotus, one should mentally recite the mantra while focusing on the power (śakti).
The practitioner of the heart-mantra should cause that Goddess, whose form is as described, to be firmly established upon this lotus-seat. (21.43)
Then, having performed the invocation (āvāhana), one should perform the rites of installation (sthāpana), presence (sānnidhya), confinement (rodhana), and the rite called veiling (avakuṇṭha);
likewise, one should perform everything up to the rite of illumination (prarocana) in due order with the limbs of the mantra accompanied by the root mantra.
Then, from the heart-mantra, the water for the guest-offering (arghya), as well as the water for the feet (pādya) and the weapon-mantra (astra),
should be offered; likewise, from the root-mantra, the bathing should be performed with the [six] limbs.
One should offer excellent garments, ornaments, fragrant garlands, fine incense, and lamps from one's own resources. (21.46)
And likewise, the sacrificial oblation (caru) prepared according to the rules, as well as excellent rice-milk (paramānna),
along with fruits and side dishes, together with water, molasses, and clarified butter.
Having offered [the oblation] together with its roots as well as well-sung water,
one should indeed offer fragrant mouth-perfume with the heart-mantra.
One should worship the previously mentioned retinue according to their respective modes of birth,
either with incense, flowers, and so forth, or mentally, as before. [This is stated] in the Anuṣṭubh meter.

One should worship those who have the bodies of children and elephant faces, playing like boys, located at the outer corners of the pedestal in the directions beginning with the northeast (Īśa). They hold nooses and goads in their hands and wear saffron-colored garlands and garments. This is the "playing of boys" (māṇavakakrīḍitaka).
[He saw] those who grant many boons, possessing their own ornaments and resembling gold, [yielding] the fruit of sovereignty.
One should worship those [deities] beginning with their own seed-syllable and *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with "namas": to Gaṇādhipa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Gaṇanātha, and Gaṇeśvara.

(p. 63) One should worship the world-protectors, headed by Indra, who are equipped with weapons and accompanied by their attendants, within the outer enclosure along the pathways, in their respective directions. (21.52)

Then, for the purpose of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), having reached the eastern direction (*indradiś*) within the fire-sanctuary, one should worship Śivā there in the excellent sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a vulva (*yoninibha*), facing the fire according to the direction of the mantra. (21.53)
In the daily rite, one should offer oblations with clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, milk, and sesame seeds;
and for rites performed for specific desires, the oblation should be made according to the other prescribed methods as before.
Having offered the tenth part of the limbs [of the mantra] from the root mantra, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) with the remainder of the clarified butter.
Then, one should scatter the remainder of the food as an offering on the ground with the words, "To his attendants," using their names.
Then, having washed his hands and sipped water, he should daily recite the root mantra three thousand or one thousand times.
A rosary made of gold or of crystal is most excellent;
if it is made of pearls, he attains manifold success (*citrapadā*). (21.56) [The term *citrapadā* means "of variegated steps" or "multifarious"].
Then, having prostrated and taken water in his cupped palms, he should offer the recitation, worship, and so forth, at the feet of the Goddess with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter:
"Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Goddess, may success be mine through your grace, for you abide within me. (21.57)
O Goddess! May whatever has been worshipped by me—though devoid of devotion, devoid of ritual action, and devoid of faith—all become complete through your grace. (21.58)

Salutation to the Śakti, the sovereign of all principles. Having joined her— whether she resides in the fire within the *bimba*, or within the *bimba* in the lotus of space, or moist with nectar— within the heart-lotus, one attains success.
If one is unable to perform external worship, one should worship with the mind alone within the lotus of the heart.
This concludes the section on the worship of the General Power (Sāmānya-Śakti).
One should worship Hṛllekhā, who has the luster of the Bandhūka flower and the shimmering brilliance of a garland of lightning.
I bow to Candrāpīḍā, who has a divine form, is adorned with red ornaments, and possesses three eyes.

(21.60) In the Kalpodyāna garden of beautiful shade, one should meditate upon that goddess Hṛllekhā, seated upon a lotus on her throne as before, possessing a divine form and appearing sixteen years of age. (21.61)

(64) One should worship the eight Śaktis located on the tips of the filaments within the limbs [of the lotus], and those situated on the tips of the petals. One should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnādhīśa), who is red, in the south, and the Lords of the Worlds (Lokādhīśas) stationed in their respective directions. Having thus worshipped her, who resides in the heart-lotus and possesses such a form, with the substances of the Buddha through meditation.
Through the practice of the mantra four hundred thousand times, the mantra known as Hṛllekhā shall be accomplished.
Moreover:

In the midst of the ocean, on the sovereign Golden Mountain, in the pleasure grove strewn with jewels, I salute the heart-pleasing Goddess—red-clad, three-eyed, and adorned with the moon as her crest-ornament. (21.64)
Having worshipped one's own limbs upon a golden pedestal and a red lotus at the tip of its filaments,
one should worship the twenty-eight Śaktis— beginning with Hṛllekhā— within the petals and situated at the tips of the petals.

One should worship Karālī, Vikarālī, Umādevī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Śacī, Māyā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā. On the tips of the petals, one should worship two Śaktis at a time, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ. Outside the path (vīthī), in their respective directions, the eight Brahmāṇīs and others should be worshipped;
outside of them, the Lords of the Worlds (Lokapālas) and finally the Weapons (astras) should be worshipped by those desiring prosperity.
The Chapter on the Worship of Hṛllekhā:

If one should desire enjoyment and sovereignty, the lords of the worlds, possessing divine forms, [reside] within seven enclosures upon the lotus-throne in the garden of the Kalpa-tree in the ocean of milk. (21.67)
The eight Śaktis beginning with Antarhṛllekhā, together with the Aṅgas, are situated on the tips of the petals;
then the eight Mātṛs, the thirty-two Śaktis, as well as the Lokapālas and the Īśas.

"One should worship"—this is the connection [of the verse]. What are those *śaktis*, and how? [They are]: for Vidyā, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rudravīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣaṇī, Ṛddhidā, Śubhadā, Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Sendukhaṇḍā, Śikhaṇḍinī, Nisumbhamathanā, Mahiṣāsuramardinī, Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī, Śaṅkarārdhaśarīriṇī, Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Śūlinī, Pālinī, Ambikā, and Hrādinī. These are to be worshipped with their names beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, while their forms and other attributes correspond to their respective names.

(65) This Pārvatī, sovereign of the worlds, red in her attire, with the luster of vermilion, wearing a radiant crown adorned with the moon, three-eyed, and richly adorned with braided hair, is to be meditated upon. (21.68)
She who bears upon her breast various gems, golden *niṣkas*, pearl necklaces, armlets, and the like,
as well as a preeminent girdle and anklets.
One messenger holds a white parasol, while others hold white yak-tail whisks;
still others, standing by the side of the Goddess, bear water-pitchers, mirrors, and other such items. (21.70)
Having thus meditated with devotion upon Pārvatī, the sovereign of the world in this form,
and having worshipped her with the seven enclosures as prescribed, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
The Chapter on the Worship of the Lord of the World. Now, the ritual procedure for those known as Bhuvanādhipati, Śakti, and Hṛdaya is written;
it consists of eleven enclosures, is common [to all], and bestows all accomplishments upon men. (21–72)

The first enclosure consists of Jayā and the others; the second, Hṛllekhā and the others; the third, the six forms (Mūrtis); the fourth, Ananga-rūpa and the others; and the sixth enclosure is formed by the Vighnas and the Mothers.
The other [enclosure] consists of sixteen powers, and likewise the [next] enclosure consists of thirty-two powers;
the ninth, however, begins with Piṅgalā and so forth, while the tenth consists of the lords of the worlds and the weapons.
The deities of the ten enclosures (daśāvaraṇa) previously mentioned are indeed present here; however, the sixty-four Śaktis beginning with Piṅgalākṣī are now written down:
Piṅgalākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Samṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Buddhi, Svāhā, Svadhā, Māyā, Abhikhyā, and Vasundharā. (21.75)
The sustainer of the three worlds, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, the sovereign of the thirty gods, she of beautiful form, she of many forms, the mother of Skanda, and the beloved of Śiva. (21.76)
Amalā, the one called Vimalā, another named Aruṇī, and also Aruṇā;
Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Sṛṣṭi, Sthiti, Saṃkhyā, and Saṃhṛti. || 21-77 ||
Jaganmātā, Satī, Haṃsinī, she who is called Mardikā,
Vajrikā, Devamātā, and the Blessed One Devakī.
She is seated in the lotus posture and has three faces; thereafter, she is remembered as having seven faces.
She is the crusher of gods and asuras, with hanging lips and long hair. (21.79)
Then there are Ūrdhvakeśī, Bahuliṅgā, the well-known Bahūdarī, Ratharekhā, Śaśirekhā, and likewise Gaganavegikā. (21.80)
Vāyuvegānaṅgarūpā, Anaṅgamadanā by name, likewise Bhuvanapālī, and then Anaṅgamekhalā. (21.81)
She who was known as Madanāturasañjñā shall thereafter be called Anaṅgakusumā; she shall become Viśvarūpā and likewise a source of terror to the Asuras.
Surarakṣiṇikā, Akṣobhyā, Satyavādā, Śucivratā, Vajravegā, Varadā, and Vāgīśī are the śaktis. || 21.83 ||
All these sixty-four [goddesses] wear garments and garlands of every variety;
their forms correspond to their own names, and they are beautiful in appearance and adorned.
Having meditated [on the mantra] ending with *namaḥ*, one should worship Tārā and all the surrounding retinues beneath a red *kalpataru* tree in a garden on a peak of the Himavat mountains.
Having meditated upon her as seated comfortably upon a lotus-jewel lion-throne adorned with footstools, and possessing the aforementioned form and other qualities, one should worship her. (21.86)

Now, having understood the ritual for worship through the *Bṛhatī* verse, she should be worshipped every day, having made the intellect— which follows the path of a serpent’s young— firmly straight in its course. (21.87) [The term] "bhujagaśiśusṛtā" means "that which has followed the path of a serpent’s young."
In this manner, one should worship Śakti with a devout mind within the lotus of the heart,
and also constantly with auspicious materials appropriate to one’s means externally.
The Chapter on the Worship of the Eleven Enclosures.
Furthermore:
[One should worship] Ambikā, who possesses the luster of a fresh cloud, who is beautiful, and who is in the bloom of youth.
Adorned with gold and jewels, possessing three eyes and clad in crimson garments; (21.89) holding a plow-shaped [implement] and also a small bell fashioned from pieces of mother-of-pearl;
adorned with armlets, bracelets, and crowns, and likewise by serpents—as before. (21.90) p. 67) Halamukhī.
Alternatively,

one should meditate on her who is clothed in a tiger skin, who has the king of serpents as her sacred thread, who is both gentle and fierce, and who holds a skull-topped trident along with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (21.91)
One should worship her together with the seven messengers (dūtīs) who are endowed with chowries, water-pots, umbrellas, and other royal insignia, as well as the aforementioned ornaments.
In the first line, one should practice the recitation of the Śakti mantra, or that of Bhuvanādhipā, for sixteen hundred thousand times;
by offering oblations with red lotuses mixed with honey, that practitioner becomes a Śuddhavirāṭ. (21.93) [Śuddhavirāṭ].
The authority for performing sacrifices involving both cruel and gentle deities.
Now, the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) is described:
A wise man should draw a red lotus, or else a *bhadraka* or a *māyācakra*.
One should worship Śakti there according to the ritual rules, upon the pericarp which holds a good seed-syllable and a goad-noose.

In the northeastern direction, upon a five-petaled lotus, one should duly fill that many pitchers made of gold or other materials with the *hṛllekhā* mantra and the rest, along with the five forms (*pañcamūrti*).

One should join these with the five products of the cow; the fifty digits (kalās) are proclaimed by means of the *praṇava*. [One should also use] milk, trees, hides, water, and the five gems along with scented water.
Alternatively,
upon a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp, one should fill nine jars in sequence with clarified butter,
milk, curd, and sugarcane juice, followed by the milky sap, the bark-juice, and water from sacred bathing places.
One should also pour the medicinal juice of the ink-letters into the central jar.
One should invoke the Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, into the eight jars according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, having invoked Ambikā in the central [jar] along with the root-mantra and its limbs, one should worship her together with the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas). || 21-98 ||
Having placed two jars filled with a decoction of *palāśa* leaves separately at each of the four doors, one should worship the *jayā* and other *śaktis* within them for the sake of protection.

Alternatively, following the procedure taught in the *Śaiva* tradition, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) and so forth for the initiation; or else, one may perform the initiation through mantra by means of the limbs (*aṅga*) of the *śakti*, originating from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *śakti*. (21.99)

Having offered a thousand oblations with the three sweet substances, and having poured the clarified butter purified by the *saṃpāta* rite into those jars, one should initiate the disciple after he has been consecrated by them.

Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks of *aśvattha*, *khadira*, *jātī*, and *bilva*, along with all kinds of grains, sesame seeds, *caru* rice, and clarified butter, and having performed worship before the image, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) for it.

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for that disciple during the night, and having discerned the future outcome through auspicious dreams, the Guru should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) together with auspicious drums, musical instruments such as the *paṇava*, songs, and other such elements. Having thus received initiation from the mouth of the Guru, he becomes one who has obtained the mantra empowered by Śakti.
Through meditation, recitation, worship, and burnt offerings, a person shall accomplish their desired objects.
The Section on the Initiation of Śakti:
Having worshipped the Fire, one should then worship Śakti, together with her attendants and limbs, within the heart-lotus of that [Fire].
By offering hundreds of thousands of lotuses, bilva fruits, ghee, and cooked rice into it, one’s prosperity shall become like gold. (21.104) — "Like gold."

One should offer eight thousand or eight hundred oblations daily with the aforementioned specific substances; furthermore, one should consume the remains of the offering, clarified butter, and bilva fruit, which bestow prosperity.

The meditation regarding prosperity is described: One who worships her—who resembles gold, holds a noose, a lotus, a goad, and a conch, and is endowed with six faces—in the heart or in the fire, shall attain prosperity through hundreds of thousands of arrows. (21.106)
At the end of the "lotus-born" mantra, the seed-syllable of Śrī-Śakti is said to be followed by "namaḥ.
By reciting and offering oblations as before, one obtains abundance of wealth. (21.107)
For one who meditates upon her— who is unfathomable as the Kalpa-tree, seated on a golden throne, whose name is Umā, who is golden-hued,
and who holds the infant Skanda upon her lap— there shall be prosperity from a hundred thousand recitations.

First, one should recite the seed-syllables of the conch-treasure (śaṅkhanidhi), the noose (pāśa), the power (śakti), and the goad (aṅkuśa); at the end, the lotus-treasure (padmanidhi) and the consort of Agni—thus one should recite for the sake of prosperity.

Then, that [syllable] situated in a long vowel, with a bindu and joined with Śakti, on a mountain peak—through a hundred thousand recitations and other rites—one obtains a long life here, or it may be obtained through the abundance of one's own power. (21.110)

Situated within the cavity of a jar or contained in the water of a jar, [the mantra] equal to a thousand suns destroys untimely death through its recitation and fire-oblation; by sprinkling that water, it destroys all diseases through its power.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of a jar-and-casket (*kumbhasampuṭa*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*);
this *mayūrasāriṇī* [mantra] removes the fear of untimely death for people. (21.112) Regarding the *mayūrasāriṇī*:
on Sundays coinciding with the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*), one should gaze at the sun with arms raised upward.
If one recites [the mantra] for a year, a hundred thousand times daily, it destroys consumption, coughs, and leprosy.
A jar-sealed vessel of four thousand [recitations] of that ash destroys diseases through its recitation;
likewise, oil removes wind-diseases, clarified butter removes bile, and long pepper destroys phlegm. (21.114)
Pippalī removes splenic disorders, and likewise, pathyā cures all diseases of the abdomen;
whatever medicines the mantra-practitioner gives, by that he destroys the diseases. (21.115)
One should recite [the mantra] twenty-five times over milk and drink it; thereby one attains supreme intelligence.
Furthermore, any other food consumed while joined with this [mantra] shall lead to long life and prosperity. (21.116)

If one offers oblations of rice grains soaked in curd, one obtains nourishment; with parched grain soaked in honey, one obtains a daughter; with milk and ghee, one obtains cattle; and if one offers food mixed with clarified butter, one obtains food.

One may bring Brahmins under control by offering *pippala* fruits, kings by *paṅkaja* lotuses, their wives by *palāśa* flowers, and other commoners (*vaiśyas*) by *kairava* lilies; furthermore, by offering a hundred thousand oblations of oil and salt, one subjugates all others. (21.118)
In rites of enchantment (*saṃvanana*), one should offer everything anointed with honey; now I shall explain [the procedure] for summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).
For kings, the mantra should begin with the syllable *Oṃ*, while for others it should be a mantra beginning with *Bhūtikā* and so forth. (21.119)

Going to the root of a banyan tree at night, the mantra-practitioner should offer three hundred thousand oblations of *raktahayāri* wood fuel smeared with ghee; he shall then behold the boon-granting Yakṣiṇī.

By practicing the Śakti [mantra] one hundred lakhs of times with meditation, from a purified place, one obtains the eightfold sovereign powers; by ten koṭis, one becomes an immortal *khecarī*. (21.121)
The Chapter on Prosperity (Abhyudayādhikāra). (p.

70) Having written the *śakti* [syllable] in the center of a lotus with petals equal in number to the *rasa* [six], and having written the vowels (*svarān*) upon the petals and outside, this [diagram], when worn by women, will surely cause a son to be born. "Born" (*upasthitam*).
One should write the mantra within the six-spoked wheel, with its own name twice in the two gaps;
outside, one should draw the abode of the Earth (the square), which, when worn by both, produces affection.

Having written the form of the enemy in a *triṣṭubh* meter upon a skull-bowl, with the root mantra placed within a hexagon, one should perform the rite of scorching (*santāpana*) at night in a cremation ground while reciting it; then the enemy shall be as if struck by Indra’s thunderbolt. (21.124) [Indravajrā]

One should offer oblations for a fortnight using lines [of grain] mixed with human bone and salt, anointed with ghee, while reciting the root mantra joined with the name of the target and the word *kṛtya*;
thus the enemy meets death, utterly uprooted. (21.125)

One should offer into the fire at night the feathers of a crow mixed with the sap of *āja-snuhī* and dust, while reciting the mantra contained within the "wind-enclosure" (*mārutasampuṭa*); thus, one shall cause the enemy to be driven away within seven days. (21.126)

By offering oblations of *kākārikā* leaves sprinkled with goat’s blood and the juice of *snuk*, while reciting the root-mantra of Sthāṇu and others for seven nights, one swiftly effects the mutual hatred of enemies. (21.127)
One should perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana) within an enclosure of earth-seeds, and eradication (utsādana) situated within an enclosure of fire and wind;
likewise, one should employ the seed-syllable of Śakti, situated within an enclosure of water, for the rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi), both in fire-offerings and in recitation.

This wheel, held within the three worlds as a means of subjugation, has the *sākhya* seed-syllable situated between two circles; it is a lotus with petals and spokes endowed with external vowels, its corners rooted in the earth-seed-syllable (*bhū-bīja*), the noose (*pāśa*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*). || 21.129 ||
Within a six-cornered power-diagram (ṣaṭkoṇa-śakti), one should place one's own name on the outside; the noose (pāśa) and goad (aṅkuśa) should be interlaced with the power-mantra.
Having encircled this with the abode of Vāyu (the wind-circle) on the outside, the "elephant-petal" (nāgadala) situated at the mouth brings about subjugation (vaśya).

Now it is said: Having attained the accomplishment of the special sword, one who possesses powerful vigor and heroism shall conquer his enemies and wander through the worlds with a splendor equal to the weapon of Upendra (Viṣṇu). [Upendravajrā meter] In a pure, secluded place such as a forest, having bathed within its waters according to the rite...
Having fasted on the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, one should be adorned with yellow garlands, garments, and sandalwood paste.

Having drawn a lotus with five pigments and having placed a water-pot upon it according to rule— equipped with the five jewels, garments, garlands, and perfumes— one should then invoke Śivā, who is both fierce and gentle.

And one should worship Śivā, who is accompanied by the Rudra-enclosures, according to the method of the ritual for the root-mantra and its limbs; having offered caru with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, incense, and lamps, and having presented the bali-oblation here.

Having placed a sword that is cleansed, free from defects such as those caused by killing a human or the appearance of lines within the blade, and distinct from the species of swords belonging to the twice-born (*dvija*), and having worshipped the royal caste (*nṛpajāti*) in the image; then, having brought a young, brave man who has been slain by a weapon in an instant, dead and still with blood— (21.135) [Upajāti meter].
Having adorned him with red garments, garlands, and perfumes, he placed the sword into his hand.

Having touched [the corpse] and recited the root mantra as long as that conscious corpse, bearing a sword, desires to rise, one should joyfully and forcefully seize the sword from its hand while shouting. (21.137)

Then, having dismissed that excellent sword with the principal members of the retinue ending with Śiva, the lord of practitioners who wields it shall indeed become invincible in the world, even if he is merely a sovereign of the earth, provided he so desires. (21.138) [Upajāti meter]. By this very method, the accomplishment of the trident, the ring, the collyrium, and so forth, is also explained.
The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Khaḍga:

In order to make known all those objects—whether past, future, or present, and even those that are doubted—which cause the fluctuations of the mind through the *dodhaka* meter, I shall proclaim the means [for their realization]. (21.139) *Dodhaka* [meter].

Having fasted on a single day, one should perform a great worship with sixteen lotuses and *karavīra* flowers for the goddess Kṛṣṇā, the lunar day of the Mothers, at Ekaśiva, accompanied by the prescribed ritual services.
Having offered milk-rice enriched with ghee into the mouth of the fire, one also offers sesame and clarified butter;
eight thousand oblations each of wood-apple wood, flowers, cooked rice, and fruits are prescribed separately.
Having placed a single, exceedingly pure mirror before the Goddess here without any gaps,
one should worship her there and then recite the root mantra one thousand times while touching the mirror.
As long as one performs the ritual of the mirror, so long should one eat vegetables, alms-food, barley-gruel, or *kṛsara* rice. It succeeds.

Or, on the eighth lunar day or on a Sunday, having fed a maiden who has bathed and is properly adorned with milk-rice and clarified butter; on the previous day, for the purpose of the spectacle, one should have her look at the mirror and other such objects. (21.143) [She is] a *śālinī*.
Having placed her upon a bed of *darbha* grass in a pure location and consecrated her with the mantra,
one should, in the morning, engage her— who has bathed, been worshipped, and is well-seated— in the act of looking at her reflection in a mirror.

In a pleasant place smeared with cow dung, having fashioned a mandala with flour-meal, incense, and lamps, and having worshipped the Goddess reflected in a mirror with red flowers, the young maiden shall see everything there. (21.145)

There, having first seen the Goddess seated upon a lion-throne beneath the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), she then perceives her entire desired object as bound within the three times. By this very method, the application [of the ritual] regarding the thumb and other fingers is explained. This concludes the section on the worship of the mirror.
Alternatively, one should meditate on oneself as identical to the Goddess, who is mounted upon a lion, fierce, black, and holding a skull and a trident.

One shall have no fear in water, nor in the ocean garlanded with waves driven by swift winds, nor in the forest, nor in battle. (21.146) *Vātormiḥ*. Now, the mantra for destroying poison is said to end in *svāhā*, consisting of the syllables *śakti* (Hrīm), *sakṣam* (Kṣam), *salilam* (Jalam), *majjā* (Mam), *kham* (Ham), *vahnistham* (Rām), and *nayana* (Ūm), followed by the word *sarva*. Having omitted the first four syllables previously mentioned, this is the mantra that destroys poison. (21.147)

Having meditated upon oneself as identical [to the deity]—white in color, holding a water-pot and a trident, adorned with white ornaments, moon-crested, and three-eyed, and pouring nectar from the pot-born [deities]—the reciter of the mantra shall destroy poison. (21.148)

In whichever field the mantra-practitioner takes soil on Saturdays during the seven days, from that [soil] he shall obtain his own [mantra] within nine months; even on a Saturday coinciding with the Aśvinī nakṣatra at midday, [the same result follows]. (21.149)
On the new moon day, at the time of fifty-seven ghaṭikās, it is likewise.

When the sun is in the Hasta constellation, as long as the mantra-practitioner writes down the name of someone using bricks numbered according to the *dhṛti* [forty-eight], that person will feel affection for him and do what he desires; the practitioner shall bring everyone under his control through touch and other means. (21.150)
Having worshipped the Goddess Paṭagā on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in a beautiful place at midnight with one hundred thousand oblations of liquid,
the practitioner of mantra, by constantly offering various fragrant flowers at the feet of the Goddess, shall become a lord of wealth.
(73) Even from a hundred thousand *homas* with *karṇikāra* flowers, the fruit is as before.

Having worshipped her at night with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and presents, one should recite [the mantra] in front of her until dawn; within six months, he shall become a lord of wealth. (21.152)
By performing worship, recitation, and other rites constantly at midnight, one becomes possessed of wealth, grain, and sovereignty.
The seed-syllable of Śakti, strung together with the letters known as "Daṣṭa," when written on a wall or similar surface, destroys poison.
Having practiced this, one should either wipe away what has been written, or sprinkle water over it while reciting the mantra, or drink that water. (21.153)
Written on birch bark with the root-mantra and its limbs, that [mantra] should be placed within grain and other such substances to cause them to increase.
Having worshipped the Goddess and also the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) therein, one should wear the "ten flowers" obtained by means of it.
With the two hands facing each other and well-joined, with the index fingers released, this mudrā—formed by the union of the middle fingers and thumbs—is known as Kṣobhaṇī. || 21-155 ||

Extending both hands with the palms joined and the fingers interlaced, with the thumbs and index fingers [extended], and the little, ring, and middle fingers pressed together, it becomes the *mohanī* [mudrā]. (21.156)
In the same way, when the hands are joined and both index fingers are extended, it is known as the *drāvaṇī* [mudrā] due to the pressing together of the middle fingers and the thumbs. (21.157)
In the same way, by pressing the two index fingers together with the hands well-joined, one forms the Karṣiṇī mudrā; likewise, with the middle and index fingers, one forms the pair of Jyeṣṭhikās.

By pressing [the fingers] together and excluding the remaining fingers, she becomes a bringer of presence (*sānnidhyakarī*). Having bound the two ring fingers below the palms with the two index fingers, [she performs this mudrā]. (21.159)
With the palms facing upward, the two middle fingers together with the little fingers are joined at their sides, while the tips of those [other fingers] remain straight and extended. (21.160)
Having touched the bases of the two little fingers with the tips of the two thumbs,
this mudrā known as the Yoni belongs to Śakti and bestows all accomplishments.
The *mohanī*, *kṣobhaṇī*, and *drāvaṇī* [mudrās], as well as the *yonimudrā*, should be employed in sequence for the subjugation of all women and men, respectively. || 21.162 ||
The Chapter on Mudrās (p.

74): On the banks of excellent rivers such as the Gaṅgā, or on the peak of a preeminent mountain by the ocean, or in a garden resplendent with bees—through ten million repetitions [of practice], one becomes equal to a sage. (21.163) [This concludes] *Bhramaravilasita*.

He may become a sky-walker within the abode of the three worlds, or he goes easily to the netherworld; or else, by the power of a human [mantra], he dwells on the Golden Mountain, long-lived, exceedingly strong, and youthful. (21.164)
It is well-established here that practitioners [inquire] what can be accomplished through the Śakti-vidyā;

for whatever desired perfection (siddhi) one prays for in this world, however lofty it may be according to one's own heart’s desire—[all that is attained]. Thus [one worships] the sole Mother of all worlds, the Mistress of the entire path of universal reality.
For those men who have firmly taken refuge in Śakti, indeed, no spiritual accomplishments whatsoever are difficult to attain. (21.166)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Śaktipaṭala, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.

Victorious is she known as Tvaritā, who, together with Gaurī in the form of a Kirāta, arrived at the edge of the forest when Śaṅkara, the granter of boons, was gratified by the austerities of Vijaya. (22.1) [The meter is] Svāgatā.
Tāra, Sārdhenduka, Kavaca, Soṣṭha, Caṇḍa, Kacchapa, Harāntavān, Ekanetra, Sargī, and the one called Saṃvartaka. || 22-2 ||
Vāmākṣa (va), agni (ra), āṣāḍhī (ṣa), śukla (u), sārdhi (r), kha (a), daṇḍi (tha), and then oṣṭhaga (o);
Krodha (huṃ) and phaṭ—this ten-syllable mantra is Trotalā and also Tvaritā. (22–3)

The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Kirātarudra, the meter (chandas) is Paṅkti, and the deity (devatā) is Pārvatī in the guise of a Śabara woman; when meditated upon with one hundred thousand recitations, she bestows spiritual perfection (siddhi). || 22-4 ||
From *tāra* (oṃ), followed by *puramitaṃ* (hūṃ), and then the seed-syllable of *śakti* (hrīṃ) before the weapon (*astra*: phaṭ), so that it may be present on both sides;
this [mantra] of twelve syllables indeed bestows accomplishment very quickly, for it is the *Tvaritā*. || 22-5 ||
(75) From the armor (*varma*) onwards, there is also the supreme speech (*paramavāk*) and the weapons (*astras*), divided by seven vowels, six consonants, and two syllables;
likewise, there is the arrangement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), so that here the former may be joined with the latter syllables. (22–6)

In this regard, the instruction is as follows: the heart [mantra] is formed with the two *kūrma* [syllables] and *soṣṭha-caṇḍa*; the head with the *kūrma*-spoken *svara* and *ekane-tra*; the crest-lock (*śikhā*) with the aforementioned *ekane-tra* and *kopa*; the armor (*kavaca*) with the aforementioned *kopa* and *bhṛgu*; the three eyes with *bhṛgu* and the aforementioned *ākāśa*; and the weapon (*astra*) with the aforementioned *ākāśa* and *saṃvartaka*. All [these mantras] are to be joined with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).

Then, the initiated disciple, having been instructed in the mantra by the Guru and having bathed his limbs with the root-mantras along with their ancillaries (*aṅga*), should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his hands: the ancillaries ending with the thumb (*jyeṣṭhikā*) on both palms, and the weapon (*astra*) on the palms of both. (22.7)
Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-vinyāsa*) with the root mantra, one should form the *praṇītā* mudrā:
with the two hands joined face-to-face, the index fingers together with the thumbs are held separately; the middle fingers are positioned upwards and their tips are bent. (22.8)
When the ring fingers are placed in the middle and the little fingers are positioned above them,
bound together in the shape of a hood, it is the *praṇītā* mudrā.
Having been consecrated by himself with the thought of offering his own identity through the mudrā, let him touch his entire body;
then, having put on his garment here, let him touch his own body once more with the mudrā.
"May we know the Vidyā of Tvaritā; may we meditate upon the Vidyā of Trotalā; may that swift one inspire us.

Having satisfied the Goddess and her retinue with this Gāyatrī of Tvaritā by reciting their respective names, he should proceed to the sacrificial ground, remaining silent, with his hands and feet washed, and using auspicious water.
Having performed the ritual rinsing as directed, he established protection all around by arranging the weapons-mantras.
Having worshipped both the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) and the lord of the site (vāstupati), and having sat down upon his own seat, remaining silent,
he should contemplate the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the purification of thought (bhāvaviśuddhi) for the sake of the welfare of all beings.

Having performed the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment), formed the mudrās, and assigned the mantras to the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should place the letters of one's own mantra in their respective locations: on the head, forehead, throat, heart, navel, genitals, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet.

Then, one should meditate upon the Goddess as being non-different from oneself. After performing the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), one should subsequently perform the external worship and meditation:
[She is] dark-complexioned, with hair as curly as bees, wearing a golden crown adorned with a garland of humming [bees].
Her face was like the autumn moon; she had three eyes, high and full breasts, and a slender waist.
Her hand was beautiful with its sprout-like forearm, lovely and delicate, and its fingers like a garland;
she possessed the pair of lotus-feet that were the descendants of the Sun, and her form was exquisite, a perfect convergence of all splendors.
She bore earrings, armlets, waist-bands, and anklets fashioned by brahmins, kings, merchants, outcasts, and serpents;
she was adorned with exquisite garlands of forest flowers and wore a garment of tender sprouts. || 22.15 ||
Visualizing her with a circle of peacock feathers, accompanied by a peacock-umbrella, a pair of chowries, and a banner,
and surrounded by a retinue of Śabarī women— even during the external rite of worship— one should contemplate her as one's own identity.

Whoever remembers Gaurī, whose form has been described even once, and worships her, shall obtain here whatever he desires, like a choice fruit fallen from its stalk. Now, on the slopes of the Himālaya mountains, one should contemplate a most beautiful and vast garden.
Even its ground consists of jewels, and within it is a beautiful throne held by the Vasus and the Haris.
One should meditate upon his Śakti, the Sustainer (Dhāriṇī), in the center, possessing the luster of molten coral.
From that [center] arises a lotus adorned with a network of petals, resembling the emergence of a *śyenikā*. Regarding the *śyenikā*:
it is characterized by the circles of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and by those presiding deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—in their respective order.
One should worship [the deity] here with its own name, preceded by "Namaḥ," using petals, filaments, and the pericarp. || 22.20 ||
Now, in the Jagatī meter:

Then, one should meditate upon the sky as a lotus of the heavens, a moon-lotus from which flows the nectar of the digits situated upon the stalks of its petals; and one should remember the earth, possessing the splendor of the sun together with the shimmering stars, joined with a handful of flowers representing the Śaktis. (22.21) [The meter used is] Vaṃśastha.
Muttering the root-mantra together with its limbs mentally, one should gradually meditate upon Tvaritā in the form described above;
having thus invoked her into the previously worshipped lotus before him, one should stabilize her with the heart-mantra and cause her to be present. || 22-22 ||

Having restrained [the breath] with the head-mantra (*śiras*), having planted [the seed-syllable] with the root-mantra (*mūla*), having rendered it immortal with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and having veiled it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, and *ācamana* waters;
then one should worship its six limbs, which are red in color, in sequence upon the petals beginning with that of Indra (East), according to their forms as female deities.
On the two petals of Dhaneśvara (North) and Īśāna (Northeast), these [limbs] are as follows:
Salutation to Gāyatrī; salutation to Praṇītā. Likewise, one should again place the eight Śaktis at the tips of the petals. (22–23)

Huṃ! To Rāvā, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, Kṣepaṇī, Strī, Huṃkārī, and Kṣemakārikā—one should worship these seven, who possess the colors and vehicles of the lords of the worlds and bear their respective weapons; then one should worship the eighth, the Earth, who is most terrifying, who holds a trident and a skull-cup, and whose body rises up with her hands placed upon her knees.

One should thus meditate upon her, who has blazing three eyes and a fierce face, who is naked, and who destroys fear, affliction, and obstacles caused by elemental spirits; one should contemplate that bringer of welfare with her own names, preceded by the seed-syllable of her power (Śakti-bīja) and ending with "Namaḥ."
In front, one should worship Phaṭkāriṇī, who holds a bow and carries a pill in her left hand;
likewise, one should worship Vijayā and Jayā, adorned with golden canes, stationed outside at the gate.
"O servant (kiṅkara)! Protect [me] according to my swift command; stand firm, phaṭ!

With this mantra, one should worship the servant Kṛṣṇa outside, who is well-adorned, holding a staff, and fierce. Then, with "Salutation to Lakulin," one should likewise worship the servant's attendant and his consort.
And one should worship the lords of the worlds situated in their respective directions;
and with the mantra "Obeisance to Caṇḍā, the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya)," one should likewise worship Caṇḍā, who is situated in the direction of Īśa (the northeast). || 22–27 ||

Having worshipped all [the deities] by their respective names ending with "namaḥ," one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and her retinue with five services (pañcopacāra), according to one's means,
with variegated red garments, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), garlands, mirrors, incense,
lamps, honey, roots, milk-rice (pāyasa), jaggery-rice (gulānna), pure food, fresh ghee, and sweetmeats (modaka).
Having performed the sacrifice and offered cool water, betel, and so forth with devotion,
he should likewise offer the remnants of the offering, along with honey, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and flowers, into the fire.

Having invoked the Goddess, one should offer oblations twenty-five times with the Gāyatrī and also with the root mantra; daily, the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) should be offered in a tenth part of that number.

Having scattered the *bali* offering—consisting of the remnants of the food—before the fire for his attendants, servants, and Antaka; having completed that rite and dismissed the fire, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and recite the mantra with his rosary.

Following the path taught in the Śaktipaṭala, one should offer the water from one’s cupped palms, as well as the worship, recitation, and other rites, at the lotus-feet of the Goddess. Having prostrated and satisfied Pārvatī with dance, hymns, song, and instrumental music as they may be available,
one should utter "nirañjane gaccha layaṃ ṭha ṭha" twice along with the root mantra and dissolve [the deity] into the heart.

But for one who, through meditation and the like, constantly worships with vigor or with the intellect in the lotus of the heart, all perfections shall remain eternal even within his lineage, just as the splendor of the Indravamśa dynasty remains constant within that lineage. (22-33) [Indravamśā meter]. This concludes the section on the daily worship of Wealth (Dhana).
Having duly invoked Ambikā into the fire within the sacrificial pit— which resembles a womb— according to the mantras,
and having worshipped her and offered oblations with sweet substances a hundred thousand times, one attains all desired fruits.

Through grains one obtains wealth; through black sesame seeds, one's desired objects; and by offering jasmine, fresh campaka, bilva, and lotus flowers soaked in honey, one attains prosperity and sovereignty.
By sacrificing madhūka flowers drenched in honey, one obtains all that is wished for.

One gains nourishment through wheat and barley, as well as through blue lotuses; through fuel-sticks of jambū wood, the abundance of wealth and grain; through white mustard seeds, the removal of calamities; through rice, health; and likewise, through sugarcane, the arrival of what is desired.

Having offered oblations here with black gram (*māṣa*), one brings about the dumbness of an enemy; with *akṣa* seeds, bewilderment; with *kodrava* grains, the onset of disease; and with poisonous *śalmali* fruits, death—having visualized that [deity] as black in color and terrifying.

There may even be an agitation of the city by offering *sumallika* flowers; one obtains women by offering *pāṭalaka* flowers; longevity by means of mango blossoms; subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) by means of white water-lilies (*kumuda*); and sons by means of *aśoka* flowers mixed with honey and clarified butter.
The Ritual of Homa: In this ritual of offering oblations (*huta*), one should not utter the mantra too quickly; likewise, it should not be so in recitation (*japa*) and other such acts.
Nor is a very slow pace desired; therefore, that which is neither too fast nor too slow always bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). [22–39] This is "neither fast nor slow" (*drutabilambita*).

Then, upon a mandala that is pleasing with white dust, resembling the source (yoni) of the measure of scattering, with the syllables of Tvaritā written in the ten directions in sequence, one should gradually place ten newly prepared jars. (22.40)
Having filled the [nine] pitchers with the nine Śaktis beginning with Hūrā, one should fill the tenth pitcher in the center of the Goddess in due order with the Mūla-mantra. || 22-41 ||
Having filled [the vessels] with gold, jewels, flowers, fruits, perfumes, and decoctions, and topped them with leaves of the jackfruit, the holy fig tree, the mango, and the bilva; 22-42.
One should properly and correctly worship those who are clothed in white, fine garments, adorned with garlands, flowers, and the like, and presided over by the powers of Tvaritā.

Then, having offered three hundred oblations into the fire with the root mantra, and having separately offered ten oblations each with the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*) and the nine powers (*śakti*), as well as ten each with sesame seeds and sacrificial porridge (*caru*);

and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), when the sun has risen at night, he should duly sprinkle that disciple— who has fasted— with the ritual jars in sequence, and through the swift initiation of the Mantra-master, he should unite him with [the deity].
Having presented this to the guru, he should satisfy him even with his own body and wealth;
then, he should mutter this mantra one million times, for he will indeed become a perfected master endowed with power.
The Chapter on Initiation (Dīkṣādhikāra).
This [body], which possesses pride born of excellent passion, is like copper; from that, it becomes silver and then gold.

Indeed, by means of the *toṭaka* ring fashioned from those [metals] melted into a single unity through the process of alchemy (*grahatoṭaka*), [it attains its true state]. (22.46) [The meter is] *Toṭaka*.

By means of that *Tvaritā*, accomplished through one hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter and recitations—meaning, by holding her with a finger—one shall indeed remove the fear of malevolent spirits (*bhūtagaṇa*), as well as venomous serpents, even by merely looking at them; she brings them under one's control, cuts them down, and destroys them. (22-47)
Outside the numerical power, one should draw a wheel situated upon the letters of the sixteen-petaled lotus, with six and four corners; when worn, that bestows desired results. (22.48)

When the diagram is inscribed on birch bark or similar material, within a square grid of lines, featuring lines extending eastward and northward from the sharp-rayed sun, and enriched with the tips of the lines forming fangs and tridents— (22.49).

In the center, however, one should place the *saṃjñā* (name); in the corners, the *tāra* (Oṃ); in the directions from the center, the *tāra* and other mantras ending in *phaṭ*, arranged accordingly in the corners. || 22-50 ||
Having drawn it there in both ways, the eight root-syllables (mūlāṣṭaka) shall be in the directions;
twenty *praṇavas* are located therein, situated in the corners of the ears (*śrutikoṇa*).
One should write the letters of the name one by one in sequence within all the compartments.
This wheel, when worn after being worshipped with recitation and fire-offerings, conquers the affliction caused by all planetary spirits.
The Trotalācakra: Alternatively, here, due to the four Praṇavas at the corners, Tvaritā should be written as before, accompanied by her name-syllables in their proper order. (22–53)
This, however, is the Tvaritā-cakra, which wards off malevolent planets and spirits;
it is the second and third [application] of this ten-syllable mantra.
And having extracted the sixth vowel, the Trikaṇṭakī mantra is accomplished;
[it is to be applied] to the head, forehead, mouth, heart, navel, secret place, thighs, and knees. (22.55)

One should place nine syllables of Tvaritā, including the vowels, upon the two feet. With the syllables of Tvaritā joined with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), using the numbers six, five, six, eight, nine, and eight, one should fashion the six limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) here; by reciting them one hundred thousand times, one shall attain perfection.
From her feet she was dark blue, then from the region of her navel she had the luster of fresh lac;
with a face as bright as the moon, she bore a digit of the moon beyond her throat, wore matted locks, and possessed three eyes.

She was surrounded on all sides by those who were four-cubit in height, adorned with serpents, vomiting flames of fire, possessing terrifying faces that were black, furrowed with frowns, and featuring white fangs and teeth.

Then, having meditated upon the Daughter of the Mountain as united with oneself—holding in her arms a white conch and a discus, and likewise a pair of lamps, one above and one below—the recitation of mantras and other rites will yield the desired result. (22.59)

Having meditated on one's own identity as Trikaṇṭakī, having bound the mudrā of the Trident-bearer (Triśūlinī), and while reciting [the mantra], one gazes upon those seized by planetary spirits; they perish instantly upon being entered [by the power].

Having meditated upon Rudra in the form of the *trikaṇṭha* [plant] as one with oneself, one may seize the planets and other such beings—so it is said by some. Alternatively, one should mutter this mantra, which consists of the syllables of the sages and is enclosed within nine syllables, for young women. If one desires to bring them under control, one should recite it three million times; furthermore, if one performs the rite of attraction at night while lying on a bed, one should recite it three hundred times. (22–61)
By giving flowers and other offerings consecrated with this [mantra], women shall become submissive.
The sixth syllable is enclosed (sampuṭa) between the third and fifth letters. (22.62)
By reciting the mantra of one's own chosen deity while maintaining the flow of breath, one destroys all poison;
furthermore, the *tvaritā* mantra fulfills every deficiency in ritual procedures.
Oṃ, the Tvaritā-pañjara should be known as that which provides all protection:
may the sound of "huṃ" be upon my head, and may Khecarī be at my throat. (22.64)
May Caṇḍā be in my heart; may Chedinī be in my belly.
May Kṣepaṇī be in my hips; may she who is designated as Strī be in my thighs.
May Huṃkārī be at my knees, may Kṣemakarī be at my shanks;
may Phaṭkārī be at my feet, and may Jayā be in all my limbs.
"May Vijayā bring me victory among all principles;
uttering this and meditating thus, I touch each respective limb. (22.67)
Oṃ! May Brahmāṇī be before me, and Māheśvarī at my back;
may Kaumārī be at my sides, and Vaiṣṇavī be above me.
May Vārāhī protect me in the water; may Indrāṇī, stationed on land, grant me safety;
may Carcā, stationed everywhere, be present; and may Cāmuṇḍā protect me.
May Caṇḍikā be my protector on mountains, in forests, in fortresses, and so forth;
may Vajriṇī be stationed before me in the east, and Śaktinī be in the southeast.
May Daṇḍinī be on my right; may Khaḍginī be in the southwest (nairṛta);
may Pāśinī be in the west (vāruṇa); and may Dhvajinī be stationed in the northwest (vāyavya).
May Gadinī come to my northern quarter; likewise, may Śūlinī be in the northeast. May Cakriṇī be situated below me, and may Padminī be above me. (22.72)
May the Śaktis, bearing the forms of the weapons of Lokeśa, protect me always;
may Tvaritā protect me in the cardinal directions and Trotalā protect me in the intermediate directions.
May Trikaṇṭhakī protect me above and below; may she always pervade me. Abiding within the Tvaritā-pañjara, I am fully protected by this vidyā.
"I have no fear from any quarter; therefore, may Pārvatī protect us. When protection for others must be performed, then one should recite the Pañjara [mantra]."
Wherever the word "me" (mām) occurs, the word "thee" (tvām) should be applied everywhere.
This is the section on the *Tvaritā* cage.
If one meditates upon the well-born one named Trotalā, who possesses the luster of a streak of fresh lightning and resides within the *kuṇḍalinī*:
One who reaches the lotus-cup at the *dvādaśānta*, moistened by the flowing nectar-essence, shall attain liberation. (22.76) The Cup (*puṭa*):

Again, having swiftly returned from the sky-lotus to the root-lotus by way of the *brahmanāḍī*, it moves upward once more, moist with light; when thus recollected, it bestows all supernatural powers (*siddhis*). (22.77)
In this world, all mantras bestow the desired fruit upon practitioners through the ripening of time;
however, this one indeed grants the desired result swiftly, and thus its name is truly meaningful.

Just as sin goes to destruction upon plunging into the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā) with its water-tossed current, so too does happiness become easily attained through meritorious deeds for a person who pursues it with haste. (22.79) "Water-tossed current": this [instruction] is not to be taught to an atheist, whose nature is like that of a serpent moving in the stream of human tradition.
It should always be given to a king, or to a virtuous son, or to one who possesses faith—even if he is a giver of his own desired objects. (22.80) [In the *Bhujaṅgaprayāta* meter.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the *Tvaritā-paṭala*, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. (22)
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.

*Pu*, *ra*, *stā*, *ra*, *śa*, *ktī*, *ca*, *vāṅ*, *ni*, *tya*, *śa*, *bdau*, *bhu*, *jaḥ*, *sā*, *kṣi*, *māṃ*, *saḥ*, *sa*, *jhaṇṭī*, *dvi*, *me*, *ṣaḥ*, *vi*, *ṣā*, *ti*, *dra*, *ve*, *cā*, *pi*, *śa*, *ktiḥ*, *ca*, *vā*, *gjaṃ*, *ṭha*-yugmaṃ, *ca*, *ni*, *tyā*: thus is declared the Nityā consisting of fifteen syllables. (22–1)
Without the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], the six limbs (aṅgas) should be formed in sequence by the syllables *krū*, *kha*, *rī*, *bha*, *va*, and *rṇa* together with the [Jāti-mantras];
just as it is when joined with the Jātis ending with the Weapon-mantra, one should again perform the limbs with the Vāgbhava. || 22–2 ||
The seer is Kāmadeva; the meter is Atiśakvarī, which is said to be beloved by Manu and eternally established.
Its deity is Umā herself, preceded by the word *klinna*; its fruit is the subjugation of the world and the attainment of prosperity. (22–3)
Having received initiation from the Guru and obtained his grace, this practitioner should first perform the purification of the self and other elements, and then recite the mantra;
furthermore, he should meditate upon the island in the midst of the ocean of Mādhava as a triangle.

In that place, it was heart-stealing with wish-fulfilling trees; and later, when the sun had risen, the sky in the eastern quarter shone with a radiant full moon and a garland of stars, while in the west it was somehow charming with the clouds of the rainy season. || 22.5 ||

And that place, which dispels sorrow with its golden grounds, was made most delightful by the swaying clusters and shoots of *aśoka* trees— rich with quivering buds and tinged with a golden-brown hue— and by the sweet warbling of cuckoos and the humming of bees.
Then, upon that lotus, one should worship a golden pedestal (*pīṭha*) shaped like a triangle, adorned with a lotus and shimmering rubies.

Having worshipped that pedestal with the mantra: *Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ, salutation to the Yoni-lotus-pedestal*, and having then worshipped [the goddesses] in the corners of the fire, water, and wind [directions] with: *Oṃ āṃ, to Drāvaṇī*; *Oṃ īṃ, to Āhlādakāriṇī*; and *Oṃ khaṃ, to Kṣobhaṇī*—then, in this [pedestal]:
Oṃ aiṃ to Madadravā; Oṃ auṃ to Rodrī; Oṃ aḥ to Madanāturā; Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ to Yoniśakti.
These should be worshipped with "namas" at the end in the cardinal directions and in the center. || 22-7 ||
Then, meditating upon the primordial Śakti— who is of subtle form, eternally moist with nectar, and the very consciousness at the *dvādaśānta*—
one should invoke her onto that yoga-pīṭha and worship her here according to the nature described.

Reddish like the *bandhujīva* flower, clad in red fragrant garments, adorned with ornaments blazing with divine jewels, possessing full and lofty breasts, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, with a golden braid of hair, wearing garlands, and possessing three eyes;
(22–9) she whose face is like the full moon, who bears upon her head the Moon-crested Śiva, the auspicious one with six arms, holding a noose and a goad. (Sragviṇī; p. 84)
Touching the *pārijāta* tree with his right hand, and holding a skull-cup filled with nectar on his left, he plays the *vallakī* lute.

The practitioner should worship Pārvatī—who is beautiful in every way and whose eyes are quickly rolling with intoxication—either in a golden image, or in a beautiful painting, or, if one possesses the necessary materials, through the intellect by means of identifying oneself with her. (22.11)

Then, one should worship the nine Śaktis from the beginning to the middle and end [of the directions]: *Iṃ* to Nityā; *Īṃ* to Subhadrā; *Uṃ* to Maṅgalā; *Ūṃ* to Naravīriṇī; *Eṃ* to Subhagā; *Aiṃ* to Durgā; *Oṃ* to Manonmanī; *Auṃ* to Madadravā; *Aṃ* to Kāmamandirā.

One should worship these Śaktis—who are beautiful, ruddy-hued, adorned with red perfumes, garments, and ornaments, and who stand playing lutes together—while meditating on them as being whirled by passion and addressed by their respective names. (22–12)
Oṃ Aṃ, to Anaṅga; Oṃ, to Smara; Oṃ, to Manmatha; Oṃ, to Kāma; Oṃ, to Kusumāyudha.

One should worship these five Kāmas in the directions and in front, on the outside, as they bear red perfumes and garments, possess beautiful forms and attire, and carry a flower-bow, arrows, a noose, a goad, and five quivers. || 22-13 ||

All [the deities] of the *Lakulīkāma* [mantra], ending with *namaḥ*, are as follows: *jaṃ ratyai namaḥ*; *jāṃ viratyai namaḥ*; *jiṃ prītyai namaḥ*; *jīṃ viprītyai namaḥ*; *juṃ matyai namaḥ*; *jūṃ durmatyai namaḥ*; *joṃ dhṛtyai namaḥ*; *jauṃ vidhṛtyai namaḥ*; *jaṃ kṛṣṭyai namaḥ*; *jaḥ puṣṭyai namaḥ*.
One should worship these ten in sequence on both sides of the *Kāmas*.
They hold lutes, are singing, are red in color, and are dressed in red garments and so forth. (22–14)
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), such as Āsāḍha and the others, situated in their respective places by their own names.
There should be milk-rice mixed with treacle, soaked in honey and ghee, along with sweetmeats (modakas). || 22-15 ||
Sweet coconut water, drinking water for rinsing the hands, as well as betel leaf with all its accompaniments, should be offered;
thereafter, one should please Pārvatī with dances, songs, and other such auspicious hymns of praise.
The Chapter on Worship:

For one who recites the mantra together with the letters of the alphabet, proceeding both in direct order (*anuloma*) and in reverse order (*viloma*), the entire world comes under control before long; moreover, even his poetry becomes *pramitākṣarā*. (22.17) [The meter is] *pramitākṣarā*.

Now, he whose mouth is the fire-pit of the womb—whoever, having meditated upon this Blessed Lady who has been duly worshipped by himself, offers oblations with red lotuses bathed in honey, shall become a giver of wealth. (22.18)
One who offers a million oblations with honey and madhūka flowers obtains great wealth;
by offering excellent food mixed with ghee, milk, and honey, one becomes possessed of cattle through the sacrifice of that food with ghee and milk.
One may bring all under one's control with red flowers sprinkled with honey, and a king with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Moreover, by looking at someone while reciting this mantra, that person and the practitioner will become mutually enamored, and the couple shall indeed be united in love. (22.20)

The one who, being faithful, constantly meditates upon and recites the mantra known as Nityaklinnā—whether thirty, fifty, sixty lakṣas, or ten million times—shall indeed attain the siddhis beginning with Bhauma, as well as those pertaining to Vaiśvadevī. [End of] Vaiśvadevī; [end of] the section on Nityaklinnā.
The subtle-eyed arm, along with the noose and goad, is the seed-syllable of Śakti in the eternal flow of Kāla;
this twelve-syllabled mantra beginning with Hṛllekhā is indeed the Vidyā named Nityā Vajraprastārī. || 22-22 ||

Āhlādinī, Klinnā, Nityakledinī, Nityā, Madadravyā, and Aṅgā—these six should be [worshipped] by their own names along with their respective *jātis*. Kāma is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *Jagatī* meter is declared.
The deity is Sarvajñā Śakti; it is perfected through one million recitations of the sun, and its fruit is the fulfillment of all desires. (22–23)
Having received initiation from a teacher and the mantra according to the rules, one whose self, station, materials, and mantra are purified should, by means of his own power,
meditate upon a sea of red lotuses with rows of lofty waves, and within it, a ship with high masts.
In the center of the nave, one should meditate upon a golden pavilion in the form of a *yoni*, enriched with networks of pearls and made beautiful by garlands of flowers.
In its center, upon a pedestal, one should meditate on a red lotus of that same [triangular] shape; its pericarp is the *vāgbhava* syllable.
Seated upon that [lotus] was the goddess of divine form, red as the bandhūka flower, with six arms and three eyes;
her limbs were adorned with ornaments rich in various jewels, her attire was crimson, and she possessed full and lofty breasts. (22–26)

One should meditate upon her who holds a goad and a noose, who bears a bow and arrows, and who carries an amṛta-skull; who has a citron fruit in her hand, who wears a garland of nine moons, and whose face is like the moon. (22–27) [She is] Navamālinī.

Having thus visualized her in this form, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), installation (*sthāpana*), presence (*sānnidhya*), confinement (*saṃnirodha*), and propitiation (*prarocana*) by means of the seed-syllable of Śakti.
And upon the filaments of the lotuses and on the tips of the young petals, which possess a reddish power through her limbs,
he should worship [the goddesses] Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Nandā, Kṣobhaṇī, Madanāturā, Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, Madanāvatī, Śekhariṇī, Drāvaṇī, Vegavatī, and Kāmā.
Having worshipped the enclosure of the eight Mothers here on the outside, he should sacrifice to the lords of the directions at the ends of their respective quarters.

He who, worshipping her here every day along with her retinue using excellent offerings, recites [her name] a thousand times at the start of each day facing the direction [of the deity], becomes as fortunate in the world as Kubera. (22–29)
Now, in the *atijagatī* meter:
Or, one who has been consecrated according to the ritual rules should meditate upon the enchantress of the three worlds, the Vajraprastārā, and recite [the mantra].
To him, Lakṣmī herself approaches—she who is not shared by many, who is auspicious, and who gladdens the hearts of her own kin. (22-30) [The meter is] *praharṣiṇī*.
Having first offered oblations with thousands of directions mixed with honey and accompanied by contradictions, the mantra then bears fruit according to one's desire;
if one were to offer a hundred thousand oblations with them, he would become beloved by the world, possessed of fortune, and live for a long time with a joyful mind.
Through milk-rice mixed with ghee, one attains great prosperity; likewise, through red lotuses or blue lotuses offered in honey, one obtains what is desired.
By offering rice grains with salt, one gains women; by offering parched grain smeared with honey, all people come under one’s control.
The Chapter on Vajraprastāriṇī:
Hṛllekhā, above that the eternal seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), followed by the two letters ending with Na; then the pair of Bhadrapīṭhas.
This Vidyā consisting of eleven syllables is indeed Mohinī. The seer and all other details, as well as the fruit, are entirely as before. (22–33)
In the meditation, however, there is a slight distinction:

one should meditate on her whose limbs are adorned with even more intensely red perfumes and so forth, who is reddish in luster, who holds in her hands the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a skull-bowl (*kapāla*), as well as a noose (*pāśa*), and who holds a goad (*aṅkuśa*) in the palm of her hand; she has three eyes, and in her braided hair she bears a crescent moon and the *pārijāta* flower. (22–34)

One should first recite this three hundred thousand times; having first offered oblations of madhūka flowers mixed with honey for that same number of times, one becomes beloved by the world, renowned, prosperous, possessed of a fortunate body, and eternally happy. (22–35)
(87) Bathing oneself, or [anointing] with perfume, or [using] water, or collyrium and so forth, with the mantra is also desired;
it removes bad dreams, brings about the pacification of disease, generates good fortune, and makes those who are to be born [or those who are hostile] submissive. (22–36)

[Mohanī: One should meditate upon her who holds a goad, the gesture of granting boons, a skull-cup, and a noose; who wears matted hair and has three eyes with the moon as her crest-jewel; who is as red as the *japā* flower and adorned with garments of jewels and other ornaments; who, through oneness with herself, is as beautiful as the God of Love—she who is the enchantress. 22-37. [Rucirā.]
Alternatively, one should meditate upon her, possessing the luster of fresh saffron, as the dawn-lotus in the ocean of the god of love;
with two hands, she bestows nectar flowing from her skull-cup—meditate on her who brings the world under her sway. (22.38)

In this regard, the instruction is as follows: having visualized one's own five faces with the short *smarabījas* (the seed-syllables of Kama), and the limbs with the long ones; and reciting the *smarabīja* joined with its name (*nāma*) while contemplating oneness with oneself, one brings the entire universe under control.
Having ascended by means of one's own name, becoming absorbed in that, one should gradually string together the syllables of the mantra and the *manmatha* (Kama-seed);
one should recite it oneself and perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's body and hands. When bound with the appropriate mudrā, it becomes a means of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). (22–39)
The instruction is that by binding the *kṣobhaṇī-mudrā*, which is joined with the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and reciting [the mantra], one brings them under control.

Thus, those whose minds are bowed low by the weight of devotion who constantly serve the Nityā here through meditation, recitation, and other means—before them, like intoxicated peacocks, the objects of desire, charming with their desired aims, shall dance at will. (22–40) *Mattamayūrā*.
The section on the three-syllabled and four-syllabled [mantras] of Nityā:
The syllable preceding the letters of the script is the seed of Manmatha; Bhuvaneśī, Meṣa, Kṣvela, and Sargi constitute the mantra of Nityā.
This five-syllabled [mantra] causes the agitation of all people; it should be mentally recited with its own constituent letters according to the ritual of the limbs (aṅgavidhi). || 22-41 ||
Kāma is its seer, Siddhilipi its deity, and Paṅkti its metre; the mantra is perfected by one hundred thousand recitations.
Having offered oblations of milk, clarified butter, and honey in ten parts of the total count, Lakṣmī remains perpetually under his control. || 22-42 ||
One should meditate upon the Goddess as one with oneself—red in hue, holding a pen and a book in her hands, adorned with red garments, and bearing a noose and a goad in her upper hands;
she is crowned by the moon, possesses beautiful matted locks, has a pair of lovely eyes, and has full, jar-like breasts. (22.43)

(88) Having pierced through the lotus-liṅga of Kuṇḍalinī from the *mūlādhāra*, she rises up—subtle as the fiber of a lotus-stalk—and is designated as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*; within her, the letters of the script are strung like pearls. (22.44)
