Meditating with a focused mind upon that goddess— who, as a streak of light with subtle radiance, proceeds through the sky via the internal path of the division of the *bindu* between the eyebrows— and who is eternally moistened by the nectar-water of the moon-lotus, one should remain intent on her recitation.

Whether seeing, hearing, delighting in touch, intent on smell, eating, walking, speaking, or performing action—even while meditating, one should find delight in mental recitation; for while he abides by his command, the entire universe remains so, how much more so anything else? (22.46)
If he desires enjoyment and sovereignty, he shall indeed obtain that; or else, the sovereignty of speech equal even to Vācaspati;
or the eightfold sovereignty of yoga beginning with *aṇimā*. If he does not desire such various sovereignties, he shall attain even liberation.
The Chapter on Mātṛkā-mālinī:

Śakti (Ś), the letter at the end of "sva" (M), Anugrahavat (Ū), Agni joined with Sūkṣma (R), Kaṇṭhī (I), Vahni (R) situated in Vahni (R), Atri himself (G), Sākṣa (KṢA), Bālī (L), those two (L and KṢA) joined with the word "Antaga" (ANTAKA), the word "Īśvarī" (ĪŚVARĪ), followed by Varma (HŪM) and Astra (PHAṬ), ending with ṬHAU—thus is the mantra of Gaurī declared. (22–48)
The meter of this mantra is Aṣṭi, and it indeed consists of these syllables; with the two initial vowels, there are six limbs endowed with their respective classes.
Gaurī is the goddess, Vāmadeva is said to be its sage, and it is accomplished by three hundred thousand recitations. (22-49)
Now, regarding the Śakvarī [meter]:
Having first received the initiation from the teacher and also the mantra, and having bathed with the root-mantras and their ancillaries, he should reach a spacious temple of Śiva;
and having worshipped both Śiva and Śivā with arghya and other offerings, having obtained permission, he should then perform our ritual worship according to the mantra. (22.50)
[Unobstructed]

Outside the door of the worship hall, one should worship Kṣetrapāla on both sides, Jayā and Vijayā above them, Dvāraśrī over the door, and Vāstupuruṣa within the door, using their respective names followed by *namaḥ*. Having entered inside and sat upon one’s own seat, remaining silent and having purified oneself by restraining the breath (*niyamitamarut*), one should perform the ritual purity (*śuddhi*). Then, having performed the assignment of the hands (*karanyāsa*) and the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), and having filled the entire body with the *arghya* water through the limbs, one should worship Gaṇapati in the western direction (Varuṇa) and the Guru in the northeastern direction (Īśa). It is as follows: "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati"; "Guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus; obeisance to the Paramagurus"; "Oṃ, obeisance to the Parameṣṭhigurus"; "obeisance to the Pūrvācāryas"; "obeisance to the Pūrvasiddhas"; "obeisance to the Yoginīs. Having worshipped thus with "obeisance to the Yoginīs," one worships in the center: "obeisance to the Kalpavṛkṣa"; beneath that, "obeisance to the Ratnasiṃhāsana"; "Iṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti"; "Uṃ, obeisance to Kūrma"; "Aṃ, obeisance to Anantāsana"; "Ṛṃ, obeisance to Dharma"; "Ṝṃ, obeisance to Jñāna"; "Ḷṃ, obeisance to Vairāgya"; "Ḹṃ, obeisance to Aiśvarya"; "Kaṃ, obeisance to Kanda"; "Naṃ, obeisance to Nāla"; "Hāṃ, obeisance to Padma"; "Saṃ, obeisance to the Kesaras"; "Haṃ, obeisance to Karṇikā"; "Kṣaṃ, obeisance to the Patras. Having worshipped thus up to the rim (*nemāntam*), one worships the eight Śaktis at the tips of the petals: "Oṃ Sāṃ, obeisance to Prabhā"; "Oṃ Sīṃ, obeisance to Jñānā"; "Oṃ Sūṃ, obeisance to Vāc"; "Oṃ Seiṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī"; "Oṃ Saiṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī"; "Oṃ Soṃ, obeisance to Vāmā"; "Oṃ Sauṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā"; "Oṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Raudrī"; "Oṃ Saḥ (Gauṃ?), obeisance to Gaurīmūrti. Having thus worshipped the ninth Śakti in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should meditate upon the Goddess with the root mantra (*mūla*) and invoke her.
She whose splendor is like the glow of the newly risen sun, whose body is composed of light,
whose face is like the full moon, who is beautiful with three eyes,
who holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and who wields a goad and a noose—
One should meditate upon Aparājitā, who holds a digit of the moon.
Having placed the limbs (aṅgas) in the cardinal directions and the weapon (astra) in the intermediate directions, one should place the eye in front;
these Veda-śaktis are at the tips of the filaments in the cardinal directions, reaching to the tips of the petals.

* Svāṃ to Subhagā; * Svīṃ to Lalitā; * Sūṃ to Kāminī; * Seṃ to Kāmamālinī. Likewise, one should worship the eight powers, beginning with Anaṅgarūpā, in pairs at the tips of the petals in the corners: Anaṅgarūpā to Anangā; Madanāturā to Pavanavegā; Bhuvanapālinī to Sarvaśiśirā; and Anaṅgamadanānaṅgamadanā to Anaṅgamekhalā. Here, outside on the enclosure wall, are the Mothers, followed by the guardians of the directions, beginning with Purandara.
Surrounded by their own retinues and accompanied by their weapons and vehicles, one should worship these [deities] individually at the enclosures with their respective names.

One should worship Nirmālyadhāriṇī in the northeast with the mantra: *Subhagāyai namaḥ*. With this Gaurī-gāyatrī: *Lupajāśaihi? Subhagāyai vidmahe, Kāmamālinyai dhīmahi, tanno Gaurī pracodayāt*, and with the seed-syllable of Śakti (*hrīṃ*), one should worship her with the ritual offerings (*upacāras*).

One should worship the Blessed Lady with flowers and perfumes, fragrant ointments, incense held in censers, fine incense and lamps, fruits filled with sweet juices, as well as with *modakas* and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee. (22–54)

One should meditate upon her who resembles molten gold, who holds a lotus for the sake of prosperity, whose hands grant fearlessness and boons, who is attended by two treasures, who possesses a mirror, who holds a collyrium-tipped brush, and who sits upon a seat of lotuses and golden splendor.

(90) Holding a noose, a goad, a thunderbolt, and a bow with its string, as well as an arrow and a sword-shield, she who crushes the sons of Diti stands here equipped with weapons for the victory of the Enemy of Smara. (22.56) [She is] *praharaṇakalitā*.
Sacrifice to the Daughter of the Mountain, who possesses the splendor of the ritual procedure, upon a lotus of eight petals where a water-pot is well-placed.
Having performed one thousand recitations and offered oblations ten times that number, he shall bathe the king; thus he becomes victorious.

He who daily worships Girijā, the bestower of boons upon the three worlds, through recitation, fire-offerings, and sacrifices, becomes possessed of abundant wealth and cattle in this world, and rejoices for a long time with land, houses, and children. (22-58)
If one worships the beloved of Śiva with ghee, honey, milk, and fresh white lotuses in the mouth of the fire,
and likewise offers oblations of sacrificial porridge in water, he shall before long become a possessor of ten times a hundred [i.e., ten thousand] riches.
For one seeking to bring the king of the twice-born under control, there should be a thousand fuel-sticks made of *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *audumbara*, or *khadira* wood;
for a vaiśya or a śūdra, with salt and rice grains; or likewise for women.
At the proper time, during the *vasantatilaka* [season], one should offer oblations with sweet substances.
(*Vasantatilakam*) With sweet-smelling red flowers, one may bring all under control; by offering a wick made from *nandyāvarta* and other plants, one obtains sons.
With red lotuses, or those born from reeds (*vetasa*), one obtains desired rain; with milk and sesame seeds, one obtains everything, including cattle. (22-61)

Through oblations of *aruṣkara*, *vibhītaka*, and pungent oil for small obstacles; and likewise with *bilva*, clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sesame seeds, one attains the fortune of sovereignty.
Furthermore, through oblations of *dūrvā* grass, milk, sesame, and ghee, as well as by ritual ablution with water, one obtains long life and freedom from disease.
Having written the name of the one to be won within the power (Śakti) enclosed between the left thigh and the city of fire (the triangle),
and having performed the mantra at night during the night, as he recites it with his hand, that woman approaches him with her left side, and another with the other.

Having mounted a chariot as lofty as a lion, bearing a thundercloud-like hue, and holding a conch, the bow of Śaṅkhāri, arrows, a vajra, a mace, a trident, a sword, a shield, and a fire—meditating on her as one with oneself, one who possesses three eyes should recite [the mantra]; thus, in times of fear, he shall become fearless. (22.64)
[This is indeed the Vasantatilaka; others call it the Siṃhonnata.

When the power (Śakti) is written outside the name by the betel-preparer, with the six limbs consisting of the noose, goad, enclosure, nectar, and the tips of the trident, there shall be the Svastika.
One should mutter the lipi-mantras at night; the nooses and the goad [are used] at the lamp. Through the heat [of the fire], one attains the desired goal. 22-65.

In a circle formed by the four directions with the *veda-bījas* called *Śaktisthirā*, and by the sequence of the syllables of *Śakti*, *Smara*, *Aṅkuśa*, and *Pāśa*, one should draw two dough effigies (*piṣṭamayaputtalikā*) provided with life-force (*sajīva*). By breaking them and feeding them sweet foods, [the target] shall come under one's control. (22.66)
The Chapter on the Ritual of Gaurī. Now, the Great Śakti is described:
"Śakti, salutations, the word Brahman, and 'O Goddess worshipped by kings'."
Oṃ, O Gaurī, O Gāndhārī, O Śaṅkarī of the three worlds, O Śaṅkarī of all the worlds, O Śaṅkarī of all women and men, O Suduhvāk! For the desire of speech, *ṭhaḥ* *ṭhaḥ*.
Aja is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Atinicṛt is the meter (*chandas*), and Gaurī is the deity (*devatā*). (22.67)
Her six limbs are formed by her own syllables numbering fourteen, ten, eight, ten, eleven, and eleven; she is perfected through ten million recitations performed before sunrise.
In the *atiśakvarī* meter:
Upon the sandy shore of the ocean of nectar, O Lotus, fragrant with heaps of blossoms from various celestial trees;
[I behold] the moon-faced one, possessing the luster of a ruby, whose face is the nectar-rayed moon and who bears a crescent moon within her mass of excellent tresses. (22.69)
[Some call her Śaśikalā, others Candrāvartā.
One should invoke and worship the goddess Gaurī, who holds a noose and a goad, is adorned with red ornaments, possesses three eyes, has full and elevated breasts, and is of divine form. 22-70.

Having constantly worshipped [the deity] within the three enclosures with the limbs, the Mothers, all the weapons, and the ritual services, using their respective seed-syllables, one should recite the mantra one hundred times.

If he performs a thousand recitations at dawn of this mantra— which is joined with a sweet-smelling, beautiful white lotus, offered into the fire, and bestows prosperity here— then Mā, like a swarm of bees following a garland of flowers, follows him.
[Some say "mālā" means "srag".
One should perform oblations with sweetened sesame seeds and rice mixed with salt;
by this, one shall subjugate all men and women and obtain whatever is desired. (22.73)

Day after day, when the divine sun has risen and its waters have subsided, he who has restrained his mind and is devoted to recitation should offer oblations to the daughter of Agastya; through the multitude of his jewel-like virtues, she brings him to the attainment of prosperity.
[Maṇiguṇanikaraḥ | p.

92] Having meditated upon and propitiated the Goddess seated amidst musical instruments, one should recite the mantra one hundred times. Whomever one has in mind during the forenoon, that person becomes subject to one’s will. (22.75)
One should employ the name of the person to be accomplished, preceded by the seed-syllable and joined with the ritual action;
in rites for subjugation (*vaśya*), success arises immediately during recitation and other practices.
Thus, through the various divisions of her own nature, the one eternal power Gaurī shines forth in the world in diverse forms;
this Mātṛkā-Mālinī bestows the desired fruit.
May Pārvatī, who brings about the pacification of all evils, protect you. (22-77) [Mālinī meter].
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on the daily rites and so forth, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. (23)
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
May that Durgā be for your prosperity—she, having entered whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra carry out the activity of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all the worlds;
she, upon whom Māyā rests, and by depending on whom the universe truly manifests, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
For the five verses beginning with "jātavedase," the seer is Marīci Kāśyapa; the meter is Triṣṭubh; and Durgā is the deity. (24-2)
Others declare the deity to be Agni Jātavedas;
the third Ṛc is known as Atidurgā, and its meter is Virāj. (24.3)

The world of the Nāgas [is formed] by the planets, sages, and days of the week, each with its own color; furthermore, one should assign the six mantras of their respective classes to the limbs separately,
and upon the body, one should place the mantra-syllables numbering fifty-one (the number of Bhava).
And following that, one should perform the six-limbed yoga with its own steps numbering according to the *dhṛti* [forty].

The pair of feet, the ankles, the shanks, the knees, the thighs, the abode of Smara (the genitals), the region of the hips, the heart, the breasts, the sides, the back, the neck, the throat, the shoulders, the arms, the forearms, the wrists, the palms, the face, the nose, the ears, the eyes, and the head—whom [does he not pervade]? 24-5.

These are the locations for the syllables. Now, the traditional teaching regarding the locations of the words is as follows: the forehead, eyes, ears, lower lip, tongue, throat, arms, heart, navel region, hips, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet; furthermore, there are two locations for the ears and eyes, and one location for each of the others. (24.6)
Devoted to the duties prescribed for him and intent on pleasing his guru, he was duly initiated by him during the northern course of the sun;
thereafter, having obtained the *manu* [the mantra] and performed the ritual ablutions and other rites, he [proceeded].
One should draw a lotus on a well-smeared surface on the ground.
Alternatively, one should draw a very beautiful two-handled lotus-wheel (cakrapadma) on the ground as an auspicious design using five-colored powders.
It is joined with the name of the practitioner, has the Lord of the World as its pericarp, and is endowed with six petals accompanied by the seed-syllable of Durgā. It is beautiful.
Therein, one should worship that seat known as Vajrāsana by its own name.
He likewise [perceived] Prakṛti with her forms possessing the three qualities, as well as the lotus.

The deities beginning with Dharma, located at the corners of that pedestal, are to be worshipped; one should likewise worship the lotus of the Śakti with the Guṇas, the Sun, the Root (Kanda), and so forth, as well as the limbs (Aṅgas) and the enclosure.

One should worship the Śaktis— Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Vyāghramukhī, Siṃhamukhī, and Durgā— who reside on the tips of the petals and occupy the ninth pericarp. And one should worship those eight quarters of the mantra outside the lotus, as is prescribed.

The syllables of the count, beginning with *mā*, *tā*, and *ātma* on the left, indeed constitute the feet; and these are individually joined with the principles (*tattvas*) and the forms (*mūrtis*) of Agni. (24.12)
Namely:

the feet are joined with the organs of knowledge and action, the elements, the seven constituents, the six waves, the six sheaths, the objects, and the vital breaths, respectively and individually. (24.13)
Jātavedas, Hutāśa, Agni, Vaiśvānara, Saptajihva, Hutavaha, Hutavartman, and Devamukha; || 24-14 ||

Thus ends the eightfold form (*mūrty-aṣṭaka*). One should worship those [deities] in sequence, ending with the word "namas," joined with the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) and so forth, using the forms [of the deities] in the vocative case at the end of the quarters beginning with *jātavedas*. (24–15)

Outside the enclosure of the [central] square, the powers beginning with their own respective letters, numbering eleven (the number of Rudras), such as Jāgatī and the others, should be worshipped in each direction. (24.16)
The Jāgatā, Tapanī, Vedagarbhā, Dahanarūpiṇī, Sendukhaṇḍā, Sumbhagatrī, and thereafter the one known as Nabhaścarā. (24-17)
Vāgīśvarī, Madavahā, Somarūpā, Manojavā, Marudvegā, as well as Rātri, Tīvrakopā, and Yaśovatī. (24.18)
She whose essence is water, who is eternal, compassionate, and captivating;
she who transcends all, the mother of the Vedas, and therefore beloved by the gods. (24.19)
Nandinī is to be propitiated, as well as Parā, Ripuvimardinī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Daṇḍinī, Tigmā, Durgā, and she who is known as Gāyatrī. (24–20)
Niravadyā, Viśālākṣī, Śvāsodvāhā, Vedanī, Vedanā, Vahnigarbhā, Siṃhavāhā, and Dhuryā. || 24-21 ||
The powers of the mantra-syllables are known as Durviṣahyā, Riraṃsā, Tāpahāriṇī, Tyaktadoṣā, and Niḥsapatnā. (24–22)
And each of these is separately surrounded by multiple powers;
they are to be worshipped outside the pedestal in the four directions with their own names followed by the word "namaḥ". (24-23)
In the fifth enclosure, [one should worship] the Mothers in the cardinal directions and Gaṇeśvara in the south.
Now, in the eighth [enclosure]:
[he who is] golden-hued, three-eyed, and with garments and flowers that are reddish-brown—

I bow to the one who wears the crescent moon on his crest, who is adorned with a single tusk, whose face is like that of an elephant, and whose neck is broad; who holds a noose and a goad, and who likewise bears a fruit in his trunk, sporting in the manner of a bull-elephant. (24) *Ṛṣabhagajavilasita* meter.
In that place, one should worship the gurus by name, white in appearance and clad in white garments and so forth. || 24–25 ||
I invoke this Tārā, born of Rudra, who is Durgā;
she whose chariot is yoked with lions and whose followers are tigers. (24–26)
"May there be fearlessness for me; may Durgā, who assumes formidable forms, grant it. To this Goddess Durgā, worshipped by gods and sages, I go for refuge; salutations! (p.

95) Having uttered this, one should invoke the Goddess from the solar orb with the root mantra and its ancillaries, and worship her in the lotus while meditating on her as described in her true form. (24–27)
Holding a conch, a shield, a bow, and a threatening gesture in her left hands,
and bearing a discus, a sword, an arrow, and a trident in her right hands, she has three eyes and a radiant crown.
I bow to Goddess Durgā, who has the moon as her crest-jewel, is adorned with ornaments, wears red attire, and is mounted upon a lion; she is accompanied by throngs of maidens eager for battle.
To Durgā, Kātyāyanī, Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, Suvarṇavarṇā, and Sarvaniṣkalā.
One should first worship the limb-mantras;
then, having worshipped the lords of the worlds together with their weapons in their respective directions,
one should worship Siṃhikā, the bearer of the remains of offerings (nirmālya), in the northeast.
Having worshipped them with primary offerings and secondary services, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times;
subsisting on the food prescribed for a vow and observing celibacy, one should also perform oblations during the nights.

One should offer oblations in sequence, each consisting of sesame, śamī leaves, white mustard, milk-rice, sacrificial fuel-sticks, and caru, along with ghee separately, while maintaining a state of being absorbed in Bhava.
If one is unable [to perform the fire sacrifice], one should worship with the mind alone and recite the mantra twice as many times as the number of oblations offered;
then this mantra becomes perfected, bestowing the fruits of its application.
The section on mantra-worship and so forth:
Having meditated upon Durgā, who possesses a rosy luster and holds a noose, a boon-granting gesture, and a goad, one offers oblations into the fire with sandalwood moistened with water.

Indeed, with flowers from the *vakula* tree or *vikaṅkata* and *sumana* blossoms, one shall surely bring under control for half a month either a sovereign king or a woman. [Regarding] the woman (*vāṇinī*):
with sweet substances and the dust from the foot of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*), mixed with salt and putty (*loṇaputtalī*), [one should perform the rite].
That which is offered as an oblation into the fire at the beginning of that constellation is known as ākarṣaṇa (attraction).

She stands upon a red lotus, possessing the luster of a *tāpiñcha* flower and adorned with various ornaments, holding in her arms, in successive order, a discus, a sword, a mace, and a lotus— thus possessing eight arms.
Recalling Candrāpīḍā, who is clothed in gold, one should offer oblations into the water with flowers and perfumes; thus he shall obtain the deer-like Fortune (Hariṇī). [The verse on] Hariṇī:
[One should meditate on her] white as crystal, dressed in white garments, standing in the waters of a great flood.

Meditating on her who bestows fearlessness and boons, holding a noose and a goad, and offering a sweet-smelling rain of fresh rice grains, one should perform the recitation while standing in water reaching up to the navel; thus, one obtains ten million [merits]. (24-37)

Holding an iron mace and a club in her hands, yellow in color, and clad in yellow garments and the like—when she is meditated upon and offered oblations of parched grain mixed with buffalo fat and Akṣa seeds, she causes paralysis. (24.38)
This smoky streak, accompanied by a spear and a mace,
causes hatred when oblations are offered with neem leaves soaked in ghee along with cotton seeds.
That same goddess, holding a trident in her threatening hand, shall cause enemies to be eradicated through oblations of black pepper, buffalo products,
poisonous leaves, and Rājī plants.
With tridents in hand, resembling fire, and with rows of wild marīca peppers smeared with sharp oil, one should perform oblations; by this, this fortress shall delude the enemies. (24.41)
Meditating upon the black goddess who bestows the quality of blood, one should offer fuel-sticks of *aruṣkara* wood; having thus sacrificed, one leads the enemies to the abode of Yama.
[One should also sacrifice] with *marica*, ashes, *idra*, *jīra*, and *rājī*, all soaked in ghee and *hiṅgu*.
The slaying of enemies at night is accomplished with funeral mounds made from wood originating from poisonous trees.
May Viṣākṣa, who possesses dark matted hair and is smeared with the blood of a shining buffalo,
offer a thousand different kinds of fuel-sticks on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
while he wallows upon the surface of the earth from that time until the end of the day.
An enemy who is intent on lamentation shall go to the city of Yama within a fortnight. [Regarding] the Earth:
one should angrily boil an image of the enemy made from *uḍumbara* wood in water from the western direction, mixed with flowers and powdered black pepper.

At the hour of midnight, one should recite the mantra while heating a doll made of *hatāma* (human hair) that has been smeared with sharp poison in reverse order; thus one shall cause death. || 24-44 ||

Having boiled an image of the enemy made of clay with asafoetida, ginger, long pepper, and cumin in water from the ocean, one should strike it with a thunderbolt made of *kṣveḍa* and *yaṣṭi*, and thus kill him. (24.45)
Meditating upon his enemy as being naked, head-downward, with his feet swallowed by the serpent that binds the horses of the sun’s chariot, and situated within the orbs of fire and wind—
one who pours water while reciting that mantra shall not become wet with water.
Remaining [in the state] after being offered oblations with salt, sharp substances, ghee, and black pepper, one should proceed step by step.

On a day of the sun (Sunday), one should worship Śivā with red garlands, perfumes, and other offerings according to the extent of one's wealth, upon a lotus marked with a wheel drawn on the courtyard;
and one should oneself [offer] white lines, sacrificial oblations, parched grain, clarified butter, and cow-products.
Let him offer the oblation, scattering the *bali* together with young water and rice-balls.

Whether one thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or a billion times, one should offer oblations according to the rite; then, at a crossroads, one should cast all the materials, beginning with fire.
This removes the fear of domestic calamities, and there shall be the pacification of all suffering.
That sacrifice, when performed with oblations, brings about the fulfillment of all desires.
Having offered oblations of the *pañcagavya* sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter, one should consume the remainder of the drops;
this destroys untimely death, brings about health, and is purifying. (24.49)
On a surface made of palāśa leaves, with flowing lines divided by sages, let him write that rite and its name again in the central square; then,
let him place the lords of the worlds in the intermediate directions and the mantra-syllables in the squares of existence.
If one should dig according to the ritual procedure for recitation and so forth, provided that one has mastery over oneself.
In the months of Leo, Aries, and Sagittarius; on days of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, and the Sun; and under the asterisms of Viśākhā, Mūla, Śravaṇa, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and Bharaṇī. (24–51)
Having constructed the nine sacrificial pits as previously described and having simultaneously established fires within them,
one should worship Mahādurgā in the eastern pit, as well as her weapons, such as the conch and others.
Having worshipped at the edges of the sacrificial pits, one should worship the trident in the center;
one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Sāvitrī and the Triṣṭubh meters separately.
Having offered [the oblation] into those weapons made of gold, copper, and so forth, one should scatter the *bali* offering and feed the best of Brahmins and young maidens. (24.54)

One should satisfy the preceptor, the officiating priests, and the ancestors with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās), in the nine directions of the city, village, house, and so forth, in their proper order. (24–55)
When these [offerings] are placed in vessels made of cow-hides and properly arranged upon the ground, they indeed effect the long-term protection of villages, cities, and so forth;
yet therein, they are like drops of water upon a bamboo leaf.
Calamities do not find a footing when shaken by the manifest wind. [This is the *vaṃśapatrapatita* meter.
Having split the tree of Brahmā into nine parts, those weapons of merit, falling in the nine directions according to the prescribed rite, [are described as being of nine kinds].
The method for protecting that [ground] consists of materials brought from outside the village, city, and so forth;
furthermore, there is another method using sand moistened by reaching the ocean. || 24-57 ||
The meaning is that by the word "others" (para), this same procedure applies to the sand as well.
Furthermore, having consecrated nine white stones equal in size to bilva fruits, one should cast them in the directions like weapons for the pacification of diseases and other afflictions. (24.58)
On Sunday, one should offer nine handfuls of sugar into the nine directions starting from the east for the planets Nanda, Durga, and Graha, using the *manu* mantra;
then, at midnight, having placed [the mixture] upon the leaf of a poisonous tree in the center, [one should perform] the *saṃpāta-homa*.
The *mandākrāntā* [mantras], when recited over a stone, are recommended for the subjugation of armies.

Regarding the *mandākrāntā*: one desiring prosperity should perform the rite with the sweet-smelling wood of milk-exuding trees, with the most excellent sacrificial porridges (*caru*) of *śāli* and *vrīhi* rice, and with milk and *bilva* fruits, according to the prescribed sequence.
Likewise, by offering eight hundred oblations daily into the fire for each respective substance, one may obtain [the fruit] in the reflection of the sun upon water with flowers.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should meditate on Durgā as she sprinkles herself with a stream of wealth;
by thus sprinkling oneself with water, one shall obtain prosperity.
Having properly invoked the Goddess in the eastern direction and offered oblations into the fire situated in the midst of the eight directions by means of their [respective] forms,
and having meditated while offering a hundred pieces [of the sacrificial substance], he then [offers] one by one into those fires.
It removes all obstacles and fear, and one shall indeed obtain all desires. || 24-62 ||

Having offered oblations with pieces of split *vāmra* leaves joined together with honey, one removes minor passion; for the pacification of the cow-pen, one should offer oblations with *paippala* leaves.
With fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* smeared with cow’s urine, one destroys afflictions caused by planets, enemies, and disease.
One should offer oblations of ghee from udumbara wood, enriched with the tips of leaves, while protecting [the ritual]. || 24-63 ||

From an oblation of *vaṭa* fruits, there shall be intoxication among the Mātaṅgas; by means of their sprouts, they shall be constantly submissive. One should purify them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Through grains, grain becomes easily obtained; and through food, food [is obtained] by means of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
And by offering *lakṣmī* flowers mixed with ghee and honey, one shall also obtain prosperity.
Having offered fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree wrapped with white, black, and reddish threads and smeared with cow-dung, one should cast an offering of red lotuses and food.
Having thrown everything at a crossroads, it brings peace to minor diseases and the like.
Then, having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of the dung of a Kapila cow from the sky (dried) and smeared it with fire, one should recite the mantra from sunrise until midnight.

If one cuts that poisonous [plant] in the forest and, with a red garment, performs an oblation at the end of daybreak on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the enemy of this person shall meet death. (24.66)
For the sake of self-protection, one should touch oneself with the mantra *sa naḥ parṣat*.
One’s own self must be protected especially by means of fire-offerings, gifts, consecrations, and so forth.
In a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), within the fire, one should fashion an image of the enemy made from the wood of the kṣvela tree,
equal in size to the enemy, with limbs variegated by honey and filth, and beautiful in appearance.

Having assumed the *adhovaktra* posture in a thorny forest (*śikhariṇīvana*) at midnight, one should offer a thousand oblations of *kṣvela* fuel-sticks along with a thousand measures of pungent ghee. (24–68) *Śikhariṇī*.
Forty-four days prior to the spring festival (*madhava*). (p. 100)
If he enters the mouth of Death and yet lives,
then, O child, by offering an effigy made from a calf born that very moment, washed with water and sprinkled with cow’s ghee, he shall likewise not remain [in that state]. (24.69)
One should recite the mantra again until it has been reduced to ashes. || 24.70 ||
In this case, self-protection must be performed by means of an ablution with the five products of the cow;
one should give a hundred cows to Brahmins, for that is remembered as the expiation.

From the offering of the five parts of the enemy’s poison-peak, there shall be the destruction of the foe; with fruits, there is paralysis; with leaves agitated by poison, the subjugation of the enemy;
likewise, with flowers, hatred arises; and with caru-oblation mixed with ghee, pacification is said to occur.
Having performed his own protection through ritual bathing and other means accompanied by mantras, he should recite that [mantra].
Oṃ! May Jātavedas and Durgā, the bestower of boons, be gracious to me. Through their favor, may all that I desire be accomplished everywhere. || 24-73 ||
This is the mantra for attendance.
Now, another method regarding the Triṣṭubh meter is being described here; Agni Jātavedas is the deity, and the remainder is prescribed as before. (24.74)

One should bathe at the three periods of the day, restrain one's speech for twelve days, and subsist on milk; or, if desired, one may practice begging for alms or even eat fruit. Furthermore, one should perform the vow known as Āgneya here, and then recite [the mantra] a thousand times.
Having offered here a sacrificial oblation of cooked rice for Agni accompanied by clarified butter, one should perform the libation. || 24-75 ||
One should feed a thousand, a hundred, or at least ten Brahmins;
remembering the divine fire, one should offer clarified butter to them after receiving their blessing.
Oṃ! May Agni Jātavedas be pleased; may my vow be fruitful.
May this mantra bear fruit quickly, and may there be eternal success. (24.77)
Thus one should complete the vow. (p.
101) Having duly immersed oneself in a river flowing toward the ocean, one who is submerged should remember the fire in the heart and mutter the mantra one thousand times.
There shall be an expiation that destroys all evils; by offering a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter with white lotuses for ten days, one shall behold the Goddess Śrī.
By offering grain for grain, one obtains grain; by offering deformed wood-apples (bilva), one obtains fortune and wealth.
By offering pills made of cow-dung and clarified butter, one becomes possessed of cattle. (24.79)

Subjugation is achieved with sweet offerings of *siddhārtha* seeds; likewise, with fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree, and with fuel-sticks of the *śamī* tree, there shall be peace. From an oblation of *audumbara* wood, food is obtained.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) from a white cow that has a calf of the same color,
and eating the remnants, one who is happy shall obtain prosperity within three months.
If one recites this for a long time at the three junctions of the day, one necessarily obtains longevity, the removal of disease, prosperity, protection, sons, and victory through destiny; moreover,
one obtains all abundant goals, and if one so desires, even liberation.
Free from desire for a thousand [worlds], he is supremely devoted to meditation within the lotus of the heart.
If one goes while reciting this, one will not be harmed by thieves and the like;
the Śakkarī verses, when practiced and cast [as mantras], shatter thieves, serpents, and other such dangers. (24.83)
One who is pure should mutter the mantra with speech; one who is impure should mutter it with the mind.
By meditating thus upon Durgā, as well as upon the god Agni, one shall attain one's desired goal.
Thus, indeed, by virtue of being the essence of the traditional teachings concerning Jātavedas,
he who always remembers [him] shall surely bear fruit in all his desired aims;
and whoever here [practices] through recitation and other means, he shall become that very [state] before long.
The frontal globes of his tusks are bowed down by the lotus-like face of Kamalā, who is known as the sovereign wealth of the three worlds.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, concerning the five Durgās beginning with Traiṣṭubhā, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.

Your pair of ears, with their eyes, is white and situated upon the plow-bearer; the fire is on the left side of the one-eyed one, together with its ear; what word is both white and possessing an eye? (25.1)
"svapiṣīti bhayaṃ śabdo me'nte syāt samupasthitam | śaḍi yakyaṃ phayakyaṃ hāṭanme bhagavati yapha śa ṭhaṭha ||" This is the thirty-seven-syllable mantra of Vanadurgā. (25-2)
The seer for this is proclaimed to be Atyāraṇya; the meter is Anuṣṭubh;
and the deity is Vanadurgā, the sovereign of all. (25.3)
One should compose the mantras for the individual limbs, measured respectively by four, eight,
six, and four syllables; and one should likewise arrange those groups of syllables within the body according to the six classes of meters.
Then, one should again perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) starting from one's own heart.
There are ten joints in the two legs— the anus, the two sides of the vulva,
the abdomen, the heart, the two breasts, the throat, and the pair of shoulders; furthermore, there are six joints in the face, the nose, the eyes, and the ears.
He should place the *viti* between the eyebrows and deposit the collection of vowels (*ke'rṇagaṇa*) there as well.
Initiated by the excellent Guru, he should perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred thousand times according to the rules;
he should offer ten thousand oblations into the mouth of the fire with sesame, sacrificial porridge, and cow’s ghee.
Furthermore, every day he should worship and also recite [the mantra] for the Guru and for Śiva and Śivā.
If he is devoted even to Hara, he shall attain perfection.
The Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras and Other Matters.
Now, regarding the *dhṛti*:
one should meditate upon a garden filled with blossoming creepers and intoxicated bees.
On the slopes of the Snowy Mountain, it is endowed with *kalpa* trees rich in various flowers;

in its center is a divine pedestal made of nine jewels with lion legs, and upon it is a red lotus with smiling eight petals, abounding in a pericarp and filaments, entwined by flowering creepers. (25–7)
Therein, one should worship that which is called the Vajrāsana by means of its own name;
likewise, one should worship Prakṛti with the three qualities (guṇas), the Image (bimba) with the forms (mūrtis), and the Lotus. (25.8)

In the filaments, there is a circle of the [eight] limbs; then, at the tips of the petals, there should be the [eight] Śaktis beginning with Āryā, bearing a discus, a conch, an arrow, a bow, a shield, and a sword.
Richly smeared with red [pigment], they hold in their hands a bowstring and another skull-bowl filled with blood.
All those on the outer enclosure have red limbs; they are surrounded by the Mothers and the World-Guardians as before.
Āryā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Ambikā, Kṣemyā, Vedagarbhā, and the eighth is Kṣemakārikā. (25.9–25.10)
Having worshipped these [deities] with their respective names,
one should then invoke Śivā in the center of the pericarp of that lotus, or in a painted image, or upon a physical ground.

One should meditate upon the Goddess Aṅgalekhā, who possesses the luster of emerald, stands upon a lion, and holds in her arms the Śārṅga bow on a lotus-petal to her left, while the discus, sword, arrow, or trident are held in the others;
she is adorned with red perfumes, garments, and other ornaments.
I bow to Durgā, who has three eyes and is adorned with bracelets, crowns, necklaces, and other ornaments. (25.12) Aṅgalekhā:
One who desires victory and the like, as well as one who seeks protection, should worship her in this form;
likewise, one who desires prosperity or sovereignty should worship her in the form that will be described hereafter. (25.13)
Resplendent with gold, seated upon a golden lotus, holding a conch and a discus,
granting the gestures of fearlessness and boons, adorned in white ornaments, possessing a divine form, three-eyed,
and beautified by golden jewels, pearl necklaces, and the like, with a lovely crown upon her head.

I bow to Durgā, who wears a digit of the moon, amidst a multitude of maidens. As before: one should worship Śivā by resorting to one of these two paths—either from the solar disc in the courtyard and so forth, or from the *dvādaśānta* in the house and so forth.
Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra and gratified him with the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) and services such as the arghya offering,
one should worship the eight weapons, beginning with the conch, in the external directions according to their sequence.
One should worship the eight Mothers, the World-Protectors (Lokeśas), their respective weapon-enclosures, Nirmālyadhāriṇī in the northeast, and Siṃhikā.
Having thus performed worship up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa), or even mentally if one is unable, by reciting and meditating upon Mahādurgā, one shall attain all desires. (25.18)
The Section on Worship:
Or else, for the purpose of subduing enemy armies and the like, [one should worship] the Supreme Goddess with extreme fortitude—

One should meditate upon her, who resembles a rain cloud, possessing three eyes, holding in her arms a conch, shield, bow, skull-bowl, mace, fist, club, goad, discus, sword, arrows, trident, thunderbolt, spear, fire, and noose, and wearing a garment of tiger skin.
Seated upon a lion, adorned with serpents, and sporting like a tiger in the slaying of enemies—this is the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita* [meter].
Or else:
seated upon a lion, possessing sixteen arms as described for the weapons, and terrifying with the brilliance of lightning—this is the *Śārdūlavikrīḍita*.

One should meditate upon Durgā, who is red in color, adorned with serpents as her necklaces and bracelets, possessing three eyes, and surrounded by hosts of maidens and the Mothers equipped with various weapons;
she is thus enraged for the slaying of the great Asuras, discharging a torrent of missiles and arms. (25–20)

Having meditated upon her and performing sacrifice according to one’s desire, whoever recites the mantra one hundred thousand times— having offered oblations of rice, sesame, clarified butter, milk, and sacrificial porridge (caru)— his mantra shall then be perfected. Or, if one offers oblations ten hundred times, or ten thousand, or even a hundred million times, directed toward her, [the same result follows].
Or even if he desires a hundred thousand [times], that devotee shall obtain all of it, provided he is devoted. (25.21)

Meditating on her as one with oneself, holding a trident in her hand, one should recite the mantra while touching [the patient]; by threatening with the index finger, one shall pacify all diseases. By reciting it while in water at the navel, one obtains one's desired goal.
Indeed, an oblation of lotus, wild sesamum, cow-products, and bilva fuel-sticks removes epilepsy.
Even from an oblation of fuel-sticks of *vaṭa* wood accompanied by *cchuṅga*, one may remove diseases, planetary afflictions, and the like. || 25-22 ||
Sunday and other such days are auspicious for all rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*).
One should commence any rite of a cruel nature (*krūrakarman*) on the ninth lunar day up to the fourteenth.
When an army of enemies is struck by thirty arrows consecrated through oblations of sharp clarified butter, it goes to destruction, fleeing in all directions out of fear;
likewise, sugar-candies prepared according to the procedure taught in the preceding chapter [produce the same effect].
Even by means of the ninefold fortress, they would certainly cause the camp of their enemies to vanish.
Exorcism (*uccāṭana*) is achieved by offering oblations of naturally fallen leaves of the *aśvattha* tree mixed with the dust from the feet [of the enemy];

immobilization (*stambhana*) by its flowers; and death at midnight by using its wood as fuel for the fire. Furthermore, one should fashion an image of the enemy, infuse it with life-force, and then break it apart.
Having thus offered [the oblation] on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should likewise [offer it] to Kākāri, afflicted by blood.
Alternatively, by offering oblations of clarified butter mixed with eternal *samidh* fuel-sticks, the pacification of elephants occurs;

by offering those same flowers soaked in honey, elephants certainly become submissive. By using their leaves, they become intoxicated. Having consecrated cow’s milk repeatedly with mantras, one should wipe [the elephant] with it.
One should protect [the fire] with milk-rice, cow-products, rice, and ghee, and cause it to increase by offering oblations daily. || 25-26 ||
Having cut above the Brahma-tree and having abandoned the lower portion in five ways,
one should likewise divide it into equal parts there, sequentially in the five directions.
Having caused [the image] to fall during an auspicious constellation, he should fashion the conch, the discus, the sword Nandaka,
the Śārṅga bow, and the mace from portions [of the image] and place them in jars containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having established [the fires] separately outside the pit according to the sequence of the directions,
one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter from a cow into each individual pit.
Having performed the *saṃpāta* rite during the counter-invocations (*pratyāhuti*) and having touched [the site], one should mutter the mantra that many times;
by burying it at a village, house, or the like, it shall become a provider of all protection.
Now, regarding the *kṛti* [mantra]:

On a Sunday, one who possesses the wheel [of power] should write this mantra—interspersed with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished—upon a leaf; then, having placed it in the heart of a clay effigy at night and touched it, he should recite it.

For seven days, or at the three junctions of the day, one who is under the power of passion may attract a beloved woman of beautiful countenance; this procedure is declared to be equally effective for attracting men as well. By offering lotuses mixed with honey, one indeed brings a king or a brahmin under one's control.

By means of *kalhāra* flowers, one gains mastery over another; with salt and honey, a village and a city; with *jātī* flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and longevity; with ghee, honey, and lotuses, one obtains wealth;
with curd, nourishment; and with grains as well as the milk of cattle, one obtains grain and cattle—just as before.
On a Sunday, one should draw the orb of the Sun, radiant with colored powders, upon the courtyard; in its center, a lotus with eight petals, complete with filaments and a pericarp;
outside of that, a twelve-spoked [wheel], and further out, a sixteen-spoked rim.
The *mātulaprabhāvṛta* consists of one hundred syllables and possesses a uniform meter (*samānavṛtta*).

Verse: Having placed the fire in the prescribed mandala, which is strewn with handfuls of *darbha* grass and encircled by arrows and swords, one should then worship Śivā in the east and offer oblations.

One should offer the *bali* outside in the various directions with clarified butter, parched grain, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), as well as a thousand red-colored cakes (*lohitāṅga-piṇḍaka*) according to the rules for daily rites and accompanied by the mantras— as before.
One should recite [the mantra] that many times and also feed young girls and Brahmins.
Having worshipped [the preceptor] with gold and garments, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher. || 25-35 ||
One should pray for fearlessness to the Goddess, to Agni, to the Brahmins, and to young maidens;
or for the pacification of planetary afflictions, diseases, and so forth—whatever is desired, that one shall obtain. (25–36)
Beginning from Sunday, by performing oblations for a week or even a fortnight in this manner,
a king shall become victorious and is liberated from all calamities.
The mantra consists of a single *akṣara*, followed by the word for water (*ambumān*), then the long vowel, and thereafter the earth (*pṛthivī*) with the suffix *sānantā*.
At the end of the fierce and difficult-to-traverse [syllables], the mantra concludes with the heart-words *balaiḥ*. (25.38)
Having fashioned auspicious rings from well-prepared triloha or gold,

one should offer clarified butter ten times a thousand or even a hundred thousand times until it drips [into the fire]. Then, having placed that [ring] in cow's milk, one should recite the mantra while wearing it after it has been duly worshipped.
He shall become long-lived and possess great wealth, sporting even in battle like a rutting elephant. [This is] the *Mattebhavikrīḍita* [rite].

In a lotus-shaped vessel called *Bhadra*, which is made of gold and other materials and honored with a water-pot (*kalaśa*), one should fill it with waters from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), flowers, perfumes, gold, jewels, all kinds of fruits, and medicinal herbs.

If he fasts for half the day while performing recitation with vigilance at night, and bathes upon the rising of the sun, he shall be cleansed of sin, freed from disease, and endowed with prosperity; such a man shall live long. (As before.
When this aforementioned consecration has been performed, or when one worships according to rule in the practice of the mudrā-sādhana, [the result follows].

Having invoked the Goddess together with her retinue into that [mandala], and having worshipped the Lords of the Field (kṣetrapālas), Skanda, Śāstṛ, Gaṇapati, the maidens, and the Brahmins at the outer corners starting from the northeast, with foods, garments, gold, jewels, variegated garlands, unbroken rice, and other offerings— (25–41). [The term *citramālā* refers to variegated garlands.]
Now, regarding the natural state:

one should pacify fever with *uttāna* and *āmla* offerings; by offering *galūcī*, one wards off untimely death; and by offering *bilva* with its roots, along with pieces of fruit, fuel-sticks, and sprouts, there shall be prosperity.

By offering fuel-sticks of *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *nitya*, and *khadira* along with weapons, there is the destruction of the enemy army. Meditating on that [goddess] Śukrā—who belongs to Varuṇa (*vāruṇā*), who is intensely yellow, and who wears a garland of golden lotuses—one should bathe, fast for one night, and perform ten thousand, or a tenth part of that, or a hundred [recitations]. (Śragdharā meter) || 25.42 ||
Having offered oblations, one should also scatter bali-offerings with balls of red rice and sleep at night.
Oṃ! Having severed all doubt, O Goddess, O Omniscient One, O Witness of All!
Come yourself in a dream and show me the truth that I desire. (25-43)
Homage to Svapnadurgā!
Having thus prayed to the Goddess, whatever auspicious and supreme matter one perceives in a dream that is connected to the three periods of time— this procedure, known as Svapnadurgā, is declared.

By performing oblations with fuel-sticks of Aruṇa-vata at night beneath a Nyagrodha tree for one month, one shall behold a Yakṣī for the sake of prosperity; one should then meditate upon that Caṇḍikā, who resembles fresh gold.

She is red, resembling a blazing fire, for subjugation and attraction; yellow for killing; smoky-colored for paralyzing and inciting hatred; white for neutralizing poison; and likewise white for liberation.
Alternatively, for all ritual actions, one should meditate upon Śyāmā standing upon a buffalo, granting boons and fearlessness,
and holding a conch and a discus.
For one who recites the Durgā-mantra here, various afflictions such as delusions and the like may torment them;

for their pacification, one should perform the rite with the Mātṛkā-syllables and lotuses according to the method of the Kamala script, using pitchers placed upon a Bhadraka diagram, joined with medicinal herbs, fruits, flowers, gold, gems, and the eight fragrances.
One should perform the consecration with the syllables of the *ṛ* vowel, filled by the Śaktis and Rudras emerging from the lotus in the sky. || 25-47 ||
Having offered those oblations with sesame and *caru* mixed with cow-products, along with parched grain (*lāja*) and clarified butter (*ājya*),
he pours that [remnant] of cow-products back into the vessel and casts it as a protection over these jars, which have been bound by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
He should then sprinkle [the subjects] with the first mantras, ending in *kṣānti*, recited in their proper sequence, for the sake of longevity, health, and prosperity.
Obstacles, planetary afflictions, diseases, and calamities perish; one shall also accomplish all desired goals. || 25-48 ||
The Section on the Forest Fortress (Vanadurgādhikāra).

Time (kāla), space (kha), witness (sākṣi), then marrow (majjā), the word "crusher" (mardani), and the human measure (manu)—this eight-syllable mantra, ending with two *ṭha*s, is known as the Heart of Durgā. (25–49)

Oṃ, salutation to Mahiṣahiṃsikā! O enemy of the buffalo, Śārvi! Huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha! Make the buffalo neigh, make it neigh! Huṃ, O Goddess, slay the buffalo, slay it! Huṃ, O destroyer of the buffalo, phaṭ!
One should arrange these five limbs together with their respective seed-syllables (jātis).
The seer (ṛṣi) is said to be named Śākavatsa, and the meter (chandas) is called Prakṛti. (25–50)
The goddess Durgā herself is accomplished through the practice of one hundred thousand recitations of her own mantra.
Having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should then recite this [mantra] beginning from the ninth day.

One should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess, who holds a bow and a mace in her arms when the planet Mercury is in the water-signs (Pisces or Cancer), while holding a chariot and a sword, as well as an arrow and a goad;
she is clad in crimson garments and other finery, possesses the luster of emerald, has three eyes, and is adorned with a crown and other ornaments.

[One should worship] Mahiṣamardanikā, who resides upon the head of a buffalo and bestows the accomplishment of all goals. Having received the mantra from the guru, bathed, and taken refuge in a recommended place for food, one should perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā) and worship the door-keepers of her temple for the sake of worship.

It is as follows: "Salutation to the attendants of Durgā"—thus everywhere; "Salutation to Kṣetrapāla"; "Salutation to Caṇḍikā"; "Salutation to Ambikā"; "Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa"—thus on both sides. "Salutation to Dvāraśrī"—thus upon the upper lintel (udumbara).
Having discharged the Nārāca weapon and entered within, he sits upon his seat.

Having performed purification of the self and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs, [he worships] with [substances] purified by his own root-mantra, limbs-mantra, and arghya-water. (54)
One should worship Gaṇeśa and the Guru with ritual substances, as well as the seat and other items.

With "Oṃ saṃ prakṛtaye namaḥ," one worships below the ground. With "Oṃ vaṃ vajrāsanāya namaḥ," one worships the lion-throne (siṃhāsana). With "Oṃ aṃ āryāyai," "Oṃ ṛṃ pralayāyai," "Oṃ ṝ mahāpralayāyai," and "Oṃ eṃ sṛṣṭyai namaḥ," one worships the four legs of the lion-throne.
[Then] one worships Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, as well as the bulb (kanda), the stalk (nāla), and the lotus (padma), by their respective names. (25.55) p. 109)
One should place the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire, as well as Ka, Ha, Rī, and Īśa, upon the petals and so forth;
then the limbs (aṅgas) at the tips of the filaments, at the tips of the petals, and in the center. (25–56)
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, Nandinī,
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā, in due order.
Having performed the ritual with long vowels and so forth,

one should place [the mantra] "Oṃ, homage to the Great Lion whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs" upon its pericarp. Then, having invoked Durgā— who is endowed with the form as previously described— by means of the root mantra.
Having worshipped with excellent offerings, one should sacrifice to the outer enclosures.

Namely: to Durgā, Varavarṇinī, Āryā, Kanakaprabhā, Kṛttikā, Abhayapradā, Kanakā, and Surūpiṇī. These, beginning with long vowels and ending with "namaḥ," should be worshipped outside the pedestal (pīṭha) in reverse order at the doors, corners, and directions as the eight weapons. (25–59)

Having worshipped the eight-syllable mantra and others, one should worship Vighna, Sarasvatī, the Mothers, and the Gurus in the [four] paths, and Guha in the cardinal directions, while Siṃhikā is in the intermediate directions.
Then the bearers of the floral remains (nirmālya) are to be worshipped, followed by the lords of the worlds in sequence;
Kālī and the others are to be worshipped in pairs at the four external gates.
Kālī, Karālī, Varadā, Madirā, Vindhyavāsinī,
Suprabhā, Siṃhavaktrā, and the eighth, Daityamardinī.
Having thus performed the sacrifice with one's own attendants through the ritual services ending with the oblation,
one should then dismiss the Goddess from either the dvādaśānta or the heart-lotus.
The Chapter on Worship:

Through offerings of sesame, ghee, and milk-rice, one gains complete subjugation; through lotuses, prosperity; through victory [offerings], triumph; and through oblations of poisoned fuel-sticks and consecrated royal ghee, one attains death [of enemies].

p. 110) With *dvija* flowers, one obtains prosperity for one’s lineage; with *anantaka* flowers, one shall conquer enemies; with white mustard seeds mixed with ghee and sprouts of *haritālī*, it removes disease. As before.
This concludes the section on the Heart of Durgā.

The mantra consists of thirty-three syllables: beginning with *Jvala* (blazing) and the repetition of *Padavī* (foot-step), followed by *Śūlini* (O wielder of the trident), then *Duṣṭapade* (O you who stand upon the wicked), then *Grahānvita* (endowed with planets), then *Pāra* (the further shore), *Bāṇa* (arrow), and finally *Astram* (the weapon).

It is as follows: *Oṃ śūlini! Durge! Huṃ Phaṭ!* *Oṃ śūlini! Varadāyai huṃ phaṭ!* *Oṃ śūlini! Vindhyavāsini! Huṃ Phaṭ!* *Oṃ śūlini! Asuramardini! Yuddhapriye! Trāsaya trāsaya huṃ phaṭ!* *Oṃ śūlini! Devasiddhapūjite! Nandini! Rakṣa rakṣa Mahāyogeśvari! Huṃ Phaṭ!*

Thus, with the limbs [of the mantra], the sage Dīrghatamas becomes [the deity]; then one should oneself mutter the *kakub* of the Uttara [Ṛgveda], which is itself the trident-bearing goddess and the indicator of the syllable that is the presiding deity. || 25-65 ||

One who has received the mantra from the mouth of the Guru, with a restricted diet and speech, should recite it and perform worship at the confluence of the lord of rivers (the Ganges), or at the face of Śiva (Kailāsa), or else on a mountain fragrant with forest blossoms;
or [one may do so] upon the lotus situated on the seat of Hari— therein the constituent limbs of the rite shall be complete.

Then there is the enclosure of the eight-petaled power (*vasudala-śakti*), followed by the enclosure of weapons (*heti-vṛti*), and the enclosure of the lords of the directions. Therein, one should worship the seat named Vajrāsana by its own name,
as well as Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) with the three qualities, the iconic forms (*bimba-mūrti*), and the lotus.

Oṃ to Durgā, Oṃ to Varadā, Oṃ to Vindhyavāsinī, Oṃ to Asuramardinī, Oṃ to Yuddhapriyā, Oṃ to Devasiddhapūjitā, Oṃ to Nandinī, Oṃ to Mahāyogeśvarī—these are the eight Śaktis. [I worship] Śivā, who holds an arrow, a discus, a sword, a mace, a spear, a bow, and a noose in her hands; who possesses the luster of Indra and the blue sapphire; and who is beautifully adorned with ornaments such as a crown.

Or else, during the recitation of mantras and other rites, one should remember her—of peerless vision, with a beautiful face, walking like the king of beasts, wearing shimmering golden garments—or rather, as four-armed and possessing a golden luster. (25–68) As before:
having thus meditated upon the Goddess from the heart or from the orb of the sun... (p. 111)
Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra, one should worship him with the limb-mantras and the various ritual services.
One should worship the four female messengers (dūtīs) situated at the sacred seats (pīṭhas) in the four directions of the Goddess:
Jayā, who is yellow in complexion and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace, with one hand raised.
In the south, one should worship the white Vijayā, who holds a noose and a staff and is accompanied by Sasphoṭā;
and in the west, the dark-complexioned Subhadrā, endowed with eight arms beginning with a conch. (25.71)
One should meditate on the goddess Śūlakātyāyanī, who is white in complexion, holding two jars filled with nectar,
and sprinkling the devotee with the ambrosial waters flowing from those jars.
One should worship Nirmālyadhāriṇī in the northeast and Siṃhikā as well. Now, regarding the form [of the ritual]:
according to the rules for daily practice, one should worship with flowers, excellent fragrant incense, lamps, and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having prostrated with his head bowed low by the weight of devotion, he performed the rite of worship;

and for one who accomplishes this mantra here through the sweet songs and instrumental music of the Madrakas, as well as dances and offerings at the feet of Śiva, there is nothing in this world that is difficult to obtain. (25.73) [Madraka]
The Chapter on Worship:
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one brings the entire world under one's control;
one may even compel yakṣas, piśācas, bhūtas, and serpents to carry out one's desired wishes here by mere word of command.
Even an army abounding in intoxicated elephants, horses, and warriors shall be held back in battle;

wherever there is a treasure-trove upon the earth, he beholds it and obtains it with ease. (25.74) As before, having meditated on Śūlinī as one with oneself, one becomes possessed by her through recitation. (25.75)
One may be liberated from poisons, planetary afflictions, diseases, and the like even by the mere sight [of this image].
One should draw the goddess Durgā upon a white cloth, endowed with eight arms and weapons. (25.76)
One should worship and recite this mantra joined with the Vāmanā, Jayā, and other [mudrās];
then this mantra is quickly perfected. Now, one should worship this [goddess] in Bāṇa.
(112) This supreme [practice] alone brings about the eradication of enemy armies;
by means of meditation and so forth upon one's own unity, one shall conquer the enemy and even delude them. (25.78)
By offering sesame seeds as oblations, one may cause all beings to die in the fire of the funeral pyre;

by casting that which has been consecrated with mantra into a white stone while enraged, one drives away monkeys and birds; and by meditating upon that [mantra], one can summon even a herd of cattle from the sky, or an army buried underground, or one stationed on the path.
Through the Vatsara-homa performed with sesame seeds mixed with honey, one becomes powerful;

by offering a thousand oblations of *pippala* wood fuel, one brings others under control; and by offering oblations with ghee, one obtains what is desired. As before, the application [of this rite] for Vanadurgā has been proclaimed here.
In this [mantra], it is considered equal to that of Mahiṣamardinī and Śūlinī.
This is the section on Śūlinī. [The mantra is: Tāra (Oṃ), two Durgās, Rakta (Raktā), Saṃvarta, and the pair of Agniṭha (Hūṃ Phaṭ). || 25-81 ||
The seer is Nārada, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Khaḍgadurgā herself; the six limbs [of the mantra] are formed by her own syllables in their proper order. (25–82)
By all those [weapons] numbering nine (the enemy of Pura) and one (the mountain), through the mantras of the missiles;
now, regarding the transformation:
may she protect us, who bears the conch and discus along with the sword and the trident in her four arms.

Possessing a splendor as dark blue as a mass of clouds or perhaps crimson, with three eyes and the slayer of Nisumbha, the Blessed Lady— adorned with golden ornaments and wearing saffron-colored garlands, perfumes, and garments— traverses [the world] for your sake, mounted upon a lion that moves with the playful gait of a horse. (25.83) — The "Playful Gait of a Horse" (aśvalalita).

Having obtained Manu from the mouth of a teacher and having contemplated one's own identity with her, one should mutter that [mantra] in battle crowded with elephants and horses, as well as in times of danger or in difficult debates.
He becomes fearless and victorious; one should worship her daily once she has been attained.

By performing special sacrifices and recitations on the White Ninth (Sitanavamī), one becomes a sky-walker (khacara) and possesses qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. As before, by offering a hundred thousand oblations of sesame, clarified butter, and mustard seeds, one becomes a Vidyādhara.
When the mantras have been consecrated by the initial piercing, enemies flee like deer;
and while reciting and meditating, one is not afflicted by thieves, diseases, and the like. (25.86)
One should indeed accomplish this Khaḍgadurgā as being entirely without obstructions.

Thus have been declared the mantras of Durgā, which pacify all poisons, diseases, sins, and fears; he who, endowed with devotion, first masters even one of these by means of ritual worship, oblation, meditation, and recitation, and then worships Śivā here every single day— [attains his desires].
Indeed, the goddess Lakṣmī, sporting with intoxicating grace, constantly resorts to him who has attained the glory of happiness and prosperity. (25.87) [The section] "Matta-krīḍā" [ends here].
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. (25)
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.

The syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), the word for water (*ambhasi*), the word for nectar (*sudhā*), the letter *sa* with the vowel *u*, fire (*agni*), and then two *ṭha*s—this is declared as the root mantra of Vasudhārā, consisting of vowels and consonants. (26.1)
Then there is Sāgnihotra, Ambaka, and Vālī ending with Harāntaga;
these three syllables are called Śrīkarī, followed by the word Dhanadhānyapada. (26–2)
The wife of Fire (Svāhā) is proclaimed when joined with the separate syllable *kari*;
this mantra of Vasudhārā, known as the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*), bestows success. || 26-3 ||
In this context, the first should be the root mantra consisting of seven syllables; with that, one should perform worship.
One should accomplish the second mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, ritual actions, and so forth. (4)
The sage is the Buddha-Muni; the meter is Uṣṇih and Atiśakvarī;
the deity is the one named Vasudhārā, Lakṣmī, who is worshipped by the entire universe. (26.5)

Oṃ vasudhāra! ṭhaṭha—this is the heart mantra. Oṃ śrīḥ vasu ṭhaṭha—this is the near-heart mantra. Oṃ vasuśriye ṭhaṭha—this is the near-heart of the near-heart mantra. Oṃ vasu ṭhaṭha—on the forehead. Oṃ vasuśriye ṭhaṭha—on the head. Oṃ vasu svāhā vaṣaṭ—on the crest-lock. Oṃ vasusvāhā vauṣaṭ—the armor for all limbs. Oṃ vasu svāhā phaṭ—the weapon mantra.
One should recite the mantra to be accomplished three hundred thousand times for the purpose of preliminary service.
The procedure for recitation and worship is prescribed for the twilights and at midnight.
With a purified body, a pure soul, observing silence, and wearing clean garments and so forth,
one should smear the circular image with sandalwood paste at midnight.
Having first prostrated to the five Buddhas and likewise to the eight Bodhisattvas—
namely Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and Ratnasambhava— [26-8]
Amitābha, likewise Amoghasiddhi, and those known by names such as Tārā;
Padmapāṇi, the embodiment of Maitreya, and he who is called Gaganagañja and others. (26.9)
And he who is named Samantabhadra, as well as the one called Yakṣādhipa;
then there shall be the one known as Mañjughoṣa, and likewise the one named Viṣkambhaka. || 26-10 ||
One should meditate upon the most enchanting Mountain of Gold arising from the seed-syllable *trāṃ*,
and likewise, a garden upon it adorned with *kalpa* trees.
In the midst of that, one should visualize a golden ground strewn with divine jewels;
there, having visualized a lotus born from the syllable Yaṃ, one should dwell within it oneself. (26–12)
"Oṃ, all things are pure by nature and equal; I am pure in every way.
With this, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) three times from the head down to the feet.
One should cultivate loving-kindness toward all who are wise and compassion for those who suffer. (26.13)
With a mind always contented, one should cultivate satisfaction toward those of virtuous character and equanimity toward those who commit evil deeds among the classes of living beings. (26.14)
Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ āṃ khaṃ hūṃ—one should perform the placement (nyāsa) three times from the thumb to the palms.
Oṃ! May all the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas be attained; may all the Tathāgatas bestow their blessing.
With these [mantras], one should perform three añjali-gestures in sequence at the navel, the heart, and the head. || 26-15 ||
Oṃ Vasudhāre! Abhitiṣṭhasva mām.
Having bowed to her by placing this añjali upon one's head, [one says]:
Oṃ Samaye! Saumye! Samayaṅkari! Mahāsamaye! Namaḥ Ṭhaṭha.
Having bound that samayamudrā, one should lift it upward and display it. || 26-16 ||
In the same way, one should display the vajra-mudrā with the vidyā of the sādhya;
then, into a golden vessel or similar receptacle filled with water, scents, and flowers—
Having placed the root [mantra] and performed worship, one should sprinkle one's own head with those [waters];
likewise, one should sprinkle the articles of worship and the location with the arghya water.

Then, having visualized [the goddess] beneath the wish-fulfilling tree upon a jeweled lion-throne lotus, one should invoke the Goddess, whose form will be described below, with this mantra: "Oṃ śriye! O Śrīkari! O Dhana-kari! O Dhānya-kari! Come, come, arrive, O Blessed Vasudhārā! Ṭhaṭha! || 26-19 ||
Then, at the time of the ritual, [he beheld] a maiden resembling gold, with full jar-like breasts, a moon-like face, hair as radiant as a cluster of bees,
clad in a bodice, with eyes like blue lotuses, beautiful arms, and a very slender, excellent waist.
Bow down to Vasudhārā, who possesses a radiant form adorned with a golden crown, ornaments made of gold and jewels, pure garments, fragrances, and beautiful garlands. || 26-20 ||
[Kāntimatī, Tanvī—some say: Standing with one foot placed upon the mouth of a jar that showers wealth, she holds a pomegranate in her left hand, which rests upon her bent knee. (26.21)
And others held in their hands a lotus flower containing a water-clock that rains down jewels, from whose dripping stalk a creeper emerged, rich with streams of flowing wealth.
Having thus meditated upon that goddess and invoked her into the mandala with the root mantra,
one should worship her in due order with the root mantra and the ritual services beginning with the water offering (arghya).
One should meditate upon the Buddha named Amitābha, seated upon a lotus below a wish-fulfilling tree; he is yellow in color, established in meditation, with a topknot and a shaven head. (26.24)
One should meditate upon Lokeśvara on a lotus at his side, likewise white, with matted hair, seated upon a radiant lotus, and adorned with a tiger-skin upper garment. (26.25)
On the left side is Vajrapāṇi, dark green in color and likewise holding a vajra;
he is richly adorned with a crown and other ornaments, and his hand rests upon the navel of a lotus.
Oṃ saṃ ṭhaṭha | Oṃ dhāṃ ṭhaṭha | Oṃ raṃ ṭhaṭha | Oṃ vasudhe! ṭhaṭha | Oṃ vasundhari! ṭhaṭha | Oṃ vasumati! śriye ṭhaṭha | Oṃ vasudhāri!

ṭhaṭha | Having worshipped these [deities] located on the tips of the lotus petals in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should worship that Goddess in the center with the root mantra, and Śrī and Mahāśrī at her sides.
To Śrīrūpa, the worshipful lotus, the showerer of wealth, and the maker of the water-vessel;

Oṃ, obeisance to the Wheel-jewel (cakraratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Gem-jewel (maṇiratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Sword-jewel (asiratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Horse-jewel (aśvaratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Woman-jewel (strīratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Man-jewel (puruṣaratna). Oṃ, obeisance to the Elephant-jewel (gajaratna).
One should worship these seven jewels situated upon the lotus in front [of the central deity]. (26–28)
On both sides of them were those called Yakṣas and Nāga-kings; above them were the sons of gods, who had come to serve him, bowing down in devotion.

In this manner, one should worship her together with her retinue with perfumes and other offerings in due order, using the mudrās to be described hereafter, along with the [eight] Vasudhās in succession. (26–30)
The mudrā known as the *samaya* consists of the two thumbs placed within;
by releasing the index fingers and the others, there are three [mudrās] known as *puṣpa* and so forth. (26–31)
Placing the tip of the little finger upon the tip of the thumb in the form of a vajra,
with the remaining fingers released, this is called the *dīpa-mudrā* by the masters.

Having joined the palms in the shape of a vessel by joining the two thumbs at the sides, this is the *naivedya* (food offering) mudrā; then, the fingers should be extended outward from each other. (26–33)
The general mudrā is prescribed for all occasions of salutation;
one should touch [the forehead] with the two index fingers, which are bent at their third joints. (26–34)
With the thumb slightly extended in the mudrā known as the "Vehicle," one should recite the fifteen-syllable mantra of the sādhya at midnight. (26.35)
One should worship her according to the prescribed rite with the seven-syllable root mantra;
within a month one obtains wealth, and after six months one becomes a giver of riches.
One should constantly recite the mantra during the forenoon and perform oblations with sesame seeds at midnight;
thus one shall bring a king under control and obtain one's desired object from him.
Alternatively, by offering oblations with white *siddhārtha* seeds, a king shall come under one's control.
A short *śrī* [syllable] situated on the lip of the *vāyu* [letter], with long vowels at the beginning and end, is a "hand" (*kari*). (26–38)
*Ḍhaṇacaṣi ḍhānyacaṣi puṣpakari ṛddhikari avighnakari sarvakari ṭhaṭha*.
This thirty-two-syllable mantra is traditionally taught with its limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth as before.
Through worship, recitation, and meditation as previously described, it shall grant the eight riches (*vasudhārā-iṣṭa*). (26–39)
Now, another ritual procedure for the previously mentioned mantra to be accomplished is described:
[on a golden beach of the Ocean of Milk, adorned with a garden of Kalpa trees]. (26.40)
In a place filled with golden birds and deer, one should visualize a golden pavilion,
ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.
That pavilion was constructed by Upendra with his intellect for the sake of the Goddess,
featuring one thousand and eight divine pillars made of jewels.
It had stairs made of lapis lazuli and floors inlaid with crystal;
it was filled with hundreds of lotus ponds and beautified by divine gardens.
It was adorned with arches, parasols, water-pots, lamps, sprouts, and chowries,
and embellished with conch shells, crystal discs, banners marked with wheels, and mirrors.
Adorned with other auspicious ornaments and draped with strings of pearls,
one should then meditate upon a jeweled lion-throne in its center.
Above that, one should visualize a great lotus adorned with a thousand petals; upon its pericarp resides the goddess Vasudhārā.
p. 118) That is to say:

at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), upon a jeweled lion-throne, on a glorious red lotus with many hundreds of petals, she whose lotus-feet are well-established, who has the complexion of a dark sapphire, whose jar-like breasts are lofty, and whose moon-like face is beautiful;

I bow to Vasudhārā, whose body is adorned with the finest ornaments such as necklaces, gem-studded garlands, and golden crowns; who is richly dressed in variegated garments, who holds a pomegranate and a skull-cup in her left hands, and who bestows fearlessness. (26-47) Having meditated upon the Goddess in this manner, [one should contemplate] the one situated at her right side. (26-maṇimālā)
The Lord of Wealth, with a water-pot in his hand enriched by streams of pearls and rubies.
And on the left, one should contemplate Samṛddhi, of divine form, constantly fanning [him] with a preeminent chowrie that has a golden handle. (26.49)

Oṃ, homage to Dharma. Oṃ, homage to Buddha. Oṃ, homage to Sahya. Oṃ, homage to Sāgaranirghoṣa. Oṃ, homage to Vajrarakṣa. Oṃ, homage to Taruṇi. Oṃ, homage to Āryāvalokiteśvara. Oṃ, homage to Prajñā. Oṃ, homage to Sarasvatī. Oṃ, homage to all Bodhisattvas.
One should worship these in sequence in the ten directions beneath the lion throne.
Having performed the placement with the previously mentioned mantras of the six limbs, one should bind the directions. (26–50)
Having thus worshipped her together with her retinue according to the prescribed rule, one should remain silent and pure while reciting the mantra, always speaking only the truth. (26.51)
One obtains the fruit of this mantra especially through truthful speech;
one should offer oblations with lotuses mixed with clarified butter, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
Then, through daily practice, worship, and oblations, the practitioner shall become glorious by means of the mudrās and mantras previously described, in their proper sequence.

By sacrificing and reciting [mantras] at midnight or at dawn, one shall obtain prosperity; likewise, by staying in the shade of a *bilva* tree while using *bilva* fuel-sticks or its fruits [for sacrifice]. (54)

Having offered oblations eight thousand times daily for six months, one shall become a sharer in a kingdom; likewise, he who, observing a vow of milk for a fortnight, recites [the mantra] every morning after having performed the libation.
Meditating upon her at midnight, one shall become a lord of wealth and grain;
and in the morning, one should satisfy her with eight thousand auspicious libations of water. (26.56)
Within one month, however, there shall be prosperity, and he shall bring the three worlds under his control,
provided he meditates, worships daily, recites the mantra, and performs the libation.
One attains great prosperity within a single year; of this there is no doubt.
By means of *dūrvā* grass one gains longevity and health; by lotuses, well-being; and by *bilva* fruits, fortune and wealth. (26.58)
By offering oblations of fresh clarified butter mixed with clarified butter, one obtains garments;
and by anointing the mandala with sandalwood paste at midnight, one likewise attains them. (26.59)
Having scattered various flowers and invoked [the deity] therein, one should worship;
having offered a hundred lamps of ghee, one should honor [the deity] in due order with perfumes and other offerings. || 26-60 ||
Beginning at midnight until the break of dawn, one should recite the mantra while remaining awake, keeping Vasudhārā in mind. (26–61)
Then, standing in water reaching up to the navel, a stream of gold as thick as a man shall fall from the tip [of the mountain] one thousand and eight times. (26.62)
Within seven days, Japan receives nourishing rain;
[this occurs] when the Goddess is worshipped according to the prescribed rite on a cloth measuring five *prādeśas*. (26.63)
Having drawn [the mandala] enriched with the aforementioned forms, one should worship it; thus one shall become a partaker of success.
This should be done at dawn and at midnight upon a mandala smeared with sandalwood paste.
