Having worshipped her and reciting [the mantra] while performing oblations as prescribed, one attains the stated fruit. This concludes the section on Vasudhārā.
Then follows: the *tāra* (om), the heart, the navel, the middle of the arms, and then water. (26–65)
*tvaksthaḥ*, *ṣaḍhi*, *bhautika-aṇḍye*, *mīnaḥ*, *araṇyaiḥ*, *dharārṇakau*, *umākāntaḥ*, *sadṛk*, *ca*, *atha*, *dharerṇau*, *ṭha-dvayam*, *manuḥ*. (26–66)
(120) This mantra, beginning with *Tārā* and consisting of more than eighty syllables, is called the *Bhūhṛdaya*.
It possesses its own letters numbering [three] Rāmas, [four] Vedas, [three] fires, and [three] Guṇas. (26.67)
One should arrange five limbs, each possessing its own meter, in due order:
the Seer is Varāha, the metre is Nicṛt, and the deity is Bhūmi. (26.68)

A hundred thousand [recitations] with the preliminary rites and a tenth part (ten thousand) of oblations of milk-rice and clarified butter shall bring this mantra to success; now the procedure for daily worship is described.
At the root of my wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), upon a jeweled pedestal of golden earth, one should meditate on a white lotus; having invoked the Goddess therein, one should worship her. (26–70)
Namely:
the supporting power, the tortoise, and likewise the seat of Ananta;
the qualities beginning with Dharma, together with the mandalas of the sun, moon, fire, and the Lord. (26.71)
Having worshipped the seed-syllable of the earth (Bhū-bīja) in its pericarp, one should invoke the Earth of divine form within that [pericarp], which is the star of its image, using the root mantra.
Now, regarding the invocation:

[I meditate upon her] who is dark-complexioned, of tender form, with eyes as tremulous as blue lotuses, in the bloom of youth, wearing a golden crown, enriched with natural ornaments, and holding in her hands a pair of lotuses and blue water-lilies.

Bow here on earth to the beloved of the Enemy of Mura, whose garment resembles the shimmering waters of the celestial river Ganges flowing between the tracks of the Krauñca bird, and who is adorned with a yellowish-golden garland of fragrant flowers.
(26.73) Having thus meditated upon the Goddess Dharaṇī, one should worship her in due order with ritual offerings.
And with the limbs, Vāsudeva and the others, stationed at the tips of the lotus petals in the cardinal directions.
One should worship Water, Fire, Wind, and Space in sequence upon the petals at the corners— having the colors white, red, black, and transparent, and possessing the bodies as previously described.
One should worship the four female messengers situated at the sides of the Goddess and those located in the corners:
the one with the fly-whisk, the one with the mirror, and the one with the casket for jewel ornaments. (26–76)
And they carried betel-boxes that shone like gold,
as well as the principal mountain ranges, the oceans, and even the rivers, trees, and medicinal herbs.
And one should offer lamps with their respective names, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) together with their retinues, weapons, and vehicles.

Outside of that, one should worship the eight elephants of the quarters, beginning with Airāvata; thus, one should worship her, together with her retinue, with the ritual offerings as previously described.
Having performed worship, one should offer rice with curd, accompanied by ghee and side dishes;
or, having offered cakes and fruit, or well-prepared rice with curd.
Having also invoked the Sāman into the fire, or into an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a ritual mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should always offer oblations with ghee and sacrificial porridge (caru), and then dismiss the Goddess.

One who desires the earth should, on a pure day during the rising of the moon, the planet Venus, or the sun, offer into the fire eight thousand oblations of milk mixed with the clay taken from that spot, or alternatively, ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, before long, the earth will come under one's control, abounding in new crops and filled with lotuses and water-lilies.

By offering oblations with fresh blue lotuses sprinkled with sweet substances, a king obtains wealth as well as the status of sovereignty. (26.82) At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should scatter the *bali* offering a number of times equal to the syllables of the mantra.
This mantra is especially a granter of all desires for one who is devoted to Viṣṇu. (26.83)
The Chapter on the Heart of the Earth: The mantra of Tripuṭā consists of three syllables, being the essence of the seed-syllable of Śrī Kāmaśakti;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) in due order by repeating those seed-syllables. || 26-84 ||
Seated upon a lotus pedestal at the foot of a celestial tree on a golden sandbank within the womb of the ocean—
possessing nine petals according to the number of Vedas, the three-eyed goddess with the luster of fresh gold, adorned with a crown and other ornaments,
six-armed, holding a pair of lotuses, as well as a noose, a goad, a flower-bow, and arrows.

I bow to the Goddess of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī), who is saluted by the universe, who wears red garments and ornaments, and who is praised by all. (26.85) As before, there should be an enclosure with her own limbs;
one should worship the first [set] on the filaments starting from the north, and the female messengers (Dūtīs) on the tips of the petals, with their hands joined in *añjali*. (26.86)

To Ghṛṇinī, to Sūryā, to Ādityā, to Prabhāvatī—having thus worshipped that Goddess, one should then perform the concluding sacrifice in due order. The illustrious one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; he shall bring the world under his control. (122) 26–87.
By offering oblations mixed with bilva leaves, fruits, and other such items, one becomes wealthy;
by offering sweet substances mixed with the powder of apāmārga seeds and bones, one may bring the world under one's control.

Then, for the sake of those desiring prosperity, power, and desire, one should worship the Goddess Bījeśī— whose form and other attributes have been described— as seated within the lotus, for the attainment of fortune.
The first enclosure should be in the six-petaled lotus outside [the central circle];
there one should worship Hari, Lakṣmī, Girijā, Smara, and Rati. (26.90)
Outside of that, one should worship her surrounded in sequence by the eight treasures beginning with Padma, by the eight Mothers in the form of women, and by the World-Guardians.
This worship brings prosperity and, in particular, grants mastery over all;
one should apply these very three seed-syllables to the *kalā* in their proper sequence.

Having joined [the breath] with the bindu in the void and meditating on it as red as vermilion, the practitioner, always intent on recitation and meditation, shall bring the three worlds under his control. (26.93)
One should offer oblations in sequence of *bilva*, *samī* fuel-sticks, and *japā* flowers, anointed with honey, for the sake of subjugating the world and for the attainment of prosperity.

The Chapter on Tripuṭā: Tāra (Oṃ), Moṣṭha (Mū), Kha (Ha), Sākṣa (Kṣa), Pārśva (Ra), Rakta (Ra), Meśvarī (Ī), and ending with two Ṭhas (ṬhaṬha)—this ten-syllabled mantra of Umā bestows subjugation. (26.95)
First, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and offer oblations of clarified butter amounting to a tenth part of that number.
In the *Utkṛti* [tantra]: "The Goddess, mounted upon a horse, three-eyed, resembling the luster of a shimmering ruby, [holding] the *bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita* [bow]..."

Having cast a noose and bound the one to be subdued—Umā, whose body is rendered helpless by hundreds of the arrows of Smara and who has attained oneness with him—one should meditate upon the Goddess as she draws her toward herself; though she is red in her ornaments, she holds in her hand a very beautiful golden staff which she is shaking.
Meditating thus and reciting the mantra, like another Manasija (the God of Love), one shall indeed bring people under one's control. (26.96)
[This is the Bhujaṅgavijṛmbhita meter:
If one offers oblations with red flowers combined with the three sweets. (26.97)
One brings everything under one's own control; attraction arises from salt.
Where the arrangement of limbs is not mentioned, there the arrangement of limbs should be conceived by means of the Śakti. (26.98)
He shall be a master of powerful mantras, and the [mantra] beginning with the Ṛṣis has been taught previously. This concludes the section on the power of attraction.
O Maheśvarī, [the centers are] the heart, the navel, the middle of the arms, and the two feet. (26–99)

The word "śabdaḥ" (sound), then the two hair-ends (keśāntau), then two "meṣau" (rams), then two "ṭha"s when full; this mantra, beginning with "tāra" (om) and consisting of forty syllables, is known as the Lord of Food. || 26-100 ||
One attains success by reciting the thousand-syllable mantra ten times the number of oblations offered;
[one who] beholds Mṛḍa dancing incessantly in a golden assembly hall while gazing upon the Daughter of the Mountain,
and who bestows upon the Brahmins food of various flavors, desired wealth, and even spotless garments.

If one meditates upon Umā as she bestows [boons], her form radiant, richly adorned with beautiful garments, flowers, and auspicious attire, and worships her while reciting prayers, then, having cast away all evil, he shall become wealthy. (26.101)
[The Apavāhaka]:
One should always recite the mantra one hundred and eight times during the morning, remaining pure. (26.102)
Within no time at all, he shall become possessed of food, wealth, and a thousandfold prosperity.
This is the section on Annapūrṇā.
O Great Goddess, the pair of goddesses together with the Heart [mantra] consists of "Devādidevī" (Goddess of the gods) and then the word "Sarva."

May the letter *ra* be at the beginning and end of the two words [of the mantra], with *viṣa* (the letter *sa*) in the middle; followed by the long vowel *ā*, the five ending letters (*pa*, *ca*, *ta*, *ka*, *śa*), and the six vowels (*a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *lṛ*, *e*).

Then the pair of *ku* joined with a crescent moon (*śa*), and the wife of fire (*svāhā*). This thirty-three-syllabled mantra of the Goddess indeed subdues the world through meditation, recitation, and other means—just as a fierce rain shower brings everything under its sway—and it bestows prosperity. (26.103)
[This is the *daṇḍaka* meter called *Caṇḍavṛṣṭiprayāta*:
it consists of syllables numbered by the *rasas*, *vedas*, *śaras*, *ṛṣis*, *bāṇas*, and *ṛtus*. (26.104)]
Having performed the assignment of the limbs ending with the weapons using [the syllables] beginning with *svā*, one should meditate on Umā for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*):
she is red in complexion, has three eyes, and holds a noose, a goad, and a pair of lotuses in her hands. (10.5)
Or else, one should meditate on Lalitāṅgī, who is Śrī in the form of Lakṣmī;
having bathed in a river, one should perform the preliminary rite by reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times.
One should consecrate water seven times with mantras and, while recollecting Śiva, wash one's face daily; this is pleasing to all. (26.107)
Having smeared one's face with oil consecrated as before, or with fragrant substances such as saffron and the like, whatever beings one may behold, one shall bring them all under one's control.
One should wear flowers touched by that [mantra], a garland, or perfume for the purpose of subjugation;
one should also recite this [mantra] upon entering villages, royal palaces, and the like.
One shall immediately accomplish one's desired aim; this rite is the same for both women and men.
By means of a mantra joined with the [deity's] name, one should perform it with *japā* flowers soaked in honey. (26.110)
One who performs oblations one hundred and eight times, or even a thousand times, acts as a subjugator;
or by reciting [the mantra] joined with the names [of those to be influenced], one shall bring each and every such person under one's control.
Having bathed in the morning on the fifth lunar day, one should worship Śrī upon a mound of sand with one thousand and eight flowers offered with palms joined in reverence.
One should worship with perfumes and other offerings and obtain wealth such as gold, clothing, and the like.
This concludes the section on the mantras of the Goddess. [The mantra] consists of the word "Hṛdaya" followed by "Bhagavatī," and joined with the words "Mātaṅgeśvarī. (26–113)
The word *sarva* joined with *jana*, followed by the enchanting term *pada*;
then *mukharāgiṇi*, the first *sarva*, and *sarvarājavaśaṅkari*. (26.114)

Then, at the end of [the mantra for] all women and men, and likewise at the end of [the mantra for] all wicked beasts, and also at the end of [the mantra for] all beings, [the word] *vaśaṅkarī* (she who brings under control) should be added separately. || 26-115 ||
At the end of the word "vaśa," [insert] "mānaya" and the two ṭha-s;
having extracted these, this is proclaimed as the *mātaṅgī* mantra, which has the color of a chariot. (26.116)
The goddess Mātaṅgikā is known as the attendant of Mahākālī.
Furthermore:
at the end of *namaḥ*, there should be the color of the ear (the letter *ka*); for Ekanetrā, there are two eyes (the letters *e* and *i*). (26.117)
Then Śveta, situated in Someśvara, followed by Caṇḍa, joined with Māṃsa and Akṣi;
at the end of Mātaṅgī and Sarvaśabda, [the word] Vaśīkariṇi, and two Ṭhas. (26.118)
This mantra of Mātaṅgī is also known as Ucchiṣṭa;
the visualization for both is the same, and its application is for subjugation.
I bow to the beautiful lady whose limbs are as tenderly dark as emerald gems, whose hair is adorned with fine locks, whose lotus-face bears a gentle smile like a jasmine flower,
and whose eyes are like blue water-lily petals; she has lips red as ripe bimba fruit, full and lofty breasts,
hands and feet as soft as young sprouts, wears deep blue garments, and possesses a radiant, divine form graced by ornaments such as the conch-shell.

Bow down for the sake of prosperity to Mātaṅgikā, who attracts all the immortals and others with her melodious songs and the sound of the lute. As before, having meditated upon the goddess Mātaṅgī, one should first recite [her mantra] during the two junctions of the day;
by reciting it ten thousand times at night, one will become a master of the mantra.
One may bring everyone under one's control; this ritual procedure is the same for both women and men.
Having eaten at night, one should offer a bali-oblation with the second [mantra] while meditating upon the food of the leftovers.
One should give [the substance] consecrated with the mantra, and one will bring the entire world under control;
or, at the king's gate or in an assembly, one should go about reciting the mantra while looking upon whomever [one encounters]. (26.123)
Having likewise offered flowers and other such items, he shall immediately become submissive;
having ground lac with the three sweets, one should fashion an image of the person to be influenced.
By offering one hundred and eight oblations in that manner, one shall bring that person under control. Having consecrated an image made of rice-flour with the vidyā, one should consume it. (26.125)
One should subjugate [a person] within seven days, beginning from the right foot;
having pierced a crow on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight through its center.
Having cast salt [into the fire], bound it, and wrapped it with a black thread, one should burn it in a funeral pyre fire; where this is practiced a thousand times, it is offered.
By the power of the mantra, he shall perform whatever is desired like a servant;
or whatever food, medicine, fragrance, and so forth is offered with his own mantra. (26.128)

One may immediately bring her under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Thus have been declared the Śaktis according to their primary importance as taught in the *Mukhyatantra*. These Śakti-vidyās are indeed the destroyers of all great sins, defects, misfortune, ill-fortune, diseases, planetary afflictions, poison, calamities, mental anguish, and other sufferings.
For those seeking the fruits of merit, wealth, desire, and liberation, they are like wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadhenu*), always granting the attainment of whatever is prayed for.
These [mantras] are like ships for crossing the ocean of existence, which is filled with the waves of birth and death; they are victorious here and bestow happiness. *Arṇaḥ*.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, beginning with the Vasudhārā [mantra], in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.

Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti—white, joined with the nasal bindu, preceded by the *tāraka* (OM), and followed by the long vowel of the sky (*vī*) and so forth—and having uttered "Sūryāya" and "namas," there arises the nine-syllabled solar root-mantra. || 27-1 ||

Oṃ aṃ, O Brahman-splendor, blaze! Homage to the heart. Oṃ aṃ, O Viṣṇu-splendor, blaze! Svāhā to the sun-like head. Oṃ aṃ, O Rudra-splendor, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Oṃ! Vaṣaṭ to the flaming crest-lock. Oṃ aṃ, O Maheśvara-splendor, O wielder of the trident! Huṃ! Hum to the armor. Oṃ aṃ, O Satyasadāśiva-splendor, O wearer of matted locks! Phaṭ to the weapon. Oṃ haṃ, O Śiva-splendor! Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes of power.
These are the limbs of the Sun, [to be placed] upon the two hands purified by his own weapons.
Having assigned [the mantras] to the fingers starting with the thumb in sequence, one should assign the weapon-mantra (astra) to both palms.
Having sequentially placed those very limbs upon the head, face, heart, genitals, feet, and the directions, one should likewise place them in sequence upon the heart and the other [limbs].
One should perform worship, recitation, and so forth; one attains the desired accomplishment.
Its seer is Śuṣkika, its metre is Jagatī, and its deity is Ravi. (27–4)
One should worship him at a river flowing to the ocean or on a mountain peak;
furthermore, one should recite his name one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rules during the rite of preliminary service (puraścaryā).
With fuel-sticks made of bilva, palāśa, udumbara, and pippala wood, smeared with clarified butter, curd, and honey, [he should offer oblations] ten times that number.
One should offer oblations according to the prescribed rule according to one's ability, and also feed Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, indeed, there are the applications for one whose mantra has been perfected. (27.7)

One should subjugate Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa*, *pippala*, and *udumbara* wood; however, women should be subjugated like Śūdras using *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.
One may bring all castes under one's control by means of apāmārga plants soaked in ghee;
standing in the water of a river flowing to the ocean with arms raised upward.
By reciting it eight thousand times daily at a height reaching the navel, one shall become wealthy.
Within the mandala of the Sun, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, golden-hued and four-armed.
Meditating upon Him who holds in His hands the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace, one should also recite [the mantra];
thus one attains all desires as well as liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to attain. (27.11)
Whatever may be desired that has been indicated by this very [deity], one obtains it through this mantra by means of recitation, meditation, burnt offerings, and so forth. (27.12)
The general procedure for the worship of this mantra and other solar mantras is now described here in summary, according to the rules. (27.13)
p. 128) It is as follows:
Oṃ! Having separately invoked Tejānvita, Tathā, Sūrya, Āditya, Tigmatejas, Vaikuṇṭha, and Tārādi—each by name—|| 27-14 ||
The mantras for the invocation of the Sun are those beginning with "I invoke" (āvāhayāmi).
Om! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ Sūrya—this is declared to be the mantra for the installation.

One should offer the arghya according to the prescribed rite with the mantra "mahābalāyai svāhā"; likewise, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) with the heart-mantra.
One should bathe the deity with the root mantra and with hymns dedicated to the Sun according to one's capacity;
likewise, one should offer garments, ornaments, armor, and a sacred thread with the root mantra.
The water for the feet and the water for sipping (ācamana) are offered as before, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*.
Then, the fragrance is offered with the mantra "To Khaṣotkā," ending with *svāhā*, and likewise the flower.
With the mantra "To the thousand-rayed one," he offers incense to the Sun with his head;
with the *śikhā* mantra, he offers a lamp, and with the mantra "To the one whose self is nectar" (*amṛtātmane*), he offers other food as an oblation.
Having recited the Sūryagāyatrī, one should likewise worship with ritual offerings, [saying]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala. Then, having entered within and sat down, one should perform the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma). || 27-20 ||
Purifying the weapons, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the limbs, beginning with the heart;
meditating upon oneself as the Sun, one should then prepare the arghya offering as prescribed.

There, one should perform the placement of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-vinyāsa) and also worship the primary limbs. Then, having sprinkled oneself, the place, the image, and the ritual materials with water, one should [proceed] with kusha grass.
"Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Oṃ Guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus.
Thus one should worship Vighna to the south and the Guru to the north.
That [Guru] is upon a seat with an abundant cushion, preceded by the syllable Om and the classes of consonants.
Having worshipped them by their own names, one should then worship their four feet as the four horses:
Vimala, Sāra, Ārādhya, and Sukha, preceded by Parama.
(129) One should worship with names beginning with the groups of consonants ending in *tāra* (oṃ) and *bindu* (m), followed by *namaḥ*.
Likewise, one should worship the Supreme Self seated upon a solar lotus throne. (27.25)
One should worship Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vimalā,
Amoghā, and Vidyutā, in sequence upon the petals of the eight directions.

The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], however, is differentiated by the long vowels; one should place it with a bindu at the beginning and the word "namaḥ" at the end for the Śaktis. || 27-27 ||
Having worshipped Tārā and the others, who face all directions, upon the ninth pericarp,
one should then display the throbbing mudrā to the Sun.
With a steady mind, one should meditate within the heart upon the God who bears the aforementioned form, situated upon a white lotus and established within the orb of his own fiery splendor.

Having filled his joined palms with flowers and having uttered the *khaṣolka* mantra together with the root mantra, [he should invoke the deity] from the lotus at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] by means of the *āvāhana-mudrā*.
Having invoked [the deity], one who is well-composed should establish it upon the lotus with the *sthāpanī* mudrā;
having brought it into close proximity with the *sannidhānī* mudrā, one should then bind it with the one called *niṣṭhurā*.
Having illuminated [the deity] with the *dhenu-mudrā* and offered the *arghya* and other gifts with the *khaṣotkinī*,
one should worship with the root mantra along with its limbs (*aṅga*) and show the lotus and the image (*bimba*).
Having offered the bath, garments, sacred thread, and so forth, one should worship the limbs in sequence:
the heart and the others on the petals of Fire, Īśa, Rākṣasa, and Vāyu. (27–33)

In the center is the Eye (netra), and then the Weapon (astra) in the cardinal petals; [the deities] in the intermediate petals, together with their respective seed-syllables, should have hands granting boons and holding lotuses, beginning with the Heart-mantra, and be beautifully adorned.
One should visualize that weapon as having a reddish luster and a smiling face, appearing in the form of a woman; it is like a mass of lightning, fierce, and possessing formidable fangs.

One should display the *dhenumudrā* for the heart and other limbs, the *govṛṣamudrā* for the eyes, and the *trāsanīmudrā* for the weapon; then one should worship again with perfumes and other offerings.
One should worship Soma, Budha, Bṛhaspati, and Bhārgava in the directions starting from the east; [and one should worship] those situated in the directions of Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśa. (27–37)
One should worship the planets— Aṅgāraka, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu— by their names, beginning with the letters corresponding to their respective stars and so forth, ending with the nasal bindu.
The nine planets, beginning with the Moon, are white, reddish, resembling bell-metal, yellow, white, bright white, black like charcoal, and smoky. (27–39)
They have two arms; their left hands rest upon their left thighs, while their right hands hold a rosary and display the gesture of fearlessness, and they are beautifully adorned.

Then, having pleased these [deities] with perfumes and other offerings, he should worship the Sun with the *vandanyā* mantra; finally, having worshipped the planets in their proper order, he should complete the rite.
Having displayed the lotus-named *bimba-mudrā*, one should offer praise;
then, having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity and offered the *arghya* water, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
Having withdrawn the mantras along with the deity and the planets, together with their limbs, by means of the mudrā,
one should unite them within the heart or at the end of the twelve [fingers] in the solar orb.
One should cause all that, including the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and so forth, as well as the fire, to be given to Caṇḍa,
using his own name preceded by the syllable Om and the group of consonants, in the domain of Īśa.
With the [mantras] well-proclaimed and with the fourth [case ending], there should be "namas" at the end for all;
these six mudrās should be displayed during the worship of the Sun as follows: || 27-45 ||

With the hands facing each other in the shape of a lotus, the two thumbs are laid down in the middle like the pericarp; this is called the *padma* [mudrā]. That same [mudrā], when the middle fingers are joined and the thumbs are touched [together], is the mudrā known as *bimba*. (27-46)

As before, when the hands are joined, by moving the thumbs from the tips of the fingers, it becomes *niṣṭhurā*. Having formed a fist with the right hand, and releasing the index and middle fingers as they spring forth, it is called *govṛṣā*. (27–47)
When the fingers of both hands are joined together, with the tips of the two middle fingers meeting at their tips while pointing upward,
and the ring fingers are crossed over so that the tips of the little fingers are joined, this indeed constitutes the mudrā known as the Cow (Dhenusamjñā).
Having formed a fist with the right hand and extended the index finger, by striking the palm of the left hand with that index finger, one becomes the Terrifier (Trāsanī). (27.49)
The Chapter on the Tilaka of Purpose:
One should extract the letter preceded by *tāra* (oṃ), ending with *s* and joined with the *bindu*; and the beloved letter (*kā*) joined with the *bindu*;
and the second letter of the second [varga] (*ṭ*), followed by the word *ṣotkāya*. (27–50)
This six-syllabled mantra of Bhāskara, along with its ancillaries, has been declared; Yājñavalkya is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is its meter (chandas). (27.51)
The deity is Savitṛ himself; as before, worship and other rites are prescribed for him.
Furthermore, the application (viniyoga) for this [mantra] is ordained to be identical to that previously stated. (27–52)
For the specific rite of *puraścaryā*, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) as before with a tenth part of that number, the mantra becomes perfected (*siddha*). (53)
The attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* occurs through the excellence of *japa*. This is the section on the six-syllable mantra.
[The lineage consists of] Lakulīśvara, born from fire, who wields a staff and possesses the grace of the sixth. (27–54)
This Sūrya mantra, named Saṅgrāmavijaya, bestows all desired objects;
it is itself joined with the long vowels, and the six limbs [of the ritual] are formed from the Astra mantra.
One should assign the syllables of the limbs from the thumb to the little finger;
reciting the sixth [syllable], one should place it with both hands at the base of the palms.
Then, having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) upon the head, face, and heart,
as well as the secret place and the two feet, one should perform the root-mantra placement and the limb-mantras (aṅga) on the heart and other locations.

Having performed the ritual placement according to the rite and having bathed, one should constantly perform worship; one should worship the Sun as before, either in a mandala or in the solar orb itself.
Having offered the guest-water (arghya) and other items up to the final oblation, and having performed worship, one should offer the oblations.
One should mutter the mantra of Sūrya three million times; as before, having offered the oblations, one attains success.
Now I shall describe [the visualization of] Aruṇa: one should meditate on him as golden-hued for the sake of peace and prosperity;
yellow for paralyzing; black for minor rites; and white for liberation. (27–60)
And for victory, one should meditate upon the Sun, who is not tawny and holds a lotus in his hand;
through recitation, fire-oblations, and so forth, as previously described, one shall attain all desires. (27–61)
The Chapter on Victory in Battle.
The mantra for victory in battle is Mārtāṇḍabhairava.
Its limbs are formed by the long vowels, and its five forms by the short vowels. (27–62)
Sūrya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, and Divākara—
these indeed are the five forms of that Mārtaṇḍa.
Everywhere this mantra, encased within the *bimba*, bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The third [letter] from the side resides in fire; it is the witness, indeed the *bimba* possessed of the *bindu*. (27.64)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five forms starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
likewise, one should place the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) starting from the middle finger and ending with the little finger.
One should also perform the pervasive placement with the root mantra from the head down to the feet;
within the form, one should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet.
Then, having placed the limbs in their respective locations like the sun itself,
one should worship while meditating upon the lotus of the maṇḍala of Vibhūti and the others on the pedestal as before.

Furthermore, one should worship the four female messengers (dūtīs)—Uṣā, Prabhā, Sandhyā, and Prajñā—who reside upon the petals of the directions, as well as the powers (śaktis) beginning with Dīptā. (27–68)
Then, having worshipped the Sun with the syllables beginning with *svā* (svāhā) accompanied by the long vowels and the crescent moon,
one should invoke him into the lotus while recollecting his form as it will be described.
He is vermilion-red, possesses eight arms, and is radiant with red ornaments;
he has his beloved seated upon half of his left side, is endowed with four faces each having three eyes,
and holds, in sequence, a beautiful noose, a goad, a pure rosary, and a skull-cup.
Then one should meditate upon him holding a khaṭvāṅga, a lotus, that discus, and a spear.

Having thus meditated upon and invoked the Sun, one should worship him according to the prescribed rule with ritual offerings (*upacāra*), as before, according to one's capacity and in accordance with that capacity. (27.71)
One should recite the root mantra four hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
and the water offering (arghya) should be presented according to the rules upon a mandala smeared with cow dung.
In a pure place, on a riverbank, in a temple, or in a house—on a courtyard smeared with cow dung and marked with a circular mandala one cubit in diameter. || 27-73 ||
Having placed his limbs [in the prescribed posture] and having invoked and worshipped the Sun according to the ritual rule,
he should take an auspicious vessel made of gold or copper, filled with a *prastha* measure.
Having fumigated and consecrated [the vessel] upon *darbha* grass, and having filled it with water using the *aṣṭavārā* mantra,
[one should add] red sandalwood, saffron, *rocanā*, *nandana*, and unbroken rice.
With camphor, agallochum, darbha grass, śyāmā, vānī, black mustard, bamboo seeds, barley, śāli rice, japā, bandhūka, and pomegranate [flowers]. (27.76)
Having mixed that water with red karavīra flowers,
together with the root-mantra of the image and its limbs, one should place it at the dvādaśānta.
Furthermore, it should be accompanied by a conscious intent, honored with perfumes, flowers, and incense,
rendered immortal by the cow’s milk, protected by weapons, and consecrated with the *avakuṇṭhana* rite.
Having illuminated [the disciple] with the Kavaca, Abjabimba, and Mudrā mudrās,
he should look upon the orb of the sun as it is either rising or already risen.
Having meditated upon the Sun, who consists of the three Vedas, in that [lotus] according to the prescribed rule,
one should worship him with the mental services as directed by the ritual injunctions.
Having recited the mantra and offered salutations, he knelt upon the ground;
holding that vessel of *arghya* with both hands, he lifted it up to his nose.
Having meditated upon that supreme nectar on the head of the solar form,
one should offer the *arghya* with the root mantra, together with its limbs, ending with "namaḥ."
Then, one should meditate upon the Lord, whose body is gladdened by the immersion in that nectar, situated within the *bimba* [image], as well as the forms and mantras within the mandala. (27.83)

Having joined [the palms] and said, "Forgive me," he should release [his hands], wash his feet and hands again, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then enter the interior of the temple where the deity is enshrined. || 27.84 ||
Having invoked the Sun into a golden or copper lotus measuring a span, one should worship him with materials acquired according to one's own means.
Whatever one desires among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, that one shall obtain;
and one should constantly recite [the mantra] ten thousand times, a thousand times, or even a hundred times. (27.86)
Through the excellence of worship, fire-offerings, prostrations, and recitation performed with supreme devotion,
the attainment of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and others occurs for him before long.
If one offers a hundred thousand oblations with human flesh, oil, and sesame seeds used for striking,
one obtains a hidden treasure that was previously unknown through the power of this rite.
By offering oblations of cow-ghee, rice, bilva, and clarified butter, one obtains a treasure;
likewise, [the smoke from] lotus filaments, fragrant stones, and the crest of a cock are equal [in effect].
An umbrella made from elephant dung, its lacquer-red resin being the elephant's ichor;
and a wick made from equal parts of white arka-cotton and the rags of the dead. (27.90)
At night, one should light a wick with the oil of human fat and marrow;
wherever there is doubt regarding a hidden treasure, it will appear clearly by the sight of that lamp. (27.91)
A wick situated in a downward flame clearly reveals the treasure.
This is the section concerning Mārtāṇḍabhairava.
Śivottama, however, possesses the nose; Umākānta partakes in the limit of vision. (27–92)
Savāmaśravaṇa, Śukla, Sākṣirakta, Māruta, Ananta, Sūkṣmayukta, Atri, Satvaksarga, and likewise Aṣaḍhī. (27.93)
This eight-syllabled mantra of the Yajurveda, beginning with "sorastāra," bestows all perfections;
its meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and its sage is Devabhāga. (27.94)
The deity is the god Savitṛ, the bestower of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.

(p. 135) *Brahmatejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. *Viṣṇutejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. *Rudratejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. *Maheśvaratejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. *Satyatejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.
[These are to be placed] on the head, between the eyebrows, the face, the heart, the navel, the anus, and the knees. (27–95)
One desiring enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should place the syllables of the mother-mantras at the feet for the sake of emanation;
for one desiring liberation (mumukṣu), the reverse of this is the placement known as withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Then, at dawn, the twice-born one, having bathed and performed the twilight rites,
stood in water reaching his navel, meditating on the Sun with his limbs and body duly disposed.
Having recited [the mantra] eight times, eight times over, one should daily sprinkle one's own head with water from the joined palms, one hundred and eight times.

One attains prosperity—the abode of wealth, grain, and happiness—without delay, even without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), through worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and other such practices. (27.99)

It certainly bears fruit for the twice-born who abide by the duties of their own caste and stage of life, provided they recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times while standing in water reaching up to the navel. (27.100)
Whatever he desires, he shall accomplish through worship, recitation, offerings, oblations, and so forth;
having established the fire in either a sacrificial pit or on a consecrated mound, he should invoke the Sun.
After the Vedic fire-offering, by making eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of the *pālāśa* tree soaked in clarified butter, one shall attain spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Through offerings of *udumbara* wood one obtains food; likewise, through *bilva* and lotuses, one gains prosperity.
An oblation offered with *dūrvā* grass sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter leads to long life.

For the daughter, [the oblation] is with parched grains smeared with clarified butter; for the son, for the pacification of sin, it is with sesame seeds and clarified butter, encircled by white, reddish, turmeric-yellow, and black threads. (27.104)
With oblations of khadira wood, one may bring the castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, under one's control in their respective order;
by offering oblations of flowers corresponding to each caste, one obtains garments.
In a pure, spacious place, well-smeared and circular,
one should properly invoke and worship the Sun within a new jar used as a ritual image.
One should also offer one hundred and eight oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter;
and for twelve days, while touching the water-pot, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Having fed the twice-born with devotion, he obtains the desired rain;
then, having fasted for three nights and worshipped the Sun according to his ability.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee eight thousand times;
having devoutly fed the twice-born with milk-rice and clarified butter according to one's ability.
For twelve days, or a fortnight, or a month, or even for three months;
thereafter, when his wife has bathed after her menses, he should cause her to consume the remains of the oblation.
Then, having empowered it one hundred and eight times with the mantra, he obtains a son;
having invoked the Sun into the water-pot as before and worshipped him with devotion. (27.111)
Having recited [the mantra] over one adorned with perfumes, jewels, gold, garments, garlands, and so forth, one should perform eight thousand oblations; by means of that, there shall be consecration.

For one who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*), the pacification of planetary afflictions, untimely death, disease, and so forth, occurs immediately; this is true whether one recites [the mantra] for one year, or year after year, or even for many years. (27.113)
The powers of flight through the sky and other such qualities are accomplished for him without effort;
he who, reciting the Sāvitrī as prescribed, should worship the Sun. (27.114)
Through the daily recitation of the path, fire oblations, and other rites, one shall attain all desires.
The verse beginning with "udyann udyati" in the eastern direction has the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The seer and the deity are as before, and the applications are likewise as previously stated.
Thus, with the solar mantras correctly recited here, there is indeed nothing that cannot be accomplished within the three worlds.
Therefore, by directing devotion toward the Sun, one shall obtain accomplishment, renown, power, and even liberation. (27–116)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Sūryapaṭala, in the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 27.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Having first paid homage to Śiva, I shall describe the six-syllabled Śiva-mantra,
as well as the five-syllabled mantra and other Śiva-mantras in their entirety.
The six-syllable mantra is "Tāram meṣam viṣam sargi śivāya";
that same mantra, when deprived of the *tāra* (the syllable Om), is known as the five-syllable mantra.
The six-syllabled mantra is to be served by Brahmins and others who are fit for the triple Veda;
likewise, the five-syllabled mantra is to be known by women, Śūdras, and so forth. (28–3)
One should employ the *prāsāda* mantra in place of this very *praṇava*.
This six-syllabled mantra is primary; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all. (28–4)
In this regard, it is stated in the *Vātula-śivajñāna-vidyā*:

"One should join that seed-syllable, which begins and ends with the Veda (the letter 'a'), is conjoined with Viṣṇu (the letter 'm'), and is endowed with the Bindu and Nāda, to the fifth long vowel (Ī) within the mantra. (28.5)

"Enveloped by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), this [mantra] should be used for ritual placements (*nyāsa*), recitations (*japa*), and so forth, by Brahmins and others; however, for women, Śūdras, and others, it should be without the *tāra*.
Thus: "The *khaṃ* (the letter *kha*) together with the Lord of Graceful Creation (*sānugrahasargīśa*) and the nasal drop (*bindu*) constitutes the *prāsāda* [mantra]."
This Śiva-mantra is also the cause of the creation, maintenance, and other processes of the universe.
For the teachers know that for all three of these, the seer, the meter, the deity, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the applications (viniyoga), are identical. (28.8)

In this regard, the *Kālottara* states: "That supreme seed called *nāda*, which resides within all beings, is the highest bestower of liberation, divine, and the granter of all accomplishments. (28.9)
It is peaceful, all-pervading, and empty, abiding within the twelve measures;
O Six-faced One, the hands are declared to be Brahman, for the limbs are indeed long.
Furthermore:
"One should join the sixth with the end of the thirteenth in the fifth;
one should know that to be Śiva, Sadāśiva, whose form is the mantra. (28.11) Thus it is said.
Therefore, the arrangement of the limbs of the temple is performed with those long vowels;
in that regard, it should likewise end with the weapon-mantras (*astra*), for there are indeed five Brahmā-mantras consisting of short vowels. (28.12)

Together with the six syllables including the palace (prāsāda) and their own respective seed-syllables ending in the nasal bindu, the heart-mantra and the others indeed become [the limbs] according to their respective classes. (28.13)
For all of these as well, Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi);
Paṅkti is the metre (chandas); and Śiva is the deity (daivata), as is generally prescribed. (28.14)

For the Śiva-principle of Tāra consists of the Prāsāda-mantra together with its power (śakti), as well as the five gross elements and so forth, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the sense organs. (28–15)
Mind, intellect, ego, the person (puruṣa), and likewise primordial nature (prakṛti); passion, knowledge, limited power (kalā), time, and necessity, along with illusion (māyā). || 28-16 ||
Similarly, Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti—these seven indeed reside within the other five groups of five syllables. (28–17)

The establishment of the thirty-five principles (tattvas) is traditionally taught as being in reverse order from what has been stated. Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta are the Nādas. (28–18)
For those desiring worldly enjoyment and those desiring liberation, Sadyojāta and the others [are worshipped] in sequence;
[their colors are] white, yellow, black, smoky, golden, and likewise ruddy.
The meters of the six colors should be understood in their respective order: the Gāyatrī for the first, and likewise the Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, and Triṣṭubh for the others. (28–20)
The Bṛhatī and the Virāj are declared as the meters in their proper order;
and Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Hara, Brahmā, and Skanda are the presiding deities. (28–21)
The locations are said to be in the heart and in the faces starting from the east;
one should place the syllables (varṇas) in sequence upon the two hands, the faces, and the body. (28–22)
Furthermore, one should place the limb-mantras upon the limbs, beginning with the heart;
for celibates there shall be emanation (sṛṣṭi), and for householders there shall be maintenance (sthiti).

For those dwelling in the forest who seek liberation, the ritual of withdrawal and placement (saṃhāranyāsa) is prescribed; one should perform the placement beginning from the right thumb up to the left hand. (28–24)
At that time, emanation proceeds from the thumb [to the other fingers], while withdrawal is the reverse.
The syllables of the mantra reside in the two hands, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger. (28–25)
Having performed the placement for the stability of the limbs, one should likewise place the mantras;
then, having placed the *tāra* (om) joined with the *prāsāda* mantra upon the two palms.
One should place the mantra-syllables on the fingers and the limbs on the two palms;
thereafter, one should also place the *tāra* (OM) and the *prāsāda* mantra upon the heart.
The placement (nyāsa) of the six-syllabled mantra, as well as that of the five-syllabled one, should be performed facing east, south, north, west, and also facing upward.
One should place the five syllables beginning with *na* on the palms, the heart, the fingers, and the seats, and assign the limbs as before. (28–29)
One should place the syllable *tāra* at the beginning and end of one's own name within the finger-joints;
one should place the *tāra* on the first and last joints and the syllables of the mantra in the middle.

For women and Śūdras, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is said to be performed with the [mantra] syllables alone, excluding the *tāra* (the syllable Om), along with the limbs of their own [mantra]. Furthermore, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra from the feet up to the crown of the head.
One should place [the mantras] on the body at the head, face, throat, heart, secret place, and feet;
in the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi) in reverse order, and in the processes of withdrawal (saṃhāra) and maintenance (sthiti) at the heart and the secret place respectively.
Then, one should place the six syllables on the feet, head, face, and throat; or, omitting the throat, one should place the syllables in the other locations in due order. (28–33)

Having thus placed the six limbs, beginning with the heart, in their respective locations according to their own seed-syllables, ending with the weapon-mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions.
Vighneśa, the Mothers, Durgā, and Kṣetreśa should be assigned to the directions in their proper order, using their own names followed by "namaḥ" and accompanied by finger-snaps (choṭikā). || 28-35 ||

By reciting one hundred thousand times the mantra of one's own [chosen] deity, by performing a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds ten times that number, and by worshipping Śiva with devotion, his preparatory rite (puraścaryā) becomes perfected. || 28–36 ||

Even without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), this [attainment] is achieved for a devotee who worships Śiva through the excellence of recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa), as well as through constant practice. || 28–37 ||

In rites such as worship and recitation, there should be three sets of three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas); furthermore, the mental repetition of the five-syllable mantra should be performed forty times. (28–38)
Prāṇāyāma for the castes is also prescribed according to a sequence of decreasing by two [units] each;
one should mentally recite the Prāsāda mantra, together with the Bindu and Nāda, one hundred times. (28–39)
Thus, the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma) has been prescribed for those mantras consisting of a single vowel as well as for others;
at the conclusion of the recitation of that mantra, one should also recite the seed-syllable one hundred and eight times.

Recitation performed by a river, in a temple of Śiva, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), on a mountain, or in the presence of fire, as well as before a guru, the sun, the moon, or a lamp, yields a thousandfold fruit. (28–41)
Moreover:
"But recitation performed at home has a single merit; in a cow-pen it has tenfold merit;
by a river it has a hundredfold merit; and in the presence of Śambhu, it is a thousandfold. (28.42)
Recitation performed in the presence of a self-manifested liṅga is said to be a hundred thousand times more effective;
likewise at divine lakes, sacred fords, mountain peaks, and on the shore of the ocean. (28–43)
In sacred fields, hermitages, and similar places, the recitation becomes ten million times more effective.
For the purposes of subjugation and malevolent rites, one should perform the recitation facing east, south, west, or north respectively.
For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), pacification (śāntika), and liberation (mukti), one should face either the east or the north,
using fingers, lines, *putrajīva* seeds, and coral.
And with beads made of crystal, lotus seeds, gold, and pearls,
as well as knots of kuśa grass and rudrākṣa seeds, respectively.
By reciting ten times for each single bead, one obtains the fruit;
pulling the rosary with the thumb is remembered as bestowing liberation.
For the destruction of enemies, it is taught that one should use the index finger; for prosperity, the middle finger;
and for rites of pacification and nourishment, the ring finger and the little finger are prescribed.
Drawing [the breath] with all [the fingers] together, including the thumb, bestows all desires.
This is the section on the practice of mantra (*mantrasādhanādhikāra*).
(p. 141) Having performed the worship of Śiva, one should then perform the recitation (*japa*) and other rites. (28.49)
One should accomplish the mantra for the sake of success, and thereafter perform its ritual applications;
having first bathed, completed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and entered the sacrificial hall, one should remain pure.
Having worshipped the Sun while observing silence, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should sit down;
then, having performed the purification of himself, he should be smeared with ashes and wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Then, having applied a tilaka mark with sandalwood paste and placed flowers upon his head,
and having sprinkled the doorway with the general arghya water, he [should worship] Vighna and Sarasvatī.
One should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as Nandi and Mahākāla, in sequence at the upper *udumbara* [post], in the middle of the branches, and on the right and left sides. (28–53)
At the base, one should strike the door-deity with three kicks of the heels;
terrestrial spirits with claps of the hands, and those dwelling in the intermediate space and the heavens with snaps of the fingers.
Having warded off obstacles with his own weapon, he should cast the Nārāca weapon and the Prasūnaka flower inside, and then enter, taking refuge at the left branch.
Having placed a flower upon the threshold with a blazing weapon-mantra,
one should worship Brahmā and Vāstvīśa by their respective names, as well as oneself seated upon the seat of Ananta.
Then, remaining silent and having consecrated his body through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
he [visualized] the light of Śiva in his own heart-lotus and then between his eyebrows by means of his intellect.
Having offered oblations into the fire of the navel-pit with the sacrificial materials produced from the "twelve-end" (dvādaśānta),
and having offered the general arghya and performed worship, provided that a *liṅga* is present.
Having removed the floral remains (nirmālya) according to the procedure for the ritual offerings (upacāra) beginning with the weapon-mantra (astra),
and having washed [the image], one should invoke Śiva into the non-empty head and worship him.
Having placed the white Ādhāraśakti upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā),
one should likewise place Ananta as the seat, as well as Dharma and the other [virtues] and the maṇḍalas.

One should meditate upon the lotus, the powers beginning with Śakti on the left and so forth, and the form of Śiva in the center—the form of the All-pervading Lord consisting of the Vidyā, as described in the Prāsāda-bīja mantra. (28–61)
(142) Having five faces as spoken of in the *Pañcabrahma*, or ten arms, or four arms, with three eyes;
bearing the Ganges, the crescent moon, and a multitude of serpents shining upon his excellent matted locks;
holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a trident, and a spear in his right hands, while granting boons and protection with the others—
A snake, a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, together with a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), a blue lotus, and a citron (bījapūra). || 28-62 ||
I take refuge in Him whose body is white, who is seated upon a lotus, who has three eyes, and who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a deer and an axe;
He whose four arms bear the celestial Gaṅgā and the moon, whose matted hair is radiant, who wears serpent-bracelets and necklaces, and who is clothed in an elephant hide. 28.63.
When performing worship with five, six, or seven palas of gold in a temple, these two forms are prescribed; one should take recourse to one of them. (28.64)
Sadāśiva, who has five faces and ten arms, is the essence of the ten vowels; he is accompanied by Manonmanī, his Śakti, who rests upon his left lap. || 28-65 ||
Having meditated, Śiva is to be worshipped in a *liṅga*, whether it be formless (*niṣkala*) or with form (*sakala*),
whether it be a fixed or a mobile *liṅga*, or even momentarily, or through non-existence.

What are those [materials] that are momentary? They are said to be eightfold: that made of sand, that made of clay, that made of flour, as well as that produced from food, that produced from fruit, that produced from fragrance, clarified butter, and cow dung as the eighth. (28.67)
Having made the momentary linga with its pedestal according to the prescribed method, one should invoke the Lord therein, perform worship, and then dismiss Him without further expectation.
Once the Śiva-liṅga has been ritually dismissed (udvāsita), and after having worshipped and released Caṇḍa,
one should cast the temporary seat (pīṭha) together with it into unfathomable waters.

One should [meditate] with the mind upon the lotus of the heart, or in the fire, or in the solar orb, or in water, or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), according to what is appropriate and according to one's preference.
Thus, having invoked the form and the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) residing therein,
[one should worship] with the Brahma-mantras consisting of five, eight, thirteen, and eight syllables.

By means of Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, as they arise in sequence, the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), beginning with the earth element and ending with Śakti, is [established]. (28.72)

Having thus meditated upon the seat ending with Śuddhavidyā, as well as the forms of Śiva ending with Śakti, the practitioner [should meditate upon] the form and the body of knowledge (vidyādeha). (28.73)
One should invoke Śiva as described in the Chapter on Ritual Conduct (Upacārapaṭala),
performing the rites of installation (sthāpana), confinement (saṃnirodha), veiling (avakuṇṭha), and pleasing (prarocana).
The rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) should be performed according to the path described for the ritual offerings (upacāra).
The limbs (aṅgas) and the faces of Brahmā [are assigned] by means of the seed-syllable of the Heart preceded by the Tāra (Om), together with the names.
Having offered a handful of flowers upon his head with the utterance "namaḥ svāhā svadhā vauṣaṭ vaṣaṭ," one should meditate upon the Lord Sadāśiva.

Then, like lamps from other lamps, the limbs of enjoyment were brought forth from those limbs and placed upon the petals of the southeast, south, and southwest, which correspond to the fires, the netherworld, and the wind.
Having placed the Eye in front and the Śiva-weapon in the cardinal directions and petals,
one should then worship the limbs of Śiva, which grant boons and protection.
There, having meditated upon the Astra-mantra as resembling a blazing fire, in the form of a woman with four arms, one should thus worship Śiva in the temple with its single enclosure.
The Chapter on the Single Obstruction:

Śiva, who is concealed by the five obstructions of the mantras beginning with the five-syllabled one, should be worshipped constantly by those who desire the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. (28.80)
Therein, the first enclosure is said to consist of the limbs (aṅgas) and the Brahmās;
the second by the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśas); and the third by Nandīśa and the others.
The fourth [enclosure] consists of the Lords of the World (Lokeśas), and the fifth enclosure consists of their weapons.
For instance, it is said that the first enclosure indeed consists of the limbs (aṅgas) and the Brahma-mantras. (82)
One should worship the eight Vidyeśvaras on the edge of the pedestal, outside the lotus:
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, the one named Śikhaṇḍin, the one named Śrīkaṇṭha, Trimūrti, and Ekavṛdra; they are situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
This refers to [the deities] beginning with Indra and those beginning with Agni, respectively.
Nandi and Mahākāla are in the east; Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka are in the south. (28.84)
In the west are Vṛṣaskanda and Devīpaṇḍa; likewise in the north. The third enclosure consists of the doors.
The fourth enclosure is known to consist of the ten world-protectors, beginning with Indra. (28–85)
"Obeisance to Indra, lord of the gods, together with his weapons, vehicle, and retinue, and to the attendants of Rudra; obeisance to his attendants," and so forth.
When a fixed liṅga is to be worshipped, there, within the enclosure of the world-lords, one should worship Vṛṣabha, lying down, by name, starting from Indra in the east. (28–86)
To the west [of him] is Vighna, and Vīrabhadra is in the west;
between those two are the seven Mothers, who should be worshipped by their own names.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍī—these [should be worshipped] again in front of her. (28–88)

Having worshipped with the mantras: "Salutation to the Mothers! Salutation to all the Mothers! Salutation to all the hosts of Mothers!", [one should place] Śāstā and his son Satyaka to the south of Nirṛti;
and to the south, the goddess Prabhā; and to the east of Vāyu, Durgā. (28–89)
To the west of Dhanada are Skanda and Caṇḍeśa in their respective stations; and to the east of Caṇḍa is Kṣetrapāla. Having worshipped these, one should worship the enclosure of weapons.
When the linga is fixed, those beginning with Vṛṣa and ending with Kṣetrapāla are to be worshipped;
however, others have declared that they are not to be worshipped on a movable linga or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 28-91 ||
The fifth enclosure consists of the weapons: the vajra, the śakti, the staff (daṇḍa), the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, and the lotus. || 28-92 ||
Having thus worshipped Śambhu along with the five obstructions, and having likewise offered oblations of ghee, cooked rice, and sesame seeds into the fire, one should cast the bali offering of food.
p. 145) For example:
"Then the Rudras, the Mātṛs, the Gaṇas, and the Yakṣas are in the eastern direction;
Śarva and the others, along with the foremost of the planets, Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, are in the center."

One should cast the constellations, the intermediate directions and the corners such as the northeast (Īśāna) and so forth, all the zodiac signs, Viśvakṣetrapati, and Durgā into those [locations] in a clockwise direction. || 28-94 ||
In the second mandala as well, the ten world-protectors beginning with Śakra [are to be placed];
and outside of them, the bali offering should indeed be cast with this mantra.
Oṃ, to the crows and others who violate their commitments, ṭha ṭha!
Having gathered the offerings for the *bali* mantra, [one should offer them] upon the maṇḍala made on the eastern courtyard:
"Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes... (28.96).
And those who are gentle, as well as those who dwell in gentle places, the Mothers of fierce form, and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas; || 28-97 ||
May all of you, with well-pleased minds, accept this offering;
may you swiftly grant me success and always protect me from fears.

Having offered the bali-oblation with the words "Obeisance to them and to those [deities]," and then having washed his hands and feet with water and sipped water (ācamana), he should remain silent; then,
having propitiated Him with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise— || 28–99 ||
If Caṇḍa is present, one should offer the food that has been presented and the remains of the garlands (nirmālya) to him;
those such as artisans and laborers should then throw it into water or into fire.
Or even female slaves may eat that, provided they do not fall [from their vows],
following the path of service according to the protocol for serving a universal monarch.
Having mentally rejoiced in the splendors of song, dance, and so forth, one should then recite the mantra before him, followed by the rites of recitation, worship, and the like. (28.102)
One should offer [the recitation] at the feet of the deity with mantras such as those beginning with "guhyātiguhya":
"O protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us. (28.103)
(146) By means of your grace, O Lord, may success be mine, for whatever action—whether good or evil—is always performed while I abide in you. (28.104)
O Śaṅkara, for me who am established in the state of Śiva, destroy [this] with "huṃ kṣaṃ"!
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world. (28.105)
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; he who is Śiva is indeed myself.
With these [mantras], "sāṅga," "mūla," and "aṅga," one should offer handfuls of water.
Now, indeed, there are applications for this perfected mantra, because a mantra falls away from its potency without an application. || 28-107 ||
By reciting [the mantra] eleven times, bathing, sprinkling, food, water, and so forth become bestowers of long life and health for men, and destroyers of sin and defects. (28.108)
A hundred thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and *chinnā* grass overcome untimely death;
they remove all diseases, planetary afflictions, and distress, and increase one's lifespan. (28.109)
By reciting [the mantra] on a mountain peak or by a great river, one shall obtain long life;
likewise, by reciting it one hundred and eight times, facing the sun, for a hundred thousand repetitions.
Offering sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter, one conquers diseases and attains long life;
likewise, on a Saturday, one should touch an Aśvattha tree and perform recitation.
One should drink either the medicinal powder obtained from one hundred and eight [applications] or parched grain flour;
thus one is freed from abdominal diseases, and even poison becomes nectar. (28.112)
Standing facing the sun in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand or a hundred times daily; this increases longevity and health. (28.113)
Having filled a jar with river water, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times according to the rule;
by touching it, there shall be an ablution that conquers planetary afflictions, diseases, and untimely death. (28.114)
The seed-syllable enclosed within its own [mantra] and placed in the belly destroys colic and other ailments;
likewise, [the mantra of] Brāhmī or the essence of ghee [is effective] during lunar and solar eclipses. (28.115)
Having drunk [the substance] while reciting [the mantra] until liberation is attained, one becomes a possessor of wisdom and a retainer of what has been heard.
This should be done on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ārdrā, or likewise on the eighth days of the dark fortnights.
Having fasted for a month prior to the eclipses of the sun and the moon, one whose limbs are smeared with ashes should worship Śiva and also recite [his mantra] according to one's ability. (28.117)
Having drunk one *pala* of white *vacā* powder mixed with four *palas* of tawny clarified butter, consecrated ten thousand times with the mantra, one shall attain omniscience. (28.118)
When the saṃkrānti of Māgha occurs on the full moon day, that is Sarasvatī;
having fasted for three nights prior to it, one should worship Śiva according to the prescribed rite.
Fasting at night and smeared with ashes, one should recite [the mantra] on the bank of a river;
then, having performed the morning bath and other rites, [one should consume] cow's ghee mixed with ashes.
Having touched the *palāśa* leaf and recited [the mantra] eight thousand times, or having drunk that fivefold cow-product (*pañcagavya*), one attains knowledge and wisdom. || 28-121 ||

Having encapsulated the six-syllable mantra with the seed-syllables of Haṃsa and Vāgīśvarī, one should recite it three hundred thousand times while meditating; before long, one will become omniscient. (28.122)
Thus, the practitioner of the six-syllable mantra, joined with Haṃsavāgīśvarī, subsisting on food according to the instructions of his vow, [should recite it] ten lakhs with devotion.
By reciting [the mantra] in sequence, having attained the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, one becomes a *vidyādhara*.
Having gone into the shade of a *bilva* tree, being pure, one should constantly recite it ten thousand times. (28.124)
One should offer that fruit with clarified butter one thousand and eight times;
having thus driven away misfortune, one will become wealthy within a month. (28-125)
He who, while reciting [the mantra], performs oblations for two months, six months, or a year, worshipping Śiva with devotion, shall become a bestower of wealth through his prosperity. (28.126)

Through oblations made with *palāśa* flowers, one shall obtain a son; by offering fuel-sticks of that same wood, there will be immediate pacification of hundreds of portents and afflictions caused by enemies. (28.127)
Having offered oblations during afflictions caused by malevolent planets, one should recite the mantra eight thousand or ten thousand times;
through oblations of *sādhya* sesame seeds, peace shall be attained, and from an offering of one hundred and eight [oblations], relief from bad dreams occurs.
Having worshipped the sign at the time of an eclipse and meditated upon it, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
thereby one obtains peace arising from that [planetary influence], as does one through ten thousand oblations.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* everywhere, one should perform the rites in its presence;
through recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*) at the three junctions of the day, there shall be the pacification of malevolent magic (*ābhicāraka*).
And that karma, once directed against someone, goes only to that enemy.
Through *vibhītaka* fruits sprinkled with poison and blood, there shall be enmity. (28.131)
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of sharp oil, even an immortal enemy shall surely die;
[one should write] the name on the left thigh, interspersed with the syllables of the mantra in their proper sequence.
At night, or during the night, one should cover [the object] with the palm of the left hand and recite that mantra;
while meditating on a woman overwhelmed by the drawing-in of the noose, one shall attract her. (28.133)
By this very practice, the attraction of men is taught;
it should be performed on six of the dark fourteenth days on the shore of the ocean.
Having worshipped the sand-phallic image (liṅga), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times while fasting;
likewise during the six other twilights, and then on the seventh day at the mandala.
Having worshipped the Lord in the center of the lotus,
one should worship Vīrabhadra and Vighneśa to his right with hibiscus flowers and the Mothers.
And one should offer ten thousand japā flowers into the fire before him;
then he beholds Vighna and Vīrabhadra together with the Mothers.
Then, having obtained his desired boon, he rejoices for a long time like a god;
by offering ten thousand *bāṇa* flowers into the fire, one shall attain victory in battle. (28.138)
By offering oblations of flowers of a particular color, one obtains that same color in the sky;
while consuming the *pañcagavya* and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times.
One is liberated from calamities and sins; there is no doubt about this.
Having ascended a mountain peak, bathing three times a day and subsisting on the food prescribed for a vow— || 28-140 ||
One who is endowed with restraints and observances, pure and observing a vow of silence, should recite the six-syllabled mantra ten million times and worship the Liṅga. (28.141)
With this very body, he became a sky-walker capable of assuming any form at will;
having attained the sovereignty of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he was honored by the perfected beings (siddhas) and the gods.
Being praised by the lords of the Gaṇas and worshipped, that all-knowing one shall travel to all worlds and behold all the gods. || 28-143 ||
The Supreme Lord, together with the Mother, will become manifest to that best of practitioners who thus recites [the mantra] three million times. (28.144)
What need is there for much speaking here? For the satisfaction of the Lord Śambhu, there is no other mantra whatsoever equal to these mantras of Śiva.
One who protects the duties of his own caste and stage of life, as well as their traditional practices,
and has been initiated by a preceptor, is fit to accomplish the mantra.
One should not take shelter in the shade of the *vibhītaka*, *karañja*, *arka*, or *snuhi* trees. Nor should one consume onions, garlic, bottle-gourd, *gṛñjana*, or water boiled with husks. (28.147)
Fish meat, liquor, kakubhaṇḍa, as well as ālupa, eating from a bell-metal vessel, śārṅgaṣṭa, nālī vegetable, and silindhra; || 28-148 ||

Food that is stale, devoid of flavor, putrid, or kept overnight; food touched by impurities such as lack of bathing; and food consumed during the periods of ritual impurity following a death or a birth. (28.149)

One should avoid the food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, and the food of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras; one should also avoid the food of those born of inverse (*pratiloma*) and natural (*anuloma*) unions. (28.150)

Without having seen and worshipped the Liṅga, one should neither eat nor drink; likewise, one should not do so without having honored cows, teachers, the Vedas, and twice-born Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva. (28.151)

One should avoid at a distance the censure of the gods and of true disciples; constantly practicing one's sacrificial rites and works of charity according to one's ability, one should always keep the senses subdued. (28.152)
By means of these mantras, a human being obtains the fruit as described above. This is the section on their application:
"The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsādabīja*), followed by *śivāya* and ending with *namaḥ*. (28.153)
This seven-syllabled root mantra of Śiva bestows all objectives;
following the seed-syllables of the limbs mentioned for the Prāsāda mantra, the syllables beginning with Śi are then added. (28.154)
Having joined them together with their respective birth-classes (*jāti*), they indeed become its limbs;
moreover, the mantra of the eye, *khaṃ* along with the *anusvāra*, shall likewise possess its birth-class. (28.155)
Dadhīca is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Śiva is the deity; the means of accomplishment and the application (viniyoga) are as before. || 28-156 ||
The six-syllable mantra beginning with *satāraḥ* and *śaktibīja* has been proclaimed;
the eight-syllable Śaiva mantra is taught as the bestower of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. (28.157)

The six limbs of this [mandala] are taught by the wise as being composed of the six colors of the respective palaces and so forth, preceded by the limbs described for the palaces, and conjoined with their own respective classes. (28.158)
The seer is Śilāda, the metre is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Śiva himself;
its means of accomplishment and applications are as before. (28.159)
The Section on the Eight-Syllable Śaiva Mantra:
When one joins the *cin-mantra* at the end of this very eight-syllable mantra, it becomes a ten-syllable Śaiva mantra that grants all desires like a wish-fulfilling tree. (28.160)
The syllable *kha* with a bindu (*khaṃ*), followed by Bhṛgu (*bha*) and the creative emission (*saḥ*), is indeed proclaimed as this *cinmantra*.
Its six ancillaries (*aṅga*) are also said to consist of eight syllables each. (28.161)
Sanatkumāra, Paṅkti, Śiva accompanied by Pārvatī, the Ṛṣis and others, as well as the Sādhanas and others—their applications (viniyoga) have been declared previously. (28–162)
For they know that this [teaching] is common to all six mantras;
indeed, these six great mantras are the root-mantras of Śiva. (28.163)
"There is indeed no human goal (puruṣārtha) desired by them that is impossible to achieve.

Having thus observed these Kalpas in brief, as well as the Śaiva mantras—six in number which are preeminent, the very essence of the Vedas and sacred compositions, and taught for the benefit of all, being distinguished and complete—[these have been set forth]. (28–164½)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 28.

Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter. The middle finger of the left arm, together with the staff and preceded by the *tāra* (Om), along with the conjunction and the syllable *bhṛgu*—this three-syllabled mantra is declared to be *Mṛtyuñjaya*. (29-1)
The seer is Kahola; its meter is said to be the divine Gāyatrī;
its application is for victory over death; and the deity is Śiva, the conqueror of death. (29-2)
The middle and final syllables of this [mantra], ending with the nasal bindu, constitute the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) through the elongated vowels;
the three seed-syllables (bīja) are placed upon the joints of the fingers of the hands, beginning with the thumb.

One should assign the limbs [of the mantra] to the fingers beginning with the little finger, and the weapon-mantra to the two palms; then, one should place the first syllable upon the body from the feet up to the private parts.
Then, having placed the second seed-syllable from the secret place up to the throat, and likewise the third from the throat up to the crown of the head. (29–5)
One should also perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in the respective locations beginning with the heart;
thereafter, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consists of three hundred thousand recitations, and from that, one-tenth as the oblation.

Having cut [the fuel sticks] four finger-breadths long and smeared them with milk, clarified butter, and honey, he should offer them while meditating on Mṛtyuñjaya as one with himself; and while performing the sacrifice, he should recite the hymn beginning with "citram" and so forth.
May he protect you— he who has the form of an eight-year-old child, seated within a moon-maṇḍala formed by the union of two upward- and downward-blossoming white lotuses,
possessing six arms and holding a trident, with a rosary of arrows and pearls resting upon his own lap.
In his right hands, Mṛtyuñjaya holds a skull-cup filled with nectar, a jar, and a mudrā; in the other [left hands], he likewise holds these. || 29-8 ||
Moreover:
White in appearance, adorned with shimmering pearl necklaces and garlands, three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon, and decorated with a crown of matted locks; (29.9)
Being bathed on all sides by streams of nectar-water dripping from the masses of lunar digits situated upon the moon-disks above and below. || 29-10 ||
The seed-syllable should be within its pericarp; between those two lunar disks, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, from which nectar-water flows. (29.11)
Remembering oneself as being flooded [by the nectar], one should meditate on Śiva, the Conqueror of Death, as one's own identity;
one should contemplate the *praṇava* at the stalk of the lotus and the second syllable upon its petals. (29.12)
In the middle of the mantra, both in its forward and reverse order,
one should utter one's own name and the purpose, and then recite it for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal.
In the same way, by performing the fire-oblation (homa) ending with "svāhā," one obtains the desired fruit;
by offering severed [blades of grass] smeared with honey, one may avert death.
Likewise, with *dūrvā* grass one obtains long life, and with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) one gains health;
an oblation (*homa*) performed with *kāśmarya* fuel-sticks shall be the remover of all diseases. (29.15)
Distress is destroyed by oblations of sesame, clarified butter, milk-rice, and sugar-cane;
one shall attain victory through offerings of milk-rice, milk, and white mustard seeds. (29.16)

Stambhana (paralysis) is performed with *busarājī* seeds; dveṣa (enmity) with the leaves of *nimba* fuel; likewise, uccāṭana (expulsion) with *vaibhītaka* wood, and māraṇa (killing) with wood from poisonous trees.
For the rites of subjugation (kṣudra), it is held that the oblation should consist of sesame oil mixed with poison;
for rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), it should be sprinkled with milk, clarified butter, and honey.
For subjugation, one should offer oblations of salt and honey; for prosperity, lotus-milk-rice. By reciting the mantra ten million times, one shall obtain all desires.
And one should perform the worship according to the sequence taught in the Śaiva tradition upon the aforementioned Śiva-seat,
[offering] with one's own limbs, the lords of the gates, the world-protectors, and the weapons as successive coverings.
