Whether in an image such as a painting, in the heart, in the solar disc, or in water, one who worships with offerings according to one's capacity attains that perfection. (29–21)
The syllable *bhṛgu* (bha), white and situated in fire (ra), followed by *jvalana* (ja) and *mṛtyu* (ma);
ending with *nāśana* (kṣa) and the wife of fire (svāhā)—this is the mantra of twenty-two syllables extracted as Manu.
The one known as Mṛtyujit (the Conqueror of Death) also has its seer and other [limbs] as previously enjoined;
facing south, one should recite this during the two twilights for the pacification of death.

One should mutter this seventeen-syllable mantra, beginning with the three-syllable mantra previously described; the practice for its accomplishment and so forth, as well as its application, are as before. (29–24)
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as before; however, the specific detail taught therein is as follows:

I bow to the Lord Mṛtyuñjaya, who sits in the midst of a pair of white lotuses and moons, holding a deer and an axe in his hands, and carrying a rosary and a skull-cup. His crest is adorned with the moon that sheds nectar, his complexion is the color of white silk, and he is moistened by the flowing waters of nectar. (29–25)
The Chapter on the Conqueror of Death: The Vedic mantra dedicated to Tryambaka is known as the "Reviver of the Dead. (29.26)
Some say the seers are the venerable Vasiṣṭha and Bhārgava;
the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Rudra preceded by Tryambaka. (29–27)
One should place the six limbs themselves upon the joints of the toes of the feet with the numbers four, three, eight, nine, and five, as well as with one's own three syllables. (29–28)
In the two joints of the feet, the knees, the private parts, the base [of the spine], and likewise the abdomen;
on the back, the heart, the throat, the joints of the arms, and also in the fingers. (29–29)
One should perform the placement of the thirty-two syllables, ending with the *bindu*, individually upon the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, the pair of eyebrows, and also on the head. (29–30)
One should place the eleven steps in sequence upon the head, the eyebrows, the eyes, the face, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the thighs, the knees, and the feet.
And as for meditation:
seated upon a lotus, holding in his own lap an amṛta-filled jar, with two hands holding a book and a rosary, [the deity] has white limbs and two jars filled with nectar.

May Tryambaka protect you—he who wears matted locks, whose head bears the crescent moon, who sprinkles himself with showers from two jars, who is adorned in white garments, possesses eight arms, and has a smiling countenance. || 29-32 ||
Now, the worship of Tryambaka with eight enclosures (āvaraṇas) must be performed.
On the Śiva-seat as declared by the Śaivas, the first enclosure consists of his own limbs (nijāṅgas). || 29-33 ||
The second enclosure of Śambhu is said to consist of his eight forms: Earth, Fire, the Sacrificer, the Sun, Water, Wind, the Moon, and the Lotus. (29–34)

The third and subsequent arrangements (vṛttis), ending with the sixth, are to be known as consisting of eight, eight, and eight [syllables] respectively, corresponding to the powers (śaktis) beginning with Ramā, Rātri, and so forth. (29–35)
What are those thirty-two powers?
They are Ramā, Rātri, Prabhā, Jyotsnā, Pūrṇoṣā, Pūraṇī, Sudhā, and then in the third enclosure, Viśvā, Vidyut, and Pāṇḍarā. (29–36)
Prahvā, Sārā, Sandhyā, Śivā, and Niśāṣṭamī.
In the fourth enclosure: Ārdrā, Prajñā, Parā, Medhā, Kānti, Śānti, Dhṛti, and Smṛti. (29–37)
Thus, the eight Śaktis of the fifth enclosure (āvaraṇa) have been declared:
Paromā, Pāvanī, Padmā, Śāntā, Moghā, Jayā, and Amalā. (29–38)
The eight powers are said to be within the scope of the sixth enclosure;
the seventh enclosure consists of the ten world-protectors, beginning with Indra. (29–39)
Indeed, on the eighth [petal], Śiva himself is present with Vajra and the others in the pericarp;
the limbs (aṅgas) are in the midst of the filaments, and the eight forms (aṣṭamūrtis) are at the tips of the stamens.
The Śaktis are located at the base, the middle, the top, and the very tip of the petals;
by means of these enclosures, according to the sequence prescribed for the offering to Śambhu (or Śarva).
One should worship Śiva by invoking him according to the prescribed rites into the heart, in a painting, in an auspicious crystal linga, or likewise in a water-pot. || 29-42 ||

Having consecrated with that [water] a Brahmin disciple who has been initiated according to the ritual agreement (sāmayika), he should give him the mantra accompanied by water; and he too should practice it.
One who has conquered the senses, subsisting on the food prescribed by his vow, should worship Śambhu constantly;
devoted to celibacy and with a one-pointed mind, he should first recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Fuel-sticks made of *bailva*, *pālāśa*, *khadira*, and *nyagrodha* wood; sesame seeds; white mustard, milk-porridge, milk, curd, and *dūrvā* grass—each used in succession. (29–45)
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations into the fire with those ten substances while Śiva has been invoked, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity. (29.46)
One should honor ten thousand, a thousand, or even a hundred knowers of the Vedas,
as well as one's own teacher, according to one's ability, with gold, garments, and other such gifts.
Then this mantra of his shall become perfected, bestowing all desires;
by means of which Śukra formerly [restored] the Dānavas slain in battle by the gods. (29–48)
With this mantra, he restored Kaca, the son of Aṅgiras, to life—
by means of which mantra Dadhīca’s body had become one of adamantine bone.
By that Traiyambaka [rite], there is nothing unattainable in the three worlds:
with ten thousand *bilva* fruits one gains prosperity (*lakṣmī*), and with *palāśa* leaves, the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). (29.50)
Through oblations of *khadira* wood one attains nourishment; through those produced from *vaṭa* wood, wealth and grain;
and furthermore, by offering black sesame seeds, one achieves victory over death and the destruction of sins.
The destruction of enemies is achieved with *siddhārtha* seeds; with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), longevity and prosperity;
and with milk, the pacification of minor diseases and the like, as well as the attainment of fortune.
With *dūrvā* grass one obtains long life and health; with curd, food; and with rice-milk (*pāyasa*), prosperity.
On one's birthday each month, [one should worship] with *dūrvā* grass and rice-milk.
Having offered one hundred and twenty oblations, one shall obtain long life;
with *kāṣmarya* fruits and milk-rice, there shall be longevity, provided it is saturated everywhere with clarified butter.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should recite [the mantra] daily for the sake of longevity;
likewise, food, milk, and medicinal herbs should be consecrated daily with the mantra seven times.
Water offered at the three junctions of the day, when drunk, increases longevity;
likewise, milk-rice or food with curd offered as an oblation on the sacred festival days bestows nourishment.
One obtains a daughter by means of fried grains (lāja), and a daughter is given to him by means of fried grains;
likewise, [one obtains a son] respectively by means of Nyagrodha, Pippala, Plakṣa, and Audumbara fruits. (29.57)

One should bring Brahmins and others under one's control by offering oblations of sesame, white mustard, dūrvā grass, and cooked rice, sprinkled with milk, clarified butter, and honey, while the moon is in the constellation Ārdrā, for the sake of longevity.
On one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), one should offer oblations of clarified butter, kṛsara, molasses, and milk-rice;
with the remainder, one should feed the Brahmins, and thus one may bring even a deity under one's control. (29.59)
She would grant him his desired boon; how much more so, then, a human being on earth who offers a thousand oblations of *śamī* wood or milk-rice on the day of the moon's conjunction? (29–60)
Having offered oblations, one should apply a *tripuṇḍra* mark on the forehead with those ashes; this brings all under control.
Having offered oblations of milk-rice and *āragvadha* wood at night, one will certainly bring [the desired person] under control.
Likewise, having offered oblations of apāmārga and milk-rice on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one who applies a tilaka of that ash upon his head shall bring a woman under his control.
One achieves hatred through khadira wood soaked in oil, and expulsion through vibhītaka fruits;
one obtains rain through vetasa wood, and may cause death with wood from poisonous trees.
In all minor rites, one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks marked with the [target] name; one should employ the name-infused rite by appending it to the end of the mantra. || 29-64 ||
Or, for the protection of houses, villages, cities, and so forth, one should scatter in all directions sesame seeds or sugar that have been consecrated three thousand times with the mantra. (29.65)
Having prepared a cord made of *rajvālu* and knotted according to the number of days—whether for a one-day, two-day, or multi-day duration—one should remove fever by binding it upon the hand. (29.66)

On one's birth-star (janmarkṣa) or during a solar transit (saṅkrānti), a water-pot filled according to the prescribed rite and consecrated through recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa), when sprinkled, shall lead to longevity and prosperity.
Likewise, a barren woman consecrated by him gives birth to an auspicious son;
for he bestows long life, health, victory, prosperity, and good fortune. (29.68)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or on the eighth lunar day under the asterism Ārdrā, or on any day specifically prescribed, the practice performed with this [mantra] grants success. (29.69)

Subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times or more by a river flowing toward the ocean; thus, one shall attain the powers beginning with *aṇimā*.

But one who eats according to the vow, being free from desire, and worships Śiva on a mountain peak, having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. || 29-71 ||
(157) What need is there for much speaking here? For those who worship with this mantra, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (29.72)
The Section on the Traiyambaka [Mantras]:
The Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, and Triṣṭubh—these three have attained unity.
This mantra consisting of three [parts] and one hundred syllables has Sūrya, Rudra, and Agni as its deities. (29–73)
Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, and Mārīca Kāśyapa himself—these sages, as they appeared in succession, are remembered as that triad of meters. (29.74)
One should oneself [perform] the six limbs with one's own syllables joined by the [seed-syllable of] birth;
therein, according to the count of the Atijagatī, Rudra, Vikāra, and Aṣṭi meters. (29.75)

Likewise, with twenty-two [syllables], one should perform the six-limbed ritual in due order; its preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*) consists of reciting it one hundred thousand times, and having offered clarified butter and milk-rice according to one's capacity. (29–76)
One should feed the twice-born according to one's capacity; thereby, the mantra becomes perfected.
For rites such as pacification (śāntika), one should begin with the Gāyatrī, while for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should begin with the Anuṣṭubh.

One should worship the Gāyatrī and other meters on the solar pedestal (saurapīṭha), the Tryambaka and others on the Durgā pedestal (durgāpīṭha), or the Triṣṭubh and others on the fire pedestal (vahnipīṭha). || 29-78 ||
In the first [mandala], the deity to be meditated upon is either Sūrya, Tryambaka, or Durgā;
the first enclosure should consist of the limbs [of the deity] and the śaktis beginning with Prahlādinī.
There are three enclosures, and four enclosures formed by the goddesses beginning with Ramā;
then one enclosure beginning with Jāgatā, and the tenth enclosure by the world-protectors (lokeśas).

Through oblations of dūrvā grass, ghee, and *aghṛta*, one gains long life and prosperity; through lotuses and water-lilies, one gains splendor; through bilva fruits, one gains fortune; through sesame seeds, peace; and [through specific offerings], one overcomes evil diseases and enemies. (29.81)
One should daily recite this with devotion in the morning and shall obtain all desires;
as for the various ritual procedures (*kalpa*) for the *gāyatrī* and other mantras that were previously mentioned.
Among those [mantras], the common applications of this [six-syllable mantra] have been described at great length.
(The section on the hundred-syllable mantra, p. 158: The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), *namaḥ*, the letter *nābhi* (na), the letter *ka* (*kumbha*), and the word *dakṣiṇāmūrti* in the dative case.
"Grant me wisdom and bestow abundance; O beloved of Agni"—this is the mantra consisting of the phonemes and syllables of the form [of the deity]. || 29-83 ||

The syllable *atri* (a-tr-i) with the eye-conjunction (*i*) at the end, followed by the long vowel *ī* at the end of the foot; then the poison-syllable (*viṣaṃ*) ending in the sixth vowel (*ū*), then the letter *ra*, the left foot (*vāmacaraṇaṃ*), and the syllables *ye tubhyam*;
then *hatapuṣaṇihāliṇe*, *dhyānai*, *dhātṛṇi*, *ṣaṭāṃśaja*, and *namorudrāya śambhave*.
This mantra for Dakṣiṇāmūrti consists of thirty-two calculated syllables;
when preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ) and joined with the Niruddha-Śakti at the end, it becomes thirty-six syllables long. || 29-84 ||
The sage of these two should be known as Śuka; some say that Brahmā is the first [sage]. (29.85)
The *chandogāyatram* is said for the first [mantra], and the *anuṣṭubh* for the latter;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the deity, and omniscience is the fruit of both. (29–86)
The six limbs of the first [mantra] are formed by its own constituent parts: six with its own vowels, then six, two, two, three, and also two. (87)

In the second [section], one should arrange the limbs (aṅgas) ending with the weapon-mantra (astra), joined with their respective birth-classes (jāti), using the syllables of Ṛtvik, Vivasvat, Mātaṅga, Bhūta, Rāma, and Nija. (29.88)
One should place those limbs upon the two hands, from the base of the thumbs to the palms;
then, one should also perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the root mantra, as well as the placement of the syllables upon the body.
As follows:
on the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, the throat, the two arms, the heart, the navel, and the private parts. (29.90)
One should place twenty-two oceans on the thighs, the shanks, and the two feet;
[and likewise] on the head, forehead, eyes, ears, nose, the two cheeks, and the mouth.
In the eight *sandhyaṣṭakas*, [the mantras are placed] respectively on the two arms, the throat, the heart, the navel, the hips, the genitals,
the thighs, the knees, and the joints of the toes.
Having performed the placement of the thirty-two syllables and then again the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*),
one should also perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the two [syllables] *tāra* and *śakti*.
Regarding the second [deity]:
at the root of the *vedanya* [channel], he is surrounded by sages, seated firmly in the full lotus posture (*gāḍhaparyaṅka*),
clad in white garments, possessing three eyes, with the luster of white ash, and adorned with a tiger-skin garment.

I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who stands with one leg raised upon his knee, holding in his straight arms the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*), an axe, and a deer, while bearing a water-pot (*kusumbha*) and a crescent moon placed within his matted locks (*jāṭajūṭa*).
This is the second *anuṣṭubh* verse of the meditation:

Seated amidst the lords of sages, with a golden cloth tied beneath him in the full-lotus posture, white with sacred ash for the sake of exposition, his matted locks shimmering like the moon upon the moving celestial river.

Constantly bow down to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who has three eyes, whose hands hold a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and a blue lotus, one arm of whom rests upon his knee, and who is clothed in a variegated animal skin.
Then, resembling the celestial river [Gaṅgā], staying on the bank of the Sarasvatī,
subsisting on the food of a vow, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at a single-liṅga temple of Śiva.
Taking refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti, with his body smeared with ashes,
he should offer oblations of sesame seeds bathed in milk and clarified butter, using a tenth part of that [number].
One should worship the God seated on the Śiva-throne, depicted in a painting on a wall or a cloth,
surrounded by disciples and sages according to the method of a single enclosure.
If the primary offerings, such as the *arghya* and others, are unavailable, one may perform them even mentally; otherwise, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times every day.
Through the excellence of recitation and meditation, one clearly becomes omniscient; even scriptures not previously heard, one explains and composes. (29.100)
By worshipping Śiva as Mṛtyuñjaya, they conquer death; by worshipping the Sañjīvana mantra, they conquer Time.
For those who worship Dakṣiṇaśiva with this mantra, Sarasvatī carries the light of eloquence within their lotus-like mouth, just like the goddess Sarasvatī herself.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the illustrious teacher Īśānaśiva. 29.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter. The white [syllable] is the seed-syllable *nāda*, followed by the final [consonant] endowed with the *anugraha* (favor) bindu;
then *bhṛgu* (s), *kha* (h), and [the letter] situated in fire (r), which is white and possesses the *bhautika* bindu.

The sixth syllable should be white and the letter *kha* (the sky), white and accompanied by fire (*ra*) and grace (*u*). One should extract the ninth seed-syllable, which possesses the *bindu*, from the mantra "Aghorebhyaḥ. (30.2)
Having extracted the seed-syllable *hrūṃ* and then the words *athaghorebhyaḥ*,
this nineteen-syllable mantra has the letter *pa* on its side, accompanied by fire (*ra*), the upper lip (*u*), and the bindu.
From the *ghoraghoratara* [mantras] comes *kham* with the *sānugraha-bindu*;
from all the *sarva-sarva* [mantras] comes the syllable *proṃ*, and immediately after that.
One should utter "namaste astu rudrānta-rūpebhyaḥ," and thereafter [place] the Sky-fire (H) with a Bindu, followed by the Vāgbhava and Mānmatha [seeds]. (30.5)
Then, having extracted Śakti, Śrī, the White One (Śukla), along with Anugraha and Visarjana,
there shall be the Aghora mantra consisting of fifty-four syllables.
In this Vedic [mantra] as well, Tārā and the others should be understood by the twice-born:
Tāram, Lohitaḥ, Sāgniḥ, and the word Sphura repeated. (30.7)
*Dantī*, *Śivottama*, *Agni*, those two, *Cāṣa*, *Ḍibhujaṅgaka*, *Aṇuṣūbhakataḥ*, *Prakataḥ*, *Kaha kaha vaṃ ghātaya* (repeated),
and *Varma* and *Astra*— this is the forty-two-syllable Aghora mantra. (30–8)
The twelve-syllable seed-mantra (bījamantra) of this very [deity] is now declared:
*pārśva* (pa), with fire (ra), the lip (u), and half-moon (anusvāra); *kha* (kha), with fire (ra), the letter *a*, and the bindu. (30.9)
Vāgbhava, Smara, Hṛllekhā, Śrī, Prasāda, Sarasvatī, and "Astrāya Phaṭ"—this is declared to be the twelve-syllable mantra. (30.10)
By joining the twelve-syllable mantra with the forty-two syllables,
the fifty-four-syllable Aghorāstra-mantra is clearly formed.
Thus, the Aghora mantra and the Aghora weapon-mantra are proclaimed;
when both are recited together, their syllables amount to one hundred and eight.
For both [mantras], the six limbs indeed arise separately from their own respective syllables. Gālava is the seer for both, and the meter is considered to be Bṛhatī. (30.13)
Śiva, whose form is non-terrible (aghoramūrti), shall be the deity for both;
the means of accomplishment and so forth are equal for both, for they do not abandon one another. (30.14)
While accomplishing the Aghora weapon-mantra, one should also recite it ten times its portion;
and while accomplishing the Aghora weapon, one should likewise recite the Aghora mantra.
In the seed-syllable of the first station, there should be *aghorebhyaḥ* and then *hroṃ*; this is the heart (*hṛd*).
Then *ghorebhyaḥ*, followed by *preṃ*; this is the head (*śiras*) conjoined with its respective [mantra] class. (30.16)
From *ghoraghoratara* [comes] *kha-m-au* together with the bindu for the *śikhā*;
from *sarvataḥ śarvasarvebhyaḥ*, the syllable *proṃ* shall be the *kavaca*. (30.17)
The eye-mantra consists of the eleven syllables beginning with "namaste";
the weapon-mantra (astra) consists of the remaining five seed-syllables, accompanied everywhere by their respective caste-designations (jāti).
The six limbs of Aghora should be joined with its own syllables;
indeed, the limbs of the Aghora-weapon likewise consist of its own phonemes.
The six limbs, each joined with its own respective class [of consonants], consist of syllables numbering respectively six, six, three, four, ten, eight, and eight. (30-20)

Whether at a self-manifested (svayambhū) site, or one established by a sage (ārṣa), or at a single-liṅga shrine of a deity, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) facing the western face of the liṅga. (30.21)
Eating only according to his vows, sacrificing to Śambhu, bathing three times a day, and with his senses restrained,
he should devoutly recite the Aghora mantra and the Aghora weapon mantra one hundred thousand times.

One should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that [total number]. If one is unable to do so, having performed the oblation according to that tenth-part, one should recite the mantra one thousand times in gold.
In Japan, one attains great siddhi after two, three, or four hundred thousand [recitations];
[the deity] has thirty-eight kalās, a form resembling collyrium, and four faces. (30.24)
He has eighteen arms, is fierce, and possesses three eyes in each face;
he wears a tiger skin and has an elephant hide as his upper garment.
A skull-topped staff, two fangs, a trident, a skull-bowl, a goad, and a noose; a plow, a spear, an arrow, a bow, a sword, a shield, and a rosary. (30.26)
He holds, in sequence, a lotus, a staff, a *ḍamaru* drum, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) with his eighteen right and left arms. (30.27)
His face was terrifying, jagged with fangs, and he bore tawny moustaches and matted locks;
indeed, he wore all the ornaments from the turban and earrings down to the anklets.
I beheld the Lord wearing ornaments fashioned by the lords of serpents,
clad in a tiger skin, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
His ornaments were entwined with spiders, scorpions, and centipedes;
his lower lip was bitten, his eyes were round, and his face was contorted by a frown.
It is surrounded by Rudras and Śaktis in the form of the syllables of Aghora,
and resides within the interior of the lotus at the center of the sixteen-spoked wheel.
Surrounded by the Rudras, Bhairavas, and Mātṛs who are about to be described, the God faces southward; that weapon is located to his west.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and other rites, either on a wall that has been plastered or upon a cloth painting (*paṭa*).
Regarding the meditation on Aghora:
while meditating on the Aghora weapon, [one should visualize it] with the luster of a mountain of crushed collyrium. (30–33)
His lower lip was clearly bitten, his face was fierce with gleaming fangs,
and he was adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments smeared with blood.
He has eight arms, adorned with seven uplifted weapons:
a trident, a corpse (vetāla), a sword, and a hand-drum, in sequence.
With his right hands and the others, he holds a skull-cup with the lowest [right hand],
and a bell, a shield, and a trident in the middle, bearing them with each successive upper hand.
With round, tawny, three-eyed faces, fierce with frowning brows,
having the form of blazing tongues of fire, and with tawny hair standing erect.
Likewise, upon the anklets, the waist-belt, and the girdle; on the bracelets and armlets, on the neck, and also upon the ear-pendants. (30.38)
Two by two, the lords of serpents bore bodies armored for battle,
with *mālaka* garlands hanging from their throats, entwined by spiders and scorpions.
Placing his left foot forward, he stands upon a red eight-petaled lotus;
he is the destroyer of all enemies, as well as of planets, diseases, fears, and minor afflictions. (30–40)

During worship, fire-offerings, recitations, and other rites, one should meditate upon the god Aghorāstra, who is radiant like a thousand suns at the end of an aeon and is compassionate toward his devotees.
Without having first worshipped Vighnarāja, the gurus, and oneself, as well as Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, the seat (āsana), and those beginning with Dharma; || 30-42 ||
Having worshipped the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, as well as Brahmā and the other lords thereof, and the powers (śaktis) such as Tāmasyā and the rest, it is known as the Aghora seat. (30–43)
Having projected that non-terrible form and its associated body of knowledge (vidyādeha) into that [liṅga],
one should invoke the Śiva who resides at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] within the heart-lotus.
Having invoked that supreme deity, the light which is subtle and whose form is consciousness,
one should establish him within the lotus of the heart through the sequence beginning with installation.
The wise practitioner should perform the worship according to the path described in the *Upacāra* [section], ending with the offering of food (*naivedya*).
Having offered oblations into the fire and presented the *bali* offering, he should circumambulate [the deity] clockwise.
Having offered salutations preceded by praise, one should recite the mantra before him;
thus one should accomplish the mantra after giving the teacher’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā). 30–47.
The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Mantras:
Now, with a mantra that has been mastered, one should perform the various applications (viniyoga) in matters of virtue, wealth, and pleasure—whatever indeed is desired by the practitioner. (30.48)
In this regard, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished here through the two mantras of the terrible (*ghora*) and non-terrible (*aghorāstra*) weapons.
One should achieve one's desired goal by means of one or the other of these two, through recitation, worship, and so forth. (30.49)
Especially in matters of state affairs, in times of fear from enemy armies and the like, during afflictions caused by planets and spirits, and in the face of fears of minor diseases. (30–50)
Likewise, when there is fear of untimely death, during droughts or excessive rains, and when great portents have arisen concerning men, women, elephants, or horses; (30–51)
For the pacification of various afflictions during calamities and epidemics,
the general Aghora sacrifice is here briefly described.
In a pure and secluded place, according to the requirements of each specific rite,
one should construct a pavilion or a water-shed, and likewise offer the *vāstu-bali* sacrifice.
Having first caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having had the twice-born pronounce blessings (*svasti*), one should,
on a well-smeared spot, drive away obstacles and worship Gaṇeśvara.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of white rice grains from the śāli variety and half that amount of sesame seeds, one should draw a sixteen-petaled lotus in its center.
Having fashioned a white lotus with colored powders and placed a water-pot in its center,
one should fill it with water, along with perfumes, gold, gems, fruits, and unbroken grains.
Having invoked Aghora in that [lotus], the practitioner should worship the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti).
The enclosure of the limbs is in the filaments; in front of that is the enclosure of the eight weapons.
The third enclosure should consist of terrifying deities such as Bhīṣaṇa and others; at the bases of the petals are Brāhmī and the other goddesses, together with Asitāṅga and the other Bhairavas.
The fourth enclosure, consisting of the Mātṛkās, is to be worshipped by those situated in the middle of the petals;
the fifth, however, by the Bhairavas beginning with Bhairaveśa, who are stationed at the tips of the petals.
The sixth enclosure consists of Śrīkaṇṭha and the other Rudras along with their Śaktis;
the seventh enclosure, situated in the pathway, consists of the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their weapons.
The outer enclosure is said to consist of sixteen [deities] beginning with Vṛṣa; this is the eighth [enclosure].
Thus, along with the weapons, it is established for the Aghora-liṅga, as well as for those made of stone, wood, or cloth.
Having worshipped him, one should offer the most excellent food-oblation according to one's capacity, and having gratified Maheśvara with instrumental music, song, and dance. (30.62)
In the east or in the northeast, according to the specific rite performed,
[one should worship] the digits (kalās) of Aghora, Astra, and the limbs (aṅgas) within the fire of Śiva in a four-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having invoked and worshipped the god Aghora, one should then perform the oblation;
thereafter, one should worship the vessel of peace (śāntikumbha) situated to the northeast of the sacrificial pit.
Fuel-sticks from the palāśa, bailva, plakṣa, vaṭa, udumbara, and pippala trees, sprinkled with clarified butter; as well as śāli rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), and ghee. || 30-65 ||
Black sesame seeds, bamboo-seeds, barley, rice, white mustard, and parched grain,
as well as milk and honey— one of each, separately, one hundred and eight times.
Having offered oblations with the Aghora mantra and likewise with the Astra mantra, as well as with the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) in one-tenth of that quantity,
the preceptor should present the bali offering at midnight with the Bhūtakrūra mantra.

Then, having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and so forth, one should scatter the bali offering to the deities of the enclosures beginning with Kalā, in their proper order.
The names of the deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇadevatā) are as follows:
Tāmasī, Mohanī, Rātri, Niṣṭhā, Vyādhi, Māraṇī, Kṣudhā, and Tṛṣṇā; these are the eight powers (śaktayaḥ) of Aghora, residing in the eight digits (kalā). (30.69)
Bhāṣaṇa, Bhairava, Bhīma, Raudra, Ugra, Bhava, Ghora,
and Ghoratara— these eight reside in order within the middle of the petals.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Caṇḍikā are the eight Mothers.
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa,
Unmatta, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
The deities beginning with Brāhmī and those beginning with Asitāṅga should be worshipped at the junctions of the petals;
likewise Bhairaveśa, Unmatta, Krūra, Mārtāṇḍa, and Kopana.
Bhīma, Saṃhartṛ, Kāla, Caṇḍa, Bhadraka, Ugra, Bhava, Pātāla, Vyomeśa, and Kṣitīśvara. (30.74)
Then there is the Overlord, as well as the sixteen Bhairavas situated at the tips of the petals,
the Rudras beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, and the Śaktis beginning with Pūrṇodarī.
There should be those previously mentioned, as well as Indra and the others, and their weapons such as the thunderbolt; furthermore, Vṛṣa, Vighna, Vīrabhadra, Śāstṛ, Devī, and Prabhā. (30–76)
Satyaka, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Śaṅkha, and then Ṣaṇmukha;
Viśākha and Naigameṣa, as well as Durgā and Caṇḍeśvara. (30.77)
And the Kṣetrapāla [should be worshipped] through the conjunction of the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the center;
thus one should worship the eight enclosures in the sacrifice to Aghora.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to the limbs of the deity according to the prescribed method;
however, one should cast the bali-offering upon the ground for the deities of the Kalā and other surrounding enclosures.
Outside of that, there should be the hosts situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions; one should offer an oblation to them as follows:
the Ādityas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Gandharvas, and likewise the Pitṛs. (30.80)
The Rudras, Rākṣasas, Nāgas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Suras;
the Suparṇas, Pretas, Kuśmāṇḍas, Vasus, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras. || 30-81 ||
The Bhūtas, Vināyakas, Viśvedevas, Piśācas, the Aśvins, the Gaṇas,
the Yoginīs, and the Ḍākinīs— these are the twenty-four classes of beings.

Situated in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the center, these sixteen [deities] are of four kinds above; likewise, those below are of four kinds. They are to be worshipped, and one should offer an oblation (bali) to them.
Outside of that, one should scatter the bali offering to the hosts residing in the ten directions.

In the eastern direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold vajras in their hands—white, with white eyes, white and red, dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth, as well as those residing in the netherworld—to them and to those [deities], salutations, salutations! *ṭhaṭha*. In the south-eastern direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold spears (*śakti*) in their hands—red, with red eyes, red and crimson, and so forth. In the southern direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold staffs (*daṇḍa*) in their hands—black, and so forth. *Oṃ*. In the south-western direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold swords (*khaḍga*) in their hands—dark, with dark eyes, dark and red, and so forth. In the western direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold nooses (*pāśa*) in their hands—variegated, with variegated eyes, and so forth. In the north-western direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold goads (*aṅkuśa*) in their hands—yellow, and so forth. *Oṃ*. In the northern direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold maces (*gadā*) in their hands—white, with white eyes, white and red, and so forth. *Oṃ*. In the north-eastern direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold tridents (*śūla*) in their hands—tawny (*kapila*), and so forth. In the upward direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold lotuses (*padma*) in their hands—subtle, with subtle eyes, subtle and red, and so forth. *Oṃ*. In the downward direction, to those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold wheels (*cakra*) in their hands—smoky, with smoky eyes, smoky and red, dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth, and so forth.
Having scattered these, he gratifies the retinue with the bali offering by means of the mantras.
Then, having bathed and entered within together with his disciples,
the preceptor should worship the Supreme Lord residing in the liṅga, the pitcher, and the sacrificial pit.
One should feed eleven excellent brahmins with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), as well as those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins), other seekers, and oneself along with one's attendants.
Having eaten, one should sleep for the remainder of the night, and again in this manner day after day,
for sixty-four days or forty-eight days.
For twenty-four days and nights, or even for twelve days,
one should first make a formal resolve according to the gravity of the task, and especially so at the conclusion.
Then, having worshipped Śiva and offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the vessel of peace (śāntighaṭa),
one should bathe the patron or otherwise sprinkle the elephants and other [animals].
One should release the Lord, who resides in the fire and is situated in the *kumbha*, into the lotus of the heart;
then, one should honor the preceptor and the others according to one's capacity with land, gold, garments, and so forth.
The patron should satisfy other Brāhmaṇas as well as those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin);
through the grace of Aghoreśa, he attains his desired objects. || 30.91 ||
(168) His terrible [obstacles] are pacified by the sacrifice to Aghora; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, they cite this example:
"Either the Lord Aghora alone, or else the Aghora-missile."
Having sacrificed according to this procedure and having offered oblations, one should accomplish the desired goals.
Thus the general sacrifice has been indicated; now the specific [sacrifice] is also described. (30.93)
The section on the general sacrifice:
Or else, one should worship the self-manifested (svayambhu) or the ancestral (ārṣeya) Liṅga with cow-derived products—
specifically, with milk that has been freshly milked, measuring one hundred *prasthas*.
One should perform the supreme worship according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual services;
having done so, one should offer the *bhūtabali* at night according to the stated injunctions.
Furthermore, one should worship the deity in a liṅga, a painting, or on a cloth;
touching the liṅga with a kūrca, one should recite the Aghora mantra one hundred and eight times.

Then, one should offer the Aghora weapon [mantra] one hundred and eight times separately into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with dūrvā grass, clarified butter, sesame seeds, milk-rice (pāyasa), and barley, while recollecting the ritual act.
One should feed eleven twice-born men a pure meal along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), saying:
"May the Blessed One, whose form is non-terrible and who holds a weapon, be pleased with me. (30.98)
In this manner, one should carry out the sacrifice for twenty-five days;
having propitiated [the deity] with special care, one should then conclude the sacrifice.
Terrible sufferings, planetary afflictions, diseases, and untimely deaths are pacified, as well as portents, pestilential plagues, and those afflictions caused by malevolent spirits. (30.100)
Peace, longevity, health, and sovereignty arise for him;
this is declared to be the supreme procedure for sacrifice for one who is capable. (30.101)
For one who is unable [to perform the full rite], it is prescribed as three-quarters or half of that;
however, for the sole purpose of pacifying disease, it is performed with ten *prasthas* of clarified butter.

One should then consecrate [the disciple] with the Aghora mantra using cow products, or with the Brahma mantras; thereafter, one should perform the consecration with milk using the Rudra and Pāvamānī mantras. (30.103)
Having smeared [the deity] on all sides with a paste of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor,
[one should worship] with unbroken bilva leaves and fragrant flowers as well.
One should burn incense made from camphor, saffron, and black agallochum mixed together, light ghee lamps, and offer milk-rice and other such foods.
Having offered the fourfold food offering (naivedya), one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
day and night, one should offer clarified butter one hundred and eight times into the fire.
There should be that many fuel-sticks of Bilva wood and eleven oblations of cooked rice;
with the remaining ashes, one should perform an anointing which removes all diseases. (30.107)
By performing the sacrifice in this manner for forty days, one shall remove all diseases; there is the pacification of every ailment.
Now, the pacification of diseases for elephants, horses, and other animals is described.
Having performed the Kumbha-yāga as before, preceded by the formal resolve (saṅkalpa),
one should bathe the Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and water scented with fragrant fruits.
Having bathed [the deity] at the three junctions of the day, one should offer clarified butter and milk-rice;
one should also perform oblations with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, milk, sesame seeds, and milk-rice.
One should recite the Mṛtyuñjaya, the Aghorāstra, and the Haṃsa mantra one hundred and eight times,
and offer a bali oblation at night for twenty-one days.
One should cause elephants and horses to drink that water from the jar over which mantras have been recited;
one should sprinkle each of them with it, and thus their peace will be attained. (30.112)
The pacification of elephants, horses, and so forth.
If nourishment (pauṣṭika) is desired, Śiva should face westward.
Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as before and having performed worship, [one should offer] fresh clarified butter derived from cow products. (30.113)

Having consecrated [the disciple] with twenty-five *prasthas* according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the aforementioned supreme and other forms of worship day by day according to one's capacity. (30.114)
One should worship with devotion a single [flower] at the liṅga, the water-pot, and the painting;
one should worship Śiva with unbroken bilva leaves that resemble tridents.
Furthermore, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times in the morning,
[offering] fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and black sesame seeds.
He performs one hundred and eight oblations for forty days;
having given a sacrificial fee according to his capacity, he attains unsurpassed nourishment.
One obtains a great nourishment, increased two or threefold; this is the *pauṣṭika* rite.
Furthermore, for the purpose of protecting one's own army, one should perform the *kumbhayāga*.
Having worshipped eight jars placed around it, presided over by Bhīṣaṇa and the others, and filled with cloth, sprouts, fruit, and gold; || 30-119 ||
As before, having consecrated the liṅga according to the prescribed rite with ten *prasthas* of milk and ghee, and with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having smeared the liṅga along with its pedestal with well-ground sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron,
[he should worship it] with beautiful bilva leaves.
Having filled [the vessel] with heaps of fragrant flowers such as *karavīra* and others, as well as with garlands, golden bands, and garments such as silk cloths; 30-122.
One should especially offer incense made from aloeswood and camphor;
one should also present ghee lamps and food offerings according to one's ability. (30.123)

With sacrificial twigs of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*, as well as with *palāśa* wood, *dūrvā* grass, white mustard, sesame, clarified butter, ghee, and milk-rice porridge. || 30-124 ||
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately during the nights in sequence;
for each jar, having recited the Aghora-weapon mantra eight thousand times.

With the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] and the waters from that jar, he should sprinkle his own commanders of the army and others, as well as their weapons, elephants, horses, and so forth, and utter benedictions. (30.126)
There shall be protection for one's own army, and one shall conquer the enemies in battle;
that is, the protection of one's own forces.
There shall be no suffering from scorpions, no fear of serpents, and no affliction from minor diseases, enemies, water, or fire.
There is no suffering from afflictions such as hungry ghosts or spirits, nor is there separation from beloved ones for one who knows the non-terrible weapon-mantra. || 30-127½ ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. || 30 ||
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.

Śiva himself, who exists until the end of creation, is proclaimed as the Śiva-weapon (śivāstra). It consists of the second letter of the sixth group [the letter ṣ], joined with the first half-mora of the fourth [the letter i]. (31.1)
By joining the first and the fifth [syllables] from the beginning, one thus forms a two-syllable mantra;
this is the Pāśupata weapon-mantra, which destroys all misfortunes.
At the beginning of this, one should employ the seed-syllable of Śiva as the weapon of Śiva;
it is divine, removes all obstacles, and bestows liberation through practices such as recitation.
The seer (ṛṣi) of these two mantras is Vāmadeva, while the deity is Śiva alone;
the metre is Paṅkti, and success is achieved through a hundred thousand recitations.
Indeed, those applications belonging to the Aghora weapon are the same for these two, the Pāśupata weapon and the Śiva weapon;
[the seed-syllable] is joined with the eighth vowel (Ū), the earth (L), the third vowel (I), and the bindu (M). (31–5)
The first seed-syllable has been indicated; the second shall be the first of the sixth [group].
The third, however, is the first of the eighth [group] conjoined with the fifth vowel. (31.6)

The five-syllable weapon-mantra known as Pāśupata consists of *varma* (the armor) and *astra* (the weapon). The syllable *prāṇa* (ha), endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, is white, creative, and pale. (31–7)

One should meditate upon the mantra that is of the nature of Śiva, consisting of consciousness, residing within the heart-lotus; it is the syllable Om (praṇava), followed by the word "Maheśāya. (31.8)
The word *vidma* is at the beginning, and *he* is at the end; we meditate upon the one whose speech is purified (*vāgviśuddhāya*).
After the word *tannaḥ*, there should be *rudraḥ*, and after the letter *pra*, there should be *codayāt*. (31.9)
One should extract the syllable enriched with the thirteenth vowel, joined with the letter of air (ya),
ending with the sixth [vowel], and place the Tāraka at the beginning of this word.

The word *vyoma* ending in the dative case, the word *vidma* joined with the letter *ha*, the syllable *śu* joined with the sixth vowel, and the final [syllable] joined with the last letter of the sixth [group]. (31.11)
Having likewise extracted the subtle sound ending in the dative case, as well as "dhīmahi" and so forth,
as before, it becomes the Sāvitrī known by the name Śiva.
The application of these two, however, is prescribed in the ritual for the worship of Śiva.
Now I shall declare the Sāvitrī-mantra known as Vyomavyāpin, which consists of eighty-one distinct words.
And of the phonemes as well, there are exactly three hundred and sixty-eight in this [system] by number.
The first word is the syllable *tāra* (Om), followed by the final letter of the seventh [vowel], accompanied by the skin (*tvak*).
Having thus extracted [the syllable] endowed with the thirteenth vowel,
and likewise again [the one] ending in the sixth [consonant], followed by "vyāpine," this is the second five-syllabled [mantra].
The word "vyoman" (space) is for the one who pervades all forms;
thus, when the five-syllabled phrase has been uttered, "Śivāya" consists of three syllables.
With the words "anantānātha" in the fourth case (dative), there is a four-syllable word;
then, with the five syllables "anāśritāya," the eighth word is formed.
In the phrase consisting of three or four syllables, [one should recite] "to the eternal and constant one," and also "to the one established on the seat of yoga, the ever-united one. (31.18)
In the five-arrow-syllable [mantra], the six-colored syllables serve as the food for meditation;
however, the five-syllable mantra beginning with Tārā is the primary six-syllable phrase.
The word *vataḥ* should consist of five syllables, beginning with *sarvaprabhava*; the word *śivāya* consists of three syllables; then follows the pentad beginning with Īśāna. (31–20)

Having spoken [the mantras] for the head, the face, and the heart, and further for the secret part and the form—thus numbering six and seven according to the count of the sages (twenty-one)—[one should worship]. (31.21)

The five words should consist of syllables numbering the oceans and the four great oceans in sequence; the first word is *tāra* (Oṃ), followed by *namaḥ* repeated, which constitutes the five-syllable word.
With six [syllables] for the one who is more secret than the secret, for the Protector; with two syllables for the word;
with five syllables for the one who has no end; and for the Lord of all Vidyās.
The eight-syllable mantra is: *saptārṇaiḥ sarvayogādhigatāya*.
With five syllables: *jyotīrūpāya*. And: *parameśvaraparāya*. (31–24)

The phrase "the state of the Supreme Self" (paramātman-pada) consists of eight syllables and is considered the color of the Vedas; the phrase "the insentient and the sentient" (acetanā cetanā) is recorded as having seven syllables.
In the sky [of consciousness], there is a pair, four-colored, and likewise a pair of pervasive ones;
formless and repeated, with six [syllables], as well as the first two.
The pair of splendors, the four colors, and likewise the pair of lights—
these three by three are formless, without fire, and smokeless.
"Abhasma," "ca," "api," and "anāde"—these four words of the Lord consist of three syllables each. Thus there are twelve syllables in total. 31-28.
The first [syllable] is *tāra* (om), followed by *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, which consist of two, three, and two syllables respectively;
the *pada*s are formed with the syllables beginning with *anidhana*, and the *nidhana* consists of three syllables.
The five-syllable mantra beginning with *nidhana* and *udbhava* is "Śiva," consisting of two syllables;
by these two [syllables], the word "Śarva" is to be understood here by the teachers. (31–30)
Then follows the five-syllable name "Maheśvara," the four-syllable "Mahādeva," the five-syllable "Sadbhāveśvara," and the four-syllable "Mahātejas. (31–31)
O Lord of Yoga, the five-syllable [mantra] releases four pairs;
the first two [are released] by six, and every subsequent pair [is released] by four.
The pair of *bhava* occurs with four [syllables], and there is a quartet of *bhavodbhava*.
Now, the eight-syllable word indeed bestows happiness upon all beings. (31–33)
The seven-syllabled mantra is the foremost of all, as is that which is said to bring about the presence [of the deity];
the eight-syllabled mantra consists of the supreme state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
"Unhonored," "honored," likewise "refined," and "repeated"—these four preceding terms are to be known as the eight-syllable feet. (31–35)
"Sākṣin" (Sākṣīn) consists of two syllables; "caturbhiḥ" (caturbhiḥ) consists of four syllables; "vedārṇam" (vedārṇam) consists of four syllables;
"turyugmakam" (turyugmakam) consists of four syllables; "pataṅga" (pataṅga) consists of three syllables; and "piṅgayugmam" (piṅgayugmam) consists of four syllables. (31–36)
The pair of knowledges, the pair of sounds, the pair of subtle [principles], the three words, the individual syllables of the Vedas, and the two pairs of Śiva and Sarva. (31–37)
With the three syllables "sarvade" and the five syllables "oṃ namo namaḥ," the three-syllable phrase "śivāya" is to be understood by the best of teachers. (31–38)
The five-syllable word preceded by *tāra* (oṃ) and followed by a pair of salutations (*natidvandva*) is thus remembered;
in this manner, exactly eighty-one words are to be understood in their proper sequence. (31–39)

Having uttered the second word of the heart-mantra, which consists of the syllable *tāraṃ* (OM) for the Universal Self (*sarvātman*) together with the [seed-syllable of] birth, it is joined with the words "Śiva" and "Brahman. (31–40)
The head-mantra is said to be joined with its own seed-syllable;
having uttered the third word, one should practice the word "jvālinī" twice.
Then one should extract the fourth word as stated with the *śikhā* [mantra] joined with the *jāti*;
having uttered the word "piṅgala," the armor (*varma*) shall be joined with the *jāti*.
Having uttered the fifth word, one should likewise [utter] Śivāghorāstraka; that weapon should be joined with its [mantric] caste-suffix. These indeed are the five limbs (aṅgas). || 31-43 ||
The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of this Vyomavyāpin mantra, as seen according to the path taught in the *Candrajñāna*, are now written down in their proper sequence.

Oṃ Vyomavyāpiśiva, Oṃ, salutations to the Self of all, the Supreme, the Supreme Lord, to Yoga, to the Source of Yoga, Turu Turu, Truth, Truth, O Bhavodbhava, to Vāmadeva, O Sadāśiva who pacifies all effects, O gracious one, homage be unto you! Ṭhaṭha. Homage to the Heart. Śiva, to the Brahma-head, Ṭhaṭha. Oṃ Śivahṛdayajvālini, Ṭhaṭha. Vaṣaṭ to the Flame-tipped Crest (Śikhā) of Jvālinī.
I invoke the Great God, whose essence is Śiva, the All-knowing, the Imperishable Lord;
I turn toward the Mahāghora, the auspicious Piṅgala armor. (31–45)

"Come, Piṅgala, you of great armor, by the command of Śiva! Bind the heart; blaze! Reel! O wielder of the Śakti, wielder of the thunderbolt, you who have the form of the thunderbolt! Having entered into him, paralyze all the wicked, huṃ phaṭ! To Piṅgala, the armor, huṃ! Oṃ juṃ saṃ, to the three eyes of the nature of light, vauṣaṭ! The Aghora weapon is indeed the weapon as before. Śiva is its deity, the Ṛṣi is Śakti, and the meter is known as Gāyatrī. Therefore, nothing else should ever be deliberated upon regarding this. (31–46)
The sixth [letter] and so forth, situated upon the seed-syllable of the earth, joined with the bindu of the fifth vowel;
likewise, water with the visarga, water, and wind joined with the end of the twelve.

The word "Vyāpina" ending in the sixth case, joined with the beloved of the Fire-eater (Agni), preceded by the Om (Tāra), consists of ten syllables; this is the essence of Vyomavyāpi Śiva. || 31-48 ||
The first syllable is *tāraḥ* (the sound Om), and the second is the vowel; these two vowels are equal in measure to the Vedas and the seasons.
This ten-syllabled mantra ends with *vyomavyāpī* in the dative case (*caturthyanta*) and concludes with *tāra*. (31–49)
Having performed the purification of the hands with the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should place [the mantras] upon the fingers of the right and left hands in sequence,
using the ten syllables of the Vyomavyāpin mantra beginning with *jyeṣṭha*.
One should sequentially place the ten syllables, ending with the nasal bindu, upon the head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, heart, navel, the secret place, and the two feet. (31–51)

Having assigned the six limbs to their respective places in the heart and other parts, and having performed the binding of the directions with the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should perform the worship, recitation, and other rites. (31–52)
Having first obtained from the Guru initiation— whether it be the *sāmayī* leading to liberation,
or the *sādhakī* culminating in consecration— one should then accomplish the mantra.
Bathing three times a day, one should worship Śiva in the liṅga according to the sequence of the five-fold enclosure (pañcāvṛti),
using the prescribed services (upacāras) beginning with the seat (āsana) and according to one's capacity.

The first enclosure should consist of the [eight] forms and limbs; the second, by the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) in sequence; the third should consist of Nandīśa and the others; and the fourth, by the ten world-protectors (Lokapālas). (31–55)
Then the fifth [stage] is declared by means of the weapons (*astra*), just as in the *Uttara-paddhati*.
This is the section on the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantra-sādhanādhikāra*).
One should recite the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra eighty-one thousand times. (31–56)
Having offered one-tenth of that amount of ten-syllable [mantra] oblations of *palāśa* wood, clarified butter,
sesame seeds, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*) becomes perfected.
Even for a devotee who worships Śiva without prior preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), this mantra accomplishes the desired goal; how much more so, then, through the recitation as prescribed? (31.58)
It brings about the great accomplishment (siddhi) as described, increasing two, three, or fourfold;
from ten lakhs of recitations, the chanting bestows the qualities such as aṇimā and the rest. (31–59)
By reciting this mantra seven times, one removes all diseases;
by eight times, all planetary afflictions; and by ten more [eighteen], all cases of epilepsy.
The mantra of Sadāśiva itself removes poisons through its recitation;
meditating on Sadāśiva as one's own self, one should perform ritual actions for the sake of accomplishment.
In rites for pacification, one should contemplate [the deity] as white; in rites for nourishment and subjugation, as red;
in attraction, as yellowish; and in rites for paralyzing and driving away, as smoke-colored.
One should meditate on Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of killing, on Śiva who has the radiance of the sun for victory over enemies,
and on him who resembles a conch, jasmine, the moon, a lotus stalk, or milk for the sake of liberation.
Meditating always upon [the deity] within the hollow of the heart-lotus, one is liberated from worldly existence;
whatever action may be desired, that should be accomplished through fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth. (31.64)
One shall accomplish [the goal] without effort within half a fortnight; there is no doubt.
When oblations are offered with sprouts and other substances, as well as the materials mentioned in the chapter, [this result follows].
One should constantly accomplish each respective rite one hundred and eight times. (The Section on Vyomavyāpin, p.
177) Sā with Īśa, Anugraha, and Sā with Agni, followed by Kāṣṭha, O, Bindu, and Nāda. (31.66)
The *piṇḍa* should be the seed-jewel (*bījaratna*), which accomplishes all aims.
One's own limbs, conjoined with the six classes (*jāti*) and the long vowels, follow in sequence. (31.67)
The seer is Aṅgiras; its metre is indeed the divine Gāyatrī;
and its deity is to be known as the Thunderbolt, possessing a splendor like the fire of time. (31.68)
It is joined with six points, sharp-tipped, and endowed with keen edges;
it is capable of the method of tearing asunder all missiles, weapons, and adversaries.
A hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), and an oblation of sesame seeds performed in ten parts [of that number] is required.
The seed-syllable (piṇḍa) situated between the orbs of the Moon and Indra is known to have the form of a vajra.
Yellow, filled with garlands of flames, it is the paralyzer of all enemies—whether in the mouths of opponents, in an army, or among rutting elephants, buffaloes, and the like. (31.71)
The *piṇḍa* situated within the moon, Indra, the disk, and fire is said to be that which is to be recited;
when visualized as yellow and filled with flames, it clearly and immediately paralyzes each respective [target]. (31.72)
When meditated upon as joined with wind and fire, the *piṇḍa* brings about paralysis;
likewise, when meditated upon in one seized by a planetary spirit (*graha*), the *piṇḍa* brings about his liberation.

Indeed, in whatever house this [image] written with yellow pigment (rocanā) on cloth or other materials is worshipped, the planets, diseases, epidemics, and minor ailments shall surely depart from it.
One should paralyze the *piṇḍa* situated in the circle of Indra, with its weapon raised;
[one should paralyze] the *piṇḍa* situated in the circle of the waters, devoid of the favor of fire. (31.75)
Poison placed upon the head of one bitten by a venomous creature will be destroyed instantly;
likewise, a *piṇḍa* [of this substance] within the center of a *piṇḍa* [placed] even upon the orb of the moon or the sun [will have the same effect]. (31.76)
Then, having written the name and the *jīva* interlaced within it, one should write the syllables of the *vipati* [mantra] upon the petals—in the west, north, south, east, and in the center. (31.77)
*Tāram*, *saṃvartakaḥ*, *sākṣaḥ*, *pārśvam*, and *ṭhaurvipatermanuḥ*—this five-syllable [mantra] is its application (*viniyoga*), which is written here below. || 31-78 ||
In the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Rakṣas, and Śarva, one should place the letters from *ya* to *va*, together with the bindu;
then, one should encircle them three times on the outside with the eye of the short *u* (the *u* with the bindu). (31.79)
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with a golden needle, using a paste of *rocanā* moistened with cow-dung water;
or one may write it during the Puṣṭyarka or Siddha yoga.
Having worshipped it with one thousand and eight recitations (japa) and burnt offerings (homa),
[the mantra] should be rolled into a pill and encased in gold and silver.
Held in the hand, or on the neck, or on the head, it grants all desires;
it bestows longevity, health, victory, prosperity, abundance, and sons. (31.82)
It removes the fear arising from spirits, seizing demons, thieves, enemies, water, fire, and existence;
when worn, it always protects one from lions, tigers, elephants, and other such dangers. (31.83)
When, however, by the force of time the withered leaf has been carried away, one should write that [letter] which is devoid of the bindu, the moon-maṇḍala, and the [vowels] beginning with ya. (31.84)
Having written [the mantra] on a black crow-feather leaf, one should cause enemies to be driven away;
for rites such as expulsion, one should recite the *piṇḍa* mantra while it is enclosed within the fire of wrath (*krodhāgni*).
One should write the syllable *khaṃ*, together with the ear (*śrī*), fire (*agni*), and half-moon (*candrārdha*), known as the seed-syllable of wrathful fire;
likewise, one should write it upon a neem leaf using the body of a crow and fire.
From the aforementioned incense, there shall be enmity between them and their offspring;
likewise, [enmity arises] from the products of poison, cats, mongooses, snakes, and buffaloes.
For the purpose of inciting hatred, one should fumigate with hairs mixed with nimba leaves;
a mass [of hair] inscribed upon a nimba leaf and enveloped by the fire of wrath.
The rite of killing is performed by offering oblations into the funeral fire with blood-soaked poison;
it is bound at both ends with a noose and enclosed within the fire of long-standing anger. (31.89)
One should recite the *piṇḍa* mantra during pacifying rites, especially for the pacification of minor evils;
for the pacification of diseases and the like, the *piṇḍa* should be recited as the "vase-enclosure" (*kumbhasaṃpuṭa*).
(179) Possessing the white luster of nectar situated within the lunar disc; this is the section on the *piṇḍa*.
Saṃvarta has skin like poisonous fire, and he bears the half-moon as his crest upon his head. (31.91)
The seed-syllable is named Cintāmaṇi; its presiding deity is Mahārudra; the seer is known as Tumburu, and its meter is indeed Gāyatrī. (31.92)
The preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations, followed by an oblation of sesame seeds amounting to one-tenth of that number;
yet that seed-syllable, devoid of the grace of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is merely joined with the long vowels. (31.93)
The six limbs are accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (jāti), ending with the *bindu* and the three eyes;
that too ends with the weapon (*astra*).
Seated upon the seat of Śiva, a red lotus, he is to be meditated upon as having a ruddy luster.
Holding an arrow, a trident, fire, serpents, a chisel, and a sword,
as well as a skull and a bow, he has eight arms and three eyes.
Clad in red garments, wearing a skin as a loincloth, with matted hair and the moon as his crest-jewel;
fierce yet possessing a serene countenance, beautiful in every limb—he is to be meditated upon. (31.96)

The limbs [of the deity] are upon the tips of the filaments; the goddesses reside within the petals of the directions; and all his messengers, possessing graceful forms, are situated upon the petals at the corners. 31.97.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā, Durgā, Subhagā, Karālī, and likewise Mohanī. || 31-98 ||

Outside of that, one should worship with the ten Lords of the World (Lokeśas), the Vighnas, the Vīreśas, and the Mothers; and outside of that again, one should worship with their weapons and the fourfold enclosure (caturāvaraṇa).
Through ritual services performed according to one's capacity, the mantra becomes perfected;
then, the various applications of the mantra come to fruition for one who is devoted to recitation, meditation, and worship.
That seed-syllable, situated before a blazing fire and with its head swallowed [by it], effects paralysis and the liberation from planetary afflictions for one who recites it in an instant. (31.101)
The seed-syllable (bīja) remembered together with the name of a woman, placed within the womb [of the triangle], is a means of subjugation;
one should meditate upon oneself as being situated within that seed-syllable which rests upon fire and wind.
This [mantra] creates protection for oneself or for another;
it is remembered as being black, located in the ear, the eyes, and the belly, O Māra. (31.103)
Deafness, blindness, and piercing pain will clearly arise as the seed [of destruction].
When visualized within the body of the enemy as a seed composed of fire, it causes burning. (31.104)
The yantra situated within the forms of fire and wind in the heart, when remembered, brings women under one's control;
it is located in the mouth of the Bhairava of the Cakrīṃ-mudrā and possesses the seed-syllable (bīja) of that name. (31.105)
It causes the paralysis of speech for an enemy; it brings about yawning, delusion, and so forth within the house of the earth;
and when placed in a jar of sweet water, it removes hunger, thirst, fever, and other ailments. (31.106)
Visualizing that hexagon above the head of the bitten person, one should bring it down to the feet;
touching this three times immediately effects the destruction of the poison. (31.107)
The pale seed-syllable, which has no upward-flaming fire and flows with nectar, when meditated upon at the throat or in the left hand, removes poison, death, and old age. (31.108)
The seed-syllable situated in the center of the hexagon is devoid of fire, wind, and the rest;
in the six corners, it is accompanied by fire, starting from the non-upward direction.
Adorned with an external maṇḍala and inscribed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on birch bark,
it is prepared by being rolled into a pill according to the procedure taught for the *piṇḍayantra*.
For this is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), accomplishing all aims as before.
Then the *praṇava*, the word, the sound, the two ears, the navel, and then water. (31.111)
The Guha-mantra consists of the vowels as its syllables; it ends with the word "namas" and resides within the Rudra-svara.
Viśvāmitra is its sage, the Uṣṇih its meter, and [the aforementioned] its deity. (31.112)

The six-faced one (Kārttikeya) should perform ten thousand recitations as the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), followed by an oblation of sesame and clarified butter amounting to one-tenth of that number, and worship according to the prescribed injunctions. (31.113)
Guha may have six faces or a single face, twelve eyes and twelve arms, or four arms or two arms; he is adorned with red ornaments and attire. || 31.114 ||
The youth Skanda, whether as a boy or a prince, should be meditated upon with a smiling face;
in his two hands he holds a lotus below and a spear and a cock above. (31.115)
Skanda, possessing four arms and seated upon a lotus throne, should be meditated upon;
he holds a lotus and a spear in his right hands, and a mātuluṅga fruit in his left.
The youthful Guha has four arms and one face; he holds a noose, bestows fearlessness, a lotus, and a spear in his right hands, and [grants] boons and a lance in his left. (31.117)
Holding a vajra and possessing six arms, he is to be meditated upon as seated on a lotus throne;
or, even when standing, he may be visualized with six faces or with a single face. (31.118)

Holding in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a spear, arrows, a thunderbolt, and a goad, and likewise holding in [his left hands] one that touches the hip and one that bestows boons; 31.119.
The all-pervading Lord has twelve arms; starting from the lower left hand and proceeding upwards, he holds a staff, a javelin, a bow, a bell, and a noose.
Having bathed with the root-mantras and the limb-mantras, having performed the twilight rites and become pure,
with his feet and hands washed and having sipped water for purification (ācamana), he should worship these two door-keepers at the entrance.
Homage to Śaktipāṇi! Homage to Vajrapāṇi!
Having entered within and sat down, one should worship Vighneśa and the Guru.
Having performed the self-sacrifice and applied the tilaka mark, one should [proceed] with water enriched by the root-mantra and its ancillaries.
Through the purification consisting of sprinkling one's own head, eyes, and the ritual substances,
[one should visualize] the powers (śaktis) seated upon the bodies of the Anantas within the auspicious mandala.
One should [place] Dharma and the others in the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus; Sattva and the others in the mandalas;
and Brahmā and the others, as well as Vidyā and the other Śaktis, with the nine syllables beginning with *ya*.

Having visualized the form of Skanda as prescribed, one should worship it after joining it with the vowels *kṣā*, *ntaiḥ*, long vowels, and the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and having placed it within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Having invoked the light consisting of the [five] elements from either the heart-lotus or the *dvādaśānta* via the path of the *suṣumṇā*, and having established it within the image, one should cause it to abide there.
Having restrained and concealed [the senses], and then having aroused interest, one should lead [the disciple] to the state of immortality;
having worshipped according to the rules with the sixteen services beginning with the water for honor (*arghya*).
One should worship the limbs (aṅgas), the powers (śaktis), the six forms (ṣaṇmūrtis), and the retinue;
[worship them] on the filaments, at their tips, on the tips of the petals, and outside of those. (31.128)
One should worship Aṅga and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas), as well as their respective weapons.
The names of the enclosures (āvaraṇas) are:
Vidyā, Śānti, Smṛti, Medhā, Prajñā, Kānti, Dyuti, and Dhṛti. (31.129)
And Vyāpinī, ending with Bindu—one should worship the ninth [deity] in their midst:
Sanatkumāra, Skanda, Viśākha, and likewise Ṣaṇmukha.
One should worship these six in sequence: Naigameṣa and Hemacūḍa, located in the directions of the East, South, Southwest, West, Northwest, and North.
In the northeast and southeast, one should worship the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, which shower wealth;
then, at each of the four gates, one should worship two deities each, beginning with Vīrasena.
Vīrasena and Mahāsena, Bhadrasena and Suṣeṇaka, Cārusena the commander-in-chief, Senānta, Pūrṇa, and Citraka. (31.133)
The meaning is that they are to be worshipped.
In the external [mandala], the twelve lords of the Gaṇas are situated in the twelve zodiac signs;
they are Bāṇa, Śākha, Bhadrasena, and Senānī, the son of Bhava. (31.134)
Subrahmaṇya, Kārtikeya, Guha, indeed Kukkuṭadhvaja, Mayūravāhana, and Gāṅgeya—these follow thereafter. (31.135)
And Deva-senāpati—these twelve are the lords of the Gaṇas.
Outside of that, the world-protectors (lokapālas) should be worshipped, together with their weapons and vehicles.
One should worship Vighna and Vīrabhadra in the south, and the Mothers;
likewise, one should worship Durgā near the northwest (Vāyu) and Dhūrtasena in the northeast (Īśa).
Having thus worshipped him together with his retinue, one should also offer worship in the fire;
the daily oblation (*nityahoma*) with sesame, clarified butter, wood-apple (*bilva*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is highly recommended.
The section on the qualification for mantra-sādhana and so forth:
(p. 183) Having offered oblations with the prescribed substances into a quadrangular or hexagonal fire-pit containing a pure *skanda*-fire, one shall attain all desires. || 31.139 ||
With fuel-sticks made of *bilva*, one attains prosperity (*śrī*); with those of *khadira*, supreme nourishment (*puṣṭi*);
with those of *aśvattha*, cattle; and with those of *plakṣa*, grain and wealth. (31.140)

One obtains intelligence and knowledge with *palāśa* leaves, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) with them; with food mixed with clarified butter, one obtains food, and with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one obtains prosperity and wealth.
One obtains sons by offering *putrajīva* fruits, and all forms of prosperity by offering sesame seeds;
by offering flowers of whatever color, one attains garments of that same color. (31.142)
Longevity is attained with *dūrvā* grass; prosperity with lotuses; victory in battle with arrows;
paralysis with *sabusa* (husks) and mustard seeds; and hatred with cotton-seed chaff. (31.143)
Likewise, eradication is performed with poison-leaves, and killing with poisonous poisons;
for a maiden, with parched grain mixed with honey, and for the destruction of enemies, with white mustard seeds.
By offering oblations with honey and salt for sixty-four days, or half of that, or even for a fortnight, the subjugation of all beings becomes certain. (31.145)
By performing oblations, a minister may obtain various results according to the gravity of the task;
for those who are unable to perform the rite of homa, the recitation of mantras (japa) shall be three times that amount.
Or, if the food consists of four qualities, one should prepare it even from double that amount;
[therein] the Child Skanda, seated upon a jewel lion-throne lotus, rests upon the lap of Śivā.
Meditating on his own body being filled by floods of the jewels that are its fruits as they shower down, and while reciting [the mantra], within just one month— || 31.148 ||
Abundance and prosperity of wealth arise like those of Kubera;
likewise, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth should be performed on the sixth lunar day under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Having quickly performed [the rite] with its specific distinctions, one shall obtain all desires.
Like the Śivāstra, the Pāśupatāstra has been declared; so too the Vidyā called Vyoma and the Piṇḍabīja.
Likewise, the Cintāmaṇibīja and the Ṣaḍvaktramanttra are presented here in this chapter in brief.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 31.

Now begins the thirty-second chapter. The heart-mantra of the Teacher [Lakulīśa] consists of the final two syllables of Śivottama, followed by Tithīśa and Sthāṇu; this is indeed the mantra for worship, joined with Lakulīśa and Tithīśa. (32.1)
"Accompanied by the nasal bindu and red in color, 'Namaḥ to the Protector of Wealth (Rāyagoptre)'—this nine-syllabled root mantra, preceded by Oṃ, grants all desires. (32-2)
The fourth letter from the sixth group (the labials), preceded by the star (the vowel *i*), long and with a bindu (anusvāra)—this word "bhūtādhipataye," ending with "namaḥ," is that mantra. (32-3)
By means of these offerings, beginning with the *arghya*, the Teacher is to be worshipped according to the ritual procedure.
The name Bhūtasena, ending in the dative case, is joined with the word *vidmahe*. (32–4)
"Bhava-putra, likewise, we meditate upon that; may the Teacher inspire us"—this is the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable *Tār*. (32.5)
To Revanta, to Śāstra, to Goptṛ, and likewise to Prabhu,
to Dīpta, and to Praśāstra— these are the six limbs associated with the [six] castes.
Śāmbo is its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī its metre (chandas), and Śāstṛ its deity.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consists of one hundred thousand recitations followed by an oblation of ten parts made with ghee and sesame seeds. || 32-7 ||
By means of this perfected mantra, one shall attain all desires;
[it is for] the sword, the dagger, the bow, and the arrow.
The weapon-mantras (śastramantra), beginning with *huṃ phaṭ* and ending with *namaḥ*, are arranged in their proper order.
Upon the lotus of the Bhūta-siṃhāsana, the Teacher (Śāstṛ) is situated at the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Four-armed, with a gentle countenance, dark-complexioned, and of tender form; seated with one lotus-foot upon his left thigh, while the other lotus-foot hangs down.
Holding a bow, arrows, a sword, and a dagger in his arms,
he has a face like the full moon and beautiful, dark, curly locks of hair.
His body was as beautiful as that of Hari and Hara, with his waist bound by a girdle;
he was adorned with a crown, lovely armlets, bracelets, and finger-rings. || 32-12 ||
In that very manner, he bears a waist-thread and two anklets;
he wears garments of blue silk and has his sword girded. (32.13)
He has red garments, well-filled shoulders, and is the banner of all beauty;
to his left is the Goddess Prabhā, who is red in color and holds a blue lotus.
Having meditated upon and invoked Satyaka, who has the form of an eight-year-old boy, as the son on the right,
one should worship the Teacher, the God, together with his retinue.
That is to say:
having meditated and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship the door of obstacles;
one should worship two doorkeepers on both sides, each holding a razor and a sword in their hands. (32.16)
One should worship the Yakṣa, the Vidyādhara, and the Door-Goddess (Dvāraśrī) above;
having cast the weapon-mantra (astra), one should enter within and place it upon the threshold.
Having worshipped the Vāstu, Brahmā, and the seats with the root mantra and its ancillaries,
one should offer the arghya water consisting of fragrance, flowers, kuśa grass, milk, sesame seeds, white mustard, and unbroken grains.
The *arghya* for the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*) should consist of sesame seeds, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water;
likewise, sandalwood and *niśā* (turmeric) are for the *pādya*, as are the lotus and sandalwood.
One should cause all of this—the water for rinsing the mouth and the water for sipping—to be offered with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Adorned with a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) and a flower on the crest-lock, one should [worship] the *śakti*, the pedestal, and the earth-element.

Having honored the feet [of the Lord] with the salutation "Obeisance to You," who possess a vast lion-throne and consist of all powers, he likewise honors Dharma and the others, whose forms are composed of the elements.
Tamas, sattva, rajas, the lotus, and likewise the powers such as Goptrī;
from these [he creates] the form consisting of the mantra-body, with its previously described appearance, weapons, and so forth.
Having performed the mental visualization (saṅkalpa), one should invoke the deity whose nature is consciousness into that image—
the subtle, supreme light risen from the heart-lotus via the support (ādhāra).
Having invoked the deity, one should establish him; having brought him into close proximity, one should restrain him;
and likewise, having delighted him and rendered him immortal, one should worship him in due order with the arghya and other offerings.
One should worship the enclosures with offerings ending with the ritual services (*upacāra*).
The limbs (*aṅga*) are at the tips of the filaments, while Goptrī and the others are located in the middle of the petals. (32.25)
One should worship those Śaktis on the tips of the petals, and Skanda and the others outside the pedestal; one should worship Ghoṣavant, the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya), in the northeast.
One should worship the horse or elephant vehicle of the Teacher in the portico, the Āryas and others on the path, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside of that.
