Then their weapons [are outside]; thus is the sevenfold enclosure (āvaraṇa-saptaka). The names of the enclosures are:
Goptṛ, Piṅgalākṣa, Vīrasena, and Śāmbhava. (32.28)
The three-eyed one, the wielder of the trident, Dakṣa, and likewise the eighth, Bhīmarūpa—these are the eight forms (mūrtis) of the Teacher, conjoined with earth and the other elements. (32–29)
Goptrī, Piṅgalākṣī, Vīrasenā, Śāmbhavī, Triṇetrā, Śūlinī, Dakṣā, and Bhīmarūpā is remembered as the eighth. (32–30)
Prabhā is said to be the ninth among them; these are declared to be the powers of the Teacher.
Then there are Skanda, Gaṇapati, Śāmbo, and likewise Madhukara. (32–31)
In the cardinal directions they are to be worshipped, and in the corners, the sword, the dagger, the bow, and the arrow;
these should be worshipped by their respective names, ending with "hūṃ phaṭ."

The noble one, the Teacher, the Great General, the Leader of the Army, the Beloved of Beings, born of Rudra, the beautiful, the desirous, the giver of boons, and the Purifier of the World. || 32-33 ||
Blue-horsed, white-elephant-mounted, dark-complexioned, and smeared with yellow unguents;
wearing a red garland, the hero Māya, who is dear to the host of Mothers.
Clad in black garments, the leader of the Gaṇas, sword in hand and bearing a bow;
born together with his consort, the one who possesses the power to enter all beings, the virtuous protector of the world. || 32–35 ||
Madhu and Śambara— these are indeed the twenty-eight lords of beings (bhūtapas),
as well as the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt.
In the case of a fixed image (sthiraberaka), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, ending with the bali offering;
likewise, for a portable image (bala) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and then mentally [visualize the deity].
Having offered the oblation (*bali*) and having invoked him into the fire, one should offer it as a libation (*juhuyāt*).
One should propitiate [the deity] with circumambulations, prostrations, hymns of praise, and silent recitations (*japa*). (32–38)
For this sacrifice of the Teacher bestows glory, nourishment, and victory;
it increases longevity, health, wealth, progeny, and prosperity. (32–39)

The Chapter on Worship: Having thus visualized the Teacher—mounted on a horse, surrounded by his retinue, appearing in the form of a hunter, and emerging from the forest for the sake of water—[one should worship him]. (32–40)
At midday, having taken water mixed with groats in his joined palms and sprinkling it while reciting the nine mantras, he should also satisfy the Gaṇas.
Then, once he has rested, one should report one's own affairs to him;
having spoken thus with a pleased mind, one should remember that he has departed. (32–42)
All undertakings, even those merely conceived in thought, are accomplished without effort;
likewise, one should offer a bali-oblation to him at night with the mantras beginning with "Ārya."

With *bhūtakrūra* mixed with clarified butter, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), [one should offer] likewise to the Lord of Beings (*bhūtādhipati*) with the mantra "Obeisance to Mahāśāstra. (32–44)
Or one may offer the bali-oblation with these mantras: "Homage be to the son of Rudra, and to Pañcakeśvaraka; homage to the virtuous one. (32–45)
In the directions beginning with the east and in the center, for the sake of protection, nourishment, and prosperity,
all the people of the Vāṅkṣāḍīs, divided into millions upon millions, [are present].
May they be united and gracious; salutations, salutations to them and to those [goddesses].

Salutations, salutations to the hosts of the East and other directions—those of terrifying form, of terrifying faces, of created forms, the stable and the fickle, the bestowers of boons, the multiform, the deformed, the of terrifying form, the existent, the non-existent, and the both-existent-and-non-existent—to all the hosts, salutations, salutations!
Dviraṇḍa, Anantadaṇḍāḍhya, Karṇānta, Nābhirāṣaḍhī.
The mantra for the Lord is nine syllables, beginning with *sākṣo mīnotha* and followed by *hṛt*.
(p. 188) Through practice, worship, and so forth as before, it bestows the fruit as previously described. || 32-48 ||
The section on the mantras of the Teacher:
The final [mantra] is rich in grace and punishment, beginning with Tārā and so forth, with the syllables of the Kṣetrapa;
the earth [syllable], along with its long vowel and nasalization, is the mantra whose deity is the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa). || 32–49 ||
The limbs [of the mantra] are formed with the first [syllable], joined in sequence with the six long vowels;
the preliminary service consists of one thousand syllables, and the meter is indeed the Gāyatrī.
The Ṛṣi is named Baṭuka, and the presiding deity is Kṣetrapāla;
one should daily recite [the mantra] one thousand times from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the end of the fourteenth.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for this [mantra] shall be performed, and now the meditation (dhyāna) is described:
May He protect us—He who resembles a mass of collyrium, a herd of elephants, or a dark rain-cloud;
who is terrifying, clad in the sky as His garment, and who holds in His two hands a fragment of a skull and a mace.
With a face bristling with fangs, tawny and round, with three eyes and hair standing erect,
his body adorned with a garland of serpents as his head-ornament, may the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśvara) protect you for a long time.

Otherwise, others [describe him] as having matted hair rising upwards with a serpent as its crest, three eyes, and the luster of a mountain of blue collyrium; holding a mace and a skull-cup in his two arms, and radiant with red garlands, garments, and perfumes.
I always worship that omnipresent Kṣetrapāla, who is terrifying with the "dhukka" sound produced by the movement of his bell, chain, and girdle, and who wears a coiled serpent as an earring.
"Come, come, O fierce one! O Ṭhalamaru! Break, strike away obstacles, O Mahābhairava! O Kṣetrapāla! Accept the offering, ṭhaṭha!
With this mantra, which is to be accomplished, one should offer the oblation (bali) into that skull.
To the left and right, and in the eight directions, [are] the others starting from Anala:
Anala, Agnikeśa, Kāla, and likewise Ghaṇṭārava.
Then there is the one named Mahākrodha, and the one known as Piśitāśana; Piṅgalākṣa and Ūrdhvakeśa are the destroyers at the end of the fourth age.
They should be worshipped in the directions, and one should cast the *bali* offering to them at midnight.
This *bali* bestows protection, victory, and prosperity. (32.57)
On the courtyard smeared with cow-dung, having established his form through mantras,
he brings together red-scented flowers and other offerings, and is sprinkled with the water of the *arghya* oblation.
One should worship the seat with the mantra "Obeisance to Anantayogapīṭha," and upon that,
having invoked Kṣetrapāla according to the prescribed rite with the root mantra.
One should worship him with the ritual services beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the lamp;
having invoked the four forms in the cardinal directions, the limbs (*aṅga*) in the corners, and [the principal deity] in front.
One should again worship the Netra-weapon in the various directions with perfumes and other offerings in a secluded place.
[The attendants are] Aticāra, Rājā, and the high-minded one named Kapālī. (32–61)
They were dark-complexioned, mountain-like in stature, equipped with bows, and resembled Rākṣasas;
then, [he took] that which was consecrated with the Bali-mantra by his left hand.
Having offered rice cooked with *kuḍuba* measures of grain, mixed with curd and clarified butter,
one should pour water over half of that food three times and cast the offering (*bali*) onto a potsherd three times.
Having offered oblations (bali) once each from the remaining portions to the [deities of the] forms and limbs,
one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the lord of the field of one's own [respective] square.
He who thus performs the bali offering to the Kṣetrapāla for the protection of his home obtains prosperity, nourishment, wealth, happiness, cattle, and sons. (32.65)
The ritual for the bali offering to Kṣetrapāla:
The left ear (va), then the pitcher (u), the fish (ma), and the letter ra, ending with phaṭ;
this three-syllabled mantra of Caṇḍeśvara grants all desires to those who worship it. (32–66)
Karṇī, Mīna, Sadṛk, Meṣa, and then the word Caṇḍeśvara ending in the dative case (caturthyanta), followed by the armor (varma) and the weapon (astra)— this is the nine-syllable mantra of Caṇḍeśvara.
For these two mantras, the ṛṣi, meter, and presiding deity are identical;
likewise, their limbs, ritual procedure, and means of accomplishment are the same. (32.68)
The meter is likewise the Bṛhatī, and the seer is Caṇḍakauśika;
the deity is Caṇḍeśvara, and there are indeed five limbs ending with the weapons. (32–69)
"Daptiṣaḍjvalaphaṭ," "Jvālinī," and "Taṭā"—these words containing "sarvajvālinī" should end in "phaṭ" and be joined with the [appropriate] jāti-mantra. (32.70)
One should sequentially assign the five limbs, beginning with the heart;
these should be placed upon the fingers of the two hands, which have been purified by the weapon-mantra, starting from the thumb.
One should place the syllables of a three-syllable mantra upon all the finger-joints, and the words of a nine-syllable mantra upon the five fingers.
Two by two and three by three, some even by single syllables;
one should place the syllables on the head, heart, and feet, while for another [mantra] of three syllables, they are placed on the head.
One should place the five steps on the face, heart, secret place, and feet;
and the five limbs in the heart and other locations in their respective places, in due order.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for both [mantras] consists of three hundred thousand and one hundred thousand recitations respectively;
and from this, a fire sacrifice (*homa*) should be performed with flowers from Śiva’s remains (*nirmālya*) in a tenth part of that amount. (32–75)
Regarding the mantra-sādhana:
having fashioned an image out of rice flour from the sand of a river, one should repeatedly cut it apart and offer it into the fire, beginning from the right foot. (32.76)
By means of that [mixture], one should bring a brahmin under control using a fire fueled by *apāmārga* wood;
using a fire of funeral pyre wood with the aforementioned effigy, one effects the subjugation of a king.
In the same way, one should bring even the Vaiśyas and Śūdras under control; of this there is no doubt.
[One should perform this] with sesame, rice, pungent substances, and clarified butter, in the fire of a golden crucible belonging to the enemy. (32.78)
For one afflicted by insanity, an oblation should be offered with milk in a khadira fire;
or likewise, an offering may be made with priyaṅgu flowers and ghee in a fire.

The mantra for obtaining garments with flowers of various colors during a city-disturbance consists of the syllable *sā*, followed by *agnivāmākṣa* (the fire-syllable and the left eye), *daṇḍa* (the staff), *atri* (the sage Atri), the dative case-ending, and *indra* (Indra). (32.80)
With these long seed-syllables, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in due order.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Āṅgirasa, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, and likewise the deity (*devatā*). (32.81)
Indra should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times; from that, one-tenth of the portion should be offered as oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds.
Thus is his preliminary rite (puraścaryā) declared, and now his visualization (dhyāna) is described.

Yellow in color, with four arms, holding a vajra, a lotus, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness; his every limb is beautiful, adorned with yellow ornaments made of wish-fulfilling gems. || 32-83 ||
Adorned with a crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, and other ornaments,
he is seated upon a golden lotus on a golden lion-throne, situated in the midst of a golden pavilion.
Seated together with the goddess Śacī and attended by the Maruts, he was served by Skanda,
Anala, Yama, and the other eight world-protectors.
One should employ the eight seed-syllables together with the *karaka*, *akṣaya*, and *vāsas*, along with the bindus;
at the beginning, one should prefix the names of those [deities], and at the end, append "namas. (32.86)

Having meditated upon and worshipped the offering of faded flowers (*nirmālya*) in the northeast, beginning with its own seed-syllable and ending with the word "namas," one should also apply the external weapons, such as the vajra and others.
One should worship Surendra in this manner for the attainment of sovereignty, nourishment, and prosperity;
having thus worshipped Śatakratu in the auspicious maṇḍala and the water-pot (kumbha).
Consecrated by this, one attains royal glory and the fruits of victory;
having offered oblations of sesame, clarified butter, and milk-rice, one shall obtain all desires. (32.89)
The Chapter on the Worship of Indra.
Now, as for the mantra of Jambhala: after the word *maṇibhadra*, then the word *mahāsena*, and then *kṣayādhipataye*. (32–90)
For Jambhala, the lord of waters, the mantra is *jambhalāya jalendrāya ṭhau*; this is the Jāmbhala mantra.
Its limbs (*aṅga*) consist of six syllables:
*namaḥ maṇibhadrāya*, *namaḥ pūrṇabhadrāya*, *namaścelimāline*, *namo vikuṇḍaline*, *narendrāya*, and *carendrāya*. These are the mantras for the six limbs.
The corners of the eyes [are adorned] with their own respective types. || 32-91 ||

One should worship the enclosure with the limbs (aṅgas) upon the filaments, then with the powers (śaktis) at the tips of the petals; and in the fourth enclosure, one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) along with their weapons (astras).
One should worship Airāvata with four tusks in front, Uccaiḥśravas, the lord of horses, behind him, and the Pārijāta tree.
The placement [of mantras] on the fingers beginning with the little finger is prescribed by means of the five root words;
the placement of the limbs [should be performed] from the thumb to the index finger, and the placement on the palms is for the eyes.

Having placed the five-fold steps upon the heart, secret place, and feet of Kāśyapa, one should meditate on Jambhala as non-dual with oneself, while placing his limbs in their respective locations. (32.95)
The Lord is seated upon a white lotus, gentle in appearance, with a yellow luster and two arms;
his crown and jeweled earrings shimmer with red ornaments.

For the sake of attaining success in mantra at the beginning of worship, one should meditate on [the deity] adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, waist-bands, and other ornaments, having three feet and a protruding belly. (32.97)
One should recite the root mantra thirty thousand times, or even half of that; one should offer oblations of bilva, lotus, and ghee, or with its fuel-sticks, for half that number.
Having offered the oblation, he should constantly satisfy Jambhala upon his head;
for previously, by some cause, he had been wounded by Hari with a discus.
By satisfying him with blood, his pain is allayed;
pleased by that, Jambhala, the lord of yakṣas, bestows wealth upon him. (32.100)
Within the lotus of the six-cornered maṇḍala, one should visualize a lotus with the syllable *hrīṃ*;
with the syllable *aṃ*, the weapon-moon; and from the syllable *jaṃ*, Jambhala therein. (32.101)
One should visualize him as four-armed, holding a citron and a mongoose, situated within mandalas of the moon and sun on his left and right sides respectively. (32.102)

Having meditated on two *cātaka* birds drinking the water of rain repeatedly trickling from a cloud accompanied by lightning and pouring down showers, one should offer libations at his two sides. (32.103)

*Gaṃ gaṃ pālaya jalajalendrāya ṭhaṭha*. This mantra of Jambhala is as before; it bestows the accomplishment of one's aims through recitation and other practices. This concludes the section on the Jambhala mantra.
The sky and fire, joined with the staff, and Pisces and Aries are red. || 32-104 ||

Aṣaḍhī, Ya, and Na are the end; Kaubera is the eight-syllable mantra. Plūṃ for Pūrṇabhadra; Pluṃ for Vikuṇḍala; Kluṃ for Celimālin; Yuṃ for Caṇḍa; Naṃ for Narendra; Nṛṃ for Nalakūbara—these six forms are the limbs (aṅgas), ending with the eyes, according to their respective classes. || 32-105 ||
Tundila is yellow in color, a bestower of wealth, adorned with yellow garments and ornaments;
he has four arms and holds two golden jars filled with jewels.
The two *karaṇḍas* are on the palms of the upraised arms upon the interior of the auspicious seat (*bhadrapīṭha*) and lotus;
the limbs [of the deity] are at the tips of the filaments, while Jambhala and the others reside at the tips of the petals. (32.107)
Outside of that are the eight treasures (nidhi), arranged in order starting from the east: Jambhala, Jalendra, Narendra, and Celimālin; [and further]... [32.108]
Vikuṇḍala, Pūrṇabhadra, Māṇibhadra, Carendraka, the treasures Padma and Mahāpadma, as well as Makara and Kūrma.
Kumuda, Ananta, Nīla, Śaṅkha, and the eighth, [Nila];

for Vaiśravaṇa, *ṭhaṭha*. For Pakvāśa, *ṭhaṭha*. For Piṅgala, *ṭhaṭha*. For Vividha, *ṭhaṭha*. For Kubera, *ṭhaṭha*. For the Lord of Kubera, *ṭhaṭha*. *Bhūḥ* *ṭhaṭha*. *Bhuvaḥ* *ṭhaṭha*. *Svaḥ* *ṭhaṭha*. *Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ* *ṭhaṭha*.
By means of these, through an oblation of *vaṭa*-wood fuel sticks, one shall become wealthy within a month. (32–110)
An oblation of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and milk-rice with clarified butter shall lead to the abundance of prosperity.
Medasākṣibhuja, Karṇī, Somākānta, and Dāruka [are the names of the deities]. (32.111)
"Sadṛk pinākī svāhā"—this is the six-syllabled mantra of Kaubera;
the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśvara) should be worshipped upon a splendid seat at the foot of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
Padmaprabhā, holding a lotus in her hand, is on his right, and [the goddess] Vajrabhūṣaṇī is on his left;
the two sons, Nakula and Saha-deva, stand at the sides of the two goddesses. (32.113)
And two female messengers with chowries in their hands— Ajitā and Aparājitā—
and furthermore, in the four directions starting from the front of that [mandala], Pūrṇabhadra and the others.
One should worship Pūrṇabhadra, Māṇibhadra, Jambhala, and Celimālin;
and the two goddesses, Śrī and Puṣṭi, who stand at the side of Pūrṇabhadra. (32.115)
The two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, belonging to Kubera, are to be worshipped on his two sides;
one should also worship Jayā and Vijayā as the two female gatekeepers.
Then, having worshipped Vikuṇḍalā and the others, one should offer oblations to all;
thus, by means of this month-long rite, one becomes wealthy, and by following it for three years in succession, one attains even greater prosperity.
He shall become as glorious as Kubera; of this there is no doubt.

Śrīkaṇṭha, Ambhovāmā, Pādādi, Agni, Āvṛti, and the ten-syllable mantra of Agnijāyā—these mantras, along with their respective syllables, should be used to perform the limb-protections (aṅgas) in pairs. This is the Kubera-mantra; by knowing it alone, one [attains success] at the three times of day.
On the eleventh lunar day, on a Saturday, at the break of dawn beneath a banyan tree.
Vaiśravaṇa is to be worshipped as before; one should recite the mantra eight thousand times daily for a full month, and at midnight, one should offer oblations of clarified butter.
By means of the oil of *jyotiṣmatī* or from the oil of *aṅkola*, one becomes a master of mantras; thereafter, day by day, one succeeds without effort.
The Yakṣa shall speak into his ear effortlessly for the sake of the three periods of time;
this is the jurisdiction of the Karṇa-Yakṣa.
Karṇī, Bhṛgu, and Pinākī are in the asterism Karṇa; Karṇaśukla is the presiding deity of the *prabhā* (radiance). (32-122)
The mantra consists of eight syllables ending with *svāhā*, and its deity is the Yakṣiṇī, who resembles molten gold and is endowed with fresh youth. (32.123)
She possessed full and elevated breasts, a beautiful braided hair, and lovely curls;
her lotus-face was like the autumnal moon, and her eyes were like trembling blue lotuses.
With beautiful eyebrows, teeth, nose, and lips; with beautiful arms and a lovely belly; with full hips and loins, and shapely thighs, calves, and lotus-like feet. (32.125)
Beautiful in every limb, radiant with variegated garments and ornaments,
she was attended by two female messengers who were busy adorning her.
The Yakṣiṇī should be properly depicted on a painted cloth and worshipped;
one should recite that mantra three hundred thousand times for exactly one month beneath a banyan tree.

At midday, one should indeed offer an oblation to Vaiśravaṇa with jujube flowers (*badarīpuṣpa*) as well as *kadamba* blossoms, along with a ball of food (*balipiṇḍa*) consisting of black gram (*māṣa*).
One should cast [the substances] during the nights according to the prescribed method,
and likewise perform oblations with ghee and *aṅkola* oil separately eight thousand times each.
Then she becomes manifest before one's eyes and grants whatever is desired;
or, sporting with her as one pleases, one may cause her to perform any action one wishes.
First, from the word *lambodara*, one should extract *trijaga*, then *dīrghāmbho*, *viṣameṣau*, *karṇa*, and *kathaya*. (32.131)

Having recited it twice in sequence, and having performed the *varma* and *astra* [mantras] with the wife of Agni (*svāhā*), this mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables is worshipped with edible fruits.

One should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times; it then whispers the desired object into one's ear. [The mantra: "O you whose body is adorned with the pure ornaments of gold, diamond, lapis lazuli, and pearl! Come, come! Go! O you who see the three times, having entered my ear, Rudra makes known the past, future, and present—Ṭhaṭha! Having worshipped the *liṅga*, one should then recite this mantra one hundred thousand times before it, using sesame seeds and clarified butter as the offering.
One should offer oblations from this [mantra] part by part according to the *paṅkti* meter; then, one should directly whisper the desired object into his ear.

O Haṃsāhi! You who have the luster of vermilion, who are naked, whose ornaments are joined with jewels and gold, whose hair is disheveled, who possess beautiful hips and thighs, and whose feet tread upon jeweled sandals of radiant splendor; you who are the net, the price, the eyelashes, the cloth, the smooth one, the grindstone for thieves, the flame, the yawn, the pillar, the delusion, and the lord of swans.

May she protect you—she who is lovely with tinkling anklets, whose slender waist shines with a delicate curve, whose beautiful brows and eyes possess the luster of the full moon, and whose lotus-face is radiant. 32-134.
Having thus meditated upon the mantra-deity as an attendant of Bhadrakālī, (verse 32-135).
One should cast nine pieces of sugar into the cardinal directions and the center with a single breath;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, thieves shall not enter that place.
"House" means [this mantra]. O Caṇḍī Śrīcaṇḍī! O you who wear a garland of bees like the immortals, O tawny-eyed one, O you who can take any form at will, O dweller in the forest! Khoṭa Ṭhaṭha!

Having recited this thousand times from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the end of the lunar day, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) on the previous day, one should [perform it] with a single maiden on the day of the sun (Sunday).

Having bathed and adorned herself in the morning, or having worshipped the student (vaṭu) with mantras, one should place a cup upon grain within the mandala, worship it, and touch it while reciting: 32-138.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he should then have the girl take hold [of it];
saying "Go," by the casting of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), she will go and seize the thief.
The word "namaḥ," the syllable "karṇa," the long vowel "kāla" (ā), then the elemental suffix (bhautikī), "vāyu," and the word "giri"—this nine-syllabled mantra ends with "svāhā. (32.140)
Having written the names of suspected thieves interspersed with the syllables of a mantra, one should burn the leaves; yet the name of the thief is not consumed by the fire.
One should bury a mantra together with its ritual manual (sākhya) inside two wooden planks;
by casting a blood offering before the Teacher while in a state of wrath, he becomes propitiated.
"O Uphā Bhaṭa Śelārvaliddhi, to you, the follower of the gods and great commander of the yakṣa army: declare this task of mine, cause it to be told! Thus as he commands: Ṭhaṭha!
One should recite [this mantra] a thousand times beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day.
Then, having mastered the mantra, one should bathe, observe a fast, and sleep at night. (32.143)

The mantra reveals the auspicious and inauspicious events of one's life in dreams, whether in times of peace or war, or in both; it is the pure yoga of great sleep. *Ṭha ṭha*. Having recited this thousand-fold [mantra] of the Sun and accomplished it, || 32-144 ||
If one scatters white sesame seeds over which the *aṣṭasāhasrikā* has been recited eight thousand times within someone's house at night, sleep shall not leave the people residing there.

Oṃ bhramareśi bhrapha phaṭi ṭha bhrama vibhrama muñca mocaya ṭhaṭha. Having meditated upon one’s own identity as Kṛṣṇā, who has many outstretched arms holding weapons, long hair, is mounted upon her [vehicle], and is within a fortress situated in the middle of the house of the sleeping lion; p. 197) oṃ bhramareśi bhrapha phaṭi ṭha bhrama vibhrama muñca mocaya ṭhaṭha | Having meditated upon one’s own identity as Kṛṣṇā, who has many outstretched arms holding weapons, long hair, is mounted upon her [vehicle], and is within a fortress situated in the middle of the house of the sleeping lion;

Having covered the house with hair, one should scatter beans that have been consecrated by recitation seven times; by circumambulating [the house], no person there will lose sleep until sunrise. (32.146)
At the end of the heart [mantra], the word "keśānta" is joined with the word "aṅguṣṭha.
Then follows: *cāli pha vācāli daśakāli caṇḍakāli lakāli ṭhaṭha*.
This mantra, having Kālī as its presiding deity, is perfected by reciting it one thousand times daily. (32–147)
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped Vighna and Kālī within a prepared mandala using japā flowers and the left thumb, and having likewise worshipped a young girl; 32-148.
By sprinkling oil on the thumb, one observes all the auspicious and inauspicious aspects of the matter at hand and speaks of them through the power of the mantra alone. (32.149)
Oṃ hidyāḍha ṣaja phaṇāśa ṭhaṭha. Having worshipped [the deity] residing in the water-pot, one should gaze upon it in a mirror as previously described.

Oṃ! O you who hold a skull, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a ḍamaru drum in your hands; you who are fierce with a mass of sharp, pointed fangs; you with crooked, tawny eyes and a mass of long, hanging hair; you whose cheeks are embraced by earrings made of human skulls; O you who bring all beings under control; O you whose mantra-body consists of all beings; come, O wearer of illusory forms! Move the spear, move the spear! Seize this human body! Having entered it, yawn! O you who cause fear on all sides! Show [yourself] in a jar, in a mirror, in sesame oil, and on the thumb of a maiden! O Mahābhairava Rākṣasī, svāhā!
This is the Vidyā Bhairavarākṣasī, whose presiding deity is Kālī.

Having propitiated the thumb with this [mantra], or by means of a mirror according to the prescribed sequence, one should perform recitation; then every object connected to the three periods of time becomes clearly visible.

Hail! From the illustrious Hanumān, who dwells within the circle [of his dominion] and whose commands are known as *dhājaṭa*, *pracatabhaṣāka*, and *phānta*, it is commanded that no one—whether rats, moths, ants, locusts, *karasumbha*, *karīṭa*, *gandhika*, or others—shall remain here. For anyone who transgresses this command, corporal punishment shall be meted out.
As that lion among monkeys strides across the ocean, the wind passing through his armpits roars like a thundercloud. (32.152)
*Huṃ phaṇnamaḥ*.
This mantra, dedicated to Hanumān, protects crops.
Having written this mantra on a leaf on a Sunday or a Tuesday, [one should employ it]. (32.153)
Having carried [the ashes] around the sacred field (kṣetra) clockwise, one should bury them for the pacification of insects and other pests.
Recite: *namo bhagavate śaktakāpuṇḍe haṃsaḥ cāmuṇḍe*, and furthermore: *vicaya haṃsaḥ kālī uccāṭaya huṃ phaṭ*.
Taking one thousand and eight portions of ash, one should recite this over the hand.

Having cast a circumambulation around the field and released a little grain, the insects and other pests of the crop will perish. Reciting "khuṣi khuṣi pravañjaṇi lukheṣiṇi ṭhaṭha" while gazing at the person to be accomplished, one should mutter the mantra with beautiful hair and draw that person into one's presence. (32.155)

Whether it be a woman or a man— this mantra, written on birch bark with one's own name interspersed, smeared with *rocanā*, wrapped in white thread, and placed within the hollow of an *aśvattha* tree, brings about prosperity for him. (32.156)
One should bring the person whose name is to be accomplished under control while [the practitioner] is situated within the hollow of a banyan tree.
*Oṃ hāṃ śu gṛhe khe he haṃ haḥ*. By reciting this, mice will not eat the grains that have been consecrated with the mantra. (32.157)
And from the binding with coconut and other materials, [one should act] with a recited red thread;
with the mantra "Oṃ hi laṣa vajra," and with this right hand moistened by the water of *śamī* ashes. (32.158)
By touching it, men become submissive; by being touched by another, they are driven away. If that ash is scattered upon merchandise, it causes the prohibition of its sale. (32.159)
Upon seeing that mark upon his forehead, even oxen and other animals become tamed.

(p. 199) Thus has the Teacher taught the ritual procedure for Kṣetrapa and Caṇḍa, complete with mantras; as well as for Indra and those headed by the Lord of Yakṣas, which is endowed with the special knowledge of the three times. (32.160½)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Scriptures and so forth, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 32.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The heart [syllable] is joined with the red of a ram and the circle of the mouth; the enclosure (pālī) is with the long vowel at the end of the feet.
The skin consists of eight syllables; the seed-syllable (bīja) of this mantra is "rāya" with an anusvāra (bindu) between.
The seventh power from that consists of the syllable *ananta*; the *praṇava* (Om) is its beginning and end, protracted (*pluta*) and to be recited (*arca*).
This mantra, accompanied by the *praṇava*, is to be chanted by the twice-born; for women and Śūdras, it is said to be without the *praṇava*.
By the word "and" (ca), [the inclusion] of the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Pārśva, and others is also intended.

The sage of this [mantra] is Antaḥpadānta; its deity is Yāmī; its meter is Gāyatrī; and its supreme self is named Viṣṇu. As for the preliminary service (pūrvasevā) performed when [the mantra] has been mastered, it consists of eight hundred thousand recitations.
In the Tretā and subsequent ages, it is said that for each syllable of this [mantra], the number of Ṛṣis and other [components] is doubled and so forth.
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and after him Jagadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, and Atri is the eighth here. (33–4)
And Agastya—these have been declared in sequence as the meters for the castes: Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. (33–5)
The Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters, as well as the Virāṭ, are the eight Vedic meters in their proper order;
likewise, Dharā, Dhruva, Soma, Āpaḥ, Agni, and Vāyu. (33–6)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are remembered as the presiding deities of the castes;
the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr, and likewise the world of Viṣṇu as the eighth.
There are eight worlds for the castes; I shall now describe the colors of the castes as well: white, resembling gold, black, reddish, and the hue of saffron.
The eighth [element] here possesses the luster of the blue lotus filament and comprises all colors;
it consists of the five subtle elements beginning with smell, as well as the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṅkāra). || 33.9 ||
The principles of the eight syllables have been explained in their proper order:
because of the acute accent (*udātta*) on the sixth and first [syllables], there is the circumflex (*svarita*) on the last and second [syllables]. (33-10)
The fifth syllable is generally hidden by the third and fourth;
the word *dyu* is used in the position of *mahāvīra*, joined with the aforementioned word *sahasra*. (33-11)
By means of their own respective classes, those five limbs are thus appropriately joined with the fourth;
Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Guru, and Vainateya are the deities located in the corners beginning with the southeast. (33–12)
Śakra and the others, as well as the lords of the fields, should be bound to the directions by their own names with a snap of the fingers.
First, there is the placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and the body, according to the procedure for the five-limbed arrangement (pañcāṅgavinyāsa) of those [deities]. // 33.13 //
Creation, maintenance, and withdrawal are the three divisions belonging to the three [stages] beginning with the student (brahmacārin).
Having purified both hands with the weapon-mantra, one should place those of one's own caste on the right side, starting with the index finger, and likewise on the left.

One should then perform the placement (nyāsa) of the finger-gestures, beginning with the *tarjanī* and ending with the *jyeṣṭhā* (the thumb) on the left hand. The seed-syllable (*tāra*) should be placed at both ends of the limb-mantras; here, one should place the letter-mantras upon the middle joints.
One should place the syllable *Tāra* itself upon the joints of the fingers, starting from the first and ending with the last, in sequence.
According to the stated order, the placement in reverse is prescribed for withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), while for maintenance (*sthiti*) of the two hands, it is done in the regular order.

In the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the [mudrās] beginning with *tarjanī* and ending with *kaniṣṭhikā* are placed on the limbs beginning with the head and ending with the feet; likewise, the regions of the eyes, mouth, heart, navel, hips, knees, and feet are also established. (33.17)
For the purpose of withdrawal, one should assign the syllables in reverse order from the navel to the heart;
for the placement on the hands, one should assign them to the two thumbs, to the fingers beginning with the tips of the index fingers,
to the two thumbs, to the middle finger, to the middle and index fingers together, and to the ring finger along with the thumb and the index finger.

One should perform the deposition on the body (*dehanyāsa*) with all the fingers—the thumb joined with the index finger, and the little finger with those that have no thumb (the middle, ring, and index fingers).
Thus, a man whose body is always thus deposited [with mantras] becomes pure and partakes of the form of Nārāyaṇa. (33–19)

Poisons, malevolent spells, diseases, and the afflictions of planetary spirits flee far away in fear when the practitioner, though impure, has performed the placement of mantras, or when he has washed his feet and sipped water (ācamana) again. (33.20)
Alternatively, having bathed and properly performed the ritual placement of the mantras upon the body (*nyāsa*), one should again perform the rites beginning with recitation (*japa*).
Having restrained the breath and recited the eight-syllabled mantra five times by means of the mind, [one should proceed]. (33.21)
This proper regulation of the vital breath (prāṇa) has been described; one should practice it at the beginning, middle, and end of the recitation (japa).
Alternatively, having honored a wise teacher who knows this [method] with service or great wealth, [one should practice]. (33.22)
Having received from him the mantra that brings satisfaction to Him, and having given an appropriate sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his own means,
he should perform all the duties of his own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), as well as the worship of Hari with devotion as prescribed.
One who eats according to the vow should properly accomplish this mantra in a place that is praised and as prescribed; as stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra. (33.24)
Absence of distraction, lack of despondency, and eating from bell-metal vessels—these are the causes for the perfection of recitation (japa).
One should also avoid garlic, fermented rice-gruel, and the meat of the śārṅga bird. (33.25)
Therefore, one should avoid those things which destroy the potency of mantras and asceticism;
one should not resort to the shade of the *karañja* tree, nor eat its fruit, nor touch its wood. (33.26)
One should never cross water while wearing an undergarment; nor should one consume food that is stale, devoid of flavor, putrid, or kept overnight. (33.27)
He should not eat [forbidden food], nor sleep during the day, nor consort with the wives of others;
[he should observe] non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession. (33.28)
Contentment, purity, self-study, austerity, and meditation on the Lord—one should accomplish the mantras while practicing these restraints (yamas) along with the observances (niyamas). 33-29.
The karañja, the onion, fish, meat, and honey; mushrooms, web-footed creatures, and the nālī, śāka, and aluka vegetables. (33–30)
One should not eat oil-seeds prepared in bottle-gourd oil;
for the sake of success in the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one should consume food that is neither pungent nor salty.
In the presence of superiors and elders, one should perform recitation, worship, and other rites only with their permission; otherwise, it will result in fault. (33–32)
Thus:
for one whose head is the Mārga and so forth, however, having fasted on the third, ninth, and so on, [one worships] Viṣṇu during the bright fortnight. (33–33)
Having performed worship on the night of the eleventh lunar day, one should then perform the preliminary service (pūrvassevā) in the morning;
four million recitations of the mantra syllables are to be performed, followed by a tenth part of that [as the fire-oblation].
He should offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter or with lotuses, and he should provide a meal for brahmins according to his capacity.
By two hundred thousand recitations of this supreme mantra, he shall be purified; likewise, purification of the self occurs within four fortnights.
Through six hundred thousand recitations, purification of one's father and mother shall occur; through eight hundred thousand, there shall be accomplishment of the mantra.
One should offer oblations into the fire ten times the number of recitations, using sesame, ghee, milk, rice, and palāśa wood fuel.
If one is unable [to perform the ritual] at home, the mantra becomes perfected through double the recitation and by feeding Brahmins;
one should thus constantly accomplish this mantra and worship it according to one's means. (33–37)
Having bathed and completed the duties of the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), and having reached the sacrificial hall, he should perform the purification of his feet;

then, having sipped water (ācamana) and holding a full offering of water (arghya) in his hand, he should worship the door-keepers with his own mantras, using unbroken rice grains, flowers, and perfumes.

One should worship Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Garuḍa by name, as well as Cakra situated on both sides; on the ground, below and above, and above that, one should duly worship Dvāraśrī located in the center.
Having cast [the flower] with the *antarastra* mantra, he enters within;
having projected a rampart outside the sacrificial hall with the *astra* mantra, he settles upon his own seat as prescribed, maintaining silence.

Having purified one's own body through the processes of drying and so forth by means of the previously mentioned path, and having meditated upon the Supreme Light situated within the heart-lotus, one should indeed worship Nārāyaṇa there with the intellect alone.

Having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) and thus made his self complete with all its parts, he should apply vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) on the forehead and other limbs using white sandalwood and similar substances.
Then, identifying the limbs with Keśava and the other deities, he should place flowers and unbroken rice grains upon his head and hold the water of honor (*arghya*).
Regarding "in the plowshare and so forth" (phālādiṣu):

[The mantras are placed] on the plowshare (phāla), the belly (udara), the disease (roga), the throat (gala), the sides (pārśva), and the arms (bāhu); then on the left side of the belly and the sides and arms;
then above that on the throat; then on the region of the back; and finally on the neck, ending each with *namaḥ* in due order. (33–43)

"By Keśava and the others" means by those named Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara. "Having offered the *arghya*"—and as for the *arghya*, it is stated in the *Nāradīya* [Purāṇa], p.
203: "Siddhārtha (white mustard), unbroken rice (*akṣata*), tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, water, barley, fragrance, fruit, and flower; this is declared to be the eightfold *arghya*. (33.44)
Having filled the vessel for the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) with *dūrvā* grass, lotuses, and water from the river Viṣṇupatnī, and having performed the ritual worship,
the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) should consist of *takola*, nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, and water.
A broom, night-blooming jasmine, śirīṣa, ādityavartinī, and sarvabhadra; likewise, darbha grass, water, and saffron—these, obtained with their roots, are to be employed for the ritual bathing.
In vessels washed with mantras and filled with water along with their roots, one should place the root-mantra together with the limbs;
then, with perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and incense, one should worship the arghya and the other offerings in due order.
Uśīra, saffron, māṃsī, mura, and sandalwood root,
along with kuṣṭha and black agallochum— this is the eight-ingredient fragrance beloved by Hari.

[The deity] is protected by all weapons and enveloped in armor. Therein, one should offer *arghya* [into the right hand], *pādya* for the feet, *ācamanīya* separately for the mouth, and *saṃmārjanīya* for the face, employing these in the special bathing ritual.
Having filled it with pure and purified waters, one should place a beautiful *vardhanikā*—either of metal or earthenware—on the left; all other articles should be on the right. (33–49)

Having sprinkled [the object] with water for the *arghya* offering from the *astra-mantra* using a *kūrca*-grass bundle, having consecrated it with the root and limb mantras, having rendered it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛtya*) by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and having shielded it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should place the well-protected object, fit for worship, in its proper position.

Having sprinkled oneself with the *arghya* and other offerings, there is purification of the head; on the ground of worship, there is purification of the collection of materials; purification of the mantra occurs by reciting the root mantra ending in a *pluta* vowel; and purification of the image (*bera*) occurs by washing. (33–50)
Having worshipped Vighneśa in the northwest by his own name, and likewise his own gurus in the northeast,
he should then worship Speech (Vāc) and the Supreme Guru right there, as well as Śrī Nārada and the ancient Siddhas.
Having removed the floral remains from the image with the Astra-mantra, having offered the *amṛta* water for the *arghya*, and having sprinkled it with waters;

having offered the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) using the head [of the mantra], and having worshipped the pedestal, invoked [the deity], and established the mantras. (33–52)
Again, having worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings, with desired perfumes, flowers, incense, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
and having bathed [the image] with fragrant oil and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should remove the coating with powders.
Having wiped the deity with a broom and with turmeric powder and saffron,
one should likewise consecrate him with fragrant flowers, scented water, and waters [mixed with] perfumes, while reciting the Puruṣasūkta and other hymns.
Oṃ! Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one! Homage to you, O creator of the universe!
O Subrahmaṇya, may your mind be gracious toward us; homage to you, O Puruṣa, O Primordial Being! (33-55)
And with this [mantra], one should offer the ritual services (upacāras) together with the root-mantra and its ancillaries:
first Ādhāraśakti, then Kūrmarāja, Śeṣa, and Pṛthivī; then the Yogapīṭha;
and thereafter Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in due order.
One should worship those lords of the directions, shaped like lions and beginning with Fire (Agni), located in the corners starting from the southwest (Adharma) and proceeding clockwise;
one should worship the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus, which consist of the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva, respectively.
The orbs of the sun, fire, and moon pervade its petals, filaments, and pericarp;
likewise, the Self, the Inner Self, and the one named the Supreme Self are to be worshipped.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yoga, and Satyā. || 33-59 ||
Then, from the east, [the goddesses] beginning with Prahvī and Īśānugrahā occupy the tips of the filaments;
in their midst, upon the pericarp of the lotus, one should duly invoke the ninth power named Anugrahā,
having first meditated there upon the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa.
His limbs are soft and dark like a blue cloud; his lotus-face possesses the luster of the full moon’s orb;
he is beautiful with a mass of dark curls parted by the radiance of his crown, which shines with the brilliance of jewels. || 33-61 ||

With beautiful eyebrows, a broad forehead, and a prominent nose, his lotus-eyes were like blossoming lotuses; the beauty of his bright crocodile-shaped earrings was enhanced by their being attached to his lovely, elegantly curved ear-lobes that hung down.
His neck is radiant with a conch-shell ornament set with gold coins; his arms are encircled by a pair of jeweled armlets;
he wears variegated garments, bracelets, and rings; and in his hands he holds a conch, a lotus, a mace, and a discus.
His shimmering, swaying necklace is adorned with six *kaustubha* gems; his broad chest is beautiful with the splendor of the *śrīvatsa* mark;
and he is lovely with a golden waistband that encircles his slender waist, resembling a ruby disk. || 33.64 ||
Upon his broad hips, which were beautiful with a special yellow silk garment,
he wore a golden thread inlaid with the finest jewels and a forest garland hanging down to his knees.
Her two calves were lovely, well-fleshed, and rounded; her pair of lotus-feet possessed well-formed ankles.
Her rows of moon-like nails were red as the hooves of a noble horse, set upon toes that were slender and soft.

Bearing the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the crocodile with the soles of his lotus-like feet and hands, he possesses the singular splendor of the quality of beauty in every limb; therefore, he is Puruṣottama. (33.67)

Having thus meditated upon the form of Nārāyaṇa within his own heart-lotus—immovable like a lamp, consisting of the *haṃsa*, enveloped by the *praṇava*, and like one light emerging from another lamp—[he beheld it]. (33.68)
Having grasped the *praṇava* with the intellect, ending in the protracted (*pluta*) vowel, one should utter it and lead it through the path of the *suṣumṇā*;
then one should unite it with Brahman, which consists of light and resides within the interior of the sky-lotus, and from there, even beyond that.

Having applied [the mantra] to his own handful of flowers, he should lead it from that form standing before him through the central channel and apply the seed-syllable "Haṃsa" together with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and Nāda into the center of the heart-lotus.
Having thus performed the invocation, the practitioner of mantra should place the letters of the mantra—excluding the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa)—upon its form;
then, from the root mantra together with the *haṃsa*, he should effect the presence [of the deity] within it.
One should sprinkle this [deity] with a stream of nectar flowing from the orb of the full moon at the dvādaśānta,
which has entered through that brahmanāḍī, while uttering the *tāra* (OM) and the mantra of Sārdhendukhaḍgīśa.
Having meditated upon him as being filled within and without as if with floods of nectar, thus delighting his divine body,
one should worship him with the prescribed offerings and, finally, the surrounding deities.
That is to say:
one should worship the limbs at the tips of the petals starting from the east, and likewise the *astra* (weapon) at the tips of the coverings in the corners;
and at the gates starting from the east, one should worship Vainateya, the discus, the lotus, and the mace in sequence.
In the corners, Pāñcajanya is to be worshipped here; Śārṅga in the south, and Nandaka as well;
two quivers in the west, and in the north the female Vanamālikā is to be worshipped by her own name.
One should worship Lakṣmī, situated on the right side of Hari, and Bhūmi, known as Puṣṭi, on his left;
and one should worship the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem in front, positioned respectively on the right and the left.
In the north, he should worship with their own names Indra, Agni, Vaivasvata, the Lord of Rākṣasas, the Lord of Waters, Vāyu, Arthanātha, Īśāna,
the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Ananta, and Soma.

Outside of them, one should worship with their own names the weapons of the world-lords: the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the *sudarśana*.
Outside the weapons, one should worship Kumuda and the others:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (33.79)
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—these lords of hosts numbering in the tens of millions, as well as Viṣṇu and the other leaders of the bhūta hosts. (33.80)
One should worship Viṣvaksena, who is situated between Someśa and [the other deity];
at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer all of Viṣṇu’s *nirmālya* to him.
Having worshipped daily according to the prescribed rules as stated, and having offered oblations of ghee and other substances into the Vaiṣṇava fire,
he should then feed the foremost of the twice-born according to his ability, or else mutter the mantra three thousand times.
Thus, one whose mantra has been perfected through the previously described service (pūrvasevā) and who desires its application (viniyoga),
should accomplish the desired collection of aims by means of those various oblations (havana) or recitations (japa) as they have been taught.

In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as previously described, or one that is square, having consecrated the fire produced by friction from araṇi wood— or any other fire— and having invoked the Vaiṣṇava fire according to the prescribed path, he should offer oblations to Hari within it.
One should offer three hundred thousand oblations of ghee and sesame seeds using the tips of green blades of grass to promote longevity;
with fuel-sticks of the *chinnā* plant four finger-breadths long, one should destroy minor untimely deaths, and with sweet substances, one should likewise overcome them.

Having touched an *aśvattha* tree at the beginning of the day, one should slowly recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times for the pacification of death and disease; by so reciting at dawn, as well as through consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there shall be long life.
Having consecrated water by reciting [the mantra] a number of times equal to the desired goal and drinking it at the three junctions of the day, one shall become long-lived.
Furthermore, having consecrated ten thousand recitations over a jar full of water according to the prescribed rite, and having placed Hari within that [image], [one attains the same result].

Having invoked and fully worshipped [the deity], and having offered clarified butter ten times the portion [of the mantra recited], one should perform an ablution for the pacification of untimely death. Food and other offerings that have been consecrated by this [mantra] and eaten daily eight times ensure longevity. || 33-88 ||
If one has consumed another poison that is difficult to digest, one should recite [the mantra] over a hundred measures of that; it will become a desired medicine.
During a lunar eclipse, having fasted for three days, one should [consume] four palas of the clarified butter of Kapila cows.
One should drink one *pala* of *vacā* powder; that will produce wisdom and enable one to obtain ten thousand [verses].
Likewise, *brāhmīghṛta*, when drunk during a solar eclipse, will also produce poetic talent.

By drinking water daily for one year, one obtains the results of eight hundred [fasts] and becomes a possessor of wisdom. Furthermore, having fasted for three nights on the full moon of Māgha during the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti), one should smear oneself with sacred ash.

If one drinks *brāhmīghṛta* five thousand times after chanting over it, it will produce wisdom. One adorned in white garments should offer ten thousand oblations of white lotuses, having sprinkled them with milk and clarified butter. (33–92)
By being consecrated according to the ritual procedure with four full jars, one obtains the desired Lakṣmī;
by the oblation of food with ghee, one finds food; and by means of clarified butter, one obtains all desires as well as cattle. (33.93)
By means of *bilva* fruits or leaves and fuel-sticks smeared with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*), one becomes like Kubera.
On the lunar day sacred to Viṣṇu during the first fortnight of Phalguna, having properly fasted for three nights, [one should worship] Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped with lotuses sprinkled with honey and having offered oblations, one obtains a treasure;
or, standing at dawn with arms held straight upward, if one recites the mantra a hundred thousand times, he shall become wealthy.

Dwelling at the root of a bilva tree, offering those fruits a thousand times every day while eating food mixed with their fruit, one who recites [the mantra] for three months shall become wealthy; indeed, he shall become a lord of riches.

Having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) from the milk of a cow that is of the same color as its calf and has a calf of the same color, and having offered ten thousand oblations of it sprinkled with clarified butter, one who eats the remainder of that oblation destroys misfortune and attains prosperity.
Whatever color of flowers one offers along with clarified butter, one shall obtain garments of that same color within a month;
indeed, by offering grains such as śāli rice soaked in ghee, one certainly obtains them after just one month.
Whoever, having recited ten million times over seeds such as rice or even [seeds] of trees, should sow them in a field, obtains the entire crop of grain, as well as their roots and fruits. (33.99)
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while consuming birch bark, cow urine, and barley gruel, one shall obtain a son;
or else, by offering guggulu resin sprinkled with clarified butter into the fire and bathing the wife with water consecrated by that same mantra. || 33-100 ||

By offering oblations of sesame and rice, Brahmins come under one's control; by offering curd-rice, kings; by food mixed with clarified butter, the Vaiśyas; and by an oblation of milk-rice, even Śūdras come under one's control. (33.101)

By offering oblations of apāmārga, one gains a wife; by offerings of parched grain (lāja) together with mātuluṅga fruits, one gains a maiden. By sprinkling [the substance] with the three sweets and salt, other women become subject to his control through these oblations performed according to the rule.

By offering oblations of apāmārga with clarified butter into a fire of aśvattha wood, one brings under one's own control the gods and asuras, the nāgas and kinnaras, the rākṣasas, the serpents, the birds, and the yakṣas, according to one's desire.
For one who worships Nārāyaṇa at the three junctions of the day while reciting [the mantra] a hundred thousand times for their sake,
all worlds shall come under their control and grant whatever is desired, through the power of firm devotion.

He who, subsisting on barley-gruel prepared with cow’s urine, bathes at the three junctions of the day and worships Hari, becomes purified by eight hundred thousand [recitations] in this world; a Brahmin becomes so even for double that number in successive order for [the killing of] those beginning with a Brāhmaṇa-slayer.
In due order, this applies to Kṣatriyas and others, as well as those who have consumed liquor unintentionally, thieves, and those who have violated the teacher’s bed—up to that point.
(p. 208) Likewise, one who stands in water for five hundred thousand [repetitions] becomes purified here from these sins.
But at the end, having consecrated and drunk the products of the cow (*gavya*), one is purified from sins by means of three hundred thousand [repetitions]. (33.106)

Standing in water reaching up to the knees, one who has eyes like the sun, consecrated by eight thousand recitations, shall destroy the sin acquired on that very day; however, for one reciting while standing at the depth of the navel, there shall be nourishment.

The practitioner of mantra, having brought together white lotus threads numbering one hundred and eight strands, should touch them and recite the mantra ten thousand times; when thus bound, it becomes a source of protection for all and bestows long life.
For men, [the mantra should be worn] on the right hand; for women, on the left hand or around the neck.
By reciting it eight thousand times before an angry person, there shall be pacification; in debate, victory is attained.
Furthermore, by reciting the mantra during the sight of a king or others, one accomplishes what is desired.

Having bathed and become purified, one should take cow-dung from a tawny cow found on a lotus leaf during the *brāhma-muhūrta*; having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times on a day when there is no moon or lunar festival, that dung, buried at the door, becomes a protector of the house.
From the cow-dung of that [cow], one should recite over the Vaiṣṇava fire and the ashes as before; this shall provide protection against planetary influences, diseases, and demons.

Through the oblation (*homa*) of white mustard seeds, *pālāśa* leaves, sesame seeds, and clarified butter, there shall be protection from all things and the pacification of planetary influences and diseases. (33.111)
One who, at midnight in the forest, naked and clad only by the directions, offers fuel-sticks of *vaibhītaka* or *vikaṅkata* smeared with royal ghee,
kills his enemies within a month and paralyzes an army.
Having sacrificed to Hari with oblations sprinkled with cow's ghee, and having daily offered a thousand fuel-sticks of apāmārga,
a lord of men, by sacrificing for nine months, conquers his enemies here and carries the earth.
Taking water in the left hand, one should sprinkle it upon the bitten person while reciting the mantra;
thus, having destroyed all poisons, one protects them by wiping away spiders and the like with *dūrvā* grass.

One desiring victory, or for the sake of pacifying fear of enemies, should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa mounted on Garuḍa, possessing eight arms equipped with the conch, discus, noose, goad, bow, arrow, mace, and sword, and as one's own identity. (33.115)

For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate upon Him who is seated upon the lotus in the center of the lion-throne within a pavilion in the garden of the Kalpa-trees on the Golden Island in the midst of the Ocean of Milk, together with Śrī and Dharaṇī. 33-116.

On the northern bank of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, one who recites the eight-syllable mantra for a year becomes possessed of wondrous power; he attains all desires and long life in this world. (33.117)

Having fasted properly for three nights during the dark fortnight, one who desires wealth should worship Kṛṣṇa on a day of the month of Kārttika; having touched His pair of feet with both hands, he should recite [the mantra] for seven days. (33.118)
In this manner, one accomplishes the respective tasks of preparing collyrium, sandalwood paste, sandals, swords, and so forth.

Having fasted for three nights at dawn and worshipped Viṣṇu with barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine, he who constantly recites [the mantra] without sleep for a fortnight will find that the sky-farers grant his desires. (33.119)

Having offered a bali-oblation with *bhūta*-water at the cremation ground during the dead of night for seven nights, and by reciting the mantra three thousand times for the *bhūtas* and other spirits, the *bhūtas* and *piśācas* shall grant his desires. (33.120)

Having worshipped Hari at the root of a banyan tree and offered thousands of oblations of *khadira* wood, a *yakṣī* will approach after a month; she shall be a granter of desires, or one may take pleasure with her.
This means [using] fuel-sticks made of *khadira* wood.

Having drawn the Yakṣa in the middle of an *aśoka* grove upon a panel made from its wood, one should likewise worship Hari with his own flowers at the three junctions of the day; having also offered oblations, after one month he will indeed become a granter of boons.

Having drawn Nāgīs upon the slabs of the Nāga trees in the midst of the Nāga forest, and having worshipped Hari with their flowers, one should offer oblations; from them, he obtains elixirs and other such things. (33.123)
Having drawn the daughter of the Asura king at the entrance of the cave and having established a fire of *vikaṅkata* wood,
one obtains whatever is desired from the Asurī by offering a hundred thousand oblations of *vikaṅkata* fuel-sticks.

Alternatively, one who is clad in wet garments may offer ten thousand oblations of *vaitasī* wood into a fire located in the sky; or even by offering fuel-sticks, there will be excellent rain. Furthermore, by standing in water and reciting [the mantra] twice that number, the same result follows.
For the pacification of calamities, he should offer oblations with *śamī* fuel-sticks, or with black sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
for prosperity and nourishment, he should offer ghee and milk-rice while reciting the mantra, and thus he beholds Śrī upon the mountain peak.
Subsisting on milk and reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, the devotee attains realization of Brahman and liberation;
by worshipping on a mountain peak and reciting for six months, he beholds Lakṣmī with his own eyes.
Having offered three hundred thousand oblations of well-purified black sesame seeds mixed with curd, ghee, and honey, the gods shall come under one's control;
he who, subsisting on the food prescribed by his vow, recites this mantra without interruption for a year in the abode of Viṣṇu [attains the same].
(210) By means of the yoga of devotion, he beholds Viṣṇu with his vision, worshipping him correctly for three years;
having properly fasted for three nights, he then fully worships Viṣṇu on the night of the twelfth day.

Having fashioned an image of Tārkṣya, touched it with red sandalwood paste, and recited this mantra, he then mounts that [image] as it begins to quiver; by that very act, he attains the world of Viṣṇu.

Whatever collection of objects this practitioner desires in the three worlds—whether effortlessly or through exertion—he obtains it all through recitation and other rites, provided he is devoted to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa. (33.131)

Thus has been declared this supreme secret of the eight-syllabled mantra, as proclaimed in the Vedas; this practice and so forth have been set forth in brief, serving as the cause for those people who possess devotion to the lotus feet of Hari to attain all their desired goals, which are dear and beneficial. (33.132)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, on the Eight Syllables, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 33.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.

First, the word *uttiṣṭha*, then *śrīḥ*, *asargaḥ*, and *brahmaśoṇite*, followed by two instances of *ṭha* and preceded by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*); this is the eight-syllabled mantra that bestows prosperity. (34.1)
The seers and so forth are Vāmadeva; the meters are Paṅkti and Viṣṇu; and the limbs, repeated twice, are "bhīṣaya" and "trāsaya. (34-2)

"Crush! "Protect! and the syllable *huṃ* are applied respectively to the hands and the limbs of the body, according to the distinctions of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*anta*). (34.3)
The knower of mantras should also perform this according to the path taught in the *Aṣṭākṣara*,
[visualizing it] upon a golden sandbank in the Ocean of Milk, within a delightful and divine grove.
Beneath the wish-fulfilling tree, upon a golden lion-throne and lotus,
one should meditate on [the deity] mounted upon Garuḍa, resembling molten gold.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with four arms,
wearing divine yellow garments, and radiant with a variegated crown.
Adorned with various necklaces, armlets, and crocodile-shaped earrings,
he was radiant with the luster of diverse jewels and wore bracelets and finger-rings.

Having meditated upon the Lord Hari, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, who is adorned with a forest garland, and who is beautiful in every limb, one should worship him. (34.8)

One should worship the limbs upon the tips of the filaments, Śrī and Rati on the petals of the directions, Dhṛti and Kānti on the intermediate petals, and the Śaktis and the Mūrtis on the corner petals as well.

Having thus worshipped Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, as well as Viṣvaksena situated in his own direction and the world-protectors (lokeśas) in their respective directions, and having worshipped the weapons in the outer enclosure according to the prescribed rule— || 34-10 ||
Then, in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) dedicated to Viṣṇu,
he should offer oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks produced from the milk and sap of the Bilva tree, as well as with lotuses.

One should offer a thousand oblations separately with clarified butter and milk-rice using the eight [mantras], and having worshipped the Guru according to one's ability with gold and other offerings.
Then this mantra of his becomes perfected and bestows desired objects;
moreover, with dūrvā grass blades smeared with clarified butter, one may ward off death and disease. (34-13)
One should feed the twice-born according to one's ability and shall attain long life;
standing in the water with arms raised toward the sun, one should recite [the mantra].
If one recites it eight thousand times, one shall attain great prosperity.

The entire collection of applications (viniyoga) prescribed for the eight-syllable mantra is stated to be the same for this *Viṣṇuhṛdaya* as well; all of that should be inferred accordingly, to be accomplished through the specific methods of recitation and fire-oblation (*japa-homa*). || 34-15 ||

The Chapter on the Heart of Viṣṇu: The seed-syllable of Smara (Klīm) ending in the dative case, followed by Kṛṣṇa, then the word Gopī, then the word Jana, then Ambubhūsthābhū with a long vowel, and then Marut [ending in the dative]. (34.16)

Agnipatnī is the seed-syllable (bīja), the mantra is said to be Manvarṇa Gopālaka; its power (śakti) is the first [syllable], and Nārada with the left eye [as his suffix] is the sage (muni). || 34-17 ||
Virāṭ is the meter, and Kṛṣṇa, in the form of a child, is the deity;
others say the meter is Gāyatrī. The limbs [of the mantra] are now written down in their proper order. (34.18)
"To Ācakra, Vicakra, Sucakra, and Jāti; for the protection of the three worlds"—thus the Destroyer of Asuras [is worshipped] with the dative case. (34.19)

Some, being low-born among the four castes, recited the Gopālamantra; its seers and other preliminary elements, as well as its ancillaries and means of accomplishment, are equal to those of the former. (34.20)

Neither the conjunction of planets such as Siddha and Sādhya, nor even the configuration of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), need be considered for this mantra; for it is indeed the bestower of success upon all.
For this [mantra] bestows the fulfillment of desires even upon women and Śūdras who are devoted;
it is also [to be applied] to the fingers beginning with the little finger on hands purified by the weapon-mantra.
One should place the syllables of the mantra upon both palms everywhere for the purpose of emanation;
for reabsorption, one should do so in reverse order, and for maintenance, starting from the middle finger and so forth.
One should likewise place the limbs— beginning with the little finger, beginning with the thumb, and beginning with the middle finger—
on both hands in sequence during the stages of emanation and maintenance.
On the crown of the head, at the point between the eyebrows, in the eyes, the nose, the two ears,
the mouth, the throat, the heart, the navel, the anus, the two knees, the two shanks, and also on the two feet.
One should place the fourteen syllables upon the body in sequence for the sake of emanation (sṛṣṭi);
for the placement of maintenance (sthiti), it begins with the heart, while for withdrawal (saṃhṛti), it is traditionally taught to begin with the feet.
One should assign the limbs, beginning with the heart, to their respective locations;
having performed the assignment (nyāsa) on the two hands, one should likewise perform the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka) upon the body.
Having received the mantra from the teacher and having pleased him, one should perform the placement of the body (dehanyāsa) and the five-limbed placement (pañcāṅganyāsa) as prescribed. (34.28)
Having meditated upon the deity at the appropriate time, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
[Suitable locations are] mountains, rivers, the roots of bilva trees, lakes, cow-pens, and temples. (34–29)
Those oceans of the shadow of awakening are likewise the locations for the practice;
one who observes the vow should eat moderately, be self-controlled, and be devoted to bathing three times a day.
In each of these places, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
After the recitation, one should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number, using lotuses, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and milk-rice.

One should worship the god Kṛṣṇa with gold and other materials according to the extent of one’s wealth; one should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to one’s ability, and thus one becomes one who has fulfilled the preliminary vow. (34.32)
And the meditation:

[one should visualize] the Child, dark as a fresh blue lotus petal or a rain cloud, with tender limbs, eyes like a full-blown lotus, adorned with excellent ornaments of gold and jewels, and clad in yellow garments.

I meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, whose face is beautiful, who wears a crest of peacock feathers, who shines with variegated and brilliant makara-shaped earrings, and who holds a lotus, a mace, a lotus, and a discus in his four arms.
His beautiful and variegated crown is fashioned from various wild flowers;

his body is enveloped by a magnificent, shimmering garland of *kadamba* blossoms interspersed with diverse peacock feathers and trailing filaments, hanging down high from his neck and following the melody of his flute-song.
Or one should meditate on him wearing yellow garments, surrounded by hosts of cows, cowherd girls, and cowherds.

One should meditate upon Him whose chest is radiant with the Śrīvatsa mark and the shimmering Kaustubha gem, whose necklaces are entwined with the Goddess Lakṣmī, whose hair and locks are as dark as a swarm of bees,
whose pure lotus-face resembles the orb of the full moon, and whose eyes are as long as blossoming lotuses.
The god Mukunda, dressed as a cowherd and being praised by celestial sages in heaven.
The Section on General Means of Accomplishment.
Now, the meditation upon Kṛṣṇa throughout the three periods of the day is described: [He is seen] amidst the herd of calves for the purpose of milking the cows. (34–36)
The playful one, delighting in the diversion of playing the flute.
It was being licked by calves and surrounded by cowherd girls,
as well as by gods, asuras, gandharvas, sages, vidyādharas, and others.
One should worship while remembering the Lord of Gods being praised by hosts in heaven, using wild flowers such as campaka, utpala, and padma, or other fragrant blossoms. (34–39)
One should worship [the deity] duly with flowers, perfumes, incense, and so forth.
In the morning, one should offer curd, roots, molasses, and honey into golden vessels.
One should offer flavorful fresh butter and betel leaf at midday upon the exceedingly beautiful peak of the lordly mountain of jewels.
In a divine garden, beneath the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) within a jeweled pavilion, upon the pericarp of a lotus on a jeweled lion-throne, [he is] four-armed. (34–42)
The practitioner should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa, adorned with the ornaments described above,
the Imperishable One surrounded by cowherd girls of divine form.
Being served by hosts of sages such as Nārada and even by the gods,
he grazed on grass and drank water in the shade of the trees of the grove.

Having meditated thus and invoked according to the prescribed rite and the procedure to be described hereafter, one should look upon [the deity] as being gazed at by cows that are well-satisfied and renowned.
Having worshipped with fragrant wild flowers, such as blooming *campaka* and *kubjaka*, and having offered milk-rice with ghee in golden vessels, || 34-46 ||
Having offered morsels of food to the cows, one should bid them farewell with the words, "Forgive me.
In the evening, [one should worship] the Lord in Vṛndāvana, situated in the midst of the Rāsa-maṇḍala.
The Lord was surrounded by cowherd girls who were most exquisitely adorned,
and he was sporting with various diversions such as dancing and singing.
Having worshipped with jasmine and *jātī* flowers, having offered ghee and milk-rice, and having presented boiled milk and water for washing the hands; || 34-49 ||
Having offered betel leaf as an oral fragrance, one should dismiss [the deity].
This concludes the section on the three daily meditations (*triṣavaṇadhyāna*).
Now, the general ritual worship (*sāmānyayajana*) of Kṛṣṇa is here described. (34–50)

Having performed the ritual bath with the *mūla-mantras* of his own limbs, he should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial hall and worship the gatekeepers in order, starting from the east, by their names.
One should likewise place Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
and similarly Śaṅkha and Padma, at the tips of the two door-posts.
Having worshipped the two middle roots and the Sudarśana in their center,
one should worship Dvāraśrī by name in the middle of the upper Udumbara.
At the southern gate, one should worship Bhadra, Subhadra, and likewise Dvāraśrī;
at the western [gate], Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Lakṣmī, Vijayā, and Jayā. (34–54)
And one should worship Lakṣmī at the door situated in the direction of the Lord of the Stars (the North);
then, having entered within after casting a flower consecrated with the Astra-mantra, [one should proceed].
Then, having placed the weapon-flower upon the threshold of the Vāstumaṇḍala-lotus,
and having worshipped his own seat and the rampart of weapons all around, [he should proceed].
Having conceived [the protection] with the *varman* mantra and having enclosed his dwelling,
he, being seated upon his own seat with a purified soul, [performs the rites] beginning with drying (*śoṣaṇa*) in due order.

Having performed the ritual placement and the rite of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one who has himself assumed the form of Kṛṣṇa should recite [the mantra] while contemplating the imperishable Kṛṣṇa within the lotus of his own heart, which is the light of consciousness.
Having prescribed the sequence beginning with the seat and so forth through mental offerings,
and having filled the arghya vessel with the root mantra and its limbs, one should sprinkle the head with that water.
Having purified the substratum and the wheel of substances with those drops of arghya water,
one should worship oneself in the form of Kṛṣṇa with excellent perfumes and other offerings.
Having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* mark and adorned his crest with flowers and *dūrvā* grass,
he should worship Vighnarāja in the south and the Guru in the northeast.

Having mentally conceived the pedestal (pīṭha) as consisting of earth and the other elements, one should worship it; likewise, one should worship the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti) and Ananta with perfumes and other offerings, using their respective names.

By means of knowledge (vidyā), one perceives dharma and its opposite, adharma and its opposite, as well as the self whose nature is light, delusion in the form of worldly activity (pravṛtti), and the principle of time (kāla).
Having fully worshipped the principle of Māyā with the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire,
one should also worship the Śaktis at the tips of the filaments in the directions starting from the east.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogā, Satyā, Prahvī, Īśā, and Anugrahā— these are the nine powers (śaktis) who are to be worshipped.

Or, having invoked Hari into an image made of gold or other materials, or onto a cloth endowed with the proper characteristics, one should worship Him according to the procedure prescribed for the eight-syllable mantra.
One should worship the limbs at the tips of the filaments and the weapon in the corners; likewise, one should worship Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmī, and Nāgnajitī. (34–67)
One should worship Sunandā, Mitravindā, Queen Jāmbavatī,
and Suśīlā, in order, at the tips of the petals starting from the east.
Outside the pedestal and within the pavilion, one should worship the conch and other items in pairs;
likewise, in the regions of the four doors, sequentially on the right and left.

One should worship the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the pestle, and likewise the sword Nandaka; then the noose and the goad in the middle, and first the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem.
Then, outside the mandala, one should worship the deities starting from the southeast corner in sequence: Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapati.
One should worship Nārada, Kūrma, and the previously established gurus starting from the east;
