outside of them, the world-protectors (lokeśas), and further outside than those, their weapons.
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then dismiss the god;
thus, when one has the means, one should worship him three times every day.
Thus, for one who has accomplished the mantra, all desires are indeed fulfilled;
by offering oblations of wild flowers and *jāti* blossoms, one may bring Brahmins and others under one's control.
Indeed, by offering all [these]— with red flowers, as well as blue lotuses,
along with rice grains and sesame seeds— one attains [the goal] through the wearing of that ash.
One should subjugate women by offering oblations of *kadamba* flowers consecrated with clarified butter, milk, and honey, while meditating on the form of Gopāla.
At the root of a Kadamba tree, one should worship that which brings all under control while singing;
one desiring food and other provisions should offer Śrī flowers mixed with white rice.
One should also offer apāmārga plants for the subjugation of all worlds;
one seeking wealth [should offer] white lotuses and the like, and for clothing, flowers of the corresponding color.
By offering fuel-sticks of *bādarī* wood smeared with clarified butter, one obtains a maiden;
by offering salt anointed with honey, there shall be the subjugation of all.
By offering cow-products as oblations, one achieves the acquisition of cattle; by offering lotuses, the abundance of food and drink;
and by offering curd, clarified butter, and *khadira* wood, one is liberated from calamities. (34.80)

For the sake of obtaining a son, one should worship Kṛṣṇa while meditating upon him at the root of an Aśvattha tree; one should then recite the Guru-mantra one hundred thousand times, and from that, perform the ten-part oblation.
One should offer oblations for prosperity; let him also offer fresh butter.
Having bathed on a Tuesday morning, he should worship Hari together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
Having performed ten thousand sacrifices and recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should go to that sacred field,
consume earth from it after consecrating it seven times with mantras, and thereby obtain the merit of that field within seven days.

Having meditated upon and worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the remover of the Pārijāta tree, one should offer oblations of well-prepared clarified butter with karavīra flowers; thus, like Indra, one conquers one's enemies.
Having meditated upon and worshipped Hari, who dwells in Dvārakā and is accompanied by the treasures such as the Śaṅkha,
and having offered oblations of rice grains, one attains stability without delay.

By meditating on Kṛṣṇa, the speaker of the Gītā to Pārtha, and worshipping Him with lotuses, one attains righteousness and liberation; and by offering oblations of dūrvā grass, one gains long life. (34.86)
Having meditated upon the one who will bring Rukmiṇī, and having offered oblations of parched grain and ghee, he should sacrifice and recite mantras; thus he obtains his desired maiden and women.

By meditating on Him as one with oneself while He drinks the breast-milk of Pūtanā, all seizing spirits (grahas) perish through that vision; [and by meditating on Him as] the crusher of Kālīya, poison [is destroyed]. 34.88
One who desires rain should meditate on [the deity] as being in Vṛndāvana;
by offering oblations with reeds (vetasa), he obtains rain within seven nights—of this there is no doubt.
One shall conquer diseases and untimely death through the oblation of *chinnā*, ghee, and sesame seeds;
by means of the oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with ghee, one shall attain all desires.
A twice-born man who desires the office of royal priest, having offered oblations with white flowers soaked in honey,
shall obtain a hundred thousand [gold pieces] or something else before long.
Thus has been fully declared this ritual procedure for the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, having observed the kalpas as perceived by the assembly of sages;
one who possesses devotion should constantly [perform] this through sacrifices, recitations, oblations, and so forth.
If the practitioner worships that which he desires, by that means he shall attain it.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Eight-Syllable Gopāla of Śrīkara," in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
The meter of the Nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubh is that very same [Anuṣṭubh], and its deity is the Man-lion (Nṛkesarī).
The ritual procedure is Prajāpati by name, and the seer (ṛṣi) as well as the limbs (aṅgas) are [the mantra] itself.

Karṇa (the letter *ra*), Khānta (the letter *kha*), Agni (the letter *ra*) rich with Daṇḍa (the letter *m*), Khaḍgī (the letter *kha*) joined with Vāmākṣa (the letter *i*), Vahni (the letter *ra*) with Daṇḍī (the letter *m*), Mahākāla (the letter *ka*), Kha (the letter *ha*), Dīrgha (the long vowel *ā*), Ayuta (the letter *ya*), and Jala (the letter *va*). || 35-2 ||
White, ending with the syllable *ḍha* and accompanied by the letter *ka*, adorned with a crescent moon, [he holds] a blazing tail... || 35-3 ||
I bow to the one who has the form of a man, the heroic, the all-pervading, the death of death;
[he who is worshipped] with four, and with four, and with eight, and indeed with three.

Then, by five and then by eight of its own limbs, one should sequentially bind the six vowels; having first bound that which is perfected by the constellations, there is likewise no need for fasting and so forth.
The accomplishment of this mantra is ordained through recitation and other practices performed with devotion.
Its seed-syllable (bīja) is known as the letter 'la' (the forty-third consonant), joined with the vowel 'u' (the twenty-first) and the anusvāra (bindu). (35–6)

Dhṛti (the letter *dh*) with the vowel *u* (*dhu*), followed by the subtle (*sūkṣma*, the letter *r*), and the power (*śakti*, the letter *e*) joined with the bindu (*m*) is traditionally taught. In fire-offerings (*homa*), it should end with "dear to Agni" (*agnipriya*, i.e., *svāhā*); the visualization (*dhyāna*) should be according to the specific rite. (35–7)
Worshipping the God at the three junctions of the day, subsisting on the food prescribed for a vow, and having conquered his senses,
he should sit in a pure place and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times without weariness.

Always pure and possessing equal devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity, one who is capable should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter; one who is incapable should perform double the number of recitations.

One should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of the number of recitations; otherwise, the mantra is not perfected. Even without prior preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), this mantra is perfected for the devotee.

The mantra consists of eleven words, [divided] by the eyes (2), the eyes (2), the Vedas (4), and the fires (3); and by the arrows (5), the fires (3), the Rāmas (3), and the tears (2); and by the Vedas (4), the eyes (2), and the horses (7) as syllables. (35.11)
One who purifies the weapons should place the [seed-syllable] of one's own color upon the joints of the fingers,
from the thumb to the little finger, and also upon the palms.

One should thus assign the pervasive [mantras] from the base throughout the body, as well as the [individual] words, to the mouth, the head, the nose, the two eyes, the two ears, and the throat. (35.13)
Having projected the mantra-body upon the heart, navel, hips, knees, and feet in their respective order, one should perform recitation, meditation, worship, and so forth. (35.14)
And the meditation:
[on her] whose radiance is as white as a thousand stainless autumn moons, and whose eyes, feet, and sprout-like hands are like full-blown red lotuses. (35.15)
With a lion’s face, gleaming fangs, and a wide-open red lotus-mouth;
three-eyed, terrifying with knitted brows, and possessing a mass of tawny manes like lightning. (35.16)
The Lord has a red silk upper garment and wears yellow robes;
his upper hands hold the conch and the discus, and his head is radiant with a crown.
His limbs were bound by a yogic belt; he was seated comfortably upon a lotus throne with his two feet crossed and both arms resting upon his knees.
His fingers were radiant with nails shaped like crescent moons,
and he was adorned with jeweled earrings shimmering as ear-ornaments.
Adorned with ear-ornaments resplendent with various clusters of gems,
and decorated with pearl necklaces fastened by white sacred threads.
His chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; his waist is bound with a belt of rubies; and he is adorned with armlets, jeweled bracelets, and finger-rings.
Adorned with a waist-cord radiant with the luster of various jewels,
his lotus-like feet shine with variegated bracelets and anklets.
Beautiful in every limb, he was the ornament of ornaments;
his lotus-like face was serene with joy at the destruction of the lord of the Daityas.

Having meditated upon Nṛsiṃha in this manner, one should perform worship, recitation, and so forth, [visualizing Him] seated within the lotus of one's own heart with the full array of mental offerings. (35.24)
The yogi should worship with the mind; if unable to do so, he should perform external worship using an image made of gold, gems, silver, or even copper.
Having prepared [an image] either on a painted cloth, or one should worship it in a *sālagrāma* stone;
in its absence, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or in fire, or in the orb of the sun.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the daily worship according to the rules as far as possible, provided that the stone image is stable and well-consecrated within the temple. (35.27)
For the protection of the king, the kingdom, and so forth, one should perform worship there;
one should sacrifice at the three junctions of the day, or at one junction, according to one's means. (35.28)
Even without prior preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), such a devotee, through daily worship, recitation, and other practices, certainly attains his desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the procedure for the daily worship (nityārcana):
having bathed and performed the twilight prayers (sandhyā), remaining silent, and having reached the hall of worship,
with hands and feet washed and having properly sipped water (ācamana), one should worship the door-keepers.
Wearing the sacrificial grass as an upper garment and having sprinkled [the area] in due order with the water for the *arghya* offering,
one should worship Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ on the two upper door-posts and in the middle space.
Below are the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma;
above, between a pair of elephants, is the Door-Goddess (Dvāraśrī) reaching up to the Udumbara post.
Having cast flowers inside from his own weapon-mantra and having dispelled obstacles while remaining silent,
he enters within and [worships] Vāstveśa and Brahmā upon his own seat.
Having sat down before [the deity], one should purify [the body] with the previously mentioned rites of drying and so forth;
then, one should meditate on Narahari as being of the nature of consciousness within the lotus of the heart, as non-different from oneself.

Having purified the weapons, one should place the limbs upon the hands and fingers; then, with the root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) upon the body and the stations of Rudra.
Placing his outstretched hands upon his knees with the fingers pointing downward, and crossing his feet while baring his mouth like a lion, [he stands]. (35–36)
Having thus bound the Nṛsiṃha-mudrā within the hollow of the heart-lotus,
one should indeed worship with the intellect the Man-Lion, who is the size of a thumb, in the midst of the light.
Having applied the vertical marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and having placed flowers upon his head,
he should then fill a vessel washed with the Astra-mantra with water for the guest-offering (arghya), along with kuśa grass and unbroken rice grains.

Having placed the *tāra* (the syllable Om) as before, having recited it and worshipped, one should display the *dhenu-mudrā*; then, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials with the waters of that *arghya*, [one proceeds].

One should worship one's own head and the sacrificial ground, and Gaṇeśa in the southwest (nairṛta); the gurus in the north (aiśa), and the sages as well in the four directions of the place of worship. (35–40)
In the east are Bhadra and Subhadra; in the south, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka;
in the west, Calapracalaka; and in the north, Vijaya and Jaya.
One should worship the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) in the center, then Kūrma and Ananta, and then the Earth; worshipping each subsequent one above the previous, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha.
Dharma and the others, as well as adharma and the others, and the qualities of tamas, sattva, and rajas, are the stalks, stems, and lotuses, which are white, black, and reddish-brown respectively.
Having provided the discs of the sun, moon, and fire as the petals, filaments, and pericarp,
and having offered the *arghya* mantras, one should remove the faded garland (*nirmālya*) and perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Having invoked Nṛhari into that [liṅga] exactly as prescribed for the eight-syllable mantra,
and having offered the arghya and other offerings in sequence, one should contemplate His presence.
Then, having performed the extensive placement of mantras (nyāsa) and honored [the deity] with flowers and incense,
one should proceed with the root mantra, the limb mantras, and Vedic mantras, along with the elaborate offerings of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth.
Having sprinkled [the image] with scented water and removed that water with a cloth,
one should then place it upon the lotus-seat and again offer the triad beginning with the *arghya*.
One should perform worship according to the ritual procedure by means of the path described as metaphorical;
one should worship the limbs at the tips of the filaments and the weapon-mantra in the directions beginning with the southeast (Agni).
One should worship Śraddhā, Medhā, Mahākāmā, Bhīmā, Mahānānā, Ārdra, and Dīpti on the tips of the petals, starting from the east in due order. (35–49)
Then one should worship Śrī in the center, Garuḍa in the east, the discus with its arrow in the south, the Śārṅga bow in the west, and the mace in the north.

In the corners, one should worship Śaṅkha and Garuḍa; at the tip of the banner, one should worship the vehicle. The outer enclosure consists of the discus, the sword, the lotus, and the mace on the right.
To the left of the God [are] the conch, the mace, the shield, and the Śārṅga bow;
to the right [is] Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi on the left, and there likewise the Kaustubha gem. (35–52)
Having worshipped the Śrīvatsa on the right side, one should worship the forest garland (vanamālā),
the yellow garment (pītāmbara), the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), the navel-lotus, and the crown (kirīṭaka).
And one should worship all the ornaments in their respective places:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (35–54)
One should worship Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita in the eight directions beginning with the east, using their respective names followed by "namaḥ" at the end.
Outside of that, one should worship the ten Lords of the World (Lokeśas) together with their weapons and other attributes;
then, having prostrated before the Guru, the Ṛṣi, the Chandas, and the Deities. (35–56)
Having performed the sacrifice before the deity, one with a serene mind should recite the mantra while holding the rosary;
he should then offer all [the fruits of] his recitation, worship, and so forth at the feet of the deity. (57)
Having bowed and offered praise, saying "Forgive me," one should dismiss him from that image.
These are the rules for the daily worship.
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall indeed describe the ritual applications (viniyoga).
One who subsists on the food of a *vratya*, having recited [mantras] ten million times in an auspicious place, attains the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇiman* and others;
through ten million recitations, there is purification even for those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātaka*), and for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
One is purified from minor sins by a hundred thousand [repetitions] and from major sins by a million;
one desiring victory over untimely death should offer an auspicious vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
Having placed it upon a pedestal filled with water for the removal of burdens during the Bhadraka period,
one should [worship] it with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha), gold, various jewels, unbroken grains (akṣata), and fruits.

With the four milks, the barks [of the trees], and waters, with fragrant fresh flowers, and with the sprouts of the śrīvṛkṣa, aśvattha, and mango trees, together with tufts of grass (kūrca). || 35-62 ||
[The vessels] were well-placed within the mouth of the jar, covered with lids containing unhusked rice, wrapped in two very fine new cloths, and adorned with garlands. || 35.63 ||
Having invoked the omnipresent Lord Nṛhari into that [seat] through the sequence beginning with the offering of a seat,
and having worshipped Him with the sixteen services (upacāras), one should worship His attendants.
Having properly established the fire and offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter,
one should pour the remainder into the jar and recite the mantra while touching the *kūrca* grass.
Having performed a great worship of the deity, one should feed the Brahmins;
the practitioner, having fasted and bathed for purification, should be seated upon a seat made of Udumbara wood.
Having established it, one should place the mantra along with its limbs (aṅgas) within that [liṅga] and worship it,
accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.
One should properly consecrate this person; he shall be liberated from untimely death.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the mantra-practitioner without withholding one's own capacity. (35–68)
One should also perform the consecration for those afflicted by spirits and demons and those who are diseased;
the pacification of their respective afflictions will occur immediately.
Ash consecrated by one thousand recitations is known to remove all diseases;
having touched oneself, one should recite the mantra a hundred times, which shall provide protection for the self.

In the event of affliction by thieves, wicked beasts, predatory animals, kings, spirits, and the like, one is liberated from those respective fears by performing recitation while meditating on one's identity with the Self. (35–71)

Having himself become Nṛsiṃha and remembering the enemy as a deer, if he should whirl [the weapon] and cast it in whatever direction, the expulsion of the enemy shall occur in that very direction. (35-72)
Being himself enraged as Nṛsiṃha, tearing apart the beast-like enemy with his claws, one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times daily; within a month, he shall cause death.
Having slain the enemy and recited the mantra, one who is consecrated with the water-pot shall become purified; that shall also constitute self-protection. || 35-74 ||
Having performed acts such as inciting hatred or expulsion, the knower of mantras becomes pure in this way; whether the rite be cruel or gentle, he accomplishes whatever he desires. (35.75)
Through meditation on one's own unity with each respective deity and through recitation, the ritual action is accomplished;
having invoked the Man-Lion (Nṛkesarin) and performed sacrifice in a fire within a four-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform oblations with the prescribed substances and thereby attain the desired fruit;
one should also perform worship of the deity according to one's ability and feed the Brahmins.

One who desires a son, by offering the fruits of the *putrañjīva* tree into a fire fed with its own wood, obtains a virtuous son; likewise, one obtains the same result by offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and clarified butter (*ājya*). (35.78)
Having performed worship of the Blessed One, when one desires a son,
one should offer milk and ghee a hundred thousand times into the fire of Putrañjīva wood.
Having poured clarified butter into that sacrificial porridge of milk-rice (pāyasa), one should also recite the mantras;
with that, one should feed the husband and wife, and also feed the Brahmins.
Before long, a son shall be born who is long-lived and possesses a beautiful body;
one desiring prosperity should offer oblations in a fire of *bilva* wood with the flowers of the *śrī-latā* creeper and lotuses. (35.81)
By offering bilva leaves and fruits smeared with ghee, one obtains prosperity;
by offering dūrvā grass, one attains long life; and by offering oblations of milk and ghee, one obtains cattle.
For the sake of pacifying calamities, one should offer three thousand or ten thousand blades of *dūrvā* grass into water; thus the calamities will come to peace.
Then, desiring victory in battle, [he offered] fuel consisting of roots, cotton, leaves, and tips into the fire of *vibhītaka* arrows. (35.84)
One who is anointed with the oil of *rāji* obtains victory over ten thousand;
likewise, one should mutter [the mantra] while meditating upon enemies as they approach. (35.85)

Having worshipped the Lord with *durvā* sprouts and unhusked rice grains in a fire of *pālāśa* wood using clarified butter, and having offered oblations of *durvā*, milk-rice, and ghee, one shall obtain a long life. (35–86)
Having offered oblations with kindled palāśa wood and clarified butter, one shall obtain health;
for rain, one should offer oblations of rice-grains with clarified butter and milk-rice.
Standing in water, one should recite the mantra; the desired rain will fall.
What is the use of saying more here? Whatever the knower of the mantra desires shall come to pass. (35.88)

The devoted practitioner, seated on a soft seat with the body straight and the mind concentrated, attains [the goal] through various acts of worship, recitation, meditation, and fire-offerings. (35.89)
One should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī four finger-breadths below the navel,
resembling a serpent in form, radiant like the sun, and eightfold in her circular coils.
Golden-hued and bearing the syllable *praṇava*, ten channels (*nāḍī*) have issued forth from her:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Gāndhārī, and Hastijihvikā; || 35-91 ||
Suyaśā, Alambuṣā, Pūṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkinī—these are the channels that serve as the pathways for the ten vital winds, beginning with prāṇa. (35–92)
The one called Suṣumnā, which moves upward, is situated in the middle of the body;
Iḍā proceeds on the left, while Piṅgalā proceeds on the right.
The Suṣumnā, having gone to the navel-lotus, reaches its pericarp;
there resides the goddess Ramā, who has the splendor of lightning and whose form is the Praṇava.
Known as the Subtle (sūkṣmā), consisting of consciousness, it should be meditated upon as radiant like a streak of lightning;
then, proceeding by way of the Suṣumṇā channel, it enters the pericarp of the heart-lotus.

One should meditate upon the power Ramā, known as Madhyamā, resembling the flame of a lamp, and manifested by the *praṇava* and *haṃsa* mantras consisting of three and a half measures (*mātrās*). (35.96)
Then, by means of the *suṣumnā*, one should lead that streak of light upward to the middle of the eyebrows,
situated within the *bindu*, as the *vaikharī* speech-sound of the syllable *praṇava*, which is the Goddess Ramā.
One should meditate on her as resembling the rays of the moon; then, having emerged through the *suṣumnā*, she resides in the center of the lunar maṇḍala within the lotus at the *dvādaśānta*. (35.98)
[She is] situated within the seed-syllable *tāra-vāruṇa* (HRĪM), being bathed by the nectars of immortality,
with a stream of nectar emitted from the multitude of digits beginning with Amṛtā.
Having traveled in succession through the *suṣumṇā* down to the lotus of the brows, the heart, and the navel, one reaches the supreme, subtle *kuṇḍalinī*. (35.100)
Then, filling [the body] with nectar and ambrosia from the soles of the feet upward, and again ascending as far as possible from that nectar, [one should contemplate her]. || 35-101 ||
One should meditate upon the supreme Lakṣmī, the creator of the entire world, who bathes [the practitioner] from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head with the waters of nectar.
One should place the four Vedas, filled with full nectar, within the *bindu*;
and those seasons, beginning with spring, filled with nectar, within the heart-lotus. (35.103)
Having placed [the fire] in the navel-lotus, one should place the Āhavanīya fire;
having likewise placed the Anvāhārya fire, one should place the Gārhapatya fire.
Being flooded with nectar and awakened by the *praṇava*,
one should place the organs of action on the left and the organs of knowledge on the right.
One should then place the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka) and the five gross elements (pañca-bhūtāni), drenched in nectar, upon the right and left feet.
There too, one should meditate upon the final [element], following it like a streak of lightning—
the mind, intellect, ego, primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the person (puruṣa).
Then, having projected the Man-lion throughout the entire body by means of pervasiveness,
and having meditated upon his identity with oneself, one should flood everything in sequence with the waters of nectar.

Then one should perform the rites beginning with worship, recitation, meditation, and fire-oblation, and ending with their conclusion; thus one obtains the fruit described for the yantra, and the perfection of the mantra arises. || 35-109 ||
This common placement (nyāsa) of the mantras of Nṛhari is thus remembered;
now I shall describe the supreme Nṛsiṃha yantra, which brings about all protection.
One should write [the mantra] on a gold plate, or on birch bark, or on a white cloth, using yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, costus (laghukuṣṭha), camphor, and sandalwood. (35.111)
With well-ground [pigments], one should draw a white lotus, radiant with its pericarp and filaments;
it should have eight petals within and sixteen petals on the outside. || 35-112 ||
There are thirty-two petals on the outside; one should encircle it three times with a noose and surround it with a hook. Then follows the single-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha.
One should write [the mantra] in the pericarp, and within it, one should inscribe the name of the person to be protected;
the eight syllables on the eight petals, and the vowels on the sixteen petals.
Within the centers of the thirty-two petals, one should also write the syllables of the root mantra;
on the tips of the petals, one should write the thirty-two letters beginning with *ka*.
One should inscribe the letters *ha* and *kṣa* three times around the joints of the petals;
having formed pellets with lotus-patterned cloth and thread, one should wrap them. (35.116)
Having coated the lotus with lac and gold, one should place the yantra upon it; then, having positioned the ritual vessels, one should proceed from the seat and so forth.
Then, having invoked [the deity], one should worship correctly; having touched [the water], one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Then, having consecrated the person to be purified with the waters from that jar, [one should give] the pill.
Having tied [this] around the neck, on the head, or on the hand, one should feed Brahmins for the sake of warding off ghosts, spirits, piśācas, epilepsy, and other such afflictions. (35.119)
And thus, the avoidance of diseases such as consumption and others will have been accomplished.
As for the ritual of the yantra: one should write the name within the seed-syllable (bīja), and outside of that, a circle; and outside of that [another circle]. (35.120)
"Oṃ hūṃ khe kṣe phaṭ jaye ṭhaṭha. One should write this mantra, with the name of the person to be accomplished inserted within it, all around.
Furthermore, one should draw a circle and within it a hexagon, and in the corners [of the hexagon], one should place the fire-syllable (raṃ). (35.121)
One should draw Mahākāla, the wrathful deity, at the tips of the corners, with a drop at the joints;
this wheel, moreover, should be drawn on the outside of the earth mandala.
By means of *dhāraṇā* alone, one may destroy *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like.
One *prastha* of the powder of *śatāvarī* and one *prastha* of *gokṣuraka*— (35.123)
The fruit of Vārāhī is twentyfold, that of Gulūcī is twenty-fivefold,
that of Bhallātaka is thirty-twofold, while for Citraka it is tenfold.
Having powdered the *palas* [of the aforementioned ingredients], one should likewise add a *prastha* of black sesame seeds and seventy *palas* of aged sugar. (35.125)
Thirty-five palas of honey and half of that amount of cow’s ghee are prescribed;
having combined all of this together, one should place it in a smooth, oiled vessel.

Having observed celibacy, one should daily eat half a *pala* of this [substance], beginning from the morning of the seventh night, having consecrated it in sequence with the *Nṛsiṃha-mantra*. (35.127)
Within six months, it shall destroy grey hair; it may even conquer old age and death, as well as the eighteen types of leprosy and the seven kinds of consumption. (35.128)

It destroys the eighty diseases born of wind (vāta), the twenty-one born of bile (pitta), the twenty pains born of phlegm (śleṣman), and those arising from the combination of all three (sannipāta). || 35-129 ||

By practicing this elixir (rasāyana) of Nārasiṃha for a long time, one shall live long. This concludes the section on the Nārasiṃha Anuṣṭubh. Then, the syllable Om (tāra), the word "hṛd," and the word "bhagavat" followed by the dative case ending [should be used]. 35–130.
Dīrgha, Meṣa, Anala, Śukla, Sākṣidaṇḍa, then Viyat;
Dīrghavāyu, and then also Devadānava—thus [the names]. (35–131)

O you who possess the brilliance equal to thousands of billions of blazing suns; O you whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, and whose mane and whiskers are fully spread out; O you whose roar has the sound of the ocean and the drum of the agitated great sea; O you who are the resonance of all other mantras; O you who are the heart of all other mantras! Come, come, Blessed One! O Narasiṃha! O Puruṣa! O Parāvara! O Brahmā! By truth, quiver, expand, rend, tear asunder all the netherworlds (pātālas)! Wander, roar, let loose the lion’s roar, put them to flight, enter, devour all forms of the yantras! Bind all the netherworlds from every side with a cage of hundreds of diamonds and infinite flames! Envelop the seven netherworlds! Summon the inhabitants of the world of the gods from all the netherworlds! Summon their hearts! Shake them quickly! Burn! Strike! Cook! Grind! Dry up! Cut to pieces! Until all my maidens have come under my control!

*Phaṭ* from the netherworlds (*pātāla*), *phaṭ* from the Asuras, *phaṭ* from those in the form of mechanical devices (*yantra*). O Lord Narasiṃha, Viṣṇu! Protect me with laughter from all sins, from all calamities, and from all fears, misfortunes, and terrors. *Oṃ hrīṃ kṣi phaṭ kāstu te hṛ phaṭ ṭha ṭha*. Its limbs (*aṅga*) are as follows: *Oṃ narasiṃhakrīḍita siṃhavidrāvaṇa sarvayantrān hana bhañjoccāṭaya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the Heart (*hṛdaya*). *Oṃ narasiṃhottamāṅgarakṣaṇāya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the Head (*śiras*). *Oṃ daṃṣṭrotkaṭāya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the Crest-lock (*śikhā*). *Oṃ narasiṃhārividrāvaṇa huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the Armor (*kavaca*). *Oṃ namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya vedavedanivedāṅge huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the Weapon (*astra*). *Oṃ phaṇāsahasrabhogakuṭilaparyaṅkāyānantāya ṭhaṭha*. *Āgaccha bhagavan! Viṣṇo! ṭhaṭha*—this is the mantra for invocation (*āvāhana*). *Oṃ namaḥ śrīhitāya namaḥ*—this is the mantra for worship (*pūjā*). *Pūjito yathāsukhaṃ namaḥ* (Salutation to the one worshipped at ease).
The mantra consisting of four hundred syllables is known as the Nārasiṃha; Yama is its seer (ṛṣi), Aticchandas is its meter, and Viṣṇu alone is its deity. (35.132)
Having approached the abode of Viṣṇu facing westward, being pure,
one should recite [the mantra] twelve thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Having performed the placement of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) upon the fingers of both hands, or having worshipped Nṛhari—who has eight arms and three eyes—upon his body; 35-134.
Emerging from the pillar and piercing the son of Diti with his claws, beak, and talons,
he was then one whose body was drenched with blood from the scattering of the entrails.
Holding a discus, a sword, a mace, a conch, a shield, and a club with his six upper arms, and with his two lower hands... [35.136]
Having split open Hiraṇyakaśipu, he cast that fierce enemy of his— terrifying with the tossing of his entrails—
down to his knees at the entrance.
Roaring with an exceedingly deep laugh that was terrifying,
he was being praised by Viriñca and the other gods, as well as by hosts of sages.
Having meditated thus, one should worship [the deity] on the variegated cloth-painting (citrapaṭaka) as being without obstructions;
one should also constantly recite the mantra, either mentally or with ritual offerings.
Having mastered the mantra, he should enter a cave and recite it ten thousand times;
seeing various kinds of obstacles there, he should continue his recitation with unwavering steadiness.
Having entered the cave, the steadfast one shall attain perfection in Pātāla;
if he is incapable [of entering], he should recite the mantra at the mouth of the cave, and then from within the cave.
And having emerged, the daughters of the Asuras grant him his desire;
he obtains an elixir, mercury, or wealth within a single ghaṭikā.
The hosts of gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and others do not approach the mantra-practitioner, and they even grant whatever is desired. (35.143)
The Chapter on Pātālanarasiṃha:

The single-syllable mantra of Narasiṃha has Brahmā as its seer (ṛṣi), the Śveta-Agni fire as its presiding deity, and it is accompanied by grace; the staff-bearer (Daṇḍin) is its form, Jagatī is its meter, Atri is its sage, and the Deity is Narasiṃha. (35.144)
Mahāviṣṇu himself, joined with his own limbs and long vowels,
is encircled by a three-pronged trident consisting of a mass of blazing fire-flames within the heart.
Placed upon the heart, it burns away even the sin accumulated in other births;
the Brahmin, well-restrained, should mutter the mantra interspersed with the *praṇava*. (35.146)
One who subsists on ghee should then recite ten lakhs [of mantras] in due order at a river flowing to the ocean or on a mountain peak.

Subsisting on almsfood for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should meditate upon [the deity] who resembles a mountain of snow, with a mass of mane shining like saffron. (35.148)
With fangs like the crescent of the young moon, a lion’s face, and three eyes;
his forehead is arched with a furrowed brow, and he is radiant with a crown.
The omnipresent Lord has four arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness;
his limbs are variegated with all kinds of ornaments, and he is adorned with yellow garments.

Meditating on Narahari as being one with oneself, one should worship Him with the mind alone—Him who is enraged by the slaughter of Hiraṇya and who seems to burn everything with His very glances. (35-151)
Whether on a cloth painting or in one's own heart, the capable person should worship with devotion;
even by reciting [the mantra] ten times, one is liberated from diseases and calamities. (35.152)
In the presence of this mantra, other mantras are thwarted;
spirits, piśācas, and the like are reduced to ashes, without a doubt. (35.153)
Even without the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), this [mantra] shall indeed be accomplished for the devotee through mere recitation;
affliction from poisons, diseases, planetary influences, and enemies is instantly destroyed. (35–154)
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, all afflictions are pacified;
the applications have been proclaimed according to the method prescribed for the Anuṣṭubh meter. (35.155)
Whatever applications (viniyoga) have been prescribed for Vārāha elsewhere, those same apply here as well;
and for the pacification of his wrath, one should recite that [mantra].
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), then *hṛt* (Namaḥ), followed by the word *bhagavate*, and likewise ending with *meṣa*.

Salutation to Vāsudeva, who has a thousand heads, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, whose couch is the coils of Śeṣa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa; salutation to you, Vāsudeva clad in yellow garments! Salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Hayagrīva, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Trivikrama, Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, O bestower of boons! Slay, burn, cook, churn, crush, seize, cause to enter, destroy, terrify, put to flight—by means of all weapons, the discus, the mace, the thunderbolt, and the trident, reduce to ashes these and other great malevolent spirits: Asuras, Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Apasmāras, Siddhas, Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, Riṭis, Ghṛṇis, Brahma-rākṣasas, Vināyakas, Pūtanās, Revatīs, Skandas, and the leaders and followers, as well as the noble and ignoble planets, constellations, and other great malevolent influences, O thousand-armed one, wielder of all missiles and weapons! Oṃ! Victory, victory! O Infinite One, Unconquered, Unassailable, Thousand-eyed One! Blaze, blaze forth! O Universal Form, Madhusūdana, Mahāpuruṣa, Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, Dāmodara, Subduer of all beings, Wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O Lord of all beings, salutation to you! O Crusher of all serpents, Destroyer of all Asuras, Great Lord of all gods, Averter of all planets, Breaker of all machines, Piercer of all seals, Destroyer of all fevers, Bestower of liberation from all bonds, Accomplisher of all purposes and goals, Destroyer of all calamities, Destroyer of all diseases, Destroyer of all enemies, Warder-off of all wicked ones, Pacifier of all misfortunes, Destroyer of all bad dreams, O God of all gods, salutation to you! O Janārdana, who draws away all beings, O God of gods, salutation to you! Thus, the ancillary limbs of this [mantra] are shown in the *Padmodbhava-saṃhitā*:

*Bhūteśvara jaya jīvana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the heart mantra (*hṛdayam*). *Tejomaya jīvana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the head mantra (*śiraḥ*). *Amṛtodbhavāya makuṭāya jaya jīvana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the crest mantra (*śikhā*). *Amṛte kṛṣṇarūpārthaṃ jīvana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the armor mantra (*kavacam*). *Dampate jīvana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*—this is the weapon mantra (*astram*). *Sarvatejasāmutkṛṣṭatejase vauṣaṭ*—this is the eye mantra (*netram*). The binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) is performed with the *darśana-mantra*. Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this; Virāṭ is its meter (*chanda*), and it has [the aforementioned] deity (*daivata*). (35-157)
For the sake of performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should recite the Viṣṇu-mantra twelve thousand times;
having offered oblations of sesame and clarified butter ten times that number, the mantra becomes perfected.
By the mere recollection of the mantra, all calamities perish;
having meditated upon Nṛsiṃha, the Lord of Gods, according to the prescribed method of the Anuṣṭubh.
Having fully worshipped the mantra, one should recite it; thus one shall obtain all desires.
Seeking victory in battle, one should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter with that [mantra]. (35.160)
Having recited this mantra twenty-one times, one shall attain victory in battle;
[one should meditate upon] the Mantra-armed Nṛkesarin (Man-lion), whose body is fortified by the mantra and who is one with oneself.
Spirits, ghosts, and piśācas, as well as tigers, serpents, and the like, and even enemies and thieves, do not approach him out of fear. (35.162)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one shall destroy smallpox;
meditating on Nṛhari as identical with oneself, while gazing with a fierce eye. (35.163)
Having recited it ten thousand times, one shall destroy epilepsy;
likewise, one shall overcome a great fever, and with twenty thousand recitations, one shall remove eye diseases.

By reciting and meditating upon the *tripañcaka* mantra five times, one removes poisons through its recitation; by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one destroys leprosy and shall annihilate consumption (*yakṣman*).
By offering oblations of *nandyāvarta* flowers with clarified butter while consuming sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one shall obtain a son;
by offering *dūrvā* grass sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter, one conquers untimely death.
Having consecrated ghee with this mantra three times starting from the full moon day, one should consume it on the day following the full moon; thereby, great intelligence arises within him.
By reciting [the mantra] twenty-four times, one shall achieve subjugation;
likewise, by offering eight thousand oblations of clarified butter while uttering the person's name, [the same result is attained].

Now, one who desires to perform an attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) should offer oblations at night, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight, using white mustard seeds and fuel-sticks of *akṣa* wood smeared with oil.
By performing oblations on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one certainly slays an enemy.
By offering ten thousand lotuses, one attains prosperity; and by offering bilva fruits, one likewise finds fortune. (35.170)
Or whatever land one desires during the yoga known as Vārāha,
having circumambulated that [land] and offered ghee from the Jyotiṣmatī plant, || 35-171 ||
One obtains that land for a full year; there is no doubt about this.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on a Friday, when there is the conjunction of the Nāgas in the Maitra constellation (Anurādhā), [this occurs].

In the *muhūrta* of Aślesha, in the asterism of Aślesha, and in the lunar phase (*karaṇa*) known as Nāga—this conjunction is called Nāgayoga; or else, it is the conjunction of the [lunar] mansion with its cause. (35.173)
For the purpose of accomplishing the subterranean realm (pātāla), by offering one million oblations of milk and ghee to the inhabitants of the underworld, one obtains abundant wealth.
Having offered clarified butter from the jyotiṣmatī plant in the shade of a banyan tree, he obtains either mercury, an elixir, wealth, or a ghaṭikā. (35.175)
One shall obtain the divine qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest; there is no doubt in this matter.
If one desires the power of traveling through the sky, [one should use] oil extracted from the aṅkola tree.
One should offer three hundred thousand oblations for each of the *jyotiṣmatī* [plants];
thereafter, having fasted for three nights, one should recite the mantra for three days.
At night, standing in knee-deep water in a river flowing to the ocean, one should recite five thousand [times]; then, having entered that water, [one should proceed]. (35.178)
One may take the fruit of the banyan tree and eat it without hesitation;
he shall become a traveler through the sky, long-lived, and possessed of perpetual youth. (35.179)
Thus, the Nṛsiṃha-mantras, having deliberated in many ways upon the various kalpas according to their primary importance,
are endowed with specific applications and the rules for image worship.
Thus has it been truly demonstrated for those possessed of devotion to Nṛhari. || 35-180 ||
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the Mantra-paṭala for Nṛhari, in the Mantra-pāda of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 35.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter. [The mantra is:
Tāra (Oṃ), Hṛt (Namaḥ), Bhagavate, Kumbha (Ka), Dīrgha (Ā), Anala (Ra), Viyat (Ha), Bhujaṅga (Sa), adorned with Vāmakarṇa (Ū), then Dīrgha (Ā) and Pārśva (Va), followed by Marut (Ya). (36–1)
The three *vyāhṛtis* are the sides; with those, preceded by *bhūpati*, [say] "tvaṃ me de"; then the sky is the right eye; [conclude] with two *ṭha*s. (36-2)
This is the mantra of Mahāvarāha; its seer and other [components] are remembered as before.
The seed-syllable (bīja) consists of the first syllable of each of the vyāhṛtis, and the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed with those very same syllables.
The three utterances beginning with the Heart, joined with the [seed-syllable] Jāti, constitute the armor (kavaca) for Mahas and Janas; Tapa and Satya are said to be the weapon (astra). || 36-4 ||

In this same manner, one should place the seven vyāhṛtis upon the fingers of the hands; then, with the root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka), and the limbs [of the mantra] beginning with the praṇava should be placed upon the [respective] body parts.
For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*, one observing the vow should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times,
meditating upon the all-pervading Lord who has the face of a boar and resembles a mass of dark rain clouds.
Four-armed, bestowing the conch, discus, mace, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons,
his body filling the three worlds, he is well-seated upon a lotus throne.
He caused the earth to tremble as he rose slightly from his seat, his fangs bared;
his chest bore the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he was adorned with ornaments such as a crown.
Having meditated on oneself as identical with [the deity], adorned and wearing yellow garments, one should perform recitation and other rites;
one should worship with mental offerings and also perform worship before images and the like.
Having taken earth from whichever ground he desires to attain, on a Tuesday, he should offer it with three sweet substances while reciting this mantra.
By performing oblations in this manner on the seven days of the week— doubling or even tripling the effort— and by constant recitation and worship, one obtains that land.
During the aforementioned yogas, one should take that excellent earth and consume it while reciting [the mantra].
That earth shall become one's own, and any offense against the sacred field is destroyed.
What is the use of much speaking here, which only causes the book to become burdensome?
For one who offers oblations directed toward whatever may be desired, [that very thing shall be attained]. (36.13)
For one who thus recites and meditates, success is indeed attained; there is no doubt.
This is the section concerning the mantra of Mahāvarāha:
Dviraṇḍa (the syllable *phaṭ*), enriched with the left ear (*va*), and followed by the creator (*sargī*)—this is the Vārāhaka mantra. (36–14)
The seer of this [hymn] is named Sāṃśika; its meter is indeed Gāyatrī;
Viṣṇu is the deity; and he himself performed the limbs [of the ritual] with long vowels. (36-15)
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should recite [the mantra] while consuming only ghee for a hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations of ghee ten thousand times, and then the mantra becomes perfected.
The seer, the metre, the deity, and the meditations and so forth have been previously stated;
the application (viniyoga) for this mantra of Mahāvarāha has now been enjoined.
The ritual for the single-syllable mantra of Varāha:
first the Tāra (Om), then the eight-syllable mantra, followed by the word "Ādidevāya" (to the Primordial God).

To the one who possesses the supreme splendor (*bhuṣurottaphāśaṃ*?), the great repository of all splendors, who consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) yet is beyond the qualities (*guṇabāhya*), who bears all marks (*sarvaliṅgin*) and all colors (*sarvavarṇa*), the creator of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds, worshipped by gods and demons, manifest and unmanifest, possessing all weapons and missiles, the destroyer of all enemies, the bestower of all boons, the affectionate follower of all, the annihilator of all sins, the breaker of all mantras, the shatterer of all mantras, the crusher of all mudrās, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, who holds the conch, discus, and mace, the wielder of the great Śārṅga bow—O God of Gods, Nārāyaṇa! Blaze! Flare up! Strike! Burn! Cook! Cut! Kill! Eradicate! Dry up! Paralyze! Melt! Attract! Create enmity! Expel! Destroy all enemies! Annihilate the Vināyakas! Grind the planetary spirits (*graha*) to dust! Terrify the Yātudhānas! Bewilder the Nāgas! Burn all poison! Cook all diseases! Wipe away misfortune (*alakṣmī*)! Summon Fortune (*lakṣmī*)! Grant good fortune! Bring the three worlds under control! Fulfill all desires! Summon the gods and demons! Withdraw the worlds! Grind the mountains to dust! Dry up the oceans! Support the earth! O Bringer of Peace and Prosperity! O You of Unfailing Power! O God of Gods, Nārāyaṇa! Protect me! *Oṃ namo namaḥ huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. This is the mantra for the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). *Oṃ namo bhagavate mahāvarāhāya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.

(236) Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāmana; *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Trivikrama; *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva; *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha; *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. These are the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Mahāvarāha, who lifted up the Earth with his tusk—white and curved like ten million moons; who possesses a great roar; who slew Hiraṇyākṣa like a dark cloud; who pervades the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); who is the illusory power of gods and demons; O Puruṣa, roar! O Great Boar! O Nārāyaṇa! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!* [This is] the Heart (*hṛdaya*). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāmana, who has a thousand bodies; who deceived the lords of the Daityas; who is the lord of all illusions; O you who are affectionate toward devotees! Bind! Protect! O Māyā-Nārāyaṇa! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!* [This is] the Head (*śiras*). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Trivikrama, who traversed the three worlds with three strides; who held the cosmic egg upon the tips of his feet; who is the subduer of Bali; who was watched by gods and demons trembling with fear; whose limits were never seen; whose feet shine with the banner of the Gaṅgā; O Victor! O Victorious One! O Great Nārāyaṇa! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!* [This is] the Crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who bears the conch, discus, and mace; the ender of the Daityas; who wears yellow garments; whose vehicle is Garuḍa; the hero of the Yadus; who has the luster of the moon; who is a forest fire to the forest-arms of Bāṇāsura; who is dark as a great rain-cloud; O Beloved of Lakṣmī! O Universal Form! O Nārāyaṇa! Act! Protect! O you who cannot be pierced even by the thunderbolt! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!* [This is] the Armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Nārasiṃha, whose splendor is equal to ten thousand times ten million blazing suns; who is difficult to behold; who has the form of the fire at the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*); who wears a garland of flames; who has tawny manes; whose terrifying form causes thousands of agitated lightning bolts to fall; who resembles the orb of the sun; who tore open the chest of the lord of the Daityas with his own claws; who made the three worlds resound with a roar as fearsome as the ocean and the sound of clouds; O Hulu! Roar! Roar! O you of unfailing power! O Nṛsiṃha! O Nārāyaṇa! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!* [This is] the Weapon (*astra*).
The seer is Nārada, and the metre is declared to be Ayutkṛti. || 36-18 ||

And for the sake of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), one should recite the mantra of Hṛṣīkeśa five thousand times as the root [mantra], and the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) at one-tenth that amount. || 36-19 ||
One who has previously performed the vow should also offer a thousand fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree smeared with clarified butter;
for the ancillary rites (*aṅga*), one should offer a tenth part of that amount. Thus, he becomes one who has fulfilled his prior vow.
Then one should behold the Lord Hari either directly or in a dream;
having bathed for the purpose of worship, one should wash both hands and feet with the root mantra and its ancillary mantras.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should worship Kṣetrapa at the door of the shrine room, as well as the Parivartakas,
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Dvāraśrī, and Vāstvīśa, as before.

The pure self is the self established by the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate nārāyaṇāya vidmahe vāsudevāya dhīmahi, tanno viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt*. By means of this Gāyatrī, one performs the purification of the substances. Having filled the *arghya* vessels and so forth with this [mantra], and having sprinkled the substances and other items with that water, [one worships] Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Ananta, and also Pṛthivī. (36-23)
One should worship the Yoga-pīṭha, Dharma and the others, Sattva and the others, the maṇḍalas, the lotus, the Śaktis beginning with Ātmā, and those beginning with Vimalā. (36.24)
In the center of the lotus is Garuḍa, and upon his shoulder is likewise a lotus.

[One should recite: "Oṃ, salutation to the God of gods, Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the universe, who possesses infinite power, beloved of Lakṣmī, worshipped by gods and asuras; come, grant your presence! Ṭhaṭha.
One should meditate on the eight-armed God, shining like gold, seated upon Garuḍa. (36–25)
Holding in sequence the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, sword, and pestle,
and bearing on both sides the noose and goad, he is clothed in yellow garments.
His chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem; he is adorned with a crown and other ornaments, wears a forest garland, and possesses beautiful, shimmering makara-shaped earrings.
With the *tāra* (Oṃ), one should invoke from the lotus of one's own heart the supreme light whose nature is consciousness,
according to the previous procedure, with: "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya supratiṣṭhito bhava ṭhaṭha."
By this, one may also establish [the deity]. || 36-28 ||
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, the Guru, and Nārada in the eight directions of the seat starting from the east, one should worship the limbs in sequence in the intermediate directions.
In the outer enclosure surrounding that, the Dūtīs are stationed in the eight directions in sequence:
Padmā, Vāc, Rati, Prīti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, and Yaśasvinī.
One should worship Śānti and Puṣṭi, holding mirrors and chowries in their foremost hands;
and outside that, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Śaṅkha in the eight directions.
One should worship Lokeśāna along with his hosts of weapons and Viṣvaksena.
With the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ puṇḍarīkākṣāya trailokyādhipataye gṛhṇa ṭhaṭha," one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*) and flowers and other offerings using this eight-syllabled mantra.
Oṃ, homage to the one dwelling in the Ocean of Milk; homage, ṭhaṭha!
With this [mantra], one should bathe [the deity] and offer garments, ornaments, and so forth.
Oṃ, homage to the God of gods, Madhusūdana, who is fond of fragrant perfumes and unguents.
"Gr̥hṇa ṭhaṭha.
Then one should offer fragrance with this:
"Oṃ namaḥ devādidevāya gr̥hṇa ṭhaṭha."
And one should worship with these flowers. || 36-33 ||
Oṃ, salutation to Hṛṣīkeśa, who is affectionate toward his devotees; accept [this], ṭhaṭha.
With this, one should indeed offer incense: Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Light, ṭhaṭha.

And with this [mantra], he should perform the *ārātrika* rite: *oṃ namaḥ paramavāsudevāya gṛhṇa ṭhaṭha*. With this [mantra] he should likewise offer the food offering (*naivedya*) as well as the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*). (36–34)
One should worship the retinue with well-spoken words, perform the recitation of the mantra,
and having invoked the deity and offered oblations into the fire,
[recite]: *Oṃ namaḥ devādidevāya śvetadvīpapriyāya garuḍavāhana āgaccha ṭhaṭha*.
With this, one should ask for forgiveness. || 36-35 ||
Having recited [the mantra] and offered oblations at a banyan tree (*vaṭa*), one will certainly bring a *yakṣiṇī* under control;
even the gods in the netherworld (*pātāla*) can be subdued by ten thousand repetitions, as observed.
In the Kali age, however, it is taught that twice the amount of oblations, recitations, and so forth, grants success;
one may overcome untimely death by offering oblations of mango leaves, cow products, and clarified butter.

Having meditated upon the deity situated in a lake filled with nectar, and having visualized him sprinkling the head of the person to be treated (sādhya) with the waters of immortality, one should destroy poisons and other such afflictions. (36–38)

To whomever one gives perfumes, flowers, and so forth, having consecrated them seven times with mantras, that person shall become subject to one's will; likewise, a woman is brought under control by means of the recitation performed upon her bed.

One who wears on his head the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) from the head of Hari, consecrated with mantras, is not afflicted by *rakṣas*, *bhūta*, *piśāca*, and other such beings, nor by serpents and the like. (36–40)

By means of that unguent applied to the eyes, one shall see treasures such as the *bhūta* and others; likewise, milk boiled with *vacā* grass, consecrated seven times [with the mantra], [should be used]. (36–41)
Having consumed it, one becomes a retainer of what has been heard, eloquent, a poet, and wise.
Meditating on the identity with the Self while reciting the mantra to the God, one is liberated even from all fears. (36–42)

Having investigated in many ways the methods established in the Harita-tantra throughout the kalpas, this king of mantras concerning the Vārāha-mantra has been revealed, complete with the procedures for fire-offerings, means of accomplishment, and sacrifice.
He is the wish-fulfilling tree for those who desire the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, named the Illustrious Varāharāja, in the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 36.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Bhṛgu, Vyoman, along with Ananta, Vahni, Śukla, and then Anala;
followed by Kavaca and Astra—these six syllables, preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ), constitute the Sudarśana mantra. (37.1)
The sage is Ahibuddhini, the metre is Gāyatrī, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity;
it may be the Sudarśana mantra itself, and its limbs (aṅgas) are written in their proper sequence.
Āviśuddhya, Mahāsudarśana, and Cakrajātiyuta;
likewise, Jvālācakra and the limbs of the mantra shall follow in sequence. (37-3)
At the end of "hṛdayāya," one should utter the word "cakrāya vidmahe," and then "sahasrajvālāya dhīmahe tanno" as well. (37–4)
The mantra "arivāritapraśabdo gāyatrī codayāt" consists of six syllables, which are as reddish as cochineal insects. (37.5)
One should contemplate the six limbs, beginning with the heart, according to their colors: white, black, tawny, yellow, lightning-like, and reddish-brown. (37–6)

One should place the colors of the weapons on the hands upon the fingers; from the thumb to the palm, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) on the body six times with the root mantra. (37–7)
One should place the syllables beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *tāra* upon eight locations on the body: the eyes, nose, mouth, heart, private parts, knees, and the two ankles. (37–8)
Kaṇva, Nārada, Brahmā, Kauśika, Vyāsa, and Gautama are to be known as the Ṛṣis for each syllable; Indra and Agni are the deities in their respective order. (37–9)
Anuṣṭubh, Virāj, Āryā, Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh are the meters; and the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, together with the Lord, are six.
"By means of the excellent wheel, I bind the eastern quarter"—with these words, one should bind the four directions;
likewise, one should bind the upward and downward directions by means of the snapping-finger weapon (*choṭikāstra*).
*Kālacakrāya hūṃ phaṭ*. At the beginning and end of going and coming, the practitioner should recite this for protection: *Trailokyarakṣakacakrāya ṭhaṭha*.
And one should recite this during the essential daily rites (*āvaśyaka*) and so forth, as well as during the eight-day sleep-rite (*śayanāṣṭi*) and others. (37–12)
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *hṛd* (Namaḥ), the word *bhagavat*, then *sudarśana* in the dative case, *phaṭ* or *kroḍa*, *mahābalāya*, *dīptarūpāya*, *sarvato māṃ rakṣa mahābalāya ṭhaṭha*.
Having recited this mantra once, one should perform the recitation and other rites. || 37-13 ||
Having placed [the mantras] in Durgā, Vighneśvara, Gurukṣetreśānana, Anala, and so forth, and having bowed down, one who performs worship and other rites shall attain success.
The fourth syllable is the seed-mantra (bīja), and the desired final syllable is the power (śakti).
For the sake of purification through the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one should abstain from pungent and salty foods.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Sudarśana two hundred thousand times in the temple of Viṣṇu,
one should then remain standing in water and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while observing a vow of subsisting on milk alone.

Facing north on a river flowing toward the ocean, subsisting on ghee, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; or else, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite it one hundred thousand times while staying at the foot of an aśvattha tree.
Eating only vegetables on a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times facing east as before;
having thus performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*), [one should offer oblations] with *apāmārga* wood and sesame seeds. (37.18)
One should offer ten thousand oblations separately with ghee and with *caru*;
if one is unable to do so, one should recite the mantra twice as many times and feed Brahmins according to one's capacity.
One should daily perform worship according to the rules for both Atri and Hari;
having performed the daily rites, one should bathe according to the procedure prescribed for the daily ritual.

Having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should purify his own body through the rites of drying and so forth; then, having performed the self-sacrifice (ātmayāga) and worshipped the wheel within the lotus of the heart.
Therein is the meditation:
[the deity] is red, adorned with red garments, with many ornaments illuminated by shimmering ruby gems;
his face is fierce with a mass of fire issuing from a wide, gaping throat, intensified by a loud, white-toothed laugh.
I bow to Viṣṇucakra, who possesses eight arms and bears a conch, a discus, a mace, two lotuses, a club, a bow with arrows, and a noose and goad; his hair and eyes are tawny-brown. || 37-22 ||
Having meditated thus upon the Enemy (Śiva) in the heart, on a sacrificial mound, or in a painting, one should worship Him;
likewise, one should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the door, as well as Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
One should worship Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Dvāralakṣmī; one should cast flowers inside while recollecting the Astra-mantra and the Nārāca weapon.

Having entered within and worshipped the Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa), sitting upon his own seat, he should prepare the *arghya* water and, with the root mantra and its limbs, purify the articles of worship using a *kūrca* brush.
Having sprinkled that ground with water for the arghya offering and having performed the protective rite (astravapra),
he should likewise worship the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the tortoise (kūrma), Ananta, and the earth.
And [he should contemplate] the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), as well as Dharma and the other [qualities], together with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire, and [the three selves:
the self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman), within the lotus.
Having worshipped the form of the Sudarśana, having meditated upon it, invoked it, and established it [within], one should,
with hands joined in a handful of flowers, [visualize] the light rising upward from one's own heart-lotus.

Having led the *bindu* into that form, one should join it within the heart-lotus by means of the *praṇava* and the root-mantra, [visualizing it] as flooded with the nectar from the *dvādaśānta*. (37.29)
Having restrained [the breath] and rendered it immortal, one should place the limbs (aṅgas) in the corners;
one should place the weapon (astra) at the tips of the petals of the directions and the eye (netra) in front.
Outside the pedestal, one should place the eight weapons in order upon lotuses;
outside of that, one should worship the ten guardians of the world (lokeśas) together with their weapons and other attributes.
One should worship that form of the wheel situated in the center of the six-spoked wheel, which is filled with garlands of flames, using the primary offerings.
In occasional rites of worship, having first properly worshipped Viṣṇu to the north of the discus, one should thereafter worship the discus itself. (37–38)
Or one may worship with the mind alone, O God; one must not neglect the daily worship.
Even without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), this [attainment] occurs through daily worship, recitation, and so forth. (37–34)
It accomplishes the goals of a devotee; how much more so through prior service!
Indeed, the ritual applications are now written down for the benefit of practitioners. (37–35)
One obtains the glory of Brahmā by offering oblations of palāśa wood;
likewise, by reciting [the mantra] six thousand times on a mountain peak with white lotuses, one attains the same.
By offering ten thousand oblations of *bailva* fruits or leaves, one attains prosperity;
or by offering a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter, one obtains either the headship of kings or a kingdom.
One should subjugate Brahmins and others with fuel-sticks made of *palāśa* wood;
likewise, one may subjugate all people, including those of the salt-trade, with fuel-sticks from the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, and *arka* trees.
One should offer a thousand oblations of a life-endowed image of Lavaṇī, sprinkled with honey, beginning from the right foot; this brings all under control. (37–39)
A sacrifice performed with severed *dūrvā* grass conquers untimely death;
it may be offered on the full moon day, under the asterism Maghā, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
Having fasted on the preceding day, with his body smeared with ashes,
he should drink that which has been consecrated by recitation for a full day and night, mixed with ashes.
One becomes a master of memory, eloquent, a poet, and wise;
or by practicing two hundred thousand [recitations] during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one becomes a lord of speech. (37–42)
By sprinkling water held in cupped hands, one obtains long life and prosperity;
by offering oblations of clarified butter and milk, one becomes possessed of cattle; and by offering flowers as oblations, one obtains garments.
Having placed a discus made of a hundred gold *niṣkas* into a vessel and having worshipped it, one should offer oblations with *aṅkola* oil; thus, the kingdom shall become one's own. (37–44)
Having fasted for three nights and offered a hundred thousand oblations of ghee beginning from the twelfth day of the dark fortnight,
one shall behold a treasure or else attain great prosperity.
By offering oblations of cane (vetasa) soaked in milk, copious rain falls;
and by reciting [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times at the entrance of a hole, one becomes a possessor of all supernatural powers (siddhis).

Or else, on a mountain peak or in a forest, one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times; having offered oblations with *aṅkola* seeds and clarified butter along with one thousand and eight [recitations], one should do so with devotion.
One may find two divine pills fallen from the sky; one should fasten one to the waist and cast the other into the mouth. (37–48)
One may become a sky-walker, possess the speed of mind, be youthful, and long-lived;
furthermore, by performing a thousand-fold recitation beneath a banyan tree with *arka* fuel, [the same results are attained]. (37–49)
Having performed five thousand oblations, the yakṣiṇī shall come under one's control;
then, having meditated on the six-syllable mantra upon the six spokes of a wheel visualized in the palm of the hand.
Having touched that which is being burned by its flames, one should remove the poison;
or, for another who has been bitten long ago, one should strike it with the fifth syllable.
There is empowerment and one certainly causes [the deity] to enter while remaining composed;
having drawn a square mandala with powders, one should then draw a wheel.
Having worshipped the mantras in the spokes, the limbs in the joints, and the name in the hub,
and having placed the one seized by the planets within that [diagram], he should mutter the mantra.
By scattering ashes with the fifth syllable, one enters [the enemy] and destroys him;
having meditated on the Sudarśana [discus], which is conch-white and bearing the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā).
Meditating on the poison as being reduced to ashes by its flames, one should recite the mantra;
then, one should flood it with nectar and destroy the poisons. (37.55)
Having worshipped Viṣṇu Sudarśana for the purpose of pacifying malevolent planets and other such influences,
[one should offer] clarified butter, apāmārga twigs, sacrificial fuel, the five products of the cow, sacrificial porridge, and sesame seeds.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee into the sacrificial porridge (caru) for each [deity];
having performed the *sampāta* rite and recited the mantra eight thousand times, one should consume the porridge.
Minor afflictions caused by spirits and planetary influences, as well as other calamities, are destroyed;
anointing with its ash brings peace to demons, minor diseases, and the like. (37–58)
Having offered oblations of *apāmārga* sprouts as fuel-sticks, the *pañcagavya* sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter, and having strewn the mandala with black and red threads; || 37–59 ||
One should place water-pots at the primary joints, nine in the center and in the cardinal directions;
[these should contain] the water of the barks of the four milky trees, the nine gems, and gold.
Provided with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and encircled by garlands and strings of cloth,
they [the vessels] contain the Sudarśana [deities] invoked into them according to the sequence beginning with their seats.
Having performed the sacrifice with them, one should bathe the person to be consecrated (sādhya), or else, having tied it with that thread,
one should place it on the hand, the crest-lock, or the neck of the sādhya while reciting the mantra.
That ritual bathing destroys minor planetary afflictions and diseases and brings about prosperity;
during an excessively high Venus, one should offer a ring made of gold weighing one hundred mānas.
Having performed ten thousand oblations of clarified butter and having sprinkled [the substance] while reciting [the mantra], it should be worn again;
by wearing it, there shall be protection, and it bestows health and long life.
When the sun is situated in Aries or Sagittarius, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight falling on a Friday,
one should bury a white stone that has been consecrated with mantras during the Abhijit muhūrta.
Facing north, one should recite the mantra; thus, any offense against the sacred field (kṣetradroha) is destroyed.
When the sun is in Aries, at the end of ten days, during the half-rising of the sun, [one should perform the rite with] a ritual stake (kīla).
The practitioner should bury an image of Aśvinī for the pacification of offenses against the field and other such harms;
this should be done when the Sun rises in Gemini or Sagittarius, during the portion of Mars, and under the asterisms Puṣya or Anurādhā. (37–67)
Having dug at a *nairguṇḍikā* [shrine], that earth which is taken shall become one's own ground.
Or, the earth should be taken during the portion of Budha in the constellation of Āhirbudhnya, or during the rising of Leo (*siṃha*). (37–68)
That respective field becomes one's own.

For the sake of pacifying minor malevolent spells (*abhicāra*), one should offer oblations with *apāmārga* plants that have been sprinkled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and are fresh; furthermore, one should smear that [field] with its ashes. (37–69)
One should sprinkle [the area] with a decoction of the bark of the four milk-exuding trees mixed with cow's ghee;
for the sake of protection, one should likewise meditate upon oneself or another as situated in the center of a wheel.
One should mentally cause that which is situated within the belly of the discus, seized and being consumed by that fire, to whirl; then the possessing spirit (graha), having entered it, releases it.
Then, in a beautiful and pure place, one should draw a six-spoked wheel;
the spokes in the center are yellow, the rims are red, and the junctions of the spokes should be dark blue.
The rim is white, and outside it is the black-cornered circle of the earth;
in the center is the seed-syllable (tāra) and its name, while the six syllables of the mantra should be placed upon the spokes.
Having thus drawn two wheels in the south and the north,
one should fill the jar in the north with gold, flowers, and other offerings.
Having properly invoked Sudarśana in that [mandala] and performed worship, one should also recite the mantra;
having established the fire upon the southern wheel, one should invoke Sudarśana there.

Then, one should offer eight thousand oblations each of wood from the *mārgasamit* tree, clarified butter, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, rice grains, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (37–76)
Having offered [the oblation], one should cast the remainder of each substance into the pitcher along with its respective mantra;
then, having placed a ball of the half-prastha measure of cooked rice upon the mouth of the pitcher.
Having performed the *nīrājana* lustration for the object of the ritual (*sādhya*) with the water-pot (*kumbha*), one should place a jar in the eighth position from that [object].
To the south of the pot, one should install the fire along with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and other implements.
Oṃ, salutations to the hosts of Viṣṇu, who bring peace to all; may they accept this for the sake of peace, salutations!
Having placed the remnants of the oblation in a vessel made of *kṣīravṛkṣa* wood filled with cow-products, one should offer the *bali* in the ten directions. (37–79)
Having offered oblations into the fire within the wheels in the four directions, the minor obstacle perishes;
[this is accomplished] by means of apāmārga fuel-sticks measuring four finger-breadths and the sprinkling of cow-products.
By offering oblations on the nights of the five Viṣṇu constellations, there shall be the destruction of minor ailments and other afflictions.
[Likewise, one should avoid] those born under the Raudra, Prājāpatya, Pitrya, and Ārka constellations, as well as those born from the Jambū, Karṇī, and Vaṭa trees. (37–81)
A sacrificial post (yaṣṭi) should be placed at the boundary; at the rising of the moon, the ground shall become one's own.
The peg (kīla) should be two tālas long, belonging to the month of Āśvina, and joined with the ritual for naming the field.
When Mars is situated in Leo, one should dig during the Viṣṭi karana at the rising of that asterism.
When Mercury and the Moon occupy a single degree, earth should be taken; such ground will be beneficial for oneself. (37–83)
Having recited the Sudarśana mantra everywhere,
one should accomplish the rite using the heartwood of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Khadira trees.
One should fashion [images] of the Jambu, Āmalaka, Nimba, and Aśvattha trees;
as well as a bull, a horse, an elephant, a snake, a donkey, a lion, and a pair [of animals]. (37–85)
And on an auspicious day (viṣṭi), one should dig a wheel in those directions all around the village and so forth;
having consecrated it with the Sudarśana mantra, it shall provide protection from all [harm].
On the fourth, eighth, and eleventh days of the bright fortnight,
on festival days, during the shooting of arrows, and when the Viṣṭi yoga occurs, one should perform [the rite] for the sages and gods in the eight directions.
On the third, seventh, and tenth days of the dark fortnight, as well as on the day of Bhūti (the fourteenth),
the rising of the quarters is recorded to occur at the watches corresponding to the seasons, the Vedas, the serpents, and the moon.

Again, the sequence is man, elephant, king, and woman; starting from the mountain (naga), the *viṣṭi* hour of that time occurs, and these [periods] are to be avoided in order starting from the bright fortnight (śukla).
The banyan, the kiṃśuka, the bamboo, the aśvattha tree, the vikaṅkata, the ghātakī, the snuhi, and the karṇī—these are the trees of the quarters in successive order. (37–90)
One should dig these [holes] in succession at the rising of Viṣṭi in their respective directions, surrounding them all around;
by recollecting Viṣṭi while facing away, the protection of the crops will be accomplished. || 37-91 ||
The lion, the tiger, the boar, the donkey, the bull, and the dog—these are the *karaṇas*; among them, the dog is called *viṣṭi*. (37-92)
And the visualization for Viṣṭi:
she has the form of a water-laden cloud; her thick legs are joined together;
she has tawny eyes and hair; and she possesses a discus-like set of tusks and a prominent nose.
Burning the entire world here with masses of fire issuing from the cavity of her mouth, the Viṣṭi [Yoga] swiftly approaches. || 37-93 ||

Now, the Sudarśana Yantra: In the center of the hexagon is the seed-syllable *tāra* (om) together with the name of the practitioner and the mantra-syllables; then, at the joints [of the corners] are the six limbs (*aṅga*).
Outside, it is enriched with the vowels on the filaments of an eight-petaled lotus; then follows a sixteen-petaled lotus with the eight-syllable mantra.

In its center, it has a pericarp formed by the pair of letters beginning with *ta* (*ta* and *tha*); on the petals are the twelve-syllable armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*) with a pair of *ṭha*s.

On the outside, it is called "interwoven" (*upavidarbhitākhya*) with *Śiva* (the letter *ha*) accompanied by the nasal bindu; it is encircled three times by the noose (*pāśa*) and likewise by the goad (*aṅkuśa*).

Then, having drawn the circle of the earth externally according to the ritual rules on birch bark, or on a golden plate, white cloth, or similar material, and having offered oblations and performed worship, that [circle] should be made into a pill with gold; when worn, it brings about protection and removes all fears.
In the center of the square, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and outside of that, six spokes;
the letters of the mantra should be placed in the six [spokes], and the limbs (*aṅga*) in the joints in due order.
Having performed worship with a water-pot containing clarified butter, one removes asthma and fever by diligently applying five parts each of *bilva* and lotus separately.
Having burned that [substance] consecrated with mantras, the resulting ash removes minor diseases and planetary afflictions.
