[One should also employ] the four milks, the bark [of the four trees], Brāhmī, Lakṣmī, sandalwood, and gorocanā.
Surasā, bilva, dūrvā, kuśa, apāmārga, rājika, guggulu, padmaka, kuṣṭha, kānta, excellent saffron, and niśā. (37–100)
Having mixed it with cow dung and combined it with other products of the cow, one should burn it in the fire with the Sudarśana mantra; that ash is then consecrated by this mantra.
The mantra of Mahāsudarśana— which destroys minor ailments, wards off untimely death, and bestows supreme fortune and health— is now written down exactly as it stands.
(248) It is because of the observation that its extraction or transposition should not be performed.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Mahāsudarśana, the Great King of the Wheel! Protect me! Destroy my enemies! Tear them apart! Rend them! Shatter them! Blaze! Set them ablaze! O you of fierce appearance, whose crest is ignited by hundreds of thousands of rays, O terrible one, whose nature is to consume the wicked! Burn! Cook! Lick! Cast down! Roast! Terrify! Grind to dust the extremely wicked persons and their magical mechanisms! Shatter the eighteen-fold collection of mantras employed by others! Seize the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) of others! Annihilate the mantras of others! Rara! O you who delight in eating the flesh, fat, and blood of the middle [of beings]! O crusher of the armies of the sharp three-day [demons] and the lords of gods and asuras! O you with hands raised holding the conch, discus, and bow! O Nara-Nārāyaṇa! O supreme weapon! Scrub! Rub! Mix! Pierce! Crush! Grind! Subdue! Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, kūśmāṇḍas, śakunis, yuvatis, vināyakas, fevers, all *lūtā* [skin diseases], poisons, and *viṣkambhakas*—seize them! Kill them! Lalaghu! O Trivikrama! O powerful one! O ancient one! O Viṣvaksena! With your excellent hand, crush and break the planets! Enter them! Drag them forth! Remember the armor of Viṣṇu! Ṭhaṭha! This is the seed-syllable of the weapon (*astrabīja*). Ṭhaṭha to the Discus of the Face—this is the heart. Ṭhaṭha to the Discus of Pervasion—this is the head. Ṭhaṭha to the Discus of Excellence—this is the crest-lock. Ṭhaṭha to the Discus of Union—this is the armor. Ṭhaṭha to the Great Discus—this is the weapon.
Ahi-budhnya is its seer; Dhṛti is its metre; and the Deity is its presiding divinity. || 37-103 ||

Mahāviṣṇu has stated that this [mantra], which requires a preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of one thousand and eight recitations, is perfected by the mere reading [of the text] once it has been learned from the mouth of the Guru. (37-104)
Then, having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should face the south in a cremation ground or at a crossroads.
If one recites the mantra at midnight, one shall obtain whatever is desired;
however, one who wishes to subdue enemies should offer oblations of mustard seeds at night.
By performing eight hundred oblations of sesame seeds at the three junctions of the day, servants such as *rākṣasas*, *bhūtas*, and others appear; they accomplish whatever is desired.
Thus is the ritual procedure uttered by the mind of Sudarśana, which accomplishes all goals for those who possess devotion to Hari;
by means of this, untimely deaths, calamities, and afflictions caused by minor diseases and malevolent spirits are brought to dissolution through the performance of recitation and other rites.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the Saudarśana, in the Mantra-pāda of the Siddhāntasāra, which is the Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati. || 37 ||
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter. Next,
for the sake of accomplishing all goals, I shall describe the Trailokyamohana mantra, along with its ritual procedures, meditations, ablutions, worship, and offerings.
*Tāraṃ*, *hṛt*, *puru* and the word *śabda*, with *sadantaḥ*, *ṣoyuga*, *ṣaḍhī*, *sānantaḥ*, the two *mahākālau*, the word *pratirūpa*, and *dharām*. (38-2)

O abode of Lakṣmī, you who cause the agitation of the entire world! You who rend the hearts of all women! You who madden the minds of the three worlds, heat, inflame, dry up, slay, paralyze, bewilder, liquefy, and attract the hearts of the beautiful women among gods, demons, and humans; O bestower of supreme bliss and good fortune, O granter of all desires, kill [Name] with the discus, the mace, and the sword; pierce all with the noose, drag them with the goad, strike, hasten—why do you stand still? Let my desire be accomplished until then! *Huṃ Phaṭ!* Homage to the one whose form is incomparable to the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), O abode of Lakṣmī! Homage to the heart! Homage to the head, O agitator of the entire world, O renter of the hearts of all women! *Ṭhaṭha!* Homage to the crest-lock, O maddener of the minds of the three worlds! *Vaṣaṭ!* Heat, inflame, dry up, slay, paralyze, liquefy, and attract the hearts of the beautiful women among gods, demons, and humans! Homage to the armor! *Hum!* O bestower of supreme bliss and all good fortune, O granter of all desires, kill [Name] with the discus, the mace, and the sword; pierce all with the noose, drag them with the goad! Homage to the weapon! *Phaṭ!* Hasten—why do you stand still? Let my desire be accomplished until then! *Huṃ Phaṭ!* Homage to the two eyes! *Vauṣaṭ!*
In this manner, there are six limbs ending with the eyes:

"Obeisance to the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, O Hṛṣīkeśa of incomparable form, O Manmatha, you who draw the hearts of all women, come! Obeisance! This is the mantra for the pervasion (vyāpaka), and it is also the mantra for invocation (āvāhana).
Vatsa is its sage (ṛṣi), though some say it is Kāma. (38–3)
The desire for supreme excellence arises, and Hṛṣīkeśa is the presiding deity;
having received the mantra from the teacher, one performs the daily rites after bathing. (38-4)
Having worshipped Viṣṇu, one should mutter the mantra fifty thousand times while standing in water reaching the navel, with handfuls of water held in cupped palms. (38–5)
The practitioner of mantras should sprinkle himself on his own head a thousand times with the recited mantras;
thereafter, he should offer milk-rice and ghee into the Vaiṣṇava fire.
One should offer twelve oblations each of curd, milk, and white rice;
and for each of the limb-mantras, one hundred oblations of *palāśa* wood fuel. (38.7)
One thousand white unbroken rice grains mixed with sesame seeds and sprinkled with ghee;
then flowers and fruits smeared with the three sweets (trimadhura). || 38-8 ||
One should offer curds as the *brahmasamidh* oblations, one hundred each;
having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should then honor and feed the Brahmins according to one's ability. (38–39)
Then this mantra is perfected through meditation, worship, oblations, and so forth.
And as for the meditation:
[one should meditate upon] Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, Śeṣa, and the Earth upon the seat (pīṭha). (38–10)
One should place the principles beginning with *dharma* within the circles of the lotus-stalk, the lotus, the sun, the moon, and fire;
the petals and other parts [of the lotus] represent the pervasion of the three *guṇas*, and the three [lotuses] beginning with the *ātman* are in the pericarp.
Upon this lotus is [the Lord] mounted on Garuḍa, his body red as vermilion, with eight arms and noble limbs, tender and with a smiling face. (38-12)
Beautiful in every limb, filled with the radiance and charm of youth, his copper-hued eyes were rolling with intoxication, and he was overwhelmed by the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa). || 38-13 ||
Adorned with divine garlands, garments, and unguents, as well as ornaments such as a crown;
his chest marked by the Kaustubha jewel and his breast bearing the Śrīvatsa sign.
Holding in his arms, in successive order, the conch, the discus, the Śārṅga bow with its arrow, the sword, the mace, as well as the club, the goad, and the noose.
Lakṣmī, whose beautiful thighs rest [upon him], golden-hued and adorned with a crown, earrings, necklaces, and other ornaments, holding a lotus in her left hand. || 38-16 ||
Embracing the Lord with her right hand, she was overwhelmed by desire;
on his chest were the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and the garland known as Vanamālā. (38.17)

One should worship the yellow garment and other items, as well as the crown and the crocodile-shaped earrings, with their respective names preceded by the *tārā* (the syllable Om); one should likewise worship the necklaces and other ornaments. (38–18)

"O Mahāsudarśana, King of Wheels, terrifier of all the wicked! Cut! Strike! Tear asunder! Devour the enemies! Swallow! Eat the spirits! Terrify them! Hūṃ Phaṭ!"—with these words, one should worship the wheel. "To Pāñcajanya, the water-dweller, ṭhaṭha!"

Salutation to the sword Nandaka; *ṭhaṭha* to the arrow. We know the host of beings, we meditate upon the fourfold [host]; may that Brahman impel us; *ṭhaṭha*. Strike with the club of Saṃvartaka! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. Bind with the noose and draw [them] near! *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. O goad, pull and threaten! *ṭhaṭha*.
Having thus worshipped the eight weapons: *oṃ* to the King of Birds, *ṭhaṭha*.
With this [mantra] one should worship Garuḍa;
then, having bathed according to the rules in the manner prescribed for the daily rites (nityaka). || 38-19 ||
Having gone to the door of the sacrificial hall, the wise one, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
should worship the Gaṇas seated upon their pedestals outside the door.
Salutations to Vainateya and all the other attendants of Viṣṇu.
Between the eastern door and the pedestal, one should worship Kṣetreśa by his own name, as well as Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, who are white and black respectively and possess four arms. (38–21)
One should worship [the two deities] holding conchs, thunderbolts, and maces, with hands that inspire wonder;
and in the center, Gaṅgā and Yamunā; and the two treasures (nidhi) on the upper sides of the door.
Then one should worship Śaṅkha and Padma, who are white and red respectively and flow with abundant wealth, situated in the middle of the upper Udumbara, as well as Dvāralakṣmī.
"Oṃ, salutation to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow together with his arrow.

Having discharged the Nārāca weapon, having expelled the obstacles, and having established a protective enclosure (prākāra) by means of the weapon-mantra, he sits composed upon his own seat, restrained in speech. (38.24)
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as well as the triad beginning with drying (śoṣaṇa),
and having remembered the Guru, one should perform the purification of the hands three times with the Astra-mantra.
Having wiped [the body] once with the root mantra, one should place [the mantras] upon the limbs;
then, from the thumb to the little finger, and finally upon the two palms for the eyes.
Having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa) upon the body with the root mantra, one should then sequentially assign the six limbs.
Then, having meditated upon oneself as Pradyumna—red in color and clad in red garments and so forth—[one should proceed].

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings that [deity] who bears the conch and discus and carries the Śārṅga bow, the Kāma-arrow, and the quiver, and then having remembered him in the lotus of the heart, (38-28).
One should worship with the mind that supreme, indescribable light which is bliss;
and having filled the vessel, which has been cleansed with the Astra-mantra, with the Arghya water by means of the Hṛdaya-mantra.

One should place the seed-syllable of Smara (Kāma) therein and worship it with flowers and other offerings. With this *smaragāyatrī*: "We know Manmatha; we meditate on Kāmadeva; may that Gandharva inspire us," one should purify the ritual substances by touching them while reciting this mantra. (38–39)
The cow [of speech] has been rendered immortal; the arghya water is protected by the *cakramudrā*.
Having sprinkled one's own head with those waters, as well as the materials for worship and the ground, [one should proceed]. (38–39)
Starting from the base of Pātāla, one should meditate upon the Power known as Ādhāra,
who has four arms and whose palms are joined in the gesture of reverence, holding a conch and a discus.
Below the netherworlds (pātālas) are Kūrma, who is red, and Śeṣa, who is white;
both have their limbs adorned, stand with palms joined in reverence, and hold a discus and a plow.
Or [one may visualize her] holding a plow and a mace;
she has the luster of a blue lotus, her limbs are adorned, and she holds a blue lotus in her hand.
Then [one visualizes] the golden lion-throne and the [deities] Dharma and the others, white in form.
One should visualize non-virtue and the other [afflictions] as black in color in the center, with the qualities such as sattva and so forth;
and a white lotus at its root, bulb, and stalk, respectively. (38–39)

Māyā, Vidyā, and the principle of Kalā, possessing the luster of dark blue, white, and yellow; the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire; and the [mantras] beginning with Tāra (Oṃ), one's own name, and ending with Namaḥ. (38–39)
One should worship, as it were: *Oṃ paramasubhaga saubhāgyakara apratirūpa keśava smara huṃ phaṭ trailokyamohanāsanāya namaḥ*.
From the northwest corner to the northeast, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī; in the lineage of gurus, one should worship these, as well as Nārada and Nalakūbara. (38–39)
One should worship the Guru, the Supreme Self-Guru (Parātmaka-guru), and likewise the Supreme Preceptor (Parameṣṭhi-guru),
as well as the two-armed ancient Siddhas who are established in meditation.

Then, having placed perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and flowers within the center of the lotus, with hands joined in a handful of flowers and recollecting the root mantra, [one should draw the deity] from the lotus of the navel. (38–39)
Having drawn up that supreme light and led it from there to the heart-lotus,
one should lead that which consists solely of bliss and knowledge upward from the lotus of the heart.
Then, having led the *bindu* from the throat and the middle of the eyebrows to the *dvādaśānta*,
and having joined it with the handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*) by way of the path of the *bindu*.
One should place [the deity] either upon an image situated on a yoga-pīṭha, or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in clarified butter;
having formed the two mudrās of the lotus and the goad, one should bring [the deity] face-to-face.
One should effect the presence and the confinement of the deity through the mudrās known as the mace and the discus, employing the appropriate prayers, skillful means, and devotion. (38–43)
Having performed the pervasive placement with the root mantra, one should display these mudrās:
the supreme [mudrā] formed by the right hand turned upward with the thumb extended.
Having grasped the thumb with the fist, one should extend the four fingers beginning with the index finger of the left hand, joined with the supreme index finger.
One should form the conch mudrā; this is considered pleasing to Hari.
Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers extended... [38-46]
With the two little fingers placed on the left and right thumbs respectively in reverse order,
this *cakramudrā* shall be formed, which brings delight to the wielder of the discus weapon.
With the hands facing each other and the fingers mutually interlaced, extend the two middle fingers and join them; this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā*.
Having bound the pair of the little fingers and ring fingers with the thumbs and bent them [inward],
while leaving the pair of the index fingers and middle fingers free, it is known as the *khaḍga* (sword) mudrā.
Having pressed the two little fingers and ring fingers together with the thumb, the tips of the middle fingers should overlap the tips of the index fingers.
The tip of the extended left hand is gradually pressed by the elbow of the other [right] hand, which is itself held over the [left] forearm. (38–51)
Having touched the tip [of the bow] with the tips of the thumb and the index finger, and then extending them,
this becomes the Śārṅga-mudrā, which brings favor to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The mudrā known as the *musala* is considered to be formed by joining the fists of both the left and right arms, with the thumbs tucked inside and extended outward. (38–53)
Having placed the tip of the index finger of the left fist upon the tip of the thumb,
one should touch it with the tip of the index finger released from the other fist.
The base of the left thumb is declared to be this noose mudrā;
[one should hold] the index finger of the left fist extended by the five-fingered [hand]. (38–55)
Having grasped its index finger with another hand in the form of a fist and having bent its tip,
there shall be the mudrā in the form of a goad (aṅkuśa).
Having pressed the middle and ring fingers with the middle and thumb [fingers],
one should place the index finger upon the pair at the base of the little fingers.
This is known by the name Śrīvatsamudrā; it brings auspiciousness to one who bears the Śrīvatsa mark.
It is formed by the little finger of the left hand turned downwards. (38–58)
Having bound the three fingers—the right thumb, middle finger, and ring finger—in sequence with the ring finger, the other index finger, and the little finger, [respectively]. (38–59)
Having positioned the left index finger with its tip pointing upward and joined [to the thumb],
one should place the right index finger at the base of the fingers of the left hand, and the left middle finger [at the base] of the right middle finger.

This mudrā, representing the Kaustubha gem, is formed by placing the two hands very closely together; starting from the throat, the tips of the index fingers are pressed down by the thumbs of both hands. (38–61)
Touching the feet, this mudrā is known as the *vanamālā*;
it is formed by turning the two hands over and interlacing the fingers with one another. (38–62)
The two index fingers are closely joined and extended, with the pair of thumbs hanging down; the middle and ring fingers are curved, forming both wings. || 38-63 ||
This mudrā of the King of Birds is the destroyer of adversaries;
it is said that the previously mentioned *yonimudrā* itself is called the *kāmamudrā*. (38–64)
Having placed the two hands, with fingers extended from the clenched fists, upon one's own head, the *trailokyamohinī* mudrā is formed by means of the tips of the thumbs. (38.65)

One should worship the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapons— having the forms of deities— in sequence upon the tips of the filaments starting from the east and so forth, and in the corners starting from the southeast and so forth.
From the limbs of the gods, his own limbs emerged like lamps from other lamps:
Lakṣmī, Vāṇī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, and Śāntivibhūṣitā. || 38-67 ||
One should worship these [deities] at the tips of the petals starting from the east: Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi;
[the others are] yellow and red, fair-complexioned, dark-blue, and white with the luster of the moon.
Lotus-colored and tawny, those goddesses hold chowries and lotuses in their hands;
outside of that, in the directions starting from the east, they possess white, red, and ruddy radiance.
And [one should place] Śyāma, along with the conch, arrow, mace, and club, each topped with its own weapon;
in the corners, those resembling yellow, sky-blue, white, and black, respectively. (38–70)
Having meditated upon the Śārṅga bow, the goad, and the noose, one should worship them by their respective names;
in the outer enclosure, one should worship those stationed in their own directions, together with their weapons and vehicles.
One should worship the ten [deities] beginning with Śakra, each joined with their own retinues. Then, in the outer enclosure thereof—
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—
these lords of hosts numbering in the tens of millions, holding swords and shields in their hands.
One should worship those adorned with crowns and other ornaments, wearing divine garlands and garments;
they have tawny beards and hair-tips, are dark-complexioned, and possess four arms. (38–74)
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena, who holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands and makes the threatening gesture with his index finger at the tip of his nose,
one should then worship the Lord.
Having offered the *arghya* on the head with the words "Om, I prepare the *arghya*," one should likewise offer the *pādya* at the feet, and similarly the water for sipping (*ācamana*) and so forth.
One should worship him with the sixteen services specified beginning with *arghya*, or, if one has the means, with the thirty-two services previously mentioned. (38.77)

Having adorned [the deity] with flowers and garlands using the words of the root mantra beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, one should offer [worship] preceded by *tāra* with the formula: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī. (38–78)
Thus, one should worship Lakṣmī as she sits upon the lap of the Lord,
according to one's ability, ending with the offering of food (naivedya), or the ritual oblation (bali), or even the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having worshipped everywhere with the *smara-gāyatrī* using the aforementioned offerings,
one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity while holding water in the hollow of the palms.
Having prepared offerings of incense and flowers, and having knelt upon the ground,
one should place the fruit of the recitation and other rites into the right hand of the deity.
Having thus performed the daily worship, one should feed Brahmins according to one's ability;
and having eaten oneself with the remnants, the man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty.
Hṛṣīkeśa himself is directly called Puruṣottama;
his seed-syllable of love (mānmathabīja) is remembered as the single-syllabled mantra. || 38-83 ||
Then follows the seed-syllable of Smara (the letter *ka*), then space (*ha*), conjoined with the seventh vowel (*ū*);
then Śveta (the letter *sa*) joined with the left eye (*ī*), and Brahmā (the letter *la*) accompanied by Rudra (the letter *ra*) and the vowel (*u*). (38–84)
Dīrgha and Baka are the heart; the mantra is proclaimed to consist of eight syllables.
This is the Trailokyamohana, whose sādhana and other details have been described previously. (38–85)
For one who recites the limbs [of the mantra] joined with the long vowels and the seed-syllable of Smara, accompanied by the ritual meters (jātis),
all desires will be fulfilled almost immediately.
*Tāraṃ*, *hṛt*, *sākṣi*, and *kumbha*; then *śveta* and *umāpati*; then *soṣṭha*, *ambhaḥ*, *karṇaga*, *śukla*, *rakta*, *pārśva*, and then *aṣaḍhī*.
Soṣṭha, Tvak, Mahākāla, Kha, Dīrgha, Chagalaṇḍaka, Dīrgha, Pinākī, and Vālī—ending with Svāhā, this is the eighteen-syllable mantra. (38–88)
The mantra is indeed without limbs or enclosures and is designated as the Lord of Food;
its seer is Gautama, its meter is Dhṛti, and its deity is Viṣṇu. (38.89)
It pacifies poverty and bestows nourishment, fortune, good luck, and happiness. (38-90)
And the meditation:
[He is] white as the milk-ocean, the moon, a lotus stalk, or a *kunda* flower; his face is like the orb of the moon;
with his two hands he holds a goblet filled with curd-rice and a jar full of nectar.
Wearing a crown and adorned with various necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments, bearing the Kaustubha gem,
the Lord of Food should be meditated upon as Vāmana, who has a serene countenance and wears yellow garments.

Recalling [the deity] as bestowing food, drink, and other necessities upon the practitioner, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). || 38-92 ||
In this Kali age, one should offer curd-rice with ghee one thousand and eight times; for in this age, recitation and fire-offerings are four times more efficacious.
One whose mantra has been perfected thereby obtains abundant food and great prosperity;
by offering oblations of rice, *śāli* paddy, and other grains, one becomes rich in food and prosperous.
By means of *maṇḍaka* cakes made from the seeds of the *śatapuṣpā*, calamity is destroyed;
likewise, the fear of a foreign army, the king, enemies, thieves, and so forth [are averted]. (38–95)
Whatever fear of poverty there may be, as well as the fear of minor ailments, one will certainly pacify them by performing a fire sacrifice with the seeds of *śatapuṣpa*. (38–96)

Whether on a difficult path, on uneven terrain, when fear has arisen, or likewise during a planetary affliction, by remembering the deity and reciting the mantra, one is liberated from poverty. (38–97)

Having meditated upon oneself or another as having the form of one who strides across the three worlds and protects from great fear, one should recite the mantra for the pacification of those respective [obstacles]. (38–98)
On a wall or even on a cloth, one who is capable should worship Hari with rice mixed with ghee,
or with ghee and rice, or with rice and curd mixed with ghee.
For one who performs the daily fire-oblation according to their ability, there is unsurpassed prosperity.
Whatever [object] one may have in mind while offering curd-rice mixed with clarified butter, [that very thing shall be attained]. (38.100)
"For this devotee, all that [is desired] surely comes to pass both in this world and in the next.

Having thus reflected in many ways upon the extensive ritual procedure for the Trailokyamohana-mantra, which is established in numerous tantras, I have here sung it in summary for the benefit of practitioners, as seen in the *Kalpa* of Hari, the Lord of Food. (38-101½)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, the Trailokyamohana-Vāmana-Mantra-paṭala, in the Mantra-pāda of the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 38.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.
It has been previously demonstrated in the *Vastunirdeśapaṭala* that [this applies] to those afflicted by poisons, planetary influences, and diseases; therefore, it is now being explained. (39-1)
Having there paid homage to his guru and to the Nāgas headed by Ananta, he condensed [the teachings] from the treatises on poisons out of a desire for the welfare of the world. (39-2)
The remedy for that [poison] is demonstrated by means of mantras, meditations, medicinal herbs, and so forth;
[it applies to] hooded snakes (phaṇin), snouted snakes (ghoṇasa), striped snakes (rājila), and likewise intermediate species (vyantara). (39-3)
Those hooded serpents are of two kinds: celestial and terrestrial;
furthermore, they are all fourfold, consisting of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (39–4)
Those divine sons of Kadrū, numbering a thousand, capable of assuming any form at will, were adorned with crowns, necklaces, armlets, tiaras, and other ornaments. (39–5)
All the Nāgas of great power were adorned with divine garlands, garments, and unguents;
among them, eight were preeminent: Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and the others.
Then Kārkoṭaka, Padma, the one named Mahāpadma,
Śaṅkhapāla, and Gulika are the protectors of the days beginning with Sunday.
The first half of Saturday has Śaṅkhapāla as its presiding deity;
Gulika is the protector of the latter half, and they are the ones who emerge from that [time]. (39–8)
Those nāgas who are the thousand sons of Kadrū, possessed of great coils—some dwelling in Pātāla, and others inhabiting the earth, the oceans, and the mountains. || 39-9 ||
Some dwell in Bhuvaḥ and Svar, while others have their abodes wherever they desire;
they are white, red, yellow, and black, corresponding to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
Some [serpents] have a thousand hoods; others are endowed with seven hundred and eight, six hundred, five hundred, three hundred, two hundred, one hundred, or five hoods. (39.11)
The number of others born in their lineage is not known;
those born in that lineage in succession were devoid of divine power. (39-12)
Those serpents, known as the single-hooded ones, dwell here and there;
by the power of their past karma, they too bite humans and other beings. (39.13)
Either due to the provocation of deities, or from the practice of cruel and evil deeds, or even for the sake of protecting their own abodes, they bite out of fear of being overcome. (39.14)
The ghoṇasas, rājilas, and others are produced through mutual cross-breeding;
for the female serpent indeed conceives her offspring during the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha.
In either the month of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa, she lays more than twenty eggs, up to forty, which produce various kinds [of offspring]. (39-16)
For after seven days, afflicted by hunger, she indeed eats them herself;
since she does not eat more than one, two, or three eggs.
Then, when seven days have passed, serpents are born from it;
there is a female egg marked with long stripes and a male egg with a golden luster. (39.18)
Likewise, a cluster resembling the Śirīṣa flower, whether white or even black, becomes split apart within ten days, yet they remain endowed with consciousness. (39-19)
The fangs appear after twenty-one days, and the movement [of the poison] after forty days;
having beheld the sun, they become intensely virulent with poison.
In six months, those born from scorpions, which are fierce and long, cast off their skins; whereas those born from archers (sagittarius) are short and peaceful. (39.21)
The Brāhmaṇas, who possess the fragrance of sacrificial offerings, dwell at the confluence of rivers and the like, on mountains, in gardens, in temples of the gods, and among lotus ponds.
O King, [the scent] of the *ketakī* flower is fragrant at the courtyards, ramparts, and so forth of houses, as well as in cow-pens, anthills, forests, fields, granaries, and homes. (39.23)
The Vaiśya has the fragrance of guggulu, while the Śūdra does not dwell in one place;
the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes [dwell] in the forenoon, midday, afternoon, and at night. (39.24)
The Brāhmaṇa king eats wind, leaves, fruits, and milk; the merchant eats mice; the Śūdra eats frogs; and the one who has attained everything eats all things. (39.25)
If he is not killed by a peacock, a hawk, a mongoose, a vulture, a cat, a cow, a donkey, a man, fire, lightning, or a wild beast, he shall live for a long time. (39.26)
The scales of the serpent are indeed as numerous as the hairs on a cow's body and are covered with skin;
for this reason, he does not move by means of feet. (39.27)
The blue lotus, the water-lily, the conch, the svastika, the utpala, and the bindu—these are indeed the marks upon the hoods, or on the head and feet, of serpents. (39.28)
There were pythons of various shapes and colors, long and variegated;
and there were striped snakes whose bodies were marked with streaks running both crosswise and upward.
One should determine the wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) [as the dominant humors], as well as the three types of snakes beginning with the hooded (darvīkara);
having understood the shape of the fangs, the nature of the bite, the cause, the movement and force [of the venom], the location, the vital spots (marman),
the messenger, the speech, the stars and other omens, and the lunar days (tithis), one may then decide whether or not to administer medical treatment.
The serpents have two hundred teeth, and they also have forty [fangs]. || 39-31 ||
The nine teeth are indeed poisonous; from being bitten by them, the *gara* poison arises.
They are Karālī, Makarī, Dhūmrā, Kālarātri, and Kapālinī. (39–42)
Kālī, Ugrā, Yamanī, and Yamadūtī have been described;
these wind-eaters bite with their few mentioned teeth. (39–33)
If a bite occurs during Āśleṣā or Gulika, there is no remedy;
likewise for one who is wounded by weapons, thorns, insects, and the like when Gulika is rising. (39–40)
Even he goes to the realm of Vaivasvata; how much more so one bitten by a snake?
During the junctions of day and night, there are great venomous male snakes and others.
The bite is to be known as fourfold: bitten, pierced, torn, and lacerated;
in the case of the bitten, a single wound is perceived. (39–36)
If two wounds are pierced, it is called *viddha*; if there are many, it is *khaṇḍita*; and if there are no wounds, it is *avalupta*. Now the causes of the bites are described. (39–37)
Fear, hunger, intoxication, oppression, guarding one's position, the command of a deity, enmity, and the bite of time—these are its eightfold forms. (39–38)
If there is a single curved wound caused by a frightened snake, no poison is found therein; however, this is not the case when there are two bites. (39)
Straight and very slight poison should be known as easily curable;
one should treat that which is smeared with saliva, located in the middle of the bite, and produced by a hungry [snake]. (39–40)
That [wound] should be known as difficult to treat; some say it is incurable when there is one or many wounds, or when the blood is profuse. (39–41)
For that [injury] born of pride is indeed incurable, or at best only barely curable;
the wounds of the station-guard are accompanied by blood, flesh, and saliva. (39–42)
"Wherever [the marks] are seen, there the goal is achieved"—this is the opinion of Vācaspati.
One should avoid a straight pair of bites and a single curved one that causes enmity. (39–43)
A wound with three openings or accompanied by blood is incurable when impelled by time;
likewise, horripilation, burning sensations, perspiration, salivation, and trembling of the limbs [indicate the same]. (39–44)
One should abandon that person bitten by Kāla, who suffers from loss of memory, delusion, and helplessness;
at the site of the bite, there is a black circle and an abundant flow of blood. (39–45)
The parting of the teeth and lips is a sign of one bitten by Kāla;
one whose eyes are bloodshot will see the moon, fire, and sun as lacking luster. (39–46)
One who is cast into water and floats does not see his own reflection; when sprinkled with water, there is no bristling of body hair, and upon being cut, there is no blood. (39–47)
If, upon being struck with a cane or similar object, no mark is seen on him, or if his mouth is wide open, he has indeed been bitten by Kāla and is dead. || 39-48 ||
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the bodily constituents (dhātus). The transition from one constituent to another is declared to be the onset of the poison's force (viṣavega).
If the fever rises within one hundred *mātrās* or half of that time, it is curable; if it rises more quickly, it is incurable. Now, the signs of the fever's onset (*vega*) are described. (39–50)
Horripilation, perspiration, dryness, discoloration, trembling, hiccup, throat constriction, sleepiness, and likewise death. (39–51)
Thus are the nine stages [of the poison].

Furthermore, the anus, the private parts, the abdomen, the palate, the ears, the breasts, the eyes, the head, the throat, the temples, the nose, the navel, the armpits, the feet, the hands, and the shanks—these are the locations of a bite that are considered censurable. (39–52)

Temples, the Aśvattha, the Vaṭa, and the Jambū trees; the Śleṣmātaka, the Tintriṇī, the Vetra, and the bamboo; cremation grounds, dried-up wells, ruined wells, crossroads, and sacred shrines (caityas)—these are also inauspicious. (39–53)
Thus end the undesirable signs.

A messenger with a serene face, flowers and other offerings in hand, with a full-bodied frame and clad in white garments and the like, is indeed desirable; whereas one whose body is smeared with oil, deformed, or diseased is likewise undesirable. (39–54)

One who carries wood and the like, or even thorns, a firebrand, or a staff; one who is soiled, or has a cloth around his neck and a rope in his hand—such a messenger is indeed contemptible, especially if his hair is disheveled. (55)
Whether he be a student, one bearing a sectarian mark, or a woman, a messenger who speaks from afar or says that a snake was bitten first is censured. (39–56)
Having placed the eight-syllable mantra of Vārada on the left palm, one should contemplate it;
when a *ketaka* flower is smelled, there will be a ladle, and when a *pāṭala* flower, a circle. (39–57)

The *rājila* [snake] is a *vyantara* spirit in the scent of jasmine (*mallikā*), and in the *karavīra* [flower], it remains in its former state; when the hand [is touched], one should say that there is no poison. (39–58)
He lives by means of the syllables of Varuṇa and Indra, such as those used in the speech of messengers;
however, he shall not exist if they are born from Vāyu and Agni, and these are written down in their proper order.
i, ī, ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, aḥ, la, ña, ṇa, na, ma are born from Mahendra;
a, ca, cha, ja, ka, la (or va), kha, kṣa, jha, ṣa, bha, and śa are indeed born from Varuṇa.
E, Ai, O, and Auḥ; the Hayavān and the Mārutas; Ā, Ū, Ṛ, and Ṝ; Aughata, Pā (or Ta), Taradasa, and Kha—the [letters] born of Fire. (39–61)
Thus ends the section on the regulation of syllables in the messenger's speech.

(p. 263) If bitten on the days of Rudra, Agni, Sarpa, Aja, Maghā, Mūla, Pūrvā, or Viśākhā; on Tuesday, Saturday, or Sunday; or on the sixth, ninth, fifteenth, first, or fourteenth lunar day—one who is bitten is as good as dead. (39–62)
Auspicious signs well-known in this world lead to success; likewise, omens announce complete accomplishment through their auspicious utterances. (39.63)
When the messenger has departed toward the eastern direction and so forth, the serpent (phaṇī) is in the corners;
the ringed snake (maṇḍalī), the water-snake (rājila), and the intermediate being (vyantara) follow in order from the directions, the intermediate directions, and the middle points. (39–64)

Whether by the command of a minister or even on his own initiative, whatever limb a messenger may touch, if there is a discrepancy regarding a bite on that spot, it shall not be a snake, nor is there any poison present. (39.65)
At the time of the messenger's arrival, on whichever side the wind blows, the bite shall occur on that side; in that case, the messenger's arrival is auspicious. (39–66)
If the auspicious naming of the snake's bite occurs first, death follows;
however, in the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa), it is nectar for men in the southern direction, whereas elsewhere it is indeed poison.
For women, it is the reverse; likewise, on the bright fortnight, it is reversed. Just as a bite on the portion of nectar (sudhābhāga) is curable, elsewhere it would result in death.
When the messenger's speech is divided into three parts, death occurs with three syllables;
if there is one syllable in excess, it is favorable, and if there are two syllables in excess, there is certainly no poison.
Likewise, the rising, transits, and aspects of auspicious planets bestow good fortune;
conversely, the aspects of malefic planets at the moment of the messenger's arrival bring inauspiciousness. (39–70)
Having first examined the omens, the physician should proceed to treat [the patient];
[he should avoid] jackals, tigers, mongooses, cakora birds, cobras, and young pigs. (39-71)
The sight of jars full of grain on the right is auspicious;
likewise, birds, wild animals, and even croakers on the left are auspicious. (39-72)
A blue jay flying from right to left and a crow from left to right during travel bestow auspiciousness; likewise, the cawing of a crow from the left is favorable. (39-73)
At the time of entering, the cry of a female mongoose from the right side is auspicious;
likewise, the movement of a crow or a blue jay toward the right at the time of entry bestows good fortune.
Standing on both sides of the path, two birds uttered auspicious cries; with their mouths turned toward each other, they called out before him at the place named Torana. (39.75)
One should know that the yawning of dogs in front [of one] is extremely auspicious;
likewise, it is favorable if a crow goes away after taking whatever food is in its mouth. (39.76)

A dog, another [animal], or a bird is auspicious; the sight of meat and wine is auspicious; a maiden, a very auspicious woman, a courtesan, a flower, a conch, and likewise unbroken rice grains [are auspicious]. (39.77)
A bow made of powder and all those that are auspicious are favorable when they come toward one;
likewise, striking with the left foot is recommended, provided it does not involve the big toe.
In that case, the big toe of the right foot is auspicious for him.
Others have also said regarding one who has sneezed:
"A prohibition at the front [of the body], cessation at the eyes, and indeed destruction at the throat on the right side."
Success in one's purpose is indicated on the back; victory on the left side; conquest at the ear; and the attainment of all gains at the eye. (39.79)
Sneezing from all sides is inauspicious at the outset; a cow's sneeze brings about death itself.
So too does that which occurs by force, even without the weak, or that caused by the elderly, those with chronic catarrh, or children. (39.80)

Thus: "The omens" refers to those that are unfavorable; they are not written down here for fear of making the text too voluminous—namely, those other than the auspicious ones already mentioned. (39–81)
Regarding the Gauliruta:

there is destruction when the sun is present; news of a desired object when the moon; misfortune when Mars; the arrival of a friend when Mercury; gold when Jupiter; food when Venus; conflict when Saturn; and death when Rāhu. (39–82)
One should place the syllable *bhṛ* with its nasalization (*anusvāra*) within the heart-lotus of the one who has been bitten.
Having meditated on the syllables of its name surrounding it, and above that a moon-maṇḍala dripping nectar, and likewise a moon-maṇḍala at the throat; (39–84)
One should utter "Bind, bind" at the drop between the eyebrows;
having thus meditated, one should recite "Namo bhagavate. (39.85)
By reciting "Nīlakaṇṭhāya" twice, the protection of life is accomplished.
One should then cause [the patient] to drink cow dung juice with clarified butter, or black pepper with clarified butter. (39–86)
Whether in one's absence or in one's presence, the protection of living beings should be performed in this manner:
[one should recite] Sākṣa, Saṃvartaka, Pārśva, Tāra, and then Vahnipriyā. (39–87)

This mantra is named Vipati; Garuḍa is the personification of sound: *jvala mahāmati ṭhaṭha*. *Garuḍaśikhe prabhañjana prabhedana vimardana ṭhaṭha*. *Apratihatabalāpratihataśāsana huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. *Ugrarūpadhāraka sarpabhayaṅkara bhīṣaya ṭhaṭha*. *Sarvaṃ daha bhasmīkuru ṭhaṭha*.
Thus have the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of Vipati been declared through the weapon-mantras (*astramantra*).
The lotus of the Mātṛkās consists of eight petals formed by the final pairs of the groups of Ṛṣis, with two vowels [per petal], possessing filaments, and having the Nārasiṃha mantra as its pericarp.

One should worship the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, and Mahālakṣmī residing on the leaf, located respectively in the east, south, west, north, southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast. (39–90)
Having remembered and worshipped with the mantras beginning with "Aṃ Āṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ Brāhmyai Namaḥ" and others, one should worship Jyeṣṭhā and the others at the middle joints,
using the five syllables of the Lord of the Twice-born (the five-syllabled mantra) along with the mandalas of the elements and so forth.

Having meditated upon an eight-petaled lotus in the heart and in the left hand, with the final pair of each of the seven groups of consonants on the petals of the eight directions and the vowels as the filaments; 39–92.
One should place the [syllable] ending with the *bindu*, accompanied by the fire (*ra*), within the pericarp;
having thus meditated upon it in the heart and also upon the palm of the left hand. (39–93)

One should then sequentially deposit the letters of the [five] castes, beginning with the big toe, as well as the letters of the mantra, the letters of the nāgas, and the syllables of the great elements. (39–94)
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the qualities (*guṇa*), and the colors upon the hand and the body.
[The area] marked by the thunderbolt at the corners of the four Vedas has flesh as its corner and Indra as its presiding deity.
The northern [direction] is white, resembling a half-moon and a lotus; in the center is the sword;
and the southeastern [direction] is red, triangular, and marked with a blood-svastika. (39.96)
The wind is circular, black, and consists of the essence of six dots situated upon a line;
it is formless, the subtle element of sound, its own reflection, and has Śiva as its deity. (39–97)

In this manner, one should place the images of the Earth and the other elements, beginning with Jyeṣṭhā, encircled by their respective serpents and accompanied by the syllables of the *vipat* [mantra], during the intermediate joints (*parvan*).
Ananta and Gulika are red, the two Brāhmaṇas have Agni as their deity;
the two Kings have Indra as their deity and are yellow, as are Śaṅkhapāla and Vāsuki. (39–99)
The two Vaiśyas are Kṛṣṇa and Mahāpadma; Takṣaka has Vāyu as his presiding deity.
The fourth pair, Padma and Kārkoṭa, are white in color, and Jala is their presiding deity.

One should place the initial syllables of the names of the Nāgas together with the initial letters of the elements, such as earth, along with the subtle elements (tanmātras) such as smell, upon the fingers beginning with the thumb. (39–101)
In the initial sections, there are the subtle elements (tanmātras); in the final sections, the elements and oceans;
and in the middle, the letters of the vowels and consonants, along with the circles of the elements and nāgas.
One should meditate upon Tārkṣya in the hand, which is endowed with the five syllables, possessed of the three qualities of the subtle elements (tanmātras), and provided with thirteen kalās.
Then one should also assign the spheres of the earth and so forth to one's own body:
from the feet up to the knees, and from the knees up to the region of the navel. (39–104)
One should place the [sections] joined with gold from the navel to the throat, from the throat to the edge of the forehead, and from the forehead to the top of the head. (39-105)
Having meditated upon oneself as Garuḍa, one should destroy poisons.
[One should visualize the body] from the knees up to the navel region as golden-colored, resembling the peak of the Snowy Mountain (Himavat);
and from the navel to the throat, as resembling a ripe bimba fruit or a freshly blossoming bandhujīva flower.

I bow to Vainateya, who is as beautiful as a mass of crushed blue collyrium from his head upward, adorned by the foremost of serpents, who pervades the center of the universe, and who is saluted by the three worlds. || 39-106 ||
Thus, when the serpents, the piśācas and other spirits, and the various grahas behold the practitioner as the Garuḍa himself, they perish instantly upon entering him. (39.107)

When the practitioner, having become Garuḍa through the identity with his own self, utters whatever [word], that very thing becomes a mantra; once bitten, the poison is released and perishes. (39.108)
Having raised the *tārkṣya* hand, by means of the transposition of the syllables of the mantra,
through the movement of the fingers beginning with the thumb, and by means of recitation (*japa*).
Having placed the first syllable in the locations of the five syllables, one effects, in an instant, the acts of paralyzing, withdrawing, stunning, and transferring. (39-110)
Through the repeated utterance of "saṃstambhaya" and so forth, paralysis occurs by means of moving the thumb. (39.111)
By reciting "kṣipa oṃ svākṣipa," one may paralyze [the enemy].
Reciting the mantra while transposing the first and second syllables:
Ananta is the necklace upon his neck, and Vāsuki is the garland upon his chest. (39–112)
Kuṇḍala is Abja and Mahāpadma; Gulika is the head-binding;
likewise, Kārkoṭaka and Takṣaka are the bindings for the belly and the waist.
With the sacred thread [represented by] Śaṅkhapāla and eyes as red as vermilion,
one should, being composed, meditate upon Garuḍa in such a form as being identical with oneself.

Having displayed the *śūla-mudrā*, there shall be a state of *stobha* from a single recitation; likewise, possession occurs with a second [recitation], and [it becomes firm] from three or four recitations. (39.115)

The neutralization of poison consists of consuming the poison five or six times. This is the section on mantras for misfortune: by reciting "saṃplava saṃplāvaya" and by moving the index finger, one removes poison.

By pronouncing *tāraṃ*, *pārśvaṃ*, *kṣivarṇaṃ*, and *ṭhau* while vibrating the middle [tongue], and by uttering the words "saṃstobhaya" (paralyze), one enters and then destroys [the obstacle] through recitation. (39-116)
Having uttered the fourth and the second, and the first and third of the fifth, and having said "saṅkrāmaye," one should then move the ring finger.
One should transfer [the breath];

having uttered "saṃ" at the end, one should draw it out by moving the little finger—[the sequence being] the long *khaṃ*, the two sides, the two arms, the witness, the contraction, and the other hand. (39-118)
The meaning is that one should neutralize the poison.
One should meditate upon a grove of white lotuses in the center, with full-blown white water-lilies, within a jar of nectar, under a full moon mandala. (39-119)
It is surrounded by the digits (kalās) beginning with the letter 'a', which have the forms of women;
it is white, marked by the digits, and flooded by the nectar of the streams of milk.
Having meditated [on her], one should recite the vowels themselves; [the practitioner] becomes free from poison in an instant.
She is the granter of desires, auspicious, blue, the giver of enjoyments, and the source of all blessings. (39.121)
Bhadrā, Bhadravatī, Saumyā, Bhoginī, Bhagamālikā, Kāmeśvarī, Kāmamālā, Siddhi, Ṛddhi, and Vāmayā. (39–122)
The new moon and the sixteen digits arise from the nectar of immortality;
Soma is manifestly composed of nectar and consists of those sixteen digits. (39.123)
They have two arms, gentle faces, and are auspicious, wearing white garments and the like. || 39-124 ||
One should visualize them with nectar-pots in their hands, adorned with ornaments;
one should then inscribe the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon a place smeared with cow dung. (39-125)
Having drawn lines in connection with that [mantra], one should cause the bitten person to step over them;
they become free from poison.
One should have the bitten person lie down on their back, visualizing them as submerged in the ocean of nectar.
Having covered that with a cloth, one should [conceive] that cloth as the lunar disc.
Having intentionally placed within the garment the one who possesses a sword, together with the anusvāra.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as flowing with nectar, one should contemplate that station and the faces;
then, with the full orb of the moon, one should recite "muḍḍha muḍḍha" for this [mantra]. (39-128)
By pulling away that cloth, one should easily remove the bite;
having placed Śrīkaṇṭha in the heart, [one should place] HĀM on the back and at the joints of the limbs. (39-129)
Incense applied to the head of one bitten by a snake immediately destroys the poison;
hailstones joined with the ears, along with the skin of a true cat and the Pināka bow, [bring about the same]. (39.130)
(269) A *bhūrja* leaf situated at the end of two *ṭha*s, when applied, shall cause the eradication of serpents;
it has fire on its side, along with a twice-born [letter] and a half-moon, and this *meṣa* possesses the triple form of fire. (39.131)

The mantra is: *sabindurlāṅgalī sargī nīlakaṇṭhīyakaḥ* | *haraḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ ṭhaṭha* | *kapardine śirase ṭhaṭha* | *nīlakaṇṭhāya śikhāyai ṭhaṭha* | *kālakūṭaviṣaharāya huṃ phaṭ* | *ugra ṭhaṭha* (the weapon). *oṃ hāṃ oṃ nīlakaṇṭhāya oṃ kapardine oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ sarvajñāya ṭhaṭha* | *trinetrāya kālakaṇṭha viṣaṃ bhakṣaya ṭhaṭha*.
The seer of this is named Aruṇi, the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity is [Śiva].
Rudra, beginning with Nīlakaṇṭha, is said to have the first syllable as his seed-syllable (bīja).
The preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) for the mantra consisting of the Śakti and the second Bindu consists of three hundred thousand recitations;
alternatively,
O Lord, having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and worshipped the Deity, one should perform ten thousand recitations.
Likewise, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
thus the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) will be accomplished.
One should place the *tāra* [syllable] on the two thumbs and on the three fingers beginning with the index finger.
One should place the three syllables on the middle joints and the *praṇava* on the two little fingers;
one should visualize the first syllable as black up to the navel and the second as red up to the throat.
One should place the third form, which is of the nature of consciousness and has the aspect of nectar, upon the head;
one should also place the three syllables on the three eyes, and the limbs upon the [physical] limbs.
From the navel it resembles collyrium; from the neck upward it has the luster of the rising sun;
and from the head upward it has the brilliance of the lunar disc, adorned by eight lordly serpents.
Meditating on the three-eyed one with the trident in hand as identical with oneself, one should recite the mantra;
this mantra consists of three syllables, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. (39–137)
One afflicted by a spear or bitten by a snake shall become happy through recitation, meditation, and other such practices.
One should worship Bhairava in a cemetery within a newly drawn mandala of the Lord of Serpents.
In front of that [image], one should fashion a nāga out of rice flour and worship it;
standing on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the recitation while remaining in the vīrāsana posture.
Seeing a nāga, he approaches it, seizes it, and shall eat it;
having seen it, his mantra becomes perfected, and it destroys poison. (39-140)
Alternatively—

if one is unable to do it in this way— one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times at night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, either in the presence of one's mother or by the ocean. (39.141)
One should offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter, milk, honey, and rice;
by this, one becomes perfected in mantra and may employ it according to one's desire.

Having visualized the bitten person situated within a fiery disc in one's own palm, and having contemplated the blazing *tāra* (the syllable Om), one should show it to him; he will then fall into a swoon.
One should visualize the first syllable, smoke-colored, situated within the wind, fire, and fire [elements];
having offered incense while entering [the victim], the bitten person becomes free from poison. (39.144)
Alternatively, having visualized the second syllable, Kṛṣṇa, which is smoke-colored, within the city of Vāyu in the body of the enemy, one should then transfer the poison.

Having meditated upon that [mantra] situated within a full moon mandala, thirdly, as being flooded with nectar, one should thus render it free from poison; in this very same way, one should treat headache.
It destroys fevers such as those occurring every fourth day; of this there is no doubt.
However, if the three syllables are devoid of the *tāra* (oṃ) and are placed within the abode of fire (the triangle), [the result is different]. (39–147)
One should contemplate [the mantra] within the body; he upon whom it falls while swooning will perish.
Having meditated on the supreme syllable raining nectar upon his head, one should recite it. (39-148)
One quickly becomes free from poison by displaying the Śūla-mudrā.
Then follows the witness: the white jar (kumbha), followed by space (kha) and fire (agni), endowed with two eyes (nayanānvita). || 39-149 ||
"Hiravarṣi kharva hiravarṣi ṭhaṭha.

One should recite the mantra while meditating upon Umā, who is dressed in white, three-eyed, as white as the moon, and adorned with ornaments; she is sprinkling the one bitten by the snake with the nectar flowing from her jar. || 39-150 ||
By reciting [the mantra] with one-pointed mind through the identity with one's own self, one renders it poisonless;
thus, the pacification of venom is demonstrated even without mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like. (39.151)

The digit named Amṛta is said to reside in the joints of the feet above the big toes, as well as in the knees, the secret place, then the navel, the heart, the breasts, the throat, the nose, the eyes, the ears, the middle of the eyebrows, the temples, and the head— corresponding to the lunar days of the first fortnight.
In the Bahulā [fortnight], beginning from the Mūrdhan [day] and proceeding in reverse order, there is the sequence of ascent and descent according to the Uditā [pattern]. || 39-152 ||
For women, the growth [of the poison] begins from the left thumb; for others, it is the descent [from the top].
The seventh station of nectar is declared by the wise to be the digit of poison (viṣakalā).

Having recognized the digit of nectar within the body bitten by [the serpent], through friction there, the poisonous digit becomes poisonless; for the seventh [digit] from the place of the nectar is indeed the poison-digit. (39.154)
In that case, by means of friction, there shall be the paralysis of all poisons;
however, a bite that is incurable therein, one should avoid treating it. (39-155)
If food is consumed while a black snake is coiled around one's neck, death will gradually occur due to indigestion, abdominal diseases, and other ailments. (39.156)
When there is a drop of poison in the throat, one should visualize a rhinoceros lying supine there and place nectar; then, recollecting the nectar, one should consume it. (39.157)
By constantly placing the nectar-syllable at the throat and meditating upon the supreme ambrosia,
one who eats will not suffer untimely death and shall live for a hundred autumns.
When the digit of nectar (amṛtakalā) has been massaged, it brings pleasure to women;
when that digit of nectar is in the secret place, then there is the first union. (39.159)
This is declared to be that which generates love between husband and wife and brings them under control;
one should always contemplate the vital breaths within that [lotus] where the digit of nectar resides. (39-160)

Just as the Śākapūrṇimata system effects the protection of life, fortune, and nourishment, [so too does this apply] to the mouth, the eyes, the throat, the two arms, the two sides, and even the feet. (39–161)
The Guru-prabhā finger-measure is the duration of existence in the signs starting from the birth sign of the crow;
having fashioned an image of the person to be acted upon, [one should perform rites] during the Vipat, Pratyari, and Naidhana yogas.

When the piercing is performed upon an effigy made of clay mixed with the dust from the feet, using the *tāra* (OM), the *viṣakalā* (poison-element), and mantras such as *Yama* and *Avidyā*, the target will die. (39.163)
May Āstīka, the son born of Jaratkāru and Jaratkārvī, a man of great austerity and true to his promise, protect me from the serpents.
Oṃ, salutations to Narmadā in the morning; salutations to Narmadā at night. Homage be to you, O Narmadā! Protect me from poisonous serpents. (39-165)
Whoever should remember Asita, Arcimant, and Sunīta, whether by day or by night, for them there shall be no fear of snakes. (39.166)
For one who recites these verses during the day, at night, and at the two twilights, no fear exists even if he is in the midst of serpents. (39.167)
Thus, for the benefit of embodied beings, the lineage arising from the Nāga-born [Garuḍa] has been briefly described through its creative causes and its role as a messenger;
and following the ritual application of the golden mantra, the meditations that remove poison have also been explained.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, on the counteracting of poisons, in the Mantra-pāda of the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 39.
Now begins the fortieth chapter:
Due to the instability of the mind during meditations, the practice of mantras,
and the deficiencies of those who undertake the practice, it is held that these must be remedied by means of medicinal herbs.

In case of doubt regarding a *daṃśaka* snakebite, if one eats the bark of the *karañja* tree, [the poison is neutralized]; however, if the snake is sweet-tasting, it is a *phaṇī*, if bitter, a *rājila*, while the *ghoṇasa* and *saṅkaṭa* are both bitter. (40.2)
One should place asafoetida, dried and made into a pill, inside a crow's egg;
by administering it through the nose with urine, one bitten by a hooded serpent shall become well. (40.3)
The powder of *mātṛghātī*, *rajaḥ*, *hiṅgu*, and *cucundarī* kept in the stomach, or *sādhāra* ground dry and administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*), removes the poison of snakes. (40.4)
(273) Ginger, asafoetida, *kāravella*, and garlic; gold, *vacā*, *tumbinī*, *naktamāla*, jasmine seeds, *vakula* wood, and seeds produced from *śigru*;
combined with the seeds of *kośātakī*, the root of the earth-born (*kṣoṇīpūrva*) *śirīṣa*, and *sarpagandhā* in equal parts.
All [these substances], ground together with goat's urine and made into pills, conquer snakes by means of nasal administration and other methods. || 40-5 ||
The application of a nasal drop or an ointment made from the root of the *ṣaḍaṅgī* plant removes poison;
one who plays with snakes here, his hands smeared with it, is not harmed by them. (40.6)

Cow’s ghee, salt, black pepper, and asafoetida, ground together and applied to the hands of one who has killed his mother, and sprinkled upon the ears, eyes, and nose, removes the poison of serpents. (40.7)
By drinking *punarnavā* and *vārāhī* with milk, one becomes free from poison;
likewise, by rubbing the lower limbs with the powders of conch-shell and *tālaka*, one is freed from venom. (40–8)

Having powdered vacā, hiṅgu, and marica, which have been properly extracted, one should administer them as a nasal drop with the juices of kāravella; this will raise the victim of the bite in an instant.
The leaves of *devadālī*, ground with *sauvīra* (sour gruel) along with seeds or without seeds, immediately remove the poison of snakes when used for drinking and other purposes. (40.10)

Having ground seeds of *guñjā* and *vakula*, along with black pepper, with human urine, one who has lost consciousness will live again by means of its administration as a nasal drop or a drink. (40.11)
Having ground bhūnāga with human urine and drunk it, one should apply it as an ointment; likewise, by using it as nasal drops and collyrium, one removes the poison of serpents. (40-12)
One may destroy even the poison born of Vāsuki by means of drinking, nasal inhalation, or collyrium, using *jananīripu*, asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*), and human urine. (40.13)
The seed of the *vākula* tree, when drunk with urine and other liquids, destroys poison; as do the seeds of *kośātaki*, *jātīphala*, *naktamāla*, and *karañja*. (40.14)
Having ground these seeds, that nasal medication (nasya) instantly overcomes snake venom;
likewise, soot from a house, dārvī, meghanāda, and haridrā [are effective]. (40.15)
Pounded with curd and clarified butter and drunk, it removes the most potent snake venom.
Ginger should be consecrated twenty-one times with the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time and has been exposed to the sun. (40.16)
Hingu, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), rock salt (sindhu), garlic (rasona), and ugragandhikā, when consumed, or used as a drink, snuff, or collyrium, destroy the poison. (40.17)

Having prepared milk from the best species of *snuhī*, *kanyā*, *snuhī*, *arka*, white *arka*, and *ajā* in bamboo vessels, one should administer it as nasal drops (*nasya*) and likewise as collyrium (*añjana*). (40.18)

And by placing [the powder] in a state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one may raise up even one who has been bitten and is dead; likewise, with seven applications of fresh *kataka* seeds to a cloth, [one may achieve the same]. (40.19)
Having performed the meditation, one should anoint the eyes with oil or with water infused with [the herb] ātmodaka;
one should also administer it as a nasal drop (nasya), for this brings about the immediate destruction of the poison of serpents.

Having finely ground black nightshade (*niśā*), asafoetida (*nāgara*), black pepper (*marica*), soot from a house (*gṛhadhūmaka*), and the leaves of *sindhuvāra* with water containing husks, [one should apply it]. (40.21)
By means of an ointment, it destroys poison and causes the discharge of blood to cease;
[the ingredients are] turmeric, soot from a house, meghanāda, ghee, and curd. (40.22)
Drinking snake venom with buttermilk destroys it; likewise, snake venom born of a bird is destroyed by buttermilk.
Ahigandhā, when placed in the mouth or smeared [upon the body], conquers the seven types of poison. (40.23)
Thus ends the treatment for snakes.
O Lavasranetra! Ulkāmukha! Viṣadahana! Viṣabhojana! Vajrahasta! Strike! Huṃ! By the binding of the fist, [destroy] the poison! Ya-ra-la-va! Pakṣi! Huṃ phaṭ pho ṭhaṭha!
Having meditated upon the body of the snake that has bitten a limb as being the very form of the Maṇḍalī [snake], [one should recite this].
And by eating a boar’s paw while reciting the mantra, one may remove poison.
Reciting "Sānantaṃ daṇḍikhaṃ śaktiralpapakṣidehā aravimaravimattavān ṭhaṭha," while chewing betel, one may remove the poison from those in the assembly.
By recollecting [the mantra] while vomiting, one may [save] a biting snake that has turned its head downward, even in the case of smoke-poison.

From rubbing the bitten limb, the swelling and the venom of the *akṣveḷa* snake are destroyed; one should remember that its poison is neutralized by consuming white *tolā* on the head and other parts. (40.26)
The poison of the *maṇḍalī* snake is destroyed.
In cases of urinary obstruction, the dung of a bull should be applied as a plaster below the navel;
even by applying the fat of a frog together with rice-water, [the urine] will flow out.
The root of the *bṛhatkadalī* plant, when applied with water below the navel, stops the flow of feces and urine; everything flows [outward] at that very moment. (40.28)

Applying a paste of *maṇḍalī* and *kṣvela* to the heart and nose, and drinking salt water, as well as placing *vākula* seeds in the breast milk of a woman or administering them through the nose, removes delusion. (40.29)
One should grind the roots of śatāvarī, akṣavāra, and ahivegā with the buttermilk of an old ewe; that ointment destroys the ghoṇasa snake. (40.30)
Saindhava salt smeared with coconut oil removes *maṇḍalīja* [disease]; likewise, the root of *guñjā* and *nīlī*, used as nasal drops and other treatments, conquers *maṇḍalī*.
Powdered *bhṛṅgī*, betel leaf, curd, and salt ground together— this pair of formulations, when applied separately, removes poison produced by a cobra.
Black ajamoda, cotton, sesame, and cakes remove poison;
one may also remove it by means of incense made from peacock feathers, deer skin, kola, and asafoetida.
This refers to the poison known as *maṇḍalī*.
An ointment made from the dung of a boar mixed with goat’s urine removes the *ghoṇasa* snake poison.
One should grind *vajravallī* and its root with cow’s milk. (40.34)
One should cause [the patient] to drink that with oil; by this, one removes the poison of the *maṇḍalī* snakes.
Likewise, the root of *snuhī* with milk, or the root of *arka* with water, [is effective]. (40.35)
The two *yoga*s, when drunk separately by those in the circle (*maṇḍalī*), remove poison;
likewise, the root of *punarnavā* and of the two types of *girikarṇī*. (36)
One should remove that [poison] by means of sour gruel (śukta) administered as nasal drops, potions, and collyrium;
likewise, by using the three pungents (kaṭutraya), curd, honey, fresh butter, and rock salt.
One should drink this, which destroys the force of *kṣvela*, blood, and the disorders arising from the maṇḍala;
it consists of *triphalā*, *trikaṭuka*, and *saindhava* salt, mixed with honey and buffalo milk. (40.38)

If ground in buttermilk and smeared [upon the body], the poison of the maṇḍalins will perish. [Likewise, it is destroyed] by a paste of kuṣṭha and sandalwood mixed with one prastha each of snuhī and cow’s milk. (40.39)
One should take cow's ghee that has been cooked [with medicinal herbs] to remove poison arising from the *maṇḍalī* snake through sprinkling.
One should cook ghee with the paste of the three fruits (*phalatraya*), turmeric (*niśā*), licorice (*yaṣṭi*), and trivṛt. (40–40)

Rich with cow's milk remaining after the extraction of butter, and four times the quantity of *brahmī* juice—this, through applications such as ointments and drinks, removes the poison of those belonging to the *maṇḍalī* class. (40–41)

Having crushed with water the powder of a skull—twice-born, struck [by a weapon], wrapped in clay, long dried, and reduced to earth along with its bones—one should mix that powder with water. || 40–42 ||

By applying an ointment of *maṇḍalī* roots, one may instantly destroy the poison of *maṇḍalī* snakes; the root of *guñjā* taken with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) likewise removes the poison of *maṇḍalī* snakes. (40–43)
By means of drinks, ointments, and nasal drops— that is to say,
the root of the *nīlī* plant destroys the poison of *ghoṇasa* snakes when used as a drink or an ointment;
"with *kāñcika*" means that is to say, with fermented gruel.
Thus ends the treatment for the maṇḍalaka.
Hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha | Hrūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha | Jhroṃ hūṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha | These three mantras destroy poison when recited over rājila snakes. (40–44)

One should cause the patient to drink the root-fiber of *kāntārakāravelī* with milk, or that of *sāribā* with urine; through such drinks and other treatments, it removes the *rājila* [type of poison]. (40–45)
One should drink poison with *varṣābhū*, *cirbhaṭa*, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
Oil mixed with house-soot, when administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*), destroys [the effects of] poisons containing *rājī*. (40–46)
Kanā, honey, and rock salt, when drunk with cow-dung water, remove the poison of *rājila* snakes; this is declared to be a secret remedy. (40.47)
The juice of cow dung, rock salt, and the root of *kaṇā*, when drunk with ghee and honey, destroys the poison of striped snakes; likewise does the root of *śvetapuṅkha*. (40–48)
That is to say, by its own natural potency.

An inhalation (*nasya*) of *droṇapuṣpa* water mixed with oil removes the poison of the *rājī* snake. An inhalation of *tintriṇī* cooked with oil likewise removes the poison of the *rājī* snake. (40–49)
Sodium carbonate, rock salt, and the three pungents (vyoṣa), ground with human urine and applied as a paste, remove the poison of small creatures such as the *rājila* snake and others. (40–50)
The drinking of a decoction made from the roots of *nandyāvarta* removes the poison of the *rājila* snake.
Thus ends the treatment for *rājila* poisoning.
Having ground the two types of *agniko* (fire-plant) with their own juices by hand... [40-51]
An ointment applied to all the limbs destroys the poison of the *rājikā* and *maṇḍalī* snakes;
likewise, the oil-cake of the *madhūka* tree mixed with *tagara* and human urine [is effective]. (40.52)
The root of the *girikarṇī* plant, combined with the leaves of the *piśāca-udumbara*, removes the poison located in the nose of both striped (*rājila*) and circular (*maṇḍalī*) snakes.
Cow’s ghee ground with [the aforementioned substances], when administered as nasal drops and so forth, removes the poison of the king of serpents.
One should drink the powder of the bark of the *arka* root stirred in cold water. (40–54)
It also removes the poison of cobras, pythons, and horses;
one should drink a fine powder of ṭaṅkaṇa stirred in clear water. (40–55)

One should administer nasal drops and an external application that destroys all snake venom; likewise, asafoetida ground with the juice of *punarnavā* and applied as a nasal drop [achieves the same]. (40–56)
Having ground mārkaṇḍa, kākamācī, vahnika, and kaṭugandhinī with breast milk, [administering it] as a nasal drop removes all snake venom. (57)
Powdered salt, fresh butter, the root of *snuhi*, asafoetida, the root of *rambhā*, and likewise *agastya*, ground together with the urine of a young child. (40–58)
Nasal drops (nasya) made from the finest inner bark of the *campaka* tree remove all snake venom.
Water from the *unmatta* plant, combined with salt, when administered as a nasal drop, an ointment, or an eye-salve, [achieves the same]. (40–59)
Even the juice of the betel vine removes all snake venom;
likewise, [the juices of] the tumbinī, bakā, kūśmāṇḍa, śairīṣa, and those born of the jātī plant [have the same effect].
Having ground the seeds with one's own urine, [this preparation] conquers all serpents when used as a nasal drop and so forth;
likewise, *meghanāda* together with its roots, combined with the root of *vegānīlī*.
Having drunk it with clarified butter, one destroys the three kinds of poison. Likewise, when touched by a goat and drunk with clarified butter, it removes all poisons. (40.62)
Punarnavā water with asafoetida, used as a nasal drop (nasya), removes all poisons.
Garlic, equal in quantity to the leaves of aṅkola, pāṭhā, and nirguṇḍī, [is likewise effective]. (40–63)
Similarly, the powdered seed-kernel of *Kataka* mixed with the root of *Punarnavā*, or the root of *Lāṅgalī*—these two, when used as incense, destroy poison. (40.64)
One should fumigate during the two twilights or in the afternoon, but never at any other time.
This means that it removes all poisons.
Furthermore, one should drink the root of *punarnavā* ground with black pepper in water. (40–65)
One should prepare an ointment and collyrium that removes the poison of all serpents;
having invoked the form of Tārkṣya made from bear’s teeth, one should recite the mantra over it. (40–66)
Whoever maintains this [mantra], for him there is no affliction from snakes;
thus ends the treatment for all snakebites.
The *tāra* (oṃ), *śukla* (hrīṃ), and *agnipuṃ* (huṃ) mantra destroys the venom of scorpions. (40–67)
One should grind betel-nut water with asafoetida by hand in a bronze vessel;
when applied as a paste, it destroys the venom of bees, as well as saliva and earwax.
Saindhava salt, asafoetida, realgar, and viśvā, with cow-dung water, as well as vṛścikaghnā, śirīṣa seed, and long pepper—by means of an ointment [made from these], [scorpions are destroyed]. 40-69.
One should grind a palāśa seed with the milk of an arka plant and apply it as an ointment;
having ground a karañja leaf with the hand, one should bind it and then remove it.
Up to the point of [the bite of] a scorpion:
betel leaf, black pepper, Vārtāka, the seeds of Karañja, and Aśvamāraka—both as an ointment and as a drink—destroy the poison born of a scorpion. (40.71)
Śirīṣa flower, mañjiṣṭhā, sandalwood, the two types of niśā, kuṣṭha, and kumuda— two parts each of these, when used as a paste, remove the poison of bees.
Pigeon dung, *nāgara*, and *sindhutālaka*, ground with the juice of *bījapūra* and applied as an ointment, overcomes the affliction of scorpion stings. (40.73)
An application of rock salt (*sindhūttha*) heated with cow’s urine and mixed with one-eighth part of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) overcomes inflammation of the ear.
Likewise, a poultice (*upanāha*) made from *barbara* grass and the crushing of its leaves [is effective]. (40.74)
One should drink the root of *punarnavā* properly extracted during the *puṣya* asterism;
the poison of scorpions will not ascend into his body. (40.75)
Equal parts of karañja seeds, śairīṣa seeds, saffron, and realgar, when made into a pill and placed in water, remove the poison of scorpions. (40.76)
Thus ends the treatment for scorpion stings.
The mantra consists of the two *kālakarṇas*, followed by *vahnipatnī* (svāhā) and *antaka* (kṣa).
Three areca nuts (*pūga*), including one with a hole, are combined with seven betel leaves. 40–77.

By writing [this mantra] upon them and reciting it, or by consuming it, one removes the poison of a rat. With "ṣe ṣe," there is the city of the servant (ceṭa). "Eka-vila-jagaru-druta-jaṭa-piṅgala phu hara viṣaṃ hara saṃhara phu.
A sunflower with a downward knot, consecrated thirty-two times [with this mantra], [should be used].
In the case of one who has swallowed the poison of a rat, one should remove the poison that has reached the teeth by means of fresh *kapittha* leaf,
the root of *cavyāghāṭa*, and turmeric at night.
One should drink [the medicine] ground with cow’s urine to destroy all rat poisons;
there is also an incense made from the leaves of the *āragvadha*, and the consumption of those leaves with clarified butter.
Cotton-seed oil drunk with water removes the poison of rats;
likewise, *kāntā*, *śirīṣa* flowers, *kustumburu*, and the two types of *niśā* [remove it]. (40.81)
That [powder], ground with cow’s urine in equal parts, removes the poison of a rat when drunk;
or one should drink the root of the *tāpiñcha* tree ground with water, or *cavya* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*). (40.82)
One should then consume black plantain fruit with sugar and milk,
or else one should cause [the patient] to swallow the seventh particle from within the interior of the plantain fruit.
These four formulations, taken separately, remove the poison of rats;
or one may drink a paste made from *navamālā*, *vāma*, and *parṇa* ground with cow dung. (40.84)

Incense made from cat dung and *dhūr* resin, combined with the skin of a *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, destroys the venom of rats when played upon; likewise, the three-leaved plant (*tridalā*) combined with *gulā* [destroys it]. (40.85)
Having cooked rice in water that has been boiled with the root of *tuṇḍī*, one should eat it;
or one should lick *mustā* mixed with honey and clarified butter, which removes the poison of a rat. (40.86)
Furthermore, having drunk the seed of the *punnāga* tree with sour gruel in the morning, a man afflicted by rat-poison will remain for a long time in the heat, even when sprinkled with oil. (40.87)

One should grind together the grains of *muṣṭika* and *kodrava*, as well as the seeds of the sun-plant (*arka*), with the milk of the sun-plant; having thus prepared them, one should vomit up even the ancient mice dwelling within the belly. (40.88)
Having made a cake and eaten it, one should vomit up the poison produced by a rat;
he should then drink gruel with water that is a decoction of *śirīṣa* leaves. (40.89)

In one afflicted by the poison of an old rat, vomiting arises from the accumulation of filth in the head, as well as skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and the like, swellings, abdominal pain, fever, and so forth. (40–90)
If there should be [excessive] heat, one should administer the aforementioned purgative:
*tuṇḍī*, *vahniśikhā*, and *vajrī*, processed with water and infused with *vikṛti*. (40.91)
One should eat betel-nut together with betel leaf as a purgative;
likewise, betel leaf containing seeds of the sea-foam plant (*sāgara*) and castor oil plant (*eraṇḍa*) removes poison. (40.92)
These are the purgatives for rat-poison.
Once he has been purged with a decoction of the leaves of *kapittha* and *aṅkola*, the bark of *śirīṣa*, and the flowers of *arka*, one should bathe him. (40.93)
