The syllable *Ā* (Ajeśa), enriched with the *bindu*, fire (*ra*), and the left ear (*va*), dripping nectar;
when placed in milk, water, or an herb and drunk, it removes the poison of rats. (40.94)
By the throbbing of the red lotus on the pair of arms of Jhaṇṭhīśa,
sugar is scattered in the ten directions, bound by the mouth of the bull.

"From one thousand and eight recitations"—this is the meaning. *Natiḥ* (obeisance) to the Blessed One; *Hajrī* and *Yaśapurī*; "O you who have the neck of a deer and the sound of a boar, devour! O Bond, command! *Huṃ Phaṭ*.
Having drawn a rat with its mouth seized by a serpent upon a cloth, one should write this mantra around it, install it facing a bull, and [the enemy] shall be expelled from the house. (40–96)

During the conjunction of Mercury, when the ascendant is Sagittarius, one should bury a seven-finger-long peg made of *vaibhītaka* wood; this acts as a *kīla* (stake) that destroys the bull [Taurus] in reverse order. (40.97)
That is to say, one should bury it in that hole.
Or, under the asterism of Svāti or Śatabhiṣaj, [one should plant] the Aragvadha tree on a bow-shaped plot;
this also destroys bulls.
Then one should set ablaze the dried tail of a *ḍuṇḍubha* snake with clarified butter.
Vajrī, karañja, madhuka, and the seeds of the two types of kośātaki, along with the root of nirguṇḍī and the two types of niśā, should be ground together with the urine of a goat and a sheep.
Pills made from ground *sauvīra* salt, when placed in a house, will remove bulls; drunk, they remove all rat poison, and when dried in the shade, they become a pill. (40.100)
Ghee prepared with the paste of white *arka*, *pāṭalī* root, *devadāru*, and the two types of *niśā*, along with cow’s urine, removes the affliction of impotence.
Red amaranth (*raktārka*) and garlic (*laśuna*), when bound [to the body], remove the poison of rats.
Thus ends the treatment for rat-poison (*ākhuviṣa*).
Spiders (*lūtikā*) are of four types of *kṛmi* (parasitic worms); they move through the air. (40-102)
Sixteen of these move upon the earth; those that move in the sky are incurable.
One kills by sight, another by touch, and the last by her shadow.
And because of the odor from the other [type of food], one should not sleep in the open air;
nor should one eat at night while in the uncovered open air. (40.104)

The syllable *khaṃ* with a fire-bindu (*ra*), the *hṛllekhā* mantra (*hrīṃ*) possessing the void (*i*), fire (*ra*), and the *arghi*-bindu (*ū*), followed by *vipatiṃ* ending with the pericarp (*kaṃ*), and the white [syllables]—this is the mantra for the armor and the weapon. (40.105)

"Laṣasraṣaśviṣāḍ ādityo vahniṣu namo 'stu te rudrāya rudrāgniṣu doṣakṣayāya phaṭ. These three mantras, which destroy worms, are each to be mastered through separate recitations and other practices, dedicated respectively to the deities Durgā, Sūrya, and Candra, and perfected by a thousand repetitions. (40–106)

The flower of the great date palm (*mahākharjūra*), combined with black pepper and *tulasī*, ground with fermented gruel (*sauvīra*), removes all spider poisons when applied as an ointment and so forth. (40.107)
With *candana*, *uśīra*, *tagara*, *pāṭalī*, *kuṣṭha*,
*padmaka*, *hnībera*, *śelu*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *śāribā* in sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

Having ground these, one may remove the poison of all spiders by means of ointments, drinks, and so forth—namely, *vacā*, *doṣā*, garlic, and half a part each of *kānī* and asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*). (40.109)
Viśvārdha, applied as an ointment with urine and other substances, destroys lūtā (scabies/eruptions).
The root of vandhyākarkoṭakī, taken with rice-water, is a destroyer of lūtā. (40.110)
The root of *vega* with water, along with water containing betel-nut, and the spittle from a spider-bite; likewise, the seeds of *jyotiṣmatī*, black pepper, and the bark of *badarī*. (40–111)

Having ground [the herbs] in milk, one should apply them as a plaster and so forth to remove the poison of all spiders (*lūtā*). Furthermore, an application of the juice of *agasti* leaves and *tulasī* overcomes spiders.
Anointing with *kadamba*, *nīlī*, *tulasī*, and *lāṅgalī*, as well as drinking the juice of *ciñcā*, *vandāka*, and cow’s milk, destroys spider-bites and similar afflictions. (40.113)
That oil, cooked with its paste, destroys spider-bites and wounds;
[as do] the leaves of aṅkola, guñjā, and nirguṇḍī, along with ginger and the two types of turmeric.
Water mixed with the seeds and marrow of the *karañja* tree, when used for sprinkling, conquers lice.
Thus ends the treatment for lice.
O Daradvara! Cut with a sword, cleave with a spear, pierce with a discus, rend—*huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*!
But for those such as donkeys who possess horns, this [act] is a cause of destruction, according to Manu. (40.115)
A potion consisting of *mustā*, *uśīra*, *abja*, *māṃsī*, *śreṣ� goat’s milk, when drunk, removes the poison of donkeys and other such creatures. (40.116)
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), cats, monkeys, crocodiles, water-monsters, mongooses, horses, and so forth are intended. (p.
283) *Vacā*, *lodhra*, and *aśvagandhā*, along with the milk of the *snuk* plant, remove poison from horses;
that is to say, by means of drinking and external application.
Indravallī, niśā, puṅkhā, jīrṇaparṇa, and pānasa. || 40-117 ||
One should drink a small amount of powder mixed with *droṇa* and *svarasa-taila*;
through drinking, nasal administration, and external application, it will destroy the poison of donkeys and horses. (40.118)

Having ground the seeds of *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *arka*, along with black pepper and the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), drinking this and other such applications will immediately remove the poison of domestic rats.
The seeds of *karañja*, *śigru*, and *kapittha* are beneficial for *gaulī* poison. An ointment of *niśā*, clarified butter (*ājya*), and *śārivā* removes the poison of leeches.
One should destroy the poison of a centipede with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree;
one should also pour lamp-oil over the bite of a centipede.
That [mixture] removes poison.
Seeds of *śirīṣa* in the milk of *snuk* destroy the poison of frogs.
Indeed, the fresh juice of *tarkārī* and *bhṛṅgarāja*, combined with *hiṅgu*, [is likewise effective]. (40.122)
The poison of a cat is destroyed by drinking, anointing, or nasal administration [of these];
by an ointment of niśā, bhṛṅgarāja, and aśvagandhā, one removes the poison from a scorpion.
The five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree, when drunk or applied as an ointment, conquer the bite of monkeys; likewise, *tṛtīyaka*, *kanda*, *vegā*, *nīlikā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka*. (40.124)
Having ground it with milk, one may remove the poison of a human bite by means of ointments and other applications.
Lodhra, together with salt and asafoetida, and mustard seeds, should be ground with fermented gruel (śukta).
One should apply this as an ointment and also drink it; it removes the poison from a fish sting.
One may also drink a paste and a decoction of *śamī*, *nyagrodha*, and *nimba*. (40.126)
The application of its paste removes the poison of nails and teeth from mortals;
likewise, [poison is removed] by house-soot, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), and rock salt ground together with vinegar.
One should destroy poison caused by the bite of a *godhā* with ointments, potions, and the like;
however, in the case of the poison of a fly, one should sprinkle heated oil mixed with salt.
An ointment made with the husk of a wood-apple (*kapittha*) removes flies.
[One may also use] the leaves of *vegā* and *anīlikā*, along with *taṇḍulīyaka* together with its roots. (40.129)
Having ground these together, one should apply them as a plaster to destroy the poison of four-footed animals;
[one should also mix] house-soot, black pepper, *vacā*, and *rātri* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
Having ground the roots of *śigru*, *kākādanī*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* together with their root-fibers, [one may apply them] as a paste or drink them; this removes the poison of all insects. (40.131)
Having ground together the seeds of *kaṭutumbinī*, *niśā*, *devadālī*, and *lāṅgalī* with milk, it serves as an ointment and other applications for the destruction of insect poison. (40.132)
Having ground these with sour gruel (śukta), an application of that paste removes the poison of all insects.
[One should also use] the root, leaves, and flowers of white Aparājitā, along with ginger (nāgara). (40.133)
Vyoṣa ground in sour gruel (kāñcika) shall be a destroyer of minor poisons.
[One should offer] the desired oblation to the Blessed Viṣṇu at the end of the heart-mantra. (40.134)

And he should place the pair of armor and weapon mantras, which conquer all insects; the final letter [Ha] situated in the center of the Mātṛkā-lotus, joined with the nasal bindu (Au), the nasal bindu (M), and fire (Ra). (40.135)

O Alarka, Aṭibhaṭeśa, Kṣarāja, O Lord of Refuges! Make this bite by Alarka poisonless for me; do not delay—Ṭha Ṭha! One should meditate upon the bitten dog as one's own self in the form of a lion in the midst of a turbulent ocean, and the bitten dog as fleeing out of fear of those two. (40.136)
Having sprinkled [the patient] with the mantra, one should recite it to remove the poison of dogs;
this is done with a combination of yaṣṭi, kustumburu, vyoṣa, svaguptā seeds, and kuṣṭha.
One part of priyaṅgu and two parts of karṇikāra,
when drunk together with a ball of milk, remove the poison of the alarka spider.
The seeds of *kośātakī* and *kuṭaja*, the juice of the root of *arka*, and the milk of *jātī* drunk together immediately destroy the poison of dogs. (40.139)
A drink consisting of yaṣṭi, vyoṣa, and cow’s milk destroys poison. Likewise, kustumburu, svayaṃguptā, rātri, kaṭu, and māgadhī [are effective]. (40.140)
One bitten by a dog should drink the juice of *karṇikāra* and *āsana* mixed with milk—this applies even to one bitten by a mad dog.
Having bathed in a decoction of all parts of the *karañja* tree mixed with sour gruel (*śukta*), one should remain in the sun. (40–141)
One bitten by a mad dog becomes free from the poison immediately even from my [remedy];
likewise, the seeds of *aṅkola* and *unmatta*, along with ginger and *māgadhī* in equal parts [are effective]. (40.142)
A mixture of black *rambhā* fruit and *alarka* destroys poison; likewise, equal parts of the roots of *rambhā*, *kāravallī*, and *nīlī* [achieve the same]. (40.143)
The poison of a jackal is destroyed by drinking goat's milk and other such remedies;
one should also grind the leaves of *apāmārga* and sesame seeds together. (40.144)
One should remove the poison of a jackal by means of an application of sour gruel (kāñcika) and other such remedies;
likewise, [one may use] bhṛṅgarāja, nīlī, nirguṇḍī, and aśvagandhikā.
One should destroy the poison of a mongoose by means of ointments and other applications made with goat's milk;
likewise, blue-flax root ground with milk, when administered through drinking and other means, shall remove the [poison] of a mongoose.
A mixture of *savyoṣa* (the three pungents), *kiṃśuka* bark, oil, and milk, when applied as a drink or an ointment, destroys the poison of ants. (40.147)
At night, *vyoṣa* ground with fermented gruel (*śukta*) removes the poison of ants;
likewise, *punarnavā*, *vacā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and black pepper ground with fermented gruel [have the same effect]. (40.148)
One may destroy poison arising from the sting of a bee by means of drinks, plasters, and so forth;
[specifically] the root of *śigru*, the two types of *haridrā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* along with its roots. (40.149)
Having ground [the plant], one should apply it as a paste; this immediately destroys the poison of the *vañcula* snake.
One should administer *ṣaḍbindu* as a nasal drop with milk, or drink equal parts of honey and clarified butter. (40.150)

At the end of the heart: To the Blessed One, the Lord of the Yakṣas, who has the form of the peak of Mount Bhāsa, [I say]: withdraw, release, move! O poisonless one, I cause this poison—which is like the great nectar of immortality—to be consumed. *ṭhaṭha*. O pure bird, cast away, remove! *ṭhaṭha*.
By means of this mantra whose essence is Tārkṣya, one should remove the poison of stationary beings;
one may play it oneself for the sake of wonder, or cause another to drink it. (40.151)
When a stable poison has been consumed, one who has vomited and been sprinkled with cold water should drink honey and clarified butter in equal proportions to effect a proper purgation.
One should drink a mixture of Niśvādvaya and Sindhūttha with clarified butter and honey; or one should lick copper powder combined with sugar and honey, or gold [powder]. (40.153)

The juice produced from *jambū* sprouts destroys the poison of the *kāraskara* tree; likewise, the juice of the *rambhā* flower and the water [extracted] from the leaves of the *kapittha* tree do the same. (40.154)
By drinking ginger with water, even the juice of *chinnā* [is neutralized]; furthermore, *snuhi*, *snuk*, and mango blossoms remove the poisons of *śṛṅgī* and *kṣvela*. (40.155)
A mouthful of oil with powdered charcoal, or a decoction of turmeric taken with the flower of the plantain tree, destroys the medicine administered by a woman. (40.156)
Bhallātaka, the juice of the Brahmavṛkṣa, and that which is produced from cow's curd—washed ten times and applied as an ointment, this shall pacify the poison and the wound. (40.157)

Ajjaṭā destroys the poison of Caṇaka, and Ārdraka destroys the poison of Lāṅgalī; Nīlī ground together with Lodhra, when administered through drinking and other means, neutralizes all stationary (sthāvara) poisons. (40.158)
One should destroy all poisons with a *khārī* measure of cow’s milk;
likewise, the flower of the *śirīṣa* tree cures the affliction arising from *kodrava* grain.
The juice of *palāśa* and *kūṣmāṇḍa* destroys intoxication and vomiting;
black pepper is for the fruit of *rambhā*, and dry ginger is for *pānasa*. (40.160)
The sour mango for the coconut, and the *kuṇḍalī* for the excellent *bhr̥ṅga*, when combined with any one of coconut water, *jambīra*, or vinegar. (40.161)
Camphor is known to counteract that poison; the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* is also prescribed.
Uśīra, along with fermented rice-gruel (*śukta*) and the root of *śāli* rice, likewise destroys poison. (40.162)
Nīlikā and aśvagandhā, when administered as a drink, nasal drops, or other applications, destroy all stationary poisons completely, just like nectar. (40.163)
A wheel made from ghee, honey, and poison, when eaten, [destroys poison]; likewise, *cakramarda*, *snuhi*, *snuhī*, and *nākulī* remove the poison of the *nīlāgama* snake. (40.164)
Elā, candana, kuṣṭha, gairika, kaṇā, sauvarcala, alo-dhra, māṃsī, yaṣṭi, nata, and uccaṭā— these, taken in equal parts, powdered and saturated with honey, when licked,
destroy the poison of corrupted blood (dūṣiviṣa), like the city of Bimba before the fire.
By visualizing [himself] as Jvālāmālin, a person shall destroy all stationary poisons. 165.

The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), joined with the fire (*hutabhuj*) from the crescent moon of the eye (*netra-śaśāṅka-khaṇḍa*), namely *saṃvartaka* (phaṭ), followed by the spear (*śakti*: hūṃ), the armor (*varma*: huṃ), and *phaṭ*, together with the beloved of Fire (svāhā)—this mantra destroys stationary poison. [One should also employ] dūrvā grass, chinnaka, pippalī, paṭola, tagara, citrā, padmaka, cavya, and vacā.
When agitated by wine and other such substances, they destroy artificial poison along with its accompaniments. (40.166)
One should dissolve in water *hiṅgu*, *śṛṅgī* poison, *kośātaki* fruit, *ghana*, *hayaripu*, *pathyā*, the roots of *viśvālarka* and *tamāla*,
as well as *bhūpota*, *niśā*, and *arkaja*; this powder, mixed with the juice of *nṛpaniśā*, is beneficial.
Cotton is used for the water-born [poison], while the *citraka* poison and the lotus are used for the *unmattaka* [poison]. (40.167)

Or else, for the purpose of removing poison from those afflicted by it, or for the sake of destroying disease, or for the sake of obtaining desired elixirs—having approached that place where the taking of medicine is intended, may he perform protection on the previous day at the time of sunset. (40.168)

Wearing white garments and having washed his hands and feet, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); facing the northern direction, he should then smear the root of a medicinal herb [with ashes].
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapa), one should then scatter barley and other grains;
then, having wound the root with a red thread, one should stand with palms joined in reverence.
One should bow to Dhanvantari and to Suprabhā, who was created by Brahmā—she who is white, beautiful, lovely-limbed, and adorned with pearls and other ornaments. (40.171)
One should worship her with principal ornaments and a prostration using the name Tārā:
"Oṃ, salutation to all medicinal herbs! You shall be full of vigor; make [the world] complete with those powers! Cook! Strike! Burn! Kill! Salutation to you!"
Having recited this ten times over the medicinal herb once again, (p. 288) || 40-172 ||
Having paid homage at dawn and having prostrated with that mantra, one should take the medicine;
it will then become potent and yield the stated fruit.
Otherwise, Suprabhā indeed grasps the potency of medicinal herbs;
having reflected thus, the extensive tantras composed by former teachers have been properly upheld.
This ritual procedure, which brings benefit to the entire world, has been shown in brief for the sake of those who desire the merit of pacifying all evils. (40.174)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, on the treatment of various types of poisons, in the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 40.
Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Herein, the medical treatment for the planets (*graha-cikitsā*) is written down, not in excessive detail.
Among those, many types of medical treatment for children (*bāla-cikitsā*) are recorded. (41.1)
Among those, first relying upon the opinion set forth by Khaḍgarāvaṇa and that declared in the Nārāyaṇīya, two paths are here described. (41–2)
On the first day, in the first month, and again in the first year, the Mother Nandā takes possession. (41.3)
His symptoms are fever, trembling, weeping, and refusal to eat;
from the mud on both banks of a river, one should fashion an image of a porpoise. (41.4)
Having wrapped it with a yellow thread, one should offer white food made from a *prastha* of rice,
along with fish, meat, and fermented liquor, together with flowers, curd, milk, and sesame seeds.
Having smeared the ground with thirteen *svastikas* made of flour and eight small lamps, and having prepared a vessel as long as an arm with plantains and other offerings; 41–6.
Having placed the image (puttalī) in the center of that, one should arrange lamps and other offerings around it;
there, during the evening twilight (aparā-sandhyā), one should worship Vighnanāyaka with perfumes and other articles.
Having performed worship in the east, south, west, and north, [one should worship] the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī;
Vārāhī and the others in the corners beginning with the southeast; and Caṇḍikā in the northeast. (41.8)
Having worshipped Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas, in the center after bringing him outside,
one should [offer] from one-fourth of the four portions of the sacrificial materials as prescribed.

One should offer the bali-oblation to Vīrabhadra and the other Mothers upon the Bodhi leaves, each separately, preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, while pronouncing their respective names. (41.10)
Having worshipped Khaḍgarāvaṇa there with the mantra that will be mentioned,
one should also offer oblations to Nandā and Śāntā by their respective names.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa, the far-sighted one! Strike! Seize! Release the child! Ṭhaṭha! With this, the oblation (bali) should be cast; having performed the lustration (nīrājana) for the infant with that, he should lead him away.
To Nandā, however, [the offering is made] by her own name, preceded by the syllable Oṃ and ending with "namas. (41-12)
Then, in the eastern direction, one should afterwards fumigate the body of the child with the remains of offerings made to Śiva, mustard seeds, neem leaves, and clarified butter.
With the sprouts of the nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, bilva, and pālāśa trees,
placed within the belly of a water-pot, one should bathe or sprinkle [the deity].
Having performed this for three days, one should likewise bathe [the child] on the fourth day;
during the second triad of days, a spirit named Sunandā afflicts the child.
There is movement [of the limbs], eye disease, and contraction of the hands and feet;
having fashioned a doll and so forth as before with the substances previously mentioned, [one should perform the rite]. (41.16)
This sequence of offerings (bali) is for Vīrabhadra and the other Mothers, for Khaḍgarāvaṇa and the obstacle-demon, and for Dināmātṛkā; it applies everywhere.
At the time of sunset, one should offer the bali-oblation in the north with the mantra:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate khaḍgarāvaṇāya dīrghadarśanāya hana gṛhṇa muñca bālakaṃ ṭhaṭha*.
During the third triad [of days], the Graha Pūtanā seizes the child.
Fever, breaking pain in the limbs, convulsions of the neck, and upward gazing;
having prepared an effigy as before, [one should offer] sesame flour, cooked rice, and curd. (41.19)
With fish, meat, liquor, cakes, perfumes, incense, banners, and so forth,
one should offer oblations as before to Vīrabhadra and the other Mothers, and to Pūtanā.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Khaḍgarāvaṇa of supreme valor! Strike! Seize! Release the child! Ṭhaṭha!

Having offered the sacrificial oblation with this, one should cast it out toward the west, consisting of white mustard seeds, the remains of offerings to Śiva, and neem leaves mixed with clarified butter. (41–21)
Having fumigated him with the horn of a goat, one should bathe him with waters of pacification. In the third set of four [days], Mukhamandika seizes the child. (41.22)
Perspiration of the limbs, fever, labored breathing, clenching of the fists, and abstention from food;
one should also employ the same materials as before, such as the effigy and so forth, in this case as well. (41.23)
One should offer the bali-oblation to Vīrabhadra and the other Mothers as before.
With this mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate khaḍgarāvaṇāya dīrghabhujāya hana gṛhṇa muñca bālakaṃ ṭhaṭha*, having cast the offering, one should carry the bali toward the southern direction.
In the fifth month, however, the seizing spirit named Vilālā seizes the child;
fever and eye disease are its symptoms, and the clenching of the fists is as before. (41–25)
All [offerings] such as the effigies (puttalī) and so forth, as well as the presentation of the bali, are as before;
one should offer the bali to Vīrabhadra and the Mothers as previously described. (41–26)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa; homage to Pūrṇa! Ṭha Ṭha!
Having offered this bali, one should likewise carry away that bali to the northeast.
One should fumigate with neem leaves mixed with ghee and guggulu.
In the third set of six days, there is the bird-omen (śakunikā), characterized by looking upward and fever. (41-28)
The dolls and so forth are as before; the distinction lies in the honey and blood.
The fifth mantra has been proclaimed, and the incense is also that previously mentioned.
Having offered the bali-oblation in the northwest, one should bathe [the image] with waters of pacification.
Furthermore, on the seventh day, the limbs become dry, there is movement, trembling, and weeping. (41.30)
As before, one should also prepare effigies and other materials here.
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa, the terrifier of the three worlds; strike, seize, release the child! Ṭhaṭha!
Having offered the sacrificial oblation with this mantra, one should seize [the child] within the range of Aditi.
One should bathe [the child] with water consecrated for peace.
During the third set of eight days, a seizing spirit (graha) seizes the child;
[the symptoms are] yawning, clenching of the fists, fever, perspiration, agitation, and gazing at the sky. (41.32)
The ritual substances consist of effigies and so forth, representing the four castes and the four banners.
Reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa, whose hands are blazing with light; slay, burn, release the child!
Ṭhaṭha!"—having offered this oblation as before, one should fumigate and bathe him. (41–33)
In the ninth triad, there is what is called Añjikā, as well as physical exertion, fever, clenching of the fists, eye disease, and the effects of Puttalī and so forth, as previously described. (41.34)
At the time of the evening twilight, one should offer *śaṣkulī* and *parpaṭī* [as oblations] with this mantra:
"Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa, whose hand is ablaze; strike, seize, release the child! Ṭhaṭha!
In the tenth and third lunar days, there arise the afflictions known as Revatī, characterized by trembling and fever. (41–35)
One should perform the offering at the foot of a tree with dolls and such, accompanied by weeping.
[The mantra is: *Oṃ namo bhagavate khaḍgarāvaṇāya dīrghadarśanāya hana gṛhṇa muñca bālakaṃ ṭhaṭha*.
Having fumigated it with the remains of the previous offering, one should also bathe him as before. (41–36)
Likewise, when three times eleven [thirty-three] have passed, there is the onset of fever known as Śilā;
there is trembling of the limbs and the striking with fists, as before, against dolls and the like. (41.37)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa! Strike, seize, release the child! Ṭhaṭha! Having offered the bali as before in the north, one should fumigate it and bathe it.
Likewise, in the three sets of twelve, there is also ripening, burning, and fever.
Clenching of the fists, diarrhea, and activity with dolls and the like;
[these are caused] by milk-porridge, milk, mung-bean rice, and curd-rice as previously described. (41.39)
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Khaḍgarāvaṇa! Accept this offering, release the child! Ṭhaṭha!
Having offered the oblation with this mantra, one should carry him out to the south;
having fumigated him with the remains of offerings and the like, one should bathe him with waters of pacification. || 41-40 ||
In this manner, the planets seize children up to twelve years of age;
others say they do so up to sixteen, and likewise up to seventeen.
Thus ends the medical treatment for Khaḍgarāvaṇa in childhood.
Now, on the day a child is born, a sinful seizing spirit (grahī) afflicts it;
in that case, there is the turning of the neck, restless movements, and the flowing of saliva. (41-42)

Having prepared a square sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) made of bamboo and other materials, one should place Vīrabhadra in its center and the Mothers in the corners and the cardinal directions. (41–43)
And one should worship Vināyaka and Cāmuṇḍā in the northeastern direction with offerings of cakes,
fish, meat, rice, sesame powder, liquor, and so forth.
One should offer the bali-oblation with their respective names preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
There, having worshipped [the deity] in the northeast corner, accompanied by eight banners and lamps... (41–45).
At the time of half-setting [of the sun], having performed the *nīrājana* rite for that infant with mantras,
one should place him either in a crossroads or in the direction of the Lord of the Immortals (Indra).
One should fumigate [the area] with the remains of offerings from Siddhārthapura, neem leaves soaked in ghee, uśīra, mārga, the tips of bodhi sprouts, and sandalwood. (41–47)
Having bathed it with water mixed [with medicinal herbs] contained in jars, one should sprinkle it;
or one should smear it with lodhra, sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, and vātakī.
Having performed this for three days, on the fourth day again,
[one should bathe the deity] with waters of pacification enriched with the leaves of the bilva, kṣīra, āgama, and mārga plants.
Having bathed the best of Brahmins according to one's capacity, one should honor them with garments and other offerings, beginning from the first day until the seventeenth year [of the vow]. (41–50)
This same procedure is prescribed, though their presiding deities differ in sequence;
on the second day there, that seizing spirit is considered to be Bhīṣaṇī.
Contraction of the limbs, coughing, and labored breathing are observed as symptoms;
[these are treated] with sandalwood, ushira, and mayura, ground together with goat's urine. (41–52)
One should fumigate with the hair of a porpoise, a cow’s tooth, and horns;
on the third day, Jhaṇṭālī is said to cause yawning and other such symptoms. (41–53)

There is movement [of the limbs], and on the fourth day, the seizing spirit is appeased by an ointment made from cow-tusks, elephant-tusks, and so forth, with goat’s milk, and by incense made from *rājī* and neem leaves. (54)
Emetics using *kākolī* and *phenaka*, as well as agitation of the eyes; an ointment made from the tusks of a striped elephant and *nimba* leaves. (41–55)
On the fifth day, incense made from snake-skin is employed;
Siṃhikā [is used] for binding the fists and other such actions, along with Lodhra, Vaca, and other substances. (41–56)
Anointing should be performed, and incense is considered to be made from the remains of her offerings and so forth.
On the sixth day, she becomes a Phaṭkārī; her activities on that day consist of weeping and other such behaviors. (41–57)
An ointment made from the aforementioned *kuṣṭha*-ghṛtas is recommended, as is incense made from those same substances.
Then, on the seventh day, she will appear with her hair disheveled. (41–58)
The symptoms are preceded by convulsive movements, crying, foul odors, coughing, and yawning.
An ointment made from *aja*, cow urine, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *vyāghranakha* [should be applied]. (41–59)
Indeed, in the eighth [chapter], Daṇḍinī is described as being preceded by cough;
her activities are considered to be accomplished with garlic, vacā, asafoetida, and white mustard.
In the ninth [chapter], there is the application of ointments and incense, known as the Great Buffalo (Mahāmahiṣī);
and the activities such as clenching the fists, eating, coughing, and so forth, [are performed] with *tagara* and sandalwood. 41–61.
An ointment composed of *kuṣṭha* and mustard seeds is recommended for that [condition];
incense made from the hair and nails of a monkey should be used, and on the tenth day, the spirit Rodanī seizes the child. (41–62)

There he seizes the child; its symptoms are a bluish complexion. Incense and ointments made from the leaves and petals of the *nimba* tree are prescribed, as well as an offering (*bali*) as previously described. (41–63)
The spirit named Pūtanā seizes a child one month old;
there will be knots and convulsions, as well as crying like a crow. (41–64)
In the second month, there is a crown-like swelling on the body due to coldness and other symptoms; incense made from neem leaves combined with garlic should also be used.
In the third month, Gomukhī, her activities consist of crying and so forth;
having bathed her with milk, *agasti* leaves, bilva leaves, and water, one should then fumigate her.
In the fourth month, Piṅgalā [is propitiated] with *siddhārthas* mixed with clarified butter;
her ritual activities, such as the emaciation of the body and so forth, as well as the bath and incense, are as previously described. (41–67)

An ointment and an incense made from the tooth of a royal elephant are excellent for that purpose; likewise, [an ointment] made from neem leaves, snake sloughs, and discarded flower offerings mixed with clarified butter.
In the fifth [chapter], the *haṃsikā* [yoga] consists of clenching the fists, looking upward, and so forth;
likewise, there are the activities of breathing and yawning, and these again apply even in the case of smearing.
Furthermore, having fumigated with the horns of a ram, stone, realgar, lodhra, and vacā,
as well as with discarded flower offerings (nirmālya) and other substances, one should protect the child vigilantly.
And in the sixth month, the lotus-eater seizes the food within the womb;
incense made from neem leaves combined with mustard seeds should be used as a remedy. (41.71)
In the seventh month, Śītalā manifested her activity through coolness and the like;
in the eighth month, Yamunā acted by first parching the mouth.
In this case, there is no need for medical treatment; during the ninth month, neither the child nor Kumbhakarṇī causes any affliction. Her symptoms are fainting and vomiting. (41–73)
An offering to Īśa should be made with cooked barley, fish, meat, rice, perfumes, and so forth;
in the tenth month, the ascetic woman, fasting, performs the closing of her eyes.
There is also movement; with yellow and red food, fish, and meat, an offering is made toward the north.
Then, in the eleventh month, a female demon named Rākṣasī [seizes] the child.
He seizes the blindness of the eyes; there is no remedy for that.
In the twelfth month, the restless activity is preceded by labored breathing. (41.76)
In the second year, likewise, there is suffering, falling, and so forth;
the ritual action involves incense made from hair and cow's teeth, and water from five petals.
In the third year, however, there is *snāna* (bathing), as well as *rodinī* (weeping) and so forth;
in the fourth year, however, there is *ceṣṭā* (movement), as well as *caṭakā* (chattering) and *vedanā* (pain) and so forth.
In that [year], incense made from piñcha, romā, and other substances is prescribed;
and in the fifth year, Cañcalā appears in the form of bodily tremors and the like. (41.79)
In this [year], there is physical exertion; in the sixth year, there is excessive urination.
Incense made from *rājī* and garlic, and bathing with water from five-leaved plants [are the remedies]. (41–80)
In her seventh year, Yamunā caused her to abstain from food;
in her eighth year, the goddess Jātavedasī afflicted the child with consumption.
In the ninth year, Kālinī causes the cracking of hands and other afflictions.
[One should counteract this] by offering sesame seeds with this mantra: "Oṃ muñca paca daha āgaccha bālike ṭhaṭha. One should also fumigate [the child] with that [sesame). 41–82.
And in the tenth year, Kalahaṃsī causes fever;
[a remedy is] an ointment made of white mustard, kuṣṭha, garlic, and cow's hair.
Incense made from *picumanda* leaves should be used during the eleventh year;
*devadūtī* always causes excessive hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions. (41.84)
In the twelfth year, Palitā causes diseases of the eyes and other ailments;
likewise, in the thirteenth year, Vāyavī is present, and her activity occurs therein.
There, a yakṣiṇī afflicts the child with ailments such as the loss of bodily strength;
in the fourteenth year, a graha causes fever, pain, and other such symptoms.
Grahi is considered to have a face like muñja grass in her fifteenth year;
however, there is no medical treatment for her in the sixteenth year, as she is then known as Vānarī.
Likewise, in the seventeenth year, the planet is always considered to be "Possessing Bonds" (bandhavatī), causing bodily pain, mental delusion, delirium, and so forth. (88)
In the eighteenth year, a girl named Kumārī afflicts the child.
Thus have the Bālagrahas been described; all these goddesses are indeed Mothers. (41.89)
One should offer the bali-oblation to all of them using their respective names preceded by the word "Kumārī" and ending with "namaḥ," and one should also recite these mantras. (41–90)
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, and Vaiśravaṇa likewise protect the child with haste, and release the young boy.
Ṭhaṭha!
With this offered oblation, one should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana) three times for the child;
at the conclusion of the offering of the oblation, however, one should recite the mantra while touching the child. (41–92)

*Namaḥ sarvamātṝṇāṃ hṛdayamoṭaka bhañja kaḍḍha sphoṭaya sphura gṛhṇa ākarṣaya troṭaya evaṃ siddhiṃ jñāpayati hara nirdoṣaṃ kuru bālakaṃ ṭhaṭha.* At the conclusion of the offering of the *bali*, one should recite this mantra: *Kūśmāṇḍi yakṣi bhagavati cāmuṇḍe muñca daha bālād gaccha ṭhaṭha.*
One should perform a fire oblation with sesame seeds, *rāji* grass, and clarified butter for liberation from that planetary affliction.

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe namo vidye huṃ hrīṃ! O evil planets and Guhyakas, go away to that place where Rudra commands you; ṭhaṭha! With this [mantra], from the first day until the end of the seventeenth year, at the conclusion of the offering of oblations (*bali*), one should throw sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *bilva*, and *palāśa* trees into the water of the jar and bathe [the child] with this mantra: *Kṣrūṃ!* Protect him, O Great God! O Blue-necked One! O Wearer of Matted Hair! Together with the planets, protect and release the young boy!
With this, an application of black mustard (*rājikā*) and incense removes the influence of the planets.
When written on birch bark interspersed with names, this binding rite overcomes the afflictions caused by child-seizing spirits.
Hasta! Mākāntaka! Sākṣau! [O you who are] repeated with *tāra* as the prefix!

*Hi cini*, *bhūcani*, *bhūtataṭi*, *vicaṇi*, *biraja*, *nārāyaṇi*! *Umē!* O you who hold a staff in hand! *Raudri*! *Maheśvari*! *Mahāmukhi*! *Vyālamukhi*! *Śaṅkukarṇe*! *Śuṣkajaṅghe*! *Alambupe*! Strike! O destroyer of all seizing spirits! *Khala*! [Take] the blood from every limb! O Goddess, whatever you perceive with your mind, delude my deluder! Born in the heart of Rudra, abiding in the heart of Rudra!
O Goddess! Come with your fierce form in Rudra; protect me. || 41-95 ||
Huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!
One should wear this *skandamekhalā* on the topknot, the neck, or the waist;
thus, a child is not afflicted by infantile seizures (*bālagraha*) or by serpents and the like. (41.96)
May Viṣṇu protect you from the east; may Rudra guard the south;
may Brahmā protect from the west; and may Skanda guard the north. (41.97)
May Sūrya protect you from above, and Vāsuki from below;
O child, may the remaining quarters and the Wind-god protect you from the depths.
May the Blessed Lord Pinākin, whose banner is the bull, grant well-being;
may cows protect [us] everywhere, and may auspicious Earth always protect us. 41-99.
May Hari, the source of all beings without exception, protect you—
he from whose navel-born lotus the universe arose.
Supported by the tip of his single tusk, he sustains the earth and the world;
may that Lord Keśava, who assumed the form of a boar, protect you. (41.101)
May the omnipresent Janārdana, who assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha and tore open the chest of his enemy with the tips of his claws, protect you everywhere. 41.102
May Vāmana protect you always— he who in an instant became Trivikrama, having traversed the three worlds with his strides and wielding flashing weapons.
May Govinda protect your head; may Keśava guard your throat;
may Viṣṇu protect your private parts along with your belly; and may Janārdana protect your shanks and feet.
May the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty is unimpeded, protect your face, arms, forearms, mind, and all your senses. (41.105)
May the pretas, kuśmāṇḍas, and those rākṣasas who are your enemies go to their destruction, struck down by the sound of the conch, discus, mace, sword, and bow.
May Vaikuṇṭha protect you in the cardinal directions, Madhusūdana in the intermediate directions; may Hṛṣīkeśa protect you in the sky, and Mahīdhara protect you on the earth.
Nandagopa always performed protection by means of this;
by chanting this and through its touch, there would be unimpaired protection for the infant Kṛṣṇa.
In the center of the *śakti*, one should place the child’s name, the *tāra* (om), the pair of *lu*s, and *jalam*;
ending with *svāhā*, one should surround this on the outside with the moon (*śaśī*). (41.109)
One should again encircle it on the outside with downward-facing crescent moons;
having thus fashioned this wheel of the heart that removes the infant's distress, one should worship it.
Clarified butter combined with neem leaves, garlic, lac, and bamboo bark;
likewise, together with white mustard, clarified butter, snake-skin, human hair, and discarded flower offerings;
and these, along with bamboo bark, lac, neem sprouts, and clarified butter, joined with white mustard—these [are the ingredients].
These three incenses, beneficial for children, are said to destroy the afflictions caused by the seizing spirits of infants. || 41-111 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, on the treatment of children, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 41.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.
Devas, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, pitṛs, heḍhras, and bhūtas deprived of their splendor;
those born from wombs, the dejected, the delirious, obstacles, those difficult to pacify, and piśācas—[all these are overcome]. || 42-1 ||
In this manner, eighteen kinds of seizing spirits (graha) take possession of human beings:
those causing insanity (unmāda), those causing epilepsy (apasmāra), and others such as the Brahmarākṣasas. || 42-2 ||
All those planets seize human beings when they desire offerings;
they are of two kinds—those who desire pleasure and those who desire to kill—and they are both gentle and fiery.
And in empty houses, lakes, ponds, mountains, gardens, and rivers;
in solitary trees and cremation grounds; and in shrines, temples, and the like. || 42-4 ||
These planets dwell here and afflict human beings when they are angry, joyful, laughing, frightened, or alone at night. (42–5)

One who is impure from eating, one adorned with ornaments at night, one who has lost or found wealth, one separated from a loved one, one about to die, a woman, and a pregnant woman [should not be looked upon]. (42.6)

One who behaves improperly, one who has bathed after her menses, one who has recently given birth, one who is menstruating, one afflicted by lust, a drinker of intoxicants, one who is naked, or one standing at a crossroads or a marketplace; || 42-7 ||

(299) During the twilights, the planets seize a woman who has not yet been enjoyed, one who is anointed with oil, or one who has been insulted; this continues as long as she [remains so], due to the censure of deities, Brahmins, or great men, or because of former enmity. (42–8)
The planetary spirits seize one because of debt and the ripening of karma, and not otherwise.
[Such a person becomes] weak, with eyes closed, lacking luster, and excessively talkative. (42.9)

Having bathed, wearing fragrant garlands and fine clothes, appearing gentle, joyful, and devoted to the gods, yet being evil-minded, fearless, and arrogant, he hated righteousness, the gods, and the twice-born. || 42.10 ||
Eating voraciously and laughing at everyone, the lord of the asuras, his limbs trembling, licked the corners of his mouth with a longing for molasses, water, milk, and other such things. (42.11)
Crawling on the ground, red-eyed, acting like a boar, afflicted by the *nāga-graha*, desiring red garlands and perfumes, and suffering with bloodshot eyes. (42.12)
One who is free from anger, quick-moving, profound, and afflicted by yakṣas;
one who desires garlands, perfumes, song, and instrumental music, and plays about, is afflicted by gandharvas. || 42.13 ||
Shameless, fond of wine, meat, and blood, and impure—such is the Rākṣasa; performing the rites of the funeral cake and water-offering while desiring meat, he is possessed by the Pitṛs.

With knees placed together, face turned downward, smiling, with fists clenched and hands held over the private parts, speaking incoherently, trembling, with cold limbs and eyes cast askance; || 42-15 ||
With pure limbs, eating much yet being pure himself, oppressed by the seizing of ashes;
with perspiring limbs and smelling of sheep, he is devoid of restraint and has flickering eyes. (42.16)
Eating much, knowing what is thought, seeking meat, and grasping at the womb;
impure, covered in filth and mud, lying in ashes, laughing and weeping. (42.17)
Hating women, always eating others' food, terrifying them, seized by dejection, dancing and laughing, with a withered body, eating excessively, and breaking his own limbs; (42.18)
One afflicted by the Pralāpa-graha should be recognized by excessive talkativeness;
one seized by the Vaināyaka-graha makes hissing sounds, vomits, and gnashes his teeth. (42.19)
(300) Dwelling in solitude, with white limbs, running with a harsh sound,
insatiable in eating, and when questioned, he who does not speak while grasping at kusha grass— 42.20.

One who smears himself with cow-dung and mud, has red eyes, threatens others, has bloodshot eyes, eats excessively, speaks piteously, is greedy, and trembles in his limbs, is possessed by an Antyajagraha. (42.21)
Foul-smelling, impure, and fickle, he is a Piśāca with exceedingly harsh speech;
imitating everyone, he strikes people and speaks out loudly. (42.22)
Altered in his gait, he climbs trees, oppressed by malevolent spirits and seizures;
slapping his limbs, laughing, singing, weeping, and tossing his body about. (42.23)

One whose body is copper-colored and emaciated, afflicted by a severe case of wind-induced insanity (vātonmāda), exhibits roaring, running about, and anger, while craving cold shade, food, and shelter. (42.24)
With a yellowish and hot body, vomiting, and insanity born of *śleṣman* and *pitta*;

with eyes rolled back, fallen, unconscious, and frothing at the mouth; with limbs and hands contracted, crying out most dreadfully and gnashing his teeth—one who is thus intoxicated is possessed by *apasmāra*, yet may eventually find relief. (42.25)
Constantly reciting the Vedas, holding *kuśa* grass, and performing the rites of the twice-born, he worships the gods and the Brahmins; yet he is a planet and a *brahmarākṣasa*. (42.26)
Running, leaping, laughing, and acting like a warrior, he was seized by the Kṣatriyas.
Yawning, laughing, weeping, scratching, crying out, seizing merchants, speaking the unspeakable, dancing, and becoming enraged—he was even made to consume excrement and urine. (42.28)
Touching his private parts and the like, laughing, hating the Brahmins, grasping at base men, shaking his hair with joy, and speaking—he beholds the minister. (42.29)

One who is falling from a tree or the like, or entering fire while weeping, or who desires to kill [the practitioner]—one should avoid such a person, for he is incurable by means of mantras and other such methods. (42.30)
Distressed, seeing [the world] on all sides, afflicted by fever, pain, and the like, overcome by hunger and thirst, and desiring an offering, he cries out, "Give me! (42.31).
One who plays with women, is agitated by passion, is well-bathed, speaks pleasantly, is fond of perfumes and garlands, is pure, and desires sexual pleasure—he is known as *ratikāma*. (42.32)
One should know that these two planets are to be propitiated; they are fond of offerings, desires, and pleasures.
[They are also affected] by the taints of great sins, such as the killing of women, cows, or gurus. (33)
At the lotus feet of Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, the planet shall speak the truth;
and having ascertained the planet's desire, it shall act accordingly. (42-34)

Having first ensured his own protection, the practitioner of mantras should perform the treatment for the planetary spirits. He should first effect the cure by offering oblations to the planets with their desired objects;
if they do not release [the patient] through these gentle applications, then he should employ a fierce treatment. (42–35)

One should effect the gradual liberation from the planets by means of ointments combined with specific incenses, as well as through fierce threats and beatings, and by the cutting, piercing, and fire-offerings (homa) of their effigies.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, on the movements of the planets, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
The heart mantra is: *Bhagavacchabda ṣudrāśagatā phacuta mandarakusumaṣaṭpada-vajratuṇḍa nīlāñjanasamaprabha idaṃ bhūtaṃ hana vilipantaṃ kha kha huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.
By reciting this over black gram and rice-mash (*kṛsara*) and striking those who are possessed, [the demon is expelled].
The seizing spirits release him instantly, becoming one with him through meditation on Rudra.

At the end of the heart [mantra]: *bhagavate phaṭ* (to the Blessed One, *phaṭ*), *iśāśa namaḥ* (obeisance to the Lord of the East), *kāśa maheśvarāya* (to the Great Lord of the North-East), *bhramari bhrāmaya* (O female bee, cause to wander), *sūkari bhakṣaya ṭhaṭha* (O female pig, devour, *ṭhaṭha*).
By consecrating black beans (*māṣa*) with this, the seizing spirit (*graha*) is released through eating them.

*Namo bhagavate śudrāśa mahābhairava devāya* (Obeisance to the Blessed One, the Śūdra-lord, the Great Terrifying God), *nartaya* (make dance), *moṭaya* (crush), *valgaya* (leap), *kroḍaya* (gape), *bhrūṃ graha caṇḍa huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.
Through the recitation of mantras and other such means, one may liberate beings from ghosts, spirits, demons, and the like. || 43-2 ||
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *hṛt* (Hrīḥ), and the fierce sound (*Caṇḍaśabda*), followed by *krodharudrāya ṭuṣu puṣu bhūtasamaye tiṣṭha ṭhaṭha*.
Having recited this seven times, one should bind the crest-lock of the one seized [by a spirit].
Then the spirit shall remain bound at that moment within the city of fire and wind. (43-3)

Having written [the mantra] with ash upon that [image], having placed the seized [person] there according to the mantra, and having recited this one hundred and eight times, one should indeed pour water into his mouth. (43-4)
And while reciting [the mantra], one who is angry should throw [a substance] into it; the seizing spirit (graha), having entered, is released.
Having bound a pillar with a rope over which this has been recited, that [spirit] is bound. (43–5)
Having fashioned an image out of flour and having invoked that planet into it,
one should perform the rite of consecrating the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and then tear it apart with a razor.
And one should pierce [the body] with a trident so that blood flows from the vital points;
by this much, whenever it does not release those seized by the grahas, [one should act]. (7)
One should offer the cut image, marked with lines, into the sacrificial pit;
having offered a thousand times, that planet, being consumed by fire, departs and flees.
When black gram, sesame, and mustard seeds have been consecrated a hundred times with this mantra and cast into the fire, the seizing spirit is released.

If one recites the *siddhārtha* mantra seven times over [the substance] while causing the seized person to whirl around toward the desired object, that spirit will transfer [its possession] immediately; of this there is no doubt. (43.10)

The heart-mantra consists of the words *hṛccaṇḍāsipa*, followed by *dhārā*, the two syllables *kilipada*, the two syllables *gaccha*, the word *namaḥ*, and [the name] joined with the wife of the fire of the Great Body (*mahākāyāgnijāyā*). (43.11)
By anointing with this sesame paste, the seizing spirit (graha) shall become terrified. [The mantra is:

*Hṛdayānte bhagavati śuddhaśālipha vācāli bhaveśca cāli nandīśvara kāli indrakāli brahmakāli paretakāli bhadrakāli vajrakāli vara pura hara turu dhara āveśaya kharja garja graha phaṇa phāleśvari! śravaṇadhāriṇi! Oṃ kroṃ proṃ adaḥ cāmuṇḍeśvari! Ṭhaṭha*.
This is joined with the seed-syllable of Nṛhari in the center of the trident situated within the *praṇava*. (43-12)

Having worshipped the spear at the tips of its two sides and having meditated upon that which is situated there as being seized and consumed by fire, one enters [the mantra] and recites it; thus, it releases [the affliction]. (43.13)
The practitioner of mantra should draw the planetary deity upon the ground with charcoal from a poison-tree;
then, with stakes of neem wood over which mantras have been recited, he should pierce it in its vital points.
The planet either dies or departs in an instant after letting out a cry;
its heart is filled with a fierce sound and it is possessed by anger on the fourth lunar day. (43.15)
*Kili mili*, the Lord of Beings commands: *ṭhaṭha*.
At the end of the heart-mantra, for the Blessed Rudra, [the mantra] *cimi* twice.
In the *vile*, the Lord of Beings commands: *ṭhaṭha*.
At night, with the *bhūtakrūra* and *andha* mantras, one should offer the *bali* oblation.
Rice-water, raw grain, parched grain, roasted grain, sesame seeds, curd, and meat—this is declared to be the food of the *bhūtas*, which brings them pleasure. (43.17)

Oṃ, you who dwell in the cremation grounds, you who roam in the charnel grounds, having accepted this offering presented according to the ritual rules, please take up residence elsewhere; protect us today—homage be to you! || 43-18 ||
And with this, one who is composed should offer the bali-oblation in the northeast, using three kuḍuba-measures of food together with spirits, cruel beings, and edible offerings.
In the same way, for the sake of pacification, one should offer a bali-oblation even at the commencement of building a house;
having constructed a three-storied house made of *saptaparṇa* wood on a pure site.
Having encircled it with red garlands, it is adorned with four gates;
and likewise with rice, śyāmāka, and the grains of priyaṅgu.

Having properly cooked three separate *caru* offerings with three *kuḍuba* measures each of curd, milk, blood, and water, respectively, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite over the ground starting from the upper direction.

Having again arranged them in sequence, one should then offer groats prepared from rice and other grains, as well as parched rice made from rice; having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should then place them in the house.
In the northeast, [he offers] rice and barley; in the southwest and southeast, groats of śyāmāka;
and then, in the west, groats of priyaṅgu and parched grain (lāja), followed by [an offering] with the powder [of these grains] mixed with water and turmeric.
Having prepared red water with eight hundred kuḍuba-measures of water,
one should take sesame seeds, mung beans, rice, and black gram, along with *droṇa* flowers.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for everything, one should place it in the northwest according to the prescribed method;
then, having invoked the elemental spirits (bhūtas) into the three layers in their proper order.
Reciting the first mantra, "bhūtāni yāni... and so forth, one should worship the spirits with fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
Having thrown sesame, mung beans, and other such substances, as well as parched flour and fried grain, one by one into red water, together with that [water] and the graha, || 43-28 ||
Having repeatedly performed the *nīrājana* rite over the seized victim with that blood-water,
one should then lead both him and the house containing the bloody water to the crossroads and deposit them there.
One should place the blood-water (raktoda) in the middle of that house and offer oblations (bali) in the cardinal directions,
provided with the remnants of the sacrificial porridge (caru) and likewise with the food for the Bhūtakrūra spirits.

Oṃ! The Niya-kashas, the Saudras, the virtuous, the non-virtuous, the virtuous-and-non-virtuous, the deformed, the multiformed, the terrible-formed, those with the faces of beasts and the faces of birds, those who bring prosperity and those who do not, and the granters of desires—they all desire the offering. To them, the swift ones, together with their hosts, to all these beings, salutations, salutations! With this [mantra], one should scatter the offering in the directions for the sake of universal peace.
Thus shall there be liberation for those seized by all the planetary spirits (grahas). || 43-31 ||
One should draw the fire-house on the ground with red powder;
one should write the seed-syllable in its corners, in the southeast, and the *praṇava* in the center.
Then, having lit a lamp in its center using a new earthen bowl filled with tawny clarified butter and a wick made of lotus fiber; || 43-33 ||
Having covered it with a jar, one should draw the Cintāmaṇi yantra upon its back;
when the Japā flower is situated there and consumed, one should draw the Cintāmaṇi.
Having fixed three staffs of *vaikaṅkata* wood—each as long as the span of the mouth and as thick as the forearm—at the three corners of the pit. (43-35)
Having placed the seized [victim] in their midst, one should encircle them with red garlands;
above them, there should be an auspicious structure made of Akṣa and Kāraskara wood.
Having constructed a pavilion, upon it,
in a shallow vessel filled with three *prastha*s of clarified butter, one should place a thousand lamps.
Having kindled [the fire] and performed the *nīrājana* rite for the one seized by a cruel spirit,
he should offer an oblation (*bali*) in the ten directions with the mantra to be recited hereafter.

"Salutations to those who cause harm, salutations to those who cause injury, to all those who cause misfortune—whether they be existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent—to the hosts of Satas, salutations, salutations!
With this [mantra], one should offer the *bali* and also perform oblations in the fire.
[One should worship] with *japā* and *kiṃśuka* flowers in a triangular *daṇḍa* [diagram] for the purpose of recitation. (43-39)
In a pit, with thousands of Vandāka and Apāmārga plants belonging to those two, one should strike [the patient] with their ashes; the seizing spirit, having entered, will then release him. (43–44)
By offering oblations of Apāmārga wood, Rājī plants, mustard seeds, and sesame seeds— either individually or mixed together— with Vanadurgā, there shall be liberation from the planetary afflictions.
On Sunday at midday, in the courtyard, within a circular mandala made with red, yellow, and black powders and surrounded by flames; || 43-42 ||
On a surface strewn with handfuls of *darbha* grass and covered with reeds and swords,
one should invoke Durgā according to the prescribed rite into a fire kindled as ordained by the rules and worship her.
Having offered clarified butter, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds one hundred times each,
he should offer eight thousand fuel-sticks of the *āditya* tree, sprinkled with cow's products.

Having performed the lustration (nīrājana) for the one who has been seized, one should offer oblations with clarified butter and other substances, as well as with sacrificial porridge (caru); likewise, one should cast offerings of blood-smeared food-balls as bali-oblations to the ten directions.
Just as the planets depart once they have released their grip, so too do minor diseases and other ailments;
likewise, enemy armies and others flee, overcome by fear. (43–46)
Likewise, white guñjā seeds obtained and recited over dispel armies;
and by fasting at a temple of Durgā and offering oblations of *āditya* fuel sticks, [one achieves the same].
Having recited [the mantra], by casting it into water, the seizing spirit and the army depart.
[One should use] the three *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*, and [the mantra]: *ṣeśvasa prajvasa jvāsā pāsiṇī sarvabhūtasaṃhārike varade jātavedasi jvala huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.
[This is done] with cotton seeds, white mustard seeds, sugar-candies, salt, and black pepper.
Or by means of *vakula* and *ariṣṭa* leaves, or with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from milk-exuding trees;
through separate oblations of these fuel-sticks combined with clarified butter, one conquers the affliction caused by the planets. (43–49)
Having offered oblations with oil using a ladle made of śelu wood, one becomes a destroyer of planetary afflictions;
furthermore, when the Puṣya asterism is present, a pill made from dārvī ground with water from the kūṣmāṇḍa plant [should be consumed].
The bark of the *chāyāśuṣka* tree, when applied as an ointment to the eyes, wards off all seizing afflictions (*graha*).
Black pepper, rock salt, long pepper, *gopī* (woodfordia fruticosa), and cinnamon bark, mixed with honey— [43–51]
Then, by means of that collyrium, all the planetary spirits perish instantly upon being entered by it.

Homage to the Blessed One, to the Three Jewels, and homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi, the great general of the host of beings; homage to Caṇḍaśṛṅkhala, the blazing one, whose hair is set ablaze and flaming, the blue-throated one, the one of wondrous form, the pot-bellied one, the one with the mouth of great wisdom, the frowning one, the four-fanged one, the formidable one, the one of greatly transformed appearance, the diamond-wombed one. Come, come! Entering the body, seize the head, move the eyes! O Hari, why do you delay? Terrify and cause to tremble the Siddhas, gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, Nāgas, and Piśācas! Remember the pledge! Strike! Abandon! Cook! Grind! Destroy! The King, the Lord of the Edge of the Fierce Sword, commands: *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*!
This mantra of the fierce sword-blade destroys planetary afflictions through recitation and other such practices.
Oṃ, salutations! We know Khaḍgarāvaṇa; we meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara; may that God inspire us.
By standing in water and reciting this ten thousand times, one becomes perfected; this [mantra] effects liberation from the planetary afflictions.

In the heart: *Namaḥ paśupataye*, *namo bhūtādhipataye*, *namo rudrāya khaḍgarāvaṇāya*. Play, sport, dance, O you whose body is offered to the cremation ground! To the wearer of a garland of bells and skulls, to the one clothed in a tiger skin, to the one who has made the moon his crest-ornament, to the one for whom the black serpent serves as a sacred thread: move, enter every hole, leap, pass over! Skull-bearer, slay the spirits, terrify the circle! Drag them in with the Rudra-hook; cause them to enter the covenant! Caṇḍāsidhārāpati Rudra commands: *Ṭhaṭha*!
This is the mantra of Khaḍgarāvaṇa, which removes all malevolent spirits and planetary influences.
Śiva is to be worshipped upon the lotus of the seat with "oṃ pūṭa bhadi ṭhaṭha. With this, one should invoke him.

Oṃ, obeisance to Paśupati, svāhā; obeisance to the heart, namaḥ. Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Beings, svāhā; to the head, svāhā. Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, svāhā; to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ. Oṃ, O you who have not obtained the sword, Rāvaṇa, sport, take away, move, dance, burst asunder, svāhā; to the armor, huṃ. [Obeisance] to him whose body is smeared with the ashes of the cremation ground, who wears a garland of bells and skulls, who is clothed in a tiger skin, and who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

To the one wearing a black sacrificial thread, Svāhā! To the *astra* weapon, Phaṭ! Oṃ! O Bala, Kila, Tasa, Khaḍga, you who follow the skull-bearer! Strike the spirits! Terrify them within the maṇḍala! Drag them forth with the Rudra-hook! Cause them to enter the pledge (*samaya*)! And summon them! Caṇḍāśidhārādhipati Rudra commands this—Svāhā! To the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ! May he protect you—he whose hands hold the *khaṭvāṅga*, trident, hand-drum, hook, sword, shield, bell, skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*); who has ten arms beginning from the right; who wears jeweled earrings; who has five faces, five heads, and three eyes.
Clad in tiger skin and a lower garment of black antelope hide, resounding with the tinkling of a network of bells at his waist;
adorned with ornaments of bells, bone-garlands, and the lord of serpents; radiant with a sacred thread of snakes;
brilliant as a mass of lightning and white with ashes; with a face made terrifying by flames—
May Śiva, who bears the moon upon his matted hair and possesses the sound of a sword, protect you all. 43–55.
Having bathed according to the rules and sipped water for purification, he should perform his daily rites while remaining silent.
Having worshipped the door and other [limbs] and sat down, and having performed the five purifications,
one should then place the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta upon the hand, the head, and the body.
Having become Śiva and having applied the three-fold long-life ash (triyāyuṣa) to his limbs,
he should worship Gaṇeśa and his Guru, and offer the water of honor (arghya) as prescribed by Śiva.
Having worshipped the spheres of Ādhāraśakti, Ananta, Dharma, Arka, and so forth, as well as Sattva and the others, and Vāmā and the others, one should then worship above them.
One should invoke the form known as Khaḍgarāvaṇa, which resides within the handful of flowers, with the mantra:
*oṃ bhūtapatiḥ svāhā*.
By means of this, one should draw forth the Śaiva light from the heart-lotus into the sky-lotus.
Having brought the *bindu* into that form through rites such as its placement within the heart-lotus,
and having worshipped it with the sixteen services (*upacāra*), one should then worship the retinue.
Then, one should place Khinkhinī, Culukundā, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā,
and Ṭiriṭillā at the tips of the petals starting from the northeast (saumya), moving counter-clockwise.
In the northeast, one should worship Mattavāṇī and also Candrāṅkitajaṭā, as well as Phalgunī with Praskhalinī, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
One should worship Aindrī, Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Cāmuṇḍā, following the sequence starting from the eastern direction;
then Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vārāhī, and Vināyaka. (43–64)
Then, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors in the corners beginning with the northeast,
the Mothers in their respective directions, and Caṇḍeśa and Kṣetreśa in sequence.
Then, having recited the mantra according to one's capacity, one should send forth the Lord.
Caṇḍa, Anugrahavat, Daṇḍin, and Bīja constitute the Khadgarāvaṇa [mantra]. (43–66)

One should visualize the limbs ending with the six weapons using long vowels together with the [six] classes [of phonemes], and the forms beginning with Sadyojāta using short vowels; one should worship them as before.
Having invoked Bhadra Khaḍgarāvaṇa, the Lord of Beings, there according to the previously mentioned procedure with sixty-four words, one should worship him as before. (43–68)

One should meditate upon the three-eyed Lord, who holds a sword, a goad, and displays the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting; whose fangs are fierce, whose body is like a peak of the golden mountain, and whose tongue is a blazing flame; who wears golden earrings and variegated necklaces, whose waist is encircled by a girdle fashioned from rows of bells, and whose hair stands upright.
Indeed, by means of meditation on one's own identity with the form of Khaḍgarāvaṇa and through the recitation of mantras and other practices,
all spirits, planetary deities, and the like depart after releasing the person who has been seized.
Śūlinī, Vanadurgā, the Aghora weapon, the Sudarśana,
the Nṛsiṃha mantras, and the two Aparājita kings of mantras.

And these Vyomavyāpin mantras, which remove the influence of the planets, have already been demonstrated in this tantra; they are to be employed according to the path prescribed in their respective Kalpas. (43–72)

Oṃ raṣṭidehiṃ coktajikādha oṃkāroṃ. Kātyāyanī in the southwest; Kālī, Mahākālī, Vajrakālī, Yaśasvinī, and Sukālī in the southeast; Kālikā, Paṅktiśakti, Śāntākṣī, Indrāṇī, Yakṣakauberī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Cāmuṇḍī, Raudrī, Vārāhī, and Kauberī in the northwest; and whatever others abide in my pledge, I shall recite their names. Seize them quickly! Oṃ lala culu pūraya dhara ānaya subhage! Enter, O Blessed One! O Mahāvajragāndhāri! Siddhacandravajrapāṇi commands: Hrīṃ haḥ hāṃ hāṃ hāṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
This mantra is Vajragāndhārī; the seer (ṛṣi) is considered to be Dīrghatamas; likewise, Aticchandas is the meter, and Viṣṇu and Durgā are its presiding deities. (43–73)
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Viṣṇu and Durgā;
eating only at night, one should constantly recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) shall be accomplished within a month by performing ten-thousandth part of the recitation as an oblation of sesame seeds;
likewise, by offering incense of guggulu that has been consecrated with the mantra ten times while it is being consumed.
One is liberated from piśācas, grahas, and fevers;
by reciting it three times while binding one's topknot, all protection is secured. (43.76)
Whether for oneself or another—up to this point—it is said:
"By five recitations of the *lūtikā* mantra, one removes the poison born of a scorpion;
likewise, by seven for mice and nine for snakes. (43–77)
By reciting it eleven times, all kinds of poison are destroyed;
by fifteen times, it destroys the poison of stationary beings as well as fevers.
By obtaining one hundred and eight mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) and by means of touch, one should offer sesame seeds or flowers to whomever; that person shall come under one's control. (7.89)
Going to war, one shall conquer enemies by tying a topknot after reciting the mantra seven times;
and for the protection of a field, one should drive in a stake made from a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Through oblations of husks, there shall be enmity; through dice, killing and the like.
Alternatively, by [offering] three hundred thousand fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree, one obtains prosperity.

Having worshipped Umāpati, the god who is the lord of the three worlds, one gains mastery over the seven unattainable [substances] through collyrium, perfumes, and the like, as well as through the *tilaka*. Oṃ. (43–82)

Now, therefore, I shall set forth the Mahāpāśupata. It was composed by the Great-Souled Tryambaka himself under the name Paśupati; it is a great scripture, fashioned like a sacrifice, its belly filled with marrow, fat, bones, blood, and grease.

(310) [It is] Rudra, of fierce form, the bringer of bliss to Rudra; the destruction of three and a half crores of supreme mantras, or the accomplishment of one’s own mantras; nourishment based on the supreme state; devoted to the *agnihotra*; the subjugation of the *vidyādharas* by means of ash-powder; the striking down of *rākṣasas* by means of charcoal-powder or iron-powder; the crushing of *daityas* and *nāgas*, the terrifying of *vidyādharas*, and the shattering of great missiles and mantras. To the one-footed, great-tusked, thousand-headed and -bellied, thousand-armed, tongue-faced, whose splendor surpasses that of Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa: *huṃ phaṭ ākaḍḍa*! [Subdue] Baladeva, Maheśvara, Garuḍa, Viṣṇu, Kumāra, Brahmā, Indra, Candra, Āditya, Yakṣa, Rākṣasa, Bhūta, Preta, Piśāca, Kūśmāṇḍa, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūpa, Virūpākṣa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Bṛhatkarṇa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Droṇakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Sthūlakarṇa, Nandikeśvara, Bhṛṅkiriṭi, Nāyaka, Vināyaka, Pāñcika, Dāmaka, Lohaka, Yaṣṭidevī, Oṃkārā, Koṭṭagirikā, Durgā, Kātyāyanī, Kālī, Yaśasvinī, Sukālī, Bhadrakālī, Cullakālī, Āgneyī, Vāyavyā, Śālikāvartī, Rātri, Śakti, Śānti, Śatākṣī, Mahāśāntākṣī, Indrāṇī, Brahmāṇī, Kaumārī, Mahāmārī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Subhagā, Cāmuṇḍī, Vārāhī, Kauberī, Aiśānī. *Gulu mulu culu julu mulu dhaṃ huṃ phaṭ*. *Oṃ kāla phaṭ*. *Oṃ kālarūpāya phaṭ*. *Oṃ kālapāśahasta phaṭ*. *Oṃ kālarūpa phaṭ*. *Oṃ kalavikaraṇa phaṭ*. *Oṃ bala phaṭ*. *Oṃ balapramathana phaṭ*. *Oṃ viśvarūpa phaṭ*. *Oṃ chinda phaṭ*. *Oṃ bhinda phaṭ*. *Oṃ hana phaṭ*. *Oṃ hanata phaṭ*. *Oṃ ghātaya phaṭ*. *Oṃ mohaya phaṭ*. *Oṃ uccāṭaya phaṭ*. *Oṃ saṃhara phaṭ*. *Oṃ saṃkṣipa phaṭ*. *Oṃ pātaya phaṭ*. *Oṃ nipātaya phaṭ*. *Oṃ yathā tattvaṃ paśupatinā samanvitaṃ tathā nipātaya svāhā phaṭ*. *Khā*! By Tryambaka, with the syllables *tvaṃ* and *huṃ*: *oṃ tsaṃ oṃ hiṃ bhakṣaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ aṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ īṃ śirase svāhā*. *Oṃ eṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Oṃ aiṃ kavacāya huṃ*. *Oṃ auṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ aḥ astrāya phaṭ*. *Oṃ*. And the meditation upon this: [The visualization follows.]
His body is tawny-red like a cluster of *japā* flowers, laughing with the flashing radiance of rising lightning;
he wears red ornaments, and his thousand heads— with their mouths possessing fierce, blazing fangs—
bear a thousand arms holding weapons, from which fire blazes forth from every mouth.
May Paśupati, adorned by the *nāgas* and bearing the moon upon his matted locks, protect you all.
This mantra is accomplished through mere recitation for one of firm devotion;
[he who is] always eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), with senses subdued, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa. (43–84)
Standing in the water of a river, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times daily until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; thereafter, this mantra becomes perfected.
One should worship [the deity] in the heart or in water according to the procedure prescribed for the temple;
one should worship the Supreme Lord by means of the path of a single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa).

Reciting [the mantra] according to one's ability, pure and self-restrained, one should meditate at the three junctions of the day; by the mere sight of such a practitioner, malevolent spirits and the like flee away. (43.87)
By merely reciting [the mantra] three times, one shall destroy all diseases;
visualizing oneself as identical with the deity through meditation and recitation, one should strike the afflicted person with prosperity (bhūti). || 43-88 ||
By fumigating with the remains of offerings, all malevolent planets immediately depart;
likewise, by using *śrīvāsa* (sal tree resin), *devadāru* (deodar), and cat dung mixed together. (43.89)

Priyaṅgu, kuṣṭha, cow’s ghee, and banyan bark, ground with honey and mixed with goat’s urine, should be made into pills and dried in the shade; by applying this as a collyrium, [the desired result is achieved].

The release from all planetary afflictions has thus been declared; this beneficial method, seen in the various Tantras, is for the sake of men afflicted by the disturbances of the spirits. Here, the rite for pacifying the terrifying planets must be performed by pure practitioners who have mastered the mantras.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, on the *bhūta*-tantras, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 43.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
Next, the pacification of insanity (unmāda) and epilepsy (apasmāra) is described:
Śatāvarī, Madhuka, Vidārī, Pippalī, and honey. (44–1)
One should drink dates, sugar, and ghee to cure all forms of insanity;
or one should apply the powder of the roots of the *unmatta* plant mixed with sour gruel and oil to the ground.
Having removed [the substance] that was placed for seven days and having smeared it, it brings an end to insanity.
Madhūka, kaṇā, yaṣṭi, mṛdvīkā, musta, and śāribā [are used]. (44.3)
Camphor, sandalwood, clarified butter, breast milk, sugarcane juice, and sugar—these, when ground together and administered as nasal drops, destroy even the most recent cases of insanity. (44–4)
With kuṣṭha, hiṅgu, vacā, yaṣṭi, śirīṣa, and garlic—these, together with goat's urine, used as nasal drops (nasya), collyrium (añjana), and for drinking, destroy delusion. (44–5)

The remains of offerings made to Śivaskandārya, the remains of offerings [to other deities], clarified butter, guggulu resin, vacā, goat hair, cow-tail hair, nimba, and the son of Aśvin (guḍūcī). 44–6.
Incense prepared with rājī and hiṅgu at the three junctions of the day destroys the influence of the planets;
likewise, [incense made from] peacock bile, cow horn, cock's egg, and cat dung [achieves the same].

A fumigation consisting of *vacā*, old hair, *unmattā*, the bone of a *mātula* (a type of lizard), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), and *rājī* and *nimba* leaves combined with *hiṅgu*, destroys the influence of the planets.

Cow’s urine, black pepper, rock salt, the root of the kapittha tree, and long pepper— by applying this as an ointment to the eyes when they are afflicted, one destroys insanity and even the influence of malevolent spirits.
The root of the *vandhyākārkoṭakī* plant together with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), soaked in human urine, dried, and made into a pill, destroys poisonous spirits when applied as an ointment. (44.10)
A plaster made from garlic, neem leaves, and bone causes that seizure-grasping spirit to release [the victim].
An ointment made from the "Mother-killer" (mātṛhā) and the "Tree-spirit" (bhūtavṛkṣa) removes those seizing spirits.
One may ward off the seizing spirits (grahas) through the application of snuff and collyrium made from śirīṣa, hiṅgula, garlic, mañjiṣṭhā, bakā, yaṣṭi, vacā, kuṣṭha, and gulī. 44-12.
From a paste of vyoṣa, hiṅgu, niśā, dāru, śirīṣa, garlic, vacā, karañja seeds, mañjiṣṭhā, and the root of kadalī; 13.
Clarified butter boiled with cow’s urine and water from a plantain tree removes the afflictions of the planets; this is to be understood as being administered by way of drinking and so forth.
One should also take *brahmadaṇḍī*, *muṇḍī*, *kumārī*, and *indravāruṇī*. (44–14)
Having ground these with human urine, [administering them] as a nasal drop (nasya) destroys seizures and insanity.
Bhārgī, salt, kuṣṭha, vṛścikālī, and pippalī—[these are the ingredients]. (44.15)
Pounded into a powder, it destroys epilepsy when used as a nasal drop (nasya).
Dog's bile, collected under the Puṣya asterism and applied as an eye-salve, also destroys epilepsy.
Incense made from that [substance] combined with cow’s ghee destroys epilepsy.
Furthermore, those sesame seeds which have been eaten by a dog on a board made of *vaibhīta* wood [are likewise effective]. (44.17)
That oil, having been reduced to the state of dung, when administered as a nasal drop (nasya), destroys epilepsy;
likewise, the smoke of a wolf's feces and saliva taken nasally shall remove epilepsy.
One should remove the flesh and bone consumed by a wolf by means of nasal drops;
likewise, the resin of *bhūnimba*, *amṛtā*, *pūtīka*, and wild *śigru* [should be used]. (44.19)
If one drinks a decoction of *vandhyākārkoṭakī*, *vyoṣa*, and *kola* for three days or seven days, it removes epilepsy and the influence of malevolent spirits. (44.20)
Vacā, aśvagandhā, kuṣṭha, the two types of niśā, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, the pungent spices, dhātrī, and saindhava salt— one should always take a paste (kalka) made from these.
The decoction of these [drugs] taken separately should measure two *prasthas*;
one should then cook this with two *prasthas* of *brahmī* juice and one *prastha* of ghee.
By drinking that, one destroys epilepsy, insanity, and even the influence of malevolent spirits (*graha*).
One *kuḍuba* each of licorice (*yaṣṭimadhuka*) and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), twenty *kuḍuba*s each of rock salt (*sindhu*) and elephant-urine separately, and five parts of cow’s ghee.

The juice of the kūśmāṇḍa fruit should be made double the quantity of urine and clarified butter; when that ghee is cooked and then drunk, or likewise applied as nasal drops, it destroys those afflicted by epilepsy.

When *śataphala*, *kaśaṅkha*, and *kusuma* have been boiled in two *droṇas* of water until reduced, six *kuḍubas* each of oil and clarified butter added to it will, when prepared and drunk, conquer epilepsy. (44.24½)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, on Epilepsy and Madness, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 44.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
