Next, the previously prepared medicine for diseases is written down,
[to be used] against whatever ailments arise during the constellations, lunar days, and weekdays, whether they be unfavorable or favorable.

Physicians or ministers should discern which [diseases] are curable and which incurable. The asterisms, days of the week, and lunar dates—namely Aśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, Svātī, Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Śatabhiṣaj, Mṛgaśiras, Pūrvaphalgunī, Bhauma (Tuesday), Śukra (Friday), Āditya (Sunday), Vighna (Bhadrā), Guha (Kṛttikā), and the ninth [tithi]—are declared forbidden for the onset of disease; medical treatment and the like will not bear fruit under these conditions.
If illness arises under Kṛttikā, its duration shall be limited to five nights.

One should offer that food— curd and rice— to the fire presiding over that [constellation], for that deity, with the appropriate mantra and the sacrificial materials (bali) as prescribed for each respective constellation deity.
One should offer the bali-oblation with one's own name preceded by "Tārā" and ending in "namaḥ.
Even in the case of Rohiṇī, liberation from disease occurs within five days; this is the decree of Prajāpati. (45–5)
An offering of perfumes, garlands, and boiled rice should be presented to the deity for this person.
Likewise, under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, illness persists for eight nights. (45–46)
One should offer a bali-oblation to Soma with mung beans, black gram, and food;
for ten nights under Ārdrā, however, milk-rice (pāyasa) is the bali-offering intended for Rudra.
If illness occurs during the eight nights of the Punarvasu asterism, its presiding deity is Aditi;
one should offer an oblation (bali) consisting of milk-rice, red perfumes, garlands, and clarified butter. 45–8.
In Puṣya, the illness lasts for five days; its presiding deity is Bṛhaspati.
One should offer him an oblation of fragrant food along with perfumes and garlands. (45–9)
Āśleṣā has the serpents as its presiding deities; an illness occurring under it brings death.
Nevertheless, one should offer oblations through fire-sacrifices, gifts, and the like, using food obtained by begging. (45–10)
Under Makhā, the Pitrya Aṣṭarātra rite is performed, with an offering (bali) consisting of food mixed with sesame seeds.
Under Pūrvā-phalgunī, the deity is Aryaman; the offering consists of perfumes, garlands, and food.
If it occurs in Uttara-phalgunī, the disease will manifest after seven days; for Bhaga, the offering is as before.
In Hasta, whose presiding deity is Savitṛ, [the result occurs] after seven days or after twenty-one days.
Liberation from disease [is attained] through offerings of sacrificial food (haviṣya) accompanied by perfumes and garlands as a bali-offering.
Citrā, however, has Tvaṣṭṛ as its presiding deity; for six days, the bali-offering consists of rice mixed with clarified butter.
In Svāti, there is either liberation from disease or death within five sets of five days (twenty-five days);
one should offer a bali-oblation to Vāyu with white food, perfumes, and garlands.
On the twenty-first day of Viśākhā, one should offer an oblation to Indra and Agni as before.
During the Maitra [Anurādhā] constellation, an oblation of ghee, rice, and other foods should be offered for the sake of liberation from disease. (45.15)
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, liberation occurs after half a month, or death generally takes place;
through gifts and other rites, one should cause an offering of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) to be presented as a bali-oblation to Indra.
Or, if it occurs in Mūlā, there is an offering to Nirṛti with nine days as before;
in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, liberation or death occurs within eight days or eight months. (45–17)
The waters are indeed the deities; for them, the offering (bali) consists of parched grains and the like, along with kṛsara.
In the Vaiśvadeva rite, after seven nights, there should be liberation [from the obstacle], and the offering should be milk-rice (pāyasa). || 45-18 ||
In the Vaiṣṇava asterism, liberation comes after a year; there is an offering of incense, garlands, and food.
In Dhaniṣṭhā, illness does not leave one for thirteen months.
An offering of ghee and green gram rice should be made to the Vasu deities;
in Śatabhiṣaj, there is liberation from the planetary affliction within a fortnight, or death, through the performance of gifts and fire oblations.
One should offer worship to the deity and present an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) to the Lord of Waters.
Under Pūrvabhādrapadā, there is liberation; the deity is Ajaikapād. (45.21)
One should offer an oblation with gifts and the like, using dhātakī flowers and red rice.
Illnesses caused by the Uttarabhādrapadā constellation [arise] over a period of twenty-eight days and nights. (45.22)
Liberation, however, comes through offerings of perfumes, garlands, and food as a bali-offering to Ahibudhnya;
and liberation within a month comes from a bali-offering of perfumes and other items to Pūṣan under the asterism Revatī.
On Aśvinī, there is the offering and weeping at the two Aśvinīs for twenty-five days;
Bharaṇī has Yama as its deity, and on that day, one may live or not. (45.24)
Nevertheless, one should offer oblations with fire-sacrifices, gifts, perfumes, food, and the like;
for an unfavorable conjunction of weekday, lunar mansion, lunar day, and astrological yoga brings about death.

When the desired lunar day and weekday coincide with a favorable asterism, one may live free from the onset of disease through worship of the gods and the twice-born, fire offerings and the like, and the recitation of mantras and so forth. (45.26)

The varieties of fever are of eight types: from vāta, from pitta, from kapha, from sannipāta (the combination of all three), from vāta and pitta, and from the mixture of vāta and śleṣman (kapha). || 45-27 ||
(316) Thus, fever has been described as being of eight types: arising from phlegm (śleṣman), bile (pitta), and injury (abhighāta).
Yawning, coldness, trembling, and pain in the waist, thighs, and head [are its symptoms]. (45.28)
In the wind-type [fever], there is a bitter taste in the mouth, thirst, cough, and lacrimation;
furthermore, there is burning sensation, fainting, delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, and vertigo. (45.29)
Excessive burning, fever, and thirst are the characteristics of a Pitta-type fever; so too are the emergence of coldness, constipation, a sense of numbness, and a sweet taste in the mouth. (45.30)
Nausea, delusion, and coldness—these are the qualities of fever born of phlegm (kapha); as well as incoherent prattle, thirst, fainting, moaning, and vertigo. (45–31)
In the Sannipatika type, there is vomiting of bile and blood, roughness of the tongue, headache, burning sensation, delusion, and dryness of the throat. (45.32)
In the condition arising from vāta and pitta, there is yawning, horripilation, and pain in the joints;
cough, coryza, constipation, vertigo, and pain in the joints and head. (45.33)
Vomiting and numbness are the symptoms in cases arising from kapha and vata;
likewise, stiffness of the limbs, sweating, and vomiting occur in cases of kapha and pitta. (45.34)
A bitter taste in the mouth are indeed the symptoms of fever born of phlegm and bile;
or it may arise from the loss of wealth, sons, and so forth, or from the curse of mantras, deities, and the like. (45.35)
Furthermore, a fever resulting from indigestion or from a minor injury may occur;
that very fever, due to its association with Vāta, becomes another type of irregular (viṣama) fever. (45.36)
Whether by day or by night, that irregular fever may occur at any time;
there is no fixed rule for it, as it may appear either after the lapse of the proper time or even prematurely. (45.37)

A fever occurring every single day is due to a constant rule; one occurring every other day is due to a different rule; and having passed two days, this fever is considered quartan (cāturthika). || 45.38 ||
Irregular fever itself is described separately by these names;
those caused by Vāta and the other humors are treated by specific remedies, as well as by gifts and the worship of gods and Brahmins.
Irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) depart through the recitation of mantras, the use of yantras, and burnt offerings (homa).
Indeed, cold-fever (śītajvara) is of the Vaiṣṇava type, while hot-fever (uṣṇa) is of the Māheśvara type.
At the outset, for those diseases, a remedy is prescribed through gifts, mantras, burnt offerings, oblations, and worship of the deities. (45.41)

One should meditate upon Jvara as fierce, three-eyed, white with ashes, having ashes for weapons, and granting boons with his left hand; he wears slightly copper-colored garlands and ornaments, has a single tusk, and a crown of tawny matted hair. (45-42)
Oṃ larvajvaṣapūṭāśa, obeisance!
Its limbs are the five [syllables] themselves, and the deity is Jvara himself.
The *paṅkti* is the meter and Vyāsa is the sage; with this, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (45–43)

Oṃ, I satiate Jvara. Oṃ, I satiate Śītajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Vātajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Pittajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Śleṣmajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Sānnipātajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Śirorogajvara. Oṃ, I satiate Mahājvara. Oṃ, I satiate Sarvajvara. Oṃ, I satiate all the attendants (pārṣadas) of Jvara.

Having meditated upon the pervasive Lord Jvara as being present on a lotus-seat at the root of a sugarcane plant, one should offer libations during the twilight hours and at night with water mixed with parched grain flour (lāja-saktu). 45–44.
Having cast the spear-offering (śūlabali) and the water for libation (tarpaṇa) into the vessel,
one should release it at the foot of a mango tree for the pacification of a fever lasting three days.
Oṃ, at the end of the heart [mantra], to the Blessed One, the destroyer of the three worlds, huṃ phaṭ khe kṣa! Enter the midst of the piśācas, huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha!

Having placed a ball of cooked rice mixed with ghee and curd in a bronze vessel, one should invoke the deity named Śūla into it with this mantra, worship him, and recite the mantra one hundred times. (45–46)

One should place three lamps in the form of a trident upon the *piṇḍa*; with that, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) for the subject, which removes diseases and the influence of malevolent planets. (45–47)
In connection with the *śūlabali*, the *kapālabali* is now described:
having filled a new earthen bowl with an *āḍhaka* measure of blood-water, one should ignite a lamp made of flour twelve finger-breadths in height in its center. (45–48)
Having meditated upon that skull and performed the ritual gesture, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times:
*oṃ hṛd brahmā pārśvabhūbījo dīrgho vāyur viṣaṃ ca hā*. (45–49)
*Mudrā ya preṃ kṣa pālaya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.

Having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony for the object of the rite (*sādhya*) with this mantra, one should place it at a crossroads, [accompanied] by the mantras beginning with Kubera and the aforementioned limbs (*aṅga*), sprinkled with milk. (45–50)
One should offer oblations with one thousand leaves of the *āmra* tree for the pacification of fever.
Oṃ!
You are Kubera; you are Rudra; bring joy and bliss to Nandin. (45–51)
[It destroys] fever, death, and terrible fear; it generates fever, [it is] fever.
Oṃ Svāhā! This is the mantra beginning with Kubera.
Seated upon a white lotus at the root of a sugarcane stalk, he holds a lotus, a trident, a horn, and a skull-cup.
Clad in white garments, three-eyed, with a lean body, white with ashes, and possessing a beautiful matted lock—such would be Jvara. || 45-52 ||
Having thus dispelled this fever of Maheśvara and having worshipped him, one should mutter this mantra: *Tāraṃ ca hṛd bhagavate śudrāśa rudrajvara kṛtāntarūpāya hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ*.
Rudra is its deity; its limbs [are assigned] by their respective syllables, distinguished by their [mantric] classes. (45–53)
Pure, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at night; having meditated upon the fever, it is mastered.
One should visualize the object of the rite within a lotus in the ocean of milk, situated in the center of a lunar disc.
Having touched [the patient] and meditated, one should recite [the mantra]; the release from fever will occur.
*Oṃ bhasmāyudhāya vidmahe | ekadaṃṣṭrāya dhīmahe | tanno jvaraḥ pracodayāt |* This is the *Jvaragāyatrī*.
With this, one should scatter ashes that have been consecrated by recitation for the pacification of fever. (45–55)

Homage to the Three Jewels! I shall now recite the heart-mantra: "O, O Fever, listen! Strike! Roar! Vomit! All fevers, move away! Vajrapāṇi commands: release the head, release the throat, release the chest, release the heart, release the belly, release the waist, release the shanks, release the feet! Caṇḍapāṇi commands: *huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*! (p. 319) This mantra has the Buddha as its presiding deity; by the natural recitation of this mantra, or by the separate burning of guggulu incense, fever is destroyed. (45–56)

A pitcher, placed within an enclosure of *vṛtta* and *svarāvṛta* diagrams inside an earthen house, destroys fever when held; it should be inscribed with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended.
This refers to that sonless Brāhmaṇa who died on the banks of the Sarasvatī. (45–57)
To him one should offer water with sesame seeds; thus the fever lasting for a single day shall be released.
In the morning, with this handful of water containing *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds— || 45-58 ||
Having propitiated [the deity] with a red flower and offered it, a fever lasting for one day is cured;
likewise by means of earth remaining after cleaning, taken from the dwelling of seven crabs.
One should prepare the *puṇḍra* for three days, destroying [the previous one] at intervals.
There should be six lines facing east and six lines facing north. (45–60)
In the outer twenty squares, on the final rows, place the syllable of the inner earth;
in the remaining [squares] at the tips of the lines where the name of the person to be accomplished remains, it is joined with tridents.
Having drawn the yantra and worshipped it with offerings of five-colored rice, one should bind [the patient];
thus, the quartan fever and even fevers appearing like those are destroyed.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllable joined with *tāra* (oṃ) and *agni* (ra) upon the sides, the space between the eyebrows, the heart, and the navel-junctions,
one should meditate upon the victim as a tiger and touch his various limbs.
One should recite [the mantra] three times while removing the white [powder], and one should meditate upon that limb which is without armor;
this should be done on the days when the fever is due to arrive, for the pacification of quartan fever.
A six-cornered [diagram] should be drawn facing south and north, with a star in the center;
on both sides of the star is *māṃsa*, and in the corners is *agni*, outside of which is that [same]. (45–65)
Having drawn six goads (aṅkuśas) at the junctions of the corners and having worshipped the Tāraka mantra, one should recite the mantra of the noose and goad; when worn, it removes all fevers.
At the end of the heart [mantra], [recite]: *bhagavate ṣudrāśabandha jvara huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*.
By this, through binding the topknot (*śikhābandha*) seven times, fever is destroyed;
the fever becomes bound.
One should wear upon the head a *cūḍāphala* fruit encircled by *tintriṇī*. || 45-67 ||

If one does not eliminate a quartan fever, one should fumigate the patient—covered with a cloth—with equal parts of *bhṛṅga*, *guñjā*, and *abhraka* mixed with oil; thus that fever will perish. (45–68)

One should drink *vandāka* originating from the *bilva* tree with either buttermilk or ghee for the destruction of intermittent fever (*viṣamajvara*); one should also perform acts of charity and other such rites. (45–69)

In a grid of nine squares formed by nine lines running east-west and north-south, one should place the *tattva-śūla* at the ends of the lines; within the squares and the enclosures on the ground, [the ritual proceeds].

One should sequentially write the letters beginning with Vāyu (Ya), colored black, red, yellow, and white, accompanied by the bindu, in numbers equal to those of the necklaces, waters, beloveds, and rays (four, four, three, and twelve respectively). (45–71)
Having performed the sacrifice and recited the mantra, one should lie down upon it for the pacification of fever;
one should write the name-inlaid with the syllable *khaṃ* in the center of a jar, and this is its offering.

An eight-petaled lotus with the sun at its center, surrounded externally by a thirty-petaled lotus joined with the letters beginning with *ka* and ending in the vowels (*ā*), and outside of that, the water mandala.
This *sañjīvana* yantra removes all fevers caused by *rakṣasas*;
it should be placed within the *mṛtyuñjaya* enclosure and have the name interlaced with the *jīva* mantra. (45–74)
Then, having covered the circle surrounded by the outermost [lotus], one should likewise [place] the Mṛtyuñjaya-mantra within the eight petals,
on the outer sixteen-petaled lotus.

In the enclosures of Mṛtyuñjaya, there is an external lotus with petals of passion; the consonants from *ka* to *sa*, along with the vowels, are arranged on the petals, and that darkness is surrounded externally by Śakti.
Having encircled this diagram called Mṛtyuñjaya three times with the seed-syllable *mā*, it pacifies all diseases, planetary afflictions, and pains when worn upon the head. (45–77)
In the corners of the square are the *tāra* (the syllable Om) and the *śakti* (the syllable Hrīṃ) located in the center;
that yantra, with the name "Śakti," is the destroyer of the appearance of fever.
One should write the name of Śakti on the exterior of an eight-petaled lotus;
the vowels should be placed in the filaments, and the consonant groups beginning with 'ka' should also be placed upon the seven petals.
In the eighth [square], one should place two at the end; outside, one should encircle it three times with a noose and restrain it with a hook. This yantra accomplishes all aims.
In cases of fever, no medical treatment is prescribed until the seventh day;
one should fast as long as strength remains, for cow's milk and boiled rice are prohibited.
Let him drink a gruel prepared without grain and cooked with *viśvā* and *parpaṭa*;
the decoction of the five roots (*pañcamūla*) is the best digestive for fever caused by wind (*marujvara*). (45–82)
In the case of Pitta-type [dysuria], a decoction of *amṛtā*, *pippalīmūla*, and *śuṇṭhī* is used;
likewise, two types of *bṛhatī* and a suppository made from *śuṇṭhī*, *bhūnimba*, and *gokṣura*. (45–83)
In fever caused by *kapha*, a decoction combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) should be drunk;
[the decoction] of *chinnā*, *gokṣura*, *mustā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*. (45–84)
By drinking a decoction of viśvā, hrībera, kaṭphala, and parpaṭaka, vāta-fever accompanied by tremors of the limbs is dispelled immediately. (45–85)

A decoction made from the five [drugs] beginning with *bilva* and a decoction made from *viśvā* are both recommended for fever caused by *vāta*, characterized by emaciation, chronic duration, and painful touch, as well as for trembling and pain in the limbs. (45–86)
One should drink [the decoction] boiled with chinnā, viśvā, pañcamūla, and pippalīmūla in cases of vāta-fever characterized by piercing pain in all the limbs, joints, bones, and head. (45–87)
Water boiled with one part each of *kustumburu* and *viśvā* (ginger) should be drunk;
it instantly destroys fevers arising from the three *doṣas*, as well as burning sensations and delusions. (45–88)
Mustā, parpaṭa, duḥsparśā, pāṭhā, and uśīra boiled with water—this formulation, when combined with a small amount of sugar, removes fever caused by pitta. (45.89)
One should drink bitter neem with sugar in water to alleviate fever caused by pitta.
[One may also use] a decoction of viśva, uśīra, gulūcī, ambu, pāṭhā, duḥsparśa, and dhānyaka. (45–90)
A decoction of *kustumburu*, *devadāru*, *nāgara*, and the two types of *bṛhatī* should be drunk in cases of fever caused by *pitta*; it removes vertigo, thirst, and exhaustion. (45.91)
This decoction, when boiled and drunk, destroys the first stage of fever;
a decoction of vāśā, viśvā, abda, and marica removes fever caused by kapha.
Or else, one may take [a decoction] boiled with *viḷaṅga*, *viśvā*, *bilva*, *abja* (lotus), and *suradāru*, with a small amount of honey added;
or [a preparation of] *niśā*, *abja*, *triphalā*, *tiktā*, *paṭolī*, and *picumanda*. (45–93)
Devadāru boiled with kaṇṭakārī, pippalīmūla, and the two types of ḍuṇḍuka destroys sannipāta fever. (45.94)
A decoction made from *tikta*, *śleṣmātaka*, *abdaka*, *marica*, *bhūnimba*, *ariṣṭa*, *vatsaka*, *chinnā*, *paṭola*, and *pāṭhā* removes all fevers. (45.95)

A man afflicted by dyspnea, one who has fallen down, one suffering from fever that is neither too cold nor too hot, one with wandering vision, one who speaks incoherently, and one afflicted by abhinyāsa [should be known]. || 45-96 ||

One should destroy *abhinyāsa* occurring at the two junctions [of day and night] by means of drinking, nasal medication (*nasya*), and collyrium (*añjana*) prepared with *sindhūttha*, *hastipippalī*, *madhuka*, *asthi*, *vaca*, and *uṣaṇa*. (45.97)

A decoction prepared from *vyāghrī*, lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), *bhūnimba*, *bhārgī*, and *duḥsparśā* destroys *abhinyāsa*; likewise, one boiled with *vyoṣa*, *ugrā*, and *bhārgī* does so as well. (45.98)
Water boiled with dhātrī, kustumburu, chinnā, and candana, mixed with sugar and honey, should be drunk; it removes fever caused by kapha and vāta. (45.99)

Water boiled with one part each of *chinnā*, *pathyā*, and *nāgara*—taken in portions of three, two, or one respectively—along with rice, cures hiccups, dyspnea, cough, throat obstruction, wasting, and delusions;
it also destroys wind-obstruction (*vāyusaṅga*) and fever caused by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). (45–100)
A decoction made from equal parts of chinnā, paṭola, triphalā, ghanasāraka, nimba, śalākā, and dhāmyāka destroys all fevers. (45.101)
A decoction of vāśā, devadruma, dhātrī, pathyā, vartī, and nāgara,
combined with sugar and honey, removes quartan fever (cāturthika).
Having thrown a single bedbug into a guḷa the size of a jujube fruit, one should swallow it;
thus even quartan fever, as well as quotidian and tertian fevers, are destroyed. (45.103)
One should fumigate with *sahadevā* mixed with cow's urine in cases of irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*).
By means of incense combined with tawny clarified butter (*kapilājya*), one shall destroy irregular fever. (45.104)

One suffering from chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), cough, loss of appetite, indigestion, or fever should drink a decoction of *chinnā*, *nidigdhikā*, and *viśvā* combined with *kṛṣṇā*. This will eliminate these ailments. (45.105)
Ghee prepared with *chinnā* and its paste conquers fever.
On the forehead (*bhrūbimba*), there are three lines extending from east to north. (45.106)
In the center, upon a five-petalled lotus, [one should place the deities] ending with those joined to their names;
outside the [central] image, in the four directions, and on the intermediate corners, [one should place] Śrīkaṇṭha.
Having written the mantra together with the *sākṣamantya* on a *citāmṛkṣī* leaf, one should worship it with *arka* flowers;
and having offered the *bali*, one should practice [this] at twilight for the sake of pacifying the breath. (45.108)
"Remove the affliction caused by the breath of Kinnaras, Kiṃpuruṣas, Garuḍas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas; [remove] that of the Pitṛs and Piśācas! Ṭhaṭha!
One should write the name within a mantra situated inside a vajra-drawn ground-palace;
having worshipped around the vajra, ghee [is offered], which destroys asthma. (45.109)
One should give the food remaining from his meal to a dog that eats with its mouth;
having mixed the fruit of the *kṛṣṇārambhā* plant into cow urine, one should consume it.
One suffering from asthma should lick a stick of *bhārgikā* in honey to remove it;
one should drink the flower of the *sāptaparṇa* with whey to cure asthma. (45.111)
It should be the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*).
A powder of *viśvā*, *pathyā*, and *abda* (musta), rolled into pills with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be held in the mouth; it is an excellent remedy for acute cough and dyspnea. (45–112)
One should lick every morning a powder of *viśva*, black salt, *śuṇṭhī*, and *marica* mixed with oil and jaggery; this immediately removes cough and dyspnea. (45.113)
One should lick a powder of viśvalā, gairika, and tryūṣa mixed with honey and clarified butter in the morning to cure asthma, according to the word of Paṭa. (45.114)
Black pepper, harītakī, ginger, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and añjana—these five, when licked with honey, are known to cure the five types of hiccups. (45.115)
Asafoetida, *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, cardamom, red ochre, black pepper, honey, sandalwood, and *indravaca*—these, when used as a linctus, remove asthma and hiccups. (1.116)
Honey and clarified butter with the ash of *śālala* destroy hiccup and asthma;
[this refers to] the ash of the *śalalī* thorn. Black pepper, ginger, sugar, and *dhātrī*, combined with the powder of a peacock's tail and saturated with honey—[these are the remedies]. (45.117)
One removes hiccup by taking black pepper, dates, and *kharjūra* with honey. Likewise:
*Vai vediṣu bandha hā ta śabhātaśa niruddha pūrṇamaṇi ṭhaṭha*.
Having visualized the earth-maṇḍala at the throat, one should drink water while reciting this mantra. (45–118)
It removes vomiting.

Blue lotus, sandalwood, *lodhra*, saffron, licorice, and honey—licked together, these remove vomiting caused by *pitta*. Alternatively, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*) with rock salt [likewise remove it]. (45.119)
Sūkṣmailā, triphalā, and honey are known to remove phlegm and vomiting;
so too are the four spices (cāturjāta), long pepper (pippalī), the juice of horse dung, and honey. (45-120)
A linctus made from parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with sugar destroys all types of vomiting.
[Likewise, a linctus of] ginger, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), parched grain, *lodhra*, *aṅkola*, *añjana*, and cinnamon bark [is effective]. (45–121)
These [medicines], when licked with honey individually as prescribed for each quarter-verse, cure vomiting.
"O Cāpha, O Brahmaṇyā, O Ilatyahāḍiṇi, you shall not exist! O Goddess Virūpā, descend according to my desire! Kāmiṣṭha phu ṭhaṭha!
By means of water consecrated with this mantra, those afflicted by desire (kāmilāḥ) should perform bathing and drinking. (45–122)
The fresh juice of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, saturated with *dhātrī*, *rātri*, and honey, when drunk with warm milk straight from the udder, destroys the five types of jaundice. (45.123)
Cow's curd mixed with buffalo urine and a small amount of cumin powder will cure the five types of jaundice. (45.124)
Especially for jaundice (*kāmilā*):
In the morning, having churned the water of *nāgabalā* mixed with buffalo curd, and having discarded the thick cream (*dhana*), drinking that liquid removes jaundice. (45–125)
One should drink *nāgabalā* with buttermilk mixed with the root of red *apāmārga*;
having anointed the head with the water of a horn, one should also constantly smell *ajjhaṭā*. (45.126)
Kāmalā departs.
A decoction of *chinnā*, *madhūka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *nimba*, drunk with plenty of honey while avoiding sour and salty foods, destroys that *kāmalā*. (45.127)
One suffering from jaundice (kāmalā) should avoid salty, sour, and hot foods.
Bitumen (śilājatu), when processed with the urine of animals, cures chronic jaundice (kumbhakāmalaka).
When medical treatment is not administered, jaundice turns into anemia;
a remedy for that is seen here to some extent. (45.129)
A decoction of *tiktā*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *vāśā*, *chinnā*, along with *bhūnimba* and *nimba*, when mixed with honey, destroys jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*) and *kāmalā*. (45.130)
One should cause [the patient] to drink viśvā, dīpyaka, rock salt (sindhūttha), bhṛṅga, pathyā, citraka, and bhūkadamba with buttermilk; this removes jaundice (pāṇḍuroga). || 45-131 ||
Punarnavā root, pathyā, bhṛṅga, nāgara, dīpyaka, balā, atibalā, citra, badarī, and candana, in equal parts. (45.132)
One should drink the iron dross (kiṭṭa) processed by them with equal parts once the liquid has been churned;
by consuming it while avoiding sour and salty foods, one may eliminate the five types of jaundice (pāṇḍu-gada). || 45-133 ||
Or one should drink *viśvābala*, *bhṛṅga*, sesame, and the dross of iron;
or one should drink *bhṛṅga* with sesame and buttermilk to conquer the disease of jaundice. (45.134)
A decoction of *bandhūka*, *vāsā*, and *chinnā* taken with honey conquers *raktapitta*; or water prepared with *chinnā* and honey may likewise be used. (45.135)
The utpala lotus with its root, grapes, plantain, the filaments of the lotus, the shoots and sprouts of the banyan tree, the heartwood of the kāśmarī, and liquorice (yaṣṭi). || 45-136 ||

One who has risen from sleep should drink the decoction of these [drugs] taken in equal parts, mixed with honey and sugar, in the morning; thus, the hemorrhagic disorder (raktapitta) is destroyed. (45.137)
And [the treatment of] prameha.
(p. 326) One should draw two lines each toward the east and the north; at the ends of the lines, eight thunderbolts, with the *tāra* (Oṃ) in the center, and outside of that. (45.138)
The syllable *Tāraṃ* (Om) should be written in that square and likewise placed upon the palm of the hand;
when shown after meditating on it as nectar, it shall destroy diseases of the head.
But in this wheel, excluding the two [squares] marked with *tāra*, one should write the poison of the solar eclipse, together with the letter *ya* and a half-moon, within the four squares. (45–140)
In the center is Supāśa-Kroḍīśa; around the circle is the mantra, namely Ananta and the syllable *ṇi*, both repeated, followed by Pinākin. (45-141)
One should double the length of the syllable *someśa* and also repeat the syllable *ṇi*;
this mantra, ending with *ṭha ṭha ṇemi ṭha ṭha*, should be written in a clockwise direction.
By performing sacrifices and offering oblations, one may destroy a bound headache;
for headache arises from wind (vāta), while from bile (pitta) it arises due to excessive heat and the provocation of that which is extremely hot. 45.143.

From phlegm (kapha) comes heaviness of the head; all these symptoms are present in the disease caused by the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika). Sūryāvarta headache increases excessively during the forenoon. (45–144)
That [disease] arising from phlegm and wind subsides in the afternoon;
it is a splitting pain in one half of the head known as *ardhāvabhedaka*, while *śaṅkhaka* is characterized by pain in the temple (*śaṅkha*). (45–145)
And those two [conditions] are dependent on vāta.
In cases of vātika disorders, one should drink kulattha, māṣa, and mudga with clarified butter;
in diseases of the head and in śaṅkhaka, one should apply that same triad with clarified butter as an ointment. (45–146)

One should grind together in equal parts *dhātrī*, *vacā*, *malayaja*, *balā*, *arjaka*, *karpūra*, *yaṣṭi*, *hirivera*, and *uśīraka* on a stone with rice-water; this paste should be applied to the head for the purpose of pacifying all types of headache. (45.147)
An old ciñcā fruit, combined with sugar and ginger,
and taken as a nasal drop (nasya) with rice-water, will surely eliminate headache.
Having ground together dūrvā roots, niśā, uśīra, yaṣṭīmadhuka, candana,
and sprouts of nandyāvarta with water, that liquid [is prepared].

When smeared with sugar, it destroys *sūryāvarta*. Likewise, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), ginger (*nāgara*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and the root-fiber of cotton (*kārpāsasya śiphā*) [are effective]. (45-150)
Indeed, this [mixture], lukewarm and mixed with clarified butter, certainly destroys diseases of the head when used as a nasal drop (nasya).
One should grind the roots of *kuśmāṇḍa* and *eraṇḍa* and apply them as a plaster with sour gruel (*śukta*). || 45-151 ||
Alternatively, for the pacification of diseases of the head, one may use the bark of the *pāribhadraka* tree;
likewise, separate wicks made from the powder of *niśā*, *marica*, and *viśva* [may be used]. (45.152)
When employed as incense, they destroy diseases of the head;
go to that Vindhya mountain, O lady of virtuous vows, where you have come from—may prosperity be yours! (45.153)
Ṭhaṭha.
The mantra beginning with *dṛk*, *puṣpa*, and *hṛdaya* is prescribed for sprinkling with water and other substances.
Having drawn lines in the earth-chamber (bhūgṛha) joined with the eight vowels, || 45-154 ||
Having been lowered here by another, those women with curved glances were seen; from drinking from the mouths of those wearing sandals, no pustules shall arise. (45.155)
Hirivera, kājīvantī, chinnā, vāsā, śārivā, dārvī, candana, nimba, the three myrobalans (triphalā), uśīra, and toyada; || 45.156 ||
A decoction with honey and jaggery wards off *masūrikā* (smallpox).
If one drinks a decoction of *paṭola* and *nimba* mixed with sugar, [the same result follows]. (45.157)
Before the eruption of smallpox, smallpox does not arise;
one should drink water produced from buffalo dung mixed with sandalwood juice. (45.158)
If one presses a *prastha* measure of the husks of *dhātrī* fruit that has been soaked in human urine for a day and drinks it, *masūrikā* eruptions will not arise for that person. (45.159)

Having ground equal parts of rock salt (*sindhūttha*), yellow myrobalan (*pathyā*), and ginger (*viśvā*) with warm water, one should drink it; this will destroy abdominal distension (*ānāha*), constipation (*viṣṭambha*), and disorders of the stomach (*āmadoṣa*). (45.160)
One should drink Pathyā, Ādīpyaka, Sindhūttha, Kaṇā, and Viśvā, boiled with whey or buttermilk, in the morning; this kindles the digestive fire. (45.161)

If one drinks in the morning *pathyā*, *kaṇā*, and so forth, along with rock salt, in proportions of six, four, two, and one parts respectively, boiled with buttermilk—how could there be loss of appetite? (45.162)
And [this is] an ignitor of the digestive fire: (p.
328) One *droṇa* of the root of *viśvā* mixed with rock salt and cooked in buttermilk, when drunk in the morning, generates the fire of wrath and destroys lack of appetite. (45.163)
Asafoetida, rock salt, long pepper, and ginger—one part of each—and double that amount of chebulic myrobalan;
when drunk with warm water, these act as laxatives and digestive stimulants for men. (45.164)
Gulūcī, rock salt (saindhava), pathyā, and ginger (nāgara) in equal parts, boiled and drunk after churning [the mixture], increase the strength of the digestive fire. (45.165)
A decoction prepared with bhallātaka, bhārgī, laghu-mūla, pathyā, agni, rājī, marica, yavānī, sindhūttha, and dīpya—when taken lukewarm—destroys disorders of vāyu and kapha. (45–166)
Equal parts of white sugar, rock salt, and black salt, finely powdered and drunk with very warm water, immediately provide relief from heart disease. (45.167)
An apūpa cake prepared with rice grains and cooked in oil, using vārāhī and citravāśā, when eaten immediately provides relief from heart disease. (45.168)

A decoction of *duḥsparśanā* (dūrvā), *nāgara* (ginger), and *balā*, with an addition of rock salt (*saindhava*), destroys pain in the flanks, heart disease, and upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*). (45.169)
A decoction mixed with the powder of *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, and *viśva*, when drunk, cures all forms of *grahaṇī* and kindles the digestive fire. (45.170)
One should drink long pepper, costus, and dry ginger with warm water at night;
this will cure all types of malabsorption (grahaṇī) as well as visual defects and other ailments. (45.171)
Burning of the hands and drinking water mixed with salt also conquer *viṣūcī* (cholera).
[A decoction] prepared with *mustā*, *uśīra*, *kaṇāmūla*, *kalaśī*, and *viśva* [is likewise effective]. (45.172)
One should drink water with the leaves of the *jambu* and *āmra* trees to destroy *viṣūci*; it should contain pungent substances, the five salts, and a small amount of *snuhi* milk. (45.173)
If taken with very warm water, it overcomes severe cholera (viṣūcikā).
Pathyā, the salt called piṇḍa, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, and vacā [are used for this]. (45.174)
Yellow [drugs] taken with pleasant water destroy cholera (viṣūcikā) along with its root;
one should drink a mixture of citra, vatsaka, viśvā, ambu, rāmaṭha, and ativiṣā.
Pāṭhā, jyotiṣmatī, karṇī, vatsaka, and kustumburu; or vacā, abda, ativiṣā, śuṇṭhī, bilva, vatsaka, and rāmaṭha. (45.176)
Warm *takrakañcika* (sour buttermilk) when drunk brings relief from diarrhea;
likewise, a decoction of *mustā* with honey cures chronic diarrhea. (45.177)
Abhayā, ativiṣā, viśvā, devadāru, vacā, and ambuda, ground with warm water and drunk, bring about the pacification of all types of diarrhea. (45.178)

Sindhūttha salt, asafoetida, black pepper, garlic, ginger, the bark of the karañja tree, ajamoda, cumin, cardamom, ginger, and long pepper—when drunk with the scum of churned buttermilk, this mixture here removes blood in cases of diarrhea accompanied by mucus. (45.179)
Amrāsthi, dipyaka, viśvāsa, aṅga, and rice sprouts, churned with buttermilk and abhayā and cooked, cure saṅgrahaṇī and grahaṇī disorders. (45.180)

One should drink a decoction of *yaṣṭī*, *vatsaka*, *bhūnimba*, *pāṭhā*, and the two types of *rātri* (turmeric and *dāruharidrā*) with buttermilk; this immediately removes diarrhea caused by recent [poison] ingestion. 45-181.
Bhṛṅgī, samaṅgā, kalaśī, sābdā, ativiṣā, and dāru—ground together or decocted, this [medicine] destroys wind-diarrhea when kept in a secure place. (45.182)
Having ground the roots of *śakravallī* and drunk them with buttermilk mixed with honey, or with whey (*mastu*) or sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one shall overcome diarrhea. (45.183)
A decoction prepared from *chinnā*, *pāṭhā*, *abdha* (musta), *bhūnimba*, *viśva* (śuṇṭhī), and *vatsaka*, when drunk, removes fever accompanied by diarrhea in an instant. (45.184)
One should drink black sesame seeds, *vayasthā*, *lodhra*, liquorice, and white lotuses with goat’s milk every morning for the alleviation of bloody diarrhea. (45.185)
From Vāta, it occurs in the bladder; from Pitta, there is burning in the navel;
and that born of Kapha involves nausea in the heart. However, if it is systemic (sarvaga), it is incurable. (45.186)

Water boiled with six leaves of castor plant (*eraṇḍa*), combined with a small amount of rock salt (*saindhava*), used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) destroys wind-pain (*vātaśūla*); likewise, water boiled with the leaves of *viśvāci* and *ciñcā* [is effective]. (45.187)
Asafoetida, the three pungents, rock salt, costus, ugrā, and powdered śilājatu—when drunk together with warm water, these indeed remove colic instantly. (1.188)
One should cook oil with the leaves of *Ladhveraṇḍa* in water, combined with a paste of asafoetida and rock salt; by using that as a nasal drop (*nasya*), pain is destroyed instantly. (45.189)
One *karṣa* each of *kuberākṣī* fruit, ginger, and garlic—
this decoction, when combined with the powders of asafoetida and *sundhūta*, destroys all types of colic.
From *hiṅgu* and rock salt, one should add castor oil in triple the quantity, and water equal to all those ingredients; this preparation with garlic conquers all types of colic. (45.91)
A decoction of the entire plant of *viḷaṅga*, taken with asafoetida and rock salt, destroys all types of colic; it must not be disclosed to those of wicked character. (45.192)
Having cut off the tip of a coconut and covered it with clay, one should burn it;
then, having ground a niṣka of castor seeds, one should stir them into that water.
One should drink it while still warm; the stone falls away instantly in a moment.
Likewise, the root of red lotus and arka, when drunk with warm water, [achieves the same]. (45.194)
It causes the stone to fall immediately and destroys dysuria;
one should drink the root of *matsyākṣī* with its own juice to cause the gravel to fall. (45-195)
Water boiled with equal parts of *sarpākṣī*, *vanamallikā*, *varaṇa*, *apāmārga*, the two types of *śigru*, *bhadrā*, *gokṣuraka*, *kāśamarda*, *subhagā*, white lotuses,
and black *kulattha* beans, along with coconut water— [This is the medicinal preparation.]
One should drink [this] together with black pepper; then the painful calculus, having been broken apart, will fall away. (45.196)

Honey enriched with a paste of *jambū* leaves and tender shoots, when drunk, overcomes urinary distress (*kṛcchra*). [Likewise, honey] with *elā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *madhūka* pollen, and *pūtīka* [is effective]. (45.197)
One should cook *śilājatu* with the separate decoction of *aśmabhedi*; one should drink that, which removes urinary calculi, dysuria, heart disease, and gravel. (45.198)
Coconut water mixed with jujube and cumin conquers *kṛcchra*;
likewise, the paste of *chinnā* with sugar and cow’s milk conquers *kṛcchra*. (45.199)
Having mixed the ashes of *pāribhadra* bark along with those produced from all parts of the *apāmārga* plant, one should drink it with castor oil; this destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
A decoction of *bilva* root, taken warm with rock salt, removes colic in abdominal tumors (*gulma*); likewise, a decoction made from wild *śigru* [is effective]. (45.201)
Madhuka, drākṣā, padmaka, and candana, mixed with honey and milk and drunk with rice-water, are an excellent remedy for removing pitta-type gulma. (45.202)
Having placed a *tulā* (ten *kārṣas*) of *snuhī* fragments mixed with an equal amount of salt in a vessel and coated it with clay, one should then burn it in a fire of dried cow-dung (*karīṣāgni*).

Once it has cooled, one should extract it and drink the boiled *kāñjika*; the five types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) are destroyed by this, and it also stimulates the digestive fire (*kāyāgni*). (45.204)

A decoction made from equal parts of *ciribilva* bark, ginger, and black *kulattha* beans, combined with long pepper (*kaṇā*) and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), brings about the pacification of phlegmatic abdominal tumors (*śleṣmagulma*). (45.205)
One should burn apāmārga together with fruits equal in quantity to those of arjuna;
then, one should cook black kulattha beans in water stirred with that ash.
One should drink that water mixed with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), which removes the five types of abdominal tumors (*pañca-gulma*).
One should boil *vilanga* with its roots and *bhallātaka* seeds in one *droṇa* of water until a quarter remains;
this, prepared with its own paste and the *ūṣaṇas*, and mixed with an equal amount of honey, shall remove colic and abdominal tumors. (45–207)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, on the medical treatment of fevers and other ailments, in the Mantra-pāda of the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 45.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Mango stone, *lāja*, salt, parched grain, rock salt, and sugar;
pomegranate, parched grain, and rock salt [are used] for the child’s hiccup, vomiting, and heart disease. (46–1)
p. 332) That is to say, the three [substances] from Prayāga along with honey;
or one should lick parched rice and blue lotus with breast milk;
or one should stir long pepper and *samaṅgā* together and lick them for the pacification of fever and diarrhea. (46-2)

By consuming a decoction of the two types of *niśā* (turmeric) together with *siṃhī*, *yaṣṭī* (liquorice), and sugar, one overcomes vomiting and diarrhea; this should be ground into a paste and administered in small quantities. 46-3.
One should have a child lick ativiṣā with honey to alleviate vomiting and fever;
likewise, water boiled with the three fruits (triphalā), sahā, śigru, and dārumegha [is beneficial].
A paste of *sadrākṣā* and *māgadhī*, combined with *triphalā*, *śāribā*, *meghanādā*, *niśā*, and the leaves of *tāpiñja*, serves to destroy worms in children. (46–5)
A decoction mixed with honey, used as an eye-wash, shall eliminate eye diseases.
[The ingredients are] khadira, kuṭaja, nimba, trikaṭu, triphalā, and vacā. (46–6)
If these [herbs], ground with cow’s urine, are drunk, they destroy worms born in the abdomen.
In the morning, one whose mouth is filled with water should perform the sprinkling (āścyotana) of the eyes with water. 46–7.
At the end of eight days of gazing at the moon, the water used for washing the hands is beneficial;
likewise are tuttha in three parts, akṣa, and the seed of āmalaka.
Having ground two parts of this in water, one should take pills that destroy eye diseases.
Tuttha, copper, iron filings, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), lead, sandalwood, rock salt, triphalā, yaṣṭimadhuka, dārvī, and tutthāñjana— [These should be used together.]
Camphor, rock crystal, borax, and *tilva*—ground with the juice of *karañja* and formed into pills—destroy cataracts and all eye diseases. (46.9)
And one nakta-māla fruit [should be taken] with equal quantities of the juices of dhātrī and rājīra. || 46-10 ||
This powder, dried in the shade, destroys the clouds of cataracts (timira) when taken with the juices of triphalā, liyaṣṭi, and śuṇṭhī, or with honey, ghee, powdered iron, and milk. (46.11)
Cow’s urine [should be used] seven times [the amount of] tuttha and lead; these two are an elixir for the eyes.
Tuttha and lead are equal in measure, and blue vitriol (*nīlāñjana*) is equal to those two. (46.12)
That powder, combined with one-sixteenth part of mercury (vikārāṃśendu), is an ambrosia for the eyes;
[it consists of] the three pungents (kaṭutraya), karañja seeds, ginger (nāgara), rock salt (sindhujam), and the two types of turmeric (niśe). 46-13.

Having ground conch and bilva fruit together, an ointment is prepared that removes eye diseases; likewise, milk from a sea-araṇḍa plant taken with breast milk will remove [discolored] spots from the eyes.
Water from a *droṇa* flower mixed with breast milk and foam removes the affliction of eye-flower (*netrapuṣpa*).
Sindhu, *rātri*, *kaṇā*, jasmine, copper, bell-metal, and cowrie shells [are also used]. (46.15)
Realgar ground with honey removes *netrapilla* (blepharitis);
likewise, rock salt ground with vinegar and placed on a cloth should be applied as drops to the eyes. (46.16)
Similarly, *lodhra* fried in clarified butter, which removes excessive secretions, or the juice of black cow dung, or earwax used as a collyrium with honey [is beneficial]. (46.17)
These three [substances] mixed with *droṇa* flower water and oil destroy night-blindness.
Inhaling breast milk and dūrvā grass water through the nose cures the flow of blood from the nose.
The root of rambhā and gṛñjana, or the juice of fresh ginger taken separately, when used as a filling in the ear along with a little rock salt, destroys earache. (46.19)
Oil prepared with goat’s urine and curd, along with *bikṣu* and *antaḥphala*, removes deafness, the discharge of pus from the ear, and other such ailments. (46.20)
One should cook oil with vacā, garlic, salt, the bark of śigru roots, and the leaves of pāṇḍu, arka, and snuhi in water; this removes earache. (46.21)
Oil cooked with equal parts of the juices of *sūryāvarta*, *śigru*, *madhupadī*, *nakra*, *sindhuvāra*, *jātī*, *rambhā*, *kāravallī*, *surasā*, and garlic,
when applied as prescribed by placing it in the hollow of the ear, cures earache and pus.
It pacifies deafness and that ulcer, just as the Bhārata pacifies the multitude of evils. || 46-22 ||
Wood of the *vilva* or *devadāru* tree, wrapped in linen cloth and soaked in oil, should be set on fire; that oil [produced therefrom] removes earache. (46.23)
An incense made from the paste of the fruit of *bṛhatī* should be employed to overcome the afflictions of the twice-born.
A physician should cook oil in a decoction of *puṅkhā*, including its roots and stalks. (46.24)
A gargle with a paste of *pathyā* is supreme for alleviating toothache;
likewise, *śyāmā*, betel nut, fermented grain-water, coconut water, and urine [used together]. (46.25)
A decoction gargled will destroy diseases of the mouth such as *adhijihva* (epiglottis) and others.
Oil prepared with the juice of *sindhuvāra*, the paste of *lāṅgalī*, and [other ingredients] should be used. (46.26)
One will destroy goiter and scrofulous swellings merely by using it as a nasal drop.
The root of *vandhyākārkoṭakī*, when drunk with rice-water, [achieves the same]. (46.27)
An ointment consisting of the paste of *gopī* and *turaga*, combined with cow’s urine and *āmalaka*, along with milk, oil, and clarified butter, removes *gaṇḍamālā*. (46.28)
A thick, non-warm plaster applied to it removes the *bidrathī* swelling when it has ripened;
or alternatively, a plaster made of sandalwood and *uśīra*, ground with milk, may be used for one who is of middle age.
For tumors that are partially suppurated or immature, [one should use] *sindhu*, *ākuli*, and *nāgara*; likewise, *nirguṇḍī*, *kaṭutumbinī*, *kiṇihī*, *tiktā*, *niśā*, *tūlaka*, *bhṛṅgī*,
the roots of *lāṅgalī* and *padma*, *surasā*, *niryāsaka*, and *āsphoṭikā*.
Oil mixed with *guñjā* seeds and clarified butter made from buffalo milk, when applied as an ointment or used for pouring over the area, destroys all types of glandular swellings (*granthi*).
With the bones of *karavīra* and *kuṭaja*, the seeds of *bhallātaka*, and *viḍaṅga*. || 46.31 ||
Kuṣṭha and tagara, when applied as an ointment with cow’s urine, remove apacī; likewise, viśvā, bilva, kuṣṭha, and rock salt, well-ground together [are effective]. (46.32)

One should destroy swelling with cow’s urine, and a glandular tumor (granthi) by the mere application of an ointment; having ground dantī, haridrā, and āmalaka with water, one should apply it as a plaster.
One should cook oil in a decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) with the paste of white-rooted plantain (sitamūlā); by sprinkling that [oil], fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) is destroyed. (46.34)
One should cook *tilaka* oil with the paste of *lāṅgalī*, *īśelu*, *kumbha*, *asthi*, *sarja*, *jyotiṣmatī*, and *vacā*, in a decoction of *pāṭhā*, *amṛtā*, and *arka*. (46.35)
By means of that, an ointment and an infusion destroy fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara).
Equal parts of *punarnavā*, *amṛtā*, *viśvā*, *vaṭa* leaves, and bricks [are used]. (46.36)
Ground with buttermilk and applied as a plaster, [these] destroy fistula-in-ano:
those derived from *vyāghāta*, *snuhī*, *pūtīka*, *śirīṣa*, *arka*, and *jātī*. (46.37)
One should conquer all skin diseases by applying a plaster made from [the powder of] *vākucī* seeds ground with cow urine;
likewise, by consuming *vākucī* seeds in equal measure with black sesame seeds. (46.38)
For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, leprosy perishes within a year;
eating the seeds of the *jalakhaṇḍanikā* plant destroys leprosy. (46.39)
An ointment made from the seeds of *karañja*, *kaṇā*, *citragṛhadhūma*, *vākucī*, and the oil of *kuṭu-tumbinikā* destroys leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). (46–40)
The roots of *sthalasārivā*, sprouts of *vacā*, seeds of *prapunnāṭaka*, *niśā*, and *pathyā*, when ground together, cure cough, root-diseases, and asthma. (46–47)
By applying a plaster made of cow's buttermilk for one year, skin diseases (kuṣṭha) are destroyed.
[This is done] with equal parts of triphalā, citraka, pūtīka, citra, rātri, and sesame seeds. (46–42)
Having ground the roots and sprouts into a powder, one should drink them with buttermilk to remove [the affliction], using vārāhī, citra, pūtīka, vandhyā, kuṭaca, and sūraṇa. (46–43)

A drink made from the flour of *śilājatu*, the root of *lāṅgalikā*, and the essence of *guñjā*, each taken in equal parts with buttermilk and barley gruel, removes diseases of the root [genital tract]. (46–44)

Having ground [the ingredients] in the milk of the *arka* plant and cow’s urine, one should cook that in an alkaline solution; having made a wick (*varti*) from it, equal in thickness and length to the thumb. (46–45)
The physician who knows [the treatment] should administer this as an enema when the sprouts of hemorrhoids (arśas) are falling away:
equal parts of the bark and fruit of pūtīka, triphalā, rātri, and karañja. (46–46)
The powder of these and their decoction, when saturated with honey, would remove urinary disorders (meha).
One part each of mercury and sulfur, along with the seed of *Mākula* and realgar (*manaḥśilā*), [should be used]. (46–47)
One should take two parts each of the husks of parched grain, the bark from the root of the black neem tree, and the root-fiber; likewise, two parts each of resin and guggulu. (46–48)
The resin of *khadira*, *kapittha*, white and black *arimeda*, and *palāśa*, as well as [the resin] of *dārvī* and the seeds of *kuṭaja*. (46–49)
Three parts each of these should be taken, as well as *kānta*, sandalwood,
the root of black *mūlā*, the root of *asumūla*, and the tubers of *musalyā* and *kulikā*.
Dhātrī and nāgakusuma— these four ingredients, each used in a fourfold quantity,
[are applied] to the root of a growing cotton plant, along with the bark of the black and white *arjuna* trees.
One should grind all five parts separately into a fine powder;
this powder should be licked with honey in the morning, or one should drink it with buttermilk. || 46–52 ||

And one should drink a decoction at night, boiled with the medicinal herbs to be mentioned hereafter: triphalā, the two types of niśā (turmeric and majoram), and the barks of jambū and āragvadha. (46–53)
Pāṭhā, amṛtā, abda, takara, śakti, patra, and punarnavā—all these taken in equal parts should be boiled down until one-eighth remains. (46–54)
When drunk cold and mixed with honey, it cures the twenty types of urinary disorders (meha).
[Likewise,] the seeds of *niṣṭheraka* and *kulī*, and the leaves of *baddhavalla*... 46–55.
One should grind the parts containing one, two, and three units of *advaita* with buttermilk;
by drinking this in the morning for three, four, or five days, one shall conquer urinary disorders (*meha*).
Six parts of the root of *śakraballī* and likewise sprouts of *karañja*:
the decoction of these, when drunk mixed with the powder of their seeds, removes [excessive] growth.
Having ground the sprouts of *kokilākṣa* with *viśva*, *sindhūttha*, and *dīpyaka*, one should drink them with cow’s buttermilk; thus, the increase of seeds is destroyed. (46–58)

When water has been infused with *karabja*, *gṛñjanī*, *pathyā*, and the tips of *kānana* shoots, it becomes *śukta*; when drunk with buttermilk and other such liquids, it removes the increase and decrease of semen. (46–59)

One should cook ghee— or alternatively, an equal measure of both ghee and oil— along with one āḍhaka of the fresh juice of *dūrvā* grass, and having made into a paste *malayaja*, *hnīberaka*, *śārivā*, *mustā*, lotus, blue lotus, *tūla*, *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, and the sprouts (*śuṅga*) of milk-exuding trees.
When drunk, it removes all spreading skin diseases (visarpaka), as does its application through sprinkling and massage.

Having cooked one *kārṣika* measure of clarified butter in a decoction of *khadira* equal in weight [to the other ingredients], along with the separate pastes (*niṣka-kalka*) of the leaves of *amṛta*, *viṣa*, *paṭolī*, *nimba*, and *dhātrī*, it should be licked at dawn.
It indeed removes erysipelas, and its decoction, when drunk, does the same. || 46-61 ||
For one who drinks in the morning the decoction of the paste of *śigru* and *viśvā*, mixed with one and two parts of milk respectively, his leprosy (*śobha*) perishes within a fortnight.

Milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla) should be one kuḍuba, along with one niṣka of madhu; the clarified butter (ghṛta) should be one and a half niṣkas, and the sugar should be double the amount of the ghee.
Four and a half niṣkas of sugar combined with the powder of black pepper,
churned or boiled in the morning, destroys vātaśoṇita (gout).
One should drink a decoction of grapes, *abdārātri*, and *kvaṭha* when there is an onset of phlegm and blood;
one should consume it twice daily along with jujube (*gulā*) to remove phlegm and blood. (46–65)
At that time, one who eats its leaves should drink the resin of *kokilākṣa*;
the *vātaśoṇita* (blood disorder caused by wind) is destroyed.
A decoction of *vyāghāta*, *vāśā*, and *chinna* mixed with castor oil [is also effective]. (46–66)
When drunk, it destroys *vātāsṛj* (blood disorders caused by wind); black hot water removes *plīhā* (enlarged spleen).

Having boiled water with three *niṣkas* each of *viśvā*, *bilva*, and *agnimantha* together with *magadhaja* (long pepper), one should add an equal amount of milk and boil that milk; then, having eaten food with that [milk].
Whoever consumes that ginger every day in this manner for just one month, their consumption (yakṣman) goes to destruction, and the body attains firm and desirable nourishment. || 46-67 ||
With vāśā, bhṛṅgendra, kāsaghnī, bṛhatī, nāgara, and amṛta; || 46-68 ||
One should drink well-boiled milk that has been processed with these decoctions; it removes pungency and cures wasting (*kṣaya*).

One should take equal parts of *bhārgī*, *gokṣuraka*, *kāsavairin* (*pippalī*), *bṛhatī*, *bilva*, and *adrikarṇī*; having prepared a decoction of these, one should then boil an amount of milk equal to the decoction over the fire.

One should drink that [mixture] consisting of powdered black iron saturated with honey; it removes the disease of consumption (yakṣma), and while it excessively dries up cough, dyspnea, and phlegm, it also nourishes the body. (46–69)
Then, that buffalo milk and its butter [should be processed] with the waters of the night.
The dung of a pigeon or that produced from a *vaṭa* tree, taken with milk, removes *vātabheda*.
When combined with the decoction of *ciribilvaka* and the paste of *rājita*, [it serves as a remedy]. (46–71)
This prepared oil removes Vāta through massage and poultices;
it should be combined with a paste of Mahājamāraka, Kola, Rātri, and its seeds.

Oil cooked with these, when used for massage, is supreme for removing diseases of the wind (vāta). [The decoction of] prasāriṇī, arka, jambīra, śigru, and ciñcā, along with curd, [is also used]. 46–73.
One should cook oil extracted from sesame seeds with a paste of *rājī*, *nāgara*, and *śigru*.
[This may also be prepared] with *śigru*, the five acids (*pañcāmla*), *saraṇi*, the two types of *karañja*, *balā*, and *arka*. (46–74)
Then, one should first sprinkle [the plant] with sour gruel (kāñjika) that has been boiled with ground *varaṇa*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), and *ciñcā* leaves. (46–75)
Through anointing with oil and food, wind-disease (vātaroga) is destroyed;
one should also immerse oneself in this very decoction when it is lukewarm.
Sprinkling with a decoction of fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla) using two vessels with their spouts cut off overcomes Vāta;
however, in cases of pure Vāta disease, sprinkling with oil alone is also effective. (76–77)
An ointment made from the seeds of *bhadrāmātula*, ground with vinegar along with *rāsnā*, *dāru*, *mahauṣadha*, and *agnimantha*, destroys swelling caused by Vāta. (46–78)
Cotton seeds, *aṅkola* seeds, *śigru* bark, and *viśvabheṣaja*, ground with fermented gruel (*śukta*) and applied as a lukewarm paste, conquer diseases of the wind (*vāta*). (46–79)
With *punnāga*, castor-oil plant, neem, *vakula*, *dhana-dāru*, *ṛṅ* (aragvadha), coconut, *karañja*, cotton,
drumstick tree, *dolāphala*, *muni*, *śaraṇa*, radish, mustard, *kola*, *aṅkola*, *kulattha*, along with garlic, *vacā*, turmeric, *devadāru*, and *dārvī*—
A medicinal packet (poṭṭala) composed of flowers, sour substances, fats, and all pungent ingredients overcomes wind disorders.
A plaster made from ḍolāṅkola, all sour substances, all fats, and rock salt, ground dry, conquers Vāta. || 46-81 ||
A decoction of triphalā and trivṛt mixed with jaggery is a purgative; likewise, a decoction of grapes mixed with trivṛt and jaggery is a purgative. (46–82)

Half a part of trivṛt, one-sixth part of each of the two types of rock salt (sindhuja), and these [other ingredients] ground into powder and mixed with honey; when drunk with water, this acts as a purgative. (46–83)
Having boiled the fruits of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and its shoots, one should then press them;
the juice, when drunk together with jaggery (*guḍa*), acts as an immediate purgative. (46.84)
Pathyā, kramuka, and nāgara in portions of four, three, and two [parts] respectively, along with saindhava salt taken with warm water, acts as a rapid purgative. (46–85)
Kokilākṣa, svayaṃguptā seeds, māṣa beans, and white sesame seeds,
taken in equal parts and drunk with milk, act as an aphrodisiac for those who approach hundreds of women.
Triphalā with sugar, as well as the root of svayaṅguptā and the powder of its seeds along with black gram (māṣa), taken with milk and sugar, is an aphrodisiac. (46–87)
A bolus prepared with the powder of sesame, rice, and mung beans, as well as the fruit of guptā, long pepper, and plantain, cooked in ghee, is an aphrodisiac known as *pramodaka*. (46.88)
This refers to taking it with milk as a post-drink (anupāna).
A woman desiring a son should drink at night a powder made from equal parts of guptā, varī, gokṣuramūla, māla, sesame seeds, and the seeds of śleṣmalaka, mixed with sugar and milk. (46–89)

A woman desiring offspring, having approached her husband during her fertile period, should drink the juice of the roots of the *aśoka* tree located toward the direction of the Lord of Wealth (the North), along with sprouts of the red *vaṭa* tree, while standing in water reaching up to her navel; thus she shall conceive.

Having ground together *dūrvā*, *akhilā*, the root of *śrīsahadeva*, the sprouts of *aśvattha* and *darbha*, and bamboo shoots with milk, a woman who drinks this during her fertile period shall conceive and obtain a son. (46.91)

One desiring a son should drink seven fig sprouts as the root of prosperity; likewise, one should drink the two sprouts of those [figs] in milk. Furthermore, having crushed the sprouts of the *sahā* plant along with those [fig sprouts], she should apply its juices to her nose during her fertile period.

Having bathed on the fourth day and performed auspicious rites, a woman who has taken medicine should not touch the earth with her feet; she should remain indoors during the day, avoid eating raw vegetables, and after eating food mixed with milk and ghee, she should approach the bed of her own husband. (46.93)
Whatever medicine a woman should drink, she who desires a son should apply that very same as a nasal drop (nasya) through the right nostril;
she who desires a daughter should do so through the other [left] nostril. She should also lie on her side according to that same rule until the end of three menstrual periods.
To pacify defects of the embryo, *tagara* seeds should be drunk with milk; however, if there is instability of the embryo, they should be taken mixed with curd.
A woman who has been barren should drink the menstrual blood of a fertile woman, ground with rice-water, along with *likuca*, sandalwood, *yaṣṭimadhu*, *lodhra*, *gopī*, and blue lotus. (46–95)
A woman desiring a son should drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* stirred with the juice of *dhātrī*, or likewise the root of *kuraṇḍa* with *āmalakī*, or the root of *paṭola* combined with ghee and curd. (46.96)
Having extracted the root of *kākamācī* at dawn during the *puṣya* asterism while remaining silent, one should have a woman drink it with milk; she will obtain a pregnancy before long. (46.97)
Let her drink a cooled decoction of sandalwood, gopī, grapes, and lodhra, mixed with milk and sugar; this, along with musta and milk, prevents miscarriage. (46–98)

For the purpose of protecting the fetus, a remedy is prescribed for each month when the fetus begins to move. One should have the woman drink a preparation of *padmaka*, *uśīra*, and *tagara* mixed with goat’s milk. (46–99)
In the second [stage], one should administer kaśeru, viśvā, śelu, and blue lotuses; in the third, one should cause [the patient] to drink pāṭala and uśīra with milk and mustā. (46.100)
In the fourth [formula], there are plantain root, blue lotus root, and uśīra;
in the fifth, milk-kākolī, milk-kañcī, utpala, and ambuja.
In the sixth [month], one should have her drink grapes, blue lotus, and saffron with milk;
and in the seventh, the bark and fruit of the wood-apple (*kapittha*), its root, sugar, and parched grain.

In the eighth [day], one should drink a decoction of coriander (*dhānyaka*), blue lotus stamens (*utpalakesara*), castor root (*eraṇḍamūla*), and *kākolī*. On the ninth day, one should administer a bolus (*modaka*).
On the tenth day, one should cause [the patient] to drink saffron, licorice, white lotus,
and sugar, mixed with milk and rice-water.

Either the root of the *vāśā* plant or the leaves of the *pappaṇa*, ground with water and applied as a plaster below the navel, result in an easy delivery; likewise, by hanging the branches [of these plants] downward. (46.105)

At the time of childbirth, by placing a *karaṅgama* upon the roof of the delivery room and by applying an ointment of oil consecrated with the recitation (*jāpa*) of the *Viloma-mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, there is a comfortable delivery of the fetus. (46–106)
A wick made from old cloth, filled with the powder of grapes, *vyāghāta*, and turmeric, along with honey and clarified butter,
cleanses a wound or the female reproductive tract.
Alternatively, one should cook sesame oil with a paste of śāriva, utpala leaves, lodhra, sandalwood, and yaṣṭimadhu, along with milk; that serves to heal wounds.

One should cook a paste made of white *pūlāsa* and *sapatra*, combined with a small amount of black pepper and rock salt, in oil; likewise, this [preparation] containing *vayasthā* destroys wounds. (46.109)
That very same [ointment], mixed with coconut oil and ghee, removes burns caused by fire;
or [it may be applied] with apāmārga leaves ground by hand, or with those of kāravallī. (46.110)
Bound with a small amount of salt, it immediately heals fresh wounds; likewise, powder from the core of a palmyra sprout, when bound on, removes fresh injuries. (46.111)

Having dried one *kuḍuba* of the three oils— sesame, castor, and *eraṇḍa*— in a *prastha* of water containing six, seven, or eight *niṣkas* of *pathyā*, *akṣa*, and *dhātrī* fruits according to the season,
one should add well-prepared *gopīcandana* powder in the measure of one *niṣka*. It should then be left to stand.
In a heap of grain, the *kālamaśī* plant removes [the poison] in twenty-one days.

Having extracted Viśvāmitraniṣka and the creeper of Mājilla along with its leaves in a quantity of one *vasu-niṣka*, and having drunk it at night, it will, upon rising in the morning, pacify great heat and burning sensations. (46-113)
Having ground one *kuḍuba* of *rājī* seeds, let it remain for three days in two *prasthas* of churned milk; when drunk after those three days have passed, it removes all types of *śītikā*.
Three niṣkas of the root of red gokṣura,
ground with milk and drunk with sugar in milk, causes the falling away of gravel and stones from the bladder.

A powder made from sea salt, Akṣatanālikera, and its root, along with the juice of Uttama-kanyā, should be placed inside a coconut shell; having covered the opening with clay and burnt it while facing the fire, it removes [the affliction] when consumed internally.

Sindhūttha, abhraka, and mākṣika, processed hundreds of times in *puṭas* with *kuṭuka*, *pathyā*, *ṛkṣa*, *dhātrī*, *śilājatu*, *bhṛṅga*, and water, along with iron (*kānta*) and earth from an anthill (*uṣāmṛd*),
are taken in equal parts; then, half that amount of *sauta* (iron filings) is added.
For one who has merely crushed the pride of Bhṛṅgī, how could there be death from mortal enemies? || 46-117 ||
But for one who is merely a "branch-person," having cut the primary root-fiber of the tender *śalmali* tree at its base, one should cause a water-pot to be placed upon that severed stump. (46.118)
Having cut that Śalmali tree to a height of one man's length,
he should smear it with clay to a depth of eight finger-breadths and burn it using cow-dung fuel.
After six or seven days, having extracted the liquid from that jar and dried it in the shade, one should mix this with the juice of *bhṛṅga* and *āmalaka*. (46.120)
Having thoroughly crushed it, one whose body is purified should consume a portion the size of a sparrow's foot upon rising in the morning; this destroys enlargement of the spleen.
Taking the root of *viśālā*, one should eat it; it destroys splenomegaly (*plīhā*) instantly.
Having avoided that [root], one should drink [the juice] in two ways to remove the spleen. (46-122)

One should drink rock salt that has been incinerated within a sealed packet made of seven arka leaves along with buttermilk; this removes the spleen disorder, according to the doctrine of Dhanvantari. (46.123)
One should drink the root of punarnavā, śukta, and pāṭhā;
and having ground two [of these] with rice-water, one should apply it as a paste to destroy abscesses (vidradhi). 46-124.
Copper dross ground with buttermilk and applied [as a paste] conquers leprosy.
Furthermore, milk that has been turned into curd within a vessel smeared with a paste of *vākucī* [removes skin diseases]. (46.125)
That buttermilk and fresh butter, when drunk or licked, conquer leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

In that regard, having licked the fresh butter together with honey, one should afterwards drink the buttermilk; this means that white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*) is destroyed. One should apply the root of white *aparājitā* as a plaster to destroy leprosy. (46–126)
Ginger ground with water and mixed with one-third part of milk decoction, combined with cow-dung water, when drunk, destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara). || 46-127 ||
Tiktā, mustā, paṭola, lūkapiñcha, and guggulu,
bound together in a black cloth— this incense dispels quartan fever.
Alternatively, the root of *balā* and the root of *meghanāda*, when drunk with milk or rice-water,
shall serve as a remedy for menorrhagia.
One should drink the juice of the red and white japā flowers during the flow of blood, both red and white;
one should take its root with milk at dawn, and its decoction with milk at night.
One should wrap a coconut flower in clay and burn it with fire;
its juice, when drunk with milk, prevents the discharge of semen. (46.131)

Having drunk the flowers of the *śalmali* tree with milk for four days during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), a barren woman will become fruitful; yet, by drinking [the same] with *abhayā* and *vyoṣa*, she remains indeed barren. (46.132)

With mañjiṣṭhā, añjana, śārivā, abda, kaṭuka, nakta, taila, jātiphala, śrīkhaṇḍa, triphalā, jaṭā, tagara, rug, yaṣṭī, the four spices (caturjātaka), uśīra, agaru, the pair of coras, mṛganābhi, palāśa, ambhas, and bisa—
Oil prepared with milk in the juice of *kumārī* cures pain in the eyes and the head. (46.133)
Having ground together the powder of *amalakī* fruit that has been roasted and the juices of *bhṛṅga*, one should then take eight *pala* of that paste.
One should cook half that amount of sesame oil with thirty-two *pala* of water from the *bhṛṅga* plant;
by anointing [the head] with that oil, even those who are bald will grow hair. (46.135)
Rasāñjana mixed with goat’s milk and powdered elephant tusks, then ground and applied to iron, produces the growth of hair. (46.136)
Even for one with a bald head (khalati), up to this point;
one should apply *japā* flowers ground with the urine of a black cow.
The root of *guñjā* in the juice of *bṛhatī* removes *indralupta* (alopecia). (46.137)
This refers to the essence contained within the fruits of the *laghu-bṛhatī*.
By grinding together *dhātrī*, *kuṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, the root of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and *balā* with water, one attains thick hair through the application of this paste. (46.138)

An ointment made from equal parts of *sagandha*, *amala*, *mātrā*, and *asthi* removes hair loss. Furthermore, three parts each of the root of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *yaṣṭi*, and *kesara* [are used]. (46.139)
An amalaka fruit smeared with these [substances] is the supreme remedy for scrofula and hemorrhoids.
[Likewise,] the leaf of *āragvadha* combined with *dhātrī*, lac, and the seeds of *punnāga* [is effective]. (46.140)
An application of *kapāla* ground with water is an excellent remedy for hemorrhoids;
likewise are the seeds of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), iron filings, and *bhṛṅgarāja*. (46.141)
The flower of the *raktāśvamāra* plant ground with indigo powder, when fumigated with *gulu* and applied as an ointment, shall turn grey hair to blackness. (46.142)
In all cases, one should grind [the ingredients] with wine (*kāñcika*).

Having anointed the hair at the crown of the head (*dharmastha*) with the seed-oil of *kākatuṇḍī* and *pīlu* in an iron vessel, and using it as a nasal drop (*nasya*), one shall remove gray hair. (46.143)
One should burn that powder with smokeless fire in the milk of the Arka plant;
when smeared with mustard oil, it removes diseases of the head.
The seeds of *dhātrī* and *punnāga*, along with the sprouts of *lākṣā* and *āragvadha*, when ground and smeared [on the head], are known to remove diseases of the head. (46.145)
The root of the kākoḍumbara tree, ground with rice-water and drunk, will indeed stop the flow of blood from the teeth. (146)
Pathyā, akṣa, nīlikā, madhukarī, vārāhī, muṇḍī, amṛtā, brahmāṇī, punarnavā, and turagā— these, along with red and yellow [oxides],
should be powdered in equal parts. Then, add half that amount of kānta iron, having subjected it to a hundred puṭas.
For one who eats [the fruit] stirred with honey for a year, that body shall become ageless like a yak-tail fan.
Pathyā, akṣa, āmalaka, agni, kīṭaripu, vākucī, bhṛṅgikā, bhallāta, asana, and śatapuṭa— these, along with kānta, should be increased in sequence.
This mixture, rubbed with honey, sugar, and ghee, should be licked from that vessel for one year.
Having attained accomplishment and conquered old age, he shall live happily for a thousand autumns.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, on various diseases, in the Mantra-pāda of the Siddhāntasāra, which is the Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati. 46.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.
Now, the rites of sorcery (abhicāra) against enemies who harm the Dharma and the Vedas are taught;
they are of seven kinds, consisting of paralyzing (stambha), creating enmity (vidveṣa), driving away (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa).

And there is the method for eradicating delusion through the use of mechanical devices, mantras, burnt offerings, and so forth, as well as through medicinal formulations, according to the indications found in their respective tantras. (47.2)

(345) Furthermore, [the mantras] belonging to Gaṇapati and others have already been mentioned in this work, as well as those belonging to the Durgā-mantras such as the Triṣṭubh, and those of Śakti and Aghora-astra. (47–3)

Those [mantras] which are separately proclaimed in the Vaiṣṇava Kalpas, such as the Nṛsiṃha-kalpa and others, should be employed by one who knows them in the domain of malevolent rites (abhicāra). || 47-4 ||
Those [mantras] which have not been shown here are written for the purpose of protecting the Dharma;
one should write the Krodha [mantra] with red ochre upon the surface of a vibhītaka fruit. (47.5)
In the center, one should write the [mantra] known as Bhāntavidarbha; then, outside, eight units of *māṃsa*; and on the exterior, the great Indra’s eight-vajra [array], followed by Vāsuki.
And having encircled it with Śaṅkhapāla, one should write their names on the mouth [of the vessel];
one should bury that [vessel] in the flower-offerings (nirmālya) and place a stone upon it.

The immobilization of enemy armies and the like is declared to be that [rite]. In the center of the lotus, one should place the name [of the target], and the armor (varma) or kavaca [mantra] in the petals of the directions. (47–8)
In each corner, one should draw the earth [element] up to its five internal parts, and a vajra-ground-house for the eight directions;
upon its spires, one should write the armor [mantra], and outside, the mandala of Varuṇa.
One should place [the deity] situated within the lap of a yellow obstacle (vighna) made of turmeric, worshipped with yellow substances;
this is the rite of paralyzing (saṃstambhana) enemies such as hostile armies and the like, as previously described. (47–10)

He who is the one to be reached by Yama, the king of the dead; he who is the great sun of the rising dawn; the source of compassion; he who is beyond the realm of death; the lord of the yakṣas; and he who is free from all affliction.

Oṃ hrīṃ vikṛtānanāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This twelve-syllable mantra of Yama has been proclaimed. Oṃ hrīṃ to the black-colored one; oṃ to the one with a distorted face; oṃ to the nine-faced one who wears a crown of tawny matted locks; oṃ huṃ to the one possessing the splendor of the rising of a thousand suns; oṃ hrīṃ to the three-eyed one, to the possessor of the three eyes, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ hrīṃ vikṛtānanāya huṃ phaṭ. [This is] the weapon-mantra (astra).
The six limbs of the mantra of Yamāntaka are [to be performed] with their respective seed-syllables. (47.12)

Oṃ dhūmāndhakārāya ṭhaṭha. This is the mantra of Yama. [One should perform] the self-consecration of the limbs. Then, having drawn two lines situated from south to north within the center of the three circles, and likewise from east to west... [47-13]
On the south and north [sides], one should draw the heads of a buffalo and a horse;
and in each of the corners, one should indeed draw a single line and tridents at their tips. (47.14)
"At the tips of the lines" means up to that point.
One should draw [the design] on a scrap of cloth using charcoal from a funeral pyre and neem water.
There, within the first circle, one should write the five syllables. || 47-15 ||
In the central, eastern, northern, southern, and western compartments, one should place five syllables in sequence;
and the name and the ritual act belong to the middle compartment.
In the second circle, having written "rā do yo ya" in the eastern, southern, western, and northern compartments, then [proceed] in the four compartments.
One should inscribe in the two compartments the [syllables] jaṅghā, aruṇa, and nirāvara;
[and] nirakaraṇā, nidana, and nirakṣo, located in the direction of the wind (the northwest).
Furthermore, having written the eight-syllable mantra of Yama within the eight side-chambers of the inner tridents, one should then write its twelve-syllable form.

One should also draw Yamāntaka upon the needle-points at the tips of the tridents situated inside and outside; [he should be drawn] on the tips of the petals, and that [deity] on the petals outside the rim.
Starting from this point, one should place the yantra between two smooth, joined earthenware bowls; then, one should bury it in a cremation ground or a similar location.
And first, one should offer a bali-oblation to Yama with these substances:
milk, curd, boiled rice, honey, clarified butter, mung beans, and black gram. (47.22)
One should cast all the sweetmeats (*modaka*), parched grains (*saktu*), and fried rice (*lāja*) first into the domain of the Lord of the East.
With the twelve-syllable mantra, one should offer them nine times into the mouths of Yamāntaka.
Then, [one offers] to the World-Protectors in the north to the Yakṣas, and then in the southwest.
One should offer oblations to the Rākṣasas and to all beings in every direction;
