to the south of the wheel, one should cast the bali with one's own names.
Yamarāja, Kāla, Yama Vaivasvata, Śānta, the King of the Pretas, Mṛtyu, and Antaka as well. (47.25)
Kṛtānta, Dharmarāja, and Yama—these are indeed the ten names of Yama.
With these mantras of Yama, ending with "namaḥ" and preceded by one's own name, one should offer the bali-oblation. (47.26)
Then one should offer [oblations] to the Mothers beginning with Vighna, and to Vīrabhadra; to the Lokapālas in the north, to the Yakṣas in the southwest, and then [to others]. (47.27)
And one should cast [the offering] toward the Rākṣasas and all beings in every direction.
The mantra is the short Śakti (PH), followed by Kha (KHA), Agni (RA), and the Bindu and Sarga (ŪṂ); thus the mantra is PHAṬ KHA RA ŪṂ. (47-28)
One should draw this [diagram] upon two shallow bowls, interlaced with the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
One should write the desired [mantra] once with a golden stylus using the juice of *rocanā* (yellow pigment).
Another [method] is with a crow's wing-feather smeared with cemetery ash;
one who desires to create mutual hatred should bury those two on the two banks of a river.

*Dharmati ke dharmati ke*, O terrible one, O you who cause hatred, O you who create enmity between such-and-such [two] persons, both terrible and non-terrible; with hands made of the wings of crows and owls, one should even satisfy them. This is the rite of causing hatred (*vidveṣaṇa*).
One should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) interlaced with the syllables of the mantra within the house of *dharma* and *vāyu*.
Then, the wind-god (*anila*) with the power of creation (*sargī*) should be placed in the eight directions upon a wooden board. (47–31)
Having written it again and again with *dharmaṭikā* ink, one should erase it;
that powder, when placed upon the head of an enemy, causes the enemy's eradication. (47.32)
Having drawn the previously mentioned yantra upon a cloth from a cemetery banner, together with *dhūrdhūra* water and ink, it should be encircled with black thread.

Having cast that [substance] into a crow-nest, one should release it into the enemy army; the destruction of the army will occur. That ash, together with crow feathers and snake skin, should be placed in a cloth from a cremation ground. (47.34)
One should bury a red thread wound around [an object], which is supremely effective for causing expulsion;
one should also dig up cemetery ash, human bone, and the *brahmadaṇḍī* plant.
A crow’s wing-feather and a human bone—these two effect the eradication of the *rājīva* plant;
one should dig up a triangular horse-stake joined with the seed-syllable of Durgā. (47.36)

Whether at the enemy's feet or even in his house, there shall be the destruction of the foe; and with this mantra ending in "svāhā" and preceded by the armor [mantra], there shall be a complete confrontation.
In the Viśākhā nakṣatra, one should drive in a stake of nimba wood at the threshold of the house;
then, having burned a house inhabited by crows with the fire of a funeral pyre, [one should perform the rite]. 47-38.
That ash, when placed at the doorway, brings about the destruction of the house;
that same ash, when thrown upon the head, causes hatred and eradication. (47.39)

Homage to the Blessed One, the Mad Śūdrāśa! O Rudra, wander, cause [Amuka] to wander, terrify, and cause [him] to roam about with your fierce form—huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha! The seer of this [mantra] is Kaivarta; its meter is Kakup; its deity is Rudra. One should recite it starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day. (47–48)
Having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times at night in a cremation ground, by means of an oblation of *dhurdhūra* wood, one causes the enemies to wander about within eight days. (47–48)
An effigy of the enemy made from gold and red ochre, with its life-force established within by means of golden needles, will cause the enemy to die instantly. (47–48)

"O you who are bitten by Time! O terrifying one! O crusher of fear! Destroy! Hūṃ Phaṭ Ṭhaṭha! To the one bitten by Time, Ṭhaṭha! To the terrifying one, Ṭhaṭha! O crusher of fear, Ṭhaṭha! Destroy, Ṭhaṭha! Hūṃ Phaṭ Ṭhaṭha!
Kucaka is its seer (ṛṣi), the *nicṛt* meter; its deity is Yama himself.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having worshipped Śiva while observing a vow of milk, [one should recite this].
Having recited [the mantra] five hundred thousand times, one then becomes a master of the mantra;
then, standing in water reaching the navel, with one's body covered by a wet cloth.
"Having performed this with the recitation of the head-mantra, the enemy shall die within a fortnight.
O firm-necked one! O Virūpākṣī! O Saṃkṣāṇī! O Mahodarī! (47-45)

"Kill the enemy with the trident! Drink the blood of the enraged one! Burn! Cook! Grind! Slay! Wither! Destroy! Annihilate! Hūṃ Phaṭ Ṭhaṭha! Its limbs are as follows: "O Reviver! O Thou with Upward-Tufted Hair! O Thou with Blazing Crest! O Thou whose Nature is the Illusion of the Three Worlds! O Thou who revolves a thousand times! O Slayer of Tārakākṣa!
These six limbs, joined with their seed-syllables (*jāti*), are to be applied in due order. (Verses 47–46)
The seer of this [mantra] is Pippalāda, its metre is Nivṛt, and its deity is declared to be Bhadrakālī; it is perfected by one hundred thousand recitations.

May Gṛdhrakarṇī protect [us]—she whose belly is lined with dried entrails and flesh, whose body is emaciated and tall, whose face is terrifying with fangs, who carries a skull and a trident, whose large, fierce eyes are tawny, whose hair stands erect and blazing, and whose long, wide nose is formidable. (47–48)

One should worship Gṛdhrakarṇī in the pericarp, the limbs (aṅgas) in the corners and also in the cardinal directions, as well as the weapon (astra) and the eye (netra) with these two; likewise, one should worship the Mothers outside. 47–49.

One should write the mantra within a skull-cup, interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished; then, facing the southern direction, one should recite the mantra at a solitary linga, for then one becomes equal to him. (47–50)
Within a month, his rites of killing and so forth will surely succeed during the nights, provided he has smeared his body with a paste made from neem leaves, mango seeds, and [mango] pulp. (47–51)
One should walk between two affectionate people while reciting [the mantra], causing those two enemies to hate each other;
and by means of the grains from the fire-oblation performed in a pit made of *pippala* wood, [one achieves the same]. (47–52)
One who desires destruction should recite with arms raised while facing the sun;
one should dig a horse-stake at the foot [of the tree], and there shall be eradication on the right side.
If [the lines] are on the left, there will be disease or death; however, a hexagon with its mantra possesses virtues.
One should recite the mantra including the name of the target: *hrīṃ ṣṭrīṃ hrīṃ praṭadhanatahuṃ śatruṃ nāśaya huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha*. By reciting this, the enemy shall suffer from quartan fever. (47–54)
Or one may suffer from colic; in such a case, one should draw an image of the victim made of red ochre (gairika) with its bones depicted.
Then, having performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) into the effigies, the subsequent rites are to be carried out.
One should accomplish this mantra by reciting it one hundred and eight times in sequence.
A twelve-finger-long effigy (*puttalī*) of the target person should be made from living plants and placed upon the heart. (47–56)

"His vital breaths are here; his life-force is established here. May all his senses, speech, mind, and vital breaths come here! *ṭha ṭha*. Wherever the word "amuṣya" (of him) occurs, one should insert the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
[The mantra] is enriched by the left ear (*vāmakarṇa*), possesses the fish (*mīna*), is tripled, joined with Ananta, and is the poison (*viṣa*). (47–57)
The eight-syllable mantra consists of *kumbha-uṣaḍhī-na-tri-yuta-ṣṭau*.
Its deity is Dhūmāvatī, who is Jyeṣṭhā and exceedingly terrifying. (47–58)
The seer of this [mantra] is Pippalāda; its meter is the Nivṛt-gāyatrī, and it is prescribed for the ritual application of the limbs.
Its specific application, moreover, is traditionally taught for the purpose of malevolent magic (abhicāra).
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at night, with hair disheveled and naked,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while eating only at night, either in a cremation ground or in a forest.
Long in form, exceedingly black, emaciated, hideous, with disheveled hair, deformed,

with a crooked and high-bridged nose, with sparse teeth, round, tawny, and three-eyed; adorned with women’s ornaments, her limbs covered in hair, wearing soiled garments, and richly marked by the banner of a crow-vehicle.
May Dhūmāvatī protect you—she who is like a newly married bride, with the tip of a winnowing basket held in her hand.

Alternatively, on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, having burned a crow in a funeral pyre at night, one should recite [the mantra] over its ashes; when these are scattered, it effects the destruction of the enemy.
Having written the neuter vowels in the corners of the letter *ma*, one should write the two names in the center; this hexagon is smeared with poison.
Having struck with a cotton stalk, one should recite the mantra for the purpose of causing enmity between two people;
by offering ashes into a funeral fire made of funeral wood, one effects death.
If one offers into a mad fire ashes mixed with the dust from his feet,
the enemy will become insane within just one month.
Having offered oblations with neem leaves inscribed with the name of the target, one should cause death;
that [inscribed] writing should be used with ghee on rajī seeds during the appropriate times for pills and other such preparations.

When the Moon is in the mandāṃśa of Jupiter or in its own asterism, or when it is in the mandāṃśa of those two planets on their respective days, provided it is devoid of Rāhu, that is the yoga named Sthavira; it is recommended for base undertakings. (47–67)
The sign of destruction (Vaināśika), the sign of slaughter (Vadharkṣa), Mars, and likewise the eighth house—these are recommended for minor rites, especially at midnight. (47–68)

Having smeared an image of the enemy made from the wood of a tree corresponding to his birth-star with the seeds of the *mārga* plant and black pepper, one should boil it at night; the enemy shall become afflicted with fever.
One should whirl [the victim] with an earring-shaped ladle and with leaves of the *prādeśa* plant;
by means of these, the fire of the Aśvins burns the enemy in the three worlds through the oblation.
Having placed her, mounted upon a trident, within the sacrificial pit, she dies from the house.
One should cause that image made of sand to be buried in this [place].
This means by performing a fire oblation (*homa*) with fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood.
Having pierced it with iron spikes, one should then dig it up while it is positioned face-downward. || 47-72 ||
By reciting [the mantra] there upon the remains of offerings (nirmālya), an enemy shall go to the state of death.
In the case of recitation and other rites, the name should be joined after two syllables of the mantra.
Having pierced a palm leaf inscribed with the mantra within a hexagon and smeared with poison, one should bury it on both banks of a river.
Enmity arises.

Having ground together yellow arsenic (*citraka*), a lump of salt, house-soot, and the three pungents (*ūṣaṇa*), as well as *sūraṇa*—which is known as "poison"—this should certainly be employed for the purpose of inciting enmity or for killing. (47–75)

The earth from seven village anthills, donkey hair, the bark of the *aśvattha* tree, the root of the *kākamūlaka*, and ash from a cremation ground—[these are to be used] during the fortnight [of the dark half]. (47–76)
Vahni-mantha, sthaviṣṭha, vandāka, markaṭī, and brahmadaṇḍikā;
the ashes of a funeral pyre from a Caṇḍāla and a Brahmin, and the hair of a Caṇḍāla and a Brahmin [are used for purification]. (47–77)
Likewise, the site of a crow’s dwelling on a neem tree burnt by a funeral pyre, dog bones, the remains of sacrificial offerings, a donkey's tail-hair, and a bone [are inauspicious]. (47–78)
Markaṭī combined with gulikā makes this the "ten-fold powder" (daśacūrṇa).
Having obtained these gulikās, they should be in equal parts within the house of Kālikā. (47–79)
This "ten-fold powder," prepared with the mantra through three hundred thousand recitations, should be cast into the houses, fire-sanctuaries, and other dwellings of the enemy. (47–80)

This secret method for causing the total uprooting [of enemies], spoken by Pippalāda, is known as the "Single-Horse Stake" (*ekāśvikīlāyasa*); it measures seven finger-breadths in length and is intended for the enemy.
One should dig at the foot [of the image] while reciting the mantra; this will bring about its eradication.
Likewise, in forest areas, one may take pebbles from the shrine of Durgā or Kālī. (47–82)

When the skull is held by three horse-pins like salt and lime, one should recite [the mantra] over it while it is being roasted with a stick; thus scattered, they cause the destruction of all [enemies]. (47–83)
At twilight, having reached the nine temples of Śiva, the naked ones rose up; those who cause the destruction of sugar were dispatched as the dispersers of sugar. || 47-85 ||
One should inscribe the Madhyādi-vidyā within a six-pointed star; it is red and great.
One should bury it in a cremation ground in the midst of a human skull between the southeast and northwest, destroying the harm caused by pretas. (47–86)

The procedure for remedying minor afflictions has been proclaimed by Sudarśana: through the fire-oblation of Vakra, consecration, and other rites, the various types of minor spirits are destroyed. (47–87)
Practical applications for the purpose of pacifying minor malevolent spells have been demonstrated using the Daurga, Nārasiṃha, and other mantras, as well as the Aghora and Aparājita weapons.
Nevertheless, the remedies prescribed by Pratyāṅgirasa are here written down in brief, out of a desire for the welfare of people. (47–89)
The Pratyāṅgirasa Sūkta is recorded as consisting of thirty-five verses;
however, in the Khila section, it was previously seen by the seer Aṅgāsa to contain one additional quarter-verse.
Pratyāṅgirasa is traditionally remembered as their seer (ṛṣi) in general; the meter (chandas) is remembered as Anuṣṭubh, and the deities (devatā) are those Mothers (mātaraḥ). (47.91)
Where there is a collection of many *ṛc* verses, that is a *sūkta*;
Yāska and Śāṇḍilya are the two teachers, and likewise the oblation is offered to the Viśvedevas.

By means of the *ṛc* that they employ through rites such as recitation and burnt offerings (*japa-homa*), minor malevolent spells (*abhicāra*) are destroyed; indeed, they return to those very practitioners themselves. (47–93)
Having established the water-pot according to the rules and having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to its south,
one should perform the final fire-installation (ādhāna) as prescribed in one's own Vedic school, or according to the ritual procedure of the Mantra tradition.
Having encircled those two with swords, one should place them even upon a skull over fire;
at twilight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and so forth, [one should offer] red perfumes, garments, and the like.
And with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* sprinkled with cow’s urine, with clarified butter, with white mustard seeds, with black mustard seeds, and with *caru*—each separately. (47–96)
With a concentrated mind, one should offer nine oblations into the fire of the skull for seven days, beginning from the southwest and ending in the northeast.
Minor ailments, malevolent spells, and even diseases perish.

Just as with the "Lightning-Struck" and other mantras, one should offer fuel-sticks produced from the *kurava* tree for the destruction of minor obstacles, using products of the cow and the *pratisara* rite. (47–99)
Having performed the homa with the Trailokyā-kara-mudrā,
one should maintain the practice by offering oblations of cow’s urine and other substances, or quickly with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga.
Or one should offer oblations of guggulu resin smeared with the five products of the cow for the sake of a rival woman.
Each of these oblations should be performed separately for the sake of malevolent rites, pacification, or subduing,
using the remaining *ṛc* verses as well as the prescribed substances, each individually.
One should perform oblations for the protection against minor malevolent rites (*kṣudrakṛtya*) and for the pacification of diseases. (p.

254) One should bury in the earth, within a copper vessel, the five products of the cow, sesame, black gram, barley, *mudga* beans, rice, wheat, *bilva*, and *māṣa* beans, as well as sesame and lotus seeds, upon a lotus leaf during the conjunction of the Nāgas. (47.103)

Having placed it in a copper casket and consecrated it ten thousand times with the Sudarśana mantra—this refers to the first *ghaṭikā* of the final half-watch (*yāmārdha*) of the new moon; for that indeed [is the time]. (47–104)
In the *sarpa* muhūrta, under the *sarpa* nakṣatra, and likewise in the *sarpa* karaṇa—
this is the *nāgayoga*.
[One should take] all five roots, the five types of earth, and all seeds, together with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
While reciting the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha, one should bury it in the earth within the interior of an earthen vessel during the conjunction of the Nāga yoga.
Minor obstacles perish and fortunes increase.

Having lit lamps with white lotus wicks in four shallow bowls using the ghee of a tawny cow, one should place them in a vessel and bury it at night; that site of dispute shall become prosperous for him. (47–106)
Having become naked himself, the Naga circumambulated the field. || 47-107 ||
At the time of seizing [the site], one should show it with the "elephant-face" [mudrā]; the ground will then become well-established for oneself.

Having filled five separate lotus petals with products of the cow (*gavya*) and bound them together at their stalks, one should bury those on the petals—which ward off minor evils—while recollecting the remainder upon the earth during the *nāga-yoga*.
*Krodhāgneḥ kalaḥ kaṭaḥ huṃ phaṭ ṭhaṭha* | *Arciṣe ṭhaṭha* | *Jvālādhūmrāya ṭhaṭha* | *Pātālarudrāya ṭhaṭha* | *Uttiṣṭha puruṣāya ṭhaṭha* | *Dhanurdharāya ṭhaṭha*.
These are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), derived from the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
The seer is Pippalāda; its metre is declared to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Rudra as Krodhāgni, the ten-armed Bhairava. (47–110)
Holding, in sequence, a noose and a goad, a sword and a shield, an arrow and a bow, as well as a khaṭvāṅga, a serpent, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with tawny hair standing erect on his head, wearing a tiger-skin garment, and adorned with various serpents. || 47-112 ||
The heart-mantra for all rites of sorcery, together with its ancillaries, has been proclaimed as the Fire of Wrath (Krodhāgni).
One should worship Bhairava, facing westward, in the place of Raudra. (47.113)
One who observes the vow of drinking only milk and performs one hundred thousand recitations shall thereby have his mantra perfected;
this should be done at the twilight hours, on the fifth day of the Rudra-pañcamī, and on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the fire of Śiva.

In a triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*), one should offer oblations for eight days beginning with the eighth lunar day, using eight thousand and eight hundred fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* wood, for the purpose of pacifying minor calamities.
Having performed the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) with *kāraskara* wood at the onset of night, he should offer oblations;
then, having released that firebrand (*aṅgāra*) at a crossroads and offered the sacrifice, the *bali* offering should likewise be cast away.
Oṃ, homage to the hosts of Rudra who bring about all peace; I cast forth this bali. May they accept it for the sake of peace! Ṭhaṭha.
With well-prepared red rice, one should cast this bali in the eight directions.
Having indeed presented the bali to the World Protectors and the Guardians of the Field (Kṣetrapālas), once again— || 47-117 ||
May those who dwell in the *pūṭas* and the *śāṇīs*, having duly accepted this offering, provide them with another dwelling and protect them today; homage be to them! || 47-118 ||

To those who are independent, those who are honey-like, those who are existent, non-existent, both existent and non-existent, those of deformed shapes, those of universal forms, those of terrible forms, those with faces like deer, those with faces like birds, those who bring prosperity, those who do not bring prosperity, and those who grant desires—all these beings, together with their hosts, to them [I offer] salutations again and again!
This oblation for the fire-sacrifice is indeed the destroyer of all petty evils.
[The fuel consists of] leaves of the *pālāśa*, *nimba*, and *apāmārga*, as well as wood from the *kuravaka* tree. (47–119)

And of the four milk-yielding trees, as well as white mustard seeds, bdellium, sesame seeds, the five products of the cow, clarified butter, milk, and the sacrificial oblation (caru)— these are used in sequence.
By offering one thousand and eight oblations, one shall destroy minor ailments; there occurs liberation from planetary spirits, ghosts, and the like, as well as the pacification of diseases. (47-121)
Likewise, one should offer oblations of Apāmārga, Aśvinī fuel-sticks, and milk;
having offered milk into the water of a jar at dawn on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
(356) By means of that consecration through the pouring [of substances], there shall be liberation for one seized by a planet;
[this is done] with charcoal from the Aśvinī tree upon its very fruit. (47.123)
Having drawn the wheel called Yamarāja and propitiated it, which bestows prosperity,
one should place [the deity] there, offer oblations with *aśvattha* wood, and sprinkle [the site] with cow’s urine.
Ten thousand recitations shall bring liberation from the planetary affliction; one should also feed the twice-born.
[The mantra is: "O Caṇḍīśa Maheśvara, quickly destroy the planet of so-and-so! Ṭha Ṭha! (47-125)
Then, having tied this mantra upon a rag, one should recite it while touching it;
or, in some place where there is a fire-sign, one should recite it separately for a thousand suns.
That ash, when thrown upon the head of an enemy, or in his house, village, or city, brings about his destruction or expulsion before long. (47.127)
For its pacification, one should dig up that ground and discard the earth; by performing the remedial rite through fire-oblations, peace will be attained.
That which has been shown as a minor action should not be employed against Brahmins or kings;
however, one may employ it for the protection of the virtuous against murderous aggressors and evildoers. (47.129)
Having first ensured the protection of oneself and one's employer, one should then carry out the suppression of enemies and other such tasks.
Once the task is accomplished, the wise man, having performed the required expiation, should establish a method for future countermeasures.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Minor [Ailments] and Their Remedies," in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*. 47.
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Now, something regarding the subjugation and attraction [of beings] is stated:
long [wood], tortoise-shell, poison from the *karṇi* plant, along with *uṣṭhoma*, *ākānta*, and wood. (48.1)

"Amukam," ending with the repetition of "dah" (burn), followed by "paca" (cook), "mama" (mine), and "vaśam ānaya agne" (bring under control, O Agni)—this is remembered as the mantra of eight syllables for the Vikṛti rite. || 48-2 ||
One should recite [the mantra] three times the number of the Guru’s years for as many days as the Guru’s age;
at the twilight [sacrifice], an oblation of white salt mixed with honey, when offered, brings about subjugation. (48.3)
*Kāphuṇḍeṇiṣiṇi kāphuṇḍāli, burn [the name of] so-and-so, cook [him], quickly bring [him] under control! *Ṭhaṭha*.
With cotton, bone, salt, tooth-sticks, and the dust from the feet, by means of this twilight oblation (*sandhyā-homa*), subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) occurs within seven nights. (48-4)
Homage to Kṛṣṇa, the Yakṣa! ṇāviri ṇāviri! O moving and unmoving mind, release the semen! Ṭhaṭha!
If one recites this seven times over a red *aśvārī* flower and causes it to whirl before a woman, she will certainly become submissive to him and her fluids will flow. (48–5)
Homage to the Yakṣas! Asame kusume ṭhaṭha! By reciting this seven times, a flower or a fruit offered [in this manner] brings about subjugation (*vaśya*).
A lotus leaf with six petals, inscribed on birch bark (*bhūrja*) and smeared with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and sandalwood paste, [is likewise effective]. (48–6)

One should worship [the deity] situated in clarified butter upon a lotus having a pericarp inscribed with the name and four petals marked with hooks; this will bring under control men and women, and even effect their attraction. 48–7.

Accompanied by fire and the Aghora mantra, he is Ardhanārīśvara; with the staff of his feet and two garments, he draws [the diagram] with funeral embers while situated in the womb-position (yonistha) to bring the subject under control. (48–8)
The bull and the ram are joined by the gaze; the two long vowels are at the end of the Brahmin [syllable];
the pair of *ṭha* letters is the delighter of the mind—this ten-syllabled mantra brings about subjugation. (48-9)
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with lac juice on the surface of the left palm;
for the purpose of subjugation, one should either show the mantra situated upon its petals or place it upon the heart.
Having written down the mantra, one should recite it for subjugation and other purposes; then the desired object comes.
Having recited it with this [mantra] and having placed curd produced from a [cow's] womb [into the vagina], through the recitation of that [mantra]: 48–11.
Therefore, collyrium prepared with clarified butter, when applied to the eyes, delights one's husband.
Now, among all those things that bring others under control, the one known as salt is the foremost. (48-12)
The mantra is indeed from the Atharva Veda; its seers are Ambarīṣa, Varuṇa, Lavaṇa, and Aṅgiras; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; and the deities are Mahārātri and Bhadrakālī. (48.13)
Others say it is Agni; furthermore, meditation is remembered as being of two kinds.

[The first is] Kālī, resembling a dark cloud, three-eyed, holding in her hands a trident, a sword, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a serpent on the right, and on the other side a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a severed head, and a shield.
She should be meditated upon as wearing a garland of skulls, radiant with the ornaments of glistening fangs and serpents,
adorned with a formidable crest of matted hair that is tawny-brown, and clad in deep blue garments.
And Agni:

three-eyed, mounted upon a ram, with matted hair, holding a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), a spear (*śakti*), and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his arms; he is saffron-pink in color, adorned with white garments and other ornaments. (48.15)
The syllable "māṃ" is a jar of flesh; it is embraced by Umā, is long, and adorned with an anusvāra. || 48-16 ||
"You are pungent, sharp, and fierce; yet the earth is the mother of salt, and Varuṇa is the father of salt.
While salt is being offered as an oblation, how can there be sleep? How can there be pleasure?
Salt cooks and causes to cook; salt cuts and pierces."
Burn my unreleased limbs; burn my flesh; burn my skin! 48.17
Burn the skin, bones, and marrow;
burn the marrow from the bones—even if [the enemy] dwells a hundred yojanas away, in the midst of rivers. (48.18)
In a city with iron walls and hundreds of black-serpent bolts,
he quickly burns it away by means of the fiery heat of salt.
In this very case, salt consecrated with the mantra comes under one's control;
it is the night during which the stake is extracted from one who has been impaled upon the point of a spike. (48.20)
That night of yours which is the Great Night, that night of yours is the Great Midnight.
*Ciṭi! Caṇḍāli! Mahācaṇḍāli! Bring so-and-so under my control, ṭhaṭha!* He who recites this while meditating [on the deity] a thousand times shall have the entire universe under his control. (48-21)

At night, standing in water reaching up to the knees and recollecting Bhadrakālī, one should perform the recitation (japa) a thousand or a hundred times; whoever is the object of this intent shall become submissive.
One should worship the Goddess and the Fire with red garlands, perfumes, and flowers;
having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) interlaced [with the mantra] upon a palm leaf, one should recite it.
If one should bury a thousand [of these] in the temple of Bhadrakālī, the person to be accomplished will undoubtedly come under his control for as long as he lives. (48.24)

Seated upon a board made from the wood of the tree of the lunar mansion of the person to be accomplished, remaining silent, on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, facing north after the first watch has passed; (48–25)
Wearing red perfumes and garments, having worshipped the fire in either a pit or on a sacrificial mound, one should worship Bhadrakālī in the eastern quarter of the fire.

On a red cloth, one should fashion an effigy of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) made of unrefined salt, provided with life-force, a heart, and the presence of the vital breaths and sense organs. (48.27)
Having drawn it out from the mouth of the fire with a ladle smeared with honey, he should offer it as an oblation;
having invoked Bhadrakālī into the fire and worshipped her, he should remain established in meditation. (48.28)
Beginning from the left foot and extending as far as the left hand,
one should divide that [limb] and offer oblations until seven offerings have been made.

Having offered clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis, one should indeed offer a bali-oblation with the Bhūtakrūra mantra, consisting of rice mixed with sesame seeds, rājikā, niśā, flour, curds, and milk.
Ṇapho ṇapho! To the hosts of Kālarātri, who bring all things under control and who effect all pacification—may they accept this offering for the sake of total subjugation and total peace, Ṭhaṭha!
Thereafter, one should place the heart of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) within one’s own heart by means of the mantra.
Recollecting "I am that very [being]," one should recite it twenty-one times. (48–31)
Having extinguished the fire during the great night, one should conclude the rite;
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
By performing a homa with salt for that duration, one shall bring everything under control;
the person to be accomplished will surrender all his possessions like a slave—of this there is no doubt. (48.33)
Standing in water reaching up to his mouth, he should perform a thousand repetitions of drawing [the water];
then, with a thousand loose flowers, he should cast them one by one into that person's feet. (48.34)
Having recited the Bhadrakālī mantra, which is supreme for attracting the one to be accomplished (sādhya),
one should write the mantra— interlaced with the name of the sādhya— upon a palm leaf.
Having boiled it in water mixed with ghee and milk while reciting the mantra, one may summon people;
for this [mantra] requires no preliminary ritual service (*puraścaryā*), nor rites such as fasting and the like. (48.36)
Once grasped, it bears fruit through the yoga of recitation, meditation, and so forth.
This is the section on the *lavaṇa* mantra.
*Pāṣaḍhī*, *sadṛgvalkau*, *klinne*, *bhāntaḥ*, [and] *atriṇā* in the liquid. (48-37)
The heart-mantra is *sadāklinnā*, which brings everything under control through recitation and other rites.
*Nityāyai huṃ phaṭ*. *Nityāyai ṭhaṭha*. *Nityaklinne hum*. *Nityaklinne namaḥ ṭhaṭha*.
Upon seeing Yamā, one should recite this vidyā; she will then flow forth [with passion] and likewise come under one's control. (48–38)
By drinking the water used for its recitation, by anointing oneself with its fragrant unguents,
and by offering flowers and other gifts, one shall bring all people under one's control.
O Devaśrī, Mukhaśrī, Yakṣi! O Padmāvati! Bring [him/her] under my control, unrelentingly! Ṭhaṭha!
A pair of palm-leaves inscribed with the Māhendra mantra, one placed over the other by oneself and kept secret, is a perfect means of subjugation. (48–49)
Homage to the Mātaṅgas! Homage to the Mātaṅgīs! Homage to the Mātaṅga maidens! It is as follows: *kuru curu ṭhaṭha*.

Having stepped upon with one’s foot an effigy made of anthill clay, whose head is that of a Sākhya and which is endowed with life, one should recite [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day; this brings her under control. (48–49)

With the right and left feet respectively, one should effect the subjugation of men and women for a period of seven days; while reciting [the mantra] joined with the noose, power, and goad, one should meditate upon Umā as being one's own self. (48–42)
By means of recitation (*japa*) and other practices, he clearly brings the entire world under his control, [repeating] "niyutaṃ sa vaśe viśvaṃ. [The mantra is:

*hṛd-dīrgha-vedhā kālaśca dhehā śalvarva gaṇadha priyāya sarvajanasaṃmohanāya jvala prajvala sarvajanasya hṛdayaṃ mama vaśaṃ kuru ṭhaṭha*. This is the Manmatha-mantra; one should meditate upon Manmatha as being identical with oneself. (48–43)
Having mentally visualized [the deity] with red attire and deeply red limbs, one should recite the mantra;
for this [mantra], when accomplished through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, is indeed a magnetizer of all. (48-44)

On another day, having placed an iron [vessel] wrapped with non-red thread along with fragrant flowers, one should take its root at sunrise when the white sun rises; by means of that, a *tilaka* mark will bring about subjugation.
Collyrium prepared with a wick enriched with the powder of the five parts of gold will bring under control even men, let alone women, for one afflicted by eye ailments. (48–49)
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and utpala filaments, along with spikenard, cloves, elephant musk, and liquorice, taken in equal parts— || 48-47 ||
Lac (ālaktaka) [is used] for the black animal; with the ashes of a crow and other such substances, it grants complete subjugation.
Gorocanā, realgar (tālaka), mica (śilā), lotus (padma), and the like, as well as red sandalwood—48–49.
The resin of the *karṇikāra*, the excrement of the *krauñca* and *pārāvata* birds, *kirātatikta*, *bhṛṅgeśvara*, *bhītā*, and the sprouts from the roots of the *vaṭa* tree. (48–49)
One should powder together equal parts of dried snuhi bark, rabbit dung, old tamarind fruit, karañja seeds, and garlic. (48–50)
When the lac-dye has been divided by the juice of the fruits of the *viśvavṛkṣa* tree,
one should sprinkle that powder with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and apply it to the head.
Having prepared a wick with honey, clarified butter, and neem oil, the soot produced therefrom, when smeared upon an elephant's temple with wine, will enchant the world. (48–52)
One should administer five parts of gold mixed with one's own five limbs and ground with honey; when consumed, it is a means of subjugation. (48–53)
Having thrown rock salt into the sour juice of *mātuluṅga* and sprinkled it with the water of the body,
one should place it for seven nights inside a sealed container formed by two shallow bowls.
At a crossroads, one clad in the directions as his garment should cook salt with *kāṣṭha*, *dhūr*, and *dhūrakā* woods;
those to whom that salt is given shall remain under one's control for the duration of their lives. (48–55)
Having ground together kuṣṭha, the resin of the punnāga tree, and the root of siṃhī, and having smeared it with honey, one may approach a woman; this is known as the "paralysis of Bhārgava. (48–56)

By applying a foot-ointment made from cow’s urine, *snuhī* milk, and the roots of white *puṅkhā* and sugarcane, one achieves paralysis; furthermore, by placing [the mixture] in the mouth and then in vinegar... (48–57)
Having ground that [substance] and smeared it upon the penis, this is the supreme method for paralyzing speech;
likewise, using the hair from the mouths of a horse and an elephant with drooping phalli [is effective]. (48–58)
Likewise, one should take the tail and the facial hair of a bull;
having fashioned a cord from them in the shape of a ring, it should be consecrated with the mantra. || 48-59 ||
Having applied [this] to the right forearm, pleasure is prevented by poetry;
it is for the purpose of binding the hair of excellent elephants and horses.
Having ground the root of *dantī* with the milk of *snuhī*, one should smear it upon the feet. (48–60)
By anointing the feet with this preparation, one becomes paralyzed in poetry; by washing them with hot water, the paralysis falls away.
[The preparation consists of] the bile of a fish, the mane-hair of a horse, and the ichor of an elephant. (48–61)
Having smeared the banner with honey is the supreme means for winning over women;
likewise are *vilaṅga*, sesame flowers, molasses, camphor, and sandalwood.
This ointment, composed by Svabhārgava, is the supreme means for winning over women.
It consists of māṃsī, vacā, aśvagandhā, kunda, and likewise vakula. (48–63)
Having ground that [substance] with water and applied it as an ointment, the organ of procreation becomes enlarged.
One should cook oil with jasmine flowers (*jātipuṣpa*); by the application of that [oil], one becomes handsome. (48–64)
Having rubbed the body with *dhurdhūra* and the leaves of *bṛhatī*, one gains control [over others];
likewise, an ointment made from *dhurdhūra* leaves and *rātri* makes one submissive. (48–65)
An ointment made from the resin of the *karṇikāra*, camphor, the pollen of the *ketakī*, rock salt, and honey, when applied to the banner, results in death. (48.66)
One should apply to the eyes a wick made of *bailva* wood, lotus with ghee, jasmine, *priyaṅgu*, and *paśurocanā*, along with the soot from a lamp fed with cow-ghee;
whomever person he looks upon, that person becomes his servant. (48–67)

Kuṣṭha, kuraṇḍa, madhuka, and two types of agaru, along with musk and sandalwood mixed with camphor—when these are ground with cow-dung water and applied as an ointment while touched with both hands, they will bring everyone under one's control. (48–68)
Having ground together oil, the juice of *vārtāka*, and the fat of a bull, and having smeared [the body] with it, she will become a girl again. (48–69)
One should chew a tooth-stick made of *kārañja* wood from the *āravāra* region;
having taken it after it has been held in the mouth for seven days, one should give it to him to eat as a means of subjugation. (48–70)
Pigeon dung, śuṇṭhī, kuṣṭha, ugrā, añjana, and gorocanā, ground with honey and smeared on a banner, bring women under one's control. (48–71)
"O Goddess! O Mātaṅgī! O you who bear the auspicious enjoyment of Rudra! Homage to you! Ṭhaṭha! This is declared to be the mantra for anointing.
Having ground lotus petals with the urine of a tawny cow into a pill, and having dried it, one should smear it on the body; thus a woman will make her husband a slave. (48-72)
One should drink grapes, licorice, and apuṣpā with milk; likewise, by using an errhine (nāvana) of mango bark and *rasa*, she will become menstruating. (48–73)
The powder of the root of black *rambhā* and the powder of *yaṣṭi*, drunk with cow’s milk in the morning, destroys menstrual hemorrhage in women. (48–74)
One should drink red ochre (*gairika*) the size of a dice with milk for three days;
it removes the flow of blood, as does honey combined with the tender leaves of the *udumbara* tree. (48–75)
Lotus stalks, sandalwood, *chinnā*, *bhīrucillī*, lime, and honey, when drunk with the sprouts of the *udumbara* tree, prevent menorrhagia. (48.76)
One should drink the juice of the red and white japā flowers during their red and white exudations;
one should take its root with milk at dawn, and its decoction with milk at night.
One should roast the flower of the coconut with fire and burn it;
its juice, when drunk with milk, prevents the discharge of semen. (48–78)

By drinking the flowers [of the *śalmali*] with the milk of a cow in season for four days, a barren woman becomes fertile; likewise, by drinking [a preparation of] *abhayā* and *vyoṣa*, she becomes non-barren. (48–79)
The drinking of *nākulī* flowers with milk destroys menstrual flow in women.
[One should take] two *kāṇḍas* of *kukkuṭāṇḍa*, *brahmī*, and the excrement of a pigeon. (48–80)
Having likewise pulverized *lakṣmī*, one should administer it; the servant shall become the master.
[This is done] in a decoction of the five parts of *hemonmatta* mixed with milk-ocean (*kṣīrodadhi*). (48.81)

Having smeared the body with the essence of that [substance] and then rubbed it with black gram (māṣa), one should place it inside a fruit; having dug a hole there, one should urinate into it. || 48-82 ||
Having extracted [the substance] after seven days and combined it with the five impurities (pañcamala), one should administer it;
this is the most excellent charm (saṃvanana), declared to be the "hook of the God of Love" (manmathāṅkuśa). || 48-83 ||
Svarakta, the dregs of poetry, the root of śvetabhānu, honey,
combined with vacā and kuṣṭha, when administered by men, is a means for bringing women under one's control.
Having drunk it and then vomited it out, one should churn that milk with a gourd-pumpkin;
from that, butter and a subjugating condiment are produced. (48–85)
One should apply a paste of earth, camphor, honey, and sugar to the private parts of a woman; her husband shall then become her slave. (48-86)

Those substances arising from the armpits, limbs, ears, nose, eyes, teeth, and tongue, when combined with sweat and one's own bodily fluids, act as a means of subjugation after consuming [the mixture] of two [partners]. (48.87)

Having smeared one's own body with musk, sandalwood, camphor, kuṣṭha, saffron, black agallochum, naktamāla, and the plant called kāma—all ground together with cow-dung water—one gains mastery over all. (48-88)
Two parts each of musk and sandalwood, and one part of camphor, ground with snow and smeared [on the body], bring about subjugation. (48–89)
A wick soaked seven times with cow-dung water and made from powdered vaṭa sprouts mixed with a sixteenth part of clarified butter produces collyrium that brings all under control. (48–90)

Saffron, yellow myrobalan, yellow pigment, collyrium, and musk, along with lotus pollen, padmaka, camphor, agallochum, iron, and the two types of sandalwood—all these ground together in equal parts and mixed with the milk of milk-exuding trees, and then encased in a wick made of lac; *Note: "alakta" refers to lac (red resin).*
A pen made from the tail-hair of a black cow, when used with ghee from a Surabhi cow, bestows mastery over the three worlds.
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kumuda, Devī, Hema, and Pārāvata—these, when made into a pill and mixed with sandalwood paste, bring others under one's control. (48.92)
With kuṣṭha, citraka, arka, mañjiṣṭhā, tagara, and red sandalwood, the Puṇḍra-rite, which deludes the entire world, brings all beings under one's control. (48.93)
Māṃsī, candana, rocanā, gajamada, nīlotpala, spṛkkā, jāti, tvak, suradāru, patra, tagara, elā, śilā, kuṅkuma,
padma, kesara, padmaka, kṛṣṇatulasī, and siddhārthaka— [these are] in equal proportions.
At the rising of the moon in the Puṣya asterism, one should grind [the medicine] with snow-water using a virtuous maiden.
With these, there should be an application of *tilaka* which brings prosperity and subjugation.
[The ingredients are: *kuṣṭha*, saffron, rock salt, *natāyasa*, sandalwood, and camphor. (48–95)
Cardamom and saffron—this collyrium, equal in parts to those [other ingredients], brings others under one's control.
On the full moon day, at twilight, one should draw three circles facing eastward.
Having fashioned a circle within the orb of the sun, and being well-seated with speech restrained,
one should place the articles of worship in the center of the orb and [arrange them] from the east.
One should worship him who stands in the center of a lotus, adorned with white ornaments, gentle, seated upon the lap of a maiden, and holding two water-lilies in his hands. (48.98)
One should worship Soma with the mantra "Oṃ sasad yadaṇḍaṃ śuklaṃ tu somāya namaḥ" and with offerings such as perfumes and the like. (48–99)
Rohiṇī, Revatī, Rātri, and Jyotsnā occupy the quarters starting from the East in sequence;
Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Kalā occupy the corners starting from the southeast.
Having worshipped [the deity] up to the offering of food (naivedya), one should fill a silver cup with milk and present it as an arghya offering to the Moon (Candra) while reciting the Vidyā-mantra.
"Oṃ vidye! vidyāmālini! candriṇi! candramukhi! svāhā"—this is the mantra of knowledge (vidyā-mantra).
In this manner, one should offer the arghya for three months; then the girl is given.
"Kāphuṇḍe cāli cāli kumārge bhagaṃ me prayaccha ṭhaṭha."
Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times every day.

Having practiced until the end of the fourteenth day, one whose mantra is perfected should then, at night, offer for a month a ball of food consisting of six kinds of condiments, reciting the *prakṛti* mantra; thereby, he obtains his desired maiden for marriage. (48–103)
One should immediately apply a paste of *kuṣṭha*, *bṛhatī*, *apāmārga*, *siddhārtha*, *tagara*, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) mixed with milk; this increases the size of the breasts. (48-104)
And on the two earlobes.
Thus have been shown these various types of subjugation rites (*saṃvanana*) established in many tantras.
These respective applications should be employed with care, by those who are skillful, vigilant, and respectful. (48–105)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, on the subjugation of others, in the Mantra-pāda of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 48.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter.

Having ground the bark of *āragvadha*, long pepper (*loṇa*), and the fruit of *ciñcā* in sour gruel (*śukta*) during the night, when drunk, it removes [diseases] and increases the size of the cows' bellies. (49-1)
Having ground sesame seeds, pāṭā root, and cotton leaves together with milk, one should give it to a cow; by administering it with cow's buttermilk, one removes bovine dysentery in an instant. (49-2)
Coconut water, milk, sour gruel, and the juice of *balā*, when drunk together, destroy diarrhea accompanied by blood in cows. (49.3)
In the case of diarrhea characterized by pus and phlegm, one should cause the cow to drink a decoction of phaṇītakam, nirguṇḍī, dīpyaka, garlic, and vacā in sour gruel (kāñjika).
The thousand-rayed Āditya, Agni, *ṭhaṭha*.
Having written this mantra on a leaf, one should place it around the neck for the protection of cattle:
"The eight-hooded Hari protects [them], *ṭhaṭha*."
This [mantra], inscribed between the Aśvinī tree and the bell, is indeed on the neck of the cow. (49.5)
When bound with a rope made of *dhātakī*, it removes the affliction caused by *gomārī*.
*Namo bhagavate vajramukāradarśanāya oṃ vila mili meli siddhi gomāri! vajriṇi! huṃ phaṭ! Protect the cattle-pen in this village; bring peace! Ṭhaṭha!* And this is the mantra:
By him, the sound of Ghaṇṭākarṇa was proclaimed as a host of great power.
May that Lord of the World, who brings about the destruction of Mārī, protect us!
*Ṭha ṭha*. And this is the *gomārihara* mantra: having written these two separately, ending with *aśvinī*, *vṛkṣa*, and *ghaṇṭā*... [49-7]
The two who ward off death were bound to the two necks of a pair of cows;
in ancient times, Kurarava performed a sacrifice with the consumption of cattle. (49.8)
Remember that the words of the God of gods, the Child (Vaṭu), are not otherwise:
*ṭhaṭha*.
Whatever [mantra] has been recited seven times, one should then cause a cow to eat it. (49-9)
Even a wicked woman shall come under one's control, especially through *girikarṇī*.
"Homage to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Purāṇas! Ṭhaṭha!
Having seized the nose of a cow with the index and middle fingers— || 49-10 ||
By means of this mantra, horses shall become submissive:
*kṣīra-gopa-vaga-yakṣīra-kṣamā-kṣa-kṣa-mā-kṣara*. (49.11)
[One should place] *namo noga gagana mogopa kṣagaty atyaga kṣapaḥ* in this [mantra] within the sixty-four squares, which are enriched by lines, points, and the *tatpaśu* [syllables]. (49.12)
One should write the Sarvabhadra mantra both forward and backward on a board made of khadira wood or on birch bark; thereafter, it is to be worshipped.
One should tie it at the entrance of the cowshed or upon the neck of a cow;
this also serves to protect the cattle.
[The mantra consists of] the name of the cow, the word "gomataḥ," and the three outer circles of the entire diagram.

One should write the root mantra ending in *svāhā* upon an eight-petaled lotus encircled by a pitcher (*kumbha*). Then, having drawn a circle provided with a water-vessel and a staff, and having enclosed it within an interval, one should apply all the oil and other substances in reverse order upon the neck of a cow.
With her single braid anointed with oil, her ears adorned with beautiful lotus-buds made of reeds,
and having fashioned the beauty of her feet for herself by binding them with a single iron chain— she who wears no garment,
whose ear-ornament is a hibiscus flower, wanders this world upon a donkey.
O Goddess! You alone understand the broom with its upward-bound flag and outstretched arms. 49-15.
Or it may be placed at the gate of the cow-pen, meaning that which protects the cattle.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the Gorakṣāpaṭala, in the Mantrapāda of the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable Īśānaśivagurudeva. 49.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Take equal parts of *coraka*, *kuṣṭha*, *murā-granthi*, *māṃsī*, and *pūtī*;
add three times as much *dhātrī* fruit, and grind them with fragrant water.
Perfumed with incense and scented even with fragrant flowers—this very *gandhāmalaka* is declared to be fit for a king. (50-2)
Cardamom, tagara, leaf, lotus, granthiparṇa, rohiṇī, pūtikā, and uraka in equal parts, with twice that amount of dhātrī—all well-ground with fragrant water. (50.3)
Fumigated repeatedly with *gulā*, *agaru*, and *sarja* resin, and scented with flowers, this becomes fragrant *āmalaka*. (4)
Granthimāṃsī, maruvaka, śaileya, dāmana, dala,
coraga, and tagara— all these in equal parts, and twice that amount [of the following].
The *āmalaka* fruit is said to be as before, and its purification is also as previously described;
likewise for *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *hastikusuma*, *devadālī*, and *mṛṇālaka*. (50–6)
When flowers are treated with powdered madhuka mixed with a small amount of honey, they release their sap through this proper application.
Having smeared an axe with honey and sprinkled it with the powdered fragments of wood cut by it,
even *mallikā* and *campaka* flowers indeed melt away.
From the application of conch powder, the melting of *ketakī* occurs; likewise, [the redness of the sun] arises from *mañjiṣṭhā*, fresh *pattaṅga*, *kusumbha*, and red sandalwood. (50.9)
With these [substances], gradually increased, mixed with lac-dye and water, strained through cloth, combined with *plakṣa* fruit, rice, and honey, and thoroughly infused; || 50-10 ||
When these are combined, they form a most beautiful incense known as *jātiliṅga*.
One part of *viśva* (ginger), one part of *gulā* (galangal), two parts of *nimba* (neem) and *hiṅgu* (asafoetida) seeds, and six parts of *guggulu* (bdellium),
along with castor seeds— all ground together in goat’s milk— become here, as before, the incense called *hiṅgu*.
This means "situated within a heap of grain.
Bilva fruit, nimba, viśvā, māṣa, garlic, and asafoetida—these are the ingredients. Measured by two, four, two, and four parts respectively, asafoetida is indeed as before. (50–12)

As before, by means of the process of grinding with goat’s milk and so forth, it becomes asafoetida (hiṅgu). [The quantities are] one, eight, four, two, fifteen, fourteen, eight, and eleven *māṣas* of bilva; along with neem, jaggery, goat’s milk, asafoetida, viśva, and garlic—this is indeed asafoetida prepared as previously described. (50–13)
The meaning is: by means of grinding goat’s milk and placing it upon a heap of grain;
likewise, a decoction of *śigru* root, goat’s urine, and honey. (50.14)
One should take four palas each of these separately, and when reduced to one-third, [they are combined with] nutmeg, kakkola, musk, camphor, saffron, and sandalwood. (50.15)
One *karṣa* of agaru, finely ground and measured separately in *palas*, should be well-prepared in a fragrant vessel; [the site] should be marked with circles using heaps of rice. (50.16)
Having extracted [the clay], formed it into a mass, and dried it in the shade,
one should take a single portion from that mass and mix it with an equal amount of earth.
That auspicious musk should indeed be moistened with water;
having cut a small piece of the root of the *śakramocā* plant and a bit of bamboo, [one should apply it]. (50.18)
One should administer the enema (nālikā) for two or three nights with that respective juice;
of that [juice] there should be a measure of two prasthas, along with kaṇā, uśīra, and coraka.
Having ground one *karṣa* [of the powder] and half a *pala* of camphor (*ghanasāra*), one should add all the powdered ingredients together with the juice of *nālikā-kadali*. (50.20)
Having blinded it, wrapped it with a rope, and smeared the outside with clay, one should burn it in a fire of husks and dried cow-dung; then, once it has cooled, one should extract it again.
Camphor placed for seven days upon a heap of grain clearly sprouts;
likewise, the sprout of the *ketakī* plant [appears] in water, and that of rice and *maṇḍa* in hot water. (50.22)
And having washed ṭaṅkaṇa separately in milk for the duration of one watch (yāma), it should be powdered and joined with camphor in a fourth part. || 50-23 ||
Having boiled it in milk and placed it upon a plantain leaf, one should dry it;
that becomes excellent camphor (*ghanasāra*).
[Alternatively,] that which is found inside a ripe *bilva* fruit, combined with half its weight of oil, [is also used]. (50-24)
Having dried it in the sun, crushed it with dharma-water, and boiled it again with clear water,
one should extract the oil by pressing it, and then add one karṣa each of karpūra and yojita.
Camphor oil is produced.
Indeed, citron fruits covered with beeswax and placed in ghee and honey remain endowed with their original juice and color. (50.26)
Mango fruits that have fallen naturally, yet still attached by a small portion of their stalks, should be placed in oil mixed with jaggery; they will undoubtedly remain fresh for a long time. (50.27)
Other fruits likewise remain fresh for a long time.
One should smear copper leaves with salt and *vajra*-milk, heat them over a fire, and then carefully quench them in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*. (50.28)
One should employ it twenty-one times in the preparation of silver and other metals.
Copper killed with sulphur and then raised again by means of borax— || 50-29 ||
Just as [iron] loses its own black odor even after seven times [of treatment], so one should cause pure copper leaves to be made smooth. (50.30)
Having repeatedly smeared [the image] with pure naga-stone mixed with sarpa-kṣī and water, and having let it dry for six days during the day, one should perform the rite of Dharma. (50.31)
Then, having driven away [the obstacles] in the light, one should sprinkle [the object] seven times with sour gruel mixed with cow dung, joined with the *tāra* (the syllable Om). || 50.32 ||
For one month, mercury (sūta) should be kept in human urine with the oil of *bhallātaka*,
along with soot (*gṛhadhūma*), oil, and jaggery (*guḍa*) in a mortar.
One should grind [the ingredients] with that and smear thin leaves of silver;
having applied this, after three *puṭa* treatments, it becomes molten gold equal in quality to pure gold.
Abhraka, whether white or black, ground with *munipuṣpa* flowers and water, placed inside a *sūraṇa* tuber within a cow-pen, and heated for one month, melts when combined with gold. (50.35)
Having ground *dhānyābhraka* in *vajrakṣīra* and having infused it therein for seven days in an extremely pure vessel made of copper or even clay; 50-36.
A breast, finely ground with the fibers of a red lotus stalk and water, and subsequently ground with safflower oil, will dissolve through this methodical application. (50.37)
Abhra that has been well-ground and mixed with the juice of *kṣīrakāñcī* liquefies;
likewise, the entire range of metals liquefies when placed in the sun. (50.38)
Quickly cooked in the juice of *khaṇḍahālī*, all metals, when reduced to powder and joined with the appropriate substances, indeed melt while remaining established in their nature. (50.39)

One should employ quicksilver (mercury) in tin, starting from two guñjās and increasing by half a raktikā for each [subsequent] sharp and red-hot iron, with the quantities being half, a quarter, and so on. 50-40.

One should melt tin in the juice of *munipuṣpa* flowers and pour it into a natural crucible; one should then sprinkle powdered *śilājatu* as a post-casting additive (*prativāpa*) for the sake of purification. (50.41)
One should add the unmentioned portions of gold and other metals to purified tin and mica;
having blinded [the mixture], it solidifies while molten.
Silver, copper, and lead should have portions equal to twelve, nine, and two [respectively]. (50–42)
One should melt it together with borax (ṭaṅkaṇa) in the light [of a fire];
having cast it into cow-dung water, it becomes silver that has returned to its natural state. (50.43)
Kṣoṇī, badarī, mūla, lavaṇa, laghu, sikthaka, tila, kṣīriṇikā, and kṛṣṇavalaya—each of these separately. (50.44)
In a kuḍuba measure of kiṃśuka water mixed with half a part of cow’s ghee, one should place a pill made of *saṅkocabandha* along with gold; this cures muteness. (50.45)
Having blinded that half of the *krama* and extracted it, one should throw it into the aforementioned liquid.
Having thus extinguished it many times, when it has indeed become digested— || 50-46 ||
Then, having melted the *samarukma* (gold) into the essence of the night (*rātrirasena*),
one should sprinkle the *nāga* (mercury) three times with it in a quantity equal to that of the pill.
When eight niṣkas of copper have been cast into that nāga, one should cause it to penetrate [the base metal] using a fresh prastha of the juice of karṇikāra flowers.
One should add one niṣka of the powder called vimalā-kāṃsya;
when that [mixture] placed on the fire has reached a solid state by means of a gentle fire, [it is ready]. (50.49)
Having mixed an equal amount of powdered stone with that [substance], one should rub it;
then, having placed it in a vessel, [one should apply it] to gold of seven colors and so forth.
One should blow [the crucible] with a humming sound while adding a flux (krāmaṇa) to the gold (niṣka).
As it is being melted, one should stir it when it reaches the weight of half a *kṛṣṇala*; then, having cooled it, one should extract it.
Thus, even without effort, the gold easily attains a state of superior uniformity of color. (50–51½)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, on various substances, in the Mantra-pāda of the Tantrasāra, which is the Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati. 50.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter.
Following from the previous discussion regarding the knowledge of the great magical illusion (*mahendrajāla*),
various forms of playful entertainment that produce wonder are here written down in brief.
If the powder of *sadbhū* and *nāgendragopa* is applied to the head, she shall be enjoyed by that very person alone for a period of one month, and not by others. (51–2)
Tambūla spat out from the mouth [and placed] upon the skin of a lizard, while kept inside a casket made of *bhallātaka* fruit, will cause diseases of the mouth. (51.3)
When [the powder] has been extracted, liberation occurs.
An ointment made from the powder of a pair of mother-of-pearl shells causes the closure of the female organ.
By washing with cow's buttermilk and powdered cowrie shells, it becomes as before. (51.4)
An application of ground [substance] to a cow-horn turned downward causes obstruction of the womb;
by applying it to a horn turned upward, she will become available for enjoyment.
By crossing over a thread sprinkled with the blood of a chameleon, [one gains power]. (51–5)

If women suffer from blood discharge due to the blood of a two-faced snake, that thread, having been washed and fasted upon, brings it to an end. If one's name is joined with the blood of a black crow on a mango leaf, [the same result follows]. (51–6)
When that very [scorpion] is thrown into its own excrement, the birds (dvikas) peck at it repeatedly;
once it is extracted and burnt, there is liberation. For her, the scorpion’s sting is like a sweetmeat, which she consumes with joy. (51–7)
A seed of the Madana tree, when applied to her excellent limb, causes a piercing sensation;
upon its removal, there is release.
[This mixture] is combined with peacock’s feathers, Malada, Durdhūra, the bark of Viṣa, and Lāṅgalī. (51.8)
That [substance] ground in buffalo blood—its smoke shall delude all beings.
Furthermore, a lamp made of a wick of lac and *ḍuṇḍuka* oil deludes every person who beholds its light.
[The powder] called *kākolūkāsṛj* (crow-and-owl-blood), when placed upon a neem leaf... || 51-9 ||
That [substance] placed in its hollow would cause enmity between those two;
likewise with the blood of a buffalo or a horse.
Also, the powder of a tail [hair], or that of a Brahmin’s son, or of a water-snake, [placed] in lac. (51.10)
Having prepared wicks, one should make lamps that leave all directions bare.
The application of incense and lamps bears fruit only at night.
For the sake of self-protection, one should insert cow’s ghee into the interior of one’s own nostrils. (51–11)
Or one may apply it as collyrium to the eyes; it will delude both oneself and others.
Having repeatedly soaked sesame seeds in the milk of the *vajrī* plant and dried them, [one should use them]. (51–12)
By the application of that oil, those hairs which are black become white;
likewise, long pepper powder (*pippalī*) repeatedly saturated with *vajrī* milk [produces the same effect]. (51.13)
Having ground *āmalaka* fruit and applied it, it is the supreme destroyer of hair;
furthermore, one should cause the dust of a princess’s feet to fall inside the nostrils of horses. (51.14)

It means that it causes those horses to fall. From drinking sandalwood [essence], there is a restoration [of vigor]. A bracelet made of the tail-hairs of two donkeys engaged in sexual intercourse, when placed upon the forearm, remains fixed there and brings about the enlargement of the penis. (51.15)
In the case of the Kṣapaṇaka, it means the erection of the penis. That which is led downward causes [the object] to fall.
Jujube seeds eaten by jackals, when placed by children upon the garments of a woman at the time of sexual union, cause her lower garment to fall off on the forearm. (51–16)
A garland of jujube fruits (*badarī*) placed on the forearm near a woman, when raised upward, causes her to fall— that is to say, she falls.
A lamp made with *arka* cotton and castor oil removes bedbugs at night.
The root of the *sthalakumbhī* plant, when applied to the bed, will remove bedbugs.
A lamp prepared with the oil of a crab, when placed upon its cheek, will certainly attract all bedbugs from their dwellings. (51-18)
A wick made from lac and *arkatūla* cotton, soaked in *rājī* and clarified butter, effects the eradication of bedbugs at night; however, the juice of *karīra* removes lice. (51.19)
The root of white Aparājitā, the fruit and flower of Arjuna, Viḷaṅga, Sarjaka, lac, Śrīvāsa, and Aruṣkara [constitute] the city. (51.20)
Incense made from these [substances] in equal proportions indeed drives away mosquitoes, bedbugs, snakes, mice, woodworms, and spiders from the house. (51.21)
Water mixed with the fine powder of *kokilākṣa* seeds becomes solid; if combined with *baddhavallī*, it takes on the form of flesh. (51.22)
Just as fire [is produced] from a sun-crystal, so too fire may arise from bell-metal placed in intense heat when there is dry cotton or cow-dung beneath it, even though its roots are absent. (51.23)
If the hands and feet are smeared with frog-fat mixed with one's own urine, they will not be burned by fire at all. (51.24)

By applying a paste made from the root of *samaṅgā* mixed with the fat of a frog, one likewise arrests the fire [of fever] through external application. Furthermore, at the time of ascending the scale, if one's breath is obstructed, one becomes light. (51–25)
Even a faultless person here should exhale the breath through the Guru [channel];
it is joined with the external desired wind, situated in the wind, within the abode of wind.
If it is buried at the base of the Tulā [pillar], even a slayer of a Brahmin becomes lightened of sin;
it should be placed within the house on the earth, situated upon a vajra, with the name [of the sinner] and the flesh of a goat outside.
One should bury that at the base of the balance; even a man who is a Guru shall become pure.
On that day, [one should prepare] a mixture of cow-dung from a calf born on that very day and tagara.
Having first swallowed the pill, the poison does not affect one who then consumes it;
thus, by creating a counter-condition for the poison, he conquers it.
One should first chew a pill made of excrement mixed with *vyoṣa* and *kaṇā*. (51–29)
Afterwards, one should make an offering of rice; such a person is victorious.
Water containing a snake's tooth placed in the mouth is divine water that bestows victory. (51.30)
The powder of *kokilākṣā* mixed with red cow’s ghee brings victory over water. Having smeared the entire face [with it], one should cause the water to enter the nostrils and ears. (51.31)
p. 376) Even one who possesses faults triumphs by creating the condition of water.
A porpoise smeared with mud is not seen when grasped in the fist;
it becomes visible upon releasing the fist.
In his wooden sandals, there were seeds of *syonāka* contained within them.
Having stepped upon it, one should wander in the water at ease and without fear, having fixed the mind motionless between the eyebrows or on the forehead. (51.33)
With his body hollowed like a pot, he floats in the water like a boat;
or else, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) with all his limbs extended.
When the wick is smeared with oil and sprinkled with resin powder (sarjacūrṇa), [it burns steadily]. (51.34)
In a vessel filled with water both inside and out, a lamp burns;
its wick, saturated with the milk of the *snuh* plant and moistened with oil, is like the foam of the ocean.
One should pour the extracted juice into a vessel filled with milk;
that vessel, containing glowing embers, will clearly remain suspended in the air. (51.36)
Having prepared a lotus stalk or a reed filled with mercury, one should place it inside that [structure] and soak it in oil; when ignited, it will fly upward into the sky by itself.
Sauvīra [mercury] situated within the womb of a woman during her fertile period should be cast into the midst of fire for seven days; therein, a man is clearly seen. (51.38)
Having placed citron oil in a copper vessel and having set it upon the sacred fire at midday, the Sun is seen here as a chariot-borne deity. (51.39)
Collyrium that has been repeatedly processed with the juice of Agasti flowers, when applied to the eyes by day, enables one to see the stars. (51.40)
A peg driven into the tree of lightning remains fixed in the sky;
mixed with a little powder and water, it becomes like oil or clarified butter. (51.41)
Salt water placed on a hand smeared with a small amount of ghee and lute-plant juice will burn when poured onto straw and such; and the fire [of that salt water] would consume it. (51.42)
Indeed, paintings weep due to incense made from a woman’s placenta;
however, *guggulu* incense stops this.
Furthermore, there is incense made from musk-rat (*cucchundarī*), *madana*, *tāla*, *kalāṅgalikā*, *sāśvāri*, *kumbha*, and *karavīra*.
The variegated paintings, when combined with lacquer, return to their natural state once incense has been applied in the city.
Having smeared a mirror with peacock bile, one should place [the image] upon it, exceeding by half.
A hidden eclipse of the sun is clearly visible when facing it;
likewise, those carp that have lost their lives after being sprinkled with *bhallātaka* oil [are seen]. (51.45)
When thrown into water, it spreads as if alive for a moment;
that powder of fish-eggs, smeared with its bile, will produce that [effect] in water. (51.46)
One produces young fish.
Furthermore, one should throw the powder of *nadīśaivala* into buffalo-milk that has been churned;
having stirred it, after a watch (*yāma*) has passed, frogs indeed appear therein. (51–47)
Having smeared neem leaves with peacock bile on one's hand and squeezing them firmly, when released, they indeed become scorpions. (51.48)
Furthermore, if leaves of *nirguṇḍī* and *nimba*,
along with a leaf from a tree brought by the wind and combined with *koladaṃṣṭrā*,
are tied around the waist using *aṅkola* oil, one causes ten men to eat their fill. (51.49)
Having invited Akṣa in the evening with the words, "You are invited," he then took the tips of those leaves at dawn,
when there was much food to be eaten.
Having stepped upon those with his right foot, he eats much rice with a foot smeared with the powder of donkey-dung, old jujube, and trikaṭu.
If a tree is struck on its left side, it will become withered of flowers and fruit;
one should feed it food mixed with stone-powder for seven days.
The *śikhin* [plant] held in a hand smeared with its own juice is not seen at all.
Having chewed the leaves of the *kuraṇḍa* for a long time, one should pierce the lip. (51–53)
Or even if a needle pierces the cheek, no pain whatsoever arises; having thoroughly chewed ginger and *cola* fruit, one may lick hot iron with ease. (51–54)
The meaning is that it does not burn.
A lamp fed with *kośātakī* oil is not extinguished by the wind.
However, the vessel [is protected] by a thread dyed with barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), moistened with oil. (51–55)
Having wrapped it in bell-metal, one should cook the milk-rice (*pāyasa*); it will not burn, nor will the thread burn. The consumption of that milk-rice removes splenomegaly and jaundice. (51–56)
An elephant conquers other elephants by applying its own ichor to its flanks;
for upon seeing a hand smeared with the powder of a muskrat, an elephant flees in fear. (51–57)
At that time, it flees from its tethering post because of the ointment and runs away from it; this is when the fruits of another tree have grown upon the *tilva* tree. (51–58)
One staying in the kitchen will make the food served there bitter;
when [the obstacle] is removed, there is liberation. Even if fire blazes while churning a pair of water-crow bones, [there is no harm]. 51–59.
And in water, one should place fragrant powder soaked in milk and left in the water;
that is to say, in places such as houses made of bundles of straw. Likewise, the excrement of a cock, a pigeon, and a peacock [should be used]. (51–60)
Powdered *hemapañcāṅga* applied to the head causes madness;
whoever has it thrown upon their head is rendered insane. By shaving the hair, one becomes healthy again.
[A mixture] of *snukkṣīra* and sesame powder, ground together and placed on an *arka* leaf... (51–61)
Having eaten that polikā cake, the mice depart from that house.
One should grind tāla, mārjāra-mala, and chāga (goat) urine together. (51–62)
By anointing with that very same mouse-dung, all mice depart;
likewise when fuel devoid of pith is sprinkled with both *gandhaka* and *aṅkola* oil.
By means of an oblation of excessively heated clarified butter, the fire blazes up of its own accord.
One should always chew white stone with the mouthfuls of the roots of the *sadābhadra* plant.
If the mouth is saturated with the juice of *indravallī* or *balā*, there shall be no itching even when consuming raw meat, wild fowl, or *āśākuṭa*. (51–65)
One who worships the bull held in his hand shall be victorious in gambling.
Having placed a lamp inside a vessel whose mouth is covered with fine *kapittha* bark and filled with buffalo ghee,
and having lit it, one should gaze upon the moon when it is full and its light is intense.

On the new moon night—that is, during the latter part of the night—the thousand-footed one with palms joined in reverence [stood] upon the head of the tortoise-legged Supporter of the Mother; and by the touch of his hand smeared with that powder, the two breasts of the young woman became invisible. (51–67)
The seeds of the karañja tree, indragopa insects, and śikhi feathers should be placed in sour gruel (kāñcika). || 51-68 ||
And with these [mantras], one who has traveled a long distance should bind a pill made from the foot of a chameleon to their waist. "In every way, stop the door of this house! Ṭhaṭha!
By digging up the bone of a monkey and placing it in urine, there shall be a stopping [of the flow] for whomever [it is applied]. (51–69)
If one buries a *lāṅgalī* plant in the urine [of a man], he becomes a eunuch;
upon its removal, there is liberation [from that state].
The ingestion of *śirīṣa* resin causes deafness in men. (51–70)

One suffering from blindness due to the consumption of liquid gold, or one with a resinous exudation from the *śalmalī* tree, shall regain their health by drinking sugar mixed with buffalo milk. (51–71)
A wooden peg belonging to a potter, which causes the destruction of his wares, [is empowered] with this:
*eṣa ṣala ṣaḍ anena nikhalala prajvala saṅgakari! huṃ sarvaprasādini! ṭhaṭha*.
By means of this, when perfected ten thousand times, [one should perform] seven recitations over a śirīṣa [flower]. (51–72)
Having led the ritual stake (kīla) clockwise around the field, one should bury it in the center;
at nineteen ghaṭikās past midnight, that indeed causes the paralysis of thieves.
A pill made of *guñjā* in the juice of *bhallātaka* causes circular spots;
likewise, poison ground into powder and applied to the body causes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). (51–74)
One shall become comfortable by drinking or using as a nasal drop (*nasya*) a mixture of *nimba* water, sugar, and honey;
and also by means of an external application (*pralepa*).
[This applies to] those who desire wondrous deeds accompanied by jests and the like.
The vital points (*marmāṇi*) of this recitation were composed in order to ordain the protections (*śarmāṇi*) for their minds.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the Chapter on Jokes, in the Mantra Section of the *Tantrasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 51.

Now begins the fifty-second chapter. Since the bitterness associated with the Kali age and so forth has been shown at the beginning, and since Kali signifies war, the means for victory in battle is now declared. (52.1)
Since Śiva possesses five forms for the purpose of the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with creation,
the universe consisting of thirty-five principles is therefore fivefold.
There too, consisting of the five elements and the winds,
Suparṇa, the king of birds, created five birds.
These, consisting of the five elements and so forth, have forms composed of written syllables;
they are arranged fivefold in the eastern, southern, western, northern, and central squares.
The wheel consists of the five elements; therein, all five birds move in five ways through the five states, both in direct and reverse order.
Kaṇṭaka, Piṅgalā, Kāraṇḍavaka, Sārasa,
and Barhin— these five birds are located in the directions starting from the east and in the center.
A-ā and ka-ḍa are the Vatsabhṛts; i-ī and kha-ma-ja are the Śaḍhas; u-ū and ga-pa are the Jhaṣas; ṇa-ya are the Ayanas; e-ai and ta-ra-sa-gha are the Phakas; and tha are the [Phakhas]. (52.7)
The eight *caṭha* syllables are the seeds of the birds, such as the *kaṇṭaka* and others;
they should be known by the wise in their respective order as eight distinct phonemes for each. (52-8)
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Vidhi, Dāruka, Ambhu, Dviraṇḍaka, Mīna, and Ekanetra—these eight are indeed the syllables of Kaṇṭaka. (52.9)
Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Caṇḍeśa, Viṣameṣa, Caturmukha, Baka, and Ardhanārīśa are proclaimed to have yellow-colored syllables. (52–10)
The two ears, the two thighs, the middle of the arms, the two sides, and the two shoulders are said to be the syllables of the *kāraṇḍava* [meter], along with the *majjā* (marrow).
On the lips there are six red ones, and likewise Śivottama and Śikhī; Ḍiṇḍī and Śukla—these are the eight colors of the sārasa birds.
Lāṅgalī and Kūrma reside in the teeth; then for three months they are in the sky (nabhas).
Chagalaṇḍa and Varṇa are the [next] two; Barhiṇa alone consists of eight syllables. (52–13)

The four [vowels] ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ, the two final vowels, and the last letters of the *ṭa*, *ṇa*, and *ña* groups—these, being devoid of the movement of the bird, are indeed the *anāma* and so forth. (52.14)
The lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) are Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, the one called Riktā, and Pūrṇā; these five, in sequence, belong to Kaṇṭhaka and the others.
On its own day, the Kaṇṭaka and other [planets] will first enjoy six nāḍīs;
the remaining birds (planets) consume their respective six nāḍīs in successive order. (52–16)
The child, the prince, and the aged king who has indeed ascended to heaven; enjoyment, conveyance, and sovereignty; likewise action, sleep, and death. (52-17)

In the case of birds, such as the *nandā* and others, the first of the six [periods] is the state; this applies likewise to all five sets of six, during the prior and posterior halves of the lunar days (*tithi*). (52–18)
In the six channels beginning with Nandā, the Bāla, Kumāra, Vanīśa, Vṛddha, Mṛta, Śyena, Kāraṇḍava, Sārasa, and Śikhin are said to be situated in due order. (52–19)
Piṅgala, Ākāraṇḍava, Sārasa, Śikhin, and Kaṇṭaka are to be known as the birds corresponding to the first group of six and the second group of five [notes] respectively. (52-20)
In the third [period], there would be *kāraṇḍava* ducks, cranes, and peacocks with necks as tawny as thorns;
in the sixth, one should know that they appear in sequence as a child, a youth, a king, an elder, and the deceased. (52.21)
In the fourth [house], the crane, the peacock, the hawk, the *piṅgala*, and the *kāraṇḍava* are the foremost birds;
in the sixth, the young, the youth, the man, the king, the old man, and the dead are the foremost birds. (52-22)
