The peacock, the porcupine, the young frog, the *kāraṇḍava* duck, and the *sārasa* crane—these five [are assigned] to the first group;
and the child, the youth, the king, the aged, and the deceased constitute the second group of five. (52.23)
Food, vehicle, kingdom, sleep, and death are the five actions of these [birds]. Their own respective desires and so forth should be known within the *śaraka* diagram of the wheel. (52-24)

In the latter part of the Nandā, there are water-jars, owls, and thorns; the peacock, the cranes, and even the female crane eat there, and he who has died goes to the kingdom even while sleeping. (52.25)
In the first hexad:

subsequently, in the second hexad, there are the lūka and śyena, as well as the kekī and sārasaka; then the kāraṇḍava, the child, the youth, the king, and the one who has reached old age and death. (52.26)

Subsequently, in the third group of six, there are the hawk, the peacock, the crane, and the crow; and the owl—these birds correspond respectively to childhood, youth, kingship, old age, and death. (52.27)
Subsequently, in the fourth group of six: the peacock is a child, the crane is a youth, the *kāraṇḍava* duck is a king, the owl is an old man, and the thorny plant is one who has died.
Afterwards, in the fifth and sixth groups, there is the young crane, then the adult kāraṇḍava; the king named Piṅgala, the hawk, the aged one, and the dead peacock. (52–29)
The owl, the crow, the crane, the peacock, and the heron; the child, the youth, the king, the old man, and the dead—these move clockwise from Bhadra onwards. (52–30)
Their actions are also as before; their enjoyment, their vehicle, their sovereignty, their sleep, and their death—one should likewise synthesize these for others as well. (52–31)
In the second [chapter], however, it begins with *kāraṇḍa*; in the third, with *sārasa*;
in the fourth, with *mayūra*; and in the fifth, with *kaṇṭaka*.
The meaning is: "in the six nāḍīs of Bhadrā.
Furthermore, in the group of six beginning with Bhadrā, Sārasa, Dhvāṅkṣa, Piṅgalā, Śyena, and Barhiṇa are to be known as Bālā and the others, respectively. (52–53)
In the second [section] is the water-crow and so forth; in the third, Piṅgalā and so forth;
in the fourth, Kaṇṭaka and so forth; and in the fifth, the peacock and so forth.
The meaning is: "in the six [groups] of the latter half. || 52-35 ||

In the group of six beginning with Jaya, there are the Kāraṇḍava, the Sārasa, the peacock, the Kaṇṭaka, the owl, and Bāla; these are [employed] through rites such as those for enjoyment and travel. (52–35)
In the second group of six, Jaya, Sārasa, Barhikaṇṭaka, Piṅgalā, Jalakāka, and Bālā—these [beings] exist according to their own past actions. (52–36)
The third [type] begins with *barhiṇa*, while the fourth begins with *kaṇṭaka*;
the fifth begins with *piṅgala*—these are declared separately for *Jayā*.

From the first half of the *Jayā* [mantra], there arise the Barhis, Sārasa, Vāyasa, Piṅgala, Kaṇṭaka, and Bāla; these six, along with others, [attain their status] through their respective ritual actions. (52–38)
Of the second [group], Jayāpara, there are the Sārasa, Dhvāṅkṣa, Piṅgala, Kaṇṭaka, Mayūra, Bāla, and others, according to their respective functions. (52-39)
On the third day of the waxing moon, the Kāraṇḍa, Ulūka, Kaṇṭaka, Barhi, Sārasa, and Kauca, as well as the Bāla and others, [attain their goals] through their respective actions. (52.40)
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight, there are the Piṅgala, Śyena, Barhiṇa,
Sārasa, Kāraṇḍa, Bāla, and others, preceded by the consumption of food.
Likewise, hawks, peacocks, cranes, ducks, owls, and young birds [are affected] by the aforementioned actions of the portion of the other arrow. (52.42)
In the first half of the Riktā tithi, the Sārasa crane and the peacock-necked bird [are favorable]; in the latter half, the owl and the crow.
These [birds] preside over the Bālā and other periods for rites such as enjoyment and travel. (52–43)
The first [division] begins with Mayūra, the second with Kaṇṭaka, and the third with Lūka and Karaṇḍava;
these belong to the remaining portions of the Riktā days.
Up to "the children and so forth" means as follows:

For the six [days] of the latter half of the Riktā [tithis], the hawk, the peacock, and the crane, as well as the crow and the owl, are to be known [to correspond] with the rites for children and so forth, as previously described. (52–45)

For the six [periods] beginning with the empty (riktā), the second (dvitīyā), and so forth, the [birds] are the Barhi, Sārasa, Kāraṇḍa, Piṅgala, Śyena, and Bālā, starting from the time of eating. 52–46.
p. 384) This refers to the latter half of the *riktā* [tithis].
For the first six of the *pūrṇā* [tithis], they are Barhi, Kaṇṭaka, Piṅgalā, Jalakāka, and Sārasa; these, beginning with Bālā, proceed clockwise. (52–47)
For those [days] beginning with the second of that [group], there are the thorn, the owl, and the crow;
and for the Pūrṇā day, the Sārasa crane and others, according to the prescribed rites beginning with the Bāla [period].
In the first six of the six periods of the second half [of the aeon], Piṅgalā, Śyena, Barhiṇa,
Sārasa, and Jalakāka are indeed the Bālā and others in reverse order.
For the second group of six and the others, the Kaṇṭaka, Śikhī, Sārasa, and Vāyasa are to be known as the first [of each], followed by Bāla and the rest in sequence. 52–50.
If a bird belonging to the letter of one's name rules the kingdom, there will be victory in battle or in debate; however, if it is a young bird (kumāra), the result will be middling. (52–51)
If [the query] concerns a child, the result will be inferior; if an elder, ruin; if one who is dead, death.
In the case of a kingdom, the result is excellent; in travel, middling; and likewise, in eating, it is inferior. (52–52)
In sleep there is loss, and in death there is death itself; thus it should be understood by the wise.
The crane is stronger than the crow, the cat is stronger than that, and the peacock is stronger than the latter. (52–53)
The hawk is stronger than the peacock; thus one should understand the relative strengths and weaknesses.
The peacock, the hawk, the kāraṇḍa crane, and the sārasa crane are strong during the day.
The owl is strong at night, as are all those who possess the strength of the twilight;
the first part of the lunar days belongs to the day, while the latter part belongs to the night. (52–55)
Having understood the strength of each respective time, the wise man should engage in battle;
by means of the movement of the bird (pakṣicāra), one should discern life, death, and disease.

Gain and loss, fortune and misfortune, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, the auspicious and the inauspicious—the king, the kingdom, and everywhere, the two excellent young princes [are the masters]. (52–57)
If the two middle planets are in the state of consumption (bhukti) or childhood (bāla), the result of the matter at hand is inferior;
if they are in sleep (svāpa) or old age (vṛddha), there is its destruction; and if they are in death (mṛti), there is slaughter.
One should likewise aggregate the results according to their suitability for each specific effect:
Garuḍa, Cat, Lion, Dog, Snake, Mouse, and Elephant. (52–59)
One should know the relative strength and weakness of those [letters] situated in the directions starting with the East (Indra), beginning with the rabbit (śa).
Those eight groups of letters beginning with *a* are embodied as Tārkṣya and the others in the various directions.
Those whose names begin with those respective syllables are also of that same nature;
for example, the Tārkṣya bird and the serpent are mutual enemies, as are the cat and the mouse.

The elephant and the lion, the hare and the dog, are mutually antagonistic; yet the Tārkṣya (Garuḍa) would conquer the serpent, whereas the serpent cannot conquer the Tārkṣya because of his inherent power.
Even a serpent may defeat Garuḍa when it stands in the direction of the serpent;
and so too is it for the lion and the elephant, as well as for the cat and the mouse.
One should also know the relative strength and weakness of the ground for rabbits and dogs;
however, the Tārkṣya, owl, lion, and dog are strong when moving against the enemy.
The remaining [beings], such as serpents and others, meet with defeat when they reach their own place;
some say that the fruit is reversed when the place is displaced.
Among those whose vowels in the letters of their names and so forth are long, their *kalās* possess superior strength. (52–65)

Those whose names begin with short vowels are weak in power; however, those whose initial syllables of their names belong to the classes of letters beginning with *tārkṣya* (the *ta* class) [are strong]. (52–66)
Those various [planets] beginning with Tārkṣya are to be known; by means of them, one should understand the relative strength and weakness in a duel, or between two kings. || 52-67 ||
Having ascertained the directions and the species such as Tārkṣya and others, one should cause battles to be fought on the fourth,
eighth, and eleventh lunar days of the bright fortnight, and on festival days.
The *viṣṭi* occurs in the watches and the directions according to the sequence of the moon, fire, sages, and Vedas;
it falls on the third, seventh, tenth, and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight.
The rising [of the breath] in the watches (yāma), directions, and seasons is traditionally taught as being equal to the number of Vedas, fires, and moons.
Again: man, woman, serpent, king, woman, and mountain. (52–70)
The *viṣṭi*-nāḍīs for that time should be avoided in their sequence starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla*).
On whichever lunar day and in whichever watch (*yāma*), the *viṣṭi* is situated in the direction of the sun. (52–71)
On each respective lunar day and during the *viṣṭi* yoga, Caṇḍarāhu remains stationary; starting from sunrise, he moves daily in a clockwise direction through the directions beginning with the east.
The rising of the Sun, Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, and the Moon, as well as that of Rāhu (Saiṃhikeya), is traditionally held to occur in the northeast at dawn. (52–73)
In each of the eight directions, Rāhu remains for half of a half-yāma (one hour) moving counter-clockwise; his motion during the night is equal [to that of the day] until sunset.
Even Rāhu, the astrologer of the year, remains in the directions during the months:
he stays in the east during the months of Leo, Aries, and Sagittarius; in the south during the months when Virgo, Capricorn, and Taurus reside there.
In the signs of Capricorn, Libra, Aquarius, Pisces, Taurus, Cancer, and Pisces—whichever sign the Sun occupies, and in that same sign the Moon and Rāhu are situated. (52–76)
Therefore, one who desires victory or rain should not go face-to-face with Rāhu;
fighting while stationed on the side opposite to Rāhu, one conquers the enemies.

The Yoginīs, beginning with Brahmāṇī, [are assigned] respectively to the directions starting from the east, according to the sequence of Pārtha, Ārambha, Ambu, Śānti, Arka, Vahni, Durga, and Atithi. (52–78)
They are stationed as follows: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Mahālakṣmī are the Mothers (Mātaraḥ). || 52-79 ||
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Roṣaṇa, Unmattaka, Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and likewise Saṃhāra— these are the eight Bhairavas.
And they, together with the eight Mothers, stand in succession according to the lunar days and weekdays,
possessing terrifying forms and holding tridents and skull-bowls.
In undertakings such as military expeditions, one who goes facing toward the Mothers and Bhairavas will perish quickly; the same applies to going toward their tridents. (52.82)
Therefore, a wise person seeking long life or victory should not go to battle when facing Rāhu, a Yoginī, or Bhairava. (52–83)
In the hands of the Rudras and the Yoginīs, there is a trident in the right hand and a skull-bowl in the left for the sake of battle; one should avoid the portion of the trident.
In the skull on the left side, however, is the path that bestows victory in battle;
within the bodies of men, the planets are situated in the constellations. (52–85)
Among the planets as well, the position of Mars during a conflict should be understood:
three [digits] from the beginning of the birth [ascendant] are in the mouth, four in the eyes, and then four in the throat. (52-86)

If there are four dots on the arms, six on the sides, and two or eight on the feet, and the body occupies the asterism occupied by Mars, there will certainly be a wound from a weapon in that limb. 52–87.
Therefore, one should carefully conceal that limb which rests upon Mars,
within the interior of an eight-petalled lotus joined with the six voids and the name.
The *tāra* (oṃ) is in the *liddhikā* cavity, with the two *ṭha*s at the end; [the letters] are also on the petals.
Outside the fire [triangle], there is the earth mandala, and in the six corners, the six *āyatas*.
One should write the letters beginning with *ṭha* and *ra*, interspersed with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the letter *a* (fire).
One should then write the letter *vi* (space) followed by the letter *sa* (creation), which has fire (*ra*) preceded by two moon-drops (*bindu*). || 52–90 ||
One should enclose the outer and inner [circles] with the *saṃvarti* and *sargi* [mantras];
this [mandala], moreover, is surrounded by the external *lipi* and encircled by the *bindu-maṇḍala*.
This armor, honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, when worn upon the forehead, shall protect one in battle and delude the enemy. (52-92)
This Sudarśana discus, known as Sañjīvana and belonging to Nārasiṃha, when placed upon the field of battle, shall paralyze the enemy host. || 52.93 ||
Worn upon the head, it shall protect one from weapons and bring victory; having firmly grasped that arrow which has struck down the enemy, [one should proceed]. (52-94)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should have a bracelet made by him;
worn on the right forearm, it is the supreme warder-off of weapons.
Vajrī, lāṅgalikā, dantī, triśūlī, śrī, mohinī, rājamohinikā, and kākabhakṣyā [are used] on the first lunar day and the others. (52–96)
Taken in the sequence beginning with *brahmāṇī* and so forth, either individually ground with snow-water or all together,
one should smear it upon the body as a supreme armor at the time of battle.
Homage to the Blessed Ones who discharge all weapons! May the Blessed Ones protect me! *ṭhaṭha*.
This mantra, when accomplished through one hundred thousand recitations, wards off weapons.
[One should employ] sandalwood, camphor, *japā* flower, *vidārī*, costus, and *agaru*... (52–98).
At that time, having smeared the weapon-shield with snow-water,
one should ward it off with *nāgakesara*, *śikhā-sūtra*, and the waters of the *nīvī*.
The *nāga* is the *bhūnāga*.
The root of *śrīparṇī*, worn facing east during the *kṛttikā* nakṣatra, when placed upon the head and bound upon the arm, wards off weapons; of this there is no doubt. (52–100)
One should drink the roots and shoots of *indravallī* with milk on the head;
or, holding white lotus stalks in the hand while drinking milk prevents the flow [of semen]. (52.101)
"Yellow" means up to that point.
The root of white Aparājitā, Nandyāvarta, lotus stalks, and the roots of the Bhūta-tree—all of these should be ground with goat's urine. (52–102)
At that time, by applying it as an ointment to the limbs, one may ward off all weapons;
the root of the white-stemmed plant (śvetapuṅkhā), when placed in the mouth, wards off the flight of arrows. (52–103)

Likewise, the root of Saṃmohinī wards off the stroke of a sword; the seed-syllable *Mā*, the bearer of the staff, the fierce one ending in *Ḍa*, with *U* and *ṢṬha*, and then the biting [syllable]. (52–104)

Having recited the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), ending with the wife of Agni (Svāhā), which brings about the cessation of the flow of blood, and having drunk water over which the mantra "Vāṇi" has been recited; || 52-105 ||
One should cause the blood to cease.
Having taken the root of *lāṅgalī* under the asterism of Hasta, one whose body is smeared with it shall conquer the enemy in a duel, remaining himself uninjured by the other. (52.106)
If one smears one's limbs with the juice of *indravāruṇī* mixed with the flour of *varuṇa*,
that cock will clearly conquer its opponent in battle.
A cock fumigated with cat-skin and cat-feces shall conquer;
the root of the peacock’s crest, when placed on the foot, brings victory, as does that which stays in the mouth. (52.108)
The root of the *ahiṃsrā* plant, which acts as a warder-off of weapons, should be placed in the mouth;
that very same root, when drunk with rice-water, remains effective until it is digested. (52.109)
It wards off weapons; that is to say, it prevents them.
Furthermore, the root of *pāṭhā* extracted under the Puṣya asterism, when placed in the mouth, wards off missiles.
[One should seek it] in places such as cremation grounds, sacred trees (*caitya*), anthills, roads, temples, and so forth. 52–110.
Wise men should not take medicinal herbs grown in an impure place;
[this applies to] the roots of white Aparājitā and white Puṅkhā.
When a clod of earth is bound on both sides, it causes the paralysis of weapons;
the right hand [is used], rolled with a wick filled with a powder of *sastrī*, locusts, and fireflies. || 52.112 ||
One whose eyes are smeared with the fat of a black cow's marrow acts like a plantain tree toward the enemy;
furthermore, one should apply the root of *kākatumbinī* to both arms under the Puṣya asterism. (52.113)
One should ward off bonds, the falling of arrows, and weapons;
having fasted for one night, being pure, [one should take] the medicinal herb in the evening on the previous day.
Having secured protection and performed the ritual, he should take it up with the mantra at dawn:
"This king is a bull, possessed of variegated heroism and great strength. (52.115)
"By that which is bound, you are bound; stay right here, do not go!
*ṭhaṭha*.
Thus one should bind [it] with a red thread. "O Suprabhā, *ṭhaṭha*. Having thrown in a handful of rice and grain.
Oṃ, O you of white flowers! O great blue one! O auspicious one! O you who possess the fragrance of sandalwood! || 52-116 ||
I take refuge in you, O herb; protect me from great fear!
May I not fall away, may I not fall down, and may my vital energy not depart.
Stay right here, O auspicious lady! Be my instrument for accomplishing my task;
once my work is done, you shall go to the heavenly world.
I bind the eyes of the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and the highly powerful Gandharvas, as well as those others who stand as obstacles.
O Gaṇḍā, Muritā, Mālinī, Caṇḍikā, Gadāpāṇinī, Stambhinī, Mohinī—homage be to you! *ṭhaṭha*.
Having thus worshipped the medicinal herb with these mantras, one should then dig it up [with the words]:
"Over such-and-such person, *ṭhaṭha*."
With this [mantra], one should dig into the earth: "Oṃ, obeisance to all medicinal herbs!
You shall become full of vigor. (52.120)
"By your own powers, make all things whole; destroy, burn, cook, and kill! Salutation to you, salutation!"—with these words, one should take [the herb].
By this procedure, the wise person should take the medicinal plant;
otherwise, its power would become very slight if it were seized by Daityas and others. (52–121)
Even a single medicinal herb, when properly gathered and mixed with other medicines, bestows strength and protects against obstacles. (52.122)
The Section on Warding Off Weapons (p.

391). Whether it be a king desiring to fight, another person, a general, or a soldier, one should thoroughly examine one's own lifespan; and if one is long-lived, [one may proceed] with diligence. (52.123)
One who wishes to fight should keep his body well-protected, wear armor, and have companions;
however, if his life is short, he should distribute his wife and others among his kinsmen by means of wealth and other assets. (52.124)
Having given gifts according to his means and performed meritorious deeds with a concentrated mind,
he should bathe, perform rites for well-being, and worship his chosen deity.
Being serene, one should enter into battle with the desire to conquer the heavenly realm;
for as long as life remains, it is clearly known through the movement of the breath and other signs. (52.126)
In the month of Puṣya, under the Puṣya asterism, having fasted on the preceding day, one should rise during the latter part of the night and perform the necessary rites and so forth. (52.127)
Seated comfortably, pure, observing silence, with the body, head, and neck held straight,
one should examine one's own breath at the time of the rising of Makara.
The wind, situated within a single fold of the ear, bestows a lifespan equal in number to the armies of Nimi, Śūra, and Khara, which are as vast as the sounds of the distant shore. (52.129)

One lives for as many years as there are syllables in these [groups], moving through one nostril for a number of days equal to the [total] count of the *pralobha* syllables; or else, one may live for as many years as there are days in the *manomaya-naya* [system]. (52–130)
The number of years of Gaurī shall be his lifespan;
the solitary wind [shall endure] for as many days as there are arrows of the god of love. (52.131)
He bestows upon him a lifespan equal to months as dear as oil, moving through days that possess the passion of the conflict between the streams of Hara and the fire. 52-132.
One should indicate the lifespan and so forth by means of the lunar days (tithi), directions, arrows, desires, horses, and the moon.
When the movement of the wind occurs during the aforementioned intermediate periods, [then... 52-133.
One should calculate the measure [of life] according to this lifespan;
for one who does not see Dhruva, Arundhatī, or the River of Heaven (the Milky Way).
Whether external or internal, one will perish within six months.
Arundhatī is the tip of one’s own tongue, while Dhruva is the tip of the nose. (52.135)
If one sees things with the luster of gold, silver, or red, or if one sees excrement, urine, or vomit, or a city of Gandharvas, his lifespan is less than a year.
If one should see lightning in a cloudless sky, a rainbow in water, or see ghosts during the day, death will occur for him within a year. (52.137)
Having seen trees made of gold in a dream, he lives for one month;
likewise if he sees his own form in a mirror or in water as deformed or smelling like a corpse. (52.138)
Or else, his life may perish without cause within half a month;
then, having fixed one's gaze for a long time upon the region of the chin of one's own reflection.
Seeing a shadow-person in the sky with all its limbs complete, a man becomes happy;
however, if it is headless, death occurs in six months, and if handless, in one year.

In a vessel that has been prepared as a maṇḍala and filled with cow-dung and water, one should observe [the reflection] in the solar disc; when it is broken in the southern, western, northern, and eastern directions, [the following occurs].
Death occurs after six, two, or three months if there is a gap in the middle; if there is a smoky appearance, the wise man should determine this within ten days on that very day. (52–142)
He who, having firmly closed his ears, does not hear that sound [of the drum], should either engage in a righteous battle or enter the Ganges, that field of merit. (52.143)
And when a man no longer perceives the scent of a lamp that has gone out—that slender radiance, resembling a firefly, arising from the pressure of the pupils—(he knows death is near). 52-144.
When he perceives that his life remains for only a single month,
having thus understood the measure of his lifespan, he should distribute [his wealth] among his sons and others.
Having given gifts such as charity and having renounced worldly life, or else undertaking the Great Departure (mahāprasthāna),
one attains a happy rebirth by performing acts of charity and dharma in every way.
Since the lifespan of mortals is very short, a wise person should strive to increase their life, for by living long, one beholds auspicious things. (52.147)
Through the yogic practices of breath-retention (*vāyudhāraṇā*), the recitation of mantras as prescribed, or the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*), one may attain a long life. (52.148)
In this regard, the *Nāradīya* states:
"When there is excellence in recitation (*japa*), one may live as a pedestrian for a thousand years, as a sky-traveler for ten thousand years, or even live for a hundred thousand years. (52.149)

Thus [it is said]. The methods for increasing longevity have already been shown here in the previous sections on the prescriptions for great mantras; now, a few remaining ones are being demonstrated. (52–150)
Having undergone purgation with decoctions of medicinal herbs, and having cleansed his body, he should remain in a windless place and administer the elixir. (52.151)
A pure knower of mantras, having taken the root of Vārāhī according to the prescribed rite,
should grind three niṣkas of it in cow’s milk and drink it even at dawn.
For three years, observing celibacy, one should eat *ṣāṣṭika* rice with milk boiled with the decoction of that root, avoiding sour, alkaline, and salty foods. (52–153)
One shall live for a thousand years, free from old age and grey hair, by consuming vegetables, curd, flat beans, and *kulattha* lentils, along with buffalo oil. (52.154)
The practitioner of *rasāyana* should avoid extreme cold, heat, and wind;
he should remain at the foot of a tender *śālmali* tree, with his arms raised as high as a man's height. (52.155)
Having dug [a pit] and cut off the tip of his crest-lock, one should place a water-pot at the spot where his head is severed;
then, having cut him down to a height of one man's measure, one should cover that *śalmalī* tree with clay.
Having smeared it to a thickness of eight finger-breadths, one should burn it with fuel of cow-dung;
after six or seven days, having extracted the jar, [one should take] its juice.
Then, having dried it in the shade and ground it with water from *bhṛṅga* and *āmalaka*,
one whose body is purified should [prepare] a portion the size of a cat's footprint.
Rising at dawn, one should eat [the elixir] while abstaining from sour, alkaline, and salty foods;
by eating only milk and rice day and night, a person shall conquer old age and death. (52.159)

Sindhūttha, abhraka, and mākṣika, processed hundreds of times in *puṭas* with pungent substances (*kaṭuka*), harītakī, vibhītaka, āmalakī, realgar, and water from *bhṛṅga*, as well as *kānta* and *uṣāmṛd* in equal proportions,
along with two measures of the ash of *saut*— these [are the ingredients].
For a mortal who eats [this] powder with the juice of *bhṛṅga* for a month, how could there be death? (52.160)
Equal parts of the powders of vandhyākṣa, āmalaka, nīlikā, madhuka, rīvara, ahimunda, amṛtā, brahmī, gāruḍa, citraka, āsana, and tuṭī,
along with two parts of sugar and iron filings (kānta) soaked in the juice of bhṛṅgarāja for a hundred times— [these should be prepared].
For one who eats that [elixir] stirred with honey for a year, his body becomes ageless and immortal. (52.161)

Having placed three *niṣkas* of gold— which has been rubbed with a paste made from equal parts of *aṅkola*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), cow dung, river mud, field soil, and so forth— into a trough prepared by one with a darkened face, and having moistened it daily with water decocted from the three myrobalans;
One shall conquer death by drinking those well-ground shoots with milk. || 52-162 ||

Thus, through the unfolding of Śakti, the universe— which consists of the expansion of letters, scripts, and sounds— is composed of mantras containing the deities according to the prescribed rules as taught in the Svatantra;
these serve for the protection of the worlds, the destruction of poisons, planetary influences, and diseases, and the [subjugation] of enemies in due order.
By means of the weapon of Īśāna, Śiva displayed both sport and victory in battle. || 52-163 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, on the ritual procedures for victory in battle and other rites, in the Mantrapāda of the Tantrasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 52.
Thus the second section of the mantra is completed;
and the first half [of the work] is finished.
May there be auspiciousness!
